CONTEXT

Context

The world the poem came out of

The Poet: Aphra Behn (1640?–1689)

Behn's origins are obscure, and she seems to have liked it that way. She was probably the Eaffrey Johnson baptised at Harbledown, near Canterbury, on 14 December 1640, though early accounts also name Canterbury, Sturry and Wye. She probably spent time in the English colony of Surinam in 1663–64, which later became the setting of Oroonoko (1688). "Mrs Behn" comes from a marriage no document confirms. The husband is usually named as Johan Behn, possibly a merchant of German or Dutch background, perhaps from Hamburg; he died, or the couple separated, soon after 1664, and it has even been suggested that the marriage was a convenient fiction.

In 1666, during the Second Anglo-Dutch War, she went to the Low Countries as a spy for Charles II's government, working from Antwerp to turn the English exile William Scot. Her code name, "Astrea", became her literary name. The mission left her in debt: she pawned her jewellery, had to borrow money to get home, and seems never to have been paid by the Crown. A warrant was issued for her arrest for debt, but there is no evidence it was served. The often-repeated story that she was jailed for debt and began writing there is apocryphal, though some accounts still give it as fact.

From her first play, The Forc'd Marriage (1670), she wrote for the London stage, producing around nineteen plays (attributions vary) and becoming one of the most prolific dramatists of the 1670s and 1680s, behind only Dryden. She also wrote poems, translations and prose fiction. A committed Tory, she was caught up in politics in August 1682, when a warrant was issued for her arrest, and for the actress Lady Slingsby's, over the epilogue she wrote for the anonymous play Romulus and Hersilia, which attacked the Duke of Monmouth, the King's illegitimate son. No record shows that she was actually imprisoned. She died on 16 April 1689.

Writing for a living, and for fame

Behn is credibly described as one of the first Englishwomen, and perhaps the first, to earn her living by writing. A woman who sold her words and staged desire laid herself open to a charge that male playwrights escaped: indecency. In the preface to The Lucky Chance (staged 1686, printed 1687) she answers critics who called the play bawdy because a woman wrote it. She asks for "the Priviledge for my Masculine Part the Poet in me", the same freedoms her male predecessors enjoyed, and ends: "I am not content to write for a Third day only. I value Fame as much as if I had been born a Hero; and if you rob me of that, I can retire from the ungrateful World, and scorn its fickle Favours." The author's payment came from the third night's takings, so she is saying that she wants fame and not just the fee.

She was buried in the East Cloister of Westminster Abbey, near the steps into the church, not in Poets' Corner. The stone reads: "Here lies a Proof that Wit can never be / Defence enough against Mortality." In A Room of One's Own (1929) Virginia Woolf wrote: "All women together ought to let flowers fall upon the tomb of Aphra Behn, which is, most scandalously but rather appropriately, in Westminster Abbey, for it was she who earned them the right to speak their minds." That is the context for a lyric in which the desiring voice claims a desire Enough to undo the Amorous World: the boldness lies less in a cruel Cupid than in a woman's wanting, stated at full scale by a woman in print.

Abdelazer, or The Moor's Revenge (1676)

The song opens Abdelazer, Behn's only tragedy. Its earliest recorded performance was on 3 July 1676 at the Dorset Garden Theatre, by the Duke's Company, with Thomas Betterton as Abdelazer and Mary Lee as Queen Isabella. Behn adapted it from Lust's Dominion (c. 1600), which was printed in 1657 as Marlowe's but is now usually given to Thomas Dekker and collaborators. The Moorish prince Abdelazer, whose father the old King of Spain conquered, has been raised at the Spanish court and made its general, and he lives for revenge. Queen Isabella loves him adulterously and has the King poisoned. Abdelazer kills the young King Ferdinand, the Queen murders Florella (Abdelazer's wife), Abdelazer has the Queen assassinated, and he is finally killed himself. Philip, the Queen's younger son, takes the throne.

The play begins in "A rich chamber", with Abdelazer "sullenly leaning his head on his hands". Music plays, then the SONG. No singer is named. Afterwards Abdelazer "rouses, and gazes": "On me this music lost? — This sound on me / That hates all softness?" The Queen enters and tells her musicians to "Play all your sweetest notes", and he snaps, "Cease that unwelcome noise". The music is hers to command, so the song works as her serenade, and the play opens with a love song rejected by the person it is sung to. The scene then reuses the song's language. The Queen sighs "Whilst we from eyes — thus — dying, fan the fire" and promises that "a thousand Cupids shall descend / And call thee Jove", deifying the man she desires. Abdelazer's replies use the same imagery ("Burning with fire of lust"; "thousand eyes throw killing looks at me"), and he tells her: "This many-headed beast your lust has armed." Before the scene is out she confesses: "This very hour, the last the king can live, / Urged by thy witchcraft, I his life betrayed." What desire arms in the song is a god; in the play it is a mob and a usurper. (Quotations from Elaine Hobby's modernised text of the 1677 quarto.)

The famous Abdelazer music, Purcell's suite (Z 570) whose Rondeau Britten used in The Young Person's Guide to the Orchestra, was written for a revival in 1695, six years after Behn's death. Purcell's song for that production was a different lyric, 'Lucinda is bewitching fair'. The 1677 text names no singer for 'Love in fantastic triumph sat', and no composer for the 1676 song is securely recorded.

Two lives in print: 1677 and 1684

The lyric was printed twice in Behn's lifetime. In 1677 it appeared in the play quarto, Abdelazer, or the Moor's Revenge … Written by Mrs. A. Behn (London: J. Magnes and R. Bentley), untitled, as the "SONG" at the head of Act I. In 1684 it was reprinted in her collection Poems upon Several Occasions: with A Voyage to the Island of Love (London: R. and J. Tonson) under the title "Love Arm'd", among her other songs. Detached from the play, it became a free-standing lyric that any voice could sing to any "thee".

The anthology prints the 1684 version (its title, and pains in line 3) in modernised spelling, keeping many of the early capitals (Fantastic Triumph, Bleeding Hearts, Killing Dart). The early printings differ only in small ways: spelling, capitals and punctuation; plural "fires" and "desires" in the play text, which also elides "t'undo" in line 8 and so keeps closer to the tetrameter; and in line 3 an early "pays", which the 1684 text reads as "paines". None of these variants changes the sense. What they show is a poem with two lives: a song inside a tragedy, sung on a queen's behalf to a man who silences it, and a printed love lyric managed by its author into an afterlife of its own.

The Restoration stage

Parliament closed the London theatres in 1642. When Charles II was restored in 1660 they reopened under royal patents granted to just two companies: the King's Company, led by Thomas Killigrew, and the Duke's Company, led by William Davenant. For the first time, women's parts were played by professional actresses, so the Queen's desire in Abdelazer was performed by a woman, Mary Lee. The Duke's Company's Dorset Garden Theatre (opened 1671) was built for spectacle, machinery and music, and songs were part of the draw. They were sung in the play and then circulated in print, which is exactly what happened to this one. The two companies merged in 1682 as the United Company.

The court culture that filled these theatres prized libertine wit, and it talked about love as campaign, conquest and game. That is the register of in sport he hurled and of the poem's final Victor. Behn's comedies traded in it, and this song anatomises what it costs the loser.

Love's triumph: Ovid and Petrarch

Love as war is one of the oldest conceits in European poetry. Ovid's Amores I.9 opens "Militat omnis amans", "every lover is a soldier", and Cupid has his camp. In this classical militia amoris the lover serves in Love's army: he keeps watch, endures hardship and besieges his mistress's door. Behn changes the lovers' role. They are not Love's soldiers but his armourers: the god arrives unarmed, and every weapon he uses has been took from them.

The opening tableau compresses the first of Petrarch's Trionfi, the Triumphus Cupidinis, which was painted and engraved across Renaissance Europe. In it the boy Cupid rides like a Roman victor, bow in hand, in a chariot of fire drawn by four white horses, leading a procession of captive lovers. The first is Julius Caesar, and even Jupiter is led in chains before the chariot. Petrarch's poet watches the procession and ends up a captive in it. Behn's version drops the famous captives for anonymous Bleeding Hearts, and her speaker does not simply join the parade but works out who supplied it.

Petrarch's love poetry, imitated in English from Wyatt and Sidney to Shakespeare, supplied the rest of the kit: the beloved's fiery eyes, the lover's sighs and tears and languishing, the cruel mistress, Cupid's dart. Behn uses every item, but as entries in an inventory of weapons. In Petrarchan convention suffering ennobles the lover. In this poem it is raw material, extracted from the lover and turned against her.

"Tyrannic" in 1676

When Behn calls Love's power Tyrannic, the word carried recent history. Charles I had been tried as a tyrant and executed in 1649, and the monarchy had been restored only sixteen years before the play. Behn was a royalist, so the song is not an attack on kings. It borrows the vocabulary of illegitimate, arbitrary power (triumph, tyranny, a ruler "set up" by his subjects, a Victor) and applies it to desire. Abdelazer then plays the metaphor out as politics: a queen's passion poisons a king, and the man she desires has himself made Protector of Spain.

The date matters for any political reading. 1676 comes before the Popish Plot and the Exclusion Crisis (1678–81) and more than a decade before the revolution of 1688. Later events can colour a modern reader's sense of the word, but they cannot have shaped Behn's.

THE POEM

The Poem

Line by line, with the analysis alongside

Song: Love Armed
TSong: Love Armed
1Love in Fantastic Triumph sat,
2Whilst Bleeding Hearts around him flowed,
3For whom Fresh pains he did Create,
4And strange Tyrannic power he showed;
5From thy Bright Eyes he took his fire,
6Which round about, in sport he hurled;
7But 'twas from mine he took desire
8Enough to undo the Amorous World.
9From me he took his sighs and tears,
10From thee his Pride and Cruelty;
11From me his Languishments and Fears,
12And every Killing Dart from thee;
13Thus thou and I, the God have armed,
14And set him up a Deity;
15But my poor Heart alone is harmed,
16Whilst thine the Victor is, and free.

Lines with a marker have analysis — click one, or just scroll.

Title
Song: Love Armed
Language & devices

Genre label: Song names the poem's original job, a lyric sung at the opening of Abdelazer (1676), and promises music and a love song. Personification: Love is capitalised as a proper name, Cupid. Past participle: Armed is a verb with its agent missing: armed by whom? Juxtaposition: the soft genre word is set against the military participle. The title comes from the 1684 printing, where the song is called "Love Arm'd"; in the play it was headed only "SONG".

Meaning & effect

The title is a riddle that the poem takes thirteen lines to answer. Love Armed suggests the oldest picture in love poetry, Cupid with his bow, but the participle hides the question that matters: who did the arming? Line 13 answers: thou and I. So the title already holds the poem's argument in compressed form: love's power is supplied, not innate. Song sets a trap as well. We expect a lyric that celebrates love; we get one that audits it, and it stays pleasant to sing throughout.

Line 1
Love in Fantastic Triumph sat,
Language & devices

Personification / Allegory: Love is a seated ruler. Trochaic inversion: LOVE in puts the first stress on the god before the iambic pattern can start. Allusion: Triumph is the Roman triumph, a victorious general's procession with his captives; behind it stands Petrarch's Triumph of Love. Diction: Fantastic in 1676 means existing in fantasy, imaginary or capricious, not "wonderful". Anastrophe: the verb sat is held back to the end, so the line closes on stillness.

Meaning & effect

The poem opens on settled, absolute power. This is not a battle but its aftermath: a conqueror already enthroned, and sat is the verb of someone who no longer needs to fight. The adjective quietly undermines the pageant, though, because a Fantastic triumph exists in the imagination. On a first reading the word is decoration. After line 14 (set him up a Deity) it reads as the poem's first hint that this god is a projection, a fantasy staged by the lovers themselves.

Line 2
Whilst Bleeding Hearts around him flowed,
Language & devices

Synecdoche / Imagery: in Bleeding Hearts the victims are reduced to the organ that is wounded, and the stock idiom of lovesickness is made literal. Verb: flowed liquefies them, as if the hearts were dissolving into their own blood or streaming round the throne like a crowd. Conjunction: Whilst marks simultaneity: his ease and their bleeding happen at once. The metre is perfectly regular, so the gore moves at a dance pace.

Meaning & effect

Love's grandeur depends on other people's pain: his throne is ringed by casualties. Flowed makes the suffering continuous, even natural, like a river, as if the supply of victims never ran out. The smooth rhythm is part of the point. The scene is offered as spectacle, the way a triumph displays its captives, and the reader is invited to watch it as comfortably as the god does. Whilst will matter later: the last line also begins Whilst, and restages this tableau with the beloved in Love's place.

Line 3
For whom Fresh pains he did Create,
Language & devices

Adjective: Fresh means new and unhealed, and hints at fresh victims too. Spondee: in FRESH PAINS two stresses land side by side. Diction: Create is capitalised in the printed text and is the verb of divine making. Emphatic auxiliary: in he did Create the did throws weight onto the act and pushes Create to the line-end. Half-rhyme: sat / Create is probably imperfect even in period pronunciation.

Meaning & effect

Love does not merely preside over suffering; he invents it, deliberately and continually. Create gives the tyrant God's own verb: he is a maker, but what he makes is pain. That matters to the argument, because the poem will reveal that Love was himself made (set him up a Deity). The creator of pains is a creature of the people he hurts. The rhyme that does not quite close is a hairline crack in the pageant's polish.

Line 4
And strange Tyrannic power he showed;
Language & devices

Political diction: Tyrannic means rule without right or limit, the vocabulary of the state. Adjective pair: strange adds alien, unaccountable, beyond reason. Verb: showed means displayed or performed, power as public show (compare Triumph). Semicolon: it closes the tableau, and the next line turns to its suppliers.

Meaning & effect

The opening quatrain ends by naming Love's rule for what it is: tyranny that is arbitrary, unanswerable and staged for effect. Strange suggests a power that cannot be understood or argued with. In 1676 the word had political weight, but Behn the royalist is not attacking kings; she borrows the language of illegitimate power to describe what desire does to people. Showed keeps the theatrical note: this tyranny is a performance, and the next lines reveal it was put on with borrowed equipment.

Line 5
From thy Bright Eyes he took his fire,
Language & devices

Direct address: thy is the first second-person pronoun, and the beloved enters the poem. Blazon reduced to a single item: Bright Eyes, the Petrarchan beloved's eyes and the conventional source of love's fire. Spondee: BRIGHT EYES. Verb: took means appropriated; it is the first of three explicit uses. Assonance: thy, Bright, Eyes and fire form a chain of long /aɪ/ sounds.

Meaning & effect

The poem turns from spectacle to supply: where did the god get his weapons? The first answer is the beloved's beauty. In Petrarchan poetry the beloved's eyes shoot fire at the lover; here Love took that fire, so beauty is requisitioned as ammunition. The beloved has done nothing but be looked at, yet that is already a contribution to the arsenal. The intimate thy also changes the situation. The speaker is no longer describing a public allegory but talking to one person.

Line 6
Which round about, in sport he hurled;
Language & devices

Adverbial: round about means scattering in every direction, without aim. Register clash: in sport (game, play, and in the period also amorous dalliance) sits against the violent, ballistic hurled. Caesura: the comma isolates in sport between the two movements. Relative pronoun: Which keeps the fire as the thing being used.

Meaning & effect

The beloved's fire becomes a toy in Love's hands, flung about carelessly at whoever happens to be near. The horror is the casualness: harm done for fun. Because sport also means flirtation, careless cruelty and flirtation become the same gesture. This is love as a fashionable game, played by someone who stands to lose nothing. The line implicates its audience too, since a song about hurled fire is itself entertainment.

Lines 7–8
But 'twas from mine he took desire / Enough to undo the Amorous World.
Language & devices

Contrastive conjunction: But turns from the beloved's contribution to the speaker's. Ellipsis: from mine means from my eyes, parallel to thy Bright Eyes, and the beat falls on MINE. Enjambment: desire / Enough is the only line-end in the poem where the sense runs straight on. Hyperbole: Enough to undo the Amorous World. Diction: undo means ruin or unravel; in the period it also meant the sexual ruin of a woman "undone". Metre: unelided, line 8 has ten syllables and overflows the tetrameter (the play text prints "t'undo").

Meaning & effect

The speaker's first appearance is as a site of theft. Her eyes supplied not fire but desire, in such quantity that it could ruin the whole world of lovers. The run-on line acts out that excess: desire is the one item in the inventory that will not fit inside its line. The hyperbole is both lament and boast. It laments that her longing has been made into a weapon, and it claims for her wanting a scale her culture rarely allowed a woman's. Undo adds a darker hint, that the whole world could be ruined the way a seduced woman is ruined. This is the stanza's biggest contribution, and it comes from the person who will end the poem harmed.

Line 9
From me he took his sighs and tears,
Language & devices

Anaphora: From me opens the stanza's ledger (From me… From thee… From me…). Fronted adverbial: the source comes before he took. Petrarchan diction: sighs and tears are the stock signs of the suffering lover. Possessive: in his sighs and tears, once taken, they belong to Love. This is the third and last explicit took.

Meaning & effect

Stanza two begins like a deposition or an account book. The speaker's own grief, the sighs and tears that in Petrarch's tradition prove a lover's devotion, is listed as raw material that Love has confiscated and made his own. The change of possessive is the point: her tears become his. Suffering here does not ennoble the lover; it equips her oppressor. The neat formula also marks a change of tone. The anguish is now being counted rather than poured out.

Line 10
From thee his Pride and Cruelty;
Language & devices

Antithesis: From thee answers From me. Ellipsis (gapping): the verb took simply disappears. Abstract nouns, capitalised: Pride and Cruelty. Rhyme: Cruelty starts the stanza's f-rhyme, the long /iː/ of thee, which also ends lines 12, 14 and 16.

Meaning & effect

The beloved's second contribution is character rather than beauty: pride and cruelty. The contrast with line 9 is exact. She supplied feelings that hurt herself; he supplied qualities that hurt others. With the verb gone, the theft is so routine it no longer needs stating; the ledger runs itself. The rhyme quietly starts a story of its own: the sound of Cruelty belongs with the beloved's pronoun thee, and that sound will dominate the rest of the stanza.

Line 11
From me his Languishments and Fears,
Language & devices

Anaphora: the third From me. Diction: Languishments is the lover's wasting, pining weakness, standard vocabulary of seventeenth-century love poetry and its languishing lover. Pyrrhic foot: the two light syllables after LAN- make the metre sag mid-line. Fears adds dread of what is coming. Rhyme: Fears completes tears; the speaker's rhyme is heard only twice.

Meaning & effect

The speaker's second deposit is her own weakness: the physical and mental wasting of longing and the fear that goes with it. The metre goes slack exactly on the word for going slack. These gifts weaken the giver, which is the pattern of all her contributions. By now the imbalance is plain: everything she gives drains her, and everything he gives arms Love.

Line 12
And every Killing Dart from thee;
Language & devices

Determiner: every signals totality: all the lethal weapons. Allusion: Killing Dart is Cupid's arrow made lethal. Plosives: the k, d and t of Killing Dart. Positional inversion: from thee moves from the start of a line (10) to the end, breaking the anaphora and taking the rhyme position. It is not epistrophe, because the phrase does not end line 10. Semicolon: the ledger closes.

Meaning & effect

The audit ends with its most damning entry: every killing weapon came from the beloved. Cupid's arrow traditionally makes people fall in love; this one kills. The moved phrase is telling. The speaker's From me stays fixed at the head of its lines, but the beloved's phrase is free to move, and it lands on the rhyme, the /iː/ sound that will finish the poem. Even the syntax gives the beloved room to manoeuvre.

Line 13
Thus thou and I, the God have armed,
Language & devices

Discourse marker: Thus means therefore, the logical conclusion of the ledger and the poem's first turn. Compound subject: thou and I is the only time the two people stand together as the subject of a verb. Hyperbaton: object before verb (the God have armed), so the god stands between the couple and their deed. Perfect tense: have armed is a completed act with lasting results. Spondee: THUS THOU. The title's word returns: armed.

Meaning & effect

The verdict: the god's whole arsenal was supplied by the two lovers, and the title's question, armed by whom, gets its answer. The couple are united grammatically only in guilt, in the very sentence that convicts them. The perfect tense makes it irreversible: the arming is done and its consequences remain. The god who owned the verbs of stanza one is now the object of human verbs. The tyrant turns out to be a creation.

Line 14
And set him up a Deity;
Language & devices

Phrasal verb: set him up means installed or erected, the way an idol or a puppet ruler is set up. Religious diction: Deity (capitalised) makes worship a kind of manufacture: Idolatry. Rhyme: Deity continues the f-rhyme (Cruelty, thee, Deity). Semicolon: a pause before the consequence.

Meaning & effect

Arming becomes deifying. The lovers have not only equipped Love but made him a god and placed him above themselves. To set up a deity is the language of idol-making: a god who exists because his worshippers built him. This is the poem's most sceptical claim. Love's divinity is a human construction, and once it is made, its makers are ruled by it. It also recolours the opening: the Fantastic Triumph was a fantasy because the lovers authored it.

Line 15
But my poor Heart alone is harmed,
Language & devices

Adversative conjunction: But is the second turn: joint cause, single casualty. Possessive: my poor Heart is the speaker's only description of herself, and poor means pitiable. Adverb: alone breaks the balanced me/thee pattern. Rhyme: armed / harmed is the same sound plus one breathed /h/. Long vowels: poor, Heart, alone and harmed slow the line down.

Meaning & effect

After fourteen lines of shared contribution, the outcome is one-sided: only the speaker is hurt. Alone is the word the whole ledger has prepared for. Trained by the parallel structure to expect fairness, the reader feels the injustice as a broken promise. The rhyme carries the argument: armed becomes harmed with one added breath, as if arming and harming were the same act seen from two sides. What the couple did together lands on her alone.

Line 16
Whilst thine the Victor is, and free.
Language & devices

Structural echo: Whilst repeats the opening of line 2. Ellipsis: thine means thy heart, parallel to my poor Heart. Military diction: Victor brings the triumph back. Inversion: the Victor is holds back the verb. Caesura: a pause before and free. Rhyme: free completes the f-rhyme with thee, so the poem's last sound is the beloved's.

Meaning & effect

The final image restages the first: someone sits enthroned in triumph Whilst others bleed. Now, though, the beloved's heart sits in Love's place, and the speaker is one of the bleeding hearts. The god has vanished from the poem, leaving a human victor, untouched and free. Freedom is exactly what the speaker gave away, and the rhyme hands even the last sound to thee. The poem's target is clear at last: not Cupid, but the person whom worshipped desire allows to rule.

THE WHOLE POEM

The Whole Poem

Stepping back: what the poem is doing, first line to last

'Song: Love Armed' is usually described as a complaint about the cruelty of love. That description is not wrong, but it undersells the poem and mistakes its direction of travel. Read from first line to last, this is an anatomy of how power is manufactured: a demonstration, conducted in two eight-line sentences, that the tyrant-god of love has no resources of his own — that every instrument of his rule was transferred to him by the two people he rules — and that the transfer, once made, cannot be recalled. The complaint is real, but it is the evidence in a larger argument, not the argument itself. The clearest way to see this is to track the poem's grammatical subject, because the poem passes it from hand to hand like a crown.

In lines 1–4, Love owns every verb: he 'sat', he 'did Create', he 'showed'. The speaker is nowhere — there is no 'I', no 'me', not even an implied vantage point, only the tableau itself, staged with the impersonality of a state occasion. This is the Petrarchan Triumph of Love — Cupid as Roman victor amid his captives — but Behn has removed the observer that tradition supplies. Petrarch watches the procession and eventually joins it; Behn's opening has no witness position at all, which is the first quiet hint that the spectacle may be internal, a pageant of someone's imagining. The diction says so too, for those reading with period ears: 'Fantastic' meant of fantasy — the triumph is announced as imagination before it is revealed as construction.

Lines 5–8 turn the public pageant intimate, and the speaker enters her own poem — but only obliquely, in the object case. 'From thy Bright Eyes he took his fire': suddenly there is a 'thy', an addressee, and the god's arsenal acquires a supplier. Then 'But 'twas from mine he took desire': the speaker's first appearance is as a possessive from which something has been extracted. She exists, grammatically, as a site of theft. This is the poem's method in miniature — agency is revealed retrospectively, through the audit of what was taken — and the stanza's one enjambment ('desire / Enough to undo the Amorous World') lets her single donation overflow the line, the largest item in the inventory and the only one that will not fit its container.

Lines 9–12 formalise the audit into double-entry book-keeping: 'From me… From thee… From me… from thee'. The frames are perfectly symmetrical; the contents are not. Her entries are inward and self-consuming (sighs, tears, 'Languishments and Fears'); his are outward and lethal ('Pride and Cruelty', 'every Killing Dart'). And the verb of theft, having appeared three times, is now gapped — 'From thee his Pride and Cruelty' has no 'took' at all — so that expropriation reads as routine, an administration too established to need stating. The parallelism does something to the reader as well: it trains an expectation of parity, entry for entry, which the ending will deliberately betray.

Line 13 is the poem's hinge, and its grammar is the argument. 'Thus thou and I, the God have armed': for the first and only time, both humans occupy the subject position — and they occupy it jointly, in the sentence that convicts them. Only here are 'thou' and 'I' the subject of a verb, and only together, in the act of arming their own oppressor. The tense matters as much as the pronouns: 'have armed' is perfect — completed action, present consequence, no undoing. 'And set him up a Deity' names the mechanism with theological bluntness: this is idol-making, worship as manufacture. The god who monopolised the verbs of stanza one is now the object of human verbs; the apparent apotheosis is, syntactically, a demotion.

Then the poem does its cruellest thing. Having dissolved the god — he never appears again after line 14 — it does not liberate his subjects. 'But my poor Heart alone is harmed, / Whilst thine the Victor is, and free': the final couplet contains no Love at all, only two human hearts, one wounded, one triumphant. The 'Whilst' of line 16 restages the 'Whilst' of line 2 — someone enthroned, someone bleeding — with the beloved now seated where the god sat. The audit succeeded; the tyrant was exposed as a fiction; and the fiction's dividends were paid anyway, to the party who felt less. Even the rhyme concedes it: 'free' completes the long /iː/ of 'thee' that has claimed every even line of the stanza ('Cruelty', 'thee', 'Deity', 'free'), so the last sound of the poem is the beloved's own.

The strongest objection to this reading is tonal, and it should be faced squarely. This is a song, written to open a tragedy of erotic obsession; its texture in stanza two is anguished, not analytic — 'my poor Heart' is the phrase of a sufferer, not an auditor; and the speaker goes on capitalising 'the God', 'Deity', as if belief survived the exposure. On this view the "anatomy" reading over-intellectualises a lament: the poem does not demystify love, it demonstrates helplessness before it, and the ledger is just the obsessive circling of a wounded mind. The theatrical frame seems to agree — the Queen whose serenade this is knows precisely what Abdelazer is, and desires him anyway.

But that objection, followed through, strengthens the thesis rather than defeating it, because the poem's most unsettling claim is exactly that disenchantment does not cure. The perfect tense of 'have armed' means the god cannot be un-made by being seen through; 'set him up a Deity' is knowledge, and the knowledge changes nothing — line 15 still begins with 'But'. The pain and the analysis are not rivals for the poem's centre; they need each other. The anguish authenticates the audit (this is not a philosopher's thought-experiment but a casualty's testimony), and the audit dignifies the anguish (this sufferer understands her suffering completely, names its mechanism, and is destroyed by it anyway). Notice, finally, what the poem never does: it never petitions. Petrarchan complaint begs — for pity, for reciprocity, for the god's mercy. This poem asks for nothing, prophesies nothing, curses nobody. Its speech-act is a verdict, delivered in a court the speaker has built herself, in the full knowledge that the verdict carries no sentence. That is the poem's whole movement: from a fantasy of someone else's absolute power to the fact of one's own unrecoverable donation — from 'Love… sat' to 'thine the Victor is', with the terrible discovery in between that we were the armourers. What begins as mythology ends as arithmetic; and the arithmetic hurts more.

FORM & STRUCTURE

Form & Structure

How the poem is built, and why it matters

Form & genre

A song: a lyric written to be sung at the opening of Abdelazer (1676), then reprinted in 1684 as a free-standing love lyric under the title "Love Arm'd". It works inside the Petrarchan complaint tradition (suffering lover, cruel beloved, Cupid's darts) but arranges the complaint as an argument in three moves: a tableau, an audit, a verdict.

Stanzas

Two octaves (8 + 8 = 16 lines). Each is a single sentence, with full stops only at lines 8 and 16. Stanza 1 is spectacle (Love enthroned, 1–4) and then supply (where his fire and desire came from, 5–8). Stanza 2 is a ledger (9–12) and then a verdict (13–16). The quatrain is the underlying rhyme unit, but the 1677 and 1684 printings and the anthology all print eight-line stanzas.

Metre

Iambic tetrameter: four beats and eight syllables a line, with every line ending on a stress. The meaningful departures are the trochee that lets Love seize the first beat (l.1); the spondees on Fresh pains, Bright Eyes, Thus thou and poor Heart; the pyrrhic sag inside Languishments (l.11); and line 8, which has ten syllables unless elided (the play text prints "t'undo").

Rhyme

ababcdcd efefgfgf. Stanza 1 has four separate pairs: sat/Create (a half-rhyme), flowed/showed, fire/desire, hurled/World. Stanza 2 breaks the pattern. All four even lines share one sound, the long /iː/ of thee: Cruelty, thee, Deity, free. The speaker's rhymes (tears/Fears, armed/harmed) sound only twice each, and the poem's last word rhymes with the beloved's pronoun.

Turns

There are two. Line 13, Thus, is the logical turn: the ledger's conclusion, with the couple joined as one subject (thou and I) in the act of arming the god. Line 15, But, is the adversative turn: joint cause, single casualty (my poor Heart alone). The Whilst that opens line 16 echoes line 2 and frames the poem.

Repetition

took appears three times (lines 5, 7, 9) and is then gapped, understood but unstated, in lines 10–12. Lines 9–11 open From me, From thee, From me; line 12 breaks the pattern by moving from thee to the line-end. That is a positional inversion, not epistrophe, because the phrase begins line 10 rather than ending it.

Lineation

Every line but one ends on punctuation. The exception is 7→8, desire / Enough to undo the Amorous World, the poem's only enjambment, placed on the one contribution too large for its line.

The form does not just hold the argument; it makes it. Metre, rhyme and syntax each show that love's power is borrowed and that its costs are unequally paid.

Scansion

Stresses are in capitals, with feet marked by |.

Line Scansion What the substitution does
1 LOVE in | fan-TAS | -tic TRI | -umph SAT (/ x | x / | x / | x /) Initial trochee. The god seizes the first stress before the iambic pattern has been set up, a small metrical coup. The line then settles into iambs as Love "sits", and the stresses frame it: LOVE … SAT.
2 whilst BLEED | -ing HEARTS | a-ROUND | him FLOWED Perfectly regular. The gore moves in procession: the metre flows as smoothly as the hearts, so the regularity normalises atrocity into music. Here the regularity is the horror, not a relief from it.
3 for WHOM | FRESH PAINS | he did | cre-ATE Spondee, then pyrrhic. The paired stresses land the blow ("FRESH PAINS"), then the unstressed "he did" hurries past, so the pain is emphatic and the agency almost casual. The filler "did" also leaves "Create" alone at the line-end, a bare, God-like act.
5 from THY | BRIGHT EYES | he TOOK | his FIRE Spondee on the blazon. The beloved's eyes are the heaviest thing in the line, given double metrical weight at the very moment they are plundered.
7 but 'TWAS | from MINE | he TOOK | de-SIRE Regular, but the beat falls on the contrastive pronoun "MINE", so the metre does the pointing. Throughout the poem thy, mine, me, thee land on beats: the me/thee contest is fought on the strong syllables.
8 e-NOUGH | to un-DO | the AM-o- | -rous WORLD (unelided) Overspill. As printed in the anthology the line has ten syllables, swelling past the measure, so desire is "Enough" to exceed the line that contains it. Elided (the play text prints "t'undo", and "the Amorous" slurs naturally to "th'Amorous": "e-NOUGH | t'un-DO | th'AM-o- | -rous WORLD"), it becomes a tetrameter with a trochee in the third foot. Either way of performing it is expressive: compression or overflow.
11 from ME | his LAN- | -guish-ments | and FEARS Pyrrhic third foot. "LANguishments" spreads two unstressed syllables across the middle of the line, so the metre goes limp exactly at the word for going limp.
13 THUS THOU | and I | the GOD | have ARMED Spondaic opening plus medial comma. The verdict is hammered in ("THUS THOU"), and the pause after "I" splits the line: the couple on one side, the armed god on the other.
15 but MY | POOR HEART | a-LONE | is HARMED Spondee on "poor Heart". Stresses crowd together, and the long open vowels (poor, heart, alone, harmed) slow the line into a lament. "aLONE" takes the central beat: isolation at the line's core.
16 whilst THINE | the VIC- | -tor IS | and FREE Promoted stress on "is". The weak beat makes the metre hesitate at the comma, a suspension before the door shuts, and then the final beat lands on "free". The last stress in the poem belongs to the beloved's liberty.

Every line ends on a stress (masculine endings throughout), so the song never lets a line fade away. Even Cruelty and Deity are forced up onto a promoted final beat, and that matters to the rhyme.

The rhyme scheme and the takeover

The scheme is ababcdcd efefgfgf. Stanza 1: sat/Create (a), flowed/showed (b), fire/desire (c), hurled/World (d). Stanza 2: tears/Fears (e), Cruelty/thee/Deity/free (f), armed/harmed (g).

  • sat/Create is a half-rhyme, probably imperfect even in period pronunciation. The poem opens on a rhyme that does not quite close, a hairline crack in the pageant.
  • fire/desire is a full rhyme that welds the two contributions together: the beloved's fire and the speaker's desire chime as one sound. It is the couple's only perfect union, and it is acoustic.
  • hurled/World rhymes the throw with its target, violence with totality.
  • The f-rhyme takeover is the poem's masterstroke. On the pattern of stanza 1, stanza 2 should run efefghgh. Instead the f-sound, the long /iː/ of thee, returns in lines 10, 12, 14 and 16 (Cruelty, thee, Deity, free) and takes every second line to the end. The beloved's pronoun becomes the stanza's dominant sound, while the speaker's rhymes (tears/Fears, armed/harmed) each sound twice and are pushed aside. The last word, free, rhymes with thee: the beloved wins the argument at the level of sound.
  • armed/harmed is a minimal pair differing by one aspirate. Add a single /h/, one exhaled breath like a sigh, and arming becomes harming. The poem's whole causal argument is audible in one sound.
  • The two polysyllabic f-rhymes (Cruelty, Deity) rhyme on an unstressed, metrically promoted -y, which was conventional in the period but is faint to the ear. The monosyllables (thee, free) ring clean. The abstractions chime weakly; the beloved himself, and his freedom, chime strongly.

The alternating rhyme suits the me/thee ledger, but the takeover shows the alternation is not even-handed. By the end only one of the two parties still has a sound of their own.

Two turns and a frame

The poem has two turns with different jobs.

Line 13, Thus, is the logical turn. The lyric has been conducting an audit (From… From… From…), and Thus is its conclusion: inventory becomes verdict. Three things converge on this line. First, thou and I is the poem's only compound subject, so the couple are united grammatically only in guilt, in the sentence that convicts them. Second, the tense shifts to the perfect, have armed: a completed act whose consequence is still present. Third, hyperbaton delays the verb (the God have armed), so that the god physically stands between the couple and their own deed on the line.

Line 15, But, is the adversative turn: joint cause, single casualty. The poem's only two Buts (lines 7 and 15) both introduce the speaker's side of the account, her desire and then her harm. The grammar of objection belongs to her alone.

The Whilst frame (2 ↔ 16) binds the poem together. Line 2, Whilst Bleeding Hearts around him flowed, shows Love triumphant and others bleeding. Line 16, Whilst thine the Victor is, and free, restages the tableau, with the beloved now in Love's position and the speaker among the bleeding hearts. The ending reveals that the opening spectacle was a prophecy: deify desire, and the person you desire becomes the tyrant.

Syntax: the ledger

  • One clause template, obsessively repeated: "From X he took Y". The middle of the poem is a deposition, exhibit by exhibit, and the pronouns alternate on the beats.
  • Chiasmus of donors. The four central donations run thee (fire), me (desire), me (sighs and tears), thee (Pride and Cruelty). This ABBA arrangement across the stanza break encloses the speaker's two inward gifts inside the beloved's two outward ones; the syntax stages a siege. Lines 11–12 then rerun the pair in miniature (me, thee), like a refrain tightening.
  • Positional inversion. Line 10 begins From thee; line 12 ends from thee. The beloved's phrase migrates from line-head to line-tail. It is mobile where the speaker's From me stays fixed at the start of lines 9 and 11, and its freedom of position previews thine the Victor is, and free. The inversion also saves thee for the rhyme, feeding the f-takeover.
  • The vanishing verb. took appears in lines 5, 7 and 9, then is gapped in 10, 11 and 12 (From thee his Pride and Cruelty). The thefts speed up into bare book-keeping: by the end of the ledger, appropriation is so systematic it no longer needs stating.

The result is that lines 5–12 form one long, balanced sentence-machine whose symmetry of contribution sets up an asymmetry of outcome. Parallelism trains the reader to expect parity, so alone (15) lands as a betrayal of the poem's own grammar.

Lineation and pointing

Fifteen of the sixteen line-ends carry punctuation, and each octave is one long sentence of semicolon-linked clauses: two long breaths, spectacle and then verdict. The one unpunctuated line-end is 7→8, desire / Enough to undo the Amorous World, where the sense cannot stop because Enough belongs to desire. Whatever the pointing of the early printings, the syntax runs on here in every text. The single overflow falls on the one commodity that exceeds all measure; everywhere else the lines close as firmly as entries in a register.

Capitals: convention and pattern

Seventeenth-century printers capitalised freely, and the early printings do not capitalise identically, so it is safer to say "the printed text capitalises" than "Behn capitalises". The anthology's capitals, inherited from the early printings, are selective, though, and the selection is readable. They cluster on the allegorical pageant (Fantastic Triumph, Bleeding Hearts, Tyrannic, Bright Eyes, Amorous World), on the finished armoury of lines 10–12 (Pride, Cruelty, Languishments, Fears, Killing Dart), on the god (God, Deity) and on the end-state (Heart, Victor). The materials as Love first takes them stay lower-case: fire, desire, sighs and tears, and also pains and power. What enters the poem as private feeling (lower-case desire) comes back from Love as reified equipment (upper-case Killing Dart), the typographic equivalent of set him up a Deity. That is a reading of the printed page, not proof of Behn's design.

Song form

The regular metre and alternating rhyme are functional, since this was written to be sung, and the clash between dance-like form and violent content becomes an argument once it is tied to the theatre. On stage the song is a seduction gift, played to a man who answers "On me this music lost?" and has it silenced: the poem's Pride and Cruelty in person. The audience, enjoying the music, are left in the god's position, taking pleasure in sport in someone else's burning.

SOUND

Sound

What the poem does to the ear

armed / harmed

The central rhyme is a minimal pair: harmed is armed plus one breathed /h/. Arming and harming sound like one act, and the extra sound is an exhalation, almost a sigh. What the couple did together (13) arrives as what she alone suffers (15).

The /iː/ of thee

In stanza 2 the long /iː/ of the beloved's pronoun closes every even line: Cruelty, thee, Deity, free. The polysyllables chime faintly on an unstressed -y, while thee and free ring out in full. The poem's last sound belongs to the beloved.

Eyes, fire, desire

Line 5 packs four long /aɪ/ sounds into thy Bright Eyes he took his fire, and line 7 answers with mine… desire. The beloved's beauty and the speaker's longing are voiced on one vowel, and fire / desire is the only rhyme that joins their two contributions.

Hard against soft

The beloved's entries strike with stops: Pride, Cruelty, Killing Dart (p, k, d, t). The speaker's are soft and sustained, sighs and tears, Languishments and Fears, dominated by s, z, l, n and the "sh" inside Languishments. Her side of the ledger hisses and drains; his side hits.

Hearts → Dart → armed → harmed

The open /ɑː/ vowel links the casualties and the weapons: Hearts (2), Dart (12), armed (13), Heart and harmed (15). The arrow's vowel is the heart's vowel, and the weapon's sound turns into the wound's.

Cadence

Strict tetrameter keeps the song singable and gives the gore a dance beat. Each stanza ends on a full stop and a stressed monosyllable, World and free, so the first stanza closes on the scale of her desire and the second on his freedom.

The poem was written to be sung. On a first hearing the ear notices how pleasant it is; on a second, that the sounds are taking sides.

The opening line is built on stops. Fantastic Triumph sat runs t, t, t, t and ends on a closed syllable, so the god's enthronement sounds clipped and final, a seated fact rather than a movement. Line 2 goes liquid: Bleeding… flowed moves on l-sounds into the long vowel of flowed, which showed picks up two lines later, tying the bleeding to the display. The b-alliteration of Bleeding Hearts returns in Bright Eyes (5): the pageant's casualties and the beloved's beauty share a sound before the poem tells us they share a cause.

Line 4, strange Tyrannic power, is the hardest mouthful in the first stanza: the three-consonant cluster of strange and then the hard t and k of Tyrannic, with the stress falling on its middle syllable. Line 6 changes key completely. round about repeats its vowel like a jingle, light and careless, then in sport is tossed off before the slow, heavy hurled, whose vowel and final -ld are matched by World. The rhyme connects the careless throw to its target, the whole Amorous World.

The /aɪ/ chain of stanza 1 (thy, Bright, Eyes, fire, mine, desire) carries into the first line of stanza 2, sighs. Then it stops. The speaker's last entries take a different vowel, the /ɪə/ of tears and Fears, while the beloved's take the /iː/ of thee. By line 16 the stanza belongs to thee: the long vowel of the beloved's pronoun has taken every second line and ends the poem.

Line 13 is thick with the voiced "th" of the beloved's pronouns: Thus thou and I, the God. The sound of thy, thee, thou and thine comes first in the line, with I joined to it second. The couple's only shared subject is spoken in the beloved's sound. Line 15 is the slowest line in the poem. my poor Heart alone is harmed is built on long, open vowels (poor, Heart, alone, harmed) with few consonants to hurry the voice, so it is hard to say quickly. Its /h/ sounds, Heart and harmed, are breaths.

The final line moves through soft fricatives, Whilst thine… Victor… free (s, th, v, f), and the comma before and free makes a small held breath before the open vowel. The last thing the ear hears is the long /iː/, the beloved's sound and the beloved's freedom, and no stop to close it.

MOTIFS & SYMBOLS

Motifs & Symbols

Images that recur, and what they accumulate

A motif recurs and accumulates; a symbol stands for something beyond itself. This poem is built from a small kit of both, each introduced in stanza one and transformed by stanza two — traceable in order on the printed page.

The armoury (motif — announced in the title, withheld in the text)

'Armed' stands over the poem as a past participle with a missing agent: armed by whom? The text delays the answer for thirteen lines. The weapons appear first as spectacle — the 'fire… hurled' in lines 5–6, ballistic and incendiary — then as itemised stock ('every Killing Dart', 12), and at each appearance they come with a supplier attached: thy eyes, from thee. What changes across the poem is the weapons' ownership history: conventional Cupid arrives pre-armed by mythology; Behn's Cupid is progressively revealed as carrying only donated equipment, until line 13 supplies the title's missing agent — 'thou and I, the God have armed' — and the rhyme immediately converts armament into its consequence, 'harmed'. The motif's trajectory: from decoration, to inventory, to indictment.

The heart (symbol, then possession)

The heart is the poem's one conventional symbol — seat of love, emblem of feeling — and Behn re-literalises it into a casualty. It enters plural, anonymous and liquefied: 'Bleeding Hearts around him flowed' (2), persons reduced by synecdoche to their woundable organ, the crowd of love's dead. It returns at the end singular and owned: 'my poor Heart alone is harmed' (15) — the speaker discovers herself inside the opening tableau, one of the hearts she had watched from apparent safety. And the final line adds a second, unbleeding heart: 'thine' (elliptical for thy heart) 'the Victor is, and free'. The symbol's movement is from generic spectacle to personal possession to antithesis — two hearts left on the field, distinguished not by what they gave (both gave) but by what they felt.

Fire and eyes (paired motif — the elemental split)

'From thy Bright Eyes he took his fire' (5) compresses the entire Petrarchan optics of love — the beloved's gaze as the channel of passion — into a single act of asset-stripping. 'Bright Eyes' is the only physical detail of any body in the poem: the sole blazon item, instantly weaponised. The fire then behaves like ordnance ('round about, in sport he hurled'), damaging at a distance, costing its owner nothing. Against it the speaker's contributions form the opposing elements: water and air — 'sighs and tears' (9) — self-consuming where fire is other-consuming; she burns inward, he outward. The play confirms the motif's currency: the Queen enters bidding music play 'whilst we from eyes — thus — dying, fan the fire', and Abdelazer complains of 'killing looks' — eye-fire is the scene's shared language of desire as harm.

The language of sovereignty (motif rising to symbol)

Trace the sequence of titles: 'Triumph' (1) — the Roman ceremony of victory, legitimate but performative; 'Tyrannic power' (4) — rule without right or limit; 'the God… a Deity' (13–14) — power theologised, beyond appeal; 'the Victor' (16) — and here the crown leaves the god entirely and lands on a human head. Each term escalates the register (military honour → political illegitimacy → divinity), and then the whole structure collapses onto the beloved, whose only qualification is that he felt less. 'Set him up' is the idiom of installation — of idols, and of usurpers. This is where motif crystallises into symbol: the manufactured Deity stands for every power — romantic, political, religious — that exists because its subjects resource and worship it. In a poem written by a Tory royalist to open a tragedy of usurpation, the resonance is hard to miss; the play immediately literalises it ('This many-headed beast your lust has armed').

THEMES

Themes

The ideas the poem is arguing about

01

Love as a manufactured power

The poem's central idea is that love's tyranny is made, not given. Love appears enthroned and violent, but the poem traces every one of his weapons to a human source: From thy Bright Eyes he took his fire, 'twas from mine he took desire, From me… From thee…. The verb took, used three times and then simply understood, turns the god into a thief, and the verdict is explicit: Thus thou and I, the God have armed, / And set him up a Deity.

The point cuts two ways. The lovers are responsible for the power that rules them, but responsibility gives them no control, because the perfect tense (have armed) marks a deed that cannot be undone. Even Create has a double edge: the god who creates Fresh pains is himself a creation. Read back from the ending, Fantastic in line 1 names the whole idea: a triumph that exists only in fantasy and still does real harm.

02

Unequal desire: who pays

The poem builds fairness into its form and withholds it from the outcome. The ledger alternates me and thee with perfect balance, but the entries are unequal. Hers (desire, sighs and tears, Languishments and Fears) are feelings that weaken the person who has them. His (fire, Pride and Cruelty, every Killing Dart) are qualities that wound other people. Then comes the result: But my poor Heart alone is harmed, / Whilst thine the Victor is, and free.

The one who desires more is the one who loses, and indifference wins. The poem's sound makes the verdict audible: armed turns into harmed, and the beloved's /iː/ (the sound of thee) takes over the second stanza and its last word, free. The injustice is felt as a broken promise, because the parallel structure taught the reader to expect parity.

03

A woman's desire at full scale

Nothing in the sixteen lines genders either person. The reading of a woman's voice comes from outside the text: the play, where the song works as Queen Isabella's serenade to Abdelazer; the inverted Petrarchan template, in which the suffering lover is no longer the male poet; and the fact of a woman writing it. Read within that frame, the poem's most striking claim is its scale. The speaker's desire is Enough to undo the Amorous World.

The line both laments and boasts. Undo carried the sense of a woman's sexual ruin, so the hyperbole imagines the whole world of lovers ruined the way a woman is ruined, while claiming for a woman's wanting a magnitude that moralists denied it. The ending shows the cost. Where one person may desire safely and the other may not, the one who admits desire pays: her heart alone is harmed.

04

Love as a false religion

The poem's titles for power rise from the military to the political to the divine: Triumph, Tyrannic power, the God, a Deity. Create gives Love the Creator's own verb, and set him up a Deity is the language of idol-making, a god produced by his worshippers' devotion. The faithful feed this religion with their offerings (the speaker's sighs and tears) and receive suffering in return; only the beloved, the Victor, profits from it.

Behn is sceptical without being irreverent. The god's divinity is exposed as a human construction, yet the poem still capitalises God and Deity, and exposing the god does not free the believer. Katherine Philips's 'A Married State' makes the same move from the other side, urging her "madam" to "Turn, turn apostate" from love. For both seventeenth-century women, love is a creed one can be devoted to, and must be argued out of.

05

Private passion, public tyranny

Triumph, Tyrannic, set him up and Victor carry the vocabulary of the state into a love song. In 1676 that vocabulary had recent memory behind it: a king tried as a tyrant and executed in 1649, and a monarchy restored in 1660. Behn was a royalist, and the song is not political allegory, but it takes power's grammar seriously. A ruler is someone his subjects arm and install, and once installed he cannot be recalled.

Abdelazer turns the metaphor into plot within minutes. The Queen's passion has already poisoned a king, and Abdelazer tells her: "This many-headed beast your lust has armed." The song's thesis, that desire arms tyranny, is played out in the state, with a usurper raised by a woman's love.

06

Pleasure, spectacle and cruelty

This is a song, music meant to please, about a god who does harm in sport. Its regular metre carries Bleeding Hearts like a procession, and its first audience came to the theatre for exactly this kind of music. Behn makes that pleasure uncomfortable. We watch the triumph as the god does, and on stage the song's addressee rejects it as "unwelcome noise".

The theme is the libertine treatment of love as a game with winners and losers (the beloved ends as the Victor), and the song counts the cost to the loser. Harm done lightly, in sport, is the poem's definition of cruelty, and its music invites us to share it.

DIFFICULT MOMENTS

Difficult Moments

Where the poem is genuinely undecidable — and what to do about it

Cruxes

Five places where the meaning is genuinely open. In each, the ambiguity is doing work, so the aim is to say what it does rather than to settle it.

1. Who is 'thou'? The ungendered addressee

The difficulty: nothing in sixteen lines genders either party. The "female speaker / cruel man" reading is imported — from Behn's biography, from the inverted-Petrarchan template, and from the play (the Queen's serenade to Abdelazer). Competing readings: (a) woman to man — supported by the frame, by the gendered feel of the inventories (her tears, his pride), and by Behn's polemical career; (b) genuinely open address — supported by the text's silence, by the stage direction, which names no singer, so the voice that first sang it need not have matched either party, and by Behn's own 'To the Fair Clarinda', which shows her deliberately engineering ambiguous address elsewhere. What a strong answer does: treats the indeterminacy as functional, not accidental — the pronouns are roles, not persons; whoever desires more occupies 'me', whoever feels less occupies 'thee'; the poem analyses a structure of unequal desire that any two people can instantiate, which is exactly why it detached so easily from its play and survived it.

2. What is 'thine' in line 16?

The difficulty: 'Whilst thine the Victor is, and free' — 'thine' needs an antecedent. Competing readings: (a) elliptical for thy heart, in strict parallel with 'my poor Heart' — supported by the poem's habit of exact antithesis and by the frame it completes (bleeding hearts at the start, two hearts at the end); (b) loose deixis for you/yours, as song grammar tolerates — supported by naturalness: 'Victor' and 'free' suit a person more readily than an organ. The evidence favours (a) — 'Heart' is the only available antecedent, one line above — but the strong answer notices what the ellipsis does: it makes the beloved's heart victorious as a heart, i.e. the organ of feeling wins the war by refusing to feel; and because 'thine' gestures at both the heart and its owner, the last line indicts both at once. Misread it as plain 'you' and the couplet loses its terrible symmetry: this was heart against heart, and one of them fought unarmed.

3. Victim or superior rhetorician?

The difficulty: tonal. 'My poor Heart' is the diction of naive pathos; the poem containing it is a machine of forensic control — balanced ledger, logical 'Thus', epigrammatic close, and the covert boast that her desire alone was 'Enough to undo the Amorous World'. Competing readings: (a) the sufferer speaks, and the formal poise is convention (songs are neat; neatness proves nothing); (b) the account is a counter-triumph — the beloved wins the affair, the speaker wins the record of it, fixing the beloved forever as 'Pride and Cruelty' in a song that has outlived its occasion by three centuries. Evidence: (a) rests on the unguarded possessive 'my poor', the only self-description in the poem; (b) rests on everything structural — she controls all the naming, and 'thou' is the subject of an active verb only once, jointly, in 'thou and I… have armed'. What a strong answer does: refuses the either/or and states the relation: the form performs the mastery the content denies; whether that is compensation, revenge, or just the only dignity available is the genuinely open question — and the poem is more interesting for not settling it.

4. Whose fantasy is 'Fantastic'?

The difficulty: the period sense — of fantasy, imaginary, capricious — makes line 1 unstable. Is the fantasy Love's (a god staging his own extravagant pageant), the lovers' (a projection they mistake for a god), or merely the observer's register for 'grotesque, extravagant'? Competing readings and evidence: the objective-spectacle reading suits stanza one's impersonal staging; the projection reading is retro-activated by lines 13–14 — 'set him up a Deity' assigns the manufacture, and therefore the fantasy, to 'thou and I'. What a strong answer does: reads the word proleptically — on first pass it is decor, after line 14 it is the poem's first confession, planted where no first-time reader can understand it. Reading it this way means pointing to the word, reading the ending, and returning to it: the poem teaches its reader to re-read, and its opening spectacle turns out to have been hindsight all along.

5. How equal is 'Thus thou and I'?

The difficulty: line 13 shares the guilt equally — one verb, two subjects — but the ledger it sums up does not. The beloved supplied beauty and indifference ('Bright Eyes', 'Pride and Cruelty'); the speaker supplied wanting and suffering ('desire', 'sighs and tears', 'Languishments and Fears'). Is the joint subject a confession or an accusation? Competing readings: (a) confession — she admits that her desire was half the arsenal: without 'desire / Enough to undo the Amorous World', the beloved's eyes would merely be bright; the line is self-knowledge, and its fairness is real; (b) accusation in the grammar of fairness — 'thou' comes first, and the silent beloved is enrolled, without being asked, in a deed that only the speaker has confessed; sharing the blame is a way of making the beloved share the responsibility. What a strong answer does: sees that the equal grammar is what makes the ending scandalous. The poem grants joint authorship so that 'alone' (15) can expose unequal payment: whether line 13 is generous or prosecutorial, it sets up the verdict that the cost of a shared act falls on one person.

CLOSE ANALYSIS

Close Analysis

The moments that repay pressure, worked through

Quotation analysis

Card 1 — 'Love in Fantastic Triumph sat,' Techniques: allegorical personification; trochaic inversion; period diction; classical allusion. Analysis: The inverted first foot lets 'Love' seize the stress before the iambic pattern can establish itself, so the god's coup happens rhythmically before it happens semantically. 'Fantastic' in 1676 meant 'belonging to fantasy, imagination, caprice' — not 'wonderful' — so the triumph is announced from the outset as a mental pageant, a staged illusion; the poem will end by telling us exactly who staged it ('Thus thou and I…'). Behind the tableau stands Petrarch's Triumph of Love — Cupid as Roman victor parading captive lovers — compressed into a single line and made sinister by the flat, settled verb 'sat': not conquest in progress but occupation accomplished. Intention/effect: Behn plants the poem's sceptical thesis in its first word-pair — this god's grandeur is fantasy — while the reader, lulled by the pageantry, only feels the trap close at line 13.

Card 2 — 'Whilst Bleeding Hearts around him flowed,' Techniques: synecdoche; grotesque imagery; regular metre against violent content; dramatic irony (frame). Analysis: The victims appear only as their wounded parts — a battlefield synecdoche in which persons have already been reduced to trophies — and 'flowed' liquefies even those, hearts dissolving into the blood they shed, circulating round the throne like tribute. The line's perfectly regular iambs make the gore processional: suffering set to a dance-beat, horror normalised into entertainment — which is literally what it was, sung to a paying Restoration audience. The idiom 'bleeding heart' lets Behn pun conventional lovesickness into open wound: the metaphor lovers use decoratively is here taken at its word. Intention/effect: Behn makes the reader complicit — we consume the spectacle as pleasantly as Love does — so the poem's later accusation of cruelty-as-'sport' quietly includes its own audience.

Card 3 — 'For whom Fresh pains he did Create, / And strange Tyrannic power he showed;' Techniques: spondee; capitalised verb of divine making; emphatic auxiliary; political diction; half-rhyme. Analysis: 'FRESH PAINS' lands two stresses together, so the new injuries hit before the light 'he did' hurries past and leaves 'Create' alone at the line-end. The capitalised verb is the Creator's own: Love is a maker, but what he makes is pain, and he makes it for victims who are already bleeding ('For whom'). 'Fresh' means new and unhealed, so the torment keeps renewing itself. 'Tyrannic' then names the regime, power without right or limit; 'strange' makes it alien and beyond appeal; and 'showed' keeps the theatre in view — this is power on display, like a triumph's captives. Even the rhyme 'sat'/'Create' does not quite close. Intention/effect: Behn gives the god a creator's verb so that the poem can take it back: by line 14 the creator of pains turns out to be a creature, 'set… up' by the people he hurts.

Card 4 — 'From thy Bright Eyes he took his fire, / Which round about, in sport he hurled;' Techniques: weaponised blazon; theft diction; register clash; medial caesura. Analysis: The Petrarchan blazon is stripped to one item, the beloved's eyes, and immediately expropriated: 'took' — the poem's obsessive verb — turns praise into requisition, beauty into ordnance. The comma-isolated 'in sport' sits between 'round about' and 'hurled' like a shrug between two violences: 'sport' in Restoration usage covers both game and erotic dalliance, so cruelty and flirtation become the same gesture. The clash between the casual adverbial ('in sport') and the ballistic verb ('hurled') is the poem's tonal signature — atrocity performed with perfect insouciance. Intention/effect: Behn indicts the fashionable libertine style of loving — desire thrown about as recreation — and the reader feels the specific chill of harm done lightly.

Card 5 — 'But 'twas from mine he took desire / Enough to undo the Amorous World.' Techniques: the poem's only enjambment; hyperbole; period pun on 'undo'; contrastive 'But'. Analysis: Uniquely in a poem of end-stopped ledger-lines, the syntax here overruns the line-break: 'desire / Enough' spills over exactly as the desire it names exceeds containment — read unelided, the second line even swells past the tetrameter. 'Undo' carries the Restoration sense of sexual ruin (a woman 'undone' is one seduced and discarded), so the speaker's desire could, in the god's hands, ruin the whole 'Amorous World' the way one woman is ruined. The hyperbole cuts two ways: it is a lament, and it is a boast — her contribution outscales everything else in the arsenal; the beloved donated a spark, she donated the apocalypse. Intention/effect: Behn insists on the world-sized magnitude of female desire — precisely what her culture minimised — and makes the reader admire the speaker at the very moment she reports her ruin.

Card 6 — 'From me his Languishments and Fears, / And every Killing Dart from thee;' Techniques: anaphoric ledger; verb ellipsis (gapping); pyrrhic sag; positional chiasmus; reifying capitals. Analysis: By this point the audit no longer bothers with its verb — 'took' is gapped, leaving bare double-entry lines — so expropriation reads as routine administration, theft become book-keeping. The metre goes slack inside 'Languishments' (two unstressed syllables mid-line): prosody performing the debility the word names, while 'every Killing Dart' answers it with hard plosives — her entries drain, his detonate. The beloved's phrase has also migrated from line-head (10: 'From thee…') to line-tail (12: '…from thee'), enclosing the stanza's gifts and seizing the rhyme position, so that even syntactic mobility belongs to him. Intention/effect: Behn converts complaint into evidence — a legal deposition rather than a sob — and the reader is manoeuvred into the jury box, obliged to convict before the verdict is announced.

Card 7 — 'Thus thou and I, the God have armed, / And set him up a Deity; / But my poor Heart alone is harmed, / Whilst thine the Victor is, and free.' Techniques: logical volta ('Thus') then adversative volta ('But'); minimal-pair rhyme; idolatry diction; structural echo of line 2; ellipsis in 'thine'. Analysis: 'Thus' delivers the QED of the whole ledger, and the poem's grammar convicts as it concludes: 'thou and I' is the lovers' only compound subject — union achieved solely in culpability — while 'set him up a Deity' is the vocabulary of idol-making, an almost blasphemous admission that this god is manufactured. The rhyme then executes the sentence: 'armed' becomes 'harmed' by the addition of a single breathed /h/ — cause and consequence one aspirate apart — and the final 'free' completes the /iː/ rhyme of 'thee' that has taken every even line of the stanza ('Cruelty', 'thee', 'Deity', 'free'), handing the beloved the poem's last sound as well as its victory. 'Thine' is elliptical for thy heart: the closing contrast is heart against heart, hers harmed, his 'the Victor… and free', restaging line 2's tableau with the beloved now enthroned where Love sat. Intention/effect: Behn ends not with the god but with the beloved who has replaced him, so the reader grasps the poem's real target: not Cupid, but the human beloved whom worshipped desire licenses to tyrannise.

CRITICAL LENSES

Critical Lenses

What each way of reading makes visible, and what it flattens

Critical lenses

Formalist

Makes visible: that the poem's meaning is executed by its form — 'armed'/'harmed' as a minimal pair one aspirate apart; the f-rhyme (/iː/ of 'thee') annexing every even line of stanza two until 'free' hands the beloved the final sound; the gapped 'took' turning theft into book-keeping. On this view the poem is its machinery, and the machinery argues. Flattens: everything the machine was built into — the theatre, the Queen, the gender politics of a woman publishing desire. A purely formalist account cannot say why the same sixteen lines scandalised anybody, or what it meant that they were sung.

Feminist

Makes visible: the gendered economy of emotional labour: 'From me he took his sighs and tears, / From thee his Pride and Cruelty' — feeling extracted from one party, licence from the other, and the products returned as weapons against the one who felt. It also restores the scandal of scale: a female-voiced claim to 'desire / Enough to undo the Amorous World' in a culture that pathologised female wanting. Flattens: the text's actual genderlessness (Difficult Moments 1) — the reading must be imported and should say so; and it risks reducing the speaker to victim, when the poem's rhetorical mastery (Difficult Moments 3) is half the evidence.

Marxist / materialist

Makes visible: an economy of extraction and alienation in the strict sense: the lovers' inner resources are appropriated ('took', three times, then silently), converted into capital — an armoury — and returned as a hostile power that dominates the producers: 'Thus thou and I, the God have armed'. The god is accumulated surplus. The lens also catches the poem's own material life: love-suffering written as a saleable song by one of the first Englishwomen to live by her pen — feeling literally monetised, twice (stage 1676, print 1684). Flattens: intimacy; tone; the fact that the poem's wound is betrayal by a person, not exploitation by a system — pressed too hard, the reading makes the beloved a class and loses the couplet's privacy.

Psychoanalytic

Makes visible: projection and splitting: two people disown parts of themselves — her longing, his aggression — and install them in an idealised external figure ('set him up a Deity') who can then be blamed, worshipped and obeyed; the god is a defence against the unbearable plain fact the last two lines state without him (he does not love her). The ending withdraws the projection, and what remains is exactly the reality the fantasy was built to avoid. Flattens: history and convention — it treats Petrarchan stock properties (darts, fire, sighs) as symptoms of a psyche when they are also simply the period's shared vocabulary; anachronism must be conceded, and 'the speaker' kept distinct from Behn.

Historicist

Makes visible: why 'strange Tyrannic power' is not a dead metaphor in 1676: written within living memory of a king's execution (1649) and a restoration, for a court culture that spoke of love as campaign and conquest, as the overture to a tragedy in which a queen's desire genuinely does arm a usurper ('your lust has armed', Act I). Love-language and state-language interpenetrate because the culture's power-anxieties ran through both. Flattens: the poem's portability — it reads the lyric as document and cannot explain why it works on readers who know none of this; the structure of unequal desire is not period-bound, and the poem knows it ('the Amorous World', not the Restoration one).

Reader-response

Makes visible: that the poem engineers its reader as deliberately as its god: the parallel ledger trains an expectation of parity that 'alone' (15) betrays — the reader feels the injustice as a broken formal promise before understanding it; 'Fantastic' only becomes legible on re-reading (Difficult Moments 4); and the theatrical frame implicates the audience, who enjoy — 'in sport' — a song its onstage addressee orders silenced. Any reader with the text in front of them is in precisely the position this lens describes: a re-reader whose responses are cued and revisable. Flattens: authorial design and historical situation; unanchored, it collapses into "I feel that…" — the discipline is to name the textual trigger for every response claimed.

(Postcolonial note, offered as a caution rather than a lens-application: the frame — a racialised Moor, a Spanish court, a source play trading in the period's stereotypes — rewards postcolonial attention, but the sixteen lines themselves contain none of it. Importing the play's racial politics into the lyric as if they were its content misreads it; the honest formulation is that the lens illuminates the poem's staging, not its text.)

OTHER READINGS

Other Readings

Contested interpretations, and where each is weak

Alternative and contested readings

1. Proto-feminist reading (the usual reading). The speaker's donations (desire, sighs, tears, languishments, fears) map onto the culturally 'feminine' position of exposed feeling; the beloved's (fire, pride, cruelty, killing darts) onto masculine display and licensed indifference; the poem anatomises a structural, gendered asymmetry — who may desire safely, and who pays. Evidence: the gendered inventories; the economy of ruin in 'undo'; Behn's own position and polemics (see Context). Weakness: it must be imported — nothing in the sixteen lines genders either party; 'the speaker is a woman' rests on biography and on the play's frame, not the text. It holds best as a claim that the poem maps onto gendered experience, not that the text names a woman speaker.

2. Queer / ungendered-address reading. Both pronouns are unmarked; the poem is an 'I–thou–god' triangle open to any configuration, and the intimate 'thou/thee/thy' register works for any beloved. Behn demonstrably wrote beyond heterosexual convention — 'To the Fair Clarinda, Who Made Love to Me, Imagined More than Woman' (printed 1688) eroticises a deliberately double-gendered addressee — so indeterminacy here can be read as licence rather than accident: a lyric of desire engineered to be singable by anyone, to anyone. Evidence: total absence of gender markers; the stage direction names no singer (see Context), so the voice that first sang it need not have matched either party; Behn's Clarinda poem as canon-internal precedent. Weakness: the theatrical frame immediately heterosexualises it (the Queen's serenade to Abdelazer), and the 1684 collection prints it among pastoral love songs of nymphs and swains; the openness is real but contingent.

3. Political-allegory reading. 'Tyrannic power', 'the God have armed', 'set him up' — the lexicon of usurpation and investiture. The lovers behave like subjects who authorise a sovereign (cf. Hobbes's covenant, 1651 — analogy, not allusion) and then discover he rules them absolutely; in the play this is literal: the Queen's desire arms Abdelazer's rise, and the scene re-uses the song's verb for politics ('This many-headed beast your lust has armed'). The song thus opens a tragedy about how private appetite manufactures public tyranny. Evidence: the political diction; the Act I echoes (see Context); Restoration memory of civil war and anxiety about arbitrary power. Weakness: Behn was a committed Tory royalist — reading her as attacking monarchy misfires; the target is arbitrary passion as usurper, and the allegory works through the play, not as free-standing political comment. Date-discipline needed: 1676 precedes the Exclusion Crisis.

4. Against the victim-reading: the speaker as rhetorical victor. The poem says she lost; it performs mastery. She controls the ledger, the logic ('Thus'), the balanced antitheses, the god's biography; her single donation is world-scale ('undo the Amorous World') while his are itemised trinkets; and she gets the last word about him. On this reading the complaint is also a counter-triumph: the beloved wins the affair, the speaker wins the account of it — and since the account is all we have, her defeat arrives already avenged in form. Evidence: the forensic architecture (see Form & Structure); the covert boast of line 8; the poised, epigrammatic close. Weakness: 'my poor Heart' is tonally unguarded — self-pity that resists the triumphant-rhetorician frame; and formal control can be read as defence mechanism rather than victory.

5. Metapoetic-sceptical reading. 'Fantastic' (fantasy), 'Create', 'set him up a Deity': the poem watches love being manufactured — out of stock Petrarchan parts, no less ('sighs and tears', darts, fire) — and says so. Cupid is a fiction assembled by lovers and by poets; the lyric deconstructs its own tradition even while singing it. Evidence: the idol-making diction; the arsenal composed entirely of literary conventions; the frame of a professional dramatist opening a play with a manufactured song. Weakness: the final couplet insists the harm is not fictional — 'my poor Heart alone is harmed' — so the poem's scepticism stops at the god, not at the suffering; a purely metapoetic reading under-reads the pain.

REVISION NOTES

Revision Notes

The working notes, quotation by quotation

Context

Analysis
  • Aphra Behn (1640?–1689): Restoration poet + dramatist; one of the first Englishwomen to earn a living by writing
