  • 1666: spy in Antwerp for Charles II, code name "Astrea" → her pen name; jailed-for-debt story = apocryphal (warrant issued, no evidence it was served)
  • Song opens Abdelazer, or The Moor's Revenge (staged 1676, printed 1677) → Queen Isabella's serenade to Abdelazer, who silences it ("Cease that unwelcome noise")
  • Play = tyranny in politics, poem = tyranny in love → power grows from exploiting the vulnerable (the Queen's "lust has armed" a usurper)
  • Reprinted on its own in 1684 as "Love Arm'd" (Poems upon Several Occasions)
Effect, style & response
  • 1676 England: male-dominated; youth + beauty decided a woman's value; scandal ruined a woman while the man stayed unscathed
  • Buried in Westminster Abbey's East Cloister (not Poets' Corner)
  • Woolf (1929): women should "let flowers fall upon the tomb of Aphra Behn… for it was she who earned them the right to speak their minds"

Overview

Analysis
  • Overarching idea: love = tyrannical, destructive force → suffering for one, the other untouched + Victor
  • Love not innate but made: Thus thou and I, the God have armed → is "Love" discovered or created?
  • Proto-feminist critique: shows how gendered conventions naturalise women's suffering in love
  • Ambiguity of thee (no gender markers) → could happen to anyone
  • Misleading positive / serene diction: Fantastic, Triumph, flowed, Fresh, Create

STRUCTURAL ANALYSIS

Analysis
  • The entire poem is written mainly in Iambic Tetrameter instead of sounding like a romantic heartbeat, it sound like the relentless march of an army (de-DUM, -deDUM)
  • Comprised of two stanza of 8 lines
  • Two quatrains in each stanza: ABAB CDCD / EFEF GFGF
  • Stanza 2 breaks the pattern: f-rhyme (/iː/ of thee) takes every even line: Cruelty / thee / Deity / free → the beloved's sound wins the stanza + last word
  • Single (masculine) rhyme, falling on the stressed syllable
  • The rhymes Harmed/armed, Cruelty/Deity are accentuated with dental T and D sounds dominating the poem and ending each line on an emphatic upbeat
  • The rhythm portrays the Tyrant’s cruel eagerness: he may be sat in lordly fashion, but his eyes are ever restless, his cruel gaze ever hunting for new victims
  • All lines but line 7 are end-stopped
  • Near-total lack of enjambment (only 7→8) shows restriction, lack of freedom, delivering a deliberate pace, offering a sense of finality and control in Love’s dominance over the speaker
  • Tone of restrained despair, with each line stands as a self-contained reflection of Love’s power and the speaker’s defeat
  • Predominantly end-stopped lines create a rhythmic regularity, mirroring the inevitability of the speaker’s emotional suffering as if each line marks the closing of an argument of painful truth
  • Manipulation of syntax to emphasis particular words and raises dramatic and elevated tone
  • Anastrophe (deliberate inversion of the usual order of words or clauses): Love in Fantastic Triumph sat rather than Love sat in Fantastic Triumph
  • Fronted Adverbial (adverbial word/phrase moved to the front of sentence): From me he took his sighs and tears, rather than He took his sighs and tears from me
  • Capitalisation in ad hoc manner (when necessary/needed): Fantastic Triumph and Bleeding Hearts
  • Capitalisation not strictly governed by rules as it is today
  • Used for emphasis to give words significance, key ideas, concepts, or personifications
  • Verb took explicitly repeated three times and implicitly repeated three times
  • Characterise Love as a parasitic creature which feeds and grows off emotions of other, giving nothing back but pain and sorrow
  • Anaphora of from enhances the one-sided, destructive and debilitating nature of love

Love Armed

Analysis
  • Love is personified and alludes to Cupid, the god of desire, erotic love, attraction and affection (Son of Venus, Goddess of Love, and Mars, God of war)
  • A youth armed with a bow and arrow (Historically)
  • Behn portrays a more dangerous, militaristic force, rather than a charming figure inspiring mutual affection, almost as if Cupid has taken on more characteristics of his father, Mars, The God of War through the adjective of Armed
  • Equipped with weapons, ready for battle and capable of inflicting harm
  • Emphasises emotional conquest and suffering, Love as an aggressor or tyrant
  • Transforms love as a symbol of power and oppression exploiting and draining the emotions of both the speaker and the beloved
  • Ready to inflict damage underscoring the one-sided, destructive nature of love in the poem, as the speaker suffers emotional wounds without reciprocation or relief
  • Portrayed as a conqueror who leaves behind vulnerability, and pain in its wake
Effect, style & response
  • Sets up the Reader’s relief to imagine it as a Love song, about beauty, romanticism or even Desire
  • Makes them feel calm, concern-free (possibly slight concern with armed but possibly physically having one in your arm[s] rather than being militarily armed
1 / 2

Love in Fantastic Triumph sat, / Whilst Bleeding Hearts around him flowed,

Analysis
  • The capital ‘L’ in Love implies proper noun and as the first word of the poem and being in the title it signals its centrality in the poem
  • Sets up and foreshadows the theme and idea of love (but subverted to an idea of evil and malevolence)
  • The very beginning breaks the rhythm with a Trochaic reversal immediately asserting the warlord (Love)’s dominance and violence before ending the first line, while revealing the all-encompassing power that Love posses
  • The diction Fantastic Triumph which presents Love in the posture of a ruling conqueror or victor surrounded by opulence and wealth
  • The term Fantastic can mean extravagant and imagined, not so much amazing but surreal, as if the poem is gazing into the speaker’s nightmare
  • The diction triumph also refers to Roman military parade celebrating victory, displaying captive and spoils of war framing Love as subjugation and Conquest (Splendid Parade)
  • Capitalisation and use of anastrophe shows Love’s self-satisfaction and self-congratulation at destructive power
  • The diction “Fantastic implies that is surpasses even the imperial grandeur of Ancient Rome; It’s so resplendent and grisly that it defies imagination
  • The aural pronunciation of FanTasTic Triumph saT and later BuT ‘Twas from mine he Took Desire all have dental sounds creating a cold, crisp, martial footstep that perfectly suits the malicious character of Love, and implies how warm emotions are cast aside struck down, and trampled upon
  • The personification of Love having sat allows for the imagery of Love being enthroned in a state of grandeur as he sits in relaxation and authority
  • The anthropomorphism merged with juxtaposition allows for a powerful contrast to Love’s relaxed state to the tormented condition of the assembled party in his court encircling him
  • The diction and anthropomorphism him also humanises Love and presents him as a callous male figure
  • The graphic visual imagery flowed and bleeding shows the broken hearts haemorrhaging blood that forms a larger blood pool, which so casually and is able to flow, as well as the pain of a broken hart
  • Anastrophe of sat and flowed contrasts Love’s serenity with carnage that surrounds him and highlights his position of unassailable power
Effect, style & response

<- The Depiction of Love as a Roman Warlord

<- Cupid

3 / 4

For whom Fresh pains he did Create, / And strange Tyrannic power he showed;

Analysis
  • The personified Love is inflicting new injuries on the already bleeding group which presents him as a psychopath because he is making their already bad condition worse.
  • Fresh Pains also provides tactile imagery of the extreme sensitivity of their wounds
  • The adjective Fresh to describe the pains of unrequited love carries the meaning of new, strong, and sharp, revealing a continuously renewing torment and the intense and acuteness of them
  • Emphasises the sharpness of the speaker’s emotional suffering
  • The perpetuity of love creating new wounds which are immediate and overwhelming, despite the old ones haven’t been healed shows the theme of relentless emotional suffering
  • Create / sat = half-rhyme, probably imperfect even in 1676 → the pageant's rhyme doesn't quite close
  • Create = God's verb: Love makes pain, but is himself made (set him up a Deity)
  • The anthropomorphised and personified Love carried out other fearful actions that presented him as a Tyrant and oppressive ruler
  • The adjective strange and tyrannic to describe Love’s power evoke the notion of love as an oppressive, alien, and cruel force which dominates the speaker’s emotional love
  • Heavily contrasts to the classical, idealised, romantic version of love celebrated in poetry
  • Diction of strange highlights emotional alienation experienced by the speaker, showing the love she feels being isolating as it drives a wedge between her and any potential for emotional fulfilment
  • Hints at disempowerment of loving someone who does not return her affection, making love itself feel alien
  • Diction of tyrannic shows a dominating, cruel and oppressive force, evoking the image of a tyrant who exercises power arbitrarily and mercilessly, exploiting its victims while subjecting them to its will without care or compassion
5 / 6

From thy Bright Eyes he took his fire, / Which round about, in sport he hurled;

Analysis
  • From thy uses the archaic second person pronoun that signals that the speaker is speaking directly to someone else from whom something was forcibly taken while bright eyes is an allusion to the vitality, health and excitement that Persona two has
  • He took his fire again anthropomorphise personified Love and presents it as a forceful raider
  • The imperious (arrogant and domineering) picture of a victorious Tyrant is amplified by imagery of fire having stolen the bright light from another’s eyes he forges this energy into arrows of fire that he hurls indiscriminately so anyone unlucky enough to get struck is guaranteed to get burned
  • The imagery of the eyes refers to the renaissance belief that the yes were powerful conduits of emotions and desire and that love could be caught through the gaze
  • Fire taken from thy Bright Eyes (the beloved's eyes, not Love's) → we imagine Love leaning forward on his throne, hunting for more victims to hurl it at
  • How causing pain is a fun distraction for him
  • The speaker silently addresses the object of her love (in Abdelazer: Queen Isabella's serenade to Abdelazer, the Moor she loves) through the apostrophe (where the speaker speaks directly to an absent person, thing or idea)
  • Love has taken the sparks of passion and transformed them into a weapon, to be hurled and thrown carelessly about with considerable force for entertainment and sport
  • His fire has struck her down, causing an ignition of her desire through the archaic possessive pronoun thy
  • Related with thou, thee, thine
  • Used in an informal and familiar manner (similar to ton, tuo or tu in French, Italian and Spanish)
  • Discusses more about her tender feelings for him rather than their relationship
  • In the play a queen to the man she loves → thou = intimacy (also the standard address of love lyric)
  • Strikingly shows the disregard with which Love toyed with what he took from Persona Two
  • The diction of “hurled’ also provides vivid Visual Imagery that he threw it with enormous force and blatant disregard as if it was a game
7 / 8

But ‘twas from mine he took desire / Enough to undo the Amorous World.

Analysis
  • Shifts the focus to the speaker and reveals that she too was a victim of Love who again like a raider drained her of zest, deep affection and enthusiasm
  • Love has taken the desire that has been ignited in her eyes recognising the destructive potential that it could even annihilate the very world and concept of love itself
  • undo = ruin; period sense of a woman undone (seduced and ruined)
  • Further emphasised through the only line with enjambment emphasising how the speaker allows her meaning to spill over from one poetic line to the next through the sheer force of her emotion
  • The hyperbole gives the degree to which the speaker has been exploited, and suggests that what was taken from her was so much that it can cause everyone in the world to become disinterested in sex and engaging in sexual relations
  • This paradoxical phrase implies that despite the overwhelming feeling the speaker experiences, desire can’t survive if the feeling isn’t returned, and how Love itself can destroy the idea of Love
  • Reinforces the Janian Nature of love: Uniting people together, separating and causing destruction
  • There is a longstanding literary tension between the opposing forces of reason and emotion, between Apollonian and Dionysian (In Greek myth, they are half-brothers who couldn’t be more different in character: Apollo stands for rational, logic, and reason; his brother for instinct passion, irrationality, and chaos (God of wine for a reason lol))
  • Her “sighs and tears’ cast the speaker in Dionysian robes, as does the extreme of her emotional pain: she feels so strongly that the Amorous World is literally undone
9 / 10 / 11 / 12

“From me he took his sighs and tears, / From thee his Pride and Cruelty; / From me his Languishments and Fears, / And every Killing Dart from thee;”

Analysis
  • Use of pairing reveals two more things that Love took from the speaker and are allusion to her groans and weeping, which reinforces that she is experiencing heartbreak
  • Continues the characterisation of “Love’’ as a parasitic force, which grows in power and strength as it feeds off the speaker’s and the man’s emotions
  • The verb took governs the subsequent phrases in lines 10, 11, and 12 despite not being explicitly repeated each time
  • The implicit repetition reinforces the relentless, one-sided nature of love in the poem
  • How Love continually draws out and takes away sighs, tears, languishments and fears and the beloved Pride, cruelty and killing darts
  • The repetition across both stanzas emphasises the act of conquest, where Love seemingly conquerors and takes over the body of the speaker
  • The anaphoric lines From me… From thee… From me… and the final inverted from thee (moved to line-end; not epistrophe), shows a constant back and forth between thee and me creating the impression that never the twain shall meet (too different to exist together)
  • Constant use of From reinforces the one-sided nature of love too
  • The rhyme scheme composed in alternate rhyme (ABAB not AABB) rather than rhyming couplets evokes the impression of two people remaining at a distance from one another
  • Alongside the subversion of romantic imagery is a subversion of poetic form as Behn defines it as a Song which was often set to music to entertain and to delight courtly listeners with musical rhythms and rhymes yet Love Armed is not a dreamy love song
  • The only song heard is the flourishing of trumpets and beating of drums that accompany the return of a victorious army as it is written in Iambic Tetrameter
  • In a more conventional love poem it might evoke the passionate beating of lovers’ hearts, but here it more readily associates with the iron-shod boots of a marching army, as those hearts are ruthlessly trampled upon
  • Shifts the attention to Persona Two and suggests that they are arrogant and sadistic and it is from them Love got both traits that he is displaying
  • The use of the anaphoric from in the fronted adverbials emphasises the multiple raids that Love engaged in, while her repetition of “took’ emphasises how forcefully he grabbed what he collected, and Love’s insatiable appetite creating a sense of exploitation and imbalance
  • Exposes two additional things that Love stripped from the speaker and are allusions to her weak physical state, sadness, and anxiety through the diction of languishments
  • The imbalance of power between the pair becomes clear as the speaker is debilitated, weak, physically and emotionally drained, overcome with misery and despair, while the man is aloof and unfeeling
  • Shifts the attention to Persona Two and presents them as the only source of the tool from which Love murders people
  • Dart is an allusion to Cupid’s arrow, not as an arrow shot playfully to inspire mutual affection but rather a lethal weapon designed to strike down and cause pain and suffering
  • The killing dart also symbolises a dark twist on the idea of being lovestruck having been physically struck with blood flow[ing] out in a grisly pool
  • The speaker is clearly prone to emotion and suffering from a depth of feel seen through the symbols of emotions “sighs and tears’
  • The softness of the sounds of the diction and long vowel sounds of the ea combination in fears/tears or the breathy onomatopoeia of the word sigh
  • Yet the speaker's beloved displays a certain heartlessness, characterised by words such as Cruelty, Pride, and Fire
  • It is the object of her affection from whom the Tyrant took his Killing Dart, words made of sharp stabbing sounds K/D/T suggesting that this person, is more than capable of inflicting wounds of his own
Effect, style & response
  • This allusion to Cupid is quite obvious In classical mythology, Cupid is the god of love, desire, attraction, and eroticism. Also known as Amor (meaning love) and Eros in Greece, commonly portrayed as a slender winged boy (as above)
  • Often conflated with cherubs (putti: small winged infants in Renaissance art), and images of Cupid as a small chubby boy carrying bow and arrow, which are the source of his power to fill others with uncontrollable love and desire, were entering the public consciousness
  • Behn faintly alludes to well-known iconography, by distorting Cupid’s kindly features with malice as he launches yet another Killing Dart at an unsuspecting victim
  • The general semantic field of war armed, Bleeding, pains, power, Tyrannic, hurled, Killing Dart, harmed, and Victor all link to Cupid, drawing out his father’s legacy as the words are not naturally suited to compose a romantic ditty (song)
  • Difficult to judge whether the speaker and this other person have had a past relationship that’s turned sour, or whether this is just a case of spurned affection
  • The diction Cruelty faintly implies the speaker has some experience of the other, and in stanza two, line 13 which is the only line of the poem to feature both thou and I briefly placing the two side by side (more so a conjecture, but interesting!)
13 / 14 / 15 / 16

“Thus thou and I, the God have armed, / And set him up a Deity; / But my poor Heart alone is harmed, / Whilst thine the Victor is, and free.”

Analysis
  • Attributes supernatural power to Love, but the arming runs the other way: thou and I (subject) put the weapons in the hands of the God (object)
  • The speaker and her beloved have both provided Love with the weapons that have enabled him to become a deity and a god
  • How Love is no god by himself, but rather enthroned as a god through others supplying him with the ability to be so
  • Despite both of them being responsible, she is the sole victim
  • The final contrast emphasises the speaker’s suffering and emotional vulnerability as she acknowledged that while they both played a role in empowering Love, only she bears the painful consequences of them both
  • Her heart is wounded and enslaved by the very force they have armed while her beloved remains untouched being the Victor and free
  • This dynamic reinforces the inequity (lack of fairness or justice) in their relationship, where love is not mutual where the speaker is trapped in emotional turmoil, while her beloved escaped unscathed
  • Underscores the parasitic nature of love where one person gives and suffers while the other benefits without sacrifice
  • Enhances the poem’s portrayal of Love in a man’s world, as a cruel and one sided force
  • Turns the focus back on the speaker and is a very direct detail of her claiming to be broken hearted, feeling pity for herself and being wounded
  • Again returns the focus to the speaker’s lover and shows that to her he won and has become unencumbered (Free and not impeded) after their breakup
  • Returning the idea of Dionysian and Apollonian, in contrast, her beloved, cast as the Victor” in this tug-of-war, seems immune to extremes of feeling (possibly his Pride holds him in check, as if he considered himself above such tawdry (showy but poor and cheap) emotions)
  • This major clash between the two is symbolised through the eyes of the speaker and her beloved, and in their brief moment of eye-contact, the fire in the other’s eyes ignited desire in the speaker’s own
CONNECTIONS

Connections

How this poem pairs with the rest of the set

Comparison hooks

1. Philips, 'A Married State' (11)

Link: This is the essential pairing: two seventeenth-century women on love as a tyranny that has to be seen through. Behn's lovers set him up a Deity; Philips tells her "madam" to "Turn, turn apostate to love's Levity". The vocabulary even overlaps. Philips's husbands "create your fears" and childbirth will "extort your tears"; Behn's Love did Create Fresh pains and took sighs and tears and Fears.

Shared technique: Patterned syntax turns complaint into a case (Behn's From me… From thee…, Philips's "No… No…"), and both arguments pivot on "Thus": Thus thou and I, the God have armed and "Thus are you freed".

Difference: Behn writes from inside desire, after the god is armed; Philips writes from outside, advising escape before any damage ("Suppress wild nature"). Freedom in Behn belongs to the beloved (the Victor is, and free); in Philips it belongs to the woman who never marries. Behn's song is the form of feeling; Philips's heroic couplets, ending on a joke ("leading Apes in hell"), are the form of argument.

2. Blake, 'The Chimney Sweeper' (Songs of Experience) (03)

Link: Both expose a god built out of the sufferers' pain. The sweep's parents praise "God and his priest and king, / Who make up a heaven of our misery"; Behn's lovers make a deity out of sighs and tears. In both, worship is the mechanism of harm.

Shared technique: Song is the delivery system: the sweep was "taught… to sing the notes of woe", and Behn's lyric is a Song. Singable metre carries the pain, and both rhyme polysyllables on a promoted -y ("injury / misery"; Cruelty / Deity).

Difference: Blake's victim is a child betrayed by institutions. Behn's speaker is an adult who co-authored her own oppression (thou and I), understands the mechanism completely, and is harmed anyway.

3. Pope, 'An Essay on Man' (12)

Link: Both are about people who make powers that unmake them. Pope warns "presume not God to scan" and shows man "In doubt to deem himself a god or beast". Behn's lovers presume further: they make a god and fall to him. Both name pride: "the stoic's pride" in Pope, Pride and Cruelty in Behn.

Shared technique: Antithesis drives both, and they use the same rhyme for scattering force: Pope's "in endless error hurled: / The glory, jest, and riddle of the world!" against Behn's in sport he hurled… the Amorous World.

Difference: Pope generalises about "mankind" in reason's impersonal voice; Behn speaks from one wounded heart to one thee. Pope's paradox (lord of all things, yet "a prey to all") is shared by every human being. Behn's is split between two people: one is lord, the other prey.

4. Shakespeare, 'Sonnet 18' (14)

Link: In both a lover's words settle the beloved's fate, and the last sound goes to "thee". Shakespeare ends "this gives life to thee"; Behn ends and free, rhyming on the same vowel. The sonneteer gives the beloved eternal life. Behn's speaker has given the beloved, by way of the god, the power to harm her.

Shared technique: Both reshape the Petrarchan kit. Shakespeare declines the comparison and never describes the beloved's body; Behn shrinks the blazon to Bright Eyes and makes it a weapon. Both personify a boasting conqueror ("Nor shall death brag" / Love in Fantastic Triumph sat) and deal in eyes and fire ("the eye of heaven" / From thy Bright Eyes he took his fire).

Difference: Shakespeare's speaker is serenely in control, and poetry defeats death. Behn's controls the account but not the outcome: her words win the record, not the love.

5. Bhatt, 'A Different History' (02)

Link: The oppressed help produce the power that rules them: Behn's lovers the God have armed; Bhatt's descendants "grow to love that strange language". Both hang the scandal on the same adjective, strange Tyrannic power and "strange language", and both open with a personified god ("Great Pan is not dead").

Shared technique: Both argue through patterned repetition: From me… From thee… in Behn; "a sin… a sin…" and the questions about "the oppressor's tongue" in Bhatt.

Difference: Bhatt's history is collective and colonial, a language imposed "after the torture". Behn's is intimate. Bhatt ends in an uneasy love for the conqueror's language; Behn ends without reconciliation.

6. Clarke, 'Lament' (07)

Link: In both, a litany becomes an indictment. Clarke's "For the…" and Behn's From me… From thee… list costs until the guilty party is convicted by accumulation. Clarke names war's suppliers, "the gunsmith and the armourer"; Behn makes the lovers Love's armourers.

Shared technique: Anaphora is the engine, and beauty is laid over damage ("the cormorant in his funeral silk" / Bleeding Hearts around him flowed), so that elegance itself feels complicit.

Difference: Clarke mourns real casualties of the 1991 Gulf War as a witness. Behn's war is a metaphor, and her speaker is both supplier and casualty.

7. Heaney, 'Follower' (08)

Link: Both end by restaging their opening picture with the power reversed. The boy who stumbled in his father's "hob-nailed wake" ends with a father who "keeps stumbling / Behind me"; Behn's second Whilst (16) repeats line 2, but now the beloved sits where Love sat.

Shared technique: An echoed word frames each poem (Heaney's stumbling, Behn's Whilst), and a final line tips the balance of power.

Difference: Heaney's reversal is time's work and comes with guilt and tenderness. Behn's is the beloved's work and comes with injustice.

Other hooks

  • Halligan, 'The Cockroach' (06): a watched spectacle becomes a mirror ("I thought I recognised myself"), as Behn's watchers discover at line 13 that they built the god.
  • Boey, 'Report to Wordsworth' (05): "insatiate man" leaves God "labouring to utter his last cry"; Behn's lovers do the opposite and create theirs.
  • Brewster, 'Where I Come From' (04): "People are made of places", benignly; Behn's god is made of donated feelings, malignly.

02Post-colonial

A Different History

Sujata Bhatt · 1988

Where it is a sin to be rude to a book, the grandchildren grow to love the tongue that cropped their ancestors' souls — and the poem asking how is written in it.

Lines
29
Form

ContextThe PoemThe Whole PoemForm & StructureSoundMotifs & SymbolsThemesDifficult MomentsClose AnalysisCritical LensesOther ReadingsRevision NotesConnections
CONTEXT

Context

The world the poem came out of

The Poet: Sujata Bhatt (born 1956)

Sujata Bhatt was born on 6 May 1956 in Ahmedabad, Gujarat, and grew up mainly in Pune (Poona). Her life crossed continents from the start. She has said that she "had learned English in New Orleans at the age of five", during a stay in the United States, and that back in India, at about eight, she was already writing poems in English with Gujarati words in them (PN Review 213, 2013). In 1968, when she was twelve, the family emigrated to the United States. She took a BA in philosophy and English at Goucher College, Baltimore (1980), and an MFA at the University of Iowa Writers' Workshop (1986). In 1988 she married the German writer Michael Augustin; they live in Bremen and have a daughter. She was Lansdowne Visiting Writer at the University of Victoria, British Columbia, in 1992, and works as a writer and translator.

Her books, all with Carcanet, include Brunizem (1988), Monkey Shadows (1991), The Stinking Rose (1995), Point No Point (1997), Augatora (2000), A Colour for Solitude (2002), Pure Lizard (2008), Collected Poems (2013) and Poppies in Translation (2015). She received a Cholmondeley Award in 1991 and the Italian Tratti Poetry Prize in 2000. So when this poem was printed she had lived in two countries and would soon settle in a third. In a short prose piece, 'Why I Write', she describes her observations as "those of an outsider". The poem depends on that double position: it speaks from inside India (Here) and looks at English from just outside it (that strange language).

Two Tongues: What Bhatt Has Said About Gujarati and English

Gujarati, the language of Gujarat, is Bhatt's mother tongue. The Poetry Archive's biography quotes her calling it, with the Indian childhood it connects her to, "the deepest layer of my identity". Yet English came early and stayed. In conversation with Helen Tookey (PN Review 213, September–October 2013) she recalled that "I had started using Gujarati words and lines in some of my otherwise English poems … when I was a child, around eight, in India". She wants readers without Gujarati to "experience the in-betweenness and 'foreignness' of what I experience", and adds: "It is not my intention to alienate or to exclude any of my readers or listeners." She describes composing as a kind of translation: "When I am most deeply absorbed in writing a poem I feel that I am 'translating' images" (Poetry Archive), and with them sounds, rhythms and an emotional tone, into words.

The companion piece is 'Search for My Tongue', a long poem from the same collection, which the critic Minnie Singh calls "an ambitious experiment in bilingual poetry". Its speaker asks what you would do with "two tongues in your mouth" and fears that, living in a foreign language, the mother tongue will "rot". Gujarati lines then appear in Gujarati script, and the lost tongue grows back overnight like a plant and "pushes the other tongue aside". The two poems use the same body-part metaphor for language and the same imagery of growth, but they run in opposite directions. In 'Search for My Tongue' the mother tongue regrows; in 'A Different History' the grandchildren grow to love the foreign one.

That contrast makes this poem's method a choice. 'Search for My Tongue' puts Gujarati on the page; 'A Different History' uses none. Everything Indian in it, from the goddess to the rules about books, reaches the reader already rendered into English and explained for someone who may not share it. Here the "in-betweenness" is not displayed by mixing two scripts. It is lived inside one inherited language, which is the very situation the last line describes.

First Printing and *Brunizem* (1987–88)

'A Different History' first appeared in PN Review 53 (January–February 1987), alongside 'The Doors are Always Open'. There, and in the text on the Poetry Archive, the second part is headed with the numeral "2", which makes the poem a two-part sequence. It was collected in Brunizem (Carcanet, Manchester, 1988), her first book. Brunizem won the Alice Hunt Bartlett Award (1988) and the Commonwealth Poetry Prize for the Asia region (Contemporary Poets dates it 1989; the Poetry Archive lists it with 1988). The title names a dark prairie soil found in Asia, Europe and North America, the three continents of Bhatt's life. Minnie Singh says the word "signals Bhatt's powerfully organic concern with language", and that concern is exactly this poem's: sacred trees, a cropped soul, and grandchildren who grow.

Singh discusses the poem as one of "an important set of Bhatt's poems" which "anticipates and answers the criticism frequently leveled against Indian poets in English — that genuine poetry cannot be written in a foreign language", and observes that Bhatt's method "moves swiftly from the discursive to the imagistic", from argument to image, as it does when the questions of the second stanza turn into the scythe. The Cambridge anthology Songs of Ourselves (Foundation Books / Cambridge University Press, 2005) drops the section numeral. It prints lines 3, 10, 12 and 14 indented, line 10 the deepest, and sets the whole second stanza as a block further to the right. Bhatt recorded the poem for the Poetry Archive in London on 1 September 2005, and the Archive's page for it carries her short first-person note on Sarasvati.

"Great Pan is dead": Plutarch's Story and Its Christian Afterlife

Pan was the Greek god of shepherds, flocks and wild places, especially Arcadia: goat-legged, a player of the reed pipes, and the source of the word "panic". In On the Obsolescence of Oracles (written around AD 100), Plutarch tells a story set in the reign of Tiberius (AD 14–37). A ship off the island of Paxi was becalmed when a voice called three times to the Egyptian pilot, Thamus, and ordered him to announce, when he reached Palodes, that "Great Pan is dead". When he shouted it, a great lament rose from the shore, and Tiberius had the matter investigated. For Plutarch the story was evidence that divine spirits could die. Christian writers gave it its famous meaning. Eusebius of Caesarea (fourth century) read it as the demons dying at Christ's coming. Rabelais (Quart Livre, 1552) identified Pan with Christ, whose death fell in the same reign. Milton's 'On the Morning of Christ's Nativity' (1629) calls the infant Christ "the mighty Pan" (l.89). Elizabeth Barrett Browning's 'The Dead Pan' (1844), with its refrain "Pan, Pan is dead", celebrates the old gods' fall. So "Great Pan is dead" became Europe's shorthand for the end of the pagan world, its nature-gods replaced by Christianity and then by reason. Bhatt's first line contradicts that whole tradition.

Two etymological footnotes add depth, though neither should be treated as Bhatt's intention. The Homeric Hymn to Pan already punned on the name and Greek pan, "all"; modern scholars instead derive it from a root meaning "guard, herd", the root of "pasture". In 1924 the philologist Hermann Collitz proposed that Pan is cognate with the Vedic god Pūṣan, guardian of roads, journeys and herds, whose chariot is drawn by goats and who guides souls to the next world. It is a respected but contested hypothesis. If it is right, Pan's "emigration" to India is a kind of homecoming.

Sarasvati, Sacred Books and Gods in Animal Form

Sarasvati began as a river goddess in the Rigveda, praised as "best of mothers, best of rivers, best of goddesses" (2.41.16). She was later identified with Vāc, Speech, and became the goddess of knowledge, language, music and the arts. She is shown holding a book and a veena (a stringed instrument), with a swan, a bird believed able to separate milk from water and so an emblem of discernment. At Vasant Panchami, her festival, books, pens and instruments are placed before her image, and children are often started on their letters. The river itself is said to have vanished underground and to flow on unseen, joining the Ganges and Yamuna at Prayagraj. The note printed with the poem on the Poetry Archive begins "in this poem I mention the Hindu goddess, Sarasvati", and explains that she is the goddess of knowledge, presides over the fine arts and is often worshipped in libraries in India.

The litany in the first stanza records real etiquette. In many Indian homes a book, paper or money is never touched with the foot or left on the floor. If it is touched by accident, you touch it with your hand and then touch your forehead or eyes in apology. The other images are equally real. Snakes are revered as nāgas and offered milk at Nag Panchami, Shiva wears a serpent, and Vishnu rests on the serpent Shesha. Hanuman, the monkey god, is Rama's devoted messenger; in Valmiki's Ramayana he even stops to consider which language to address Sita in, learned Sanskrit or ordinary speech, so that she will not take him for Ravana in disguise. Trees such as the peepal and the banyan are worshipped, and the Buddha's enlightenment took place under a peepal, the Bodhi tree.

English in India: From Wonder to Policy (1786–1947)

The East India Company, chartered by Elizabeth I on 31 December 1600, won control of Bengal after Clive's victory at Plassey (1757). Its early scholars were often admirers. In 1786 Sir William Jones told the Asiatic Society in Calcutta that Sanskrit was "more perfect than the Greek, more copious than the Latin, and more exquisitely refined than either", and the Company funded Sanskrit and Arabic colleges and printed classical texts. That changed with Thomas Babington Macaulay's Minute on Indian Education, dated 2 February 1835. Macaulay claimed that no orientalist could deny "a single shelf of a good European library was worth the whole native literature of India and Arabia". He called the spoken dialects of his region "so poor and rude" that valuable works could hardly be translated into them, and complained that the Committee's Sanskrit and Arabic books "find no purchasers". His aim was "a class of persons Indian in blood and colour, but English in tastes, in opinions, in morals and in intellect", who would one day "refine the vernacular dialects". Lord William Bentinck's resolution of 7 March 1835, often called the English Education Act, decided that "the great object of the British Government ought to be the promotion of European literature and science", and that education funds "would be best employed on English education alone". No new stipends were to go to students at the oriental colleges, and no further funds to printing oriental works.

Some of this was softened later (Lord Auckland restored money to the oriental colleges in 1839), but the direction held. In 1837 English and the local languages replaced Persian, the courtly language of the Mughals, in the Company's courts and administration. From 1844, English-educated Indians were given preference for government posts, and English-medium universities opened in Calcutta, Bombay and Madras in 1857. After the rebellion of 1857 the Crown took over (the Raj, 1858–1947). English thus became the language of law, office and advancement, which is part of why the grandchildren "grow to love" it. The poem's torture is not only metaphor either: a commission in Madras reported in 1855 that torture was routinely used to extract the Company's land revenue. Gandhi, writing Hind Swaraj in Gujarati in 1909, attacked the English education built on Macaulay's foundations as a form of enslavement, and then translated the book into English himself.

Can a Language Murder? The Debate the Poem Enters

Bhatt's second stanza enters one of the central arguments of postcolonial literature. Chinua Achebe, in 'The African Writer and the English Language' (1965), argued that the colonial language could be taken over and remade to carry African experience. Ngũgĩ wa Thiong'o, in Decolonising the Mind (James Currey, 1986), renounced English for Gĩkũyũ. He argued that while the bullet had subjugated the body, language had subjugated the spirit, and that imperialism's "cultural bomb" works "to annihilate a people's belief in their names, in their languages". For Ngũgĩ, "Language as culture is the collective memory bank of a people's experience in history." Sociolinguists later named the process "linguistic imperialism" (Robert Phillipson, 1992) and even "linguistic genocide" (Tove Skutnabb-Kangas, 2000), the vocabulary of murder applied to languages that drive out others.

'A Different History', in print by early 1987, takes up the question without joining either camp. Its first question says every language has served an oppressor; its second says no language "truly meant" to murder; its ending grants the grandchildren's love. Indian history supports its refusal to blame English alone. Persian was imposed as the language of the courts for centuries before English, and after independence the plan to make Hindi the sole official language provoked violent protests in Madras State in 1965. English survived as an official language alongside Hindi, defended by many as a neutral link between India's languages. Gujarat itself became a separate state on linguistic lines in 1960. The question Which language / has not been the oppressor's tongue? has Indian answers as well as British ones.

Kindred Tongues: Why the "Strange" Language Is a Lost Relative

Jones's 1786 discourse is also the founding moment of comparative linguistics. He saw that Sanskrit, Greek and Latin (and, he suspected, the Germanic languages) "sprung from some common source". Gujarati descends from Sanskrit's family, and English from its Germanic branch. So the "strange language" of the last line is a distant cousin of the grandchildren's own. Sanskrit Dyaus Pitar, the sky father, is Greek Zeus Patēr and Latin Jupiter. Sanskrit deva, a god, is related to Latin deus; Gujarati nām is English "name"; Gujarati dānt, tooth, is related to Latin dens, the source of English "dental". If Collitz was right, even Pan and Pūṣan are a separated pair. In that light the poem's history is a family story: one root, long divergence, and a violent reunion.

Kinship has not made translation easy, and the gaps sharpen the poem. Gujarati builds respect into grammar, with an intimate tũ and a respectful tame for "you", where English has a single word. A Gujarati speaker has many words for uncle, kākā (father's brother) and māmā (mother's brother) among them, where English has one. And the English sin, shaped by Christianity's idea of an offence against God, is not an exact equivalent of Gujarati pāp (wrongdoing, with its consequences in the chain of karma). When the first stanza says sin, the reader is already hearing Indian reverence through the conqueror's vocabulary.

THE POEM

The Poem

Line by line, with the analysis alongside

A Different History
TA Different History
1Great Pan is not dead;
2he simply emigrated
3to India.
4Here, the gods roam freely,
5disguised as snakes or monkeys;
6every tree is sacred
7and it is a sin
8to be rude to a book.
9It is a sin to shove a book aside
10with your foot,
11a sin to slam books down
12hard on a table,
13a sin to toss one carelessly
14across a room.
15You must learn how to turn the pages gently
16without disturbing Sarasvati,
17without offending the tree
18from whose wood the paper was made.
19Which language
20has not been the oppressor's tongue?
21Which language
22truly meant to murder someone?
23And how does it happen
24that after the torture,
25after the soul has been cropped
26with a long scythe swooping out
27of the conqueror's face –
28the unborn grandchildren
29grow to love that strange language.

Lines with a marker have analysis — click one, or just scroll.

Title
A Different History
Language & devices

Indefinite article A: one history among several, not the history. Compare the colonial "The" of James Mill's The History of British India (1817), a book written without its author ever visiting India. Adjective Different implies a comparison but withholds it: different from what? The word comes from Latin differre, "to carry apart". Noun History comes from Greek historia, "inquiry", and English "story" comes from the same word.

Meaning & effect

The title promises a counter-history, told from the side that is usually written about rather than doing the writing. Because it leaves out its comparison, the reader supplies the version they already hold: the European story in which Pan dies, or the imperial story in which English brings enlightenment. The first line then contradicts it. "History" in its old sense of inquiry suits a poem whose second half is three questions, so this is history as asking rather than as record. The title also hides an irony. The pattern the poem finds is not different at all: Which language / has not been the oppressor's tongue? says that conquest through language is the oldest story there is. What is different is the ending, where the conquered come to love what conquered them. Read that way, the title and the last lines answer each other. The "different history" is the one the grandchildren live in that strange language, and the poem, written in English, belongs to it. Read counterfactually, the title also imagines the history that might have been, in which India's gods and books were left undisturbed. The poem holds both meanings: a history that should have been different, and one that turned out stranger than anyone could have predicted.

Line 1
Great Pan is not dead;
Language & devices

Allusion to the cry in Plutarch's On the Obsolescence of Oracles. In the reign of Tiberius (AD 14–37) a voice ordered the Egyptian pilot Thamus to announce, as his ship passed Palodes, that Great Pan was dead. The epithet Great comes from that cry. Negation not dead opens the poem by contradicting a sentence the reader is assumed to know, asserting life by denying death. Heavy monosyllables give four strong stresses (Great, Pan, not, dead). The Caesura at the semicolon is a pause that promises an explanation, not a full stop.

Meaning & effect

Bhatt starts mid-argument by correcting Europe. From Eusebius onwards, Christian writers read Plutarch's cry as the death-notice of the pagan gods at Christ's coming, and Rabelais and Milton turned Pan into a figure for Christ himself. To say not dead is to say that what Europe recorded as an ending was only an ending in Europe: Western history is not world history. The tone is calm and certain rather than angry. The speaker informs instead of arguing, and that authority wins the reader's trust before the poem turns to questions it cannot answer. The semicolon refuses closure and leans the sentence forward into its surprise. An ancient pun linked Pan's name with Greek pan, "all", so the line can also be heard as a claim about all the old gods. That is wordplay, not etymology, but it suits a poem about a land where the gods (plural) live on.

Line 2
he simply emigrated
Language & devices

The Adverb simply is Understatement that tips into Bathos: the death of a whole world-order shrinks to a change of address. Diction emigrated is a modern, administrative word for moving permanently, so a god is given a migrant's verb. Enjambment carries the sentence over the line-end towards its destination.

Meaning & effect

The joke has an edge: Europe's most famous obituary is reduced to paperwork. Emigrated is chosen precisely. It is not "fled", which would make Pan a refugee from Christianity, and not "travelled", which would imply he means to return. Emigrants leave in order to settle, so Pan has chosen India as home, and India becomes the place where the old world survives rather than a place of loss. The verb also points at the poet. Bhatt emigrated too, but the other way: her family moved to the United States in 1968, when she was twelve. A god travels east as the poet travelled west, and each carries a culture with them. The poem will need that contrast. Pan's migration is voluntary and preserves what he is, while the language of the second stanza arrives by conquest and replaces what was there.

Line 3
to India.
Language & devices

An indented line (as printed in the anthology): the destination is given its own ledge of white space. It is a short, two-word line, End-stopped with a full stop, so the first sentence closes on India. The Enjambment across ll.2–3 makes the reader cross the line-break as Pan crosses the border.

Meaning & effect

Because it is delayed, India arrives as a small revelation: the reader travels over a line-break to reach it, and the full stop gives the arrival weight and calm. The indentation works two ways at once. India is pushed off the main margin, a country history has placed at the edge, and it is also isolated so that it becomes the focus of attention. It is the only place the poem ever names. No Britain, England or Europe appears anywhere, which keeps the poem's frame wider than any one empire. In ten words Bhatt has moved a European god to the subcontinent and quietly made India the keeper of what the West let die, and the full stop presents this as calmly as a fact of geography.

Line 4
Here, the gods roam freely,
Language & devices

Deixis Here is a "pointing" word that places the speaker inside India; the comma isolates it as a beat of arrival. The subject widens from singular to plural, Pan to the gods. Verb roam means wander without a destination, as grazing animals do. Adverb freely.

Meaning & effect

Here is a position, not just a place: the voice speaks from inside India, although the poem was written abroad (it was in print by early 1987, before Bhatt settled in Germany). Its silent opposite is "there", the Europe where Pan was declared dead. Here is also answered by the poem's last pointing word, that strange language: near and far mark its two ends. The gods are now a population rather than one refugee, and they roam. They are not housed in churches or fixed in doctrine; they are at large in the living world. Freely carries an irony the second stanza will make felt: the gods are free in a country that, for nearly two centuries, was not. The line is literal as well as theological, since monkeys and cattle do wander freely through Indian towns and round temples, so the belief is anchored in what anyone could see in the street.

Line 5
disguised as snakes or monkeys;
Language & devices

Diction disguised means hidden divinity, and it is an outsider's word. This is not a Simile: as means "in the form of". The animal imagery: snakes, as in the nāgas (serpent deities), Vishnu resting on the serpent Shesha, and Shiva's snake; monkeys, as in Hanuman. Sibilance in disguised as snakes, with hard /k/ in snakes or monkeys. A semicolon keeps the list running.

Meaning & effect

The line finds holiness in creatures the West tends to fear or mock, the serpent of Eden and the monkey of colonial caricature, and quietly reverses that ranking. Disguised, though, is the word of someone translating for outsiders. In Hindu thought a god's animal shape is a form, not a costume: Vishnu's avatars (the word means "descent") include a fish, a tortoise and a boar. So the speaker is already explaining her culture in the terms of another, a small early sign of the problem the second stanza names. Disguised can also suggest survival under pressure, since a god who must hide is a god in danger. The next lines then rebuild the Eden story with its values reversed: a snake, a tree, a book of knowledge and the word sin. In Genesis the sin is to take from the tree of knowledge; here the sin is to fail to respect it.

Line 6
every tree is sacred
Language & devices

Absolute every: no exceptions. Diction sacred. A short declarative line in the present tense of permanent truth. Sibilance is sacred leads the ear into sin.

Meaning & effect

This is the poem's first general law, and the premise of all that follows: the tree is holy, so whatever is made from it inherits that holiness. Real devotion stands behind it, since the peepal and the banyan are worshipped and the Buddha's enlightenment took place under a peepal, the Bodhi tree. Every, though, extends the belief into a whole world-view in which nature is not raw material. The line begins the stanza's chain of tree, wood, paper and book, which closes in ll.17–18. It also introduces the vocabulary of growing things, which the second stanza will turn violent: if every tree is sacred, a soul cropped with a scythe is sacrilege as well as cruelty. The plain, unqualified syntax gives the claim the authority of a creed.

Line 7
and it is a sin
Language & devices

Line break suspense: the solemn noun sin hangs at the end of the line before we learn its object. The Anaphora begins here; sin comes four times (ll.7, 9, 11, 13). Diction sin is the vocabulary of Christian theology, standing in for the Sanskrit and Gujarati pāp. The conjunction and joins the holiness of trees and of books into one law.

Meaning & effect

The pause prepares the reader for a grave offence, and the next line delivers a book. Sin is the stanza's quiet joke and its quiet problem. A passage describing Indian reverence speaks in an English word with Christian weight, so the coloniser's moral vocabulary is already inside the "pure" stanza. (Pāp, wrongdoing with consequences in the chain of karma, is not an exact match for a Christian offence against God.) Sin also sets the moral scale by which the second stanza will be judged: it is used four times for mishandling a book, and not once for torture. When the poem reaches real atrocity its moral word falls silent, and the reader has to measure that gap.

Line 8
to be rude to a book.
Language & devices

Bathos, or a clash of register: the theological sin meets the nursery word rude. Personification: a book that can be offended. End-stopped. The book is introduced as the poem's sacred object.

Meaning & effect

Rude is the word a parent or grandparent uses, so the line sounds like teaching in the home rather than religious decree, which is how reverence is actually passed on: through small corrections. A Western reader may smile at the idea of being rude to a book, and that smile is the reflex the poem examines. What looks like quaint etiquette is a complete ethic, in which respect is owed to the objects that carry knowledge. History makes the point sharper. In 1835 Macaulay judged the spoken languages of his part of India "poor and rude", and declared that a single shelf of European books was worth "the whole native literature of India and Arabia". That was rudeness to a whole culture's books, carried out as education policy. Bhatt never names him, but the line measures him. The book now becomes the hinge of the poem: here the sacred object, and in the second stanza the language it carries.

Line 9
It is a sin to shove a book aside
Language & devices

Anaphora It is a sin repeats l.7. Verb shove is rough and contemptuous. Sibilance runs through sin, shove and aside. At ten syllables this is one of the poem's two longest lines: the verse expands where the handling of books is at stake.

Meaning & effect

The general law of l.8 now becomes particular actions. The litany lists gestures, which is how the poem makes reverence concrete enough to be learned: not a doctrine about books but a list of things a child must not do with one. Shove is contempt more than violence, the book moved out of the way as if it were nothing, and aside names where it ends up. Read as a figure, this is how one culture handles another's learning, pushing it aside as worthless, which is what the second stanza shows happening to a whole language. The capital It restarts the sentence, so the rule is said again, as rules are repeated to children, and the tone stays half-amused: the speaker knows how fussy this sounds to an outsider. Yet this is one of the poem's two longest lines, and the verse lengthens exactly where it describes a careless act, lingering on the offence until the reader feels its weight.

Line 10
with your foot,
Language & devices

An indented line, isolating the instrument (it is the most deeply indented line in the anthology printing). Second person your implicates the reader. The foot is the lowest and least clean part of the body. Assonance links book and foot across the break on the same short vowel.

Meaning & effect

With your foot is the worst version of the act: you do not even use your hands. In many Indian homes a book, a piece of paper or money touched by the foot is touched with the hand and then raised to the forehead or eyes, a small apology to Sarasvati. The poem records a gesture children are really taught. Your turns description into accusation: the reader is the one doing it. The indentation acts out the offence, since the line itself is shoved aside on the page. And the vowel-chime binds the sacred object to the offending limb, so the sound commits the very act the sentence forbids. This is also the closest of the three offences, body against book: the first point on a scale of distance that the litany will widen.

Line 11
a sin to slam books down
Language & devices

Ellipsis: It is is dropped, and the litany speeds up. Onomatopoeia slam. The plural books escalates the number. Plosives /b/ and /d/ in books down.

Meaning & effect

The prohibitions now come faster, and the grammar sheds words as a chant does: It is drops away, leaving only a sin to…. Slam moves the scale on from contempt to aggression, an act with noise and force behind it, so the reader hears the impact rather than imagining it. The plural matters, because the offence now falls on books in general rather than on one, and the scale of the harm is growing. The sound lands like the blow it describes, on two stressed, stopped syllables, books down. Under the comedy of being told off for slamming a book lies the idea the second stanza will make literal: how a thing is handled shows what it is thought to be worth, and violence to the vessel of knowledge is the small-scale version of violence to a culture.

Line 12
hard on a table,
Language & devices

An indented line. Adverb hard; Plosives /d/, /t/ and /b/ in hard on a table. The table is ordinary domestic furniture, a place for reading and eating.

Meaning & effect

The second indented completion isolates the impact, hard, as the first isolated the instrument. The setting is domestic: these sins happen at the table where one eats and studies, not in a temple. That is the poem's view of the sacred. It lives in everyday gestures, so it can be lost through everyday gestures too, and it is passed on in ordinary rooms by ordinary correction. Each completion is given its own ledge of white space, like evidence laid out item by item, so the list reads as a record of offences as well as a set of rules. The distance has also grown: the foot touched the book, but the slammed book is flung against furniture, one step further from the hand that should hold it.

Line 13
a sin to toss one carelessly
Language & devices

Anaphora a sin, the fourth and last time. Verb toss; Adverb carelessly. The pronoun one reduces the book to a unit. The Tricolon of shove, slam and toss is complete.

Meaning & effect

The three verbs form a scale: contempt, then aggression, then indifference. The last is the lightest in force and the worst in attitude, because carelessly names the real sin, which is not damage but the absence of care. One makes the book a mere item, something counted rather than cherished. Read as a figure, the three gestures are the ways a culture can be mistreated: pushed aside, struck, and finally simply not cared about. Indifference needs no effort and leaves no mark, which is why it is the hardest to resist. This is also the fourth and last sin. After this line the word disappears from the poem for good, so its absence from the second stanza, where the offences are far worse, is all the more noticeable.

Line 14
across a room.
Language & devices

An indented line, end-stopped, completing the spatial phrase. Through the litany the directional words accumulate: aside, down, across.

Meaning & effect

Each sin moves the book further from the hand: first the foot (contact), then the table (impact), then across a room (distance). As distance grows, care shrinks. The second stanza completes the pattern with a long scythe that harms from far away, so the litany quietly rehearses the poem's account of violence: the further the agent is from what he damages, the less he needs to care. The directional words, aside, down and across, also echo Pan's journey in ll.1–3, but as careless displacement rather than chosen migration: things moved by force, not by will. The full stop closes the list of sins. What follows is instruction, and the tone softens with it.

Line 15
You must learn how to turn the pages gently
Language & devices

Direct address You; Modal verb must (obligation); learn how to names a skill. This is the poem's longest line, eleven syllables with five main stresses: the nearest it comes to Iambic pentameter, with a feminine ending. Internal rhyme learn / turn. gently is placed at the line-end.

Meaning & effect

The prohibitions turn into positive teaching. Reverence is a skill to be learned, like a craft, and You puts the reader in the place of the child being taught. After the choppy lines of the litany, this long, smooth line performs the gentleness it asks for, and gently sits at the edge of the line as if handled with care. Learn is the stanza's key verb, and the last line will answer it with grow to love. Reverence is taught and deliberately passed on; love of the conqueror's language simply grows, and nobody chooses it. The near-pentameter carries a quiet irony too: this Indian lesson moves to the rhythm of English poetry's most traditional line.

Line 16
without disturbing Sarasvati,
Language & devices

Anaphora without… / without… begins a second litany, this time of care. Allusion to Sarasvati, the Hindu goddess of knowledge, speech, music and the arts, and the only Indian deity the poem names. Diction disturbing is domestic and tender. Soft Fricatives in without, Sarasvati.

Meaning & effect

Sarasvati lives in the book, so turning a page roughly is like waking someone. Bhatt's own note on the poem (Poetry Archive) explains that she is the goddess of knowledge and is often worshipped in libraries in India. The choice of name is pointed. Of all the gods who roam freely, the one named is the goddess of speech and learning, which tells us the poem's real subject is language, the word the second stanza will finally say aloud. The verb is gentle: you do not "anger" her, you disturb her, as one disturbs a sleeper, so the sacred is intimate and close at hand. The soft consonants restore calm after the plosive violence of ll.9–14. The name carries one more resonance for a reader who knows it: Sarasvati was first a river, and tradition says the river vanished underground and flows on unseen, a fitting presiding goddess for a poem about a culture that may survive beneath a conqueror's language.

Line 17
without offending the tree
Language & devices

Anaphora without. Personification offending. The tree of l.6 returns.

Meaning & effect

The sacred chain now runs backwards: first the goddess in the book, then the tree in the paper. To offend a tree sounds comic at first; the stanza makes it serious by showing that every page has a living source and a cost. Reverence here does not mean leaving nature untouched, because the tree has already become paper. It means using it with respect: an ethic of use rather than of avoidance. The line also asks the reader to remember origins, which is exactly what the second stanza fears the grandchildren will no longer do.

Line 18
from whose wood the paper was made.
Language & devices

The relative pronoun whose is normally used for people, here for a tree. The chain is complete: tree, wood, paper. Passive voice was made, with no agent named. Alliteration on /w/ in wood and was (whose, spelt wh but sounded /h/, joins the pattern only to the eye); long, low vowels. End-stopped: the stanza closes on made.

Meaning & effect

The stanza ends where it began, in the natural world of l.6, with the book fully traced back to its living origin. Whose quietly gives the tree personhood. The passive is harmless here, since nobody needs to know who made the paper, but the poem will repeat the construction in has been cropped, where the hidden agent is no longer innocent. The slow, soft sounds bring the stanza down to a near-whisper, so it ends at rest, on a made thing. This is the world the reader has been taught to value before the stanza break takes it away.

Line 19
Which language
Language & devices

The stanza break makes a Volta: from statement and instruction to questioning. Interrogative Which, on an isolated two-word line. The word language appears for the first time (it occurs three times, in ll.19, 21 and 29). A Tone shift: no images, no setting.

Meaning & effect

The white space between the stanzas is the poem's only transition. There is no "but" and no explanation, and across it everything changes. The mood moves from command and statement to question, the tense from timeless present to history, the tone from amused tenderness to anguish. The first stanza never said "language": it spoke of books, pages, paper and Sarasvati. Now the abstract word arrives alone on its line, as if called to the dock. The isolated phrase also hangs like a mind searching history for an answer. The emotional temperature changes with it: after eighteen lines of amused tenderness the voice turns to accusation, and the bareness of the line, two words and no image, is the first sign of the anger this stanza holds. In the anthology printing the whole second stanza is set further to the right, so the eye registers the shift before the mind does.

Line 20
has not been the oppressor's tongue?
Language & devices

Rhetorical question, with the implied answer "none". Present perfect has not been covers the whole of history up to now. Metonymy tongue for language turns the idea of a "mother tongue" upside down. The generic the oppressor names no nation, and the negative not makes the claim universal.

Meaning & effect

The question convicts every language: none has not served some oppressor. That includes English, and also Latin and Persian (Persian was the court language of the Mughals, kept by the East India Company until it was replaced in 1837). In honesty it also includes the speaker's own Gujarati and India's other languages. This is why the poem names no coloniser. Its occasion is British India, but its claim is universal, and reading it as an attack on Britain alone flattens it. Tongue makes language a part of the body, and that dead metaphor comes back to life in l.27, where the conqueror's tongue becomes a blade. The generality can be heard as even-handed (no language is innocent, so blame power rather than speech) or as bitter (no language is innocent, so every people's turn will come). Either way, the target has shifted from English to power.

Lines 21–22
Which language / truly meant to murder someone?
Language & devices

Anaphora and Parallelism repeat Which language, but this time there is no negative, and the verb is active: truly meant. A Pun on meant: intended, and signified. Diction murder, the strongest word so far. The singular someone.

Meaning & effect

The second question looks like a twin of the first but asks the opposite. A language cannot mean (intend) anything; only the people who use it can. So the implied answer, again "none", acquits language: the guilt belongs to the wielder, not the word. Together the two questions are the poem's core. Every language has been an oppressor's, and no language ever intended murder, which leaves power as the real defendant. Truly concedes the appearance (language has seemed murderous) while denying the essence. Someone brings the abstraction down to a single person: however large the empire, murder happens to individuals. The pun on meant asks a further question, whether a language's meaning can ever be separated from its history.

Line 23
And how does it happen
Language & devices

The third question. Conjunction And; the vague pronoun it; the present tense does it happen (something that recurs). This begins a seven-line Periodic sentence: the subject and verb of its that clause are held back until ll.28–29.

Meaning & effect

The first two questions were rhetorical, their answers implied; this one is genuine bewilderment. The opening And is conversational, even weary, as though the speaker has stopped expecting a neat answer and is thinking aloud. It is hard to name: the thing the whole poem has been circling, which the sentence will take seven lines to identify. The present tense makes this something that goes on happening, generation after generation, rather than a single event in the past. Because the subject and verb are delayed, the reader has to pass through the torture and the scythe before reaching the love, so the grammar enforces the order of history: there is no way to the grandchildren's love except through what was done to their grandparents. The question is not whether the conquest was wrong, which the stanza never doubts, but how love can come after it.

Line 24
that after the torture,
Language & devices

Definite article the torture treats it as known, shared history. An Abstract noun. Anaphora after… / after… begins. A comma pause.

Meaning & effect

The torture is the poem's first literal word for violence: no metaphor now, only the fact, and the plainness is itself a form of anger. The definite article treats it as something everyone knows about and nobody needs to explain, which is chilling, because the history is assumed rather than described. After begins a structure of time that layers the past beneath the present question, and its repetition in the next line makes the sequence feel like counting. The poem gives no details and refuses to turn suffering into spectacle; it trusts the single word to carry the weight. Set against the first stanza's careful scale, the word lands hard. A stanza that called it a sin to slam a book down now names torture with no moral comment at all, and the silence says more than a judgement would.

Line 25
after the soul has been cropped
Language & devices

Agentless passive has been cropped: the culprit disappears. Metaphor cropped, meaning harvested and cut short (the verb once also meant cutting off ears as a punishment). the soul is singular and collective. Present perfect.

Meaning & effect

The growing world of the first stanza returns as violence. The soul is treated as a crop, owned, cut and harvested for its yield, which is exactly what colonial extraction does to people. The passive hides who did it at the moment of greatest guilt. The same construction that was innocent in was made has become an evasion, as if history had no agents. Yet cropped also keeps something back: cropping cuts what is above ground and leaves the roots, which prepares for the regrowth of l.29. A reader who knows the Hindu idea of the ātman, the eternal self, will feel a further irony: what should be uncuttable has been cut.

Line 26
with a long scythe swooping out
Language & devices

Metaphor scythe: a harvesting tool, and also the emblem of the Grim Reaper and Father Time. Adjective long suggests both reach and duration. Verb swooping is what a bird of prey does. Sibilance in scythe and swooping, carried on from soul in l.25. Enjambment out / of.

Meaning & effect

The image moves from harvest to hunt. A scythe does not swoop; a predator does, so the reaping becomes an attack, and the conqueror is a bird of prey as well as a reaper. Long gives the blade reach, so the harm is done at a distance, without touching. This completes the litany's widening distances (the foot, the table, across a room), and long may also suggest a conquest lasting generations. The hissing sounds make the blade audible as it cuts the air. The line ends on out, and the reader has to wait across a line-break to learn where the blade comes from, so the enjambment performs the swing. The scythe also brings Death's own emblem into the poem: this conqueror does not only harvest, he ends lives.

Line 27
of the conqueror's face –
Language & devices

A grotesque, almost surreal image: the scythe comes out of a face, that is, out of the mouth, so the tongue of l.20 is made literal. A lexical escalation from oppressor to conqueror. The Dash, the only one in the poem.

Meaning & effect

Speech itself is the weapon. What comes out of a face is a tongue, and here it is a blade, so the dead metaphor of the oppressor's tongue revives as a murder weapon: the conqueror's language is pictured as his body's instrument of violence. Conqueror is stronger than oppressor: the language now belongs to someone who has won. Face is also the one moment when the agent hidden by has been cropped is glimpsed, though still only as a type, never a name. The image is nightmarish, so the violence is felt in the body rather than filed away as "cultural loss". The dash opens a gap: between the atrocity and its strange consequence, and between the generation that suffered it and the generation that will not remember it. It also works as a held breath before the hardest clause in the poem.

Line 28
the unborn grandchildren
Language & devices

Temporal leap with the Adjective unborn. grandchildren, not children: a generation is skipped. The definite article the.

Meaning & effect

The grandchildren had not yet been born when this happened, so their innocence is complete: their love cannot be called betrayal. The skipped generation matters. The children, who lived with the loss, are missing from the sentence, and by the grandchildren's time living memory has faded; two generations is the distance at which an imposed language stops feeling imposed and starts feeling native. The makes them a definite, known group, and readers may place Bhatt herself among them, born in 1956, nine years after independence, and writing in English. Unborn also tilts the sentence towards the future, as if more grandchildren were still to come: the pattern is not over. Both sides inherit something here. The colonised inherit a language, and the colonisers' descendants inherit the history that came with it, including this poem, written in their language.

Line 29
grow to love that strange language.
Language & devices

Verb grow is organic, gradual and unwilled, and completes the crop metaphor. love is the strongest possible verb. Deixis: the distant that answers Here (l.4). Adjective strange comes from Latin extraneus, "from outside", and means both foreign and wondrous. A full stop stands where the grammar expects a question mark. Liquid /l/ in love and language. The poem ends on language (its third use), on an unstressed syllable.

Meaning & effect

The sentence began as a question, how does it happen, and ends as a statement: the full stop hardens bewilderment into fact. The love happens whether or not it can be explained or justified. Grow completes the farming metaphor. What was cropped grows again, and love comes up in the cleared field, which is hopeful (life returns) and dark (the conqueror planted the seed). That holds the language at arm's length even inside love: India was Here, but English is still that. Strange carries both senses at once, foreign because it came from outside, and wondrous. The poem then becomes evidence for its own last line, since one of those grandchildren wrote it in that language, and this loops back to the title: the "different history" is the one in which the conquered take the language and make poems in it. It can be read as healing, the language now truly theirs, or as defeat, the conqueror's final victory being to be loved. The full stop declines to choose.

THE WHOLE POEM

The Whole Poem

Stepping back: what the poem is doing, first line to last

The poem is usually filed as anti-colonial protest, and its second panel earns the label: torture, murder, a scythe out of a conqueror's face. Read continuously from first line to last, though, it is something less comfortable and more valuable. It is an essay on transmission, on how the sacred and the violent are both taught and both inherited, written by a poet who is herself an example of its final image.

It opens by correcting Europe's most famous obituary. Great Pan is not dead flatly denies the sentence Plutarch's pilot was ordered to proclaim, which Christian tradition took as the pagan world's death-notice. Then the denial is deflated further: he simply emigrated. The joke has a blade in it, since what the West recorded as the death of the old gods was only their departure from the West. A "universal" history is exposed as local in ten words. The direction of travel matters too. Pan moves east as Bhatt's family moved west, a god's immigration mirroring the poet's emigration, but his journey is chosen and preserves him. Here, the gods roam freely: that comma'd Here is the emigrant's word, a pointing gesture of return performed from abroad (the poem was in print by early 1987, before Bhatt settled in Germany). The poem begins by demonstrating that where you stand determines what counts as dead.

The first panel then builds its ethnography of reverence. Divinity lives in despised creatures (disguised as snakes or monkeys quietly inverts Western contempt), every tree is sacred, and a litany of four sins scales holiness down to the hand: how a book is shoved, slammed, tossed, turned. Two things complicate the idyll, and both carry weight. First, the moral vocabulary is borrowed. Sin is Christianity's word, standing in for the Indian pāp, so the stanza describing uncolonised reverence is already conducted in the coloniser's vocabulary, and the second panel's problem is present in the first panel's diction. Second, reverence here is discipline: it is a sin… You must learn. The sacred world also polices, instructs and forbids. The poem needs this severity, because it is establishing that culture travels through teaching, which is exactly the channel conquest will use. It also needs the scale the litany builds. Four times the poem says sin about the mishandling of a book, so that the reader carries a precise moral measure across the stanza break.

The break is the hinge and the wound, and nothing announces the turn. The two questions that open panel two pull in opposite directions, and their grammar repays precise reading. Which language / has not been the oppressor's tongue? convicts every language, not English alone; the not universalises guilt. Which language / truly meant to murder someone? looks like its twin, but it contains no negative and its verb is active. Languages do not mean, in the sense of intend, anything; wielders do. One question finds every language historically guilty; the other finds language intrinsically innocent. Between conviction and acquittal, the true defendant is identified: power, not speech. This is why the poem names no coloniser and no language. Pan, India and Sarasvati are its only proper nouns. The occasion is British India, but the grammar is universal.

Then comes the long sentence that cannot be answered, in which panel one's pastoral returns as weaponry. The tongue of l.20 becomes a scythe swooping out / of the conqueror's face, speech literally the blade, and the soul is cropped: harvested, processed as yield, the metaphor colonial extraction deserves. Two silences make the passage worse than its images. The moral word is gone, since the poem that called a shoved book a sin uses no such word for the torture. And the agent is gone, since the soul has been cropped by no one. That passive voice was innocent when the paper was made; here it is the grammar of an empire that never signs its work. The reader, trained by the first stanza to name every offence, is left holding a crime without a criminal.

But cropped also seeds the ending, because what is cut regrows: the unborn grandchildren / grow to love that strange language. Growth is the crop's own word. The grandchildren are the next planting in cleared ground, and their love is real: a gnomic present tense, recurring in every generation, the poet's included. They are grandchildren, not children. The generation that lived the loss has dropped out of the sentence, and with it the memory. The final deixis answers the first: India was Here; English is still that strange language, loved at arm's length, intimate and foreign in one phrase. And the sentence that grammar wants as a question ends with a full stop, bewilderment hardened into fact.
