The strongest objection comes from two sides at once. A reader in Ngũgĩ wa Thiong'o's camp will say the ending is capitulation: to "grow to love" the language of the people who tortured your grandparents is the conquest's last and most complete victory, and a poem that reports it without protest has surrendered. A reader from the other direction will say the even-handed question (Which language / has not been…?) lets the British off: if every language is guilty, no one is. Both objections mistake what the poem is doing. It does not excuse the conqueror. It gives him a scythe and a face, its nouns (murder, torture) are angry ones, and it makes his absence from the grammar conspicuous, an accusation by omission that the reader is trained to notice. Nor does it celebrate the love. It surrounds it with after the torture and after the soul has been cropped, calls the language strange, and withholds the question mark that would let us feel the matter was still open to argument. What the poem refuses is the comfort of a single verdict. It holds anger at the history and attachment to the language in the same breath, because that is how the grandchildren actually live.

That is also where the title finally lands. "A Different History" promised a counter-narrative, but the pattern the poem uncovers is the oldest there is: every language has been an oppressor's. What is different is the ending, and the ending is the poem itself. Bhatt writes in the strange language, gently, about a goddess who must not be disturbed, and so does the thing she cannot explain. The poem neither forgives the history nor disowns the love. It closes as a grandchild's act of love performed in the conqueror's tongue, which is evidence for its own last line and the most honest answer it could give to its own question.

FORM & STRUCTURE

Form & Structure

How the poem is built, and why it matters

Form & genre

A free-verse lyric argument in two verse-paragraphs of 18 and 11 lines. In its first printing (PN Review, 1987) and on the Poetry Archive the second part is headed "2"; the anthology prints it as two stanzas. It works as a diptych: two linked panels, blessing and violence, set side by side.

Metre & rhyme

No regular metre and no rhyme scheme, but the stresses are carefully managed. It opens with heavy monosyllables; l.15 comes close to an iambic pentameter; and the last line ends on an unstressed syllable. There are local chimes (learn / turn, book / foot) but no pattern.

Layout

In the anthology printing ll.3, 10, 12 and 14 are indented, l.10 most deeply, and the whole second stanza is set as a block further to the right. Every line begins in lower case unless a new sentence begins.

Syntax

Stanza 1 has four sentences: myth (ll.1–3), law (ll.4–8), a litany of sins (ll.9–14) and an instruction (ll.15–18). Stanza 2 has three questions: two short and parallel, then a seven-line periodic sentence that ends with a full stop.

Punctuation

Semicolons at ll.1 and 5. Question marks only at ll.20 and 22. One dash, at l.27. A full stop at l.29 where the grammar expects a question mark.

Voice & address

There is no "I": the voice is a teacher's, then a questioner's. you is addressed at ll.10 and 15. Two pointing words frame the poem: Here (l.4) and that (l.29).

A diptych of unequal panels

The poem is built from two free-verse panels, eighteen lines and then eleven, and the proportions are an argument. The sacred world is given expansive, unhurried space: a whole panel to establish what reverence looks like, down to the fingertips. The violence arrives late and compressed, takes up far less room, and yet overturns everything. The white space between the panels is the poem's only transition. There is no conjunction, no "but", no announcement, yet once it is crossed the pronouns, tense and mood have all changed. The gap is a border, an incision and a historical rupture at once. The unwritten middle of the poem is colonisation itself, which happens, as it were, between the stanzas.

The panels are also quietly symmetrical. The first traces a chain of material transformation upwards into holiness: tree, wood, paper, pages, book, each stage inheriting sanctity from the last. The second traces a chain downwards into harvest: tongue, scythe, cropped soul. One panel consecrates matter; the other processes souls as if they were matter. That mirroring is why the diptych holds together despite its tonal break. The critic Minnie Singh notes that Bhatt's method "moves swiftly from the discursive to the imagistic", and the second panel shows it in miniature: two abstract questions harden into the poem's most violent image.

Stanza against stanza

Read side by side, the two panels use the same tools for opposite purposes.

Stanza 1 (ll.1–18) Stanza 2 (ll.19–29)
Anaphora a sin… / without…: rules, certainty Which language… / after…: questions, doubt
Violence shove, slam, toss: done to books murder, torture, cropped: done to souls
Agent your foot: active verbs, a named offender has been cropped: passive, the culprit vanishes
Moral word sin four times, for mishandling a book no sin at all, even for torture
Learning must learn: chosen, taught grow to love: unchosen, absorbed
Sound plosive blows give way to soft fricatives: order restored a sibilant blade, and no calm after it
Deixis and length Here (near), eighteen lines that (far), eleven lines that undo the eighteen

Metre: scansion

The poem keeps no metrical contract, but its stresses are deployed with care. In the table, bold marks a stressed syllable.

Line Scansion What the rhythm does
l.1 Great Pan is not dead; Four heavy stresses in five monosyllables: a tolling, spondaic opening that sounds like the death-sentence it quotes. The semicolon then refuses the toll a full close.
l.2 he sim-ply em-i-grat-ed Two beats, then a run of light syllables: the grand death deflates into the shrug of an administrative word.
l.6 ev-ery tree is sa-cred A falling, trochaic rhythm, chant-like: the first panel's creed in miniature.
l.8 to be rude to a book. Two light, skipping anapaests: a nursery rhythm under the theological sin, bathos carried in the metre.
l.15 you must learn how to turn the pa-ges gent-ly Eleven syllables, five beats, a feminine ending: the nearest the poem comes to iambic pentameter, English verse's home metre, at the moment an Indian lesson in reverence is taught.
l.19 Which lan-guage Two stresses and a fall: a two-word blow, then silence.
l.25 af-ter the soul has been cropped Two falling triple rhythms land on the stressed monosyllable: swing, swing, cut.
l.26 with a long scythe swoop-ing out A light run-up jams into three consecutive stresses: the weight of the blade at the top of its arc.
l.29 grow to love that strange lan-guage. Heavy monosyllables, then a final falling trochee: the poem ends on an unstressed syllable, a dying fall exactly where a question would rise.

The two longest lines in the poem, l.9 (ten syllables) and l.15 (eleven), are both about handling books. The verse expands where care, or the violation of care, is greatest.

Rhyme and chime

There is no scheme, but there are structured chimes, worth naming precisely:

  • learn / turn (l.15): a full internal rhyme that makes the instruction memorable, like a proverb.
  • book / foot (ll.9–10): assonance on the same short vowel, binding the sacred object to the offending limb across the line-break. The chime commits the sin the sentence forbids.
  • tongue / someone (ll.20, 22): a faint chime on the same vowel, yoking the two questions together.
  • freely, tree, gently, Sarasvati: a thread of bright "ee" sounds through the first panel's moments of grace.

The volta

The stanza break is a turn, but not the sonnet's kind, where an argument turns inside continuous discourse. This is a cut. The subject continues (books, language, reverence), but the mood flips from declarative and imperative to interrogative. The tense flips from timeless present (is, roam) to historical perfect (has been cropped). The tone flips from amused tenderness to anguish. It is a turn of mode hidden inside a continuity of subject, which is the argument in structural form: the language cradled in panel one is the weapon of panel two. A second, smaller turn comes at l.23 (And how does it happen). There the paired, almost forensic questions deepen into genuine bewilderment, and the final seven lines become one long suspended sentence.

Syntax and punctuation

Panel one moves from declarative assertion (ll.1–6) into litany (a sin four times, ll.7, 9, 11 and 13, a grammar of commandment), and closes in a double without… construction hanging from an imperative (You must learn). The sacred world's syntax is the syntax of instruction. Its four sentences also tell a story in order: a myth corrected, a law stated, sins listed, a skill taught.

Panel two is three questions with a withheld third question mark. The first two are short, parallel and complete. Each isolates Which language on its own line, putting language itself in the dock, before the predicate arrives. The third (ll.23–29) is a long periodic sentence: And how does it happen / that…, then two after… clauses, the scythe image running up to the dash, and only then the delayed subject and verb of the that clause, the unborn grandchildren / grow to love that strange language. The grammar demands a question mark; the poem prints a full stop. This has three effects. The question has hardened into fact: the loving happens whether or not it can be explained. After two properly punctuated questions, the withheld mark enacts the exhaustion of asking, as if history had outrun the interrogative. And the flat stop refuses both protest and absolution, declining to tell the reader how to feel.

The dash at l.27 is the poem's second hinge in miniature. It separates the atrocity from its strange consequence, a visual gap between torture and love that mirrors the stanza break's gap between reverence and torture.

Lineation, indentation, enjambment

In the anthology the four indented lines (3, 10, 12, 14) hang like stepped ledges. to India. gives the destination its own shelf. That is arrival honoured with white space, and also a physical image of marginality, which nonetheless makes India the focal point. The three indented completions of the litany, with your foot,, hard on a table, and across a room., isolate instrument, impact and trajectory, one ledge for each offence. with your foot, is pushed furthest from the margin: the book shoved aside on the page itself. The second stanza is printed as a block set further right, so the eye registers the shift before the mind does. (That offset may be the typesetter's rather than the poet's, but it is how the poem is read on the page in front of you.)

Enjambment does local work. he simply emigrated / to India. crosses its own border in the line-break. a sin to shove a book aside / with your foot shoves the end of the thought down and aside. and it is a sin / to be rude to a book. delays the object, so the solemn word sin dangles over what turns out to be an almost comic offence; the line-break engineers the bathos. In panel two the enjambment accelerates and stretches: cropped / with a long scythe swooping out / of the conqueror's face – keeps cutting through three line-endings, the blade emerging in the gap between out and of.

Person, tense and deixis

The poem's pronouns trace its history: he (Pan), then the gods, then you (the child being taught, and the reader), then the oppressor, someone, the conqueror, and finally the unborn grandchildren. The you who must learn to turn pages in panel one is implicitly the same person as the grandchild who grows to love English in panel two. Both are being formed by teaching. grow is a gnomic present, neither past nor future: this keeps happening, generation after generation, the poet's own included.

Two pointing words hold the structure together. Here (l.4) is near: the speaker stands inside India. that (l.29) is far: the language is loved but held at arm's length. The poem moves from the deixis of belonging to the deixis of distance, and the space between those two words is the history the title promises.

SOUND

Sound

What the poem does to the ear

Sibilance

It runs through holiness and offence alike: snakes, sacred, Sarasvati, but also sin, shove, slam. In the second stanza it becomes the swish of the blade: soul, scythe, swooping.

Plosives

Stopped consonants (/b/, /d/, /t/, /k/) score the abuse of books: book, foot, books down, hard on a table.

Fricatives & nasals

The consecration in ll.15–18 goes soft: without, disturbing, Sarasvati, and the /w/ of wood… was in the stanza's last line.

Cadence

Stanza 1 ends on a stressed, settled word, made. The poem ends on the unstressed second syllable of language, a fall with no click of closure.

The first panel builds a soundscape in which the sacred and the transgressive share one hiss. Sibilance carries holiness: disguised as snakes, every tree is sacred, Sarasvati. The identical sound carries offence: a sin to slam, shove a book aside, toss one carelessly. The ear learns early what the argument will state late. Sanctity and violation are made of the same material, just as love and oppression will turn out to be made of the same language. That is also why the snake-hiss reading of disguised as snakes should not be pushed too far: the same /s/ runs through sacred, so the sound marks a family of ideas rather than imitating one animal.

Against the hiss, the abuse of books is scored for percussion. It is a sin to shove a book aside / with your foot, / a sin to slam books down / hard on a table knocks with stopped consonants, book, foot, down, hard, table, striking like the impacts described, while book and foot thud on the same short, dull vowel. The triad shove, slam, toss is a scale of curt monosyllables. Each verb is lighter in force than the last, from contemptuous push to careless throw, force giving way to indifference, which the poem treats as worst. The nasals that hum through the litany (sin, slam, down, one, room) keep the chant insistent rather than angry.

Then the consecration goes soft. In You must learn how to turn the pages gently / without disturbing Sarasvati, / without offending the tree / from whose wood the paper was made, fricatives and nasals (w, th, s, v, n) replace the plosives, and the bright vowels of gently, tree and Sarasvati open the line out. The last line's /w/ alliteration (wood… was, with whose joining it only to the eye, since it is sounded /h/), set in slow rounded vowels, lowers the stanza to a near-whisper before its full stop. The panel ends on made: a made thing, at rest.

The second panel opens with bare interrogation. Which language, twice, sets the tight affricate of which against the swallowed /ŋgw/ of language, with no verb to soften either, and oppressor's spits a plosive /p/ into a cluster of hissing sounds. Torture strikes the hard /t/ twice. The scythe passage is the poem's most concentrated sound-effect: after the soul has been cropped / with a long scythe swooping out. The sibilants (soul, scythe, swooping, then face) make the swish of a blade through air. The long vowels of long scythe swooping stretch the backswing. And cropped is shut off by its own stopped ending, /pt/, so the word is cut short as the soul is. This is a rare case of sound doing argumentative work: it insists the violence is physical, bodily and audible, not an abstraction called "cultural loss".

The final line slows into liquids and long vowels: grow to love that strange language. The /l/ of love returns in language, binding the feeling to its object, and the line ends on the unstressed second syllable of language. It is a dying fall with no click of closure, the audible equivalent of the missing question mark. The poem does not end; it exhales.

MOTIFS & SYMBOLS

Motifs & Symbols

Images that recur, and what they accumulate

A motif is a recurring element; a symbol is an element that stands for something beyond itself. In this poem the motifs accumulate into its symbols.

Motifs

The religious register

sacred, sin (four times), gods, and the devotional-social verbs disturbing and offending. The recurrence builds panel one's litany-like texture. It also carries the poem's deepest irony: sin is the English word of Christian theology, standing in for the Indian concept of pāp. The stanza describing uncolonised reverence is already conducted in translation, so the problem of stanza two is present in the diction of stanza one. And the register stops dead at the break. Stanza two has no sin, no sacred, no gods, only murder and torture: the language of reverence has nothing to say about atrocity.

The material chain of the book

Tree, wood, paper, pages, book. It recurs and closes a loop: every tree is sacred (l.6) returns as the tree / from whose wood the paper was made (ll.17–18). Reverence is not mystical but material, traceable through manufacture, and the book is holy because its origin is.

Growth and harvest

every tree is sacred, then cropped, a long scythe, and finally grow. The vocabulary of plants runs through both panels and changes function. In the first it is literal and sacred; in the second it is a metaphor for what is done to people. Farming words make violence sound natural, like the seasons, until the torture breaks the spell. Then they make love sound natural too, since the grandchildren grow as a crop regrows. Pan, a shepherds' god, brings the pastoral with him, and the poem shows what happens to pastoral under conquest.

Motion and migration

emigrated, roam freely, shove… aside, toss… across, swooping out, grow. Everything in the poem moves or is moved. Sacred motion is self-directed: roaming, emigrating, turning pages. Violent motion is done to things: shoved, slammed, tossed, cropped. The grammar of motion is the poem's moral grammar.

Teaching and learning

You must learn is answered by grow to love. Instruction recurs as the channel through which both reverence and conquest pass themselves on. What is taught with the hands in panel one is absorbed with the soul in panel two.

Interrogation

Which language… Which language… And how does it happen: asking escalates from forensic to anguished and finally collapses into the non-question that ends with a full stop.

Symbols

Pan

Pan stands for the supposedly dead older world, pre-Christian Europe and by extension everything "official" history declares finished, surviving by relocation. He is also a quiet double of the poet: one emigrant crossing eastward as she crossed west.

Snakes and monkeys

The gods' animal forms put holiness exactly where the West tends to put fear or ridicule. Together with the tree, the book of knowledge and sin, they rebuild the Eden story with its values reversed. In Genesis the serpent tempts and the sin is to take from the tree of knowledge; here the snake is divine and the sin is to disrespect the tree and the book.

Sarasvati

She stands for language and knowledge as a living presence rather than a commodity. The book-reverence around her is not a metaphor but lived practice. In many Hindu households books and paper must not be touched with the foot, and someone who does so by accident touches the object and then their forehead or eyes in apology. At her festival, books are placed before the goddess, and Bhatt's own note on the poem points out that in India she is often worshipped in libraries. The litany describes etiquette children are actually taught, which is why its tone is domestic (rude) as much as theological (sin). Because she is the goddess of speech, naming her is the first sign that the poem's real subject is language.

The book

The book is the vessel of culture, and the one object in the poem that can be sinned against. It is also the hinge between the panels: a cherished object in one, and in the other the instrument of the oppressor's tongue.

The scythe

The scythe is language turned into a weapon. It carries the death-shadow of the Grim Reaper and Father Time, but its precise horror is agricultural, because a scythe harvests. That makes the crop the poem's darkest symbol. the soul has been cropped treats souls as yield and colonialism as an extraction industry. The ending completes the metaphor rather than abandoning it: the grandchildren grow to love, new growth in cleared ground. Love is what comes up after harvest, and the tenderness of the last line is planted in the field the scythe made.

The tongue and the face

These are metonyms for language and identity which the poem makes literal again. "The oppressor's tongue" is a dead idiom (as in "mother tongue") until ll.26–27 revive it: the scythe comes swooping out / of the conqueror's face, out of the mouth. Speech itself is the blade.

THEMES

Themes

The ideas the poem is arguing about

01

Language: Vessel and Weapon

The poem treats language in two ways at once. In the first stanza it is a vessel: the book holds knowledge, Sarasvati, the goddess of speech, lives in its pages, and the reader must learn how to turn the pages gently. In the second stanza it is a weapon: the oppressor's tongue becomes a long scythe swooping out / of the conqueror's face, speech issuing from the mouth as a blade. The poem's argument is that these are one thing in different hands. Which language / truly meant to murder someone? makes language a tool without intentions, so the guilt belongs to whoever swings it. Yet a tool is never quite neutral. A language also carries the values of the people who imposed it, which is why the grandchildren's love is both natural (people love the language they grow up in) and disturbing (the language they grew up in arrived by conquest).

The poem stakes its own medium on the question. It is written in English by a poet who calls Gujarati "the deepest layer of my identity" yet learned English at five, and it uses the conqueror's tongue gently, to honour a goddess and to question the conquest. The poem is itself a demonstration that a weapon can change hands. It does not pretend the change is clean, though: the last line still calls English that strange language.

02

The Sacred, Taught and Broken

The first stanza builds a complete theology of everyday reverence. The gods live in animals (disguised as snakes or monkeys), every tree is sacred, and the book inherits the tree's holiness through the chain of wood and paper. Its sins are tiny gestures: shoving a book with your foot, slamming books hard on a table, tossing one carelessly / across a room. Sacredness here is not a feeling but a practice, and practices must be taught: You must learn. That makes it fragile. A reverence that lives in gestures passed from adult to child can be broken simply by breaking the teaching.

The second stanza shows that break. The poem's moral vocabulary is placed with care. Sin is used four times about mishandling a book and never about the torture or the soul cropped, so when real atrocity arrives the stanza's moral word falls silent. The reader measures the violence against the scale the first stanza built: if it is a sin to be rude to a book, what is it to crop a soul? And the word sacred never returns.

03

Power Without a Name

The poem never names a coloniser, a country or a language. Its only proper nouns are Pan, India and Sarasvati. Power appears as generic types, the oppressor and the conqueror, and at the moment of greatest guilt it vanishes into the passive voice: the soul has been cropped, by no one. The same grammar was innocent in the paper was made; now it hides an agent. This namelessness is part of the argument. Which language / has not been the oppressor's tongue? indicts every language that has served an empire, from Latin to Persian to English, so the subject is how power works rather than one nation's crimes.

The violence is also distant and growing more impersonal. Through the litany the book moves from contact (with your foot) to impact (on a table) to distance (across a room), and the climax is a long scythe, a weapon that reaches from far off and cuts without touching. Against all this abstraction the poem sets one small word: murder is done to someone. Power is general; harm is always particular. None of this makes the stanza cool. Its anger is in its nouns, murder, torture, conqueror, and in the image of a face from which a blade swings. What the poem withholds is not anger but a single, named target.

04

Inheritance and the Skipped Generation

The poem is full of handing down. The first stanza is a lesson, a voice teaching a child how to handle books, and the second ends with heirs: the unborn grandchildren. The word is exact. It is not the children, who lived with the loss and are missing from the sentence, but the grandchildren, born after it, for whom the language is simply home. They inherit innocently. They were unborn when the torture happened, so their love cannot be called betrayal. And they grow to love, an organic and unchosen verb that sets their inheritance against the deliberate one of must learn.

Both sides inherit. The colonised inherit a language; the colonisers' descendants inherit a history, including this poem, which is addressed in English to readers on both sides. The ending's uncertainty is about what has been inherited along with the language: is the past remembered (as Bhatt remembers it, in the first stanza's details), or erased by the very fluency the grandchildren have gained?

05

Migration: Chosen and Imposed

Two movements frame the poem. Pan simply emigrated / to India. He moved by choice, and the move preserves him: the god Europe declared dead survives Here. English moved too, but by conquest, and its arrival replaces: it cropped a soul to make room. One migration keeps a culture alive across a border; the other overwrites the culture it arrives in. Bhatt's own life runs through the middle. She was born in Ahmedabad, moved to the United States at twelve and settled in Germany, a migrant who carries Gujarati with her and writes in English.

The poem's deixis maps these journeys. Here (l.4) plants the speaker in India, although the poem was written abroad, and that strange language (l.29) holds English at a distance even while it is loved. Between those two pointing words lies the whole poem: a culture seen from inside, and a language seen from just outside.

06

Love Without Absolution

The poem's most daring claim is that love can grow out of violence without excusing it. Grow to love is the strongest verb in the poem, and Bhatt does not undercut it with irony. The love is real. But the sentence that delivers it is built on after the torture and after the soul has been cropped, so the love is permanently aftermath. Strange keeps both readings alive, a language foreign and marvellous at once, and the missing question mark keeps the bewilderment alive: the sentence that began how does it happen ends as a flat statement that it does.

The poem neither forgives the history nor disowns the love. It offers no reconciliation and no denunciation, only the fact. This is what makes it disturbing and honest rather than a slogan: anger at the conquest and attachment to its language can live in the same person, and in this case in the same poem.

DIFFICULT MOMENTS

Difficult Moments

Where the poem is genuinely undecidable — and what to do about it

Cruxes

Five places where the poem will not settle. In each, the meaning lives in the unsettledness, so the evidence for both sides matters as much as the verdict.

1. Do the two questions convict language or acquit it?

The difficulty. Which language / truly meant to murder someone? arrives as the visual twin of Which language / has not been the oppressor's tongue?: the same opening, the same two-word line. The parallel tempts the reader to carry the first question's not into the second. But the negative is not there, and the verb is active: as printed, the question asks which language ever truly intended murder. These two questions open the second stanza and carry its argument, so how they are read decides what the whole poem says.

Competing readings. Acquittal, supported by the words on the page: languages do not mean (intend) anything; intention lives in their users, and the implied answer is "none". Truly concedes the appearance while denying the essence: language has seemed murderous, has been the oppressor's tongue, but never truly meant it. Indictment by momentum, supported by the parallelism and the stanza's torture: readers complete the pattern as "which language has not truly meant to murder", making every language a murder weapon. The grammar forbids this; the design invites it. Intention moved: meant to murder heard as "was meant to murder", the purpose of those who imposed it. Strictly that is not what the sentence says, but it is where the poem's argument goes, since it relocates intention to the hand that swings the scythe.

What a strong answer does. Notices that both questions have the same one-word answer, "none", and that it delivers opposite verdicts: no language has escaped serving an oppressor (universal guilt); no language ever meant to kill (universal innocence). Between them the real defendant appears: power, not speech. The trap is part of the meaning, because a reader who blames English for what was done in English has made exactly the confusion the poem examines. And someone, singular, insists that whatever the verdict on language, the victim is a person, not a population.

2. Whose crime? The unnamed conqueror

The difficulty. The poem's occasion is plainly British India, and the language the grandchildren love is plainly English. Yet the poem names no Britain, no England and no English. Its only proper nouns are Pan, India and Sarasvati, and its agents are types: the oppressor, the conqueror. Is it an attack on British rule, or a reflection on conquest anywhere?

Competing readings. A specific indictment: the stanza is angry (murder, torture, a blade swooping out / of the conqueror's face), and the history behind the torture is the Raj's. Leaving the conqueror unnamed can even be read as contempt: he is not given the dignity of a name. A universal claim: the first question says every language has served an oppressor, which takes in Latin, Persian (the Mughal court language the East India Company kept until 1837) and India's own languages, so the subject is power working through language, and the refusal to name a nation is the point. A strategy: the abstraction lets a particular history be told so that it cannot be waved away as one people's grievance.

What a strong answer does. Holds the anger and the universality together: the stanza's nouns are furious, its grammar even-handed. It treats the namelessness as evidence rather than omission. It notices that the agentless passive has been cropped hides the culprit exactly where the guilt is greatest, and that the face lets him be glimpsed, for one line, as a body without a name.

3. Stanza 1's reverence: ideal or constraint?

The difficulty. Is the first panel a loving portrait of a sacred culture, or does its litany of prohibitions carry its own severity? And if both, how do they fit together?

Competing readings. An ideal: the tenderness of gently, the warmth of roam freely, and a coherent material theology (tree, wood, paper, book) in which respect is logical, not superstitious. The practice is real and lovingly rendered. A constraint: sin four times, must, a code that polices gestures as small as how a page is turned. The accumulating rules can feel like surveillance of daily life, and a poet who left India at twelve writes this Here from a distance that allows ambivalence.

What a strong answer does. Finds the job the severity does. The first panel shows that culture passes itself on through teaching (You must learn), and the second shows conquest using the same channel, imposition ripening into grow to love. Reverence and constraint are one process seen before and after: discipline is how both the sacred and the colonial get into a child. The discipline is also voiced in the borrowed word sin, so the "pure" tradition the ideal-reading wants, and the native orthodoxy the constraint-reading wants, both reach us already in translation.

4. The ending: bitter, resigned or reconciled?

The difficulty. the unborn grandchildren / grow to love that strange language. can be heard in at least three tones, and the final punctuation withholds the usual cue. Tone decides what the poem finally means, and it is bound up with the title.

Competing readings. Bitter: love is the last clause of a sentence governed by after the torture, affection as the conquest's deepest victory, the coloniser winning the heart last; that strange keeps a cold distance even as love is asserted. Resigned: grow states a recurring law, not a choice; And how does it happen has the flatness of someone no longer expecting an answer; the full stop files the mystery as fact. Reconciled: love stands without irony; grow is organic and unforced, the opposite of imposition; and the poem's own English, supple, tender and exact, is the love it describes, made audible.

What a strong answer does. Treats the missing question mark as evidence that the ambivalence is designed: after two correctly punctuated questions, the poem visibly declines to grade its own feeling. It links the ending back to the title. The different history turns out to be this one, in which the conquered love the conqueror's tongue and write poems in it. And it finds the word built to hold all three tones, strange, foreign and wonderful at once, so that the ending is less a tone than a suspension.

5. "That strange language": whose word is "strange"?

The difficulty. Every word of the final phrase is contested: the distancing that, the double-valued strange, and whose point of view the phrase carries.

Competing readings. Merely foreign: strange as plain description of a language from elsewhere (Latin extraneus, "from outside"). Estranged: the history has made the language uncanny. It might have been merely foreign, but the torture made it strange, and that holds the acquired thing at arm's length even inside love. Wonderful: the older sense of "strange" as marvellous, love's own word for what it cannot fully possess.

What a strong answer does. Maps the poem's pointing words (India is Here, l.4; English is that, l.29) and then asks the sharper question. To the grandchildren the language is not strange at all; it is the one they grew up in. Strange must therefore be the ancestors' word, or the speaker's, surviving inside a sentence about the grandchildren's love, so two generations' viewpoints share one phrase. That is an argument rather than a fact about the text, but it best explains how a language can be loved and called strange in the same breath.

CLOSE ANALYSIS

Close Analysis

The moments that repay pressure, worked through

Close analysis

1. A Different History (title)

Techniques: indefinite article; a comparison withheld; etymology (Greek historia, "inquiry"); the loop between title and ending.

A makes this one history among several, not the history Europe wrote, and Different withholds its comparison, so the reader supplies the version already held: the European story in which Pan dies, or the imperial one in which English brings light. The first line contradicts it at once. Historia means "inquiry", which suits a poem whose second half is three questions. But the title also sets a trap. The pattern the poem uncovers is not different at all: Which language / has not been the oppressor's tongue? makes conquest through language the oldest story there is. What is different is the ending, the conquered coming to love what conquered them, and the poem itself, written in that language by one of those grandchildren.

Intention and effect: Bhatt promises a counter-history and delivers a stranger one, so that only at the last line does the reader learn which history the title meant.

2. Great Pan is not dead; / he simply emigrated / to India. (ll.1–3)

Techniques: allusion; negation; bathos; semicolon caesura; enjambment and indentation.

The opening takes Europe's obituary for its own pagan world, the cry that Great Pan was dead, told by Plutarch and read by Christian writers as the old gods' death at Christ's coming, and refuses it in five heavy monosyllables. Simply emigrated then deflates apocalypse into paperwork: the death of a world-order becomes a change of address, and the bathos is aimed at Europe's habit of mistaking its local endings for universal ones. The enjambment makes the reader cross the border the sentence describes, and the indented to India. gives the destination its own ledge of white space, marginal on the page and central to the poem. There is a quiet self-portrait too. The god travels east as the poet's family travelled west, two carriers of culture crossing in opposite directions.

Intention and effect: Bhatt opens with amused, unarguable authority, so the reader trusts a voice that will shortly turn and ask questions it cannot answer.

3. Here, the gods roam freely, / disguised as snakes or monkeys; (ll.4–5)

Techniques: deixis; singular to plural; connotation reversed; diction (disguised).

Here, set off by its comma, is the emigrant's word: a poet writing from the United States plants herself on Indian ground, and the word will be answered at the end by the distant that. The plural gods widens Pan's welcome into a theology of divinity at large in the living world rather than housed in institutions, and freely sharpens once the oppressor arrives, since freedom is what conquest ends. Disguised puts holiness in creatures the West fears or mocks, the serpent of Eden and the monkey of colonial caricature, so the line reverses a hierarchy. It is also an outsider's word. In Hindu thought an animal form is a form of the god, not a costume, so the speaker is already translating her world for someone else.

Intention and effect: the divine is presented as an ordinary fact of the street, so that its later cropping feels like sacrilege, not only cruelty.

4. every tree is sacred / and it is a sin / to be rude to a book. (ll.6–8)

Techniques: absolute (every); line-break suspense; register clash; personification; the start of the anaphora.

Every makes the first law universal and starts the chain that will end in the book: tree, wood, paper. The solemn noun sin then dangles at the line-end before landing on the nursery word rude, and the swerve is the point. What looks like quaint etiquette is a complete ethic, in which respect is owed to the things your hands touch, and the Western smile it invites is the reflex the poem examines. The deeper irony is lexical: sin is Christianity's word, drafted in to translate an Indian idea, so the coloniser's vocabulary is already inside the poem's most Indian sentence. Measured against history, with Macaulay in 1835 calling the local languages "poor and rude" and dismissing "the whole native literature of India and Arabia", the line also asks who was really rude to books.

Intention and effect: the reader is handed a moral scale, sin for a mishandled book, which the second stanza makes devastating by never using it.

5. shove, slam, toss one carelessly (ll.9–14)

Techniques: anaphora; a tricolon of verbs; indented completions; plosives; second-person accusation.

The rule is repeated as rules are to children, and each repetition sheds words, It is a sin shrinking to a sin, so the chant speeds up. The verbs make a scale: shove is contempt, slam aggression, toss… carelessly indifference, the lightest act and the worst attitude, because the real sin is the absence of care. The indented completions isolate instrument, impact and trajectory on separate ledges, and with your foot is pushed furthest out, the book shoved aside on the page itself. The stopped consonants of books down and hard on a table land like blows. And the distances grow: foot against book, book flung on a table, book thrown across a room. The second stanza completes the series with a long scythe that harms without touching.

Intention and effect: comedy and accusation at once (your foot): gesture by gesture, the reader learns the scale on which the coming violence will be weighed.

6. You must learn how to turn the pages gently / without disturbing Sarasvati, (ll.15–16)

Techniques: modal of obligation and direct address; near-pentameter; internal rhyme; anaphora (without… without); allusion.

The gentlest lines in the poem are also commands. Must turns tenderness into obligation: reverence is not a mood but a discipline passed on by teaching, the same channel through which, a stanza later, a conquering language is absorbed. Learn / turn gives the lesson the memorability of a proverb, and the line's eleven syllables fall into the shape of an iambic pentameter with a feminine ending, English poetry's home metre carrying an Indian lesson. Gently sits at the line's edge as if handled with care. And the goddess is not figurative: Sarasvati, goddess of knowledge and speech, is understood to dwell in books, which is why a book touched with the foot is apologised to. She is the only Indian deity the poem names, and her name tells us that its real subject is language.

Intention and effect: the reader becomes the addressed child, You, raised for two lines inside the tradition, and cannot afterwards look at it wholly from outside.

7. without offending the tree / from whose wood the paper was made. (ll.17–18)

Techniques: anaphora; personification; the material chain reversed; passive voice; soft /w/ and long vowels.

The chain of holiness now runs backwards, goddess in the book, tree in the paper, so the stanza ends where it began, with every tree is sacred. Whose, a pronoun normally kept for people, gives the tree personhood, and offending sounds comic until the reader sees that every page has a living source and a cost. This is an ethic of use, not of avoidance: the tree has already become paper, and the sin would be to forget it. The passive was made names no maker, harmlessly here; the same grammar returns in has been cropped, where the hidden agent is no longer innocent. The soft /w/ of wood… was and the long vowels lower the stanza to a near-whisper.

Intention and effect: the first panel closes at rest on a made thing, a world the reader has been taught to value just before the stanza break takes it away.

8. Which language / has not been the oppressor's tongue? (ll.19–20)

Techniques: volta at the stanza break; isolated two-word line; rhetorical question; present perfect; metonymy.

Nothing announces the turn. Across the white space the mood changes from instruction to interrogation, the tense from timeless present to history, the tone from tenderness to accusation. Language, never said in the first stanza, arrives alone on its line as if called to the dock. The question convicts every language: the implied answer is "none", and has not been gathers the whole of history into one tense. That includes English, but also Latin, Persian and India's own languages, which is why no coloniser is named. Tongue is a dead metaphor for language that also overturns "mother tongue", and the poem will bring it violently back to life in the scythe swinging from a face.

Intention and effect: the reader's comfort is broken without a single image; the plainness of the question is the first sound of the stanza's anger.

9. Which language / truly meant to murder someone? (ll.21–22)

Techniques: anaphora and parallelism; rhetorical question; pun on meant; personification withdrawn; singular diction.

The line-break isolates Which language a second time, but this question is not the first one repeated, and misreading it flattens the poem. There is no not, and the verb is active: the question asks whether any language ever intended murder. The implied answer, none, acquits the very thing the previous question convicted, because intention belongs to those who wield a language, not to the language. Guilt slides off the tongue and onto the hand of power that holds it. Meant also asks what a language means, and whether its meaning can ever be separated from its history. Someone, singular, refuses the anaesthetic of scale: murder happens to one person at a time.

Intention and effect: Bhatt builds the parallel so that the reader enacts the confusion the poem is about, blaming the language and then catching themselves, which prepares the ending's refusal to condemn English.

10. And how does it happen / that after the torture, (ll.23–24)

Techniques: conversational And; a genuine question; definite article; anaphora (after… after); periodic sentence.

After two rhetorical questions comes a real one, and its opening And is weary, as if the speaker no longer expects a neat answer. It is hard to name: the thing the poem has been circling, which the sentence takes seven lines to reach. The torture is the poem's first literal word for violence, no metaphor now, and the definite article treats it as known history that needs no explanation, which is more chilling than description would be. Because the subject and verb of the that clause are held back to the last two lines, the reader has to pass through the torture and the scythe before reaching the love.

Intention and effect: the grammar enforces the order of history: there is no way to the grandchildren's love except through what was done to their grandparents.

11. after the soul has been cropped / with a long scythe swooping out / of the conqueror's face – (ll.25–27)

Techniques: agricultural metaphor; agentless passive; revived metonymy; sibilance; enjambment; the poem's only dash.

Cropped treats the soul as a crop, owned, cut and harvested for its yield, which is what colonial extraction does to people, and the verb is itself cut short by its stopped ending. The passive hides the agent at the moment of greatest guilt: the grammar that was innocent in was made now belongs to an empire that never signs its work. Then the image turns grotesque. The scythe swings out / of the conqueror's face, and what comes out of a face is a tongue, so the oppressor's tongue of l.20 revives as a blade and speech itself is the weapon. Swooping turns the harvest into a hunt, long gives the blade reach, and the hiss of soul… scythe… swooping makes it audible. The enjambment keeps cutting across three line-endings, and the dash opens a gap between the atrocity and its strange consequence.

Intention and effect: the violence is felt in the body, not filed away as "cultural loss", and the farming metaphor quietly prepares the regrowth of the last line.

12. the unborn grandchildren / grow to love that strange language. (ll.28–29)

Techniques: temporal leap; the agricultural metaphor completed; distancing deixis; a question mark withheld; a falling last syllable.

Unborn places the grandchildren beyond blame: they were not conceived when the torture happened, so their love is inheritance, not betrayal, and the generation that lived the loss is missing from the sentence. Grow completes the harvest metaphor with terrible economy. The soul was cropped, and what comes up in the cleared field is love: organic, slow, unforced, and therefore impossible to denounce. That strange language holds intimacy and estrangement in one phrase, the distant that pointing away even as love closes the gap, strange meaning both foreign and wonderful. The sentence is grammatically a question, but the full stop prints it as fact, and the unstressed last syllable of language lets the poem fall away rather than close.

Intention and effect: Bhatt ends by describing herself without saying so, a grandchild writing in the strange language, so the reader is left holding evidence of the paradox, and the title's different history turns out to be this one.

CRITICAL LENSES

Critical Lenses

What each way of reading makes visible, and what it flattens

Critical lenses

Each lens below says what it makes visible in this poem, anchored in quotation, and what it flattens. The blind spot matters as much as the insight: it is what keeps a reading answerable to the text.

Formalist

Makes visible. That the meaning is carried by layout and grammar before it is stated. The unequal panels (eighteen lines against eleven); the punctuation system of two question marks and a withheld third; the indented ledges (to India., with your foot,); the second stanza set apart as a block; the near-pentameter of You must learn how to turn the pages gently; the last line falling away on the unstressed second syllable of language. A formalist could teach this poem from its punctuation alone.

Flattens. Everything that needs the world: that book-reverence is lived practice rather than a conceit, that sin is a word doing translation, that a real empire stands behind the conqueror. Form alone cannot say why the scythe image is earned rather than gothic decoration.

Postcolonial

Makes visible. The poem as "writing back". Great Pan is not dead reverses Europe's obituary for its own gods and shrinks its "universal" history to a local one. The ending renders what postcolonial critics call colonial ambivalence, attachment and estrangement fused in grow to love that strange language. The medium itself, English used with tenderness and exactness, performs the in-between condition it describes, with a Greek god and a Hindu goddess sharing a coloniser's tongue. The lens also hears the argument the second stanza enters: Achebe's case for remaking English to carry other experience, against Ngũgĩ wa Thiong'o's view of the imposed language as a "cultural bomb".

Flattens. The poem names no coloniser, no Britain, no English, and its first question convicts every language, including those of the colonised. A strictly anti-imperial reading has to ignore that universalising grammar, read the final love as false consciousness against the poem's tone, and treat stanza 1 as pure pre-colonial authenticity when its key moral word, sin, is already borrowed. The lens finds the poem's occasion and can miss its refusal to prosecute a single nation.

Ecocritical

Makes visible. Culture with an ecology. Every tree is sacred is premise, not scenery: the book's holiness comes from the tree inside it, and without offending the tree / from whose wood the paper was made is an ethic of use, reverence that acknowledges the cost of consumption. The violence of stanza 2 is agricultural (cropped, scythe, a love that will grow), so cultural conquest is pictured as the clearing of land.

Flattens. The poem's centre of gravity, which is language. Trees matter here as the source of books and knowledge; a reading that turns the poem into a conservation argument mistakes the vehicle for the tenor.

Feminist

Makes visible. The guardian of language in the poem is female (without disturbing Sarasvati puts a goddess, not a god, inside the book), and culture is passed on through intimate household teaching, the grandmotherly rude and the patient You must learn. A woman poet claims both the goddess of speech and the contested language.

Flattens. The text's reticence. Neither the teacher of You must learn nor the conqueror is given a gender, so casting the violence as male is inference, not evidence. Pressed hard, the lens supplies a cast the poem declines to name.

Marxist / materialist

Makes visible. The material basis of the grandchildren's love. The soul has been cropped frames colonisation as extraction, people processed as yield, and history supplies the mechanism the poem leaves unstated: after 1835 English became the language of education funding, the courts, government posts and the new universities, so affection for it grew where the rewards were planted. Love, in this reading, has a salary attached.

Flattens. The spiritual register (Sarasvati, sacred, sin), which materialism must translate into ideology, and the ending's tenderness, which it can only read as disguised self-interest. The poem does not sneer at the love; a reading that must sneer has left the text.

Reader-response

Makes visible. A poem that builds its reader and springs traps. You must learn casts whoever reads as the child being taught; rude to a book invites a Western smile that the stanza then quietly judges; the parallel questions are built so that the reader supplies a negative the grammar forbids and catches themselves blaming language. A reader raised to apologise to a dropped book reads description where another reads charm, and the poem knows it.

Flattens. The poem's assertions. The torture happened whether or not a reader feels implicated, and treating everything as an effect on the reader dissolves the historical claim on which the poem's anger rests. The lens explains the poem's manners, not its wound.

OTHER READINGS

Other Readings

Contested interpretations, and where each is weak

Other readings

1. An anti-colonial elegy: the poem mourns a murdered soul and indicts the conqueror

Evidence. The second panel's semantic field (oppressor's, murder, torture, cropped, scythe, conqueror's) and its central image of harvest, which frames colonisation as the extraction of souls. The anger is real, and the history behind it, the Raj and English as the price of advancement, is unmistakable.

Weakness. The grammar refuses a single target. Which language / has not been the oppressor's tongue? extends guilt beyond Britain; no coloniser, country or language is named; and the ending grants the grandchildren's love of English without irony or rebuke. A pure protest poem would not acquit the weapon in l.22 and bless the outcome in l.29.

2. A celebration of Indian syncretism: the "different history" is a history of hospitality

Evidence. ll.1–6: a Greek god welcomed into a Hindu world where the gods roam freely and every tree is sacred. India appears as the place where all traditions survive and mingle, against a Europe that lets its gods die.

Weakness. Disguised hints that survival needs concealment, and the second panel shows what actually happened when cultures met under empire: not hospitality but the scythe. The reading also overlooks the first panel's own severity (must, sin four times). This paradise has rules.

3. The acquittal of language: tools are innocent, wielders are guilty

Evidence. The active grammar of l.22 (truly meant): languages have no intentions, so guilt belongs to those who use them; and the poem's own English, supple and loving, shows that the tongue can be repossessed. PoetryProf reads the faint personification the same way, as language made an innocent party, misled into murder.

Weakness. ll.19–20 have just found every language historically complicit (has not been is a perfect tense of accumulated fact), and the last line still calls English that strange language, keeping the acquitted defendant at arm's length. The acquittal is argued for and withheld at once.

4. Reverence as discipline: the first panel is quietly ambivalent about orthodoxy

Evidence. The litany's four prohibitions, the imperative You must learn, the slide from theology (sacred) to the policing of tiny gestures: tradition felt as weight as well as gift, a view open to a poet who left India at twelve and writes Here from abroad.

Weakness. The tone is tender, not satirical (gently, the loving chain of tree, wood and paper, the domestic rude), and the severity has a structural job, establishing teaching as culture's channel of transmission, rather than a critical one. The panel honours the discipline more than it chafes at it.

5. The ending as reclamation: love wins, and the strange language now belongs to the grandchildren

Evidence. Grow to love is organic, unforced and in a present tense that keeps recurring; the poem itself, written by one of those grandchildren, is proof that the language now serves the people it was used against.

Weakness. The love never stops being aftermath: it arrives only after the torture, and the full stop keeps bewilderment rather than triumph. Reclamation is what the poem does; it is not what the poem claims, and the gap between the two is deliberate.

6. The ending as a graft: English grown onto a Gujarati root

Evidence. The poem thinks in plants: every tree is sacred, cropped, scythe, grow. Grow to love suggests new growth from an old root, and strange suggests that the two never fully merge, as a grafted tree keeps rootstock and scion distinct. Bhatt's own case fits the image: Gujarati, which she calls "the deepest layer of my identity", beneath the English she writes in.

Weakness. A graft needs a wound, and the rootstock does not consent; the poem's word for the cut is torture. It promises nothing about fruit: the language is strange, not "better". And the hopeful version depends on the root being remembered, which the skipped generation of the unborn grandchildren puts in doubt. The poem itself remembers, in its whole first stanza, and that may be its answer.

REVISION NOTES

Revision Notes

The working notes, quotation by quotation

Title

A Different History

Analysis
  • A = indefinite → one of many histories, not the history (vs James Mill's The History of British India, 1817, written without visiting India)
  • Different from what? → reader supplies the coloniser's version
  • Latin dis + ferre = carry apart → Pan, English, Indo-European branches
  • History < Greek historia = inquiry → st.2 = 3 questions
  • "history" & "story" share a root → a chosen narrative
  • focus = cultural & intellectual history (language, books, religion), not wars & treaties
Effect, style & response
  • irony: promises difference, finds sameness (which language has not… = oldest pattern) → only the ending differs (love)
  • ambiguous: colonial history / Pan's new life / the history inside a language
  • asks: whose history were we taught, and is it complete?
  • title ↔ last lines: the "different history" = the grandchildren's, lived in English → this poem

Core argument

Analysis
  • st.1 → sacred world · language = vessel (book)
  • st.2 → violence · language = weapon (tongue / scythe)
  • ending → grandchildren love the coloniser's tongue
  • written in English → the poem is the paradox
Effect, style & response
  • my reading (wielder, not word): language = neutral, malleable tool → guilt lies with the wielder (truly meant; scythe from the conqueror's face)
  • almost every language spread by conquest
  • humans need language → love whatever they're raised in
  • nuance: still that strange language → innocent, but carries history

Bhatt · *Brunizem*

Analysis
  • b. Ahmedabad, Gujarat, 6 May 1956 · grew up Pune
  • English at 5 (New Orleans) · English poems with Gujarati words at ~8
  • USA 1968 (aged 12) · Goucher BA 1980 · Iowa MFA 1986 · married Michael Augustin 1988 → Bremen
  • Gujarati = "the deepest layer of my identity"
  • wants readers to feel "the in-betweenness and 'foreignness'" of her experience
  • first printed PN Review 53, Jan–Feb 1987 (part 2 headed "2") → Brunizem (Carcanet, 1988)
  • Brunizem = dark prairie soil of Asia / Europe / N. America → 3 worlds · Alice Hunt Bartlett Award + Commonwealth Poetry Prize (Asia)
Effect, style & response
  • 'Search for My Tongue' → Gujarati script on the page, mother tongue grows back = opposite direction
  • this poem: no Gujarati → in-betweenness lived inside one borrowed language
  • Bhatt = one of the unborn grandchildren → poem = the love it describes
1

Great Pan is not dead;

Analysis
  • allusion: Plutarch → a voice orders the pilot Thamus to announce "Great Pan is dead" (reign of Tiberius) → Christians (Eusebius on) read it as pagan gods dying with Christ
  • negation not dead → starts mid-argument, refutes a belief the reader already holds
  • Great = Pan's epithet from the cry · ancient pun Pan = "all" (pantheon) → all the gods aren't dead
  • plosive monosyllables Great… dead → firm halt · semicolon caesura → pause before the explanation
Effect, style & response
  • Western history ≠ global history → an ending only in Europe
  • calm, informing tone (not angry) → wins trust before the questions
  • ideas thought "dead" survive elsewhere
2–3

he simply emigrated / to India.

Analysis
  • simply = understatement / bathos → death of a world-order shrinks to a change of address (the litotes-like negation is l.1's not dead)
  • emigrated = permanent, bureaucratic move → god treated as a migrant · not "fled" / "travelled"
  • enjambment → reader crosses the line-break as Pan crosses the border
  • indent to India. → pushed off the margin (India marginalised) and isolated → why India?
  • full stop → calm fact
Effect, style & response
  • Pan east, Bhatt's family west (USA 1968) → diaspora
  • chosen migration preserves (Pan) vs forced arrival replaces (English, st.2)
  • Pūṣan: Vedic god of roads & journeys, herds, goats → "emigration" = homecoming (⚠ contested hypothesis, 1924) · Pūṣan faded too → India didn't keep everything
4

Here, the gods roam freely,

Analysis
  • deixis Here → speaker inside India (imaginative return, written abroad) · silent "there" = Europe · answered by that (l.29)
  • singular → plural: Pan joins the gods
  • roam = grazing, no destination → divine immanent, not housed in churches
  • freely = irony → gods free in a country that wasn't
Effect, style & response
  • India = refuge for what the West let die
  • literal too: monkeys & cattle round temples and streets
5

disguised as snakes or monkeys;

Analysis
  • disguised = outsider's word → avatar ("descent": fish, tortoise, boar, man-lion) = a form, not a costume → speaker translating for the West
  • hidden divinity in humble things · disguise = survival under threat
  • snakes: nāgas · Shiva's serpent · Vishnu on Shesha · Nag Panchami milk · shed skin = rebirth
  • monkeys: Hanuman → in the Ramayana weighs which language to speak to Sita · monkeys mocked in colonial racism → made divine = inversion
  • sibilance disguised as snakes hisses · hard /k/ snakes… monkeys = lively bounce
Effect, style & response
  • Eden inverted: snake + tree + knowledge + sin, values flipped → the sin = disrespecting the tree, not taking from it
6–8

every tree is sacred / and it is a sin / to be rude to a book.

Analysis
  • absolute every · sacred → harming nature = spiritual crime
  • real devotion: peepal · banyan · tulsi · Bodhi tree
  • line-break suspense: it is a sin hangs → expect something grave → a book (bathos)
  • sin = Christian lexis, not pāp → coloniser's moral vocabulary inside the "pure" stanza
  • personification rude → book has feelings · grandmotherly word → teaching at home
  • synecdochic progression tree → book: natural → cultural → book inherits sacredness
  • anaphora begins → litany
Effect, style & response
  • Macaulay 1835: local dialects "poor and rude" · "a single shelf of a good European library" worth "the whole native literature of India and Arabia" = rude to a whole literature
  • builds the moral scale st.2 is judged by: sin ×4 for a book, never for torture
9–14

shove · slam · toss one carelessly

Analysis
  • anaphora a sin ×4 (ll.7, 9, 11, 13) → rule repeated, as to a child
  • tricolon shove / slam / toss = contempt / aggression / indifference → carelessly = worst sin
  • with your foot → lowest, unclean · touch book, then forehead / eyes = apology to Sarasvati · your implicates the reader
  • ellipsis of It is → chant speeds up · slam onomatopoeia · plural books escalates · one = book reduced to a number
  • plosives book… foot… books down… hard… table → the blows · nasals sin… slam… down… one… room → dull, insistent hum
  • indents ll.10, 12, 14 = instrument, impact, trajectory → book shoved aside on the page
Effect, style & response
  • distance map: with your foot (contact) → hard on a table (separated) → across a room (careless) → long scythe (cuts without touching) · distance ↑ care ↓
  • my historical reading: Company rulers in India (1700s) → ruled from London (after 1857) → Radcliffe, who had never been to India, draws the Partition line (1947)
  • cruelty: personal → impersonal (Milgram: obedience rose as the victim got further away · Bauman: distance breeds moral indifference)
  • aside / down / across echo Pan's journey → careless displacement, not chosen migration
15

You must learn how to turn the pages gently

Analysis
  • You must = modal of obligation · not a bare imperative ("Learn…") · direct address → reader = the child being taught
  • longest, smoothest line (11 syllables) → enacts gently after the choppy litany · adverb gently at the line-edge
  • near iambic pentameter + feminine ending → English poetry's home metre carries an Indian lesson
  • internal rhyme learn / turn → proverb-like
Effect, style & response
  • learn (chosen, taught) vs grow to love (unchosen, absorbed)
  • reverence = a taught skill → fragile: break the teaching and it's lost
16

without disturbing Sarasvati,

Analysis
  • anaphora without → second litany, of care
  • only named Indian deity → goddess of speech & knowledge → language = the real subject
  • disturbing = domestic, tender → like not waking someone
  • fricatives without… Sarasvati → soft lattice, order restored
Effect, style & response
  • Rigveda river goddess ("best of rivers") → merges with Vāc (Speech) → book · veena · swan (discernment) · Vasant Panchami: books rest with her
  • Bhatt's own note: often worshipped in libraries
  • river said to vanish underground and flow on unseen → beneath the English, an older tongue may still flow
17–18

without offending the tree / from whose wood the paper was made.

Analysis
  • personification offending → funny at first, then serious
  • reverse chain tree → wood → paper → traces the book to its living source
  • long O / A + soft /w/ wood… was made (whose sounds /h/) → low sounds fade reverently
  • passive was made → hidden agent harmless here → sinister in has been cropped
Effect, style & response
  • reverent use: using nature is fine, disrespect is the sin · the sacrifice behind every page
  • ambivalence: 4 sins, must, 2 withouts → rules can feel overwhelming → not pure nostalgia
  • stanza ends at rest, on a made thing

Structure · the stanza break

Analysis
  • diptych (two linked panels) · 18 + 11 lines · volta in white space, no "but"
  • anthology: st.2 set further right as a block → visual border between two Indias
  • free verse = speech: elder → interrogator · the unforced English = the love
Stanza 1 Stanza 2
Anaphora a sin… without = rules Which language… after = questions
Violence shove · slam · toss → books murder · torture · cropped → souls
Agent your foot, active has been cropped, culprit vanishes
Moral word sin ×4 none, even for torture
Learning must learn (taught) grow to love (unchosen)
Deixis Here (near) that (far)
Effect, style & response
  • missing ? (l.29): Q1, Q2 rhetorical → ? · Q3 genuine bewilderment → . → fact over explanation, closure without resolution
  • tone: amused tenderness → anger (in the nouns) → bewildered love
19–22

Which language / has not been the oppressor's tongue?

Analysis
  • abrupt tone shift → no imagery, no setting, only questions · first language (×3: ll.19, 21, 29)
  • isolated Which language → language in the dock · hangs like a mind searching
  • rhetorical Q1 → implied answer: none · present perfect has not been = all of history
  • metonymy + pun tongue → organ = language · inverts "mother tongue" → revived as the scythe (l.27)
  • generic the oppressor → not just Britain · Persian (Mughal court tongue until 1837) · Sanskrit (caste)
  • Q2: no not, active truly meant → intention → guilt on the wielder · pun meant · someone = one indefinite victim
Effect, style & response
  • Q1 convicts every language; Q2 acquits language as such → defendant = power
  • not "British bad, India good"
  • language = vehicle for expression and oppression (Janus-faced)
23–27

after the soul has been cropped / with a long scythe swooping out

Analysis
  • Q3 = genuine bewilderment · weary And · vague it · 7-line sentence (ll.23–29): subject & verb held back → we sit through the violence first
  • the torture: definite article → known history, unexplained · metaphor drops → brutal fact · anaphora after layers time
  • agentless passive has been cropped → culprit vanishes when guilt is greatest
  • cropped = harvested · cut short · (old sense) ears cut off as punishment → the roots survive
  • atman irony: the self that "weapons cannot cut" (Gita 2.23) is cropped → colonialism cut the uncuttable
  • scythe = harvest + Grim Reaper / Father Time · long = reach, power from a distance · swooping = bird of prey → harvest becomes hunt
  • sibilance soul… scythe… swooping → blade's hiss · cropped /pt/ cuts itself short
  • conqueror's face → blade out of a mouth = tongue → speech is the weapon · oppressor → conqueror escalation · only dash → gap between generations, memory lost
Effect, style & response
  • Ngũgĩ: bullet = physical subjugation, language = spiritual subjugation
  • sin silent here → the moral word fails at the real crime
  • Bhatt's anger in the nouns, not a slogan
28–29

the unborn grandchildren / grow to love that strange language.

Analysis
  • temporal leap unborn · skipped generation → those who lived the loss are missing · grandchildren innocent
  • grow = organic, unwilled → the cropped field regrows · love = the strongest verb
  • that (far) vs Here (near, l.4) → language kept at arm's length
  • strange < Latin extraneus "from outside" → foreign + wondrous
  • full stop, not ? → the question becomes fact · liquid /l/ love… language → soft, unprotesting close · ends on language
Effect, style & response
  • healing (Achebe: remake English) or final victory (Ngũgĩ) → the full stop won't choose
  • grafting (my reading): English scion on Gujarati rootstock → parts stay distinct ("strange", not blended) · needs a wound; rootstock didn't consent → best of both only if the root is remembered (Bhatt remembers: st.1)
  • "Stockholm syndrome", tweaked: they never saw the captivity → innocent love, erased history · "a house built on stolen land"
  • Bhatt = one of the grandchildren → the poem is the love it describes

The gods · the language family

Analysis
  • Pan: Greek god of shepherds, flocks, wild Arcadia · goat legs · pipes · "panic"
  • Pan vs Pūṣan: shared herds, goats, paths · Pan wild, lustful · Pūṣan gentle guide of roads & souls, toothless, eats gruel
  • Indo-European: PIE → Sanskrit → Gujarati · Greek / Latin · Germanic → English
  • Dyaus Pita = Zeus Pater = Jupiter ("sky father") · deva / deus / "divine" · Uṣas = Eōs (dawn) · nām = name · dā̃t ≈ dental
  • Jones 1786: Sanskrit "more perfect than the Greek" · all "sprung from some common source"
Effect, style & response
  • one root → divergence ("different histories") → violent reunion → grandchildren · strange = a lost relative, uncanny · a branch cut from its own tree
  • Gujarati vs English: kākā / māmā → "uncle" · tũ / tame → politeness built into grammar (cf. rude) · pāp ≠ sin
  • weak linguistic relativity (Sapir–Whorf): language influences what you notice and value → English can't fully carry what it replaced

Colonial context

Analysis
  • East India Company: charter 31 Dec 1600 (Elizabeth I) · Plassey 1757 (Clive) · after the 1857 rebellion → the Raj, 1858–1947
  • 1786 Jones (admiration) → 1817 Mill (contempt, never in India) → 1835 Macaulay's Minute → policy
  • Macaulay: "a class of persons Indian in blood and colour, but English in tastes, in opinions, in morals and in intellect"
  • Bentinck's resolution, 7 March 1835 (the "English Education Act") → funds for "English education alone"
  • 1837 English & local languages replace Persian in the courts · 1844 English-educated preferred for posts · 1857 universities (Calcutta, Bombay, Madras)
  • 1855 Madras commission: torture used to collect revenue → the torture not only metaphor
Effect, style & response
  • Ngũgĩ, Decolonising the Mind (1986): language = "carrier of culture" · Achebe (1965): take English and remake it
  • Aotearoa: Native Schools Act 1867 → English-medium schooling (punishing te reo = school practice, not the Act) · Māori Language Act 1987 → te reo an official language
  • Bhatt names none of it → the poem is wider than one empire, but this history explains torture and why the grandchildren grow to love English (law, office, advancement)
CONNECTIONS

Connections

How this poem pairs with the rest of the set

Comparison hooks

1. Where I Come From — Elizabeth Brewster

Link. Both ask what a person is made of, and answer: something inherited before any choice. Brewster opens "People are made of places"; Bhatt's grandchildren are made of a language. Both build identity from concrete particulars, Brewster's "acres of pine woods" and Bhatt's trees, books and pages.

Shared technique. A two-part structure setting one world against another (Brewster's city of "smog" and "museum smell" against the woods of home; Bhatt's sacred India against the conqueror's violence), and a final image that carries the argument: "A door in the mind blows open", grow to love that strange language.

Difference. Brewster's inheritance is benign and kept by memory; home blows back into the mind like weather. Bhatt's arrives by torture and is loved anyway. Brewster's place survives in the mind, while Bhatt fears that the place may be lost inside the new language.

2. Follower — Seamus Heaney

Link. Two poems about what passes between generations, both ending by reversing who follows whom. Heaney's boy wanted to "grow up and plough"; at the end his father is the one stumbling behind him who "will not go away". Bhatt's grandchildren grow to love what their grandparents suffered. In both, the past refuses to stay in the past.

Shared technique. A way of handling things learned by watching and imitation: the father is "An expert" whose son longs to "close one eye" and plough like him; Bhatt's child is told You must learn how to turn the pages gently. Both are also farming poems. Heaney's furrow and sod are literal; Bhatt's crop is a metaphor, cropped, scythe, grow.

Difference. Heaney's inheritance is loving and chosen, and its weight is personal: an ageing father. Bhatt's is imposed by violence, and its weight is historical. Heaney's plough masters land; Bhatt's scythe masters people. The same agricultural world serves opposite ends.

3. Storyteller — Liz Lochhead

Link. Both are about culture passed down through words handled with care. Lochhead's woman makes telling "her work", work "like spinning", and her stories end up in the children's "sleeping heads". Bhatt's first stanza is household teaching of the same kind (You must learn), and her last lines show what happens when a different tongue takes over the children's heads.

Shared technique. Language as a physical, living thing: Lochhead's "tongue clacked" while hands worked, and the stories dissolve "in the whorl of the ear" at dawn only to fly again at night. Bhatt's tongue becomes a blade swinging out of a face.

Difference. Lochhead's tradition survives its own daily disappearance; nothing threatens it but morning. Bhatt's is broken by force and replaced, and the children grow up loving the replacement. A tongue that clacks in a kitchen, against one that swings as a scythe.

4. Carpet-weavers, Morocco — Carol Rumens

Link. Both turn a craft of patient hands into a question about culture and power. Rumens's children sit "at the loom of another world" knotting a carpet that "will travel in the merchant's truck" and be spread in the mosque; Bhatt's household treats books as holy things.

Shared technique. A sacred object made by human hands from natural material: Rumens's carpet will "give when heaped with prayer"; Bhatt's book is traced back to the tree / from whose wood the paper was made. Both also fold the future into the past. Rumens's colours of "all-that-will-be" freeze into "all-that-was"; Bhatt leaps to the unborn grandchildren.

Difference. Rumens's children are bound to a pattern they did not design, inside their own culture's faith and commerce, in "the school of days". Bhatt's grandchildren are shaped by a foreign power and love it. Rumens watches as a visitor from outside; Bhatt speaks Here, from inside.

5. Before the Sun — Charles Mungoshi

Link. Two poems in which the sacred lives in everyday acts. Mungoshi's fourteen-year-old chops wood, roasts maize and invites the sun to "come share" it; the woodsmoke rises like "a sacrificial prayer", and "the sun just winks". Bhatt's gods roam disguised as snakes or monkeys, and a page must be turned so as not to disturb a goddess.

Shared technique. The divine treated with intimacy rather than awe, and ordinary actions given ritual weight: Mungoshi's shared bites of maize, Bhatt's gentle verbs (disturbing, offending).

Difference. Mungoshi's ritual is playful, private and unthreatened, a boy's morning with no conqueror in sight, and it ends in the "two little skeletons" of the eaten cobs, the residue of a shared meal. Bhatt's sacred world is shadowed by what comes next, and she ends with love growing in a cleared field. (Mungoshi, who wrote in both Shona and English, also knew the colonial language from inside.)

6. Report to Wordsworth — Boey Kim Cheng

Link. The exact counter-case on the fate of the old gods. Boey's classical sea-gods are dying in the modern world, Proteus "entombed in the waste / we dump" and Neptune "helpless as a beached whale", while Bhatt's Pan survives by emigrating east: Great Pan is not dead.

Shared technique. Argument through classical allusion: Boey answers Wordsworth's 'The World Is Too Much with Us', which longs to see Proteus and Triton; Bhatt answers Plutarch's cry. In both, gods are the gauge of a culture's health.

Difference. Boey names the culprit, "insatiate man", and includes himself in the "we" who dump the waste; Bhatt's culprit is a nameless conqueror, glimpsed only by his face. Boey ends with God uttering "his last cry"; Bhatt ends not with a death but with a strange love.

7. Lament — Gillian Clarke

Link. Both end at the same wound: language after violence. Bhatt asks Which language / has not been the oppressor's tongue?; Clarke's last line mourns "the ashes of language".

Shared technique. The litany: Clarke's anaphoric "For the…" and Bhatt's a sin to… both count violations one item at a time, inside a reverence for the natural world (ocean and creatures; trees and books).

Difference. Bhatt's poem holds a future, the unborn grandchildren; Clarke's unborn are turtle eggs "in their nest of sickness". Bhatt's violence has a face; Clarke's has no agent but "vengeance". Bhatt's language survives and is loved; Clarke's is ash.

8. The Chimney Sweeper — William Blake

Link. Institutions teach the oppressed to bless their oppression. Blake's parents have gone "to praise God and his priest and king" after they "taught me to sing the notes of woe"; Bhatt's grandchildren grow to love the conqueror's tongue.

Shared technique. Religious vocabulary as an instrument (Blake's "a heaven of our misery"; Bhatt's borrowed sin), and a calm voice that leaves the reader to do the condemning.

Difference. Blake names his culprits; Bhatt names none. Blake's child sees through the comfort ("They think they have done me no injury"); Bhatt's grandchildren never need to, because they were unborn when the harm was done.

Also worth setting beside it

Love Armed (Behn) — the dominated supply the dominator's power. Behn's lover arms Love ("From me he took his sighs and tears") as Bhatt's grandchildren sustain the conqueror's tongue with their love, and Behn's god shows "strange Tyrannic power" where Bhatt's language is strange: both poems study consent inside subjection.

The Cockroach (Halligan) — the animal as mirror of a hidden order.
