Bhatt's gods hide in snakes and monkeys; Halligan's speaker wonders whether the insect's restlessness is "due payment for some vicious crime" in a former life, a karmic idea in a Western room, and ends having "recognised myself". Both unsettle the observer's sense of superiority, and both end without resolving.

A Married State (Philips) — two lessons built on anaphoric lists. Philips counsels "be advised by me" and lists what the single woman escapes ("No Blustering husbands", "No pangs of child birth"); Bhatt's You must learn follows a list of sins. Philips urges escape from an institution; Bhatt describes people who come to love the power that conquered them.

An Essay on Man (Pope) — human doubleness. Pope's man is "Great lord of all things, yet a prey to all"; Bhatt's language is vessel and weapon at once, and the grandchildren's love is a "riddle" of Pope's kind. Pope holds his paradoxes in balanced couplets; Bhatt leaves hers as a question that ends with a full stop. (Pope's "rudely great" uses rude in its older sense, unpolished.)

Sonnet 18 (Shakespeare) — two opposite accounts of what language does. Shakespeare's verse preserves ("So long lives this, and this gives life to thee"), and his beloved grows into "eternal lines"; Bhatt's language crops souls, yet the grandchildren grow into it. Both use growth for what a language does to people over time.

Hunting Snake (Wright) — the snake as sacred or awesome rather than evil. Bhatt's gods go disguised as snakes; Wright's watchers freeze before "The great black snake", "Cold, dark and splendid", and lose breath in awe. Both overturn the Edenic reflex of fear, and Wright, like Bhatt, wrote from a country whose land and first peoples bore the cost of colonisation.

A nursery rhyme is turned against the adults who sing it: the child’s happiness is the very thing they punish him for.

CONTEXT

Context

The world the poem came out of

The Poet: William Blake (1757–1827)

William Blake was born on 28 November 1757 at 28 Broad Street, Soho, London, the son of James Blake, a hosier. He left school once he could read and write, at about ten, and was otherwise taught at home by his mother; at ten he also joined Henry Pars's drawing school in the Strand. On 4 August 1772 he was apprenticed for seven years to the engraver James Basire, and in October 1779 he entered the Royal Academy Schools. Engraving — cutting other people's designs into copper for book illustrations — remained his trade for life: Blake was a London craftsman who worked with his hands for a living, not a gentleman-poet. In 1782 he married Catherine Boucher, who learned to print and colour his books with him.

He was also, from childhood, a visionary. His Victorian biographer Alexander Gilchrist reports that at eight or ten he saw 'a tree filled with angels, bright angelic wings bespangling every bough like stars' on Peckham Rye. In notes written in 1810 he imagined being asked whether the rising sun was not 'a round Disk of fire somewhat like a Guinea', and answered 'O no no I see an Innumerable company of the Heavenly host crying Holy Holy Holy is the Lord God Almighty' — a refusal to see the world in money terms that is the temper of this poem. Except for three years at Felpham in Sussex (1800–03) he lived in London all his life, largely unrecognised. He died on 12 August 1827 and was buried in Bunhill Fields, the Dissenters' burial ground.

Illuminated printing: *Songs of Innocence* (1789) and *of Experience* (1794)

In 1788 Blake developed relief etching, which he called 'illuminated printing'. He wrote the words (backwards) and drew the designs in acid-resistant varnish on a copper plate, etched away the rest, printed from the raised surface and coloured each print by hand, with Catherine's help. Words and picture were made in one process, every copy differs, and the books were produced by hand in small numbers. Songs of Innocence is dated 1789 on its title page. Songs of Experience is dated 1794 — the year Blake began issuing the two together as Songs of Innocence and of Experience Shewing the Two Contrary States of the Human Soul, although he also went on offering the two books separately. He was living at 13 Hercules Buildings, Lambeth (1790–1800), when the Experience songs were made.

On the plate this poem sits above a small design: a sweep, black from head to foot, trudges towards us through driving snow down a street between houses, a sack of soot on his back, under a dark band of sky. The picture is line 1 made visible — a small black figure on the white of the paper, among the snow.

The text: Notebook, plate and anthology

Blake drafted the poem around 1793 in his Notebook (British Library Add MS 49460, also called the Rossetti Manuscript), alongside drafts of many other Experience songs, including 'London' and 'The Tyger'; this one runs across two pages (pp. 103 and 105). Two revisions are revealing. In line 6 he first wrote 'winter's wind', then changed it to 'snow', so that the line deliberately repeats line 1. And the last line first read 'Who wrap themselves up in our misery' — the powerful keeping themselves warm in the children's suffering — before he struck it out for Who make up a heaven of our misery.

The etched plate is punctuated differently from the anthology. Blake used no quotation marks at all, wrote the cry 'weep, weep,' without apostrophes, used ampersands ('father & mother', 'God & his Priest & King'), capitalised 'Priest' and 'King', and spelled 'smil'd' and 'winters'. The text in Songs of Ourselves — and therefore on the exam paper — is a modernised edition: it puts the child's speech (lines 4–12) in quotation marks but leaves the question in line 3 unmarked, italicises weep, prints smiled, keeps Blake's colon after injury, and prints priest and king in lower case. Exactly who speaks which line is partly an editor's decision.

The climbing boys

London flues were narrow and crooked (as late as 1840 Parliament had to require new ones to be at least fourteen inches by nine), and the cheapest way to clear them was to send a child up inside. Master sweeps used 'climbing boys' from as young as four or five. The 1788 Act allowed churchwardens and overseers of the poor to bind pauper children — those 'chargeable' to the parish, or caught begging — as sweeps' apprentices, or any boy 'with the Consent of the Parent or Parents', until he reached sixteen; the Innocence sweep puts it more bluntly: 'my father sold me'. The boys advertised by crying their trade through the streets, often in the dark before dawn — 'Sweep!', which in a very small child's mouth came out as 'weep.

The work meant burns, suffocation in the flues, falls and lung disease. In 1775 the London surgeon Percivall Pott published his observations of cancer of the scrotum in chimney sweeps and traced it to soot — the first cancer to be linked to an occupation. The philanthropist Jonas Hanway (1712–1786) campaigned for the boys; his Sentimental History of Chimney Sweepers in London & Westminster (1785) argued, in its subtitle, for 'putting them under regulations, to prevent the grossest inhumanity to the climbing boys'.

The 1788 Act — and eighty years of failure

Parliament responded with 'An Act for the better Regulation of Chimney Sweepers and their Apprentices' (in force from 5 July 1788). No boy was to be apprenticed under eight; a master could keep no more than six; each boy was to wear a leather cap with a brass plate bearing his master's name; he was to be washed once a week, never forced up a chimney 'actually on Fire', and not made to 'call the Streets' before seven in the morning in winter. The indenture also bound the master to make the boy 'attend the Publick Worship of God on the Sabbath Day', not to let him wear 'his Sweeping Dress on that Day', and to treat him 'with as much Humanity and Care as the nature of the Employment of a Chimney Sweeper will admit of'. A clause to license master sweeps was voted down in the House of Lords, and with no one to inspect, the Act went largely unenforced.

The poem appeared six years later, and its child is everything the Act regulated: out in the street in his sweeping clothes, crying his trade, while his parents are at church. If, as church-going suggests, the day is a Sunday, he is exactly where the law said he should not be. Reform took most of another century. The 1834 Act raised the minimum age for apprentices to ten; the 1840 Act made it an offence, from 1842, to compel or allow anyone under twenty-one to climb a chimney, and was widely ignored. Only the Chimney Sweepers Act of 1875 — pushed through by Lord Shaftesbury after eleven-year-old George Brewster died after being sent up a chimney at Fulbourn Hospital, near Cambridge — required every sweep to be registered with the police, which finally gave the law an enforcer.

Two Chimney Sweepers: the contrary states

The combined title page promises 'the Two Contrary States of the Human Soul'. In The Marriage of Heaven and Hell (composed 1790–93) Blake wrote that 'Without Contraries is no progression': Innocence and Experience are not simply good childhood and bad adulthood but two ways of seeing the same world, each exposing what the other misses. The Innocence 'Chimney Sweeper' (1789) is spoken by a boy whose mother died and whose father 'sold' him. He comforts little Tom Dacre, who dreams that an Angel unlocks thousands of sweeps from 'coffins of black' and promises that if he is good he will 'have God for his father & never want joy'. It ends: 'So if all do their duty, they need not fear harm.'

The Experience child is not the same boy: his father and mother are both alive, and at church. He has no dream and no angel, and the bargain the Innocence poem repeats — do your duty now, be rewarded in heaven — is exactly what he exposes as a heaven of our misery. The Experience poem is half the length of its twin (12 lines to 24). Elsewhere in Songs of Experience, 'London' puts the same two things side by side: 'How the Chimney-sweepers cry / Every blackning Church appalls'.

Church and King in the 1790s

The Church of England was the established Church: the monarch was its Supreme Governor, its bishops sat in the House of Lords, and much of its preaching to the poor stressed contentment with one's station and reward in the life to come. Blake was baptised in it, at St James's, Piccadilly, but his mother had once belonged to the Moravian congregation in Fetter Lane, and he was hostile to the Church of England and to almost every organised religion — while remaining a passionately Christian visionary. His target in this poem is not God but God's managers: the possessive in God and his priest and king describes a God who has been taken over.

The poem also belongs to the years of the French Revolution. Blake moved on the edge of the radical circle of the publisher Joseph Johnson, which included Joseph Priestley, Mary Wollstonecraft and Thomas Paine, and in 1791 he wrote The French Revolution, a poem that was set in type but never published. In Britain 'Church and King' became the loyalist rallying cry: in July 1791 a Birmingham 'Church and King' mob burned Priestley's house and laboratory. Britain went to war with revolutionary France in 1793, and in 1794 — the year Songs of Experience is dated — leading reformers were tried for treason. In that climate, naming God, priest and king together as the makers of a heaven out of children's misery was a political act as well as a religious one. Blake's own clash with authority came in 1803, when a soldier, John Scolfield, accused him of damning the King and calling soldiers slaves; he was tried for sedition at Chichester in January 1804 and acquitted.

THE POEM

The Poem

Line by line, with the analysis alongside

The Chimney-Sweeper
TThe Chimney-Sweeper
1A little black thing among the snow,
2Crying ‘weep, ‘weep, in notes of woe!
3Where are thy father and mother, say?
4‘They are both gone up to the church to pray.
5‘Because I was happy upon the heath
6And smiled among the winter’s snow,
7They clothed me in the clothes of death
8And taught me to sing the notes of woe.
9‘And because I am happy and dance and sing,
10They think they have done me no injury:
11And are gone to praise God and his priest and king,
12Who make up a heaven of our misery.’

Lines with a marker have analysis — click one, or just scroll.

Title
The Chimney-Sweeper
Language & devices

Definite article The names a type, not a person: no name, age or family. The anthology hyphenates Chimney-Sweeper into a single job-title (Blake's plate reads 'THE Chimney Sweeper', with 'THE' in capitals). Occupational noun: the '-er' suffix identifies the child entirely by the work he does for others. Intertextuality: the same title had already been used for a poem in Songs of Innocence (1789), so the title itself sets up a comparison between Blake's two 'contrary states'.

Meaning & effect

Blake introduces the child the way a trade directory or a street-cry would — by his function. The title sounds like an ordinary service ('the chimney-sweeper is coming'), and the poem will show that the 'service' is a small child. Repeating the Innocence title tells us the circumstances have not changed between the two books (soot, cold, the cry); what has changed is the understanding. The plainness of the label is the first of the poem's polite surfaces that the child will strip away.

Line 1
A little black thing among the snow,
Language & devices

Dehumanising noun: thing where we expect boy or child. Indefinite article A: one of many, unnamed. Diminutive little invites pity in the same phrase in which thing withdraws personhood. Colour contrast: black soot set among white snow. Minor sentence: lines 1–2 have no main verb — the child is presented as a sighting, not as someone who acts. The four beats fall on LIT-, THING, -MONG, SNOW; said naturally, black thing becomes two heavy syllables together.

Meaning & effect

The poem opens inside an adult onlooker's way of seeing: before the child is a person he is a size, a colour and a shape in the street. Blake is not calling the child a thing; he is recording how a society that uses climbing boys sees them. Little shows the onlooker can still feel pity, which makes thing worse — pity and dehumanisation share one phrase. Among the snow places him in the white world but not of it: the soot that makes him useful is what makes him invisible as a child. The line sets up the poem's reversal: this thing is about to speak, and will understand more than anyone looking at him.

Line 2
Crying ‘weep, ‘weep, in notes of woe!
Language & devices

Pun: 'weep is the trade's street-cry 'sweep!' with its first sound lost, as a child too young to manage sw- would say it; the elision mark shows the dropped s, and the anthology italicises the word as a quoted cry (Blake's plate has no apostrophes: 'weep, weep'). Epizeuxis: 'weep, 'weep — the call repeated like a street-cry. Spondee: two stressed monosyllables side by side stall the lilt. Auditory imagery: notes of woe hears the cry as music; Alliteration on /w/ in weep… woe. The line's only exclamation mark comes after woe, so it belongs to the onlooker's reaction, not to the cry.

Meaning & effect

The child is doing his job: calling through the streets for work. But the word the city hears as 'sweep' comes out as weep, so the advertisement is also a lament — his labour and his grief are the same sound. Blake did not need to invent the pun; it is what a very young sweep's call would actually sound like, so the line tells us how young he is as well as how unhappy. The onlooker hears notes of woe and exclaims: the first adult response in the poem is to hear the grief as a kind of music. When notes of woe returns in line 8 as something taught, this cry is retrospectively revealed as a trained one.

Line 3
Where are thy father and mother, say?
Language & devices

Interrogative followed by an Imperative: Where are… then the bare command say?, set off by a comma. Archaic pronoun thy: the familiar form, used to children and social inferiors — it can sound tender or condescending. Unmarked speech: in the anthology text this line has no quotation marks, so the question comes in the same narrating voice as lines 1–2; the child's reply (from line 4) is in quotation marks.

Meaning & effect

The adult assumes there must be a local explanation: a child alone and crying in the snow must have lost his parents. It is a kind question, but it is the wrong size for the problem — it looks for an accident where the poem is about to show a system. The tag say? turns concern into a demand: the child must account for his own situation. Because the line is unquoted, the voice that called him a thing is the voice that now addresses him; the poem moves from looking at the child to speaking to him, and in the next line, at last, to listening.

Line 4
‘They are both gone up to the church to pray.
Language & devices

Shift of voice: the opening quotation mark hands the poem to the child, who keeps it to the end. Determiner both: neither parent is dead or missing. Directional verb gone up: the church above, the child below in the street. Declarative closed by a full stop: no complaint, no exclamation. Couplet rhyme: pray answers say.

Meaning & effect

The answer is devastating because it is so ordinary: his parents are alive, together and respectable, and they are at church. Both cancels every excuse the question offered — orphan, widow, family crisis — and replaces misfortune with a choice. Gone up starts the poem's vertical pattern: the parents rise towards church and heaven while the child stays at street level in the snow, a pattern the last line completes. The flat statement sounds like something he has said many times; the neglect is routine. Rhyming say with pray makes piety the neat, nursery-rhyme answer to the question.

Line 5
‘Because I was happy upon the heath
Language & devices

Causal conjunction Because opens the stanza: the child gives reasons, like someone making an argument. Past tense was: the happiness belongs to a time before. Pastoral setting heath: open, uncultivated common land — the opposite of a narrow flue. Alliteration of breathy /h/ in happy… heath. Run-on line: no punctuation at the line-end, so the clause flows straight into line 6.

Meaning & effect

The child begins to explain how he came to be here, and the explanation is shocking: his happiness is given as the cause. Read one way, this is a child's logic — first he was happy, then he was punished. Read another way it is accurate: a contented child could be put to work without anyone feeling cruel, and untaught joy could look like something that needed disciplining. Blake keeps both meanings in the one word. Heath stands for a childhood lived freely in the open air, the life the trade has replaced.

Line 6
And smiled among the winter’s snow,
Language & devices

Repetition with variation: among the… snow repeats line 1. Sibilance: smiled… snow. Contrast: the same snow that now frames a black thing was once where he smiled. Recycled rhyme: snow repeats line 1's rhyme-word, and line 8's woe repeats line 2's, so stanza 2 is built on stanza 1's sounds. In Blake's Notebook draft he first wrote 'winter's wind' and changed it to 'snow' — the echo of line 1 was chosen.

Meaning & effect

He remembers being happy even in winter, which shows that the cold was never the problem: the snow has not changed; what was done to him has. Line 1 shows a black shape in the snow; line 6 shows a smiling child in the same snow. Side by side, the two lines separate hardship a child can bear from harm that adults inflict. The repeated rhyme makes past and present chime, as if he cannot get out of the snow and the woe of the opening.

Line 7
They clothed me in the clothes of death
Language & devices

Polyptoton: clothed… clothes — the act and the garment from one root. Metaphor: clothes of death — the soot-black working clothes as a shroud or mourning dress. Ambiguous pronoun They: grammatically the parents, but wide enough to take in everyone who profits from his work. Half-rhyme with line 5: heath/death share the final /θ/ but not the vowel — the poem's only imperfect rhyme. Another Run-on line into line 8.

Meaning & effect

Clothing a child is a basic act of care; here it is the instrument of harm. The black working clothes mark him as a sweep, and the trade killed children — by falls, suffocation and the soot cancer the surgeon Percivall Pott described in 1775 — so clothes of death is close to literal. It is also symbolic: he has been dressed for his own funeral while still alive, his childhood buried. The rhyme that ties his free past (heath) to this death does not quite fit, as if the poem's own music registers that the join is wrong.

Line 8
And taught me to sing the notes of woe.
Language & devices

Repetition: notes of woe returns from line 2. Verb taught: suffering as something instructed. Irony: teaching a child to sing is normally an act of love. Rhyme: woe again repeats line 2's rhyme-sound.

Meaning & effect

In line 2 the notes of woe sounded spontaneous; now we learn they were taught. The street-cry was drilled into him as part of the trade, so his grief has been turned into work: his voice advertises his labour. Blake's point is that oppression does not only cause suffering; it trains its victims to express it in forms useful to others. It also changes how we hear everything that follows — even this answer comes in a voice that others have trained.

Line 9
‘And because I am happy and dance and sing,
Language & devices

Parallel structure: And because repeats line 5's Because. Tense shift: was happy becomes am happy. Polysyndeton: and… and… and. Anapaestic rhythm: and be-CAUSE | I am HAP- | py and DANCE | and SING — three anapaests, the most dance-like line in the poem. Echo: sing repeats line 8's taught singing. A fresh opening quotation mark marks the new stanza of the child's speech.

Meaning & effect

His happiness is still real in the present — he dances and sings — and that is exactly the trouble. This time because explains the parents' state of mind: his cheerfulness is the evidence they use to tell themselves he is fine. In line 5 happiness was the reason he was put to work; now it is the reason no one feels guilty. Blake does not say the joy is fake (though sing recalls the singing he was taught); the poem is more disturbing than that — real joy can still be turned against the child. The skipping rhythm performs the cheerfulness it describes, so the reader is charmed by the very thing that fools the parents.

Line 10
They think they have done me no injury:
Language & devices

Cognitive verb think: belief, not knowledge. Understatement: no injury — the cold vocabulary of a court or an account-book. Alliteration of the soft dental sound in They think they. Colon at the line-end (in the anthology and on Blake's plate): it links their belief to what they do next. Weak rhyme: the rhyme falls on the unstressed final syllable of injury.

Meaning & effect

The parents are not hypocrites who know they are lying; they genuinely believe they have done nothing wrong. That is worse than conscious cruelty, because it shows how a society can make ordinary people comfortable with harm. Injury is an official word — as if harm were something to be inspected and found absent — and the child repeats it with an irony they cannot hear. The colon makes the next line follow from this one: because they think they have done no injury, they can go to church with clear consciences.

Line 11
And are gone to praise God and his priest and king,
Language & devices

Echo: are gone repeats line 4's are both gone. Polysyndeton and Tricolon: God and his priest and king. Possessive his: priest and king presented as God's own servants. Capitalisation: the anthology capitalises only God (Blake's plate has 'God & his Priest & King'). Rhythm: and are GONE | to praise GOD | and his PRIEST | and KING — the same skipping beat as line 9.

Meaning & effect

The parents' absence is explained a second time, and now it has a destination: they have gone to praise the powers at the top of society. Church and Crown are joined to God in one breath, as a single authority — in Blake's England the monarch was the Supreme Governor of the established Church, and 'Church and King' was a loyalist slogan. The line's rhythm matches line 9 exactly, so the parents' worship and the child's dancing sound like the same tune: both are performances that keep the system running. Praise flows upward, away from the child.

Line 12
Who make up a heaven of our misery.’
Language & devices

Relative clause: Who carries the sentence on past king, and turns a list of the revered into the subject of an accusation. Polysemy: make up = invent (a made-up story), assemble (their comfort made out of the children's pain) and make up for (heaven offered in return for misery). Paradox: heaven made of… misery. First-person plural: our — the child speaks for all climbing boys. Falling ending: the line ends on the unstressed tail of misery. In the Notebook draft this line first read 'Who wrap themselves up in our misery', which Blake struck out.

Meaning & effect

The final accusation: the powers the parents praise turn the children's misery into heaven. That heaven is both the reward promised to the poor for patient suffering and the warm, comfortable life of the households whose chimneys they sweep; make up lets Blake say that the promise is a fiction and the comfort is real, built out of the child. Our shows he has been speaking for a whole class of children all along. The cancelled draft line pictured the powerful wrapping themselves warm in the children's misery; the final version makes the larger charge that they manufacture heaven itself. Ending on the falling sound of misery leaves no consolation.

THE WHOLE POEM

The Whole Poem

Stepping back: what the poem is doing, first line to last

The easy account of this poem — small child, cruel parents, wicked Church, reader duly moved — mistakes it for a plea. It is not a plea. Nothing in the child's nine lines asks for anything: no appeal, no 'help me', no address to the adult at all after the first answering line. The poem's real subject is the machinery by which a society converts a child's suffering into everyone else's comfort, and its real scandal is not that the child suffers but that he understands — better than his parents, better than the questioner, and at least as well as the reader. The poem is built to disqualify, one by one, every adult position from which the child might be viewed comfortably — including the position of feeling sorry for him — until the only stance left standing is his own analysis.

Begin where the poem begins, in the wrong voice. A little black thing among the snow is the adult world's perception rendered with terrible fidelity: not a boy but a thing, its size noted (little), its colour noted (black), its setting noted (among the snow) — the grammar of an object in a landscape, almost a connoisseur's grammar. The line can be read as compassionate; it is at best pre-compassionate, the seeing that comes before recognition. The cry in line 2 is what forces the upgrade from thing to someone who can be spoken to: 'weep, 'weep is the trade-cry 'sweep! sweep!' as a very young mouth actually delivers it, the /s/ not yet manageable, and the mangling turns advertisement into lament without the child intending either. London heard this cry daily and heard it as commerce. The observer at least hears notes of woe — and responds with the poem's one question: Where are thy father and mother, say? It is a kind question and a hopeless one. It assumes the child's condition is an anomaly with a local cause — lost parents, a family misfortune — when the poem is about to demonstrate that the cause is not local at all. Pity personalises; the child is about to show the structure.

His answer opens with the poem's quietest devastation: They are both gone up to the church to pray. Not dead, not lost: at church. Both closes the escape-route the question offered — this is no orphan, but a complete, functioning, respectable family, which has chosen. The rest of his speech is organised as an argument, and the conjunctions carry it: Because I was happy… They clothed me… And because I am happy… They think… And are gone. Twice the child identifies his own happiness as the operative cause. The first time it is the pretext: his visible contentment on the heath made it possible to put him to work without the appearance of cruelty — you can sell a smiling child and call it providence. The second time it is the alibi: his persistent cheerfulness is now the evidence by which his parents acquit themselves — They think they have done me no injury. The logic is airtight and monstrous: happiness before the harm licenses the harm; happiness after the harm proves there was none. The child's joy — the one thing that is authentically his — has been converted at both ends into an instrument of his exploitation. This is a subtler claim than 'his happiness is fake'. The poem never says it is fake. It says something worse: that its being real is no obstacle to its being used.

The form is running the same argument in parallel. The poem wears the metre of the nursery — couplet chime, four-beat lines, an anapaestic skip — and the skip intensifies precisely where the content darkens. And because I am happy and dance and sing runs on three anapaests (and be-CAUSE / I am HAP- / py and DANCE / and SING), the most dancing line in the poem, and And are gone to praise God and his priest and king moves to the identical tune. Praising and dancing, worship and performance, are metrically one activity: the parents at their devotions and the child at his compulsory cheerfulness are keeping time to the same song, and the song is the system's. Blake could have broken the metre to signal outrage. He does the opposite — he lets the pretty music play on, because the horror he is diagnosing is exactly that everything continues to sound lovely.

Then the trap closes grammatically. God and his priest and king looks like a list of the venerable; the line ends on a comma; and the sentence does not end. Who make up a heaven of our misery carries the objects of praise over the line-break and into the dock. Make up will not settle: they fabricate heaven (a consoling fiction, invented to keep the poor patient); they constitute heaven (their comfort is literally assembled from child labour — warm rooms, swept flues); and they make up for misery with heaven, the compensatory bargain the Church actually preached. The genius of the phrase is that the ideological reading and the economic reading are the same reading: the story told about heaven and the comfort extracted from the child are one manufacture. Blake's Notebook shows him arriving there: the line first read 'Who wrap themselves up in our misery', an image of the comfortable keeping warm in the children's pain, before he widened it into the manufacture of heaven itself. And our — the child's only plural — quietly reveals that he has never been speaking merely for himself. Behind the single black figure in the snow stands the class of children for whom he speaks.

Set the Innocence poem beside this and the pairing sharpens rather than softens it. There, Tom Dacre dreams the angel's bargain — if he'll be a good boy, 'He'd have God for his father & never want joy' — and the poem closes on its moral: 'So if all do their duty, they need not fear harm.' The Experience child has seen through precisely that transaction: They think they have done me no injury answers 'they need not fear harm' across the five-year gap, and make up a heaven names the bargain as a fabrication. What changed between 1789 and 1794 is not the child's circumstances — both freeze, both climb — but his understanding. Innocence believes the consolation; Experience has costed it and knows who profits.

The obvious objection: no real climbing boy talks like this; the poem puts a pamphleteer's analysis in an infant's mouth, and its portrait of the parents — punishing a child for happiness — is caricature. The objection fails twice. First, the implausible articulacy is the device, not a flaw: every plausible voice in the poem has been shown to be compromised — the parents by self-deception, the questioner by the smallness of his pity — so the truth is given to the one speaker with nothing to gain from illusion. Making the child the poem's best thinker is the point at which pathos becomes accusation. Second, the parents are not caricatured; they are excused into something more frightening. They are believers, not monsters — They think they have done me no injury grants them sincerity, and the final line transfers the deepest guilt from them to the system that manufactures their sincerity for them. Blake's target was never two individuals; it was the alliance — God's priest, God's king, joined by that single possessive his — which arranges matters so that ordinary, pious, even loving people can sell a child and feel righteous on the way to church. The questioner has long since vanished from the poem. Whom, then, is the analysis for? The reader — the only adult left in the snow, holding a pity the poem has just shown to be insufficient, and an understanding it has made impossible to refuse.

FORM & STRUCTURE

Form & Structure

How the poem is built, and why it matters

Form & genre

Three quatrains, twelve lines — half the length of the 1789 Innocence 'Chimney Sweeper' (six quatrains). A song, as its book's title says, in the manner of a nursery rhyme or simple hymn: short stanzas, a strong four-beat pulse, chiming rhymes. It is not a ballad in the strict sense (no alternating four- and three-beat lines, no ABCB rhyme). It is a tiny dramatic lyric with two voices.

Voices

Lines 1–3: an adult onlooker, who describes the child and asks him a question (in the anthology text the question has no quotation marks). Lines 4–12: the child. His speech opens with a quotation mark at line 4, reopens at the start of each later stanza (lines 5 and 9) and closes only after misery. After line 3 the adult never speaks again.

Rhyme

AABB / CACA / DEDE. Stanza 1 is two couplets (snow/woe, say/pray). Stanzas 2 and 3 cross-rhyme, and stanza 2 reuses stanza 1's sounds: snow and woe return as rhyme-words in lines 6 and 8. heath/death is the one imperfect rhyme; injury/misery chime mainly on their weak final syllables.

Metre

A loose four-beat line (tetrameter) mixing iambs (da-DUM) and anapaests (da-da-DUM); lines run from 8 to 11 syllables. The onlooker's lines are the most irregular. The child's lines lengthen and grow more anapaestic as his argument builds, until lines 9 and 11 share an identical rhythm.

Syntax

The onlooker speaks in fragments: lines 1–2 have no main verb, and line 3 is a question. The child speaks in three complete sentences — one line (4), then one sentence per stanza (5–8 and 9–12) — built on Because… They… and And because… They…. In the anthology text his nine lines contain no internal punctuation at all.

Punctuation & lineation

Line-ends in the anthology text: comma, exclamation mark, question mark, full stop; none, comma, none, full stop; comma, colon, comma, full stop. Lines 5 and 7 run straight on into the And… lines that complete them. The colon after injury (also on Blake's plate) ties the parents' belief to their worship; the comma after king lets the sentence carry on into Who make up….

Stanza logic

Twelve lines against the Innocence poem's twenty-four: the halving is expressive. The Experience child seems to have less life left, and he needs fewer words because he understands more. The stanzas move inward. Stanza 1 is the street: an adult sees a thing, hears a cry, asks a question. Stanza 2 is the past: the child's history, told as cause and effect. Stanza 3 is the present: the child's analysis of what his parents believe and whom that belief serves. Sighting, history, ideology — the poem's camera moves from outside (a black shape in a white field) to the furthest inside possible, what They think.

Two voices, one handover

Lines 1–3 belong to an adult observer — a passer-by, a stand-in for the reader, or Blake himself. The poem never says which, and that is useful: whoever it is stands where we stand. In the anthology text the observer's question is not in quotation marks, so the voice that calls the child a thing is the same voice that asks after his parents; only the child's words are set off as speech. (Blake's plate has no quotation marks at all, so every voice-boundary is an editor's choice.)

The handover at line 4 is the poem's real turn: the object of line 1 becomes its only intelligence. Asked a small question — where are your parents? — the child answers a much larger one: why am I here? A second, quieter turn comes at line 9, where Because I was becomes because I am: history becomes diagnosis. The third comes in the last line, when a list of the revered turns out to be the subject of an accusation.

Rhyme

  • Stanza 1 rhymes in couplets (AABB): snow/woe, say/pray. This is nursery-rhyme certainty, and it makes the question chime with prayer, as if piety were the natural answer to anything.
  • When the child's explanation begins, the couplets open into cross-rhyme (CACA, DEDE): argument replaces jingle. But stanza 2's alternate rhymes are stanza 1's first rhymes again — snow (line 6) and woe (line 8). The poem cannot get out of its opening sounds: the remembered happy snow is locked to the present woe by the rhyme scheme itself.
  • heath/death (lines 5 and 7) is the only imperfect rhyme: the final /θ/ matches, but the vowels do not (/iː/ against /ɛ/). The rhyme that binds the child's free past to his sentence of death is audibly forced, which is exactly what the syntax claims: Because I was happy… They clothed me in the clothes of death.
  • injury/misery (lines 10 and 12) share a stressed vowel and an identical unstressed ending, but nothing firm: after the strong one-syllable rhymes (snow, woe, say, pray, sing, king), the poem's last rhyme is weak and falling. The nursery music runs down like a clockwork toy at the moment the largest accusation is made.

Metre

The base is a loose four-beat line mixing iambs and anapaests — the metre of songs, hymns and nursery rhymes — but the variations do precise work. Scansion of the anthology text (stressed syllables in capitals, feet divided by ·):

Line Scansion What the rhythm does
1 a LIT · tle black THING · a-MONG · the SNOW Iamb, anapaest, iamb, iamb. The beat lands on thing; black is a demoted stress, so said aloud black thing is two heavy syllables together, and the line's weight falls on the dehumanising noun.
2 CRY-ing · 'WEEP, 'WEEP · in NOTES · of WOE Trochee, spondee, iamb, iamb. Two stresses side by side stall the line: the cry will not fit the lilt.
3 WHERE are thy · FA-ther and · MO-ther, · SAY Two falling triple feet, a trochee and a lone stress: a sing-song, solicitous rhythm that ends abruptly on the command say.
4 they are BOTH · gone UP · to the CHURCH · to PRAY Anapaest, iamb, anapaest, iamb. The child answers in the swinging rhythm that becomes his signature.
5 be-CAUSE · I was HAP · py up-ON · the HEATH Iamb, two anapaests, iamb: the remembered happiness skips.
6 and SMILED · a-MONG · the WIN · ter's SNOW Four iambs, with natural stresses exactly on the beat: the steadiest line in the poem is the memory of being whole.
7 they CLOTHED · me IN · the CLOTHES · of DEATH Formally four iambs, but the beat on in is weak; the voice gives three heavy stresses — clothed, clothes, death.
8 and TAUGHT · me to SING · the NOTES · of WOE The anapaest falls on to sing: the skip that was taught.
9 and be-CAUSE · I am HAP · py and DANCE · and SING Three anapaests and an iamb: the most dance-like line in the poem performs the dancing it describes.
10 they THINK · they have DONE · me no IN · ju-ry The fourth beat can only fall on the weak -ry: the harm is played down even by the cadence.
11 and are GONE · to praise GOD · and his PRIEST · and KING Exactly the rhythm of line 9. The parents' worship and the child's dance move to the same tune.
12 who MAKE · up a HEAV · en of our MIS · er-y Iamb, anapaest, then a rush of light syllables into misery, which falls away unstressed: the poem cannot end on a strong beat.

The central metrical fact is the match between lines 9 and 11. Both have eleven syllables and the same three anapaests and closing iamb, so dancing and praising, the child's compulsory cheerfulness and the parents' devotion, are set to one tune — and the tune is the system's. Blake could have broken the metre to signal outrage. He does the opposite: he lets the pretty rhythm play on, because what he is exposing is a world in which everything goes on sounding pleasant.

Syntax

The onlooker's lines are fragments: A little black thing among the snow, / Crying 'weep, 'weep, in notes of woe! has no main verb, and the question that follows is a single short line. The child's answer is syntactically complete and builds two long sentences on the same frame: Because I was… They clothed me… And taught me… and And because I am… They think… And are gone… Who make up…. This is the syntax of proof — premise, agent, consequence. A child in a protest poem might be given exclamations; this child is given subordinate clauses, the grammar of someone who has worked out the mechanism.

Note what the syntax leaves out: no but, no yet, no plea. There is no contrasting conjunction anywhere in his speech because, from where he stands, nothing contradicts anything — the system is working as designed.

Punctuation and lineation

In the anthology text every pause inside a line belongs to the adult's part: the cry in line 2 is set off by commas, and the question in line 3 pauses before say?. The child's nine lines have no internal punctuation at all, so his speech runs fluently, like something said, or sung, many times before. The poem's only exclamation mark comes at the end of line 2, after woe: it is the onlooker's outburst, not the child's.

Stanza 2 has no punctuation at the end of lines 5 and 7, so it moves in two two-line breaths: Because I was happy upon the heath / And smiled among the winter's snow (what I did) and They clothed me in the clothes of death / And taught me to sing the notes of woe (what they did). The stanza's shape puts the child's happiness and the adults' response in exact balance.

In stanza 3 the punctuation becomes argument. The colon after injury turns the parents' belief into the premise of their worship: they think they have done no injury, and so they are gone to praise. Line 11 ends with a comma, after what looks like a complete list of the great and good — God and his priest and king — but the sentence does not stop: the relative clause Who make up a heaven of our misery carries it into the last line and turns the objects of praise into the accused.

SOUND

Sound

What the poem does to the ear

The missing /s/

The cry 'weep, 'weep is the sweep's street-cry, 'Sweep!', as it sounded in the mouths of children too young to manage the opening cluster: /sw/ collapses to /w/. Two things follow. First, Blake invented nothing: London heard small children cry 'weep, weep' every day and chose to hear 'sweep'. The poem transcribes the sound with the self-deception removed — the pun was found in the street, and the mispronunciation is itself evidence of how young the child was when he was put to work. (The elision marks are an editor's; Blake's plate simply reads 'weep, weep'.) Second, the poem keeps making the sound the child cannot: snow, say, smiled, sing, snow, sing — /s/ everywhere, including the title's Sweeper. The trade-word 'sweep' never appears in the twelve lines; its only trace is the maimed cry.

Keening and moaning

'weep, 'weep is built on the thin, high /iː/, a keening vowel at the pitch of a small child's voice. Against it the poem sets a spine of long /əʊ/: snow, woe, notes, both, clothed, clothes, snow, notes, woe — a moaning vowel that recurs like a tolling bell. Read aloud, the poem alternates the two sounds; its two registers of grief are phonetic before they are verbal.

The th-web

Soft dental fricatives knit the poem's agents together: thy father and mother → They clothed me in the clothes of death → They think they have done me no injury. The whisper-consonant links the parents, their act and their belief in one hushed thread, and makes the reading voice gentle: the poem never raises its voice about them, which is more damning than if it did.

Hard sounds and the -ing chime

A little black thing: after the light A little, black is spat out on its /b/ and /k/, and thing shuts the line. Hard consonants recur at the points of accusation — clothed, taught, God, priest, king — giving the last stanza its bitter edge. The -ing of thing also returns as a rhyme: sing (lines 8 and 9) and king (line 11). The child who is a thing is taught to sing for a world crowned by a king; the sound links the three.

Breath

Happy upon the heath is open-mouthed and breathy: the aspirated /h/ is the sound of exhaled ease. It returns, softened, in happy (line 9), have and his, and finally in heaven — where the breath of the child's happiness has been taken over for someone else's paradise.

Polysyndeton as liturgy

And… And… and dance and sing… and his priest and king: the chained ands are at once a child's breathless chatter and the cadence of the King James Bible, which strings clauses together the same way. The poem attacks the Church in the Church's own rhythm — scripture's syntax turned against scripture's managers. That double quality, childish and biblical, is why the last stanza sounds both naive and prophetic.

Cadence

The poem's music runs down as its argument completes. Firm one-syllable rhymes dominate early (snow, woe, say, pray); the last stanza ends on the weak, falling pair injury/misery, and the final line closes on two unstressed syllables. A reader cannot end the poem with emphasis — misery can only be let fall — and that enforced quietness is the final effect. The Innocence poem closes on a firm stressed rhyme and a promise ('they need not fear harm'); this one closes on misery, with neither.

MOTIFS & SYMBOLS

Motifs & Symbols

Images that recur, and what they accumulate

A motif recurs; a symbol stands for something. This poem's method is to take a motif, repeat it once, and let the repetition turn it into a symbol — the second occurrence always arrives bent.

1. Snow

Line 1: among the snow — an environment, an engulfing white field with a black object in it. Among does the engulfing: the child is surrounded by the whiteness, half-hidden in it, almost invisible. Line 6: smiled among the winter's snow — the same phrase-shape, but now the snow is where a happy child once played: real cold that a loved child could smile in. Blake chose the echo: in his Notebook draft line 6 first ended 'winter's wind', and he changed it to snow. The repetition proves the snow has not changed; the child's relation to it has. Only across the two occurrences does snow become a symbol — of a world whose whiteness (purity, respectability, the churchgoers' image of themselves) is indifferent rather than clean, and which now excludes the blackened child it once delighted. Any reading that fixes snow as 'false purity' from line 1 has to ignore line 6; the motif's movement is the meaning.

2. The cry that becomes a song

Line 2: Crying 'weep, 'weep, in notes of woe! — involuntary, heard in the street. Line 8: taught me to sing the notes of woe — the same phrase, now the object of instruction. Between the two stands the poem's whole theory of oppression: the child's spontaneous grief has been turned into a trained performance, his voice made into his product (the cry advertises his labour; his labour causes the cry). By line 9 the conversion is complete: dance and sing — woe professionalised as visible cheerfulness. The motif traces a production line, cry → lesson → performance. As a symbol, the notes stand for every form of suffering that a system teaches its victims to present acceptably.

3. Clothing and blackness

Line 1: black thing — the child is his covering; soot has replaced skin as his surface. Line 7: They clothed me in the clothes of death — the polyptoton folds the act and the object into each other: the dressing and the shroud are the same event. Clothing a child is the most basic parental act of care; here it is the transfer of death onto his body. The image can be read as an inverted christening: instead of the white robe that welcomes a baby into the community of the saved, black garments induct him into the condemned. Blake's Notebook shows the clothing idea running to the end of the poem: the last line first read 'Who wrap themselves up in our misery' — the child is clothed in death so that the comfortable can wrap themselves in his misery. Across the poem, blackness moves from description (line 1) to investiture (line 7): he is not merely dirty; he has been dressed in his fate by his own family.

4. Going, and going up

Line 4: both gone up to the church; line 11: And are gone to praise. The parents are defined twice by absence, and the absence has a direction: upward. Church sits above street, heaven above church, the child at the bottom in the snow. By line 12 the vertical motif produces the poem's final symbol — a heaven at the top of a structure whose foundation, the syntax insists, is our misery. The geometry matters because it is also the trade's geometry: a sweep climbs upward, inside the flue, so that the household around it may be warm. Every ascent in this poem is made on the child.

5. Happiness

I was happy (5) → smiled (6) → I am happy and dance and sing (9). The strangest motif, because it survives. Past happiness was the pretext (Because I was happy… They clothed me); present happiness is the alibi (because I am happy… They think they have done me no injury). Happiness never belongs to the child as a private good: each time it appears, the adults turn it into a licence. That is the motif's terrible trajectory — joy as provocation, then joy as exoneration. The one thing the child cannot afford to show is the one thing he cannot stop doing.

THEMES

Themes

The ideas the poem is arguing about

01

Joy turned against the child

The poem's most disturbing idea is carried by one word used twice. Because I was happy upon the heath… They clothed me in the clothes of death: the child's happiness is given as the reason he was put to work. And because I am happy and dance and sing, / They think they have done me no injury: his happiness is now the reason no one feels guilty. Before the harm, joy is the pretext; after it, joy is the alibi.

Blake never says the joy is fake — the child still dance[s] and sing[s] in the present tense — and that is what makes the theme so bleak. Real vitality, the best thing about the child, is exactly what the adult world uses to excuse itself. (There is a shadow of doubt, since sing recalls the singing he was taught in line 8; the poem lets genuine joy and trained performance blur, as they would to the parents.)

02

Respectable cruelty and self-deception

There are no villains in the poem. The parents are alive (both), together, and pious: gone up to the church to pray. The child is precise about their state of mind — They think they have done me no injury — and think grants them sincerity. They believe they are good people, and their belief is what lets the harm continue. The colon after injury joins that belief straight to their worship: a clear conscience is what they take to church.

Even the kindest adult in the poem fails. The onlooker pities the little figure and asks Where are thy father and mother, say?, assuming a lost child. The child's answer shows that the problem is not a missing family but a functioning one — and a society that makes its harm feel normal.

03

Church and State as one system

God and his priest and king names the alliance at the top of Blake's England in a single breath: polysyndeton chains the three together, and the possessive his presents priest and king as God's own servants. In the 1790s 'Church and King' was a loyalist slogan, and the monarch was head of the established Church; Blake writes them as one power that the parents praise while their child works in the snow.

That power's product is the poem's final paradox: a heaven of our misery. The heaven promised to the poor as a reward for patient suffering keeps them working; the comfortable heaven of warm, swept houses is built out of their work. Blake is not attacking faith — the poem's cadences are biblical, and its quarrel is with those who have annexed God — but the use of religion to make exploitation feel holy.

04

The trained voice: labour and expression

The child's voice is part of his labour. His street-cry 'weep, 'weep is the trade's advertisement, 'sweep', made into a lament by a mouth too young to say it; then we learn he was taught… to sing the notes of woe. His grief has been drilled into a form that sells his services, and by line 9 he dance[s] and sing[s] — suffering presented in the shape most convenient for others.

Blake's insight is that oppression controls not only what people endure but how they are allowed to express it. Yet the poem also returns the voice to the child: from line 4 to the end, the adult never speaks again, and the trained singer becomes the poem's clearest analyst.

05

Seeing and not seeing

The poem begins with a failure of sight: A little black thing among the snow. The onlooker sees size, colour and setting, but not a child. The question that follows is kindly but too small — it looks for a missing parent where there is a whole system. The child's reply outgrows it so far that the questioner disappears from the poem.

The final pronoun redraws the lines: our misery belongs to the climbing boys, and the heaven to everyone who benefits from them — which includes the poem's readers, who live in warm houses. The poem works as a trap for pity: it invites the tear in lines 1–2 and then shows that feeling sorry is not the same as seeing.

06

Childhood buried alive

Blake sets two worlds against each other. The heath is open, free and unowned, and the winter's snow once held a smiling child; the trade gives him the clothes of death, the black of soot and of mourning. The snow itself does not change — he smiled among it once and is a black thing among it now — so the damage is shown to be human, not natural.

Clothes of death is close to literal (the trade killed through falls, suffocation and soot cancer) and also symbolic: the child has been dressed for his own funeral while still walking the streets. Innocence in this poem is not simply lost with age, as in a story of growing up; it is taken, and then used.

DIFFICULT MOMENTS

Difficult Moments

Where the poem is genuinely undecidable — and what to do about it

Cruxes

1. Because I was happy upon the heath… They clothed me in the clothes of death — what causal claim is this?

The difficulty. Read literally, the parents punished the child for being happy, which seems psychologically absurd.

Competing readings. (a) The child's bitter after-the-fact logic: he knows only that happiness was followed by betrayal, and his because is the reasoning of someone making sense of the senseless. (b) The economic reading: his evident contentment made the sale feel harmless — a thriving child will cope, a smiling child cannot be being wronged — so happiness genuinely was the enabling condition. (c) The doctrinal reading: to a certain kind of piety, untaught natural joy looks like idleness or sin, something to be corrected into discipline and duty, so happiness attracted correction. Evidence: (a) leans on the child's age and the simple chain of And… And…; (b) on the exact parallel with stanza 3, where happiness demonstrably works as evidence (because I am happy… They think they have done me no injury); (c) on taught me to sing the notes of woe — woe as a lesson implies an institution that thinks woe is good for you.

What a strong answer does. It refuses to pick: the line is written so that the child's naive logic and the system's real logic coincide, and that is its horror. The mistake is to soften because into 'although'; the poem means its preposterous causality.

2. And because I am happy and dance and sing — is the happiness real?

The difficulty. The poem's alibi-structure tempts you to call the joy performed, trained, fake — but the child himself asserts it in the present tense, and elsewhere Blake treats a child's joy as an energy that is hard to kill.

Competing readings. Performance: the dancing and singing are literally his trade — the sweep's public cry — so happy names the professional surface the parents mistake for wellbeing. Resilience: the joy is genuine and unkillable, which makes the parents' inference almost reasonable and therefore more terrible. Dissociation: the learned cheerfulness of a child who has got used to his treatment and can no longer feel the injury he knows exists. Evidence: for performance, taught me to sing makes song a lesson two lines earlier; for resilience, the was happy / am happy symmetry insists the same quality persists through the catastrophe; for dissociation, They think they have done me no injury is knowledge held at arm's length, stated without anger.

What a strong answer does. It notices that the poem needs the happiness to be real and used. If it is fake, the parents are merely fooled; if it is real, they have done something worse than deceive themselves — they have made the child's own vitality testify against him. Holding the question open deepens the parents' guilt.

3. Who is accused — They, they, Who?

The difficulty. The pronouns' reach keeps shifting. They are both (4) is unmistakably the parents. By They clothed me (7) the agent could be the parents, the master sweeps or the adult world; They think (10) again reads as the parents; then Who make up a heaven (12) grammatically attaches to the nearest nouns — God and his priest and king — moving the final, largest charge from the parents to the institutions.

Competing readings. Tight grammar: the child ends by accusing the institutions, having half-excused his parents as their instruments. Loose grammar: the relative clause gathers everyone — the parents who praise and the powers praised — into one Who. There is also a textual complication: Blake's plate has no quotation marks at all. The anthology marks lines 4–12 as the child's and leaves the question in line 3 unmarked, so even the boundaries of the voices are an editor's decision. Evidence: the possessive chain his priest and king builds the institutions into a single system, a natural antecedent for Who; but the subject of the sentence throughout has been the parents (They think… And are gone…), and Who caps their sentence.

What a strong answer does. It uses the wobble: the pronoun-drift is the analysis. Responsibility in this poem is a chain along which guilt travels upward, from father and mother to priest and king to the God they claim, and the grammar refuses to let any link detach itself.

4. Who make up a heaven of our misery — fabricate, constitute or compensate?

The difficulty. Make up has three senses and of has two, and every combination gives a different theology.

Competing readings. (i) Invent: heaven is a made-up story, sold to the poor so that present suffering feels like an investment — religion as management of the exploited. (ii) Assemble: their heaven — comfort, warmth, clean flues, moral self-satisfaction — is physically made out of the children's misery, as a house is made of bricks. (iii) Compensate: heaven is offered in exchange for misery, the bargain actually preached to the poor (endure now, be rewarded later). Of as raw material supports (ii); of as source supports (i). Evidence for (i): make up as fabrication sits naturally with They think — the stanza is about manufactured belief. For (ii): the poem's economics — everything the adults have, from a warm church to an easy conscience, has been extracted from the child. For (iii): the Innocence poem states the bargain openly ('So if all do their duty, they need not fear harm'), and this line is its audit. Blake's Notebook adds a fourth piece of evidence: the line first read 'Who wrap themselves up in our misery'. That cancelled version is pure (ii) — the comfortable warming themselves in the children's suffering — and the revision to make up a heaven keeps that sense while adding fabrication and theology.

What a strong answer does. It shows that the senses are not alternatives but a mechanism: the fiction (i) is what enables the extraction (ii), and the promised exchange (iii) is the fiction's selling price. Then it notes the order of the last two nouns: after heaven comes misery — the poem ends by placing them as the system prefers, heaven on top and misery underneath, carrying the weight.

CLOSE ANALYSIS

Close Analysis

The moments that repay pressure, worked through

Quotation analysis

1. A little black thing among the snow,

Dehumanising noun; visual antithesis; indefinite article.

The line performs the perception it condemns: whoever speaks it sees size, colour and category, but not a child — thing is not Blake's cruelty but the world's, transcribed. The indefinite article does quiet work: a thing, one of an unnumbered many, glimpsed and generalised in the same instant — against which the title's definite The Chimney-Sweeper reads as the label for a social type rather than a person's name. Among the snow sets the poem's palette (one black mark on a white field — the composition Blake etched below the text on his plate) and its politics: the child is in the whiteness but not of it, an inclusion that the preposition makes feel like engulfment. The four-beat pattern lands a beat on thing, so the metre itself objectifies him.

Intention and effect: Blake opens inside the language of the passer-by, so that the reader begins the poem complicit, using the very grammar the child will spend nine lines correcting.

2. Crying 'weep, 'weep, in notes of woe!

Found pun; spondee; auditory imagery.

The cry is the trade's street advertisement, 'sweep! sweep!', in a mouth too young for its opening sound: the /s/ drops and what remains is, by accident of pronunciation, the truth — weep. The pun is found, not made; London had been hearing it for years and choosing to hear commerce rather than grief, so the line simply removes the city's earplugs. The anthology italicises the word and sets each cry off with commas; the line's single exclamation mark comes after woe, so the outburst is the onlooker's, not the child's. Metrically the two stressed monosyllables jam the nursery lilt — the cry will not scan, will not be carried by the song, and that resistance is its pathos. Notes of woe turns the cry into music, and notes looks ahead: six lines later we learn the music was taught, which retrospectively poisons even this spontaneous-seeming grief.

Intention and effect: Blake makes the reader's ear repeat society's failure — you must hear 'sweep' inside weep to understand the line, performing the substitution the adult world refuses.

3. Where are thy father and mother, say?

Question and imperative; archaic second person; unmarked speech.

The question is kindness at its least useful: it assumes absence, misfortune, an anomaly — that a crying child alone in the snow must have lost someone. Thy cuts two ways: it is the intimate form used to children and social inferiors, so it can be warmth or condescension, and the poem does not decide. The appended say? — a bare command after a comma, with its own stress — tips concern into demand: even compassion, addressed downward, arrives as an order to account for yourself. In the anthology the line carries no quotation marks, so it comes in the same voice that called him a thing. The child's answer will expose the question's scale-error: the parents are not missing but present elsewhere, at prayer, which no where question can reach.

Intention and effect: Blake plants the reader's stand-in inside the poem and gives him the wrong question, so that the child's outsized answer measures the distance between pity and understanding.

4. They are both gone up to the church to pray.

Matter-of-fact declarative; both; directional irony.

The line's flatness is its horror: no protest, a full stop, the tone of a child reporting a routine — because it is one. Both quietly dismantles every softening story the question offered — not orphaned, not a broken home, but a complete and functioning family whose two adults have made the same choice. Gone up gives the poem its vertical axis: the parents ascend (to church, towards heaven) while the child remains at street level in the snow, and the last stanza prices that ascent. The church is where they are instead of here; piety becomes a location, and the location is 'away'.

Intention and effect: Blake lets the most damning sentence in the poem sound the most ordinary, so the reader feels the normalisation before being told about it.

5. Because I was happy upon the heath

Causal conjunction; pastoral setting; past tense.

Because is the poem's most audacious word: it claims that happiness was not incidental to the child's fate but its cause. The claim works at every level the poem contains — psychological (a visibly thriving child can be sold without visible cruelty), doctrinal (untaught joy can look to the pious like idleness needing correction) and rhetorical (the child has learned that in his world consequences follow joy). The heath is everything the flue is not — open, level, unowned — and was seals it in the finished past. The aspirated happy… heath opens the mouth, a sound-memory of ease that the poem lets back in only as happy again and finally heaven.

Intention and effect: Blake forces the reader through a logic that should not make sense but, in this society, does — the shock is not that the reasoning is alien but that it is recognisable.

6. They clothed me in the clothes of death

Polyptoton; inverted care; metaphor.

Clothing a child is elementary parental care; here the act of care is the transfer of death onto the body, and the polyptoton (clothed… clothes) seals act and object into a single gesture — the dressing is the shroud. The metaphor is both literal (the sweep's soot-blackened garb, the uniform of a trade that killed by cancer, suffocation and falls) and sacramental: an inverted christening, black garments in place of white, induction into the condemned rather than the saved. Of death hangs ambiguous — clothes belonging to death, made of death, leading to death — and the line does not choose. The agent remains They: by now the pronoun has widened past two parents towards everyone whose comfort requires the uniform.

Intention and effect: Blake corrupts the tenderest domestic verb in the language, so that the reader cannot get an innocent sense of clothed back afterwards — the poem's method in miniature.

7. And taught me to sing the notes of woe.

Repetition with variation; institutional verb; irony of song.

Notes of woe returns from line 2 transformed: there it was heard in the street, involuntary; here it has a syllabus. Taught is the poem's coldest verb — suffering not merely inflicted but instructed — and it turns the child's grief into a skill that serves his masters: the cry advertises the trade; the trained voice is the product. This is the poem's theory of oppression in one line: systems do not only cause pain, they manage its expression, licensing the forms in which the victim may be heard. The disquieting consequence is that everything the child says to us, lines 4–12, comes in a voice we have just been told was trained: his testimony arrives in the enemy's medium.

Intention and effect: Blake implicates expression itself, leaving the reader to wonder whether even this poem's song is one of the notes of woe the system taught.

8. And because I am happy and dance and sing,

Anapaestic metre; polysyndeton; present tense.

The scansion is the analysis: and be-CAUSE / I am HAP- / py and DANCE / and SING — three anapaests at a run, the poem's most dancing line, so that the metre performs the compulsory lightness it describes. The polysyndeton is double-voiced: a child's breathless chatter (and… and… and) and the cadence of the King James Bible, so the sentence sounds at once naive and liturgical — the Church's own rhythm carrying the evidence against it. Am insists the happiness is current and real; the line's grammar is the first premise of the parents' reasoning ('because happy, therefore unharmed'), and the child recites it knowing exactly what it will be used to prove. Two lines later the parents' worship, And are gone to praise God and his priest and king, moves to the identical tune: dance and devotion are one music.

Intention and effect: Blake sets the alibi to the prettiest rhythm in the poem, so that the reader is charmed by it in the act of seeing through it.

9. They think they have done me no injury:

Verb of belief; understatement; colon.

Everything rests on think: not lied, not pretended — believe. The parents are granted sincerity, which is far worse than hypocrisy, because sincere belief is what institutions manufacture; the line's target is the machinery that produces a good conscience. No injury is the vocabulary of the court and the account-book, the register in which harm is inspected and found absent; the child borrows their language for his own case, deadpan. The colon then turns belief into action: what follows from thinking you have done no injury is going to church. The soft They think they whispers, and the line falls away on the weak ending of injury: the poem never raises its voice where an accusation is largest.

Intention and effect: Blake moves evil from cruelty to self-excusing belief, and the reader — another adult who thinks well of themselves — is not allowed to stand outside the diagnosis.

10. Who make up a heaven of our misery.

Relative clause; word with several meanings; first-person plural.

The sentence seems complete at king, — but the relative clause carries it over the line-break and arrests the objects of praise. Make up refuses to settle among its senses — fabricate (heaven as a consoling fiction), constitute (their comfort literally assembled from child labour), compensate (heaven as the promised exchange for patience) — and the phrase's power is that the senses describe one mechanism: the story is the extraction. Blake's first draft, 'Who wrap themselves up in our misery', had only the image of comfort; the revision adds the manufacture of heaven itself. Our is the child's only plural, and it detonates quietly: he has been speaking all along for a class, not a case — the single black figure in the snow stands for many. The poem ends on misery, falling away unstressed, the word physically underneath heaven in the line as in the world.

Intention and effect: Blake compresses his whole critique of institutional religion into one relative clause, and leaves the reader holding the question that survives it — who is heaven for, and who pays?

CRITICAL LENSES

Critical Lenses

What each way of reading makes visible, and what it flattens

Critical lenses

Marxist / materialist

The lens makes visible that this is a poem about production. The child is a commodity (a little black thing — the grammar of goods, not persons), his voice is his advertising ('weep, 'weep cries his availability through the streets), and heaven is the surplus extracted from his labour: Who make up a heaven of our misery describes, with economic precision, comfort assembled from the exploited. Put bluntly, sweeps died so that the better-off could have warm rooms free of smoke. Religion appears as ideology in the strict sense — the belief-system (They think they have done me no injury) that reconciles the exploiters to the exploitation — anticipating by half a century Marx's 1844 description of religion as 'the opium of the people'.

What it flattens: Blake's own faith. The lens has to call the child's clarity 'class consciousness' and heaven a pure fiction, but Blake attacked the priest's heaven on behalf of a real spiritual life, not against one — the poem's rage is that of a believer watching belief used as a weapon. It also has little to say about why the poem is beautiful, and why the nursery music matters.

Historicist

The lens restores the poem's documentary edge. Climbing boys were set to work as young as four or five, because small bodies fit narrow flues. Their trade's cancer had been identified by the surgeon Percivall Pott in 1775, the first cancer traced to an occupation. Jonas Hanway had campaigned for them (his Sentimental History of Chimney Sweepers appeared in 1785), and Parliament had legislated: the Chimney Sweepers Act of 1788 set a minimum age of eight and even required masters to send their apprentices to Sunday worship out of their sweeping clothes — but its clause licensing master sweeps was voted down in the Lords, and the Act went largely unenforced. Blake published this poem six years later. Read historically, They think they have done me no injury indicts not just two parents but a nation that had already passed its law, filed the problem as solved, and gone back to church; the poem is written in the tense of failed reform.

What it flattens: the poem's designed timelessness. Blake strips out every date, name and place, so that the mechanism — joy converted to labour, misery converted to heaven — stays readable in any century; historicism pressed too hard turns a diagnosis of ideology into a period piece.

Psychoanalytic

The lens illuminates both minds the poem contains. In the parents: disavowal — They think they have done me no injury is the structure of knowing-and-not-knowing, belief kept up against the evidence because the alternative (we have sold our child) is unbearable, and the church visit is the ritual that launders the knowledge. In the child: the compliant cheerfulness of a victim who has adapted — I am happy and dance and sing as a false self presented to keep the adult world manageable, while the true account (clothes of death) is delivered flatly, without feeling, to a stranger. The cry itself is overdetermined: weep is what his mouth makes of 'sweep', grief speaking through the very word that denies it — a slip institutionalised as a street-cry.

What it flattens: agency and accuracy. The child is not a case study; he is the poem's best analyst, and his conclusions are presented as true, not as symptoms. A purely clinical reading also privatises what Blake insists is systemic: it treats as family pathology what the last line assigns to priest and king.

Formalist

The lens takes seriously what the poem is made of: a nursery quatrain carrying an indictment. Couplet chime (snow/woe, say/pray), four-beat lines and an anapaestic lilt — the sound of childhood safety — are made to carry their opposite, and the mismatch is the meaning: the form performs the society it accuses, pretty on the surface, with misery holding it up underneath. Within that frame the local effects are unusually economical: the steadiest iambic line (6) is the unbroken past; the one spondee ('weep, 'weep) is the cry the lilt cannot absorb; the sentence that runs on past king, into Who… is the exposure; the one weak rhyme (injury/misery) is the dying fall.

What it flattens: the referent. A purely formalist account can describe the machine and miss that soot cancer is not a verbal effect; the poem's occasion — real children dying — presses on its language in a way form alone cannot register, and Blake built the poem to keep that pressure impossible to ignore.

Reader-response

The lens notices that the poem contains a reader: the questioner of lines 1–3, who sees, pities and asks — exactly what we are doing. His question is well meant and structurally useless, and the child's answer overshoots it so far that the questioner never speaks again; the poem dramatises the uselessness of sympathetic curiosity. By the end the only person left to receive the analysis is us, and the child's our misery quietly redraws the boundary: he speaks for a class we are not in, from which our warmth is extracted. (The Innocence poem makes the point openly — 'So your chimneys I sweep' — and this poem inherits that pointed second person silently.) The poem is a trap for pity: it invites the tear and then demonstrates the tear's insufficiency.

What it flattens: certainty. Read purely as an experience-machine, the poem becomes open-ended, a mirror for each reader — but Blake is not open-ended here. The poem has a verdict, and a response-centred account risks replacing the verdict with our feelings about it, which is precisely the parents' manoeuvre.

Ecocritical (briefly)

The lens foregrounds the two environments: the heath — open, unowned, unproductive ground where a child can simply be — against the street and the flue, nature converted into infrastructure. The child's path (heath to chimney, green to black) is enclosure in miniature: a creature of the commons captured by the economy of coal and smoke. Even the snow changes function, from a place of play to a place of exposure.

What it flattens: the poem's insistence that the agents are not 'industrialisation' as a kind of weather but named institutions with addresses — church and crown. The ecocritical frame can dissolve responsibility into process, which the final stanza exists to prevent.

OTHER READINGS

Other Readings

Contested interpretations, and where each is weak

Alternative readings

1. The poem as an attack on religion itself

Evidence: the unbroken chain God and his priest and king; prayer presented as abandonment (gone up to the church to pray); heaven as fabrication (make up).

Weakness: the God of the poem is a God claimed by others — his priest and king describes a deity annexed by institutions — and Blake, a Christian visionary hostile to churches, is attacking the annexation. The reading also cannot explain why the child's own idiom (polysyndeton, biblical cadence) stays scriptural: the poem fights the Church in the Bible's voice, which an atheist reading flattens into confusion.

2. The parents as fellow victims

Evidence: poverty made selling children to sweeps a survival economy; They think they have done me no injury grants them sincere belief; the final accusation moves upward, to the powers who make up both heaven and the parents' good conscience. On this reading the poem indicts a system that manufactures its agents' innocence.

Weakness: Because I was happy — the child twice makes his parents' motive his happiness, which no economic explanation requires; and the poem pointedly notes they have both gone to church. Blake leaves the parents their sincerity but not an excuse: the system-reading risks doing their 'thinking' for them a second time.

3. The child's joy as indestructible innocence

Evidence: I am happy and dance and sing in the present tense; the was/am symmetry insists that the same vitality persists; elsewhere in Blake, a child's energy is the divine thing institutions fail to kill. On this reading the poem is not about destroyed innocence but about innocence surviving and being harvested.

Weakness: taught me to sing has already made his performances a lesson, so the dancing may be trade patter rather than joy; and the reading drifts towards consolation — precisely what the Experience version exists to refuse.

4. The sweep as a ghost
