Evidence: clothes of death read as literal grave-clothes; the eerie calm of the analysis; a black figure in white snow addressing a passer-by has the look of an apparition; our misery spoken for the dead sweeps collectively.

Weakness: the poem's present tenses are stubbornly physical — crying, dancing and singing in the street now — and its documentary force (this is happening, six years after Parliament claimed to have regulated it) drains away if the child is already past saving. The reading buys atmosphere at the cost of urgency.

5. The child as a ventriloquist's dummy

Evidence: no small child analyses ideology in subordinate clauses; the official word injury and the tricolon of powers are a pamphleteer's tools; Blake has plainly lent the child his own conclusions. On this reading the poem's flaw (or device) is that Experience speaks through rather than as a child.

Weakness: the poem anticipates the objection — it shows us the training (taught me to sing) that produced this articulacy, and it needs the child's analysis to outstrip every adult's precisely to invert the hierarchy of who understands. The implausibility is the engine of the accusation, not a leak in it.

6. The poem as a trap for the reader's pity

Evidence: the questioner — the reader's stand-in — asks a compassionate, useless question and is never heard again; the child's answer exceeds and so exposes it; the Innocence poem's 'So your chimneys I sweep' points the finger outward, and this poem inherits the aim. On this reading the poem's subject is the insufficiency of sympathy — feeling sorry being the emotional wing of they think they have done me no injury.

Weakness: lines 1–2 are not satirised — their pity is rendered with real tenderness (little, the grieved exclamation after woe) — and Blake plainly wants the tear as well as the verdict. A reading that treats compassion as the poem's dupe mistakes a starting-point for a target.

REVISION NOTES

Revision Notes

The working notes, quotation by quotation

Title

The Chimney-Sweeper

Analysis
  • Title itself is relatively self-explanatory
  • Anthology/exam spelling: Chimney-Sweeper (hyphen); Blake's plate: 'THE Chimney Sweeper'
  • The not 'a' or a name → a type/archetype: all oppressed children, not one individual
    • Suffering is systemic, not isolated
  • Plain job-title → sounds like 'just a job' but hides abuse + neglect
    • Irony: society normalises injustice by reducing it to an ordinary label
  • When compared alongside its companion poem 'The Chimney Sweeper' in Songs of Innocence, acting as a powerful commentary on Blake's view of the human experience
    • Songs of Innocence: optimism, naive light, where suffering can be overcome through spiritual faith and innocence
    • Songs of Experience: darker side of life where child's suffering is more fully acknowledged and criticised
      • Harsh reality of exploitation and societal neglect
  • Blake underscores stark contrast between the two states of being
    • Innocence (naivety, purity, and spiritual faith)
    • Experience (disillusionment, suffering, and societal critique)
  • Repetition of title creates sense of unity, while highlighting the profound shift in perspective between the two volumes
    • Perspective (not circumstance) has shifted: the suffering was always there, now seen with awareness + anger

Structure + overview

Analysis
  • Made up of three quatrains (four-line stanzas)
  • Masking the complexity of the ideas by the simplicity of the structure
  • Split up into two main sections:
    • Initial sighting of the little black thing (the chimney sweep) in the snow
    • And the child's reply which demonstrates his knowledge of his position using his 'experience'
  • Contrast in length with Songs of Innocence (12 lines vs 24) shows the deterioration and weakening life-force/death of the chimney sweep from one poem to the next
  • This poem (Experience):
    • Unnamed adult speaker chances upon a weeping chimney-sweep in the snow, he asks him where his parents are
    • Young boy takes over the narrative and explains his parents are in the church praying
    • A child once full of innocence and joy, is now full of despair, condemned to a short and brutal life
    • Parents are ignorant of their child's real suffering believing that they have acted in his best interests as they went up to church to offer their praise

Songs of Innocence and of Experience

Analysis
  • Songs of Innocence and of Experience Shewing the Two Contrary States of the Human Soul (1794) is the full title of his collection (illustrates Blake's belief of dual nature of human condition)
    • Coexistence of innocence and experience, light and dark, joy and suffering
    • Contrasts the joy, freedom, and happiness that are the natural state of childhood with the oppression and exploitation of contemporary society
  • Songs of Innocence (1789) present idealised and optimistic view of life, focusing on purity, joy, and the innocence of childhood
  • Songs of Experience (1794) explore much darker and more cynical view of the world, exploring themes of corruption, suffering and the loss of innocence, often criticising social and religious institutions
    • This volume reflects Blake's growing disillusionment with the world
  • Blake's original punctuation (plate): no quotation marks, 'weep, weep' (no apostrophes), '&' for 'and', 'Priest & King' capitalised
    • Anthology modernises: quotation marks, smiled, priest and king lower case
  • Blake's draft (Notebook, c. 1793): 'winter's wind' → snow; last line first 'Who wrap themselves up in our misery' (crossed out)

Context — climbing boys + the Church

Analysis
  • Poverty drove families to sell their children into chimney sweeping (few options for survival + lacking stable income)
    • By selling them a master chimney sweep provided financial benefit + alleviated the responsibility of child care
    • Parishes also bound pauper children to sweeps
  • Started as young children (as young as 4–5) due to small bodies needed to climb into narrow, soot-filled flues
    • Hazardous, causes respiratory illnesses, burns, and even deformities due to prolonged crawling in confined spaces
    • Soot → scrotal cancer ('chimney sweep's cancer'): Percivall Pott 1775 = first cancer linked to a job
    • Harsh reality of child labour deeply troubled social reformers (Jonas Hanway)
  • 1788 Chimney Sweepers Act: min age 8 → largely unenforced (Blake writing 6 years later)
    • Act even said apprentices must go to church on Sunday, not in sweeping clothes → poem: child in clothes of death while parents pray
    • Not properly enforced until the 1875 Act (sweeps registered with police)
  • Church justified child labour through religious, economic, and moral reasoning which aligned with the broader societal norms of the 18th and 19th centuries
    • Everyone had a God-given place in society and poverty and hardship were a part of God's plan
    • Suffering faithfully would lead to rewards in heaven while emphasising obedience to parents and employers being virtuous
    • Hard work was equated with moral goodness
    • Character-building and a way to instil discipline and responsibility in children since idleness was believed to be sinful

Rhyme + metre

Analysis
  • Not regular couplets throughout:
    • 1st quatrain: rhyming couplets (A, A, B, B)
    • 2nd and 3rd quatrains: alternate rhyme (A, B, A, B)
  • Partial rhyme: the heath/death rhyme suggests something's not quite right, speaking to the way that the chimney sweep's natural enjoyment of being outdoors has been replaced by a kind of death — the death of his childhood
  • Mainly single/masculine rhyme (emphasis on the final stressed syllables) e.g., snow and woe
  • Weak/falling rhyme in last stanza: INjury / MISery — stress on the first syllable, chime mainly on unstressed '-ry' → dying fall
  • Line lengths vary between 8 and 11 syllables
  • Metrical/rhythmic structure is irregular
    • Combination of iambs (de-DUM) and anapaests (de-de-DUM)
    • a LIT- | tle black THING | a-MONG | the SNOW,
  • Occasional spondee (DUM-DUM)
    • WEEP, WEEP (for emphasis) and uncontrollability
  • Lines 9 + 11 same rhythm (3 anapaests + iamb) → dancing = praising, same tune
  • The poem develops a very sing-song feel to it, like a nursery rhyme, reflective of the chimney sweep being a child (making childish rhythms appropriate)
    • Also singing the notes of woe reflects the poem being the song of the child's misery
    • Also appropriate as the main subject is the exploitation of childhood
  • Diction is characteristically quite plain and simple with highly symbolic and richness in meaning
    • Accessible to a wider audience
    • Simplicity used to communicate powerful messages in a direct way (resonant and impactful)

Speakers + voice

Analysis
  • Speaker 1 (lines 1–3) could be a stranger, the reader, or just Blake, aware of the child's neglect
    • Anthology: line 3 has no quotation marks → same voice as the thing description
  • Speaker 2 (lines 4–12) is the chimney sweep telling his tale (most chimney sweeps were male, but there were still female sweeps too)
  • Contrasts to the first 'The Chimney Sweeper' from Songs of Innocence, where the sweep comes across as indoctrinated by what the authorities tell him, this sweep talks from experience and thus has perspective and understanding on why he finds himself in such a dire situation
  • He acknowledges his parents and more widely, organised religion are to blame for his exploitation. He talks wisely, and is able to neatly sum up the hypocrisy of the age through the paradox in the final line: Who make up a heaven of our misery
    • That is the church and society who thrive off exploitation
  • This sweep could be a ghost or visitation as he states clothes of death, hinting that he may be speaking from beyond earthly experience, revealing that society has doomed him to a short and difficult existence
1–2

A little black thing among the snow, / Crying 'weep, 'weep, in notes of woe!

Analysis
  • Literally it characterises the boy's physical condition as a chimney sweep, being covered in soot to the point of being unrecognisable
    • Contrast between child's blackened appearance and the white snow, which shows the child's degradation and isolation from the natural world, while dehumanising the child through the diction thing suggesting that he is viewed as a mere creature
    • He becomes unidentifiable as a mere black shape, a dark mark on the conscience of society
  • Metaphorically the contrast between the black of the boy and the white of the snow becomes symbolic
    • (One reading) ironically describing how society sees him as a being besmirched, stained, and blackened by 'original sin' (Adam and Eve) among the snowy white 'purity' and idealised virtue of the Church and society
    • Using original sin, it justifies the suffering of the innocent child as a form of redemption/expiation (making amends for guilt) for humanity's inherent sinfulness
    • By opening the poem in this way it immediately exposes the dissonance between the Church's teachings of purity and salvation and the grim reality of its complicity in human suffering
  • The child, which acts as an emblem/symbol of innocence is paradoxically branded as impure by the very system that should protect him
  • The sound patterning emphasises the child's distress
  • The epizeuxis (repetition of words in immediate succession) 'weep, 'weep
    • Acts as an echo (allusion) to the other 'The Chimney Sweeper' where it undoes the false moralising of the first poem where despite 'weep[ing]' they find comfort in the idea that God will grant them happiness if they only work obediently and dutifully
    • Not the same boy: Innocence speaker's mother is dead + father 'sold' him; here both parents alive, at church → a whole family chose this
  • Alliteration of the semi-vowel (a speech sound intermediate between a vowel and a consonant like /w/ or /y/) through weep and woe links the further action of crying to the sweep's life of misery
  • Repetition of the long 'ee' sound creates a high-pitched, reedy quality, aurally mimicking the thin weak voice of a young child crying for help
  • Youth, physical frailty and vulnerability is also emphasised through the assonance of notes of woe (nOtes of wOE) mimics a sound of despair and a depressing song
  • Delicate consonance of A little black thing among the snow acts as a gentle reminder that despite the sweep being world-weary and experienced, he is still small and vulnerable
  • The apostrophe before 'weep (added by editors — Blake's plate just has 'weep, weep') indicates a letter is missing: chimney sweeps normally chant out 'sweep! sweep!' to advertise their services (elision: purposeful missing letter(s))
    • Thus the diction 'weep transforms a cry of labour by a young child with underdeveloped language skills which lead to him struggling to pronounce his words clearly into a cry of pain and despair
    • The pun reinforces the dehumanisation of the child as his voice is reduced to the very labour that defines his existence, creating a strong sense of pathos
Effect, style & response
  • Makes the reader feel distraught, uncomfortable, sad, empathetic and Blake intends to put the reader in that position as part of an argument that everyone bears some responsibility for the way society works (or doesn't work) where the reader becomes a spectator to the small child's suffering
3–4

Where are thy father and mother, say? / They are both gone up to the church to pray.

Analysis
  • The unidentified adult speaker addresses the child using the archaic possessive pronoun thy
    • Used to express familiarity and among people who were intimate or to people who were of a younger age or lower status (like 'ton'/'tuo'/'tu' in French/Italian/Spanish)
    • A sudden intimacy that contrasts with the earlier dehumanisation of the child
  • The direct question subtly accuses the absent parents while drawing the reader's attention to the broader systems that permit such suffering to persist
    • Sets up child's response as devastating in its naivety and acceptance of his fate
  • The 4th line is the child's voice which emerges to take over the narrative
    • Child's voice contrasts between the adult's perspective and the child's innocent yet resigned explanation of his plight (unfortunate circumstance) makes the situation more poignant (emotional, bitter and regretful) through the naivety
    • Internalised his suffering as normal
    • Blake empowers a figure that society typically silences, using this as evidence against these systems of exploitation and hypocrisy
  • The juxtaposition between the parents' spiritual pursuits with their neglect of their child's physical and emotional needs
    • The abandonment is literal being physically absent and symbolic by relinquishing (giving up) their responsibility by entrusting the child to harsh labour where the parents believe they have fulfilled their duties by seeking divine approval for their choices
    • Pervasive influence of religious teachings that prioritised suffering as a path to salvation
  • The consonance (voiced and not) runs throughout both of the lines, where the gentleness of this sound suggests the physical weakness of the chimney sweep, while linking directly to the father and mother which helps highlight the fact they aren't around due to the lack of sound and presence
  • Solidifies the rhyme scheme for the stanza as AABB, where they also continue the poem's tetrameter in a mix of trochees (DUM-da), anapaests (da-da-DUM) and iambs (da-DUM)
    • Allows for a very intuitive sound for the poem making it flexible so that the rhythm of the first speaker's voice contrasts with the rhythm of the child's voice
    • The initial stress in the speaker's question Where captures the forceful inquiry of a concerned adult
    • Meanwhile, the two unstressed syllables in the first anapaest of the child's response capture both his weakness and his innocence and his inability to make out strong forceful words due to his dehumanised and malnourished state
Effect, style & response
  • More personal and heartbreaking for the reader as they imagine if this someone they were familiar with, submitted to this cruelty
5–8

Because I was happy upon the heath / And smiled among the winter's snow, / They clothed me in the clothes of death / And taught me to sing the notes of woe.

Analysis
  • Remembers a time of happiness, purity and innocence
  • Diction of heath meaning a vast grassland suggesting a contrast between the open countryside in his earliest years to the claustrophobic and filthy urban conditions where he now lives and works
  • Breathy alliteration of the aspirated /h/ in heath and happy and sibilance of smiled and snow emphasises former contentment in the natural setting
    • Juxtaposition with the child's previous smiled with his current 'weep[ing]' revealing his loss of innocence
  • The snow symbolises his coldness and suffering now — but he once smiled in the same winter snow → an indication of his prior emotional and spiritual warmth
    • The juxtaposition of him having smiled in the snow then, when now he is just Crying 'weep, 'weep, in notes of woe!, showing how he was once happy to be out in the snow but no longer
    • Whiteness of the snow, suggesting purity, contrasts with the way the sweep is now disfigured by his covering of soot and ash
    • Blake's draft had 'winter's wind' → changed to snow = deliberate echo of line 1
  • The causal conjunction at the beginning of the line implies the child's former state of happiness and ignorance of sin was intolerable to the Church's doctrine like a problem that needed correcting
    • Subtly criticises a system that thrives on guilt and suffering rather than fostering natural joy and freedom
  • Boy's punishment for his former happiness being lines 7 and 8
    • How he was put into labour because he was caught being happy
  • Ambiguity in the pronoun They which is deliberate and powerful in implicating both the parents and the church creating a web of blame
    • Parents are directly responsible for the child's suffering even though they are unaware of it
    • Church is responsible for the ideological framework which justifies the idea
    • Lack of clarity forces the reader to see the child's suffering as systemic, enabled by societal norms, parental actions, and religious teachings
  • Diction of clothes of death can be literally the soot-covered rags that blacken the child or metaphorically allude to the inevitability of an early death due to the physical toll that chimney-sweeping had on very young, under-developed and often malnourished boys
    • Helps draw out competing forces at work in society: life and joy vs. death and misery. While the child wants to live joyfully, society forces him towards death and misery
  • Polyptoton (repetition of words derived from the same root) of clothed and clothes intensifies the claustrophobic tone and underscores the oppression that these boys have suffered
    • Suggests that whoever put the sweep in the clothes of death did so intentionally. That people exploit children with full knowledge of what they are doing
    • The soft consonance in They clothed me in the clothes of death (THey cloTHed me in THe cloTHes of deaTH), which recalls the unknown whereabouts of thy father and mother (THy faTHer and moTHer) in line 3
  • The diction taught shows how he had to be forced to learn to sing the notes of woe while smiled came to him naturally
    • Criticism of religious and societal institutions, where instead of fostering joy and freedom, they impose suffering as a moral and spiritual obligation
    • The child's learnt sorrow contrasts to the innate happiness he once knew
    • Suffering is an artificial construct rather than a natural state (contrasts to Christian belief that suffering is natural after the original sin where Adam and Eve caused all generations after them to be cursed)
  • Repetition of notes of woe emphasises the enduring and cyclical nature of this suffering
    • Also acts as a kind of refrain like in a song, which is in keeping with the sweep's act of singing the notes of woe where the assonance of this phrase also adds to the songlike quality
  • In the poem's companion in Songs of Innocence, the child is 'taught' to believe that society is a certain way, and that its harshness and brutality is just a fact of life
    • The church persuades people that if they don't complain in this life, they will be rewarded by God in the next (heaven) thus preventing people from striving for improvements in this world
    • Misery and suffering, then, are things that the child has to learn, and not innate characteristics of life itself, where the poem argues that some institutions like the Church actively suppress the more joyful elements of life
  • The polysyndeton ('And… And…') in this stanza and the next subtly mimics the language and tone of the King James Version of the Bible, and thus by harnessing the Bible's tone the poem seems to mock the Church, arguing that the Church has lost the true spirit and meaning of Christianity
9–12

And because I am happy and dance and sing, / They think they have done me no injury: / And are gone to praise God and his priest and king, / Who make up a heaven of our misery.

Analysis
  • The present tense of am offers a confusing contrast as we question how he can be happy and dancing if he is woeful in the snow
    • Past tense ('danced and sang') wouldn't rhyme with king
    • Could also indicate an enduring hope of salvation, a temporary relief from despair, from clinging to religious promises, even if they are ultimately hollow
    • Links to the companion poem in Songs of Innocence as the children find genuine solace in religious belief, imagining angelic visions of freedom and warmth
      • 'Then down a green plain leaping laughing they run' (Innocence)
      • 'Tho' the morning was cold, Tom was happy & warm, / So if all do their duty, they need not fear harm.' (Innocence)
  • Polysyndeton of 'and' in the first line and the simplicity of the syntax reveals the child's own simplicity and ingenuousness (innocent, naive)
    • Also gives the line a playful, jumpy feel that fits with the image of a happy child
    • Also evokes the sound of the KJV Bible (a version full of polysyndeton) pitting its own vision of Christianity against the corrupted version of the church
  • Lack of any sign of distress from the child allows the parents to be in a state of blissful ignorance or wilful denial as They think they have done me no injury:
    • Rationalised their actions as being in the child's best interest (both spiritually and materially)
    • Turning a blind eye to the terrible conditions
    • Colon after injury → their belief leads straight to their worship
  • The gentleness of the /th/ alliteration in They think they (THey THink THey) echoes the consonance in line 3 linking the They to the father and mother figures
  • The repeated pronoun They has an accusatory tone, making it clear that the sweep knows, from experience, who is to blame for his miserable existence
  • More polysyndeton in God and his priest and king which implies the connection between religion and government in a unified system of exploitation
    • Both are complicit in perpetuating the suffering of the vulnerable and that an individual's relationship with God and/or spirituality is mediated by more worldly concerns and that you can't have one without the others
    • Alliteration between gone and God emphasises the link between societal neglect and organised religion, that people who praise God are gone from their responsibilities
    • Linking the priest to king draws the full picture of blame (Blake's plate capitalises: 'Priest & King')
    • The distortion of the Trinity — rather than being 'Father, Son, and Holy Spirit' it becomes God, priest and king, named in a single line, which is rhetorically devastating. It refuses to separate theology from politics, saying these forces are not incidental to the child's suffering but rather that they are its authors
  • The verb make up suggesting fabrication or invention, implying that the promise of heavenly rewards is a constructed narrative designed to pacify and control the oppressed
    • Blake's draft: 'Who wrap themselves up in our misery' (crossed out) → final version = they invent heaven itself
  • Oxymoron of heaven of our misery is very ironic as it underscores the hypocrisy of the system
    • A true heaven cannot coexist with misery
    • Church and state claim to be working towards a moral and spiritual paradise, built on the suffering of the vulnerable
  • Literally the heaven could refer to the comfortable lives led by the wealthy who prospered as a result of the misery of the poor (effectively slave labour)
    • Forces the reader to confront the paradox of the system which purports (claims) to save souls while destroying lives
    • Chimney sweepers are an emblem of the way that the powerful in society create their comfort and luxury by exploiting others, in this case the young and the poor
    • How the chimney sweeps literally die so that the middle and upper classes can have warm cosy homes to live in
Effect, style & response
  • Implores the reader to also think about who this They might be

Innocence vs Experience — the two sweeps

Analysis
  • Innocence (1789): 'When my mother died I was very young, / And my father sold me' → cry 'weep weep weep weep' (can barely talk)
    • Tom Dacre: head shaved; dreams angel frees sweeps from 'coffins of black'
    • Moral: 'So if all do their duty, they need not fear harm' → comforted by religion
    • 'So your chimneys I sweep' → reader = customer
  • Experience (1794): different boy — both parents alive, at church
    • No dream, no angel → sees through the bargain: make up a heaven of our misery
    • They think they have done me no injury answers 'they need not fear harm'
  • Same title, same cry, same snow/soot → perspective changed, not circumstances

Allusions + Blake's beliefs

Analysis
  • Blake = Christian visionary but against organised religion (Church of England) → attacks the institution, not faith
    • his priest and king → God claimed by the powerful
  • Parents at church while child freezes → echoes James 2:14 ('What doth it profit, my brethren, though a man say he hath faith, and have not works?') → Bible turned against the church
  • Lamb imagery in Innocence (Tom's hair curled like a lamb's back, shaved for the job) → stripped away in Experience: no lamb, only blackness + death
  • clothes of death → baptism inverted: christening robe is white; this child is clothed in black
  • heaven of our misery → attacks 'providential suffering' (hardship = God's plan; patience rewarded in heaven)
  • 'Mind-forg'd manacles' ('London') → the parents' belief that his dancing means they have done 'no injury' = a manacle of the mind
  • 'London': 'How the Chimney-sweepers cry / Every blackning Church appalls' → sweep + church again
CONNECTIONS

Connections

How this poem pairs with the rest of the set

Comparison hooks

With 'Carpet-weavers, Morocco' (Carol Rumens)

Link: children's hands making something sacred and comfortable for adults. Rumens's children sit at 'the loom of another world', weaving 'the garden of Islam' into a carpet that will be 'heaped with prayer' in a mosque; Blake's sweep keeps other people's houses warm while his parents pray, and his misery becomes their heaven. Shared technique: religious imagery fastened to child labour, and children heard as music (her 'melodious chime', his notes of woe). Both poems are twelve lines long. Difference: Rumens never lets her children speak and withholds judgement — their absorption and the beauty of the craft are held in balance with 'the school of days'; Blake hands the poem to the child, and the child delivers a verdict.

With 'Before the Sun' (Charles Mungoshi)

Link: a child's working morning in a completely different key. Mungoshi's boy chops wood and roasts maize before sunrise, and the work is a joy: at 'fourteen', the bigger the log the better. Shared technique: sacred language around a child's labour — his rising smoke is 'a sacrificial prayer', while Blake's parents leave to pray — and an adult power watching the child (a sun that winks 'like a grown-up'; God and his priest and king). Difference: Mungoshi's boy works for himself and shares his food freely with the sun, bite for bite; Blake's boy works for others, and what he 'shares' is taken from him. Free verse and freedom against a nursery cage — though Mungoshi's 'two little skeletons' leave a faint shadow too.

With 'Follower' (Seamus Heaney)

Link: a child and a parent's work. Heaney's boy idolises his ploughman father — 'An expert.' — and longs to 'grow up and plough' in 'his broad shadow'; the work is an inheritance he wants. Blake's parents hand their child a trade that will kill him and walk away to church. Shared technique: four-beat rhymed quatrains, a child's-eye view, and a final reversal — Heaney's father 'keeps stumbling' behind the grown son; Blake's child becomes the one who understands and judges. Difference: 'Follower' is about love, admiration and the guilt of outgrowing a parent; 'The Chimney-Sweeper' is about parents who have failed their child and think they have done me no injury.

With 'An Essay on Man' (Alexander Pope)

Link: providence and the order of things, questioned. Pope tells man 'Know then thyself, presume not God to scan', and to accept his place 'on this isthmus of a middle state'; the Essay as a whole sets out to 'vindicate the ways of God to Man'. Shared technique: the balanced paradox — Pope's 'Great lord of all things, yet a prey to all' and 'The glory, jest, and riddle of the world!' beside Blake's a heaven of our misery. Difference: Pope speaks from the top of the cultural order, in polished couplets, about 'man' in general, counselling humility before God's design; Blake speaks from the bottom, through a child, and does not scan God at all — he scans God's managers, his priest and king, and finds the design man-made.

With 'A Different History' (Sujata Bhatt)

Link: the oppressor's deepest conquest is what the young are taught to love and perform. Bhatt's 'unborn grandchildren' come to love 'that strange language'; Blake's child is taught… to sing the notes of woe. Shared technique: a pivotal question — Bhatt asks which language has not been 'the oppressor's tongue', Blake's onlooker Where are thy father and mother, say? — and sacred frames (Sarasvati and the sacredness of books; church, prayer and heaven) tested against cruelty. Difference: Bhatt's history has no named culprit and ends in troubled wonder; Blake names his defendants in one line and convicts them. Hers is a poem of implication, his of indictment.

With 'Lament' (Gillian Clarke)

Link: the blackened innocent. Clarke's cormorant 'in his funeral silk' and her soldier with 'his uniform of fire' are cousins of the sweep in the clothes of death: in each, a covering — oil, fire, soot — is costume, stain and shroud at once, put on the innocent by the powerful. Shared technique: liturgical repetition (her intercessory 'For…', his biblical and… and… and). Difference: 'Lament' is a litany of many victims, none of whom speaks; Blake gives one victim the whole poem, and he does not mourn — he explains.

With 'Report to Wordsworth' (Boey Kim Cheng)

Link: religion failing in the face of damage done by people. In Boey's sonnet 'poetry and piety' are failing while 'insatiate man' closes in, and the poem ends with God 'labouring' towards 'his last cry'; in Blake, piety carries on — the parents are gone to praise God — but has been captured by his priest and king. Shared technique: a compact traditional form (sonnet; nursery quatrains) carrying protest, and religious words turned into evidence. Difference: Boey's culprit is mankind and the damage is to nature, so his poem ends in grief without a defendant; Blake's culprits have titles, the damage is to one child, and the poem ends in a verdict.

With 'Song: Love Armed' (Aphra Behn)

Link: people make a god out of suffering. Behn's lovers supply Love's weapons — 'From me he took his sighs and tears' — until 'thou and I, the God have armed, / And set him up a Deity'; Blake's priest and king make up a heaven out of our misery. Shared technique: a pretty song-form carrying harm; power given regal and religious trappings. Difference: Behn's victim is an adult in a rigged game of love, and her balanced antithesis ('my poor Heart alone is harmed, / Whilst thine the Victor is, and free') keeps both sides in view; Blake's victim is a child in an economy, and his last line refuses balance — one side is made out of the other.

With 'The Cockroach' (Kevin Halligan)

Link: a small dark creature, closely watched, turns out to be a mirror — but the mirrors face opposite ways. Halligan's speaker ends by half-seeing himself in the insect ('recognised myself'); Blake's little black thing refuses to stay an object and answers back with an analysis of the watcher's world. Shared technique: the observed creature as emblem, inside a tight rhymed form. Difference: Halligan's poem is private — a conscience auditing itself through an insect; Blake's is public — a person made thing-like by named institutions.

❋

Where I Come From

Elizabeth Brewster · 1977

The city clings to people like a smell and drops away; home is carried in the mind — until, in the last two lines, it stops being carried and blows back in.

ContextThe PoemThe Whole PoemForm & StructureSoundMotifs & SymbolsThemesDifficult MomentsClose AnalysisCritical LensesOther ReadingsRevision NotesConnections
CONTEXT

Context

The world the poem came out of

The Poet: Elizabeth Brewster (1922–2012)

Elizabeth Winifred Brewster was born on 26 August 1922 in Chipman, New Brunswick, a logging village on the Salmon River near Grand Lake: in Thomas Hodd's words, "a lumber, coal and brick town that offered her few opportunities". (Hodd's 2013 memorial essay gives 22 August; the New Brunswick Literary Encyclopedia and The Canadian Encyclopedia give 26 August.) She was the youngest of the five children of Frederick John and Ethel May Brewster. Her friend the New Brunswick writer Robert Gibbs remembered that "The family was desperately poor" and "They had to move around." Physically frail, with patchy early schooling, she read whatever she could find, from literary classics to the Eaton's mail-order catalogue, and poverty delayed her finishing high school until after most of her friends had graduated.

She began writing poems at nine or ten, and her first was published when she was twelve, in the Saint John Telegraph-Journal (her father sent it in). She went on to publish more than twenty books of poetry and fiction, was made a Member of the Order of Canada in 2001, and died in Saskatoon on 26 December 2012, aged ninety. The home of the poem's second stanza (wooden houses, poultry, the bush, poverty) is the world of that childhood, which is why its details are a resident's, not a visitor's: nobody who had only passed through would think to say the farmhouses were in need of paint.

Away from Home: the Cities behind Stanza 1

Brewster left Chipman for the University of New Brunswick in 1942 on an entrance scholarship (BA 1946), and was a founding member there of The Fiddlehead (1945), now one of Canada's longest-running literary magazines. Then came an MA from Radcliffe College, Harvard's women's college in Cambridge, Massachusetts (1947); a year at King's College London on a Beaverbrook overseas scholarship (1949–50); a library degree from the University of Toronto (1952 in the NB Literary Encyclopedia, 1953 in Hodd); work as a librarian and cataloguer in New Brunswick, Ontario, Alberta and British Columbia; and a PhD from Indiana University (1962). From 1972 until she retired in 1990 she taught English and creative writing at the University of Saskatchewan.

Her two memoirs are called The Invention of Truth (1991) and Away from Home (1995), and Hodd described her as "a transplanted Maritimer who never forgot her roots". This matters for the poem. The subways, museums, offices and rush hours of stanza 1 are things she knew at first hand, and the title's idiom (people say "where I come from" only when they are somewhere else) is the speech of someone living away from home.

The Poem: Probably 1950s, Collected 1977

'Where I Come From' was collected in Sometimes I Think of Moving (Oberon Press, 1977). It is not in Passage of Summer: Selected Poems (Ryerson, 1969), a date sometimes wrongly attached to it. Gillian Harding-Russell, reviewing The Essential Elizabeth Brewster (ed. Ingrid Ruthig, Porcupine's Quill, 2021) in The Fiddlehead, describes the poem as "written in the 1950s" and says it "seems to fit thematically with the first collection", East Coast (Ryerson, 1951); LitCharts also dates it to the 1950s. No primary source for the dating has been found, so treat it as probable rather than certain.

If it is right, the poem was written after Cambridge, London and Toronto, by a poet in her thirties, and kept back for some twenty years. The title of the book it finally appeared in, Sometimes I Think of Moving, suits a poem about what people take with them when they move. It has since been anthologised as Atlantic Canadian writing (in Coastlines: The Poetry of Atlantic Canada) as well as in Cambridge's Songs of Ourselves.

A "Plain Poet"

The critic Desmond Pacey called Brewster "a 'plain poet'", meant as praise for her restraint, and she described her own aim as "a language which is clear, straightforward, and with little adornment". Friends insisted it was a choice. "She deliberately wrote plainly, and strove to make it that way," said Nancy Bauer; "she didn't bow to fashion," said Robert Gibbs. Her doctoral subject points the same way: her Indiana thesis was on George Crabbe, whose poem The Village (1783) attacked the pastoral habit of prettifying country poverty and promised to paint the cottage as truth would paint it, not as poets usually did.

'Where I Come From' practises that plainness. It has one coinage (almost-not-smell), one simile (like the smell of smog), one rhyme and almost no unusual words, and its home stanza admits peeling paint, battered schools and hens clucking aimlessly. The plainness works as honesty: neither the city nor home is prettified, so when the poem does reach for a metaphor at the end, A door in the mind, it carries the more force.

Canada and "Where Is Here?"

In his conclusion to the Literary History of Canada (1965), Northrop Frye wrote that the Canadian imagination is "less perplexed by the question 'Who am I?' than by some such riddle as 'Where is here?'": identity asked as a question of place. He also described a "garrison mentality" in early Canadian writing, small communities huddled against a huge, threatening wilderness, and a "deep terror in regard to nature" in Canadian poetry. Margaret Atwood's Survival (1972) went further, arguing that survival is the central theme of Canadian literature, with nature often cast as a hostile force to be endured.

If the poem dates from the 1950s it predates both books, and it answers neither directly, but they show where it stands. Its title asks Frye's question and answers it, and it turns the garrison inside out. The cold is not an enemy beyond the walls; it is inside the mind, and it is the self. ice and the breaking of ice is a rhythm of survival, but lived as identity rather than fought as terror.

The Real Places behind the Images

The poem names no place, but its details are exact about one.

  • The pine woods. Chipman sits in the forests of central New Brunswick, on the Salmon River, which flows into Grand Lake: acres of pine woods is the landscape of a logging village.
  • The burned-out bush. Wild lowbush blueberries come back strongly after fire, and Maritime blueberry fields were traditionally pruned by burning: a Nova Scotia fact sheet (1997) notes that "Burning has been used most often in the past", usually on a two-year cycle, because the fruit comes on new growth. blueberry patches in the burned-out bush is accurate: sweetness that depends on fire.
  • The breaking of ice. New Brunswick's rivers freeze in winter, and spring arrives with the break-up: the freshet and ice jams that regularly flood the Saint John valley. In April 1994, for example, ice jams and the spring freshet closed roads around Chipman, and in 2018 floodwaters again threatened road access to the village. The breaking of ice is a yearly event before it is a metaphor.
  • The glue factories. Animal glue was made by boiling down hides and bones, and glue works were notorious for their stench.
  • The violets. New Brunswick's floral emblem is the purple violet, adopted in 1936, when Brewster was thirteen; the province's schoolchildren helped to choose it. The poem does not name the province and need not be alluding to this, but a reader from there would recognise the flowers growing behind the schoolhouse as their own.

Wordsworth's 'Tintern Abbey': the Same Return, a Different Temperature

Wordsworth's 'Lines Written a Few Miles above Tintern Abbey' (1798) describes the same experience: a landscape carried away and returning in the city.

These forms of beauty have not been to me, As is a landscape to a blind man's eye: But oft, in lonely rooms, and mid the din Of towns and cities, I have owed to them, In hours of weariness, sensations sweet

(1798 text; later editions print "'mid".) The parallel shows Brewster's difference. Wordsworth's remembered landscape brings "sensations sweet" and "tranquil restoration"; Brewster's arrives as a frosty wind from fields of snow, neither sweet nor restoring. And Wordsworth draws on memory when he needs it, "In hours of weariness", while Brewster's door blows open on its own. Boey Kim Cheng's 'Report to Wordsworth', also in the set, writes to the same poet about a natural world being destroyed; Brewster's subject is the inner world a natural place has made.

"Place Identity": a Later Name for Line 1

Environmental psychology later gave a name to the claim of line 1. In "The City and Self-Identity" (1978) the psychologist Harold Proshansky defined "place identity" as the parts of a person's identity defined "in relation to the physical environment": the memories, feelings, values and habits tied to particular places. Brewster's poem owes nothing to this, and was probably written twenty years earlier, so the term is useful only as an analogy: a sign that People are made of places is a claim later thinkers took seriously enough to test. Proshansky's subject was the city, and he argued that urban places make selves too, which is a useful check on any reading that has Brewster's city leaving nothing but a smell.

THE POEM

The Poem

Lines with a marker have analysis — click one, or just scroll.

Title
Where I Come From
Language & devices

Colloquial formula Where I Come From: the phrase people use about home when they are somewhere else ("where I come from, we…"). A Noun clause as title: the answer to an unasked question, "Where are you from?", given without a place-name. Where puts place first; I is the speaker's only self-reference, and it returns just once more, at l.12. Present tense Come, not "came": origin as a continuing condition. Repetition: the title comes back word for word as the opening of stanza 2 (l.12), so the poem reaches its own title only after eleven lines about other people's places.

Meaning & effect

The title promises a place and delivers a person. It sounds like the start of a description of somewhere (geography, landscape, a map reference), but the poem never names Chipman, New Brunswick, or anywhere else: what it describes is what a place does to the people who come from it. The idiom also tells us where the speaker is standing. Nobody says "where I come from" at home; it is said elsewhere, to people from somewhere different, so the title already implies distance, and the city of stanza 1 is where the speaker seems to be now. The present tense matters as much as the place: you never stop coming from somewhere, and the last two lines prove it by having home arrive in the present. In Canadian terms the title answers a question of identity with a place, the habit Northrop Frye summed up as asking "Where is here?" rather than "Who am I?". The phrase can be heard as tender, but it can also carry the edge it has in speech, where it usually introduces a contrast with the listener's world. Either way the stress falls first on Where and then shifts to I come from: a question of location becomes a question of self.

Line 1
People are made of places. They carry with them
Language & devices

Aphorism: a five-word general law in the simple present, with no hedge. Metaphor made of: the language of materials (made of wood, of stone), so places are what people are composed of, not just what influenced them. Passive voice with no agent: nobody does the making. Alliteration on plosive p, People… places, binds the two nouns. Caesura: the full stop falls mid-line, so the thesis is complete before the line is. Then They carry with them opens the evidence: the verb carry returns at l.13, and Enjambment holds back what is carried until the next line.

Meaning & effect

Brewster sets out her stall in the first five words: identity is not chosen but made by place, and the flat declarative allows no argument. On nature versus nurture, the line comes down on nurture, with place as the nurture. made of is stronger than "shaped by" or "influenced by": a person is a material made from a place, as a table is made of pine. Yet the second sentence quietly loosens the first. carry is portable and ongoing where made of is fixed and finished, so places are both what we are and what we take with us: substance and luggage. The claim is universal (People, not "country people"), which matters later, because city-dwellers are made of places too, and the poem will have to say what their places give them. The tone is calm and conversational rather than polemical, a woman telling the reader something she is sure of, and the enjambment carries her straight on, as people carry their places into wherever they go next.

Line 2
hints of jungles or mountains, a tropic grace
Language & devices

Diction hints: traces rather than proof, faint and partial, felt more than seen. Metonymy jungles or mountains: landscapes standing for the whole way of life lived in them. Listing on or: the examples are offered as alternatives, the grammar of guessing. a tropic grace fuses a climate adjective with a personal quality, so the place becomes the person's manner. Every landscape here is distant and non-urban, and none is Brewster's own.

Meaning & effect

The evidence for the bold thesis is deliberately faint. Places show in people only as hints: not clothes, skin or accent, but something in the way a person moves or holds themselves, a tropic grace that suggests the ease of a life lived outdoors in warmth. Brewster does not explain how a jungle makes someone graceful. She leaves the mark as something hard to name that one can faintly detect, and invites the reader to test the idea on people they know. The geography matters: the poem starts at the far edges of the world, in tropics and mountains, and will travel inward through cities to the speaker's own woods, so this line is the outermost ring of a funnel. grace is the poem's first admiring noun, and it is given to strangers. Read sceptically, though, the line sorts humanity by climate, and tropic grace edges towards a postcard stereotype of hot countries. The hedges (hints, or) are the poem's defence: this is a speaker guessing tentatively about strangers, not laying down a law of character.

Line 3
or the cool eyes of sea-gazers. Atmosphere of cities
Language & devices

Transferred epithet cool eyes: the sea's temperature passes into the watcher's temperament. Coined Compound noun sea-gazers: people named not by their work (fishermen, sailors) but by where they look. Spondee cool eyes slows the line to the pace of a stare. Caesura: the full stop after sea-gazers ends the admiring portraits mid-line, and a new sentence starts abruptly. Fronting Atmosphere of cities, with no article: the city arrives as a substance, not a place. At 14 syllables this is the poem's longest line, and it holds two worlds.

Meaning & effect

The sea-gazers' eyes are cool: calm, reflective, a little detached, the look of people who have spent their lives watching something always changing and always the same. The coolness is admired. It is composure, not coldness, and it starts a thread of temperature that ends twenty lines later in a frosty wind: the poem begins by admiring coolness in other people and ends by finding cold in the speaker herself. Then the line changes direction in its middle. The caesura closes the gallery of human portraits, and the city enters with no article and no people, only an Atmosphere. So the two halves of the line already set out the contrast the poem will develop: places that give their people qualities (grace, cool eyes), and cities that give them an air. The abrupt turn can be heard as reluctance, as if the speaker comes to the city because the argument needs it rather than by choice.

Line 4
how different drops from them, like the smell of smog
Language & devices

Exclamatory interpolation how different: an exclamation dropped into the sentence without commas, breaking its grammar. Ambiguity drops from them: falls away from them, or is given off by them like a smell. Simile like the smell of smog: the first of five smells, and the first is pollution. Sibilance smell of smog; Alliteration on plosive d, different drops. them points back to the They of l.1, people in general.

Meaning & effect

This is the poem's untidiest sentence, and it belongs to its tidiest place. Atmosphere of cities / how different drops from them will not parse cleanly: it can be read as "the atmosphere of cities (how different!) drops from them", or as "how differently the atmosphere of cities drops from them". Either way the grammar breaks as the city arrives. The verb has two readings. If it means "falls away", the city never gets inside its people: its mark is shed like a coat, which is exactly what will not happen to people who carry woods in their minds. If it means "gives off", city people exude their city as a body gives off a smell. Both readings make the city's mark a surface thing, not part of the self. The simile then picks smell as the city's sense and smog as its first smell, and the hiss of smell of smog hangs in the air like a sour note. how different is the poem's one exclamation, a flash of feeling quickly muffled, and the nearest it comes to stating a judgement. The disapproval is in the diction and the images; it is never said outright.

Line 5
or the almost-not-smell of tulips in the spring,
Language & devices

Neologism almost-not-smell: a hyphenated Compound noun with a double qualification (almost, not) built in, so the noun names a smell by its near-absence. The stress-jam on -not-smell makes the voice stumble where perception fails. Juxtaposition with smog: the city's two smells are pollution and next to nothing. tulips: cultivated bulbs planted in beds by city gardeners. in the spring: the city's spring, against the Spring of l.18. The line-end comma keeps the catalogue moving.

Meaning & effect

Even the city's beauty is defined by what it lacks. Tulips are planted for colour and display rather than scent, and in city air their fragrance is so faint it might as well not be there. Brewster invents a word for it, the almost-not-smell, and the coinage is exact about a real experience: bending to a flowerbed and getting almost nothing. Two explanations sit inside the phrase: the scent is overpowered by the smog, or the flowers are too ordered, municipal planting grown for show. The hyphens box the vacancy into one tidy compound, so even the word for the tulips' smell is a little plotted square. The detail also plants a contrast the second stanza will answer. Here spring is a faint smell in a park; where the speaker comes from, Spring is one of the mind's two chief seasons, and it arrives as the breaking of ice. A gentler reading is possible, in which catching the faint scent at all teaches city people to find beauty in unlikely places, but the line's weight falls on the not.

Line 6
nature tidily plotted in little squares
Language & devices

Pun plotted: laid out in garden plots, plotted on a plan, and schemed. Irony in the adverb tidily: neatness, usually a virtue, becomes the charge. Diminutive little squares: rigid geometry, small and bounded. The abstract noun nature stands in for any actual plant. There is no finite verb: plotted is a participle, and the sentence has loosened into a list of exhibits.

Meaning & effect

In the city, nature is administered. It is not a forest or a field but nature in the abstract, an idea of nature laid out by planners in parks and public squares, where plants grow only where they have been planned. tidily carries the irony: wild nature is never tidy, so to make nature tidy is to turn it into something else. The pun in plotted stacks three meanings (a garden plot, a planned layout, a scheme), and the third hints that the arrangement is a contrivance: nature reduced to decoration, visited as an escape rather than lived alongside. little squares sets up one of the poem's clearest visual contrasts, because the hens of the second stanza will circle about: the city's geometry is squares, home's is circles. The tone stays dry rather than angry. There is no open condemnation in the line; the judgement lives in a single adverb.

Line 7
with a fountain in the centre; museum smell,
Language & devices

Imagery a fountain in the centre: symmetrical design, water pumped round and round. Semicolon mid-line: the list moves from park to museum with no connective. Olfactory imagery museum smell: a verbless noun phrase, one more exhibit.

Meaning & effect

Every square has its fountain in the centre: the planned city is organised around centres, and its water does not run anywhere but is pumped up and falls back into the same basin. The image adds symmetry to the geometry, and it will be answered by hens circling about with no centre at all. Then, with no transition, the line turns from park to museum, and even art is first known by its smell: shut-away mustiness, polish, closed air. Making the museum a smell rather than a collection is telling. The speaker registers the building's air, not the paintings, as a visitor passing through takes away an impression rather than a possession. The semicolon sets park and museum side by side as items in one inventory, which prepares the word also in the next line.

Line 8
art also tidily plotted with a guidebook;
Language & devices

Repetition tidily plotted, word for word from l.6. also: the hinge that files art with nature. Symbol guidebook: experience arranged in advance, a set route through recommended sights. Semicolon at the line-end.

Meaning & effect

Art gets exactly the same treatment as nature: arranged, labelled and routed in advance, tidily plotted with a guidebook. The repetition is the argument. A city keeps nature and art as proof that it has a soul, and here it processes both with the same three words. The flat word also is the most damning in the stanza: the city has one relation to everything, arrangement. The guidebook is the symbol of this world. It tells visitors which works to look at and in what order, so it removes the chance of finding something for yourself and the thrill of discovery; and if People are made of places, a place where even wonder comes with instructions will make people with less spontaneity and imagination. The guidebook also places the speaker. She knows the city as visitors know it, from outside and by the book, whereas nothing in the second stanza needs instructions: she knows where the violets grow.

Line 9
or the smell of work, glue factories maybe,
Language & devices

Metonymy the smell of work: labour known by its odour. glue factories: animal glue was made by boiling down hides and bones, a byword for stench. Hedge maybe: a casual shrug, the poem's only open admission of guesswork. or returns: the catalogue is still a set of alternatives.

Meaning & effect

Leisure and work come down to the same sense: after the park's faint tulips and the museum's closed air comes the smell of work. The glue factory is the stanza's harshest image, the reek of animal remains boiled into something useful, and it brings the city's industrial underside, and a whiff of death, into a list that began with flowers. The key word is maybe. It can be read as dismissive, as if the city does not matter enough to be precise about, or as honest: the speaker knows the smell but not the world it comes from, and says so. Either way it labels the whole stanza's kind of knowledge: impressions gathered by someone passing through. Nothing in the second stanza is hedged, because there the speaker knows exactly what grows behind the schoolhouse. And the poem keeps its manners: there is no criticism of the people who do this work, only observation.

Line 10
chromium-plated offices; smell of subways
Language & devices

Compound adjective chromium-plated: a hard, shiny coating laid over another metal, so the sheen is surface only. Semicolon mid-line. Sibilance smell of subways, the fifth and last smell. The line has no verb: two exhibits side by side. Near-echo plated / plotted (ll.6, 8, 10).

Meaning & effect

The offices gleam with modernity, but they are only plated: chromium is a surface over something else, so the image suggests a world impressive on the outside and not rooted at its core. The metallic sheen throws light back, a building that pushes nature away rather than living with it, and it stands directly opposite the wooden farmhouses of l.15, which are wood all the way through. Then the subway: city people out of sight underground, penned in metal boxes at both ends of the working day, and the hiss of smell of subways gives that crowded heat a nauseating intensity. plated chimes with plotted: coated surfaces and mapped surfaces, the same gesture. The line has no verbs, so for all its rush the city feels strangely still, a run of exhibits rather than a life.

Line 11
crowded at rush hours.
Language & devices

The stanza's shortest line, five syllables, End-stopped with the poem's first line-final full stop. Spondee rush hours. crowded is a participle: the nine-line sentence that began at Atmosphere ends with only one finite verb in it, drops. The line stops short, leaving white space that l.12 will fill.

Meaning & effect

The city section ends compressed, as crowded as the carriage it describes: the line is cut short and packed with stresses. Its last words are rush hours, so the city's time is clock time, timetable and commute, against the second stanza's seasonal time of Spring and winter. The crowd is the only form in which city people appear. The tropics had grace and the coast cool eyes; the city's people appear only as a mass in a tunnel, which is the poem's quietest and sharpest comment on what cities leave on their people. Yet the sentence describing all this rush has almost no verbs, so the busy city feels curiously empty and still. The short line is also structural: it leaves half a line of white space, and the next stanza begins exactly there.

Line 12
Where I come from, people
Language & devices

Dropped line: printed indented, starting where l.11 ends, so the two half-lines share one line across the stanza break. Repetition of the title, word for word. Volta: third person becomes first person, the city becomes home. The poem's only I, immediately followed by people. Enjambment people / carry: the subject waits at the line-end for its verb.

Meaning & effect

This is the hinge of the poem, and the layout makes it visible. Because the line is dropped, it both continues and divides: it completes the city's unfinished line, so home is one more case of the opening thesis, yet it starts a new stanza, so home is a different world. The step down the page can look like the two halves drifting apart like continents. The title returns here, and the poem reaches its subject only now: other people's places first, then Where I come from. The single I appears and at once dissolves into people. She claims the origin but speaks for a community, so the self is defined by belonging, which suits a poem arguing that places, not individuals, make people. And the voice changes: there is no more maybe, and certainty arrives with the first person. Some readers hear nostalgia in the repeated title; it can as easily be heard as quiet pride, the speaker's turn after the city has had its say.

Line 13
carry woods in their minds, acres of pine woods;
Language & devices

Parallelism: carry repeats the verb of l.1 (They carry with them), now at the head of the line and stressed. Metaphor woods in their minds. Amplification woods… acres of pine woods: the general word, then the measure and the species. Repetition woods… woods. The first of three minds (ll.13, 19, 20). Assonance on long i, minds… pine.

Meaning & effect

The same verb, the opposite cargo. The people of stanza 1 carry faint hints; her people carry woods in their minds, acres of pine woods. Where the city's atmosphere hangs on its people and drops away, the woods are inside, and they never leave the people even when the people leave the woods. The image grows as she remembers it (woods, then acres, then pine), and acres lays a surveyor's measure over the inside of a head: space, freedom, more room inside than out. Pine is evergreen, so these woods are permanent where the city's tulips are seasonal, and pine forest is what surrounded Brewster's logging village. The woods can be read three ways: as a lasting kinship with nature; as privacy and secretiveness, since woods are dense and shadowy; or as a tendency to dark moods. carry has two weights as well: pride, an inheritance carried with dignity, or a burden that can never be put down. What the line does not claim is that minds are superior to bodies. The contrast is between surface and depth.

Line 14
blueberry patches in the burned-out bush;
Language & devices

Alliteration on plosive b and p, blueberry patches… burned-out bush. Juxtaposition of sweetness and fire damage. The preposition in: the fruit grows inside the burn, not beside it. bush: the Canadian word for uncleared forest. A real detail: wild lowbush blueberries thrive after fire, and blueberry fields were traditionally pruned by burning.

Meaning & effect

The image is fact before it is symbol. Wild blueberries come back strongly on burned ground, and growers burned the fields to make them fruit, so in this landscape sweetness really does come out of fire. The colour arrives inside damage, shocks of blue in a grey, burned landscape, and the preposition carries the tenderness: not blueberries next to the burn but in it. The burst of plosives gives the line a strong pulse of life after the city's thin hiss. The poem does not explain the burn (wildfire, controlled burning, something else) and leaves the reader to feel both the ruin and the renewal. As a symbol it is hard-won beauty, nature's stubborn will to thrive, and by extension the people it shapes, who survive and flourish in hard conditions. burned-out can also suggest exhaustion, so even the stanza's first sweetness sits in a used-up landscape. The poem neither laments the burn nor celebrates it: it is simply part of home.

Line 15
wooden farmhouses, old, in need of paint,
Language & devices

wooden against the city's chromium-plated: solid and natural against surface sheen. Postposed adjectives old, in need of paint, set off by commas: the voice pauses, looks again and appraises. Understatement in need of paint. Three halting phrases make this the most broken rhythm in the poem.

Meaning & effect

This is not a pastoral idyll. The farmhouses are real buildings in a poor place: wooden, old, peeling. Against the plated offices they suggest authenticity and simplicity, wood all the way through, the farming and logging life of the region. But the commas make the voice slow down and look honestly, like someone describing a house they know well, and what she sees is wear. in need of paint is left open. Do appearances matter less in a tight-knit rural community? Is it neglect, or the decline of farming? Is the house still loved and used? Have the young left for the cities? The poem does not choose. What it refuses is prettification, and the refusal is a form of respect: she describes home as it is, and her affection is believed because of it. If there is beauty here, it is in run-down things, the bare wood showing through old paint.

Line 16
with yards where hens and chickens circle about,
Language & devices

circle about: round, unhurried movement with no destination. Juxtaposition with the city's little squares and fountain in the centre: circles with no centre. hens and chickens: in older usage "chickens" are young birds, so the phrase can picture hens with their brood. Guttural c and k begin (chickens circle). circle is the catalogue's first finite verb since carry.

Meaning & effect

The farmyard is unplanned. Hens and chickens circle about with no fountain to circle round and no plan; life simply goes on. Against the city's squares the shape is softer, and against the subway's rush the pace is slower: free, calm, without hurry. If chickens means the young birds, the yard also holds generations, mothers and their brood, which suits a poem about what is passed on. The line also restores what the city stanza lacked: verbs of movement. After the almost verbless city, the home catalogue moves (carry, circle, grow), so by contrast the rush-hour city looks the stiller of the two. The circling prepares the next word, aimlessly, which tips the image from freedom towards drift.

Line 17
clucking aimlessly; battered schoolhouses
Language & devices

Onomatopoeia clucking, with its c/k sound spread through the neighbouring words: chickens circle… clucking. The adverb aimlessly is the direct opposite of tidily. Semicolon mid-line. battered: worn, beaten, weathered. Enjambment schoolhouses / behind which.

Meaning & effect

aimlessly is the stanza's most double-edged word, and the opposite pole to the city's tidily. Read one way it is freedom: unscheduled life with no rush hour, nobody deciding where the hens go or when. Read another way it is purposelessness: a region adrift in economic decline, the community's condition displaced onto its poultry. The hens are both, and the poem does not choose. There is some gentle comedy in it too, an affectionate, unidealised picture of a farmyard. Then the battered schoolhouses: weathered by wind and snow, used hard and still standing. The building meant for making futures is the most worn thing in the poem, an honest detail about rural poverty. The line clucks in its sound as well as its sense, and the guttural c/k gives the yard a pulse the city's sibilance never had.

Line 18
behind which violets grow. Spring and winter
Language & devices

Enjambment schoolhouses / behind which violets grow: the violets are hidden behind the line-break as they are behind the building. The formal relative behind which is unusually stiff in a plain-spoken poem. The finite verb grow ends the home sentence mid-line. Juxtaposition: wild violets against the city's planted tulips. After the Caesura a new sentence begins, Spring and winter, enjambed onto the next line.

Meaning & effect

The violets are the stanza's quiet climax. They are wild and unplanned, growing out of sight behind a battered building, the opposite of tulips plotted in squares: delicate life reclaiming a forgotten corner. You have to know where to look to find them, so they are insider knowledge in the shape of a flower, the reverse of a guidebook. Like the schoolchildren the building implies, they shelter from the weather and thrive in a bleak place, an image of people who survive against the odds. The home sentence ends on grow, a verb of life, where the city sentence ended on rush hours, a timetable. Then, mid-line, the poem lifts from inventory to generalisation: Spring and winter begins a statement about minds rather than places, and the line-break makes the reader wait for it.

Line 19
are the mind's chief seasons: ice and the breaking of ice.
Language & devices

Metaphor the mind's chief seasons: the second mind. Omission: no summer, no autumn. Colon: the poem's only colon, introducing a definition. Repetition ice… ice: the phrase begins and ends on the same word (Epanalepsis). Gerund breaking: a process rather than a single event. At 13 syllables the line is the poem's second longest, after l.3.

Meaning & effect

Here the poem states its deepest claim. A place does not only give people pictures to remember; it gives the mind its seasons. The climate governs the psyche, and only the extremes count: winter, the ice, and spring, defined not by flowers but as the breaking of ice. Summer and autumn, the comfortable seasons, are left out, so a polarised climate makes polarised moods: withdrawal, coldness and endurance, then relief, renewal and opening up. The repetition makes the two seasons two sides of one coin, each handing the baton to the other year after year. Literally, spring in New Brunswick comes with river ice breaking up, often with floods; figuratively, breaking the ice means overcoming reserve, or breaking through a hard barrier, which suggests the grit this life builds. A bleaker reading is available too: life lived mostly in cold and dark, spring a short relief before the next snow. Either way the line prepares the ending: a mind whose chief season is winter will be visited by a winter wind.

Line 20
A door in the mind blows open, and there blows
Language & devices

Metaphor A door in the mind: the third mind, now a house with a door, and the mind, not "my": even the climax keeps the first person out. blows open: sudden and involuntary, with no human agent. Repetition blows… blows. Inversion there blows: the old-fashioned word order holds the subject back. Enjambment: the subject, the wind, arrives only in the next line. A separate two-line stanza, cut off by white space that nothing bridges.

Meaning & effect

The poem stops describing, and something happens. The mind has been moving inward all along: woods in their minds, then the mind's chief seasons, now a door in the mind, so the landscape is fully inside. Nobody opens the door. It blows open by itself, and the agency of the whole poem reverses: people carried places; now a place acts on a person. This is memory as involuntary and unstoppable, an upbringing that cannot be suppressed, past and present merging in an instant. It need not be a memory at all: it may be a mood, a sudden bleakness that feels like the winters she knows. After two calm catalogues the change of mode is a jolt, and the ending is meant to jar with what came before. The inversion there blows delays the wind across the line-break, so that it arrives with full weight in the last line.

Line 21
a frosty wind from fields of snow.
Language & devices

Rhyme blows / snow: the poem's only end-rhyme, and imperfect, since the z of blows goes unanswered. Assonance on long o, blows open… blows… snow. Alliteration on f, frosty… from fields. Iambic tetrameter: a FROS-ty WIND from FIELDS of SNOW, the only fully regular line in the poem. The sense is now touch, cold air on skin, after the city's smells.

Meaning & effect

What comes through the door is not a warm glow of nostalgia but cold, a frosty wind from fields of snow: harsh rather than welcoming, yet clearly hers, the native weather of a mind whose chief season is winter. Comforting or chilling? It can be read as home always with her at full sensory strength, the clearest proof of the opening thesis, or as a breach, a cold draught through a mind that cannot be sealed, and Brewster's refusal to explain it makes it the more unnerving. The image also overturns the usual associations of winter with loneliness and isolation: here the cold is the source of identity, what she is made of (endurance, an eye for nature's austere beauty, a mind left open). The form seals it. After twenty lines of speech-rhythm, the free verse falls into its one rhyme and one perfectly regular line, as if the mind falls into its native measure once it stops steering. The city reached only the nose; home reaches the skin. The poem's journey from the general to the specific to the personal ends inside one mind.

THE WHOLE POEM

The Whole Poem

Stepping back: what the poem is doing, first line to last

'Where I Come From' opens with the most confident sentence in it, People are made of places., and then spends twenty lines appearing to illustrate that thesis while actually revising it. The revision, not the illustration, is the poem. Read as illustration, it is a tidy compare-and-contrast of city and country with a decorative flourish at the end, which is how it is often read. Read as revision, it is a drama about two ways of knowing places and people (acquaintance from outside, constitution from inside), which stages the second overtaking the first and ends by discovering that its own opening aphorism was not quite right.

Start with how oddly the thesis is supported. made of is total, passive and finished: manufacture completed at some point in the past. But the evidence is immediately hedged: hints of jungles, a tropic grace / or the cool eyes, glue factories maybe. The first stanza is written from the position of an observer, someone reading strangers' surfaces in transit, guessing at origins from a posture or a stare, guessing at a city's life from what it smells of. And the guessing is done in the city's own idiom. The stanza's vocabulary is the vocabulary of curation (tidily plotted, guidebook, museum), and its speaker does to people exactly what the guidebook does to nature: she sorts them into little squares. Jungle people are graceful; sea people are cool; city people smell of subways. The typology skirts the postcard and the stereotype, and the poem knows it: that is what hints and maybe are for. Grammar completes the demonstration. The city sentence sprawls across eight and a half lines with a single finite verb, drops, before decaying into a verbless inventory (museum smell; smell of subways). Knowledge about a place piles up but cannot predicate; it cannot make anything happen. This is not city-hatred. It is a demonstration of how thin outside knowledge is, offered in the voice of anyone who has changed trains somewhere and thought they knew it.

The dropped line, Where I come from, people, changes the ground of authority, and the economy of that pivot is remarkable. The first person enters once, a single I buried mid-formula and never repeated, and immediately dissolves into people. The restraint is the argument. A poem claiming that persons are made by places, communally and involuntarily, would undercut itself with an insistent lyric "I": whatever an "I" makes of itself is exactly what it was not made of by anywhere. So the speaker claims origin without claiming ownership, speaks for a people she belongs to, and lets the certainty of the new catalogue do the self-revealing. And it is certain: no more maybe. The acres, the blueberries, the paint, the hens, the violets behind the schoolhouse: this is the exactness of memory rather than research, a knowledge that includes what is behind buildings because the knower has stood behind them.

Yet the inventory refuses the reward it seems to promise. Home is peeling, battered, economically becalmed; its hens go nowhere, clucking aimlessly; its bush is burned-out. The stanza's tenderness is real, but it is placed rather than stated, carried by prepositions: blueberries grow in the burn, violets behind the battered school. Sweetness and delicacy are not compensations set beside the damage; they are located inside it, inseparable from it. This is where the poem's honesty cuts deepest. What home gives is not beauty but constitution, and the constitution includes the damage. Then a definition names the deepest layer of the inheritance: Spring and winter / are the mind's chief seasons: ice and the breaking of ice. This is not scenery any more but a shape of feeling, a calendar of two extremes, stillness and rupture, with the mild seasons deleted. There is no summer: the mind this place makes has no season of ease. What you inherit from such a place is a rhythm, long freeze and sudden thaw, and the sentence performs it, two stressed ices flanking a loose run of syllables.

Everything up to this point, however vivid, is willed: catalogues composed by a speaker in full control of her material. That is exactly why the poem cannot stop there. If places really make people, recitation proves nothing; a tourist can recite. The proof must be something that happens to the speaker, against her will, in the poem's present tense. Hence the couplet, which jars against everything before it and is meant to: A door in the mind blows open, and there blows / a frosty wind from fields of snow. Agency has drained out of the human. People carried, hens circled, violets grew; now a door blows open, unlatched from the far side, and weather arrives. The form seals it. The poem's only rhyme and its only metrically regular line, a strict iambic tetrameter, close the free verse like a mechanism engaging, or, better, like the mind falling at last into its native measure, the cadence of where it comes from, once it stops steering.

The obvious objection says the poem is rural chauvinism: the city rendered as smells and sterility, the country as flowers and growth, with a dash of climatic stereotype (tropic grace) in the set-up. Concede the tilt; the stanzas are not neutral. But the tilt is about knowing, not morals. The city passage criticises a way of knowing (mediated, curated, known by smell, guessed at) and flags its own guesswork while doing so, and its human specimens get the poem's most admiring nouns (grace, cool eyes). City-dwellers are inside the opening thesis too: they also carry their places; it is just that what an observer can know of them is residue. Meanwhile the country is given poverty, aimlessness and burn scars, and its climactic gift is a cold draught through the skull. The voice throughout is reflective and accepting: it neither hates the city nor sentimentalises home. A chauvinist poem would end warm, at the hearth. This one ends frosty, in a mind that cannot be heated.

The second objection is formal: that the couplet is a bolted-on epiphany, a rhymed and faintly gothic flourish that betrays the catalogue's hard-won specificity (a door in the mind could be anyone's; a blueberry patch in a burn is Brewster's). The preparation answers most of this. The mind has been a container since l.13 and has had a climate since l.19; the long o of the rhyme is laid down three lines early, in grow; and the rhyme itself is left imperfect, blows against snow, one consonant short of tidy, so the poem declines full closure even while closing. But the generality of the last image should not be argued away, because it does the final piece of work. At the moment origin returns as a force, it stops being listable.
