In 1982 the International Whaling Commission voted for a moratorium on commercial whaling, which took effect from the 1985–86 season, making the whale — and the beached whale of news photographs — an emblem of the environmental movement. And the birds are few stands in a line of literary alarm: Rachel Carson's Silent Spring (1962), often credited with starting the modern environmental movement, carries as its epigraph Keats's "And no birds sing". Set beside these, the poem's sea-gods and Wordsworthian echoes are not an escape from the present: they are how Boey makes a contemporary emergency feel ancient, sacred and final.

THE POEM

The Poem

Line by line, with the analysis alongside

Report to Wordsworth
TReport to Wordsworth
1You should be here, Nature has need of you.
2She has been laid waste. Smothered by the smog,
3the flowers are mute, and the birds are few
4in a sky slowing like a dying clock.
5All hopes of Proteus rising from the sea
6have sunk; he is entombed in the waste
7we dump. Triton's notes struggle to be free,
8his famous horns are choked, his eyes are dazed,
9and Neptune lies helpless as a beached whale,
10while insatiate man moves in for the kill.
11Poetry and piety have begun to fail,
12as Nature's mighty heart is lying still.
13O see the wound widening in the sky,
14God is labouring to utter his last cry.

Lines with a marker have analysis — click one, or just scroll.

Title
Report to Wordsworth
Language & devices

Register: Report is an administrative noun — the account an inspector, official or journalist files upward, to someone with the power to act. It promises facts, findings and a neutral voice.

Apostrophe announced in advance: to Wordsworth makes the poem an address, not a description. The addressee is William Wordsworth (1770–1850), the English Romantic poet who made Nature a moral and spiritual teacher.

Allusion: the title names the poet whose sonnets the poem quotes and rewrites — 'London, 1802', 'The World Is Too Much with Us' and 'Composed upon Westminster Bridge'.

Irony: a report to a man dead since 1850 can never be acted on. A faint second sense of report — the bang of a gun — suits a poem in which man moves in for the kill.

Meaning & effect

The title sets up the whole situation before line 1: a modern poet files an official account of damage with the poet who made Nature sacred in English. Choosing a bureaucratic genre for a lyric is a deliberate clash — the poem promises the cool objectivity of a document and delivers myth, lament and prophecy, as if the facts were too terrible to be told in a factual voice. to Wordsworth makes him both the authority who must be informed and the standard against which the damage is measured: the report is, in effect, on the state of everything he loved. It is also homage and inheritance — a younger poet reporting back to the master of the tradition, as Wordsworth himself had called on Milton. The title only works if Wordsworth is heard in it: once he is, every image that follows becomes one of his images, returned damaged. And because the recipient cannot read it, the real recipient is the living reader — the futility of the address is built in, and so is its appeal to us.

Line 1
You should be here, Nature has need of you.
Language & devices

Apostrophe: You addresses the dead Wordsworth as if he could hear.

Modal verb: should carries two senses at once — obligation (you ought to be here) and impossible longing (you are not here, and cannot be).

Allusion: the line rewrites the opening of Wordsworth's 'London, 1802' — "Milton! thou should'st be living at this hour: / England hath need of thee" — keeping should and need of, swapping Milton for Wordsworth and England for Nature.

Archaism: has need of (not "needs") imitates Wordsworth's "hath need of". Personification: capitalised Nature is a being with needs.

Comma splice: two main clauses joined only by a comma — the grammar of an urgent message; You … you frames the line.

Alliteration and Assonance: Nature has need (n); the long vowels of be here, need and Nature — open, carrying sounds that make the line a call rather than a statement.

Meaning & effect

Boey opens by doing exactly what Wordsworth did in 1802: calling a dead poet back because the present has failed. In Wordsworth's sonnet the patient was England, sick with selfishness; in Boey's it is Nature itself — the emergency has grown from a nation's morals to the living world, some 140 years after Wordsworth's death. should makes the line a summons and a lament at once: the speaker demands Wordsworth's presence while knowing he cannot come, so the poem is shadowed by grief from its first words. Capital-N Nature is Wordsworth's own idea of nature — a presence close to divine — so Boey speaks to him in his own terms, which makes what follows more painful: this is the Nature Wordsworth trusted. The comma splice gives the line the breathless run of speech rather than the composed syntax of a report, and the line begins and ends on you, surrounding the absent poet with need. A sharper voice is possible too: You should be here can carry reproach — come and see what has become of the Nature you promised "never did betray / The heart that loved her".

Line 2
She has been laid waste. Smothered by the smog,
Language & devices

Personification: She — Nature as a woman, the traditional Mother Nature, here the victim.

Passive voice: has been laid waste deletes the agent; the present perfect says the damage is done and still lying there to be seen.

Military idiom: laid waste is what invading armies do to conquered land.

Allusion: Wordsworth's "Getting and spending, we lay waste our powers" ('The World Is Too Much with Us') turned from active to passive, and from our inner powers to Nature's body; and the sentence shape of 'London, 1802' — "England hath need of thee: she is a fen / Of stagnant waters" — need, then She and her diagnosis.

Caesura: a full stop after five syllables kills the sentence mid-line.

Alliteration / Sibilance: Smothered by the smog — the shared sm binds cause to effect.

Dangling modifier: Smothered belongs grammatically to the flowers (line 3) but arrives directly after She.

Meaning & effect

The first finding of the report is a blunt verdict: Nature has been devastated, like territory sacked in war. The passive voice withholds who did it; the culprit is not named until we dump in line 7, so for five lines destruction seems simply to happen, the way it does when everyone is responsible and no one is accountable. The borrowed verb carries an argument: Wordsworth warned that "getting and spending" lays waste our own "powers"; Boey shows where that waste ended up — no longer inside us, but spread across the world. Echoing "she is a fen / Of stagnant waters" makes Nature the new England, the "she" in need of rescue. Smothered by the smog begins the poem's imagery of breath: smog — smoke and fog — is pollution you breathe, and to smother is to kill by stopping breath. Because Smothered sits right after She, it seems at first to describe Nature herself before it settles on the flowers — the damage drifts across the full stop like the smog itself. And the full stop after waste stops the sentence dead: the grammar is already rehearsing the deaths it will report. Making Nature a woman in distress also sets up an old story — the lady in danger, the hero summoned to save her — and casts Wordsworth as the rescuer; the rest of the poem quietly denies that plot, because no one comes.

Line 3
the flowers are mute, and the birds are few
Language & devices

Metaphor / Personification: the flowers are mute — silenced, as if they once had a voice.

Parallelism: two matching clauses (the + noun + are + adjective) joined by and — items on a list.

Understatement: few, not "gone" — the language of a survey count.

Monosyllables and an Anapaestic rhythm: the flowers are mute, and the birds are few lilts in four beats, almost like a nursery rhyme.

Echo: Keats's "And no birds sing" ('La Belle Dame sans Merci'), the line Rachel Carson set as the epigraph of Silent Spring (1962) — an association rather than a certain allusion.

Meaning & effect

Line 3 lists what the smog has done in plain, almost childlike clauses: the flowers have no voice, and there are fewer birds. mute is the poem's first word of silence and starts its master motif — voices failing one after another: flowers, Triton's notes and horn, poetry, God's cry. It implies that flowers once spoke: for Wordsworth they did — nature had a "language of the sense" that poetry translated — so if the flowers are mute, poetry has nothing left to hear. few is chilling because it is measured: the voice of a report counting survivors, a decline still in progress rather than a finished extinction, which is what makes it urgent. Flowers and birdsong are the stock materials of English nature poetry — Wordsworth's daffodils, Keats's nightingale — so these losses are also the lyric tradition's losses. The simple lilt makes the damage sound like a child's plain statement of fact, final and unarguable. Another reading puts the fault in us rather than in the flowers: they are mute because we can no longer hear them — the failure of perception that line 11 will call the failure of piety.

Line 4
in a sky slowing like a dying clock.
Language & devices

Enjambment: few / in a sky — the scarcity is spread across a whole failing sky.

Simile: like a dying clock. Paradox: dying clock gives a machine a living death.

Present participles: slowing, dying — actions still under way.

Alliteration and Assonance: sky slowing (s); sky … like … dying (the long i sound).

Rhythm: the line stalls — two light syllables (in a), two heavy ones together (sky slow-), two light again — so the even tick of the pentameter falters. The full stop closes the first quatrain.

Meaning & effect

The sky itself is running down: its movement of weather, cloud and birds is failing like the last ticks of a clock before it stops. The simile turns ecological damage into a countdown — time is running out — and introduces the poem's sense of apocalypse not as an explosion but as a slow winding-down that we are living through. Comparing the sky to a clock, a made machine, suggests that nature has already been reimagined as a mechanism — something to be run and used — which is part of how it came to be exploited; yet calling the clock dying gives the machine a body that can suffer. slowing and dying begin the poem's run of continuous tenses: the death is happening now, as we read. A stopped clock is also a traditional sign of a death in the house, which looks ahead to Nature's mighty heart … lying still in line 12. Read literally, a slowing sky is also one where the air hangs thick and stagnant with smog — nothing moves in it. The faltering rhythm enacts the meaning: the measure stumbles in the line about time failing.

Line 5
All hopes of Proteus rising from the sea
Language & devices

Classical allusion: Proteus, the shape-shifting, prophetic "Old Man of the Sea" of Greek myth; in Homer's Odyssey (Book 4) Menelaus has to hold him fast through all his transformations to learn the way home.

Quotation: Wordsworth's "Have sight of Proteus rising from the sea" ('The World Is Too Much with Us') is lifted almost word for word; only "Have sight of" becomes All hopes of.

Hyperbole: All hopes — not one hope but every hope.

Imagery of ascent: rising.

Enjambment: the subject All hopes must wait a whole line for its verb.

Meaning & effect

Boey turns from land and sky to the sea, and to Wordsworth's sonnet against materialism. There Wordsworth, sickened by a world of "getting and spending", wished he were "A Pagan suckled in a creed outworn" so that he might at least see Proteus rising from the sea — the old gods were his consolation, a way of seeing nature as alive and holy again. Boey quotes the wish exactly and, for one line, lets it stand: the line still holds the hope (rising), and only the line break will tell us what became of it. Proteus is a precise choice: a god of transformation and truthful prophecy, he stands for nature's power to renew itself and for the hope of a revelation that might show the way out. All hopes widens the loss from one myth to the whole Romantic belief that nature might restore us. The line also opens the poem's longest movement: the next six lines belong to the sea and its gods.

Line 6
have sunk; he is entombed in the waste
Language & devices

Antithesis: rising (line 5) is answered by sunk.

Literalised idiom: hopes sink as a heart sinks — here they literally go down into the sea.

Semicolon: a hinge from the abstract (hopes) to the physical (Proteus's body).

Metaphor: entombed — sealed in a tomb.

Repetition with shifted meaning: waste — line 2's devastation has become literal rubbish.

Enjambment: the waste / we dump holds back the agent.

Metre: nine syllables — a syllable short of the pentameter — sagging through two slack pairs, he is and in the.

Meaning & effect

The hopes do not just fail; they have sunk — the idiom made literal, dropping to the sea floor where Proteus lies. entombed is the cruellest word in the passage: the god whose whole nature is escape — the shape-shifter no grip could hold — is sealed in, unable to change or rise, and a tomb promises no resurrection. waste now means rubbish, not ruin: the grand military image of line 2 collapses into the ugly fact of garbage on the seabed, and the bathos is the point — myth buried under trash. The line ends on waste, leaving the dumping without a dumper for one more moment, so the reader is pulled across the line break to find out who is responsible. Its short, sagging rhythm makes the verse itself seem to lose something, as though matter had gone overboard. The tenses place us after the burial: have sunk, is entombed — we are reading the report of a grave, not of a battle.

Line 7
we dump. Triton's notes struggle to be free,
Language & devices

Enjambment / Delayed agent: we dump lands at the start of the line.

First-person plural: we — the only first person in the poem.

Colloquial register: dump, a blunt, ugly verb against the mythic vocabulary.

Caesura: the full stop after two syllables isolates the admission.

Classical allusion: Triton, son of Poseidon and Amphitrite, herald of the sea, whose conch horn could calm or raise the waves.

Personification of sound: notes struggle to be free — music behaving like a trapped creature.

Allusion and Rhyme: Wordsworth wished to "hear old Triton blow his wreathèd horn"; free rhymes with sea (line 5) — the pair Wordsworth rhymed in praise of Milton's voice, "like the sea … majestic, free" ('London, 1802').

Meaning & effect

we dump is the poem's moral turn: after six lines of agentless destruction the culprit is named, and it is us — the speaker included, and the reader with him. Holding the words back until a new line gives them the force of a sudden confession, and the blunt monosyllable dump lands like rubbish hitting water; the full stop after two syllables leaves the admission standing alone. Then the poem moves to the second god. Wordsworth longed to hear Triton's horn; Boey lets us hear Triton, but only straining — it is the notes, not the god, that struggle, so the image is of sound trying to escape a blocked instrument: the sea's voice imprisoned. The rhyme is a quiet irony: in 'London, 1802' Wordsworth praised Milton's voice as "like the sea" and "free"; here the sea's own voice is anything but free. notes may also glance at the poem's own medium — a report is made of notes — as if the reporter's voice, too, were struggling to get out.

Line 8
his famous horns are choked, his eyes are dazed,
Language & devices

Parallelism: two matching clauses — his famous horns are choked, his eyes are dazed — divided by a central Caesura.

Metaphor: choked gives the instrument a throat. The participles choked and dazed record damage already done.

Epithet with an allusive charge: famous — the horn is famous because poets made it so: Spenser's "Triton, blowing loud his wreathed horne" (Colin Clouts Come Home Againe, 1595), then Wordsworth's line (1807). The plural horns replaces Wordsworth's single "horn".

Iambic pentameter, perfectly regular: five even beats, falling on fa-, horns, choked, eyes, dazed.

Meaning & effect

The sea's most famous instrument is choked, blocked like a windpipe — god, conch and poem share one obstructed airway. In myth Triton's horn could command the waves (in Ovid's Metamorphoses it sounds the retreat of the great Flood), so its silencing means the sea has lost its voice of authority over its own waters. famous is the most knowing word in the line: famous where? In English poetry — Spenser and Wordsworth made it famous — so what is being choked is a celebrated image of the tradition as well as a god's horn. His eyes are dazed: stunned, as if poisoned or concussed, so the god cannot even see clearly what is being done to him. The two balanced clauses read like entries on a medical chart — voice gone, sight gone — and the calm, perfectly regular rhythm makes the injuries sound clinical, which makes them colder and more disturbing. Read another way, dazed suggests gods bewildered by a world that no longer believes in them. And read literally, as PoetryProf suggests, the choked horns are real shells and real sea-creatures, clogged with waste and tangled in lost fishing nets: the myth is a costume worn by an actual ocean.

Line 9
and Neptune lies helpless as a beached whale,
Language & devices

Classical allusion: Neptune, the Roman king of the sea (the Greek Poseidon), bearer of the trident — the third and greatest of the gods.

Listing: and adds him to the catalogue.

Simile and Bathos: helpless as a beached whale — a god compared downward to a stranded animal.

Verb: lies — prone and defeated, looking ahead to lying still (line 12).

Spondee: beached whale ends the line on two heavy stresses.

Structure: line 9 is where an English sonnet's third quatrain, or an Italian sonnet's sestet, would turn; and refuses the turn. In 'The World Is Too Much with Us', line 9 is exactly where Wordsworth turns to the pagan gods ("Great God! I'd rather be / A Pagan…"); Boey's line 9 lays the last of them on the beach.

Meaning & effect

The sea's sovereign is the last of the three gods and the most humiliated. The order of defeat is an escalation — Proteus (renewal), Triton (voice), Neptune (power itself) — so by now power has gone too: helpless is the exact opposite of what Neptune means, the god whose trident raised storms unable to move. The simile is shocking because it runs downhill: we expect a god to be compared to something greater, but Neptune is likened to a stranded animal — and to an image from the news of the 1980s, when the whale had become the emblem of the environmental movement (a moratorium on commercial whaling took effect in 1986). A beached whale is the sea's mightiest creature made helpless by being out of its element, which is what pollution does to every sea-creature by making the sea itself unliveable; and a beached whale dies without help, so the image is also a deathbed. The all-powerful figures of myth are made as weak as the creatures they ruled, and the reversal of power is what shocks. Beginning the line with and carries the list straight across the point where a sonnet traditionally turns: there is no turn, because the damage simply goes on.

Line 10
while insatiate man moves in for the kill.
Language & devices

Conjunction: while — simultaneity: as the gods lie helpless, man attacks.

Archaic diction: insatiate — "unable to be satisfied", the word of Renaissance moralists (Shakespeare's John of Gaunt calls vanity an "insatiate cormorant" that "soon preys upon itself").

Generic noun: man — the species, not a nation or an industry.

Hunting metaphor / Idiom: moves in for the kill — a predator closing on weakened prey.

Register collision: an archaic adjective and a modern idiom in one line.

End-stopped: the long sentence of lines 7–10 ends on the perpetrator.

Meaning & effect

Here the poem's anger breaks into the open and names the cause: human greed. insatiate means an appetite that is never filled and grows with what it consumes; it sharpens Wordsworth's "Getting and spending" and his "We are selfish men" into something older and more damning — the vocabulary of deadly sin. moves in for the kill is the language of predators in a wildlife film, of hunters, and of the sales floor closing a deal: man waits until the prey is helpless — Neptune beached — and then finishes it, so the image is of opportunism, not combat. while makes the timing deliberate: the attack comes as the victim lies helpless. man, without an article, turns the accusation into a charge against the species, and because the poem has already said we dump, the reader cannot stand outside it. The shift from gods to man also moves from myth to fact: the gods are images, but the predator is real. The archaic word and the modern idiom collide in one line, as if the old moral language and the new language of power meet exactly where humanity meets nature.

Line 11
Poetry and piety have begun to fail,
Language & devices

Alliteration: Poetry and piety — near-twins in sound, each opening on p followed by two vowels, each with a t and a final -y.

Abstract nouns: after the concrete gods, human faculties.

Present perfect + infinitive: have begun to fail — a process started, not finished.

Shift / partial Volta: from Nature's body to human culture and spirit.

Metre: the slackest line in the poem — twelve syllables unless squeezed, crowded by two triple-syllable words that each carry only one stress (po-e-try, pi-e-ty).

Allusion: Wordsworth's sonnets of 1802 — 'London, 1802' laments that England's "altar, sword and pen" have lost their "inward happiness"; 'Written in London, September, 1802' complains "No grandeur now in nature or in book / Delights us".

Meaning & effect

The poem turns from what is happening to nature to what is happening inside humanity. Poetry — the art of celebrating nature, everything Wordsworth stood for — and piety — reverence, religious devotion — are failing together, and the alliteration binds them so closely that they sound like one faculty with two names. Boey suggests that our capacity for wonder and for worship depends on the natural world that calls them out; he has said that in the years of his early collections "poetry and spirituality were inextricable" for him, so the line records the failure of the two things he held most closely together. have begun to fail is the tense of dread — the decline is under way and being watched, not yet complete. Wordsworth in 1802 had already complained that "pen" and "altar" were failing England and that neither "nature" nor "book" delighted any more; Boey's diagnosis goes further, because now the arts are failing not from fashion but because their source is dying. There is a paradox in the line: it announces poetry's failure inside a working sonnet — though its own overcrowded rhythm sags, as if the verse were beginning to fail as it speaks. The line also leaves the cause open: are poetry and piety failing because nature is dying, or did their failure — our loss of reverence — let nature be destroyed? Line 12's as keeps both possibilities alive.

Line 12
as Nature's mighty heart is lying still.
Language & devices

Allusion / near-quotation: the last line of Wordsworth's 'Composed upon Westminster Bridge, September 3, 1802' — "And all that mighty heart is lying still!" — with "all that" replaced by Nature's and the exclamation mark by a full stop.

Personification / Metaphor: Nature as a body whose heart has stopped.

Ambiguous conjunction: as means both while and because.

Iambic pentameter, perfectly regular: as Nature's mighty heart is lying still falls into five even iambs — the da-DUM of a heartbeat.

End-stopped, closing the third quatrain's rhyme (kill / still).

Meaning & effect

This is the poem's most devastating borrowing. In Wordsworth's sonnet "that mighty heart" is London's, seen from Westminster Bridge at dawn: the city asleep, "All bright and glittering in the smokeless air", its stillness a rare peace — the one moment the industrial city is beautiful, because it has stopped working. Boey transplants the line to Nature, and the stillness changes its meaning: a heart lying still now suggests cardiac arrest, a body on a deathbed — not sleep but death. The reversal carries a historical argument: London's heart was still because, for an hour, it was not at work; Nature's heart has stopped because the city's work never stops, and its smoke has become the smog of line 2. mighty measures the loss — the vast power of the natural world brought to a standstill. as binds the line to line 11: poetry and piety fail while Nature dies, or because Nature dies — simultaneity or causation — and Boey lets both stand. The rhythm is the cruellest touch: perfect iambs, a steady heartbeat, carrying the news that the heart has stopped. Wordsworth's exclamation of wonder becomes a flat full stop — the finding of a report.

Line 13
O see the wound widening in the sky,
Language & devices

Apostrophe / Exclamation: O — the vocative of prayer, psalm and ode.

Imperative: see — the poem's only command.

Metaphor: wound — the sky as an injured body.

Alliteration: wound widening.

Present participle: widening — still opening.

Rhythm: two firm stresses collide (wound wi-), then the line slackens through -dening in the — it gapes in the middle.

Echo: Wordsworth's "Little we see in nature that is ours" and "Ne'er saw I, never felt, a calm so deep!" — and a homophone the ear can catch: O see / "O sea".

Meaning & effect

The couplet begins with a cry for attention. The poem stops reporting and starts pleading, its register rising from document to prayer. The command see is aimed past the dead Wordsworth at whoever is reading — you cannot tell the dead to look, so it is the living who are being told — and it answers Wordsworth's own complaint, "Little we see in nature that is ours": Boey insists that we see what we have done. The wound widening in the sky makes the sky a body — the same suffering body as Nature's stopped heart — and the damage an injury that is still opening. Many readers connect it with the hole in the ozone layer, reported over Antarctica in 1985 and the subject of the Montreal Protocol of 1987: real damage, widening in the real sky, in the years before the poem. But Boey chooses the old bodily word wound, not a scientific term, so the damage is felt as violence against a living, sacred body rather than measured as data. A wound in the sky also prepares the last line: the sky becomes God's body, and wound carries the Christian memory of Christ's wounds.

Line 14
God is labouring to utter his last cry.
Language & devices

Personification: God as a suffering body.

Double meaning: labouring — straining with effort, and being in labour (childbirth).

Infinitive: to utter — the cry is attempted, not yet made. Adjective: last — finality.

Present progressive: is labouring — still happening.

Rhyming couplet: sky / cry — a full rhyme closes the sonnet.

Spondee: last cry — two heavy final stresses, ending on an open vowel with no closing consonant.

Allusion: the Crucifixion — "Jesus, when he had cried again with a loud voice, yielded up the ghost" (Matthew 27:50) — and a reversal of Wordsworth's exclamations "Great God!" ('The World Is Too Much with Us') and "Dear God!" ('Westminster Bridge').

Meaning & effect

The destruction reaches its summit: the poem's list of casualties — flowers and birds, sea-gods, poetry and piety, Nature's heart — ends with God. labouring means straining for breath, like a dying person; it is also the word for giving birth, and the birth is inverted: labour should end in a first cry, a baby's, but this one ends in a last cry. to utter means the cry has not yet come — the poem ends before it sounds, leaving the reader inside the final moment before silence. What it means for God to die is left open: the God who lives in nature — Wordsworth's "presence" whose "dwelling is … the round ocean, and the living air, / And the blue sky" — dies when nature does; or the line echoes the Crucifixion, making the destruction of nature a kind of deicide; or the failure is ours, and God strains to speak with no one left with the piety to hear. Wordsworth cried "Great God!" and "Dear God!"; here the roles are reversed and it is God who cries out. The full rhyme sky / cry closes the sonnet with a firm chime, but the sense stays open — the cry is still being laboured toward — so the form closes while the catastrophe does not. last says the end is almost here; labouring and the unfinished cry keep a sliver of time open, and that sliver is the space the poem leaves its reader.

THE WHOLE POEM

The Whole Poem

Stepping back: what the poem is doing, first line to last

The usual account of Report to Wordsworth — modern poet updates Wordsworth's complaint for the age of pollution — is true and insufficient. Read closely, the poem is not primarily a report on dying nature. It is a report on the death of the apparatus for seeing nature: the gods, the piety, the poetry — the whole Romantic optical system that made "Nature" (capital N, feminine pronoun, sacred presence) visible in the first place. Its deepest subject is the failure of its own inherited instruments, staged in those instruments; and its pessimism, I want to argue, is strategic rather than total — a despair performed with such formal vitality that it contradicts itself, deliberately, in the reader's hands.

Begin with the rhetorical situation. "You should be here, Nature has need of you" is Wordsworth's own gesture returned to him: in London, 1802 he called on the dead Milton: "Milton! thou should'st be living at this hour: / England hath need of thee". Boey files the same requisition one poet further down the chain — except that where Wordsworth summoned Milton to repair a nation ("England hath need"), Boey summons Wordsworth to repair the biosphere ("Nature has need"). The substitution measures the escalation: in 1802 the emergency was civic virtue; in 1992 it is the planet. And the gesture knows its own futility in a way Wordsworth's did not. Milton could at least be imitated; what is a returned Wordsworth supposed to do about smog? The apostrophe to the dead is poetry's oldest power move and its most transparent fiction, and Boey chooses it precisely because both things are true: the poem performs the only act poetry has left — calling to the dead — while admitting, through the administrative deadpan of "Report", that no reply is coming. A report to Wordsworth is a report to a filing cabinet in the sky.

The octave then conducts its survey through borrowed equipment, and the borrowing is the analysis. "She has been laid waste" converts The world is too much with us — "Getting and spending, we lay waste our powers" — from active to passive, from reflexive to transitive: in 1807 the casualty of materialism was our inner powers; by 1992 the waste has migrated out of the psyche and into the world's body. Wordsworth's sonnet then offered a fantasy consolation: better a Pagan creed than this numbness, so that one might "Have sight of Proteus rising from the sea; / Or hear old Triton blow his wreathed horn". Boey's middle lines take that consolation and drown it. Proteus does not fail to rise; the hope of him sinks, and he is "entombed in the waste / we dump" — the god of escape buried under specifically our garbage, the enjambment reserving "we dump" for the moment maximum guilt can be handed across the line-break. Triton's horn — "famous", Boey slyly says, famous because of Wordsworth's line — is choked. The allusion works like an audit: item by item, the 1807 imagery is checked against 1992 stock and found destroyed. Even paganism, Wordsworth's last-resort religion, is no longer available; you cannot be "suckled in a creed outworn" when the creed's gods are dead of poisoning.

This is why the sea-gods matter beyond decoration, and why their order matters (renewal, then voice, then sovereignty; see Motifs). It is also where the grief turns to anger: "while insatiate man moves in for the kill" is the one line that points at a culprit, and its predator's idiom makes the destruction an act of appetite rather than accident — an accusation that already includes the speaker, who has admitted "we dump". It is also why line 12 is the poem's most devastating theft. "As Nature's mighty heart is lying still" rewrites the ending of Composed upon Westminster Bridge — "And all that mighty heart is lying still!" — where the stilled heart is London's, asleep at dawn, and the stillness is a blessing: the one moment the city is beautiful because it has briefly stopped doing what cities do. Boey lifts the line, swaps the patient, and lets the tense curdle. Nature now wears the city's stillness, and it is not sleep. The intertext carries the whole historical argument in a single line: what industrial civilisation once borrowed from nature (calm, majesty, "the beauty of the morning") it has repaid by exporting its own condition — stoppage — back onto nature. Wordsworth's serenest line becomes a flatline.

Then the couplet, where the poem stops reporting and starts prophesying: "O see the wound widening in the sky, / God is labouring to utter his last cry." The register breaks upward — "O" is the vocative of psalm and ode, the least bureaucratic syllable in English — and the addressee silently widens from Wordsworth to anyone holding the page. The ozone reading is available and historically earned, but the poem insists on "wound", keeping the sky a body and the damage a wound in the sacred: the report reaches the place where data should go and finds only scripture. And the last line performs the poem's boldest theological move: not "God is dead" (Nietzsche's completed past) but God dying, in labour, straining toward an utterance that never arrives. The poem ends before the cry does.

Now the objection: surely this is simple despair — the heart already "still", the cry already "last", nothing left to save. Three features of the text push back. First, the tense: the damage already done is in the perfect ("has been laid waste", "have sunk"), but the dying is held in continuous forms — "slowing", "lying", "widening", "labouring" — and even the failure of poetry has only "begun". Nothing is finished; the poem fixes us in the final minute and holds the minute open. Second, the recruitment: the poem's only first-person is "we dump", and its only imperative is "O see" — guilt, then summons, both aimed at the living reader over the dead addressee's shoulder. You do not command corpses to look; the imperative proves the poem believes in a survivor. Third, the form: every voice in the poem chokes except the poem's, which keeps rhyme, keeps a strained pentameter, and closes on a clean couplet chime. A poem that truly believed poetry had failed would hardly trouble to rhyme sky with cry. The sonnet's own persistence is a quiet counter-argument running under all fourteen lines — the tradition is damaged, "laboured", half-choked, and still speaking.

So the strongest reading holds both truths at once: Report to Wordsworth announces the death of Romantic nature-piety in a living specimen of it. The report is filed to the dead, but it is delivered to us; the cry is "last", but it has not yet sounded; the heart is "lying still", but the line describing it still beats in iambs. Whether that residue of form amounts to hope or only to a beautifully disciplined way of grieving is the poem's finest, most deliberate uncertainty — and the reader, holding the text the poem says is failing, is the experiment still running.

FORM & STRUCTURE

Form & Structure

How the poem is built, and why it matters

Form & genre

A sonnet: fourteen lines printed as a single block, rhymed as an English (Shakespearean) sonnet — three quatrains and a couplet. Its genre is mixed on purpose: an official report (the title), an apostrophe to the dead (line 1), a lament for a dying world, and, in the couplet, something close to prayer.

Metre

Loose iambic pentameter. Lines 8 and 12 are perfectly regular; line 6 is a syllable short (nine); line 11 is crowded (twelve). Trochaic openings (Nature, Smothered, Triton's, God is) and heavy stress-clusters (beached whale, last cry) bend the pulse where the damage is worst.

Rhyme

ABAB CDCD EFEF GG. The B and D pairs are half-rhymes — smog / clock, waste / dazed — and every rhyme from line 9 on is full: whale / fail, kill / still, sky / cry.

Turn (volta)

No turn at line 9: and Neptune carries the list of casualties straight across. The poem turns twice, late: at line 11 (from Nature's body to the human spirit) and at line 13 (from report to plea).

Sentences

Seven sentences in fourteen lines. Two end mid-line (laid waste., we dump.); the longest (lines 7–10) piles up casualties with and and while.

Wordsworth's sonnets

All three Wordsworth sonnets the poem rewrites — 'London, 1802', 'The World Is Too Much with Us', 'Composed upon Westminster Bridge' — are Italian (Petrarchan), rhymed ABBAABBA in the octave. Boey answers them in the English pattern.

The sonnet as the report's official form

A report should be prose; Boey files his as a sonnet, and the choice is the poem's first argument. The sonnet is the form in which Wordsworth conducted his own most serious business with the state of England — 'London, 1802', 'The World Is Too Much with Us' and 'Composed upon Westminster Bridge' are all sonnets, all from the burst of sonnet-writing that began when his sister read him Milton's sonnets in 1802. Writing back in the same form is a way of writing on the tradition's own letterhead: the report is addressed to the master of the form, in the form.

The imitation is deliberately inexact. Wordsworth's three sonnets are Italian in build (an eight-line octave rhymed ABBAABBA, then a sestet); Boey's rhymes fall into the English pattern of alternating quatrains and a closing couplet — the form of Shakespeare's sonnets, and so of another English master. The copy is made at almost a century and a half's distance, by a Singaporean hand, and its variations from the model are part of what it reports.

Rhyme: hoarse, then clear

lines rhyme kind what it does
1 / 3 you / few full the absent poet and the counted survivors: the two ends of the report
2 / 4 smog / clock half-rhyme same vowel; the end consonants differ only in voicing (g voiced, k voiceless) — a rhyme with the breath taken out of it, in the quatrain about smothering
5 / 7 sea / free full the two words of escape and openness, pinned at the line-ends of a passage about burial and blockage
6 / 8 waste / dazed half-rhyme again a voicing mismatch (s–t against z–d): the rhyme goes hoarse as Triton's horn is choked
9 / 11 whale / fail full the beached god and the failing arts sound as one collapse
10 / 12 kill / still full cause and result: the predator's attack and the stopped heart
13 / 14 sky / cry full the wound and the utterance; the couplet closes on an open vowel

The pattern tightens as the poem goes on: blurred rhymes while the damage is being described, clean rhymes once the poem moves into verdict. So the sonnet's rhymes recover their voice as Nature loses hers. The full rhymes of lines 9–12 also pair the poem's two kinds of loss — natural and spiritual — in sound: the god whale with fail, the hunter's kill with the heart still. The couplet's sky / cry rings clear, but it carries a sentence whose action is unfinished (God is still labouring to utter): the form closes while the event does not.

The free/sea rhyme carries a private irony: Wordsworth used the same pair in 'London, 1802' in praise of Milton's voice — "Thou hadst a voice whose sound was like the sea: / Pure as the naked heavens, majestic, free". In Boey the sea's own voice is the thing that is not free.

Metre: key lines scanned

Stressed syllables in capitals; ‖ marks a strong pause.

line scansion what the variation does
1 you SHOULD be HERE, ‖ NA-ture has NEED of YOU two iambs, then a trochee on Nature after the comma: the metre turns over as the subject is named, and the line ends on you, the stress it began with
2 she has been LAID WASTE. ‖ SMOTH-ered by the SMOG two heavy stresses together on laid waste, then the earliest full stop in the poem, after five syllables; a trochee (SMOTH-ered) restarts the line from below
4 in a SKY SLOW-ing like a DY-ing CLOCK two light syllables, two stresses colliding, then the falling -ing rhythm: the even tick of the line falters in the line about time running down
6 have SUNK; ‖ he is en-TOMBED in the WASTE nine syllables and only three firm stresses: the line is a syllable short, sagging through he is and in the — something has sunk out of the measure
7 we DUMP. ‖ TRI-ton's NOTES STRUG-gle to be FREE the run-on sentence lands on the thud of dump and stops; then notes struggle crowds two stresses together — sound pushing against blockage
8 his FA-mous HORNS are CHOKED, ‖ his EYES are DAZED perfectly regular: five even iambs and a central pause. After the strain of line 7, injuries recorded in a calm clinical rhythm
9 and NEP-tune LIES HELP-less as a BEACHED WHALE stress-clash on lies help-, a quick run as a, then two final heavy stresses: the line runs aground on beached whale
11 PO-e-try and PI-e-ty have be-GUN to FAIL twelve syllables carrying four main stresses; the two three-syllable abstractions crowd the line, and it sags as it announces failure
12 as NA-ture's MIGH-ty HEART is LY-ing STILL the most regular line in the poem — the da-DUM of a heartbeat carrying the news that the heart has stopped
13 o SEE the WOUND WI-den-ing in the SKY two firm iambs, a clash on wound wi-, then three light syllables (-dening in the): the line gapes in the middle, as the wound does
14 GOD is LA-bour-ing to UT-ter his LAST CRY a trochee puts the final subject first; labouring makes the mouth work; two heavy stresses end the poem, the last on an open vowel

Even allowing for elisions, the pentameter is never comfortably itself after the octave: lines 6 and 13 run light, 9 and 14 heavy, 11 crowded. The two perfectly regular lines (8 and 12) are the two clinical ones — the inventory of Triton's injuries and the stopped heart — so regularity itself becomes sinister. A traditional measure is still standing, and audibly failing.

The missing turn

A Shakespearean sonnet leads the reader to expect a shift at line 9 (the third quatrain) or, in its Italian ancestor, at the octave–sestet border. In 'The World Is Too Much with Us' line 9 is exactly where Wordsworth turns — "It moves us not.—Great God! I'd rather be / A Pagan suckled in a creed outworn" — towards the consolation of the old gods. Boey gives his line 9 to the last of those gods, and opens it with and: and Neptune lies helpless as a beached whale. The list of casualties (lines 5–10) rides straight over the border, as if the damage paid no attention to the form's internal divisions, any more than to nature's.

The poem does turn, twice, and late:

  • Line 11 — from the seascape to the human spirit: Poetry and piety have begun to fail. The report moves from what is happening to Nature to what is happening inside us. PoetryProf calls this an escalation rather than a change of direction, and the sound bears that out: the rhyme pairs fail with the beached whale.
  • Line 13 — from report to plea: O see breaks the documentary voice with the oldest lyric gesture there is, and the addressee widens from Wordsworth to whoever is reading.

So the poem has three shapes laid over each other: an English rhyme-grid (4 + 4 + 4 + 2); a suppressed Italian expectation at line 9; and a rhetorical structure of survey (1–10), diagnosis (11–12) and appeal (13–14). The mismatch between them is part of the meaning: the form promises turns and resolutions that the catastrophe refuses.

Syntax, punctuation and lineation

The seven sentences trace the report's changing voice:

  1. You should be here, Nature has need of you. (line 1)
  2. She has been laid waste. (line 2, first half)
  3. Smothered by the smog, … like a dying clock. (2–4)
  4. All hopes of Proteus … the waste / we dump. (5–7)
  5. Triton's notes struggle … moves in for the kill. (7–10)
  6. Poetry and piety … lying still. (11–12)
  7. O see the wound … his last cry. (13–14)

The poem opens in the clipped manner of an incident report — subject, verb, full stop — and the sentences then lengthen as the disaster outruns the reporting style, peaking in the four-line sentence 5, which keeps adding casualties (and Neptune…, while insatiate man…) like a list that cannot be closed. The two sentences that end mid-line both stop dead on violence: She has been laid waste. (after five syllables) and we dump. (after two). Elsewhere sentences end with the line — at lines 1, 4, 10, 12 and 14 — and lines 12 and 14 are the two moments of arrest, the stopped heart and the last cry.

There are three enjambments, and each does work. the birds are few / in a sky spreads the scarcity across a whole failing sky. All hopes of Proteus rising from the sea / have sunk makes the reader wait a line for the verb, so the hope rises before it falls — and then drops over the line-edge. he is entombed in the waste / we dump withholds the agent until the next line, so that the reader steps across the gap into the confession. Elsewhere the lines are end-stopped or comma-paused: a poem of containment rather than flow, as dammed as the sea it describes.

The single semicolon is a hinge: have sunk; he is entombed — from the abstract (hopes) to the physical (a body in a tomb). The comma splice of line 1 and the chain of commas in lines 7–10 (free, … choked, … dazed, … whale,) give the poem the breathless run of speech under pressure, not the composed syntax of a document.

The title as part of the form

A report is an administrative genre: filed upward, to someone with authority, in expectation of action — and Boey, who worked as a probation officer before he emigrated, knew the genre from the inside. Report to Wordsworth therefore casts Wordsworth as the absent superior of English nature poetry, and quietly admits the futility, since a report to the dead brings no action. The poem's two registers — bureaucratic notification and lyric lament — are both announced before line 1 begins, and the poem's form is the movement from one to the other.

SOUND

Sound

What the poem does to the ear

Sibilance: breath escaping

She has been laid waste. Smothered by the smog — the shared sm welds smog to smothering, and the s sounds running through lines 2–5 (waste, smog, sky slowing, hopes, sea, sunk) sound like air leaking out of a system.

Stops: air blocked

The violent words end on stopped consonants: dump, entombed, choked, dazed, beached, clock, kill. choked begins with a stop released into friction (ch) and ends on two stops (-kt); dump closes the lips on the waste.

Two vowels of grief

A long ay sound runs through Nature, laid waste, famous, dazed, whale, fail, labouring; a long i through sky, dying, rising, eyes, while, piety, mighty, lying, widening, cry — the sounds of wail and cry.

The last sound

cry ends on an open diphthong with no closing consonant: the poem's final sound is a vowel left open, like the unfinished cry it names.

The opening line is a call rather than a statement: Nature has need alliterates on n, and the long open vowels of be here, need and Nature carry — PoetryProf hears the voice as strident, even desperate. Then line 2 turns the sound inward. Smothered by the smog is hissed through the teeth, and the soft m inside both words muffles them: the line sounds like breath being pressed down, which is what it describes.

Lines 3–4 slow the mouth. the flowers are mute, and the birds are few lilts in four light beats, but its long oo (mute, few, echoing you) is the sound of lament, and it returns in entombed and wound. In line 4 the l sounds — sky slowing like a dying clock — slide the line downhill, and the two -ing endings fall away like the last irregular ticks of a clock. The line about slowing time is itself hard to say quickly.

The sea passage is built from obstruction. Triton's notes struggle to be free packs consonant clusters together (tr, n-t-s, str) so that the reading voice has to push, as the notes do; then his famous horns are choked, his eyes are dazed lands two hard endings (-kt, -zd) either side of the central pause. Against all this the C rhymes sea and free are the only pure, open ee rhymes in the poem — escape and openness audible for a syllable at a time, then shut in.

Poetry and piety are near-twins in sound: both open on p followed by two vowels side by side (po-e, pi-e), both carry a t, both end on the same light -y. The alliteration argues what the sentence argues — that art and reverence are one capacity, failing together. The ay chain gathers on whale and fail, binding the beached god to the failing arts in the rhyme itself.

The couplet asks the voice to rise — O is an intake of breath, a wordless cry before the words — and wound widening repeats the w like a mouth opening. The last line is effortful to say: labouring to utter his last cry crowds b, r and t sounds, and last cry puts two heavy stresses together with a cluster (st-kr) between them. Then the poem stops on the open vowel of cry. Read aloud, it does not resolve; it breaks off.

MOTIFS & SYMBOLS

Motifs & Symbols

Images that recur, and what they accumulate

(Motif = an image or idea that recurs and accumulates; symbol = a thing that stands for something beyond itself. This poem's motifs run in strict sequence — each can be traced line by line, and each degrades as it goes.)

Motif 1: silenced utterance (the poem's master-motif)

Track every image of voice, in order: the flowers are "mute" (3) → Triton's "notes struggle to be free" (7) → his "horns are choked" (8) → "Poetry" begins "to fail" (11) → God is "labouring to utter his last cry" (14). The trajectory is a progressive laryngitis of the cosmos: first the small voices (flowers, whose "speech" is scent and colour), then the sea's official music, then human art, then the divine voice itself — and at each stage the failure moves closer to the poem's own medium. By line 14 what is dying is utterance as such, and the only voice still functioning is the sonnet we are reading. The motif turns the poem reflexive: a report on the death of speech, delivered in speech; the last breathing thing in a world of stopped throats. That is why the final image is not a flood or a fire but an unfinished sentence.

Motif 2: the vertical collapse — rising defeated by lying

Every vertical in the poem points down: Nature is "laid waste" (2), hopes of Proteus "rising" have "sunk" (5–6), he is "entombed" (6), Neptune "lies" (9), the heart is "lying still" (12). One word of ascent is permitted — Wordsworth's own "rising", quoted from The world is too much with us — and it appears only inside a negation ("All hopes of… have sunk"). The motif ends on the repeated posture of the deathbed — Neptune "lies", the heart is "lying still" — and Wordsworth's phrase for a city asleep now describes a body that has stopped. What changes across the poem: early, things are put down ("laid waste" — passive, an agent implied); by the end things simply are down ("is lying still" — stative). Violence has become condition.

Motif 3: the failing mechanism — time running out, in the present progressive

The clock enters as simile ("a sky slowing like a dying clock", 4) and never really leaves: "begun to fail" (11), "is lying" (12), "widening" (13), "labouring" (14). Grammatically, the poem's dying happens in continuous forms — the grammar of the not-yet-finished — while only the damage already done is in the perfect ("has been laid waste", "have sunk"). Nothing in the poem has completed: the birds are "few" not gone, poetry has "begun to fail", the wound is "widening" not open, the cry is being laboured toward, not uttered. The motif accumulates into the poem's temporal signature: apocalypse as wind-down rather than explosion, witnessed from inside the final minute. The dying clock also quietly indicts a whole cosmology — the Enlightenment's clockwork universe, wound by a watchmaker God; here the mechanism is running down and the watchmaker is on his deathbed. What changes: at line 4 time is failing out there, in the sky; by line 14 the reader realises the poem itself has been the clock, fourteen lines ticking to a stop.

Motif 4: the wounded body of Nature

The poem assembles a single composite patient, examined top to tail: smothered (2, breath), mute (3, voice), sunk and entombed (5–6, burial), choked (8, throat), dazed (8, eyes), beached (9, whole body), heart "lying still" (12, cardiac arrest), "the wound widening" (13, open lesion), "labouring" (14, the body in extremis). The clinical sequence moves inward — surface, airway, senses, heart — then bursts outward to a wound in the sky, as though the autopsy discovered the injury was bigger than the body. Two transformations matter: "laid waste" (a war-term: land as ravaged territory) becomes literal "waste / we dump" (garbage) — the metaphor of devastation degrading into the fact of litter; and "labouring", the childbirth word, arrives inverted — a body in labour to deliver not a first cry but a "last cry". The motif's endpoint fuses Nature, God and mother into one dying body, and the reader is left holding the question the poem will not answer: attending a deathbed, or a delivery?

Symbols

  • The three sea-gods, in this order. Proteus — the shape-shifting sea-elder who, if you could hold him, prophesied truly: he stands for the sea's capacity for renewal, metamorphosis and revealed truth (and, since Wordsworth wished for "sight of Proteus rising", for the Romantic hope itself). Triton — herald of the ocean, whose conch-blast calmed or roused the waves: the sea's voice and authority over storm. Neptune — not a messenger or a seer but sovereignty itself, king of the element. The order of defeat is an escalation staged with forensic logic: first the possibility of renewal dies (Proteus entombed — the escape-artist buried, the one god whose essence is slipping free now fixed under garbage), then expression dies (Triton choked), then power as such dies (Neptune beached — and note the demotion: the god is compared to an animal, "as a beached whale", divinity explained by way of a carcass on the news). Prophecy → voice → sovereignty: hope, then speech, then being. By the time "insatiate man moves in", the kill is of something already down.
  • The dying clock (see Motif 3): entropy, the mechanistic cosmos failing, and — since a clock is a made thing — the suggestion that Nature has already been reconceived as machinery, which is part of how it was killed.
  • The wound widening in the sky: the poem's one symbol that history has since "solved" (the ozone hole — and the dates fit) but which the text keeps unscientific: a wound, in a sky that by line 14 is God's body. It stands for damage that is (a) overhead, i.e. above human reach and remedy, (b) widening, i.e. ongoing, and (c) inflicted on the sacred itself. The refusal of the technical term is the meaning: a report that breaks down into scripture exactly where the data should go.
  • "Nature's mighty heart": lifted from the last line of Composed upon Westminster Bridge, where "all that mighty heart" is London's, lying still in beautiful early-morning sleep. Transplanted here, the symbol carries its provenance as irony: the city's borrowed stillness has become Nature's literal cardiac arrest — Wordsworth's most serene line converted into a death certificate (see Close Analysis).
THEMES

Themes

The ideas the poem is arguing about

01

Environmental destruction and human greed

The report's findings come in the order of a survey: land and air first (She has been laid waste. Smothered by the smog), then flowers and birds (mute, few), the sky (slowing like a dying clock), and the sea, where every god is disabled. The damage is total — breath, voice, sight, movement, heartbeat — and it is told through verbs of violence: laid waste is what armies do, Smothered and choked are ways of killing by stopping breath, entombed is burial. The cause is held back until the sea passage. First it is buried in passives (has been laid waste), then it surfaces as habit (the waste / we dump), and finally it is named as an appetite: insatiate man moves in for the kill.

insatiate — never satisfied — makes greed the root of the destruction, and the archaic word gives it the weight of an old sin rather than a modern policy failure. moves in for the kill adds opportunism: man attacks when the victim is already down, while Neptune lies helpless. The theme is not only destruction but its motive: the same "Getting and spending" Wordsworth warned against in 1807 has grown from a waste of our powers into a waste of the world. This is where the poem's grief turns to anger — the one line that points a finger is also the one with a predator in it.

02

The loss of the sacred

For Wordsworth, Nature was holy: a "presence" dwelling in "the round ocean, and the living air, / And the blue sky". Boey's report is written from inside that belief — capital-N Nature, a She with a mighty heart — and it records the sacred dying layer by layer. The pagan gods Wordsworth hoped to glimpse are entombed, choked and beached; reverence itself (piety) is failing; and the last line reaches the top of the hierarchy: God is labouring to utter his last cry.

The poem never decides what kind of death this is. It may be the death of a God who lives in nature and so dies with it; a Crucifixion re-enacted, so that destroying the world becomes a kind of deicide; or a God still crying out to people who have lost the piety to hear. What is clear is the link the poem insists on: the natural and the sacred stand or fall together. Boey has said that in his early writing life "poetry and spirituality were inextricable"; the poem imagines that bond broken by the destruction of the thing both were turned towards.

03

Complicity: who did this?

The poem's grammar is a short history of blame. In lines 1–6 the destruction has no agent — has been laid waste, Smothered, have sunk, is entombed — the way environmental damage seems to happen when everyone is responsible and no one is accountable. Then the line break after waste delivers we dump: the only first person in the poem, a blunt two-syllable confession that includes the speaker and pulls the reader in with him. By line 10 the culprit has become man, the whole species.

So the report is not filed by an innocent observer. The poet who mourns Nature belongs to the we that buries Proteus, and the imperative O see in line 13 — the poem's only command — is aimed at the living, who share the guilt and might still act. The anger in insatiate man is therefore partly self-accusation, which is what keeps the poem from being a sermon delivered from safety. Wordsworth's own sonnets set the precedent: "We are selfish men" ('London, 1802'), "we lay waste our powers".

04

What poetry can and cannot do

A report should bring action; this one is addressed to a man dead since 1850. The poem knows the gesture is impossible — Wordsworth cannot come — and makes that futility part of its meaning: poetry's oldest power, calling the absent into presence, is used at the very moment the poem says Poetry and piety have begun to fail. The voices of the poem fail one after another — flowers mute, Triton's notes struggling, his horns choked, God labouring to utter — so the failure of utterance is the poem's master image, and poetry is one of the casualties.

Yet the sonnet itself keeps working: it keeps its rhyme scheme, keeps a strained pentameter, and closes on a full chime, sky / cry. Whether that survival is a sign of hope or only a disciplined way of grieving is left open. Either way, the poem tests the Romantic claim that poetry binds us to nature, and finds that claim weakest exactly when it is most needed.

05

Inheritance: answering Wordsworth

The poem is made out of Wordsworth's sonnets: the summons of 'London, 1802' (should, need of), the lay waste and the sea-gods of 'The World Is Too Much with Us', the mighty heart … lying still of 'Composed upon Westminster Bridge'. Wordsworth had called on Milton in the same way, so Boey places himself in a line of inheritance — Milton, Wordsworth, Boey — and writes in the form that line made its own, the sonnet. The allusions work like an audit: Wordsworth's images are checked against the present and found destroyed, and his consolation (the pagan gods) becomes a casualty list.

The heir is a Singaporean poet, born in the year of independence, educated in the English canon. The poem does not quarrel with that inheritance — its tone is filial, closer to a pupil reporting to a master than to a rebel — but the report carries an uncomfortable message to its source: the industrial modernity that grew up alongside English Romanticism has poisoned the world that Romanticism worshipped. Boey keeps the tradition and finds it damaged in his hands.

06

Time running out: an apocalypse in slow motion

The poem's end of the world is a winding-down, not an explosion. a sky slowing like a dying clock sets the image: time itself failing tick by tick. The damage already done is in perfect tenses (has been laid waste, have sunk, have begun to fail); the dying is in continuous forms that keep it happening as we read (slowing, dying, is lying, widening, is labouring). Nothing is quite finished: the birds are few, not gone; poetry has begun to fail; the wound is widening; God is still labouring to utter the cry.

That incompleteness is the source of the poem's dread and of its one sliver of possibility. last says the end is almost here; the unfinished cry means it has not yet come. The poem stops inside the final moment — grief for what is going, anger at who is doing it, and the implied question of whether O see can still make anyone look in time.

DIFFICULT MOMENTS

Difficult Moments

Where the poem is genuinely undecidable — and what to do about it

Cruxes

1. What kind of speech-act is line 1 — summons, elegy, or accusation?

The difficulty. "You should be here, Nature has need of you" can be voiced at least three ways, and the poem never adjudicates. (a) Summons: the London, 1802 template — come back, we need your vision; "should" as moral requisition. (b) Elegy: "you should be here" as the idiom of the bereaved and of postcards ("wish you were here") — nothing is being requested because nothing can be; the line mourns an absence it knows is permanent. (c) Accusation, or bitter irony: you should be here — you, who promised that Nature never did betray the heart that loved her; come and look at her now. On this voicing the report is a subpoena, and Wordsworth's absence is a kind of luck ("you are well out of it" flickers underneath).

Evidence. For (a): the modal "should", the businesslike second clause, the report frame (reports go to someone empowered to act). For (b): everything that follows — a dead addressee, gods "entombed", a "last cry"; you do not brief a corpse, you grieve at it. For (c): the poem's systematic demolition of Wordsworth's specific images (his Proteus, his Triton, his "mighty heart") reads almost like an itemised refutation; and "Poetry… ha[s] begun to fail" indicts the very art Wordsworth claimed would bind man to nature.

What a strong answer does. Refuses to pick, and instead observes that the poem's genre is precisely the impossible speech-act: an apostrophe to the dead is always simultaneously summons (in form) and elegy (in fact), and Boey chooses it because the gap between the two is his subject — poetry's grandest power (calling absence into presence) exercised at the exact moment the poem says poetry is failing. The accusatory shimmer is what keeps the reverence from sentimentality.

2. "Smothered by the smog," — who or what is smothered?

The difficulty. As punctuated ("She has been laid waste. Smothered by the smog, / the flowers are mute"), the participial phrase belongs grammatically to "the flowers". But it arrives hard on the heels of "She", whom we have just seen "laid waste", and most first readings attach it backwards to Nature herself. The modifier genuinely dangles between two hosts.

The readings. (a) Careless-reader version: it modifies Nature — wrong by the punctuation, but revealing. (b) Strict version: the flowers are smothered, and the sentence performs a camera-cut from the whole ("She") to the parts (flowers, birds, sky). (c) The sophisticated version: the drift is the device — pollution does not respect clause boundaries; the participle floats like the smog it names, settling on whatever stands under it. Notice too that the agentless passives ("has been laid waste", "Smothered") keep deleting the perpetrator, so that for six lines destruction simply happens — until "we dump" abruptly files the missing agent, and it is us.

What a strong answer does. Uses the ambiguity as evidence about agency rather than resolving the grammar: the poem's syntax reproduces the structure of environmental harm — diffuse cause, drifting damage, deferred culprit — and then springs the trap of the first person plural. Grammatically the participle belongs to the flowers; its drift back towards "She" is the effect, not an error.

3. "the wound widening in the sky" — what is the wound?

The difficulty. The poem's climactic image is its least specified. Three readings compete. (a) Historicist: the ozone hole — announced 1985, treatied 1987, ubiquitous in early-90s environmental discourse; a Singapore poet writing in 1992 could count on every reader supplying it. (b) Theological: a wound in the body of God — the sky as divine flesh, preparing line 14; "wound... widening" as crucifixion imagery in slow motion (a spear-wound that will not close), so that pollution becomes deicide. (c) Deliberately unnameable: the report reaches the point where a real report would give the measurement and the chemical name, and instead produces the oldest, least technical word for damage there is. The failure of nomenclature is the point — piety's vocabulary surviving where science's should be.

Evidence. For (a): the dating; "widening" as the literal behaviour of the ozone hole; the poem's other eco-specifics (smog, dumping). For (b): "God is labouring" immediately after — the syntax invites us to read line 13 as God's wound; "O see" echoes liturgical address (ecce — behold). For (c): the poem's consistent preference for archaic register ("insatiate", "piety", "O") over technical terms; a poem happy to say "smog" chose not to say "ozone".

What a strong answer does. Notes that (a) and (b) require each other: the image only works because a real, measurable hole in the sky existed and could be seen as a wound — the metaphor's power is that the literal referent was itself apocalyptic. It also notices how much the single word "wound" carries: without it the image would be an abstract "widening"; with it the sky becomes a body, which is what allows line 14 to make that body God's.

4. "Poetry and piety have begun to fail, / as Nature's mighty heart is lying still" — cause or consequence?

The difficulty. The conjunction "as" can mean while or because, and the two lines can be read in either causal direction. Did the death of nature bring about the failure of poetry and piety — or did the failure of poetry and piety, our loss of reverence, allow nature to be killed?

Competing readings. (a) Nature first: poetry and piety are responses to the natural world — Wordsworth's "language of the sense" — so when Nature's heart stops, the arts of wonder and worship lose their source and fail. The sea-god passage supports this: the poem's sacred figures are nature-figures, and they die of pollution before poetry is mentioned. (b) Reverence first: the destruction was possible because reverence had already gone. Wordsworth made this diagnosis in his sonnets of 1802–07 ("Little we see in Nature that is ours"; "We are selfish men"), and the poem's chain of agents — passive, then "we dump", then "insatiate man" — describes people who no longer treat nature as sacred. PoetryProf reads "piety" in this sense, as humanity's loss of accountability to any higher power. (c) Simultaneity: "as" means only while — two declines happening together, the cause left unspoken because both are symptoms of the same appetite.

What a strong answer does. Treats the ambiguity as the poem's argument rather than a lapse: by refusing to say which came first, Boey makes the natural and the spiritual crises one crisis, each the cause and the effect of the other. It also notices the irony of form: the line announcing poetry's failure is followed by the most regular line in the poem, as if the verse were still doing what it says has stopped.

5. "God is labouring to utter his last cry." — dying God, dying meaning, or deaf mankind?

The difficulty. The last line commits the poem to an extraordinary theological claim, but which one? (a) Literal deicide: God is dying of what we did to his creation; the strongest, most disturbing reading, and the one licensed by "last". (b) Pantheist/Romantic: "God" here is not a person but the sum of meanings nature carried (Wordsworth's "presence… deeply interfused"); when nature dies, that God dies by definition — the line is rigorous, not hyperbolic. (c) Failure of reception: God labours "to utter" because no one is left who can hear — the cry may be perfect and perpetual; it is our organ for hearing it ("piety") that has failed.

Evidence. For (a): the escalation pattern (flowers → gods → God) demands a real casualty at its summit; "last" is unambiguous about finality. For (b): the poem's God appears only through nature (sky as his body); and the gods already killed are nature-personifications — the poem has trained us to read divinity as ecology's face. For (c): "labouring to utter" locates the failure in transmission, not existence; and line 11 blamed our faculties ("piety ha[s] begun to fail"), not heaven's.

And the second layer: "labouring" is the childbirth word. A last cry delivered by labour inverts the first cry of the delivery room — but an inversion still carries its original: is something being born here (a new dispensation, a warning that could still be heeded), or is birth-language the cruellest possible frame for extinction? The cry, note, never sounds — the poem ends inside the labour.

What a strong answer does. Keeps the cry unuttered. The line's genius is that the poem must end for the cry to happen, so the cry falls into the white space after line 14 — either it is sounding now, unheard, or the silence after the sonnet is the cry. Choosing between God-dying and man-deafened matters less than seeing that both leave the reader in the same position: the last functioning listener, reading the last functioning voice.

CLOSE ANALYSIS

Close Analysis

The moments that repay pressure, worked through

Quotation analysis

(Twelve moments chosen because they repay pressure, not because they are the most quoted. Format: quotation — techniques — analysis — intention/effect.)

1. "Report to Wordsworth" (title)

Genre-word; apostrophe announced in advance; allusion; irony. The title has to be read with Wordsworth in it, or the opening and the three sea-gods lose their point. "Report" is the vocabulary of officials and inspectors — an account of findings filed upward to someone with the power to act — and it promises a cool, factual voice that the poem will not keep: the report breaks into myth, lament and prayer, as if the facts were too terrible for a factual style. "to Wordsworth" names both the addressee and the standard: William Wordsworth (1770–1850), the English Romantic who made Nature a moral and spiritual teacher, and whose sonnets supply line 1, the "laid waste" of line 2, Proteus and Triton, and the "mighty heart" of line 12. A report to a man dead since 1850 can never be acted on — the futility is built into the title — so its real recipient is the living reader. It is also a gesture of inheritance: a younger poet reporting back to the master of the tradition, as Wordsworth himself had called on Milton. Intention/effect: before a line is read, Boey sets two registers against each other — bureaucratic notification and lyric grief — and the poem's movement from one to the other is its shape.

2. "You should be here, Nature has need of you." (1)

Apostrophe to the dead; modal verb; allusion (London, 1802); balanced two-part line. The line is a rewrite of Wordsworth's summons to Milton — "England hath need of thee" — with one substitution that carries the whole poem: England has become Nature. The endangered polity is no longer a nation but the biosphere; patriotism has been superseded by something larger, and Wordsworth is being drafted as its laureate. "Should" is doing double work: obligation (you ought to be here) and counterfactual longing (the "wish you were here" of the bereaved postcard) — command and grief in one auxiliary. The archaism "has need of you" (rather than "needs you") deliberately fakes Wordsworth's period voice, as if the report were written in the recipient's dialect out of courtesy — or as if Boey can only speak of Nature in borrowed Romantic English, which is precisely his predicament. Intention/effect: Boey establishes homage and hopelessness in a single breath, and the reader is positioned as eavesdropper on a letter to the dead — which quietly makes us its actual recipients.

3. "She has been laid waste." (2)

Agentless passive; military idiom; personification; terminal caesura (sentence dead after five syllables). "Laid waste" is what armies do to enemy territory: the idiom declares, before any detail arrives, that the relation between humanity and nature is a war, and a finished one — this is the language of aftermath, not battle. The passive deletes the perpetrator, and the deletion is the meaning: environmental destruction arrives with no signature, everyone's doing and no one's fault, until "we dump" (line 7) belatedly files the confession. Hear also the buried Wordsworth: "Getting and spending, we lay waste our powers" — in 1807 the waste was inward, a squandering of human capacity; Boey flips the verb into the passive and the damage outward onto Nature's body. The full stop after five syllables kills the sentence mid-line: the poem's syntax starts practising for the deaths it will describe. Intention/effect: a war-report register that makes the reader a citizen of the aggressor nation before we have agreed to be.

4. "the flowers are mute, and the birds are few" (3)

Personification; parallel clauses; understatement; four-beat lilt. Two short, matched clauses — the + noun + are + adjective — read like items in an inventory, and their plainness is chilling. "mute" implies the flowers once had voices: for Wordsworth they did, since nature spoke a "language of the sense" that poetry translated; so the first silence in the poem is also the first loss to poetry, which now has nothing to hear. It starts the poem's master motif, the failure of voices, which runs through Triton's notes and horns to God's unfinished cry. "few" is the word of a survey count, not of an elegy — a decline still in progress, which makes it urgent rather than merely sad. Flowers and birdsong are the stock materials of English nature poetry, so these are the tradition's losses as well as nature's; behind "the birds are few" many readers hear Keats's "And no birds sing", the line Rachel Carson set as the epigraph of Silent Spring (1962). Intention/effect: the almost nursery-rhyme lilt makes the damage sound like a child's flat statement of fact — final, unarguable, and more disturbing for being calm.

5. "in a sky slowing like a dying clock." (4)

Simile; mechanistic conceit; participial chime ("slowing… dying"); decelerating rhythm. The obvious reading — time running out — is the least of it. A clock is a made thing: comparing the sky to one quietly concedes that nature has already been reconceived as machinery, the Enlightenment's clockwork universe — and a clockwork universe can break. "Dying clock" fuses the organic and mechanical into one impossible corpse: clocks do not die, creatures do not run down, and the collision says the categories themselves have failed. The simile also works meteorologically: a "slowing" sky is one where nothing moves — no wind, no birds (line 3 has emptied it), weather itself winding down. And a stopped clock is how a household marks a death. Intention/effect: Boey wants dread with a long fuse — entropy, not explosion — and the reader's inner metronome is made to drag through the falling "-ing… -ing" rhythm.

6. "have sunk; he is entombed in the waste / we dump." (6–7)

Enjambment; semicolon; irony of myth (the escape-artist buried); pronoun ambush; metrically short line. The subject that "sinks" is not Proteus but "All hopes" — abstraction given physics, hope with displacement and weight. "Entombed" is the precise cruelty: Proteus is the god whose essence is escape — shape-shifter, uncatchable, the one being no grip could hold — and Boey pins him under garbage; not defeated in contest but landfilled, a burial with no resurrection grammar anywhere near it. The line-break then performs the poem's moral pivot: "the waste" hangs innocent at the line-end until the turn delivers "we dump" — agent and crime in two syllables, the only first-person in the poem, positioned where the eye cannot see it coming. The verse line itself is a syllable short (see Form & Structure): matter has gone missing from the pentameter. Intention/effect: the reader is manoeuvred into confession — we finish the line and discover it was about us.

7. "Triton's notes struggle to be free," (7)

Personification at the level of sound; pun on "notes"; allusion. The notes — not Triton — do the struggling: agency has retreated from the god into his music, which now behaves like something trapped and animate, a creature scrabbling at a blocked pipe. The pun is quietly devastating: "notes" are music, but they are also what reports are made of — jottings, memoranda; Triton's notes and Boey's notes are failing together, the sea's herald and the poem's author caught in the same sentence. (A student can legitimately hear the poem describing its own composition: these fourteen lines are notes struggling to be free.) After Wordsworth wished to "hear old Triton blow his wreathed horn", Boey grants the wish acoustically and ruins it — we do hear Triton, and what we hear is obstruction. Intention/effect: the poem makes the reader listen for a sound that never arrives, training us in the attentive failure that is its subject.

8. "his famous horns are choked," (8)

Epithet with intertextual payload; transferred physiology; plural revision of the source. "Famous" looks like filler and is the most knowing word in the line: famous where? In poetry — the horn is famous because Wordsworth's sonnet made it so ("Or hear old Triton blow his wreathèd horn" — the last line of one of his best-known sonnets). The adjective is a citation: Boey is not describing a god's attribute but a canonical image's afterlife, and what has happened to it — the tradition's best-known instrument now blocked with waste. The plural "horns" (Wordsworth's was one "wreathed horn") suggests multiplication and degradation at once — as if mass reproduction of the image (in a thousand anthologies) has left many horns, all choked.
