"Choked" transfers a windpipe to an instrument: god, conch and poem share one obstructed airway. Intention/effect: readers who know the source feel the canon itself gag; readers who don't still hear the strangling — the line is built to work at both depths.

9. "helpless as a beached whale," (9)

Simile (god → animal); bathos as method; topical image. The comparison runs downhill — a god explained by way of an animal, and not a living animal but the era's most public image of marine death: the beached whale of the news photograph, the "Save the Whales" placard (the whaling moratorium was six years old in 1992). Neptune is not overthrown by a rival god, which would at least be mythologically dignified; he is stranded — removed from his element the way pollution removes every sea-creature from its element, by making the element unliveable. The simile's logic cuts deeper: when the sacred needs the creaturely to explain it, the hierarchy of being has inverted — myth now borrows its images from ecological disaster, not the other way round. "Helpless" before "beached" doubles the passivity: power's defining figure defined by what he cannot do. Intention/effect: Boey collapses the mythic into the documentary so the reader grieves for both at once — the picture from the news lends the god its pathos, and the god lends the news its scale.

10. "while insatiate man moves in for the kill." (10)

Register collision (archaism + thriller idiom); synecdoche ("man"); predation metaphor; conjunction of simultaneity. "Insatiate" is the poem's oldest word — the moral vocabulary of Renaissance epic and sermon (Shakespeare's "insatiate cormorant" that "soon preys upon itself"), the deadly sin of avarice in period costume. "Moves in for the kill" is its newest: the idiom of the nature documentary, the hitman film, the sales floor. Their collision in one line is the poem's whole method in miniature — Romantic-archaic diction laid against modern demotic until the gap between them measures the fall. And the predation is dishonest predation: you "move in for the kill" on wounded prey; after nine lines of choking and beaching, man arrives not as hunter but as finisher. "While" makes it simultaneous with Neptune's helplessness — opportunism, not combat. The universal "man" (no article, the species) turns indictment into anthropology. Intention/effect: the reader is denied the comfort of blaming an industry or a nation; the charge sheet names the species, and the archaic word makes the greed feel ancient, constitutive, confessed.

11. "Poetry and piety have begun to fail, / as Nature's mighty heart is lying still." (11–12)

Abstract pairing bound by alliteration; allusion (Westminster Bridge); ambiguous conjunction; iambic flatline. The line pivots the poem from ecology to epistemology: not what is dying, but what dies in us when it does — the twinned faculties of art and reverence, near-anagrams sharing their sounds as they share their fate. "Begun to fail" is the tense of dread: we are watching the decline live, not mourning after. Then the theft: "all that mighty heart is lying still" is the last line of Wordsworth's Composed upon Westminster Bridge, where the heart is London's and its stillness is dawn sleep, the one moment the city deserves wonder. Boey swaps the patient — Nature now wears the city's stillness — and lets provenance do the accusing: what civilisation borrowed from nature it has repaid by exporting stoppage. Finally the conjunction: "as" means both while (two declines, simultaneous) and because (our arts fail since their source has stopped) — temporal grief or causal diagnosis in a single syllable, and the poem needs both. The scansion is the cruellest touch: perfect iambs — the heartbeat metre — carrying the news that the heart has stopped. Intention/effect: Wordsworth's serenest line is converted into a death certificate, and a reader who knows the source feels the tradition close over like water.

12. "O see the wound widening in the sky, / God is labouring to utter his last cry." (13–14)

Apostrophe/vocative "O"; imperative; symbol; birth-labour inversion; withheld climax; full couplet rhyme. The register breaks upward out of the report into psalm: "O" is the least administrative syllable in English, and "see" — the poem's only imperative — is aimed past the dead addressee at whoever is actually reading. The wound makes the sky a body and the damage sacrilege; "widening" keeps it in the merciless present progressive, unhealed and unhealing. Then the final line stages the largest event conceivable — the death of God — as a delivery: "labouring" is the childbirth word, and its object is an inverted nativity, a last cry where labour should produce a first. The cry itself never sounds; the poem ends inside the contraction, and the silence after line 14 is either the cry (unheard, because piety has failed) or its absence (unuttered, because it is not yet too late) — the two readings between which the poem deliberately expires. The couplet chime (sky/cry) closes the form with a click while the event is left open: sound resolved, sense suspended. Intention/effect: Boey engineers an ending that cannot be finished reading — the reader is left holding a breath the poem never releases, which is as close as a sonnet can come to making silence audible.

CRITICAL LENSES

Critical Lenses

What each way of reading makes visible, and what it flattens

Critical lenses

Ecocritical

The home lens, but push past "the poem is about pollution". First-wave ecocriticism celebrates the poem's prescience: smog, ocean dumping, the ozone layer, species loss ("the birds are few") — a 1992 inventory that reads as reportage now. Second-wave ecocriticism turns the lens on the poem itself and finds something stranger: its "Nature" is not an ecosystem but Romantic Nature — capitalised, feminised ("She"), sacralised, populated by European gods; its animals are the charismatic shorthand of the movement poster (flowers, birds, whale); no organism is named at species level; and the catastrophe is measured by its cost to poetry, piety and God — that is, to human meaning-systems. On this view the poem mourns an idea of nature at least as much as nature, and its grief is (knowingly) anthropocentric: the sky matters because God lives there. What the lens makes visible: the whale — in 1992, after the 1986 whaling moratorium, the single most politicised animal body on earth; "beached" imports the news photograph into the sonnet. What it flattens: the intertextual machinery — treating "Proteus" as mere ornament misses that the poem's true ecology is textual (Wordsworth's images are its endangered species).

Postcolonial

A Singaporean poet, born in the year of independence, files a "report" — the genre of colonial administration, the paperwork empire ran on — upward to the imperial canon's official priest of Nature, in the empire's prestige verse-form. The ironies stack: the periphery informs the metropole that the metropole's myth-stock (Greco-Roman gods, Anglican piety, Romantic Nature) is dead; the "smog" smothering Her is the exhaust of exactly the industrial modernity Britain exported; and the report's implicit accusation — your civilisation did this — hides inside perfect deference ("You should be here"). Yet the poem refuses the Caliban posture: unlike Bhatt's A Different History, which asks "Which language / has not been the oppressor's tongue?", Boey writes as a loving legatee — no Singaporean place-name, no vernacular, no quarrel with English itself. The sharpest postcolonial reading is therefore about inheritance without restitution: Boey arrives to claim the Romantic estate and finds it already asset-stripped; the colonised subject's classic tragedy (educated into a tradition, then discovering its promises void) replayed as ecological fact. What the lens flattens: the poem's universalism — "insatiate man" indicts a species, not an empire, and the lens must not turn a lament into a lawsuit the text never files.

Formalist

Everything in the Form & Structure section is this lens at work; compressed to its thesis: the poem's meaning is the condition of its form. A Shakespearean rhyme-grid whose early rhymes are voiced/voiceless pararhymes (smog/clock, waste/dazed) — rhyme half-choked, then recovering to full chime exactly as the poem moves from description to verdict; a pentameter that goes short in the line about sinking (6) and gapes dactylically in the line about the widening wound (13); a volta suppressed at 8/9 by the flat conjunction "and Neptune" — catastrophe ignoring the form's internal borders; two flatline-regular lines (8, 12) for the body on the monitor; a couplet that closes the rhyme (sky/cry) while refusing to close the sentence's action (the cry unuttered). The form is a working scale-model of its content: a canonical structure, still standing, audibly failing. What the lens makes visible is precision; what it flattens is address — formalism has no way to register that the "you" is Wordsworth, and that half the poem's devices are quotations with the ethics of quotation attached.

Marxist / materialist

Follow the agents. The poem opens with agentless passives ("has been laid waste", "Smothered") — destruction with the perpetrator redacted; mid-poem the agent appears as "we" ("the waste / we dump") — universal consumer guilt; by line 10 it is "insatiate man" — a species-essence, appetite as anthropology. A materialist reading says: this sequence mystifies. "Man" did not lay Nature waste; specific arrangements — industrial capital, developmental states (Singapore's among them), the growth imperative — did, and the poem's archaic moral vocabulary ("insatiate": the deadly sin of avarice) converts a political-economic system into a timeless flaw of the species, which is precisely how such systems prefer to be described. Meanwhile "Poetry and piety" — superstructure — fail when the base (nature as means of production of meaning) is consumed. What the lens makes visible: the strange class-blankness of "we"; the poem written from inside one of history's most aggressive developmental states without naming it; the fact that "moves in for the kill" is the language of the market (closing the deal) as much as the hunt. What it flattens: the poem's actual register of loss — you cannot audit "God is labouring to utter his last cry"; the lens reads grief as ideology and so misses that grief may be the only universally available politics the poem trusts.

Psychoanalytic

The poem is a work of incomplete mourning — technically, closer to melancholia: the lost object (Nature, and behind her the Romantic father-poet) is kept alive by address ("You should be here"), by present-progressive tenses that refuse the past tense of the truly dead, and by introjection (the poem swallows Wordsworth's lines — "mighty heart", Proteus, Triton — and speaks as him, in his form, the classic melancholic incorporation of the lost object into the self). The family structure is oedipal in the gentlest sense: Wordsworth as dead father and ego-ideal, the son filing a report that is simultaneously homage (I have kept your forms), plea (come back), and announcement that the father's God is dying — the son surviving the father's whole symbolic order. The imagery runs on oral catastrophe: smothering, choking, muteness, the strangled cry — and against it, "insatiate man", the devouring mouth; the poem's world divides into blocked throats and one open, endless appetite. What the lens makes visible: why the poem cannot end (the cry withheld = the mourner's refusal to let the death be final); "labouring" as birth fantasy inside a death — the wish that loss deliver something. What it flattens: the ecological referent's reality — smog is not a symbol of the mother; sometimes a dying sea is a dying sea.

Ecofeminist

The poem's Nature is a woman — "She has been laid waste" — and her destroyer is "insatiate man"; the summons goes to a male poet, as if a lady in distress needed a rescuer, and every god in the poem is male. An ecofeminist reading, in the line of Carolyn Merchant's The Death of Nature (1980), connects the two dominations: Merchant argued that the old picture of the earth as a living, nurturing mother had restrained its exploitation, and that when the scientific picture of nature as a machine replaced it, the restraint fell away. Boey's poem holds both pictures in a single line — "a sky slowing like a dying clock", a machine that dies like a creature — and its violence is gendered: "laid waste" and "Smothered" are done to a female body by an appetitive "man". What the lens makes visible: the buried plot of violation, and the way the poem still casts Nature as passive and voiceless, waiting to be saved. What it flattens: "man" here is the species rather than the male sex, and this Nature is also "mighty"; the poem uses the inherited image of Mother Nature rather than examining it.

OTHER READINGS

Other Readings

Contested interpretations, and where each is weak

Alternative readings

  1. The eco-protest reading (the default): the poem is an environmentalist alarm-call — smog, dumping, ozone, extinction — using Wordsworth as a measure of what has been lost and "we dump" to indict the reader. Evidence: the documentary nouns; the topical fit with 1985–92 environmental history; the recruiting imperative "O see". Weakness: it cannot explain why over half the poem is about utterance (mute, notes, choked, poetry, utter, cry) rather than ecology, nor why the casualties are literary gods rather than actual species; taken alone it reduces a meta-poetic elegy to a poster.
  2. The elegy-for-imagination reading: the true deceased is the Romantic way of seeing; the poem mourns the death of a tradition — its gods, its piety, its "poetry" — and performs the mourning in the tradition's own failing forms. Evidence: the systematic quotation-and-inversion of three Wordsworth sonnets; "Poetry and piety have begun to fail" as explicit thesis; the choked famous horn (a canonical image, not a sea-creature). Weakness: pushed hard, it aestheticises the disaster — smog and dumped waste are stubbornly literal, and a reading in which nature dies merely to symbolise poetry's decline gets the poem's priorities backwards.
  3. The postcolonial report: a Singaporean poet returns the empire's own administrative genre ("report") and prestige form (sonnet) to sender, notifying the centre that its myth-stock is dead and that the industrial modernity it exported has poisoned the world. Evidence: the loaded genre of the title; the poet's biography (born at independence, 1965); the exclusively European god-machinery being declared defunct. Weakness: the poem's tone is filial, not insurgent — it petitions Wordsworth, it does not arraign him; there is no Singapore in the text, no quarrel with English; the reading supplies a politics of resistance the poem conspicuously declines to state.
  4. The theological reading (jeremiad/psalm): the poem is a religious poem in ecological dress — pollution as sin, the wound as sacrilege, the ending a deicide; its nearest genre is the prophetic lament, and its subject is the killing of the sacred. Evidence: "piety"; "O see" (liturgical ecce); the sky as God's body; "his last cry" with its Passion overtones (a labouring death, a final cry — Golgotha shimmer). Weakness: the poem's gods are pagan-classical and openly literary; "God" arrives in the final line as rhetorical summit rather than doctrine; and the poem never prays — it reports. A reading that makes Boey a believer must explain why the divine appears only as casualty.
  5. The ironic-futility reading: the poem knowingly stages its own impotence — a report no one will action, addressed to a dead man, in a dying art, ending in an unuttered cry; its deepest note is not warning but the elegance of despair. Evidence: the constitutive absurdity of the address; "Poetry… ha[s] begun to fail" inside a poem; the refusal of any imagined remedy, future, or "unless". Weakness: despair does not bother to rhyme. The poem's formal vitality — the couplet's chime, the engineered ambush of "we dump", the imperative flung at the living — is the behaviour of a text that believes rhetoric still works; pure futility would not try so hard to be heard.
  6. The historicist reading: the poem is best understood as a document of the early-1990s environmental moment — ozone panic (Montreal Protocol 1987), the whaling moratorium (1986), acid rain and marine dumping in the headlines — written from Singapore at the crest of its own hyper-development, the year of Another Place (1992) and five years before the poet's emigration. Evidence: every image has a period referent (smog / beached whale / widening sky-wound); the poem's despair matches Boey's documented disillusionment with Singapore's transformation. Weakness: the poem universalises on purpose — no event, place or date appears in it; historicism explains where the images came from but not why the poem strips their labels off, and it risks shrinking a poem about the death of the sacred into a time-capsule of 1992 anxieties.
REVISION NOTES

Revision Notes

The working notes, quotation by quotation

Title

"Report to Wordsworth"

Analysis
  • Report = official account filed upward, to someone with power to act
  • Bureaucratic genre → promises facts, neutral voice; delivers myth, lament, prophecy
  • to Wordsworth → Apostrophe to William Wordsworth (1770–1850), Romantic poet of sacred Nature
  • Irony: report to a dead man → can never be acted on → real recipient = living reader
Effect, style & response
  • Younger poet reporting back to the master of the tradition (as Wordsworth called on Milton)
  • Every image that follows = one of Wordsworth's images, returned damaged

Context

Analysis
  • Boey Kim Cheng — b. 1965, Singapore (year of independence); family name Boey → "Boey", not "Cheng"
  • Poem in his 2nd collection Another Place (1992)
  • Emigrated to Australia 1997 → later taught in Newcastle (NSW) and at NTU Singapore
  • Grew up as Singapore was rebuilt: kampongs cleared → HDB high-rises; coast pushed out by land reclamation
  • But poem names no place, date or event → speaks of the whole Earth
Effect, style & response
  • Wordsworth = founding voice of English nature poetry → the right authority to report to
  • Early-90s backdrop: ozone hole (1985), whaling moratorium (1986), smog

Wordsworth intertexts

Analysis
  • 3 Wordsworth sonnets inside the poem
  • 'London, 1802' → "Milton! thou should'st be living at this hour: / England hath need of thee" → line 1
  • 'The World Is Too Much with Us' → "we lay waste our powers" (l. 2); "Proteus rising from the sea" (l. 5); "old Triton blow his wreathèd horn" (ll. 7–8)
  • 'Composed upon Westminster Bridge' → "And all that mighty heart is lying still!" (l. 12)
  • Chain of inheritance: Milton → Wordsworth → Boey
Effect, style & response
  • Allusion as audit → Wordsworth's images checked and found destroyed
  • Wordsworth's consolation (pagan gods) becomes a casualty list

Form & structure

Analysis
  • Shakespearean sonnet: 14 lines, ABAB CDCD EFEF GG, loose iambic pentameter
  • Wordsworth's 3 sonnets are Italian → Boey answers in the English pattern
  • Half-rhymes smog/clock, waste/dazed → rhyme "choked"; full rhymes from l. 9
  • Sea-god list runs ll. 5–10 → and Neptune at l. 9 = no volta; damage ignores the form's borders
  • Real turns: l. 11 (Nature → human spirit), l. 13 (report → prayer)
  • Continuous tenses: slowing, dying, widening, labouring → end still happening
Effect, style & response
  • Sonnet = Wordsworth's own form → report written on the tradition's letterhead
  • Couplet closes the form; sense stays open
1

You should be here, Nature has need of you.

Analysis
  • Apostrophe to the dead Wordsworth
  • should → obligation + impossible longing (he can't come)
  • Rewrites 'London, 1802': Milton → Wordsworth; England → Nature
  • has need of → archaic, Wordsworth's "hath need of"
  • Capital N → Nature as a being / near-divine presence
  • Comma splice → urgent, breathless; You … you frames the line
Effect, style & response
  • Summons + lament at once → grief from the first words
  • Can carry reproach: come and see the Nature you trusted
2

She has been laid waste. Smothered by the smog

Analysis
  • She → Nature personified as a woman (Mother Nature) → victim; Wordsworth cast as rescuer
  • Passive voice → agent hidden until we dump (l. 7)
  • laid waste → military idiom (conquered land)
  • Flips Wordsworth's "we lay waste our powers": active → passive; our inner powers → Nature's body
  • Full stop after 5 syllables → sentence killed mid-line
  • Sibilance sm–sm → smog welded to smothering; smother = kill by stopping breath
  • Smothered = the flowers grammatically, but sits right after She → drifts like smog
Effect, style & response
  • Damage that seems to happen by itself → everyone responsible, no one accountable
  • Reader's own breath hisses the line
3

the flowers are mute, and the birds are few

Analysis
  • mute → flowers once "spoke" (beauty, scent) → silence motif begins
  • few → survey count; decline still under way
  • Simple parallel clauses → childlike, final
  • Echo (association, not certain allusion): Keats "And no birds sing" — epigraph of Carson's Silent Spring (1962)
Effect, style & response
  • Flowers + birdsong = stock materials of nature poetry → the tradition's losses too
4

in a sky slowing like a dying clock

Analysis
  • Simile: sky running down like a clock → time running out
  • dying clock → machine given a living death (paradox)
  • Nature reimagined as mechanism → something to run and use
  • Stopped clock = sign of a death in the house → lying still (l. 12)
  • Rhythm stalls → pentameter falters
Effect, style & response
  • Apocalypse as slow winding-down, not explosion
5–6

All hopes of Proteus rising from the sea / have sunk

Analysis
  • Proteus = shape-shifting, prophetic sea-god (Homer, Odyssey 4)
  • Quotes Wordsworth's wish "Have sight of Proteus rising from the sea"
  • rising → sunk = antithesis; idiom made literal (hopes sink into the sea)
  • All hopes → whole Romantic hope that nature restores us
  • entombed → god of escape sealed in; tomb = no resurrection
Effect, style & response
  • Wordsworth's consolation drowned
6–7

the waste / we dump

Analysis
  • waste → l. 2's ruin becomes literal rubbish → bathos (myth under trash)
  • Enjambment holds back the agent → we dump = sudden confession
  • we → only first person in the poem → speaker + reader implicated
  • dump → blunt, colloquial monosyllable vs mythic vocabulary
Effect, style & response
  • Moral turn: culprit finally named — and it's us
7–8

Triton's notes struggle to be free, / his famous horns are choked

Analysis
  • Triton = sea's herald; conch calms or raises the waves
  • notes struggle, not the god → sound trapped in a blocked instrument
  • famous → made famous by poets (Spenser, Wordsworth's "wreathèd horn")
  • choked → instrument given a throat; eyes are dazed → sight gone too
  • free rhymes with sea → pair Wordsworth rhymed praising Milton's voice
Effect, style & response
  • Balanced clauses + regular metre → reads like a medical chart
9–10

helpless as a beached whale

Analysis
  • Neptune = Roman king of the sea → power itself
  • Order of defeat: Proteus (renewal) → Triton (voice) → Neptune (sovereignty)
  • Simile runs downward → god compared to a stranded animal (Bathos)
  • Beached whale = 1980s emblem (whaling moratorium 1986)
  • and at l. 9 → refuses the sonnet's turn
Effect, style & response
  • All-powerful made as weak as the creatures they ruled
10

while insatiate man moves in for the kill

Analysis
  • insatiate = never satisfied → archaic, sin of greed (Shakespeare's "insatiate cormorant")
  • moves in for the kill → predator / hunter idiom; attacks prey already down
  • while → as the gods lie helpless
  • man → the species, not a nation or industry
  • Archaic word + modern idiom → Register collision
Effect, style & response
  • Anger in the open: cause named = human greed
11

Poetry and piety have begun to fail

Analysis
  • Alliteration p–p → art and reverence sound like twins
  • Turn: Nature's body → human spirit
  • begun to fail → decline being watched, not finished
  • Wordsworth's 1802 sonnets: "pen", "altar" failing England
  • Paradox: says poetry fails inside a working sonnet; line's crowded rhythm sags
Effect, style & response
  • Cause open: dying nature kills reverence — or lost reverence let nature die?
12

as Nature's mighty heart is lying still

Analysis
  • Near-quotation: Westminster Bridge "And all that mighty heart is lying still!"
  • There: London asleep at dawn (peace) → here: Nature's heart stopped (death)
  • as = while + because
  • Regular iambs = heartbeat rhythm carrying news the heart has stopped
  • Wordsworth's ! → Boey's full stop
Effect, style & response
  • Wordsworth's serenest line → a death certificate
13

O see the wound widening in the sky

Analysis
  • O → vocative of prayer and ode; report becomes plea
  • see → only imperative; aimed at the living reader
  • wound → sky as an injured body; widening → still opening
  • Ozone hole (reported 1985; Montreal Protocol 1987) → a reading, not a decode
  • Answers Wordsworth's "Little we see in Nature that is ours"
Effect, style & response
  • Damage felt as violence against a sacred body, not measured as data
14

God is labouring to utter his last cry.

Analysis
  • Summit of the casualty list: flowers → gods → poetry → Nature → God
  • labouring → straining + childbirth inverted: first cry → last cry
  • to utter → cry not yet made; poem ends before it sounds
  • Crucifixion echo: Jesus "cried again with a loud voice" (Matthew 27:50)
  • Full rhyme sky/cry closes the form; sense left open
Effect, style & response
  • God dies with nature — or no one left with the piety to hear him
  • Unfinished cry = the space left for the reader

Motifs

Analysis
  • Voice failing: mute → notes → horns are choked → Poetry → utter his last cry
  • Downward: laid, sunk, entombed, lies, lying still
  • Body of Nature: smothered, choked, dazed, beached, heart, wound, labouring
  • Time: dying clock → begun → widening → last
CONNECTIONS

Connections

How this poem pairs with the rest of the set

Comparison hooks

With 'Lament' (Gillian Clarke)

Link: the set's other elegy for a damaged natural world, written in the same years (Clarke's war is the Gulf War of 1991). Both poems contain a silenced whale — Clarke's "whale struck dumb by the missile's thunder", Boey's Neptune helpless as a beached whale — and both end by recording damage to language itself: Clarke's "ashes of language", Boey's Poetry and piety have begun to fail. Shared technique: a catalogue of casualties in a borrowed form of grief — Clarke's litany ("For the green turtle…", "For the cormorant…"), Boey's report turning to prayer (O see); and a sky put out ("the sun put out", the wound widening in the sky). Difference: Clarke names a war and gives her victims bodies — turtle, cormorant, dugong, "Ahmed at the closed border", a soldier; Boey names no event and routes the grief through literature and myth. Clarke laments the world; Boey laments the world and the words that once held it sacred.

With 'Hunting Snake' (Judith Wright)

Link: the opposite encounter between people and nature. Wright's walkers "froze half-through a pace" as a snake passes, "lost breath" in awe and let it go; in Boey nothing stops, and the breath is taken by smog (Smothered). In Wright the hunter is the animal, with its "fierce intent"; in Boey the hunter is man, who moves in for the kill. Shared technique: a tight rhymed form (Wright's four quatrains; Boey's sonnet) and the imagery of breath — Wright's humans take a "deeper breath" when the snake has gone; Boey's world can barely breathe. Difference: Wright's nature is intact, indifferent and magnificent — "Cold, dark and splendid" — and the people are the ones made still; Boey's nature is the one made still (lying still), and the people are the danger. Awe that restrains, against appetite that destroys.

With 'Before the Sun' (Charles Mungoshi)

Link: the reverence Boey reports as dying is alive in Mungoshi's boy. He shares his roasted maize with the sun, bite by bite — "one for the sun" — and his wood-smoke climbs "a sacrificial prayer", where Boey's smoke has become smog that smothers the flowers. Shared technique: a personified sky — Mungoshi's sun arrives like "some / latecomer to a feast" and "winks / like a grown-up"; Boey's sky is a body with a wound, and God in it is dying. Difference: dawn against ending, play against prophecy, free verse against the sonnet; a relationship of sharing against one of consumption. Yet Mungoshi's morning also ends with the cobs as "two little skeletons" — even a reverent appetite consumes — which sharpens what Boey means by insatiate.

With 'An Essay on Man' (Alexander Pope)

Link: what kind of creature man is. Pope's man stands on "this isthmus of a middle state", "Great lord of all things, yet a prey to all"; Boey's insatiate man has abandoned the balance and become pure predator, moving in for the kill. Pope warns "presume not God to scan"; Boey's man has gone further than presumption, and God is labouring to utter his last cry. Shared technique: paired abstractions and balanced sound — Pope's "darkly wise, and rudely great", Boey's Poetry and piety — and a closing exclamation (Pope's "The glory, jest, and riddle of the world!", Boey's O see). Difference: Pope writes inside a confident, God-ordered universe and counsels humility within it; Boey's dying clock shows that ordered, clockwork world running down, wrecked by the creature Pope told to know its place.

With 'Sonnet 18' (William Shakespeare)

Link: the same form making opposite claims for poetry. Shakespeare promises that poetry outlasts death — "So long as men can breathe or eyes can see, / So long lives this" — and Boey reports the conditions of that promise failing: breath Smothered, eyes dazed, a command to see that may come too late, and Poetry … begun to fail. Shared technique: the Shakespearean rhyme scheme with a summarising couplet, and a personified sky — Shakespeare's "eye of heaven", whose "gold complexion" is sometimes "dimmed"; Boey's sky with its widening wound. Difference: Shakespeare's nature changes by its own "changing course" and his poem defeats time; Boey's nature is destroyed by people and his poem cannot save it. A living beloved promised immortality, against a dead poet sent a death notice.

With 'A Different History' (Sujata Bhatt)

Link: two postcolonial poets weighing what the old gods and the English inheritance are worth. Bhatt opens "Great Pan is not dead; / he simply emigrated / to India", where "every tree is sacred" and it is "a sin / to be rude to a book" — the piety towards nature and books that Boey reports as failing is still alive there. Boey's classical gods do not emigrate; they are entombed. Shared technique: classical allusion carrying the argument, and pointed address — Bhatt's rhetorical questions ("Which language / has not been the oppressor's tongue?"), Boey's summons (You should be here). Difference: Bhatt questions English and ends with grandchildren who "grow to love that strange language" — survival after damage; Boey never accuses the tradition he inherits, and ends with a last cry.

With 'Where I Come From' (Elizabeth Brewster)

Link: both poems smell the smog of the modern city — Brewster's "like the smell of smog", Boey's Smothered by the smog — and both argue that people are shaped by the nature around them: "People are made of places". Put together, they make one argument: if people are made of places, destroying the places destroys the people — and Boey's next step is exactly that, Poetry and piety have begun to fail. Shared technique: a catalogue of sensory evidence (Brewster's smells, Boey's silences) and a city that tames or kills nature ("nature tidily plotted in little squares"; laid waste). Difference: Brewster's ending opens "A door in the mind" onto remembered fields — the Wordsworthian consolation of memory; Boey's report has no such door. Brewster mourns what the city does to the human spirit; Boey what it does to the world itself.

With 'The Cockroach' (Kevin Halligan)

Link: two modern sonnets in which the observer turns out to be implicated. Halligan's speaker begins "I watched" and ends "I recognised myself"; Boey's report begins with agentless passives and arrives at we dump. Shared technique: the sonnet's order set against disorder, and a turn delayed past its traditional place — Halligan's comes in his last line, Boey's at lines 11 and 13 after the and of line 9. Difference: Halligan's crisis is private and uncertain ("I don't know"); Boey's is public and cosmic, and the report is certain of the damage, unsure only of whether anyone will see it. Self-recognition in an insect, against self-accusation before a dying world.

With 'The Chimney Sweeper' (William Blake, Songs of Experience)

Link: Blake's London soot (1794) and Boey's global smog are the beginning and end of the same industrial story, and both poems are full of failing voices — Blake's child crying "in notes of woe", Boey's Triton's notes struggling and God's last cry. Shared technique: a plain traditional form carrying protest, and religion turned into evidence — Blake's parents "gone to praise God and his priest and king", Boey's failing piety. Difference: Blake's culprits have titles and his religion is an accomplice that "make[s] up a heaven of our misery"; Boey's culprit is mankind and his God is the final victim.

With 'Follower' (Seamus Heaney)

Link: a son measuring himself against a master. Heaney's boy follows his ploughman father — "An expert" — in "his broad shadow"; Boey writes in Wordsworth's shadow, in Wordsworth's form and words. Shared technique: inheritance figured through craft, ploughing for one and the sonnet for the other. Difference: Heaney's father ends up as the one who "keeps stumbling" behind the grown son and will not leave; Boey's father-poet is summoned and cannot come.

Further pairings

Behn's 'Love Armed' shows people building a god ("And set him up a Deity"); Boey's people unmake their gods. Rumens's 'Carpet-weavers, Morocco' gives a craft still bound up with faith ("the garden of Islam"), the union of making and piety that Boey's poem watches failing.

CONTEXT

Context

The world the poem came out of

Kevin Halligan: what can actually be established

Very little, and it is worth knowing exactly how little. Halligan's Wikipedia entry runs to three sentences: a Canadian poet and writer, born in 1964, best known for 'The Cockroach' and for his collection Utopia, with many individual poems in the Times Literary Supplement between 1998 and 2006. Its only reference is a library-catalogue search, and the page carries a "multiple issues" warning. Library catalogues confirm two books. Utopia was published by Springfield Books, Cambridge (England), in 2009, 55 pages, and the Library of Congress files it under Canadian literature. An earlier book, Blossom Street, is dated 2001 in Open Library's record. PoetryProf quotes the English poet Peter Reading (1946–2011) praising Halligan's "quietly amusing and observant poems"; where Reading wrote this could not be traced.

Everything else repeated in study notes is unconfirmed: birth in Toronto; years in Cambodia (or Phnom Penh); work for the Cambodia Daily; study of Buddhism; a poem "written in Cambodia"; a "1999" publication; even that the poem is collected in Utopia (likely, but no contents list was available to check). No interview, essay or publisher's biography by or about Halligan has turned up. The poem itself names no country, no religion and no history, so no reading of it should depend on where its author lived.

The poem in print: *Songs of Ourselves*

Almost every reader meets the poem in Songs of Ourselves, the Cambridge anthology of poetry in English for international students, first published in 2005 by Foundation Books (Cambridge University Press India) and now reissued by Cambridge University Press as Volume 1. The anthology is the earliest printing that can be dated, which rules out the "2009" often attached to the poem: that is the year of Utopia, and a poem anthologised by 2005 was not written in 2009. When it was written is not documented. It has been one of the anthology's most studied poems since the early 2010s.

The anthology prints it as a single fourteen-line block, with no stanza break. The octave and sestet are there in the rhymes but not on the page, so it is accurate to speak of the poem's "octave" and "sestet" but not of its "stanzas".

The sonnet the poem bends

Two models stand behind the poem. The Italian or Petrarchan sonnet, named after Francesco Petrarca (1304–74), whose Canzoniere contains 317 sonnets, divides into an octave rhymed ABBAABBA and a sestet on new rhymes (CDECDE, CDCDCD and other patterns). Its volta, or turn, comes at line 9, where the sestet answers, qualifies or reverses the octave. The English or Shakespearean sonnet, shaped by the Earl of Surrey and made famous by Shakespeare's Sonnets (1609), uses three cross-rhymed quatrains and a couplet (ABAB CDCD EFEF GG). The couplet usually clinches the argument, as Sonnet 18's does: "So long lives this, and this gives life to thee."

Halligan starts English and finishes Italian. His octave is two Shakespearean quatrains (pace / floor / trace / door, rings / back / wings / attack), which teaches the ear to expect a third quatrain and a couplet. The last six lines instead bring three new rhymes in two tercets, in the Italian manner, but the second tercet comes back out of order: EFG EGF. So both of the sonnet's great gestures of resolution are missing. The volta at line 9 is swallowed by an enjambment (attack / Of restlessness), and the couplet never arrives: the last line rhymes with line 10, four lines back.

The choice of form is itself a statement. The sonnet's subjects are love, time and the self under scrutiny, and handing it to a cockroach is mock-heroic. Wordsworth's sonnet about sonnets, 'Nuns fret not at their convent's narrow room' (1807), praises the form as a chosen confinement: it was "pastime to be bound / Within the Sonnet's scanty plot of ground", a "brief solace" for those "Who have felt the weight of too much liberty". Halligan's poem reads like a test of that claim. His creature seemed quite satisfied while its world had walls, and it stalls at the one place without them, an open shelf. The form stays immaculate while the creature inside it gets lost.

Creatures read for a moral: fable, bestiary, emblem

The title follows an old naming habit: the definite article and a creature, as in 'The Fly', 'The Flea' and 'The Tyger'. It is the formula of the fable, the bestiary entry and the emblem. Aesop's fables give animals human characters and end with a moral. Medieval bestiaries described real and fabulous animals, then explained what each signified for a Christian reader. Renaissance emblem books, such as Andrea Alciato's Emblemata (1531) and Geffrey Whitney's A Choice of Emblemes (1586), set a picture of a creature or object beside a motto and a short poem drawing out its lesson.

All three train a reader to look at an animal and ask what it means for us. Halligan's poem behaves like an emblem for thirteen lines, with close description followed by interpretation (As if…), and then declines to draw the moral. The only lesson it reaches is private and hedged (I thought I recognised myself), not a maxim for everyone. The gap between a fable-shaped title and a non-moral ending is part of the poem's quiet comedy.

Insect poems before Halligan: Donne, Burns, Blake, and Kafka's vermin

Poets have long used insects to cut people down to size. In Donne's 'The Flea' (published 1633) a flea that has bitten both the speaker and the woman he is courting becomes a witty argument for sleeping together. That insect is a tool of argument, never a mirror. In Burns's 'To a Louse, On Seeing One on a Lady's Bonnet at Church' (1786) a louse climbs to the top of a proud woman's bonnet, and the poem ends with the famous wish "O wad some Pow'r the giftie gie us / To see oursels as ithers see us!" Blake's 'The Fly', in Songs of Experience (1794), the collection that holds 'The Chimney Sweeper', comes closest. Having brushed a fly away, the speaker asks: "Am not I / A fly like thee? / Or art not thou / A man like me?"

Halligan's last line belongs to this line of recognition, with one difference: Burns and Blake turn the insect into a lesson about "us" or "man", while Halligan's speaker only thought he recognised myself. PoetryProf suggests two modern companions, D. H. Lawrence's 'The Mosquito' and Miroslav Holub's 'The Fly'. The nearest prose relative is Kafka's The Metamorphosis (1915), in which Gregor Samsa wakes to find himself turned into a monstrous insect. He is lying on his hard, armoured back, his thin legs waving helplessly, which is the image flipping right over calls up. Kafka never names the species (the charwoman calls Gregor an "old dung beetle"). The poem contains no verbal echo of Kafka, so this is a comparison readers bring, not an allusion the poem makes.

Karma, rebirth and A former life

Lines 12–13 borrow an idea without naming it. In Hindu and Buddhist thought, karma (Sanskrit for "action") is the principle that intentional actions bring consequences to the one who acts, which may ripen in a later life. Rebirth as an animal is one of the unfortunate births that bad actions can lead to: the Chandogya Upanishad, an early Hindu scripture, says that people of good conduct attain a good birth and those of evil conduct an evil one, such as that of a dog or a pig.

Two cautions. First, in Buddhism there is no judge passing sentence: karma works as cause and effect, not as punishment. Second, the poem uses none of the tradition's own words. Its version is a law court and an account book, due payment for some vicious crime, a debt falling due. That is karma as a Western mind might picture it. The idea of a soul passing between human and animal bodies is not only Asian, either. Ovid gives Pythagoras a long speech on it in the Metamorphoses (Book 15). In Don Marquis's newspaper columns (from 1916, collected as archy and mehitabel, 1927), archy is a cockroach who was a free-verse poet in a former life, typing at night by diving head-first onto the keys. The poem's hypothesis is half serious and dropped within a line: I don't know.

The absurd: a frame the poem invites but never names

Albert Camus's essay The Myth of Sisyphus (1942) describes "the absurd": the collision between our need for meaning and the world's silence. Camus says it often starts in routine. Getting up, the tram, work, a meal, sleep, the same rhythm every day: that "path" is easily followed until one day "the 'why' arises". His emblem is Sisyphus, condemned by the gods for his offences against them to roll a rock up a mountain forever. Camus dwells on the pause at the summit, when the rock rolls back and Sisyphus becomes conscious of his fate, and he ends: "One must imagine Sisyphus happy."

The poem has the same shape: a traced path, futile repeated motion, a climb, a stop, then a question about crime and payment. It does not have Camus's defiance; its speaker gets to I don't know, not to happiness. Kierkegaard's phrase "anxiety is the dizziness of freedom" (The Concept of Anxiety, 1844) suits a creature that climbs to an open shelf and freezes. Sartre's claim that we are "condemned to be free" ties freedom to the language of sentence and crime. None of these thinkers is named in the poem, and none needs to be. They are frames that help explain why fourteen lines about an insect feel so large, but treating them as the poem's subject inflates a poem that works by staying small.

What cockroaches actually do

The poem's details are closer to natural history than they look. Cockroaches are thigmotactic: they prefer to keep their bodies in contact with surfaces and run along walls and edges, and laboratory studies of the American cockroach show it steering by touching the wall with an antenna as it runs. A path between the wainscot and the door, along the foot of the wall, is exactly the route a real cockroach takes. The largest common house species, the American cockroach, is about 4 cm long and has working wings, so giant is not far from fair description and his wings are a real power left unused.

A cockroach on its back, however, is usually in trouble. Healthy ones right themselves; a roach stranded belly-up on a smooth floor is typically sick or poisoned. Household insecticides (pyrethroids) attack the nervous system, causing spasms, tremors and loss of balance, and the insect's rounded back and high centre of gravity tip it over. Nothing in the poem says the creature is dying. Its sequence of circling, flipping over, a restlessness that worsened over time, a climb and a stop fits a creature in distress at least as well as one exploring, and that darkens the comedy.

The wainscot, wooden panelling on the lower part of a wall, is also the traditional home of household vermin in English writing. In Tennyson's 'Mariana' (1830), a poem about restless waiting in a decaying house, "the mouse / Behind the mouldering wainscot shriek'd".

THE POEM

The Poem

Line by line, with the analysis alongside

The Cockroach
TThe Cockroach
1I watched a giant cockroach start to pace,
2Skirting a ball of dust that rode the floor.
3At first he seemed quite satisfied to trace
4A path between the wainscot and the door,
5But soon he turned to jog in crooked rings,
6Circling the rusty table leg and back,
7And flipping right over to scratch his wings –
8As if the victim of a mild attack
9Of restlessness that worsened over time.
10After a while, he climbed an open shelf
11And stopped. He looked uncertain where to go.
12Was this due payment for some vicious crime
13A former life had led to? I don't know,
14Except I thought I recognised myself.

Lines with a marker have analysis — click one, or just scroll.

Title
The Cockroach
Language & devices

Definite article + creature: The Cockroach uses the naming formula of fable, bestiary and emblem ('The Fly', 'The Flea'), which promises a typical specimen and a lesson to draw from it. Singular noun: one creature, not "cockroaches", which prepares for the individual he of line 3. Connotation: the cockroach is the least loved of household insects: dirty, nocturnal, hard to get rid of. Deadpan: there is no adjective or comment, just a label, like a specimen card.

Meaning & effect

The title points at an object of study and hides the real subject. It presents the poem as being about an insect, and only the last line reveals that it has been about the man watching. Read again after line 14, the title becomes a double label: it names the creature and, by implication, the speaker. That gives the ending a sting, because the creature he finds himself in is the one most people flinch from, so the recognition comes with a charge of self-disgust that a neutral animal could not carry. The fable-like title also sets up an expectation the poem refuses: we expect a moral, and get only a hedged personal impression. And a poem in the high tradition of the sonnet under the title of a household pest announces mock-heroic comedy before the first line, a comedy the poem will turn serious.

Line 1
I watched a giant cockroach start to pace,
Language & devices

First-person pronoun: I is the first word; the last word will be myself, so the self frames the poem. Verb: watched means sustained, deliberate attention (not "saw"), and its past tense makes the poem a report given afterwards. Hyperbole / Mock-heroic: giant magnifies the insect, though large house species really are big. Anthropomorphic verb: pace is how anxious or confined people walk, to and fro. Inchoative verb: start to catches the beginning of a process. Metre: regular iambic pentameter; in cockroach start (COCK-roach START) three heavy syllables crowd together and slow the line on the creature's name.

Meaning & effect

The poem opens on a man watching, and the watcher is introduced before the insect. We learn nothing about him except that he is watching a cockroach closely and for a long time, and that is already telling: this is the attention of someone with nothing he can bear to do, or nothing else to look at. Giant is the first sign of how he sees. He magnifies, making the creature worth a sonnet, which is both fair description and a comic inflation of scale. Pace is the first human word, and it sets the mood before anything has happened, the walk of the anxious, the waiting and the imprisoned. Start to frames everything as a process with stages, so a reader senses a story of change, and probably decline, from the first line. The matter-of-fact past tense makes it sound like a naturalist's log, which is exactly what will make the final confession surprising.

Line 2
Skirting a ball of dust that rode the floor.
Language & devices

Initial trochee: Skirting (SKIRT-ing) swerves off the iambic beat as the creature swerves round the obstacle. Participle: Skirting means going round the edge of something; the figurative sense, avoiding, is close by, and "skirting" is also the board along the foot of a wall, where cockroaches run. Imagery: a ball of dust is a small, exact sign of an unswept room. Metaphorical verb: rode gives the dust a jaunty verb of travel, but riding is being carried. End-stop: the full stop closes a two-line opening sentence.

Meaning & effect

One precise, unglamorous detail sets the scene: a dust ball drifting on the floor. It tells us about the room (neglected) and about the watcher (looking closely enough to see dust move). It also sets up the poem's question about agency. Two things move in this line, the cockroach, which moves itself, and the dust, which is moved, carried along by a draught. By the end the self-propelled creature gets nowhere, and is no better directed than the dust that merely rode the floor. Skirting plants avoidance: the creature goes round things rather than through them, a habit the poem never explains, but one that lightly suggests whatever the watcher himself is avoiding. With the scene set and the full stop placed, the poem has its stage; the next sentence will run on for seven lines.

Line 3
At first he seemed quite satisfied to trace
Language & devices

Temporal marker: At first signals that things will change, so the outcome is foreshadowed. Pronoun: he, not "it". English calls an animal "he" when it is seen as an individual, so this marks the shift from specimen to someone. Epistemic verb: seemed flags the inner state as the watcher's inference. Anthropomorphism: satisfied is a human state of mind. Qualifier: quite (fairly, or entirely) is a measured, dry word either way. Enjambment: to trace / A path sends the verb over the line-end in search of its object.

Meaning & effect

This line gives the creature's first phase, apparent contentment in routine, and in doing so it defines contentment as following. To trace is to follow a line that already exists, not to choose or make one. The poem's first picture of satisfaction is therefore a life on rails, which is why it cannot last. The speaker is scrupulous: he says seemed, because he cannot know what an insect feels. That honesty matters later, when the hedges thin out and he starts reporting feelings as facts. He quietly turns the insect into a person-like individual eleven lines before the speaker admits why it matters. The line scans perfectly, so the metre is as orderly as the behaviour it describes, and the satisfied phase gets exactly one regular line before But soon.

Line 4
A path between the wainscot and the door,
Language & devices

Noun: A path is a route between two points, the most ordered shape of movement in the poem. Diction: wainscot means wooden panelling on the lower part of a wall; it is an old-fashioned word and the traditional lodging of vermin in English writing. Paired limits: between… and… fixes two boundaries, a wall and a way out. Full rhyme: door / floor completes the first cross-rhymed quatrain (ABAB). Metre: regular, with the fourth beat on the weak word and, a level line for a level route.

Meaning & effect

The creature's world is bounded: the wall on one side, the door on the other. That is accurate natural history, since cockroaches run along walls and edges, keeping contact with the surface. It is also the poem's picture of a limited life that feels satisfying because it is limited. The door matters because it is the poem's only exit. The path runs up to it and never through it, and the creature never leaves the room, which may be the speaker's situation too. The line ends on a comma, not a full stop, so the contented phase does not even get a sentence of its own: the next word is But. Some readers map this onto the settled routines of early adult life; the poem allows it, though it offers a shape, not a key.

Line 5
But soon he turned to jog in crooked rings,
Language & devices

Conjunction: But is the first turn, coming at line 5, well before the sonnet's appointed turn at line 9. Verb: turned means both a literal change of direction and a change of state. Comic diction: jog, the leisure-exercise verb, names running that ends where it began. Paradox / Imagery: crooked rings are circles that fail even as circles; "going round in circles" is the idiom for getting nowhere. Metre: perfectly regular, so the line about crookedness scans dead straight. Rhyme: rings opens the second quatrain (C).

Meaning & effect

Contentment collapses almost at once: But soon the route becomes circling. This is the poem's argument in one image, movement that goes nowhere and is not even regular in its going nowhere. Jog is comic casting. It makes the creature's crisis sound like a fitness routine, and the reader laughs at the symptom before seeing what it is a symptom of. Crooked suggests something going wrong, a wobble or disorientation, and faintly carries its moral sense (dishonest), which vicious crime will pick up seven lines later. The verse stays perfectly orderly, so at this stage the disorder belongs to the creature and not yet to the poem or the watcher. That distance will not last.

Line 6
Circling the rusty table leg and back,
Language & devices

Initial trochee: Circling (CIR-cling) makes the line begin by turning. Participle: a chain of present participles (Circling, then flipping) gives continuous motion with no main verb and no arrival. Imagery of decay: rusty means corrosion, neglect and time at work. Perspective: table leg is the room seen from the floor, at insect height. Syntax: and back hangs at the line-end like the futile return leg it describes. Rhyme: back ends on a short vowel and a hard stop (D).

Meaning & effect

The circling now has a centre: one rusty table leg, a single fixed point the creature orbits. And back turns the movement into a return journey to nowhere, out and back, the shape of routine without purpose. Rusty adds to the room's decay (dust, then rust) and lets time into the poem before the speaker names it in worsened over time. The viewpoint has dropped to the floor. The watcher sees the leg, not the table, which means he is looking from very near the creature's level, a first physical hint of the closeness he will admit at the end. One reading sees the creature clinging to a safe point it will not leave; either way, it is circling, not exploring.

Line 7
And flipping right over to scratch his wings –
Language & devices

Polysyndeton: And heaps one action on another. Mid-line trochee: in right over (RIGHT O-ver) two stresses collide and the rhythm flips over in the line describing the flip. Colloquial intensifier: right over is spoken and faintly amused. Significant detail: his wings means the creature has flight available and does not use it. Dash: the line is left hanging, the creature upside down and the meaning withheld. Rhyme: wings / rings (C).

Meaning & effect

This is the poem's most physical and most comic image: the creature upended, legs in the air, scratching. The humour lies in the loss of dignity, but a cockroach on its back is usually in difficulty. Healthy ones right themselves, and one stranded belly-up is often sick or poisoned, so the comedy has a darker edge for anyone who knows the insect. His wings is the detail most readers pass over. The creature could fly, so escape is possible, yet it spends its energy on its back on the floor, a capacity left unused that comes close to describing the watcher's own life. The dash suspends the image and the reader waits for an explanation, which the next line supplies. That explanation will be the watcher's invention, not the insect's.

Line 8
As if the victim of a mild attack
Language & devices

Simile: As if openly marks what follows as interpretation, and from here the poem explains rather than describes. Ellipsis: As if [he were] the victim. Medical and legal diction: victim and attack make the creature passive, something done to rather than doing. Oxymoron: mild attack, since attacks are not mild. Enjambment: the line ends on attack and leaves its kind (heart? panic?) in suspense. Rhyme: attack / back completes the octave (ABAB CDCD).

Meaning & effect

The watcher moves from observing to diagnosing. The creature's behaviour is recast as an illness, with the insect as a victim suffering something it did not choose. That changes the poem's terms: aimlessness becomes affliction, and the question of responsibility (who or what is to blame?) quietly enters. As if is honest, because he knows this is his reading, but once spoken, the diagnosis stays. The phrase mild attack is exact about the kind of suffering at issue: low-grade, undramatic, chronic, not a crisis. This is the octave's last line, where a reader expects a pause, and the sentence runs straight on. Victim is also crime's word, the first entry in a legal vocabulary that ends in vicious crime.

Line 9
Of restlessness that worsened over time.
Language & devices

Bathos: after the suspense, the attack turns out to be one Of restlessness, an anticlimax. Abstract noun: restlessness names the poem's condition, and its three hissing /s/ sounds fidget. Enjambment across the octave–sestet seam: the sestet's first word is Of, the weakest word available, so the sonnet's turn is refused. Prognostic diction: worsened over time is the language of chronic illness. Double time-scale: over time suggests a longer span than an afternoon watching an insect. End-stop: the full stop ends the poem's longest sentence (lines 3–9). Rhyme: time (E) will chime with crime.

Meaning & effect

The poem names its subject, restlessness, and does it through a joke: a mild attack / Of restlessness sounds trivial after the build-up. Then the clinical follow-up, that worsened over time, takes the joke away. This is a condition that deepens rather than passes, and that is the poem's darkest claim about the state it describes. Over time quietly breaks the realism. The watch has probably lasted minutes, yet the phrase sounds like months or years, a span that fits a human life better than an insect's evening, and so the diagnosis begins to fit the man making it. Structurally, this is where the sonnet expects to turn, and the poem does not: the sentence simply carries on through the form's resting point, so restlessness overruns the place appointed for a pause. The full stop ends seven lines of unbroken motion, and what follows is shorter, broken, and stops.

Line 10
After a while, he climbed an open shelf
Language & devices

Initial trochee: After (AF-ter) tips the line forward into the last phase. Vague duration: After a while is unmeasured time, the watcher no longer counting. Caesura: the comma after while is the poem's first mid-line pause. Verb: climbed is the first upward movement, effort and aspiration. Polysemy: open means exposed, empty and unbounded. Enjambment: the line runs on into And stopped. Rhyme: shelf (F) waits four lines for myself.

Meaning & effect

The creature tries something new: up instead of round. If the poem is a life-story, this is the climb towards achievement, and the line holds a moment of hope, a creature leaving the floor at last. But where it arrives is an open shelf: open as in exposed, open as in bare, with nothing stored there, and open as in unbounded, with no wall to follow. Compared with the bounded path where he seemed quite satisfied, the shelf is pure freedom, and freedom is where he stalls. After a while also tells us the watcher is still there, still watching, and the duration is part of the portrait. The comma is the first crack in the poem's smooth surface: its punctuation, like its creature, begins to break up.

Line 11
And stopped. He looked uncertain where to go.
Language & devices

Caesura: in And stopped. the poem's only mid-line full stop follows two syllables, its shortest sentence. Enjambment: the run-on from line 10 tips the reader over the line-end onto the stop. Plosives: the /st/ and /pt/ of stopped close the word at both ends. Metre: five regular iambs, so the syntax breaks but the pentameter does not. Monosyllables: He looked uncertain where to go is plain and bare. Ambiguity: looked means appeared, and looked about. Anthropomorphism: uncertain is stated without any seemed. Rhyme: go (G) will rhyme with know.

Meaning & effect

All the movement of ten and a half lines halts. The creature reaches the top and does not know where to go: the poem's central image of paralysis, arriving at the moment of greatest freedom. The full stop after stopped makes the reader stop too, and the metre ticking on regardless is like a clock in an empty room, the world's rhythm indifferent to the creature's arrest. Then comes a crucial shift. Earlier the watcher hedged (seemed, As if); now he simply states an insect's mind as fact. That is the sign his projection is complete, and he is reading his own uncertainty into the creature. Looked carries both senses, appeared uncertain and looked around, so the uncertainty is active, a creature scanning for a direction it cannot find. This line is the poem's hinge: everything before it is motion, everything after it is thought.

Line 12
Was this due payment for some vicious crime
Language & devices

Question: narration becomes interrogation, a shift of mood. Demonstrative: this could be the restlessness, the paralysis, or being a cockroach at all. Financial-legal diction: due payment is a debt that falls due, cosmic justice as accounting. Spondee: due payment (DUE PAY-ment) bunches the stresses on the payment. Moral adjective: vicious means wicked, savage (from Latin vitium, vice). Vague determiner: some makes the crime unknown. Rhyme: crime / time (E), as if time served were the sentence. Enjambment: the line runs on into 13.

Meaning & effect

Now the speaker asks why, and reaches for the largest explanation available: that suffering is payment for wrongdoing, perhaps in an earlier existence. The idea is close to karma and rebirth, but the words are those of a Western court and ledger, a crime, a debt, payment falling due. The question works on two levels. About the cockroach, it imagines a sinner reborn as vermin; about the speaker, it voices the fear that his own condition is deserved. Some is telling: whatever the crime was, nobody remembers it, guilt without an offence. The tone hovers between mock-solemn (a man asking whether a bug is paying for its sins) and genuinely troubled, and the poem does not choose. The rhyme with time from line 9 links the two ideas: a condition that worsens over time, as if time itself were the punishment.

Line 13
A former life had led to? I don't know,
Language & devices

Enjambment: the break falls between crime and A former life, a white space where the gap between lives would be. Syntax: crime / A former life had led to makes the life the cause and the crime its destination. Allusion to rebirth: A former life. Caesura: the question mark falls mid-line. Present tense: I don't know is the poem's only present-tense main verb. Monosyllables and Comma: plain words, then no full stop, so the sentence leans on into Except. Rhyme: know / go (G), what he cannot know chiming with where the creature cannot go.

Meaning & effect

The question ends and is answered at once: I don't know. It is the most honest moment in the poem, a refusal to supply a grand answer to a grand question. It is also the first time the speaker speaks in the present. Everything else is narrated from afterwards, and the one thing he says now is that he does not know, which moves the poem from report to confession. A former life can mean an earlier incarnation, the creature's or the speaker's, or simply the speaker's own earlier years. On that second reading the question becomes autobiographical: has the way he lived led to where he is? The syntax supports it, since a life that led to a crime suggests a drift that adds up to guilt rather than a single deed. I don't know can be heard as giving up or as honest agnosticism, but the comma keeps it from being the last word.

Line 14
Except I thought I recognised myself.
Language & devices

Conjunction: Except makes one exception to his ignorance. Hedging: I thought, past tense and uncertain. Verb: recognised, to know again, implies prior acquaintance, and recognition can be mistaken. Reflexive pronoun: myself is withheld to the last word. Circular structure: the first word I, the last myself. Distant rhyme: myself / shelf reaches four lines back, and there is no couplet. Metre: smooth, regular iambs with no internal pause, after the broken lines 11 and 13.

Meaning & effect

The poem's meaning arrives in its final words: the speaker sees himself in the cockroach. Everything has prepared for it, from he and the human verbs to the illness and the question of guilt, so the recognition feels both surprising and inevitable. But it is hedged on every side: an exception, past tense, thought, recognised. That makes it more believable and more unsettling than a grand declaration; he claims only what he can honestly claim. What he recognises is unflattering: a creature that moved restlessly, got worse over time, climbed and stopped, not knowing where to go, possibly paying for something. The rhyme binds myself to shelf, the place where movement ended, and closes the poem so quietly that the ear barely registers it. There is no couplet to sum up. The poem ends on a line with no internal pause, unbroken after two lines that stuttered, and the confession lands exactly because it is said so flatly. The poem never says "we", but it leaves room for the reader to wonder what they would recognise.

THE WHOLE POEM

The Whole Poem

Stepping back: what the poem is doing, first line to last

The standard account of this poem (insect as allegory of human aimlessness, sonnet subverted, turn delayed, moral delivered) is not wrong. But it files the poem under a grandness the poem spends fourteen lines declining. The better reading is this: 'The Cockroach' is less a finished allegory than a demonstration of how allegories get made. We are not handed a symbol. We watch a man make one, hedge by hedge, out of a dusty room and a passing insect, and in its last line the poem confesses that this is what it has been doing. Its subject is the mind's habit of planting meaning in whatever it watches, and the self-portrait that habit produces.

Track the making. The poem opens in the grammar of pure observation, I watched, and at once begins to tilt. Giant magnifies. By line 3 the insect is he, and seemed quite satisfied plants an inner life while seemed admits that the planting is guesswork. The realist furniture of dust, wainscot and rusty table leg does alibi work: this is mere reportage, the details insist, while the verbs anthropomorphise. Satisfied, jog, restlessness, uncertain: each is a human word carried across the species line under cover of description.

The simile is the poem's one moment of open honesty about its method: As if the victim of a mild attack / Of restlessness concedes that the diagnosis is the watcher's. By line 11 the pretence has thinned to nothing, and He looked uncertain where to go reports an insect's mind as plain fact. Once the creature has been filled with human uncertainty, the metaphysics follows as if naturally: Was this due payment for some vicious crime, a question that only makes sense about a person. The final line names the person. Except I thought I recognised myself is less a twist than an audit. Of course he recognised himself; he had been drawing his own portrait since satisfied.

Read this way, the poem's structure falls into place. The sonnet machinery keeps perfect time: every rhyme is full, every line has ten syllables, and the pentameter runs on even through And stopped. Meanwhile every ordering system inside the poem fails in turn. The traced path decays into crooked rings, the climb tops out on an empty shelf, the karmic hypothesis dies in I don't know, and knowledge itself decays from watched to thought. By the last line the verse-form is the only machine in the poem still working. That is the deep joke of writing this experience as a sonnet. Form persists the way habit persists, the way the roach goes on scratching its wings upside down: a leftover order no longer connected to any purpose. The withheld couplet is the point of greatest tact. A couplet is the English sonnet's gesture of confidence, and confidence is the one thing this speaker cannot honestly perform. So the poem ends instead on a rhyme four lines distant, technically resolved and barely audible: closure for those who check, uncertainty for the ear.

The obvious objection is that this makes the poem cold: a clever machine about projection, its unhappiness dissolved into technique. The answer is that projection is not an alternative to self-portraiture but its most reliable form. What a mind plants in a trivial object tells you about that mind. Nobody content projects a mild attack / Of restlessness that worsened over time onto an insect. The poem's unhappiness is real precisely because it is found, planted, in so small a thing: a mood that spreads into whatever is at hand, and the triviality of the host measures how far it has spread. The vigil itself is evidence before any interpretation begins. Only a man with nothing he can bear to do watches a cockroach this long and this closely. The symptom is the watching; the interpretation merely catches up.

A second objection comes from the other side: that the poem is slight, a shaggy-dog sonnet with a mock-solemn punchline. The joke-structure is undeniably there. Giant is mock-heroic, the grandest lyric form in English is handed to vermin, and the octave's last enjambment winds up a mild attack / Of and pays off with restlessness, pure bathos. Except I thought I recognised myself has the timing of a deadpan curtain-line. But the comedy is load-bearing, not decorative. Deadpan is the only register in which this confession could be made without curdling into self-pity. The moment the poem said I am in despair, it would become the kind of poem its speaker could no longer trust. Instead it says something much smaller, I thought I recognised myself, and the smallness is what makes it credible.

This is also why inflating the poem misreads it. Kafka's insect, Camus's Sisyphus and the karma the poem borrows are useful comparisons. Made into the poem's subject, they convert understatement into exactly the grandiosity the poem was built to avoid, and so does the history of a country the poem never names. The poem's scale is one man, one room, one insect, a few minutes. Its biggest metaphysical question is asked and dropped inside a line and a half. Smallness is not a limitation it fails to transcend; it is the argument. Despair here is not tragic or historical but domestic, mildly comic and chronic, a condition that worsened over time while nobody was watching except the sufferer, who was watching an insect.

So the movement from first line to last is best described not as observation followed by revelation but as a closing loop. The poem begins I watched and ends myself: first word the watcher, last word the watched, and the fourteen lines between are the discovery that these were the same. The sonnet, historically the form in which a self addresses its beloved, is here the form in which a self, by way of a cockroach, finally addresses itself. What it finds to say is four hedges deep, in the past tense, and hangs off I don't know. The creature, meanwhile, is left where it stopped, on its shelf, unaware of having been used. That too is part of the poem's honesty. The roach was never the subject. It was the mirror, and the poem never once pretends otherwise.

FORM & STRUCTURE

Form & Structure

How the poem is built, and why it matters

Form & genre

A hybrid sonnet: fourteen lines of iambic pentameter printed as one unbroken block. Its octave is Shakespearean and its sestet Italian-style, and it has no couplet. The subject is mock-heroic: the form of love and self-examination is given to a household pest.

Rhyme

ABAB CDCD EFGEGF, every rhyme full. In the octave each rhyme-partner sits two lines back. In the sestet the gaps are three lines (time/crime), two (go/know) and four (shelf/myself).

Metre

Iambic pentameter, ten syllables in every line. There are initial trochees in lines 2, 6 and 10, a mid-line trochee in line 7 (right over) and spondaic weight on due payment (12). Line 11 is five regular iambs.

Sentences

Six: lines 1–2; 3–9 (seven lines); 10–11 (And stopped.); 11 (He looked uncertain where to go.); 12–13 (the question); 13–14 (I don't know, / Except…).

Lineation

Four enjambments: 3–4, 8–9, 10–11, 12–13. Lines 1–9 have no punctuation inside the line. The internal pauses all come in the sestet: a comma (10), a full stop (11) and a question mark (13).

Turns

The turn is spread out. But comes early (5); speculation begins with As if (8); the formal turn at 9 is refused; the action stops at 11; narration becomes a question at 12; the recognition comes at 14.

The block and the title

On the page the poem is a single fourteen-line block with no stanza breaks. The sonnet's architecture exists only in the rhymes, audible but invisible: a structured interior under a featureless surface, which also describes the speaker. The title follows the fable and emblem formula of definite article plus creature, and so promises a moral. The poem then declines to draw one, and that gap between the fable-shaped title and the hedged non-moral of line 14 is the form's first joke.

Rhyme, worked letter by letter

Line End word Letter
1 pace A
2 floor B
3 trace A
4 door B
5 rings C
6 back D
7 wings C
8 attack D
9 time E
10 shelf F
11 go G
12 crime E (rhymes with time)
13 know G (rhymes with go)
14 myself F (rhymes with shelf)

The scheme is ABAB CDCD EFGEGF, and two things follow from it. First, the opening eight lines are pure Shakespearean procedure, which trains the reader to expect a third cross-rhymed quatrain and a clinching couplet (EFEF GG). Instead the poem swerves into an Italian-style sestet of two tercets, and then warps even that. A standard EFG EFG would repeat the tercet's order exactly; Halligan's second tercet comes back out of order, E-G-F.

Second, and decisively, the couplet never arrives. The English sonnet's couplet is the form's engine of confidence, the two-line snap that resolves, summarises, moralises. Halligan's fourteenth line rhymes not with line 13 beside it but with line 10, four lines back. That is the longest wait for a rhyme in the poem, so long that most readers half-lose the chime. Closure technically happens and is barely heard. A poem about a creature that looked uncertain where to go is written in a form that, at its own ending, cannot find its expected way home.

Look at the rhyme distances. In the octave every rhyme-partner sits a tidy two lines back (1→3, 2→4, 5→7, 6→8). In the sestet the gaps go three, two, four. The even alternation frays exactly as the creature loses its pattern. The pairings carry meaning too. Time rhymes with crime, the karmic equation in miniature, with duration itself as the sentence. Go rhymes with know, the two things neither roach nor speaker can do. Shelf rhymes with myself: the self's rhyme-partner is the place of arrest, the bare ledge where movement ended.

One more fact, easy to miss because it is an absence: every rhyme is full. There is no half-rhyme anywhere. The disorder the poem describes never roughens its sounds; its table manners stay perfect throughout the breakdown. Disorder lives in the large structures (the withheld couplet, the reordered tercet, the drifting distances) while the local finish stays polished. That is the speaker's condition too: outwardly composed, structurally lost.

Metre

The base is iambic pentameter, kept with almost sinister reliability: every line has ten syllables. Stressed syllables are in capitals and feet are marked |.

Line Scansion What it does
1 i WATCHED | a GI | ant COCK | roach START | to PACE Regular, but roach, a heavy syllable, sits in a weak position. Three heavy syllables in a row slow the line on the creature's name.
2 SKIRT ing | a BALL | of DUST | that RODE | the FLOOR Initial trochee. The metre swerves off its path as the creature swerves round the dust.
3 at FIRST | he SEEMED | quite SAT | is FIED | to TRACE Regular: an orderly line for the orderly phase.
4 a PATH | be TWEEN | the WAIN | scot AND | the DOOR Regular, with the fourth beat on a weak and: a level line for a level route between two fixed points.
5 but SOON | he TURNED | to JOG | in CROOK | ed RINGS Perfectly regular. The line about crookedness scans dead straight, so the disorder still belongs to the creature, not to the verse.
6 CIR cling | the RUS | ty TA | ble LEG | and BACK Initial trochee (circling is two syllables). The line starts by turning.
7 and FLIP | ping RIGHT | O ver | to SCRATCH | his WINGS Mid-line trochee after a stressed right: two stresses collide and the rhythm flips over in the line about the flip. This is the poem's most mimetic substitution.
8 as IF | the VIC | tim of | a MILD | at TACK A light third foot (-tim of): the line goes hollow before attack lands, enacting mild.
9 of REST | less ness | that WORS | ened O | ver TIME A light second foot. The line that opens the sestet, the sonnet's most important position, begins with Of, the weakest word available: bathos built into the architecture.
10 AF ter | a WHILE | he CLIMBED | an O | pen SHELF Initial trochee, the third of three. All three (Skirting, Circling, After) fall on words of moving on or time passing: the inversions cluster where the creature changes course.
11 and STOPPED. | he LOOKED | un CER | tain WHERE | to GO Five regular iambs. The syntax breaks after two syllables, but the metre does not: it ticks straight through the full stop like a clock in an empty room, indifferent to the creature's arrest.
12 was THIS | DUE PAY | ment FOR | some VI | cious CRIME Spondaic weight on due pay-: the stresses bunch and thud where the invoice is presented.
13 a FOR | mer LIFE | had LED | to? I | don't KNOW The question mark falls inside a foot, mid-stride. The metre puts a beat on I while speech also stresses don't and know, so the three words come out almost evenly weighted: a flat, heavy close.
