14 ex CEPT | i THOUGHT | i REC | og NISED | my SELF Regular and docile, the tamest line in the poem, with no internal pause. The last stress falls squarely on -self: four hedges in the syntax, but the poem's final beat lands without hedging on the self.

The turns

A sonnet is a machine with one pivot. This one spreads the pivot's work across several sites, which is what a turn looks like when the turner is uncertain where to go. But soon (5) is an early micro-turn, from contentment to circling. With As if (8) the poem stops describing and starts speculating about causes. The form appoints its turn at line 9, and the syntax refuses it: a mild attack / Of restlessness enjambs straight across the octave–sestet seam, and the poem's longest sentence (lines 3–9, seven lines: restlessness as syntax) pours over the boundary where the sonnet asks for a pause.

The narrative hinge comes at line 11 with And stopped., the poem's shortest sentence and its only mid-line full stop, arresting ten and a half lines of continuous motion. The change of mode comes at 12, where narration becomes interrogation. The disclosure comes at 14. (Difficult Moments weighs which of these is "the" volta.)

Syntax and punctuation

There are six sentences, and their shape is eloquent: a two-line establishing shot; a seven-line sentence that will not stop; then syntax breaking into short units exactly where the creature halts. Time-markers run the narrative like a log-book (At first, soon, over time, After a while).

The first nine lines contain no punctuation inside the line, so the poem streams. The sestet holds its first internal comma (10), its only mid-line full stop (11) and its only question mark (13), so it stutters. Then the last line runs whole and unpunctuated to its full stop. After the caesurae of lines 11 and 13, that clean final line arrives with extra force: the poem's only unbroken line in the sestet carries its only certainty. Note too that I don't know is not even given a full stop. A comma lets the sentence lean on into Except, so the poem's whole self-knowledge is grammatically a tail hanging off a confession of ignorance.

Enjambment

There are four run-ons, each crossing a meaningful edge:

  • 3→4, to trace / A path: the path continues over the line-end as it does over the floor.
  • 8→9, a mild attack / Of restlessness: the seam-crossing analysed above, and also a bathetic reveal. A mild attack of what? Heart? Panic? Restlessness.
  • 10→11, an open shelf / And stopped.: the reader tips over the line-end and lands on the stop. The enjambment delivers the arrest bodily.
  • 12→13, some vicious crime / A former life had led to?: the line-break falls between the crime and the life, the white space standing where the gap between lives would be.

Lines 1 and 2 are end-stopped (comma, full stop). The octave's fluency comes from its lack of internal punctuation, not from a string of run-on lines.

Line 11 as hinge

Everything before it is motion; everything after it is mind. And stopped. ends the poem's physical action. He looked uncertain where to go. (seven words, all but one of them monosyllables) is the plainest sentence in the poem and the first to read a mind into the creature without any hedge. The caesura is the poem's centre of gravity. The silence after stopped. is where watching turns into thinking, and the remaining three and a half lines all happen inside that silence.

SOUND

Sound

What the poem does to the ear

The poem's sound-world divides at the same hinge as everything else. The octave is built on friction: a scuttle of sibilants, Skirting, dust, seemed quite satisfied to trace, soon, rings, scratch. Insect-leg noise is carried in the consonants, so the reading voice performs a light, continuous rustle while the creature moves.

Under the hiss runs a guttural /k/ and /g/ line, hard sounds made at the back of the mouth: cockroach, wainscot, jog, crooked, circling, leg, scratch, back, attack. PoetryProf hears these as the broken sound of a creature's jerky movement, and they cluster exactly in the lines of circling and flipping. The /k/ also travels: from cockroach through crooked and attack to climbed, crime, recognised and Except. The consonant of the creature's own name migrates through violence (attack) and indictment (crime) to cognition (recognised). The accusation moves phonetically from insect to speaker before the syntax admits it.

The word restlessness deserves its own note. Three hissing sibilants are packed into the poem's diagnosis, so the noun performs the fidget it names. And it arrives, after the line-break's suspense, as bathos: a mild attack / Of sets up something grave and pays off with a word that merely seethes.

The sestet drops the friction for stops and open vowels: stopped, uncertain, go, don't know. The mouth closes and the busyness falls away. Read aloud, the poem audibly loses its scuttle at line 11, which is why the caesura lands so hard. The full stop after stopped comes straight after the plosive cluster /st…pt/, a word walled in by consonants at both ends, and is followed by nothing the voice can rustle on.

Vowel length does the emotional shading at the rhymes. The octave's A and B rhymes are long and open (pace / trace, floor / door): stately, unhurried sounds for the period of apparent purpose. Against them the D rhyme back / attack snaps shut on a short vowel and a stop, so the octave's two shut sounds land on its two violent words. In the sestet, go / know leaves the mouth open on a long o, the vowel of irresolution, heard twice and the second time on the confession of ignorance. Shelf / myself closes on the short, shut /ɛlf/: the self filed away on its ledge.

Cadence completes the effect. The octave's rhymes ring at even two-line intervals, a metronome under the scuttle; the sestet's chimes come at three, two and four lines. In line 13 I don't know is three nearly equal stresses, a flat, heavy monotone. The final line is all evenness: five soft iambs with no cluster, no hiss and no pause, closing on the stressed -self. The quietest line in the poem is the only one that lands its last beat squarely on its subject. That is deadpan as a sound-effect: the voice must not rise exactly where the meaning does.

MOTIFS & SYMBOLS

Motifs & Symbols

Images that recur, and what they accumulate

A motif recurs and gathers meaning; a symbol stands for something. The cockroach itself becomes a symbol only at line 14, after the event and hedged. For thirteen and a half lines it is stubbornly an insect, and the poem's power depends on how long it withholds symbolic status. Around it, five motifs run the poem's length.

1. The geometry of movement

The poem's plot is told as shapes:

  • pace (1): a straight line, to and fro.
  • Skirting (2): an arc round an obstacle.
  • trace / A path between the wainscot and the door (3–4): a fixed segment with two endpoints, the most ordered figure in the poem.
  • crooked rings (5): closed curves, and deformed ones, a ring that fails at being a ring.
  • Circling the rusty table leg and back (6): an orbit round a single point.
  • flipping right over (7): rotation about the body's own axis. Movement now centres on the creature itself, going nowhere at all.
  • climbed (10): a sudden new axis, vertical, promising escape from the plane.
  • And stopped (11): a point.

Line, arc, segment, ring, orbit, spin, vertical, point: the degrees of freedom collapse one by one to zero. The whole existential argument is conducted in geometry before a single abstract noun appears.

2. Dust, rust, vacancy: decay in three glimpses

  • A ball of dust that rode the floor (2): loose matter, mobile, passively carried.
  • The rusty table leg (6): corrosion, fixed, eaten into the structure.
  • An open shelf (10): a bare board with nothing stored on it, open as in empty.

The decay moves inward, from floating debris to corroded furniture to sheer vacancy at the top of the climb. Time is present in the room's objects long before it is named (worsened over time, After a while, A former life), and the neglected interior shows the watcher's state eight lines before he admits to having one. English poetry has long used the decaying room this way: in Tennyson's 'Mariana' the restless, waiting woman's house has its mouse behind the "mouldering wainscot". The shelf is the one object that hardens into a symbol: the summit that contains nothing, exposure and emptiness at the top of every climb. The room's one way out, the door, is reached by the creature's path and never used.

3. The language of law and debt

  • victim (8): someone wronged.
  • attack (8): an offence, though here medicalised.
  • due payment (12): an invoice.
  • vicious crime (12): an indictment.
  • had led to (13): a case history establishing cause.

Watch the register shift from medical (mild attack… worsened) through forensic (victim) to financial and judicial (due payment for some vicious crime). Across the poem a prosecution is quietly assembled out of natural history, and cosmic justice, when it surfaces, speaks the language of bookkeeping: karma pictured as an unpaid bill. The verdict never comes, and the court adjourns on I don't know.

4. The verbs of knowing: the poem's real plot

  • watched (1): confident perception.
  • seemed (3): appearance flagged as appearance.
  • As if (8): open simile, interpretation admitting itself.
  • looked uncertain (11): projection wearing the grammar of observation.
  • I don't know (13): the collapse.
  • thought… recognised (14): knowing, hedged twice.

The trajectory runs from seeing to seeming to not knowing to thinking one recognises: a steady decay of confidence that is the poem's true narrative arc. The creature's movements degrade from line to point, and the watcher's knowledge degrades in parallel, from observation to confession. By the end the two collapses turn out to have been one thing, which is what recognised means.

5. The pronouns: I, he, myself

I is the first word. A giant cockroach becomes he at line 3 and stays he (his wings, He looked), never "it", so the creature is an individual long before it is a mirror. In the sestet the I returns in force: I don't know, I thought I recognised myself, three uses in two lines after twelve lines without one. The last word, myself, absorbs the he. The pronoun chain tells the whole story in miniature: a self looks outward at an other, and the other turns out to be the self.

THEMES

Themes

The ideas the poem is arguing about

01

Restlessness: motion without purpose

The poem's story is a loss of direction, told in the creature's movements. It begins with a route, trace / A path between the wainscot and the door, a line between two fixed points. That path decays into crooked rings, then into an orbit round one point (Circling the rusty table leg and back), then into the body's own axis (flipping right over), then into a climb that ends in And stopped. Each stage has fewer degrees of freedom than the last, until the creature is a point on a shelf, uncertain where to go.

The diagnosis the poem gives this condition is restlessness that worsened over time: not a crisis but a chronic, low-grade condition that gets worse rather than better. That is its bleakest suggestion. Restlessness does not lead anywhere, not even to a breakdown with a clear cause; it simply deepens, and the moment of freedom at the top of the climb is the moment of paralysis. Movement in this poem is not progress. Jog, the most purposeless kind of running, is the poem's own joke about it.

02

Projection: the mind that reads itself into things

Nobody in the poem knows what a cockroach feels, and the poem keeps saying so. The watcher seemed to see satisfaction; he explains the scratching As if the creature were the victim of a mild attack; by line 11 the hedge has gone and he simply reports He looked uncertain where to go. The human vocabulary (satisfied, jog, restlessness, uncertain) arrives under cover of description, and the poem gives the reader the evidence to notice it happening.

The theme is how meaning gets made. The speaker does not find a symbol; we watch him build one, word by word, from a dusty room and a passing insect, until the creature can bear a question that only makes sense about a person: Was this due payment for some vicious crime. The last line then names whose portrait it has been. What a mind reads into something trivial tells you about that mind, so the description of the cockroach turns out to have been a self-portrait all along.

03

Self-recognition: the watcher becomes the watched

The poem begins I watched and ends myself: first word the observer, last word the observed, and the fourteen lines in between are the discovery that they were the same. The distance closes by degrees. The insect becomes he in line 3, and the room is seen from floor level (a table leg, not a table). The diagnosis outgrows its patient: worsened over time fits a human life better than an insect's afternoon. The only present-tense words, I don't know, belong to the speaker, not the creature.

What he recognises is unflattering. It is not a lion or an eagle but vermin, the creature people flinch from, and what they share is aimlessness, chronic restlessness, a climb that leads nowhere, and perhaps guilt. Recognition here is a shock of self-knowledge rather than consolation. Yet it is also the poem's only certainty: everything else is I don't know, Except this.

04

Guilt, debt and deserving

Line 12 asks whether suffering is earned: Was this due payment for some vicious crime / A former life had led to? The idea is close to karma and rebirth, the belief that actions bring consequences across lives and that a soul may be reborn as an animal. The poem phrases it in the language of a court and a ledger: a debt falls due, a crime is vicious, and victim and attack have already brought crime into the poem's vocabulary at line 8. Some is the crucial word. The crime is unknown, guilt without any memory of the offence, which is the vaguest and most corrosive kind.

The question works on two levels at once. Asked about the cockroach, it is half a joke (an insect paying for past sins). Asked about the speaker, it is the private fear that his own restlessness is deserved. The syntax even lets A former life mean simply his own earlier life, the way he has lived, which had led to this. The poem never settles it. It tries out the explanation and puts it down: I don't know. That refusal is the theme's point. No account of desert, cosmic or personal, is allowed to make sense of the suffering.

05

Not knowing: uncertainty as honesty

The poem's verbs of knowledge decline steadily: watched (confident perception), seemed, As if, looked uncertain, I don't know, I thought I recognised. It moves from seeing to seeming to not knowing to thinking one recognises. Even the one revelation is hedged four ways: an exception (Except), past tense, an uncertain verb (thought) and a fallible one (recognised).

The form agrees. A Shakespearean sonnet normally ends with a couplet, its gesture of confident summary. This one withholds it, and its last line rhymes with a word four lines back, a closure so faint most ears miss it. The poem's honesty lies in claiming no more than the speaker can know. I don't know is not despair or giving up but a refusal to supply a grand answer to a grand question. That restraint is why the small claim that survives it, I thought I recognised myself, carries such weight.

06

Smallness: the comic made serious

The poem is mock-heroic. The grandest lyric form in English, the sonnet, is handed to a household pest; giant inflates it; jog turns its crisis into a fitness routine; a mild attack / Of restlessness is a set-up and an anticlimax across a line-break; the last line has the timing of a deadpan punchline. The incongruity of a man comparing himself with an insect is funny, and the poem knows it.

But the comedy carries the seriousness rather than relieving it. A deadpan voice is the only one in which this confession could be made without self-pity: had the poem said "I am in despair", its speaker could not have trusted it. The smallness is the argument. The scale is one man, one room, one insect, a few minutes, and unhappiness that is domestic, chronic and undramatic. That the speaker's whole state can be found in so trivial a thing measures how far it has spread.

DIFFICULT MOMENTS

Difficult Moments

Where the poem is genuinely undecidable — and what to do about it

Cruxes

1. Where is the turn: line 8, 9, 11, 12 or 14?

The difficulty. A sonnet reader arrives expecting one turn, and this poem offers several candidates. Line 8 is the speculative turn (As if: description becomes explanation). Line 9 is the formal boundary, where the octave ends. Line 11 is the narrative reversal (And stopped.). Line 12 is the modal shift, from statement to question. Line 14 is the revelation.

Competing readings. - For line 9: the sestet's new rhymes (EFG) begin here, and restlessness that worsened over time turns movement into diagnosis. Against: the syntax pointedly refuses the turn. The sentence enjambs straight across the seam, and the line it delivers opens on Of, the least turn-like word in the poem. This is a refused volta, and the refusal is expressive. - For line 8: As if is where the speaker starts explaining rather than describing, the start of the speculation that ends in self-recognition. Against: it is a simile, not a change of direction, and the description carries on. - For line 11: everything reverses here, motion becoming stillness; the full stop after stopped is the poem's centre of gravity. Against: the speaker's stance has not changed. He is still outside, still reporting; the arrest is an event, not a turn of mind. - For line 14: the allegory completes here, and the idea of a "displaced volta" honours the fact that the meaning arrives in the poem's last breath. Against: a volta is a change of direction, and line 14 is better described as a landing. The direction changed earlier; this is where the ground arrives.

The strongest single case is line 12. Was this due payment for some vicious crime changes what kind of poem this is. Past narration becomes interrogation; the room's physics gives way to metaphysics; and the speaker's mind, hidden until now behind observational grammar, enters as a questioner. One line later the poem produces its only present-tense main verb, I don't know. Tense, mood, register and subject all pivot at 12 in a way they do not at 9, 11 or 14.

What a strong answer does. It does not just pick a line and defend it to the death. It argues that the poem distributes the volta's functions: explanation begins at 8, the form's turn is refused at 9, action turns at 11, mind at 12, meaning at 14. Then it makes the interpretive move: a sonnet whose turn cannot be located in one place is enacting a speaker who is uncertain where to go. The scattered turn is not indecision in the writing; it is the poem's most precise imitation of indecision.

2. He looked uncertain where to go — whose uncertainty is this?

The difficulty. Looked carries two grammars: appeared (the roach seemed uncertain to me) and gazed (the roach looked about, uncertain). Beneath both sits the harder question. Can an insect be uncertain at all, or is this the moment the speaker's projection completes itself and he starts reporting his own mind as the creature's?

Competing readings. Taken as honest observation, the line is the poem's most touching moment: hesitation legible in an insect's body, animal experience continuous with ours. The he of line 3 has been preparing this reading. Taken as ventriloquism, the line is the crucial slip. Earlier projections wore flags (seemed, As if); here the hedge is gone, and the speaker states an insect's inner state as fact. This is the moment the mirror silvers, after which the karmic question and the recognition follow. The evidence tilts towards ventriloquism precisely because of the missing hedge: the poem has trained us in scrupulousness and then conspicuously drops it. There is also a literal possibility. A cockroach that has been flipping onto its back and is now motionless on a shelf may be sick or dying, so what the speaker reads as indecision may be failing. That reading makes his projection even more pointed, since he would be reading a mind into a body's collapse.

What a strong answer does. It refuses to choose and finds the poem's honesty in the undecidability. The speaker cannot know whether he observed uncertainty or installed it, and that is exactly what Except I thought I recognised myself concedes. This line is where watching and mirroring become indistinguishable, and the final hedge (thought) acknowledges that they were never separable. Resolving the line one way loses either the pathos or the self-knowledge; the poem keeps both.

3. Was this due payment for some vicious crime / A former life had led to?

The difficulty. There are three tangles in sixteen words. Whose former life: the cockroach's (a soul demoted into vermin, paying off an old debt), or the speaker's (his own past surfacing, disguised as a question about an insect)? What is this: the restlessness, the paralysis, or existence as a cockroach at all? And the least noticed: the causality runs backwards. The syntax does not say a crime was committed in a former life. It says the former life had led to the crime, so the life is the cause and the crime the destination, as if simply living a certain way accumulates, by itself, into an offence.

Competing readings. Read as the roach's biography, the question is a real, if half-smiling, engagement with rebirth: demotion down the ladder of beings as a penalty, the insect as a soul in a debtors' prison. Read as displaced autobiography, it rehearses the speaker's private dread that his condition is deserved, that restlessness is a sentence rather than a symptom, asked at one remove, where it is safe to ask. The reversed causality quietly supports the second reading. "A life that leads to a crime" describes not a single sin but a drift, a way of living culpable in total, much more like a watched life than a legal case. And the tone will not settle. Due payment is bookkeeping language, cosmic justice as an invoice, which either deflates the metaphysics into comedy or makes it more sinister: debts fall due whether or not you remember incurring them.

What a strong answer does. It keeps the question double, asked about the roach and meant about the man, and reads I don't know as the only honest settlement of it. Then it presses the syntax. The poem's darkest suggestion, available but never stated, is that the former life is simply the speaker's own earlier life, and the restless present is what it led to. On that reading line 14 does not change the subject; it answers the question of line 12.

4. Except I thought I recognised myself — what, precisely, is being claimed?

The difficulty. The poem's whole payload is delivered through four stacked hedges, and a careless paraphrase bulldozes them into "the speaker realises he is the cockroach", which is exactly the paraphrase the line was built to prevent. Grammatically the line is not even a sentence of its own. It is a subordinate tail on I don't know,, the one exception to a declaration of ignorance.

The hedges, in order. - Except: a swerve, rescuing one thing from not-knowing. The bleak consequence is that the only certainty on offer is a resemblance to vermin. - I thought: past tense and weak. The writing self reports an impression it does not now endorse. By the time we hear of the recognition it is already over, and I don't know (present tense) formally outranks it. - recognised: not "saw" or "realised" but a verb of fallible matching, since you can recognise wrongly. Yet the word also brings in intimacy, because recognition presupposes earlier acquaintance: you cannot recognise what you have never met. The verb hedges the claim while conceding that the face was familiar. - myself: withheld to the last stress. The syntax delays the object of recognition to the last possible position, so the meaning arrives on the closing beat, where the metre lands its one unhedged commitment.

Competing readings. - (i) Full allegorical identification, hedged only for politeness, supported by everything the imagery has built. - (ii) A momentary illusion, honestly reported and already half-disowned, supported by the tense and by the subordination after Except. - (iii) The answer to line 12: the former life was his, and the recognition is an admission of guilt, not of kinship. - (iv) A deadpan punchline: the mock-solemn form finally tips its hand.

What a strong answer does. It treats the hedging not as modesty about the claim but as the claim itself. The line asserts exactly as much as this speaker can honestly assert, and its four qualifications are the most precise thing in the poem, not the least. Removing the hedges to get at "the meaning" removes the meaning.

5. Comic or desolate?

The difficulty. The poem is funny: a giant insect, a creature that goes for a jog, the bathos of a mild attack / Of restlessness, a curtain-line of perfect deadpan timing. The incongruity of a man comparing himself with a cockroach is a joke in itself. Yet its content is chronic suffering that worsened over time, paralysis, guilt, and a self-image as vermin. Readers split over whether the poem is a wry squib or a bleak confession, and both have the text on their side.

Competing readings. The comic reading sees mock-heroic throughout: the sonnet's dignity lent to a pest, solemn metaphysics (due payment, A former life) applied to a bug, the anticlimax of I don't know. The desolate reading sees the comedy as surface. The natural history is grim (a cockroach on its back is usually in trouble), the decay of the room is real, and the last line confesses a low opinion of the self. A third reading holds that the comedy is how the confession becomes possible: deadpan lets the speaker say the unbearable without self-pity.

What a strong answer does. It locates the humour precisely (in diction, bathos and timing) and then tracks how it drains away. The comic verbs belong to the octave (jog, flipping right over); the sestet has none (stopped, uncertain, crime, don't know). The poem starts as a joke about an insect and ends as something no one laughs at, while keeping a joke's shape to the end. The last line has a punchline's timing without the release a laugh would bring. That unreleased tension, comedy that turns serious without changing its tone, is why the ending unsettles.

CLOSE ANALYSIS

Close Analysis

The moments that repay pressure, worked through

Quotation analysis

Twelve moments that repay pressure, in the order of the poem.

1. I watched a giant cockroach start to pace, (1)

First-person frame; mock-heroic hyperbole; anthropomorphic verb. The watcher is introduced before the watched, and watched is the verb of long, deliberate attention: the poem's first piece of evidence about the speaker is simply what he chooses to spend time on. Giant does two jobs. It is fair description (large house species really are big), and it is comic inflation, raising an insect to the scale of a sonnet. Pace gives the creature a human walk, the to-and-fro of the anxious or the imprisoned, and start to frames what follows as a process with stages. The tone is a naturalist's log, plain past tense and no comment.

Intention and effect: Halligan sets up apparently neutral observation, so that the confession at the end comes from inside a report the reader had trusted as objective.

2. Skirting a ball of dust that rode the floor. (2)

Initial trochee; participle; metaphorical verb. The metre swerves off the iambic path on Skirting exactly as the creature swerves round the obstacle, so the poem's first substitution is mimetic. Skirting also carries its social sense of evading, giving a wide berth, and names the board at the foot of a wall where cockroaches run. The dust rode the floor: passive matter given a jaunty verb of travel, while the genuinely self-propelled creature will end up going nowhere. It is the poem's first quiet joke about the difference between moving and being moved. The precise trivial detail (a dust ball, watched closely enough to see it drift) is also evidence about the watcher: this is the noticing of a man with nothing else to attend to.

Intention and effect: Halligan grounds the allegory to come in small, checkable fact, so the reader trusts the eye long before doubting the mind.

3. At first he seemed quite satisfied to trace / A path between the wainscot and the door, (3–4)

Temporal frame; epistemic hedge; enjambment; bounded interval. At first announces a narrative after the fact (you only say at first when things changed), so deterioration is promised before it begins. Seemed is the earliest confession that the creature's inner life is the watcher's construction, and quite measures that contentment in a dry, grading tone. Trace is not "choose" or "make": you trace a line that already exists, so contentment is defined at once as obedience to a given track. The enjambment sends the verb over the line-end to find its object, a small performance of path-following. The track runs between two fixed limits, wall and door. Wainscot is an old word for wall-panelling and English literature's traditional lodging for vermin. It is also exact natural history, since cockroaches run along walls and edges.

Intention and effect: purpose arrives already ironised. The reader sees limits where the creature seemed to see satisfaction, an irony the poem will turn on the speaker himself.

4. But soon he turned to jog in crooked rings, (5)

Conjunction pivot; comic register; failed geometry. But is the poem's first turn, a micro-volta at line 5, well before the form's appointed one, as if the poem cannot wait to start failing. Jog is superb comic casting. The leisure-exercise verb, aimless by design (jogging ends where it began), demotes the creature's crisis to a fitness routine. Crooked rings fail twice: a ring returns you to where you began, and these are not even true circles. Meanwhile the metre stays perfectly iambic. The line about crookedness scans dead straight, the verse withholding its sympathy: disorder has reached the creature but not yet the poem.

Intention and effect: Halligan lets aimlessness arrive in comic dress, so that its later escalation (worsened) catches the reader having laughed at symptoms.

5. Circling the rusty table leg and back, (6)

Initial trochee; synecdoche; floor-level perspective. The trochee makes the line pivot at its head; it starts by turning. The orbit has shrunk to a single point of reference, and the point is telling: not the table but the table leg, furniture seen from the floor. The poem's camera is lowered to insect height eight lines before the speaker admits to sharing the view. Rusty puts corrosion at the centre of the creature's circuit, so it orbits decay. And back hangs off the line like the futile return leg it describes, the syntax retracing its own steps.

Intention and effect: the reader is brought physically down to the roach's scale, so the final identification has been rehearsed by perspective long before it is stated.

6. And flipping right over to scratch his wings – (7)

Mid-line trochee; colloquial intensifier; suspended dash. The rhythm flips with the creature: right over jams two stresses together and inverts the foot, the poem's most mimetic substitution. Right over is spoken register, the phrase you would use of a toddler or a beetle, amused and faintly fond. The detail everyone forgets is wings. The creature has flight available and spends the poem on the floor, on its back, scratching them: escape technically possible and never taken. And a cockroach on its back is usually in trouble. Healthy ones right themselves, and one stranded belly-up is often sick or poisoned, so the comic tumble may be a symptom. The dash suspends the line mid-air, the creature upended and the interpretation withheld for a beat.

Intention and effect: comedy and diagnosis arrive fused. The reader smiles at the tumble and inherits the image of unused wings.

7. As if the victim of a mild attack / Of restlessness (8–9)

Simile; medical and legal register; bathetic enjambment. As if flags the diagnosis as invention even as the speaker commits to it; these are the poem's most honest two words until I don't know, and the start of its speculation about causes. Victim converts behaviour into affliction: the creature no longer acts but suffers, passive before its own movements. A mild attack / Of is engineered suspense. The line-break holds open the grave possibilities (heart, panic, seizure) and pays off with restlessness, bathos that deflates and, in deflating, smuggles the medical frame past the reader's defences. The oxymoron (attacks are not mild) captures the low-grade, chronic, undramatic suffering at issue.

Intention and effect: Halligan makes the reader laugh at the anticlimax and then discover that the laughter has accepted a clinical account of the speaker's own state.

8. that worsened over time. (9)

Prognostic diction; end-stop; double time-scale. Four flat words close the long sentence with a chart-note: not an event but a course, the language of chronic illness. The phrase quietly breaks the poem's realism. The vigil has lasted minutes, yet over time speaks of a longer span than any session of cockroach-watching contains. Two clocks are superimposed, the insect's evening and the man's years, and the sentence only makes literal sense on the second. This is the poem's first unguarded autobiographical leak, five lines before myself. The full stop, the first since line 2, ends seven lines of unbroken motion.

Intention and effect: the reader registers, perhaps without noticing, that the diagnosis has outgrown its patient, and starts looking for the real one.

9. After a while, he climbed an open shelf (10)

Initial trochee; vague duration; polysemous adjective. After a while is the diction of boredom, unmeasured time from a watcher no longer counting, and its trochee tips the line into the poem's last movement. Climbed brings in the vertical for the first time: after nine lines of wandering on the floor, ascent, aspiration itself. But the summit is an open shelf: open as in exposed (no cover), open as in available (nothing stored yet), open as in empty and unbounded (no wall to follow). The reward for the poem's one upward effort is a bare board, and every meaning of open converges on vacancy. The comma after while is the poem's first internal pause: the surface begins to crack.

Intention and effect: the reader receives the poem's bleakest irony, that climbing changes the view but not the condition, one line before it is enacted in And stopped.

10. And stopped. He looked uncertain where to go. (11)

Caesura; enjambed arrival; regular metre against broken syntax; dropped hedge. The run-on from line 10 tips the reader over the line-end onto two syllables and a full stop, the shortest sentence in the poem and its only mid-line full stop. Stopped is walled in by plosives (/st/, /pt/), a word that shuts at both ends. Yet the pentameter does not break: five regular iambs tick straight through the stop, the rhythm of the world indifferent to the creature's arrest. Then the hedge disappears. After seemed and As if, He looked uncertain where to go states an insect's mind as fact, in plain monosyllables, with looked meaning both appeared and looked about. This is where the projection completes itself.

Intention and effect: motion ends and mind begins. The silence after the full stop is where watching turns into thinking, and the reader feels the poem's centre of gravity in a pause.

11. Was this due payment for some vicious crime / A former life had led to? I don't know, (12–13)

Interrogative turn; legal-financial lexis; enjambment; present tense; refused full stop. Narration becomes a question, and the question borrows karma and rebirth in the language of a court and a ledger: a debt falls due, a crime is vicious. Some leaves the offence unknown, guilt without a memory. The line-break falls between the crime and the life, white space where the gap between lives would be. The causality deserves pressure: the life had led to the crime, living itself as the road to the offence, guilt gathered by drift rather than by a single act. The question mark falls mid-line, and what follows is the poem's only present-tense main verb. I don't know is spoken now, the one thing the writing self asserts in its own moment, and it is a disclaimer. It is not even given a full stop: a comma, and the sentence leans on into Except.

Intention and effect: the reader watches the poem's one metaphysical structure collapse in real time, and is handed the question the speaker drops.

12. Except I thought I recognised myself. (14)

Exceptive conjunction; stacked hedges; withheld object; distant rhyme; unbroken line. The one certainty is rescued from ignorance by Except, and it is a resemblance to vermin. I thought puts it in the past and makes it weak; recognised implies prior acquaintance (you can only recognise what you have met) while admitting it could be mistaken. Myself is held back to the last word and the last stress. The first word of the poem was I, so the poem closes its loop. The rhyme reaches four lines back to shelf, binding the self to the place where movement stopped, and there is no couplet to sum up. After the broken lines 11 and 13, this line runs whole: no internal pause, regular iambs, a flat delivery.

Intention and effect: the confession lands precisely because it refuses emphasis. The reader feels the largest claim in the poem made in its smallest voice, and is left to supply the scale the speaker declined to claim.

CRITICAL LENSES

Critical Lenses

What each way of reading makes visible, and what it flattens

Critical lenses

Formalist

This is the lens under which the poem gives most, because its deepest ironies are structural. An octave that promises a couplet is followed by a sestet that withholds it. The second tercet comes back out of order (EGF). The pentameter ticks undisturbed through And stopped. Full rhymes polish the surface of a breakdown. A seven-line sentence enjambs across the form's main seam at attack / Of restlessness. Formalism sees the poem's real drama, a mind keeping perfect table manners while getting lost, enacted in verse-machinery rather than stated.

What it flattens: the I. Formalism can describe the hedges of line 14 as devices but has nothing to say about why a person hedges. It also brackets the karmic material, which is doing real work, as mere "content".

Psychoanalytic

This lens shows that the poem is a study in projection and displacement. The speaker deposits his own inner life in a creature (seemed quite satisfied, looked uncertain) and is then ambushed by it. Except I thought I recognised myself is a textbook return of the repressed: the disowned self met as an other, and uncanny precisely because it is half-familiar (recognised). The choice of host matters. Vermin is the culturally abject, the thing people flinch from; self-disgust selects the one creature the self can safely despise, and the recognition therefore carries a charge of shame that no neutral animal could deliver. Some vicious crime, guilt without a remembered offence, is the language of a superego that accuses without telling you the charge.

What it flattens: the comedy, which it must read as defence. It also flattens the poem's scruple about knowledge, turning I don't know into resistance rather than honesty, so the reading starts diagnosing the patient instead of the poem.

Existentialist

This lens shows a poem that never uses the vocabulary of existentialism but follows its plot. Routine first: a traced path, the kind of rhythm Camus says is easily followed until "the 'why' arises". Then futile repeated motion, the Sisyphean circle. Then a climb to a summit and a pause, at the point where Camus locates consciousness, and the question of why, framed as crime and payment, as Sisyphus's labour is a punishment. The open shelf, freedom without walls, is where the creature freezes: Kierkegaard's "dizziness of freedom" made literal. I don't know is the absurd confrontation itself, a demand for meaning met by silence.

What it flattens: the poem's refusal of grandeur. Existentialism tends to make every unhappiness heroic, and this poem's unhappiness is mild, chronic and slightly comic. It also misses the difference in outcome: Camus's Sisyphus must be imagined happy, while Halligan's speaker gets only to an uneasy recognition.

Ecocritical

This lens shows what every other reading uses without noticing: the actual insect. Much of what the speaker pathologises as restlessness is ordinary cockroach behaviour, such as running along walls and grooming; what is not ordinary (lying on its back, stopping) may be a creature sick or dying, which the speaker turns into a parable about himself. The disorder exists in the watching mind, and the poem half-knows it (As if). Ecocriticism catches the anthropomorphic machinery in the act (he from line 3, human verbs throughout) and names the method for what it is: a colonisation of animal life by human meaning, in which the creature is never itself, only a mirror. Yet the lens also credits the poem's countercurrent. Giant grants scale, he grants individuality, and the last line levels the hierarchy: the human does not stoop to the insect but finds himself already there.

What it flattens: the poem's real interest, which is unashamedly the human. Done stubbornly, an ecocritical reading ends up reviewing the poem for a moral failure it openly performs and confesses.

Marxist / materialist

This lens shows the material preconditions nobody in the poem mentions. A man with time to watch an insect at length is a man released from work, whether by leisure, unemployment or simple vacancy, and the shabby interior (dust, rusty) is a material environment being read as a metaphysical one. Sharpest of all, it notices that when the speaker reaches for cosmic justice he can only imagine it as an economy: due payment, a debt falling due. And the roach jogs, a leisure-exercise verb of the comfortable, pasted onto an insect's survival. Even this poem's transcendence is counted in money.

What it flattens: the interiority. A strictly materialist account has to treat the drama of knowing (seemed, I don't know, thought) as superstructure, and so misses that the poem's subject is consciousness, whatever its economic base.

Reader-response

This lens shows that the poem's ending is completed in the reader or not at all. I don't know hands the metaphysical question across the page. The four hedges of line 14 leave a gap exactly the shape of a reader. The poem never says and so are you, but the fable-promising title, the universalising sonnet form and the pointed smallness of the occasion all press the reader to extend myself to themselves. The reader's own flinch at cockroaches is energy the poem imports: the turn from revulsion to recognition happens in us, unstated.

What it flattens: the specificity of the one speaker the poem actually has. It also licenses precisely the inflation ("this is all of us, the human condition") that the poem's deadpan holds at arm's length.

OTHER READINGS

Other Readings

Contested interpretations, and where each is weak

Alternative readings

  1. The existential allegory (the standard reading). The roach's trajectory of purpose, restlessness and arrest maps human aimlessness, and the poem universalises through smallness. Evidence: the geometry's collapse (path → rings → stop); uncertain where to go; the fable-promising title. Weakness: it flattens the hedges. The poem says myself, once, four qualifications deep, and never "ourselves"; read as a universal statement it becomes the grand, solemn poem its deadpan was built to avoid.

  2. The clinical reading. The poem describes a psychological condition, anxiety or depression, in deliberately medical language: pacing, agitation (a mild attack), chronic course (worsened over time), arrest (And stopped.), emptiness at the summit. Evidence: the sustained language of prognosis; the double time-scale of line 9; the long vigil itself as a symptom. Weakness: the whole diagnosis sits inside As if, a simile flagged as the watcher's invention, and the karmic question belongs to a different explanatory world that the clinical frame cannot absorb.

  3. The karmic confession. The metaphysics is meant. The speaker half-believes his condition is due payment, and line 14 answers line 12: the former life is his own past, and the recognition is an admission of guilt. Evidence: due payment, vicious crime, the reversed causality of had led to; I don't know (not no); Except rescuing one certainty from the ignorance. Weakness: the tone will not hold still, since due payment is bookkeeping comedy as much as doctrine, and the poem's only stated position is unbelief (I don't know).

  4. The mock-heroic comedy. The poem is a sustained joke: the grandest lyric form handed to vermin, giant inflation, the bathos of a mild attack / Of restlessness, a punchline curtain-line. Evidence: the engineered anticlimax of the 8–9 enjambment; jog; the deadpan timing of line 14; the incongruity of man and insect. Weakness: it cannot account for what is left over. Worsened over time and And stopped. are not funny, and the last line, if it is a punchline, doubles its tension instead of releasing it.

  5. The life-course allegory. The poem compresses a biography: the given track of youth (trace / A path between fixed limits), the crooked circling of middle age, the climb to achievement, the summit that turns out bare, the arrest. Evidence: the time-markers (At first, soon, over time, After a while), a lifetime's connectives spent in minutes; climbed as aspiration. Weakness: a point-for-point "ages of man" mapping is mechanical and has to be asserted more than shown (what is the dust? the table leg?). The poem offers the shape of a trajectory, not a key, and readings that allegorise every noun end up writing their own poem.

  6. The literal reading: a creature in distress. Read as natural history, the poem may describe a dying insect. A cockroach on its back is usually sick or poisoned (household sprays cause spasms, tremors and loss of balance); a restlessness that worsened over time followed by stopped is the course of a poisoned insect as much as of a troubled mind. Evidence: flipping right over, victim, attack, worsened, stopped. Weakness: the creature also climbs a shelf, which a collapsing insect is unlikely to do, and the poem never hints at death. The reading is most useful not on its own but for what it adds: if the roach is dying, the speaker's self-recognition becomes darker, and his karmic question more callous or more desperate.

  7. The biographical frame (to handle with care). Many study notes place Halligan in Cambodia, a Buddhist country with the recent history of the Khmer Rouge genocide (1975–79), and read some vicious crime and A former life as shadowed by that place's guilt and its belief in rebirth. Evidence: the poem's karmic vocabulary; the expatriate isolation of a single, placeless room. Weakness: the biography is unconfirmed (no reliable source places Halligan in Cambodia), and the poem names no country, no religion and no history. Its karmic language is that of a Western court and ledger, not of Buddhist teaching. At most this is context brought to the poem, not found in it.

REVISION NOTES

Revision Notes

The working notes, quotation by quotation

Core argument

Analysis
  • Extended allegory: cockroach's restless, aimless movements mirror the speaker's existential uncertainty
  • Speaker travels from detached observation → self-recognition
  • Purpose → Restlessness → Paralysis → Self-identification
  • First word I watched → last word myself: watcher becomes the watched (loop)

Form & rhyme

Analysis
  • Hybrid sonnet: 14 lines, printed as one block (no stanza break: octave/sestet only in the rhymes)
  • Octave (1–8): English/Shakespearean ABAB CDCD
  • Sestet (9–14): Italian-style tercets EFG EGF (second tercet out of order)
  • No couplet → last line rhymes with line 10 (shelf/myself), 4 lines back → closure barely audible
  • Every rhyme full → polished surface, lost creature
  • Iambic pentameter throughout, incl. line 11 (five regular iambs): line 11 breaks the syntax (caesura), not the metre
  • Real substitutions: initial trochees (2, 6, 10), mid-line trochee (7, right over), spondee (12, due payment)

Structure: four movements

Analysis
  • 1–4 ordered + purposeful: regular metre, ABAB; lines 1–2 end-stopped, only enjambment to trace / A path
  • 5–8 restlessness intrudes: But soon, circling, trochee in line 7
  • 8–11 boundary bridged: enjambment attack / Of restlessness runs over the octave–sestet seam → form's pause refused; then caesura And stopped. halts poem + insect
  • 12–14 question + recognition: caesurae in 11 and 13, then an unbroken last line → sharpens its impact
  • Turn spread out: speculation from line 8 (As if), refused at 9, action stops at 11, question at 12, recognition at 14

Sonnet form: ironic deflation

Analysis
  • Sonnet historically for love + grand subjects → Halligan gives the grandest lyric form to a cockroach (mock-heroic)
  • Deflation → human existential suffering as absurd + universal, but no bigger than an insect's aimless wandering
  • Form keeps order (rhyme, metre) while the creature loses it → order vs chaos
  • Couplet = sonnet's gesture of confidence → withheld because the speaker can't claim any

Context: what's verified

Analysis
  • Kevin Halligan: reported born 1964, Canadian poet (sources thin)
  • Utopia (Springfield Books, Cambridge, 2009); Blossom Street (2001, per Open Library)
  • In Songs of Ourselves (first pub. 2005) → in print by 2005; date written unknown (not "1999", not "written 2009")
  • Cambodia / Buddhism claims unconfirmed; poem names no place, religion or history
  • Kafka (Metamorphosis), Marquis (archy, a cockroach with a former life) = frames readers bring, not references
  • Karma/rebirth borrowed in 12–13, phrased as law + money (due payment, crime)
Title

The Cockroach

Analysis
  • The + creature = fable/emblem formula (cf. Blake 'The Fly', Donne 'The Flea') → promises a moral; poem withholds it
  • Cockroach = most despised household insect → final self-recognition carries self-disgust
  • Title names the insect, hides the real subject (the speaker)
1

I watched a giant cockroach start to pace,

Analysis
  • Line opens with first person pronoun I
  • Immediate and direct, places the speaker in the moment; lack of distancing suggests a connection between the cockroach and the speaker
  • watched → sustained + deliberate attention rather than glancing → invites the question why he watches a cockroach
  • Could hint at the speaker's boredom, drawn to a conventionally unattractive creature → pointlessness of his life
  • Hyperbole giant captures attention; size grants it presence, centre of the poem
  • Also mock-heroic: magnifies an insect to sonnet scale (large house species really are big)
  • pace → anxious restlessness from the start
  • Subtly anthropomorphic: pacing is a human quality → links humans + insect
2

Skirting a ball of dust that rode the floor.

Analysis
  • skirting → agility and movement, almost lively
  • Line 1 ends on a comma → sentence runs on into line 2; full stop closes the opening
  • Initial trochee (SKIRT-ing) → metre swerves as the roach swerves
  • Skirting also connotes avoidance, possibly of tasks till it snowballs at the end, where the speaker is forced to confront what he avoids
  • Dust rode the floor = carried along (passive) vs roach self-propelled → irony: roach ends up no better directed than the dust
  • Dust → unkempt room, contrasting the even and tidy form of a sonnet
  • Neglected room establishes atmosphere and the speaker's inner state
3 / 4

At first he seemed quite satisfied to trace / A path between the wainscot and the door,

Analysis
  • Temporal At first → narrative progression; signals change to come
  • Begins with a purpose: defined path between two fixed points = baseline
  • seemed → speaker can't know the cockroach's inner state; satisfaction may not be real, only apparent
  • he not "it" → an individual
  • trace → mechanical, path designated from the beginning (humans' purpose set by peers or parents) → undermines the satisfaction; mindless motion rather than living
  • wainscot and the door → defined limits; could suggest the safe parameters of early adulthood (one reading: a shape, not a key)
  • Accurate: cockroaches run along walls and edges
  • Door = the only exit, never used
  • Wainscot: wooden panelling on the lower part of an interior wall
5 / 6

But soon he turned to jog in crooked rings, / Circling the rusty table leg and back,

Analysis
  • But → flaw/hiccup in the journey: certainty → restlessness
  • crooked → wobbliness, a lapse, uncertain which path to take; path no longer laid out (adults struggling with life's complexities)
  • rings → circular, purposeless; straight-line satisfaction dissolves into aimless circling (midlife crisis?)
  • jog → comic: exercise that ends where it began
  • Line 5 metre perfectly regular → disorder in the creature, not yet in the verse
  • Circling a table leg → wound about one point, won't leave where safety is guaranteed → entrapment, no progress
  • Initial trochee (CIR-cling) → line starts by turning
  • rusty → degraded, neglected world; passing of time
7

And flipping right over to scratch his wings –

Analysis
  • Rolling onto its back → momentary loss of control and vulnerability, paralleling a human's willingness to sacrifice for momentary pleasure
  • Total loss of footing → captures his directionless journey
  • Undignified; dash suspends the moment before the explanation arrives
  • Trochee (right over, RIGHT O-ver) → two stresses collide, rhythm lurches → mimics the flip
  • A healthy cockroach rights itself; one stuck on its back is often sick/poisoned → darker edge
  • wings → flight available, never used
8 / 9

As if the victim of a mild attack / Of restlessness that worsened over time.

Analysis
  • Simile As if → watcher's interpretation, flagged; speculation starts here
  • victim → passive, suffering rather than choosing → hints at the speaker's own emotions, involuntarily consumed by existential crisis
  • mild attack → oxymoron; enjambment suspends it (heart? panic?) → bathos: just restlessness
  • Enjambment runs over the octave–sestet seam (no stanza break on the page), ignoring the traditional volta
  • worsened over time → clinical, ordered account of a disorderly state; time worsens rather than heals
  • over time → sounds like years, not one afternoon → diagnosis fits the speaker
10 / 11

After a while, he climbed an open shelf / And stopped. He looked uncertain where to go.

Analysis
  • After a while → time passing; long, slow watch
  • Reaches the metaphorical peak (top of the shelf) where achievement brings not satisfaction but bewilderment
  • open shelf → possibility + exposure + emptiness; no walls to guide him → freedom paralysing
  • Full stop → finality, anticlimactic: still uncertain
  • Caesura after stopped → reader feels the silence → enacts the epiphany of emptiness
  • Metre stays regular (five iambs): syntax breaks, not metre
  • No seemed now → projection complete
12 / 13

Was this due payment for some vicious crime / A former life had led to? I don't know,

Analysis
  • Alludes to karma + reincarnation: speaker ponders questions reaching beyond the cockroach
  • due payment → debt/court language, karma as an invoice
  • vicious crime → guilt, self-blame; some = crime unknown
  • I don't know → only present-tense main verb → out of detached observation; direct link between speaker + cockroach
  • Flat, simple answer → grand question deserves no grand answer; refuses to pretend to certainty
  • A former life could = speaker's own past → his life led to this
14

Except I thought I recognised myself.

Analysis
  • Final revelation (last stage of the spread-out turn): speaker sees himself in the cockroach, allegory completes itself; cautious thought rather than "knew"
  • The poem's entire point: his own restless, aimless trajectory; reader invited to extend it to themselves
  • recognised → confirming a suspicion; re-cognise = know again → the self was already familiar
  • Detached observation → confession: honesty rather than resolution
  • I … myself → loop composition
  • No couplet: rhyme reaches back to shelf

Sound

Analysis
  • Guttural /k/ /g/ run: cockroach, wainscot, jog, crooked, circling, leg, scratch, back, attack → scuttling, broken sound
  • Sibilance in restlessness → fidgeting
  • stopped → plosives /st…pt/ close the word at both ends
  • go / know → open long o of irresolution; shelf / myself → shut /ɛlf/
CONNECTIONS

Connections

How this poem pairs with the rest of the set

Comparison hooks

1. Wright, 'Hunting Snake' (15)

Link: Both poems watch an animal move, and both turn on a moment of human stillness. Wright's walkers "froze half-through a pace" as the snake passes; Halligan's cockroach starts to pace and ends And stopped.

Shared technique: Close description of a creature's movement inside strict form (Wright's regular rhymed quatrains, Halligan's sonnet), with verbs carrying character: the snake "quested", the roach goes for a jog.

Difference: Wright's snake has purpose ("fierce intent") and the humans are the ones who stop; Halligan's creature loses purpose and the human finds himself in it. Wright's watchers keep their distance, "scarcely thought" about what the snake was hunting, then took "a deeper breath" and moved on. Halligan's watcher cannot stop thinking, and ends inside his creature. One poem lets the animal stay other; the other makes it a mirror.

2. Pope, 'An Essay on Man' (12)

Link: Both are studies of what a human being is, and both find us suspended between purposes. Pope's man "hangs between; in doubt to act or rest". Halligan's cockroach acts restlessly, then rests, uncertain where to go. "The proper study of mankind is man" is the project Halligan carries out sideways, through an insect.

Shared technique: The paradox of rise and fall ("Created half to rise and half to fall") against a creature that climbed an open shelf / And stopped. Both make error and ignorance central: "Sole judge of truth, in endless error hurled" against I don't know.

Difference: Pope generalises with total confidence in closed heroic couplets, ending on the exclamation "The glory, jest, and riddle of the world!" Halligan's speaker can only say I thought I recognised myself, and withholds the couplet. Pope's man is "in doubt to deem himself a god or beast"; Halligan's man has found the beast, and it is vermin. (Earlier in the Essay, Epistle I, Pope reasons that we lack "a microscopic eye" because "man is not a fly". Halligan's poem suspects otherwise.)

3. Heaney, 'Follower' (08)

Link: Both watch a figure move and end with the watcher discovering his own relation to the watched. Heaney's father ploughs with mastery, "Mapping the furrow exactly"; Halligan's creature goes in crooked rings. In the last lines both relationships flip. Heaney's father now follows the son, "keeps stumbling", and will not leave him; Halligan's speaker recognised myself.

Shared technique: A final turn that rewrites everything before it, and movement verbs that carry character: Heaney's "stumbled", "tripping, falling"; Halligan's jog, flipping right over, stopped.

Difference: Heaney's is a poem of family, inheritance and guilt, and its reversal is stated with certainty in the present tense. Halligan's creature is a stranger, and his reversal is hedged in the past tense (thought). Heaney's haunting figure cannot be shaken off; Halligan's self is left on a shelf, uncertain where to go.

4. Shakespeare, Sonnet 18 (14)

Link: The set's two sonnets about whether a comparison holds. Shakespeare proposes his in line 1, "Shall I compare thee to a summer's day?", and rejects it. Halligan never proposes his; it is forced on him in the last line.

Shared technique: Legal and financial diction: "summer's lease hath all too short a date", "that fair thou ow'st", against due payment. Time as damage: "every fair from fair sometime declines" against worsened over time.

Difference: The confidence of the form. Shakespeare turns cleanly at line 9 ("But thy eternal summer shall not fade") and ends on a clinching couplet, "So long lives this, and this gives life to thee." Halligan's line 9 is swallowed by an enjambment and his couplet never comes. Shakespeare promises the beloved will never "wander" in death's shade; Halligan's creature does nothing but wander. One sonnet claims power over time; the other claims only I don't know.

5. Boey, 'Report to Wordsworth' (05)

Link: Two sonnets that use creatures to measure what is wrong with people. In Boey, "insatiate man moves in for the kill", man as predator; in Halligan, a man finds himself as vermin.

Shared technique: The sonnet under pressure. Boey keeps the couplet but makes it apocalypse ("God is labouring to utter his last cry"); Halligan withholds it. Both give exact images of creaturely helplessness: Neptune "helpless as a beached whale", the roach flipping right over.

Difference: Boey's poem is public and addressed to a dead poet about a world laid waste; Halligan's has no addressee and stays in one room. Wordsworth's own sonnet on sonnets ('Nuns fret not') is a bridge: the form as a narrow room that comforts those who feel "the weight of too much liberty". Boey uses the room to mourn; Halligan's creature gets lost in it.

6. Brewster, 'Where I Come From' (04)

Link: Both read minds through places and their creatures. Brewster's farmyard has "hens and chickens" that "circle about, / clucking aimlessly", the same aimless circling as Halligan's crooked rings.

Shared technique: An inventory of plain particulars trusted to carry the mood: her farmhouses "in need of paint" and "battered schoolhouses"; his ball of dust and rusty table leg.

Difference: Brewster's aimlessness is affectionate, part of a remembered home that makes a self ("People are made of places"). Halligan's room is placeless, and the self it reveals arrives as a hedged glimpse, not an identity. Her poem ends as "A door in the mind blows open"; his creature never goes through the door.

7. Blake, 'The Chimney Sweeper' (03)

Link: Both depend on how an observer sees a small, dark figure. Blake's speaker first sees "A little black thing among the snow", a child reduced to a thing; Halligan's speaker sees an insect and makes it he. Blake's Songs of Experience also contains 'The Fly', whose speaker asks "Am not I / A fly like thee?", the closest ancestor of Halligan's ending.

Shared technique: A question at the poem's heart ("Where are thy father and mother, say?"; Was this due payment…?) and imagery of confinement.

Difference: Blake's irony indicts institutions, "God and his priest and king"; Halligan's has no culprit but, perhaps, the self.

8. Philips, 'A Married State' (11)

Link: Both read hidden unhappiness from outward signs. In Philips, wives' misery is something "in wifes Carefull faces you may spell"; Halligan spells restlessness from a cockroach's movements.

Shared technique: Rhymed pentameter arguing towards a closing joke.

Difference: Philips argues in confident heroic couplets and ends on a punchline that clinches ("There's no such thing as leading Apes in hell"). Halligan's punchline has no couplet and no certainty. She knows the cause of the lack of "ease" (marriage) and offers a remedy; he knows neither (I don't know).

Quick links to the rest of the set

Poem Link
Behn, 'Song: Love Armed' (01) An inner state given a body and watched in action (Love as a tyrant; restlessness in an insect); both speakers cast themselves as victims: "my poor Heart alone is harmed".
Bhatt, 'A Different History' (02) Gods "disguised as snakes or monkeys" and the idea of "a sin" against a book, against a soul perhaps reborn as vermin. Both turn on unanswered questions ("Which language / has not been the oppressor's tongue?"; I don't know), but Bhatt's history is collective, Halligan's private.
Clarke, 'Lament' (07) Creatures as casualties of human action, including "the restless wader", against a creature used as a mirror. Clarke's grief is certain and shared; Halligan's unease is hedged and private.
Lochhead, 'Storyteller' (09) A swept, scoured kitchen against an unswept room. Lochhead's stories, bat-like, "hung themselves upside down" in the children's heads, an upside-down creature that will fly again; Halligan's upended insect never uses its wings.
Mungoshi, 'Before the Sun' (10) A boy's purposeful morning ritual, sharing his maize with the sun as a companion, against a man's aimless solitary watch; both are poems of one small scene made to carry a whole state of being.
Rumens, 'Carpet-weavers, Morocco' (13) Repetitive work with a destination (the carpet will leave for a mosque floor) against repetitive motion with none; both make a pattern of movement carry an argument about time.

Lament

Gillian Clarke · 1991

A prayer with no god in it: eleven dedications beginning For mourn a war’s casualties without ranking them, until language itself joins the dead.

CONTEXT

Context

The world the poem came out of

The Poet: Gillian Clarke (born 1937)

Gillian Clarke was born in Cardiff on 8 June 1937. Like R. S. Thomas and Emyr Humphreys before her, and many Welsh children of the time, she had Welsh-speaking parentage but was brought up speaking English. Her father, a radio engineer, made sure her childhood was "steeped in Welsh culture if not in the language, which she learnt as an adult" (Diane Green, Rhizomes, 2007). Her grandmother's farm, Fforest, above a small bay near Fishguard in Pembrokeshire, gave her the shore, sea and seabirds that run through her poems; she now translates from Welsh, including the early war-elegy Y Gododdin (Faber), but writes her own poems in English.

After university in Cardiff she worked for a year for the BBC in London, then taught, edited The Anglo-Welsh Review (1975–84), moved to rural Ceredigion in the mid-1980s, and in 1990 co-founded Tŷ Newydd, the writers' centre in North Wales. She was National Poet of Wales from 2008 to 2016, received the Queen's Gold Medal for Poetry in 2010 and the Wilfred Owen Award in 2012. Her poems have been set for GCSE and A level for more than thirty years.

Two habits of hers matter for 'Lament'. She writes about distant public catastrophes from the reports that reach Wales: of 'Neighbours', her poem on the Chernobyl disaster of 1986, she says "Every detail in the poem is true, and taken from reports in the press and media". And she builds poems out of lists — of 'Letter from a Far Country' she says simply, "It's made of lists." Her open letter to students also says something the last line of 'Lament' depends on: "Language is not frozen. It's alive and it changes and grows with every generation of readers and writers and speakers." In 'Lament', it is war that turns it to ash.

Writing and publication, 1991–97

'Lament' answers the Gulf War of 1990–91, and Clarke says it was assembled from the news: "All the details in the poem came from reports in the media." Her notes list them: "newspaper photographs of cormorants covered with oil" (in his funeral silk); the stain on sand and sea; the burning oil that seemed to put out the sun and poisoned land and sea; the boy fusilier and the farmer's sons, which "came from hearing radio interviews with their mothers"; creatures "listed by Friends of the Earth as being at risk of destruction by oil pollution"; and "a horrific photograph of a soldier burnt when his tank was bombed".

The exact first printing is not certain. Clarke's next collection after the war was The King of Britain's Daughter (Carcanet, 1993), whose drafts date from 1990–91 (National Library of Wales), and 'Lament' was probably first collected there; it is certainly in her Collected Poems (Carcanet, 1997), and PoetryProf gives 1997 as its publication date, adding that it "had been several years in the writing, its inception going back to 1990/91". The war marks the 1993 book as a whole: its title sequence retells the Mabinogion story of Branwen, daughter of Llŷr, whose marriage to the King of Ireland ends in war between the two islands, and the critic Diane Green calls it "a poem about war and its causes", noting that the present-day war behind the myth, for Clarke, is the Gulf War. The poem is now best known from Cambridge's Songs of Ourselves anthology.

Clarke's own notes, and PoetryProf's text of the Cambridge selection, give For the soldier in his uniform of fire; some copies and study guides print "with his". In dresses the soldier in flame; "with" would issue fire to him like kit.

The Gulf War, 1990–91

On 2 August 1990 Iraq, under Saddam Hussein, invaded and occupied Kuwait after long-running disputes over territory and oil. A US-led coalition — "the United States, with Britain's help, bombed Iraq", as Clarke puts it — began its air campaign in mid-January 1991; a ground offensive launched on 24 February drove the Iraqi army out of Kuwait in days, and a ceasefire followed on 28 February. Clarke's notes add a sentence that explains why the poem names no year: "This war has never really stopped."

Closed borders were part of the story. When uprisings against Saddam were crushed in March and April 1991, Iraqi Kurds fled towards Turkey, which at first closed its frontier, leaving hundreds of thousands of people stranded in the mountains along it. Clarke does not say which border, or which Ahmed — the poem keeps him general.

It was a war most people in Britain met through television, newspapers and radio, and through military briefings. A few images broke through: the oiled seabirds, and the burnt bodies of soldiers. In March 1991 The Guardian published Tony Harrison's poem 'A Cold Coming', which begins from Kenneth Jarecke's notorious photograph of an Iraqi soldier incinerated in his vehicle at the war's end. Clarke names no photographer, and her soldier was "burnt when his tank was bombed", so her photograph may well have been another — but the poem belongs to the same moment, when poets were answering pictures that the language of the briefings could not hold.

Oil and fire: what the images record

The spill. At the end of January 1991 Iraqi forces released crude oil into the Gulf, chiefly from Kuwait's Sea Island oil terminal, apparently to hamper a US Marine landing; Iraq blamed American air strikes on its tankers. Early Pentagon figures were around 11 million barrels; later government studies put it at 4–6 million — still one of the largest oil spills in history. Tens of thousands of seabirds are thought to have died, grebes and cormorants above all, and years later oil still lay in the salt marshes and mudflats of the Saudi coast. Both sides used it as propaganda; Washington called it "environmental terrorism".

The fires. As they prepared to leave, Iraqi forces sabotaged Kuwait's oilfields and set fire to between 605 and 732 wells (estimates vary). The fires began in January and February 1991 and peaked as the ground war started; experts predicted they would burn for years, but the last well was capped on 6 November 1991. At their peak the smoke absorbed 75–80 per cent of the sun's radiation. Carl Sagan, who had predicted worse, later admitted that "it was pitch black at noon and temperatures dropped 4–6 °C over the Persian Gulf". So the veiled sun and the sun put out are close to plain report.

Clarke's own note attributes the veil of iridescence on the sand and the shadow on the sea to "the spreading stain of oil from bombed oil wells". Historically the slick at sea came mainly from the terminal and tankers, while the wells produced the smoke, burning oil lakes and burnt earth on land; the poem fuses them, as the news did.

The casualty list: creatures and people

Clarke's creatures, she says, were on a Friends of the Earth list of species at risk from oil pollution, and each is exact. Green turtles (endangered) often return to nest on the very beach where they hatched — hence the breeding ground, a single place. The hook-beaked turtles are hawksbills, named for their narrow, hooked beak and now critically endangered; later surveys suggested the Gulf's turtles came through the 1991 spill better than feared. The Gulf holds the world's second-largest population of dugongs, gentle grazing "sea cows".

The oiled cormorants that filled Western television were probably mostly Socotra cormorants, a threatened species found only in the Gulf and along the south-east coast of Arabia — a local bird, not a symbol. Terns, gulls and waders are birds of shore and passage, many of them long-distance migrants.

The people are exact too. "Fusilier" is not antique decoration: it is the private soldier's rank in British fusilier regiments, and the 3rd Battalion, Royal Regiment of Fusiliers, fought in the 1991 war. The boy and the farmer's sons come, by Clarke's account, from their own mothers' words on the radio.

Lament, elegy and litany

Clarke's definition: "'lament' is an elegy, an expression of grief. It can be a sad, military tune played on a bugle. The poem uses the title as the start of a list of lamented people, events, creatures and other things hurt in the war, so after the word 'lament', every verse, and 11 lines, begin with 'for'." An elegy usually reflects and works towards consolation; a lament is grief's cry, often sung and communal — and 'Lament' offers no consolation at all. The bugle sense points to the wordless military lament, the call played at soldiers' funerals and on Remembrance days.

Some of the oldest poetry in Welsh is lament. Y Gododdin, which Clarke has translated, is a sequence of elegies for warriors who fell at Catraeth, and many of its stanzas open with the same words ("Men went to Catraeth…"). The Canu Heledd poems, set in a woman's voice, mourn her brother Cynddylan and his destroyed hall, returning again and again to the same opening phrase. Repeated openings, and grief that widens from the dead to a whole ruined home: 'Lament' belongs to a very old line.

A litany (from Greek litaneia, "entreaty") is a prayer of petitions in a fixed, repeated form. Cranmer's English Litany of 1544, later part of the Book of Common Prayer, asks God to "preserve all that travel by land or by water, all women labouring of child, all sick persons, and young children; and to shew thy pity upon all prisoners and captives" — a roll-call of the vulnerable, as Clarke's is; church intercessions still often run "For the sick… For those who have died…". Clarke keeps the form and removes the addressee: there is no "Lord", no "hear us". Compare Gerard Manley Hopkins's 'Pied Beauty' (1877), a litany of praise — "Glory be to God for dappled things – / For skies of couple-colour…", ending with "all trades, their gear and tackle and trim". 'Lament' reads like its negative image: a list of creation spoiled, its trades now the gunsmith's and the armourer's.
