Lines with a marker have analysis — click one, or just scroll.

Title
Lament
Language & devices

Noun: Lament — one word, the name of a genre: a song or poem of grief. Clarke's own gloss adds that it "can be a sad, military tune played on a bugle". The word also means a complaint, so it protests as well as mourns.

Syntax: the title is grammatically unfinished. Every stanza opens with For, so the title becomes the first half of a phrase the poem keeps completing — Lament / For the green turtle… — the traditional title pattern of the genre ("Lament for…"). Ellipsis: no object, no possessive, no "I": nobody is named as the mourner.

Meaning & effect

Clarke names the act, not the occasion: no war, no date, no place, only grieving. Because the title heads every sentence that follows, the reader silently re-says "Lament" before each For and so takes part in the rite instead of watching it.

The missing object is the poem's first argument: so much has been lost that the title cannot say what, and the next twenty-one lines are the attempt to list it. The double sense, grief and complaint, sets the tone held to the end — mourning that is also an accusation, though it never raises its voice.

Line 1
For the green turtle with her pulsing burden,
Language & devices

Anaphora: the first For — the word of dedication used in prayers for the sick or the dead; it completes the title. Specific noun: green turtle names a real, endangered species, not "a turtle". Pronoun: her — a person's pronoun instead of "it" (accurate, not personification: a nesting turtle is female, but the choice dignifies her).

Transferred epithet: pulsing burden — the pulse belongs to the life inside her, but is given to the load itself. Pun: a burden is a weight and also the refrain of a song. Plosives: pulsing burden — /p/ and /b/, a heartbeat in the consonants.

Meaning & effect

The first casualty is not yet dead: she is alive, carrying life, and moving. Clarke begins at the most intimate scale — one creature, one body — and with the most hopeful act in nature, breeding, so that everything after reads as damage done to the future.

Pulsing makes the reader feel a heartbeat inside burden: the weight is precious and already a strain. The pun on burden quietly says what the poem itself will be — a song carried on a refrain, borne as the turtle bears her eggs.

Line 2
in search of the breeding ground.
Language & devices

Pattern break: the only line in the poem that begins with neither For nor the. Prepositional phrase: in search of — a noun of effort, with no verb and no arrival. Definite article: the breeding ground, not "a": green turtles often return to the very beach where they hatched, so there is one place and no substitute. End-stop: the full stop closes the sentence where the search cannot end.

Meaning & effect

The cruelty here is instinct in a ruined world: the turtle is built to go to one place, and that is the place that has been poisoned. Search admits that what instinct knew is no longer true — the ground cannot be found as it was.

The line is the shortest of the stanza (seven syllables, three stresses) and stops hard, so the reader meets the full stop as the turtle meets the end of her map. Fittingly, the one line that has lost the poem's opening pattern is the line about losing the way.

Line 3
For her eggs laid in their nest of sickness.
Language & devices

Anaphora: a second For inside the stanza — the eggs are mourned separately from their mother. Past participle: laid — the act is finished and cannot be undone. Possessive: their nest — the nest belongs to the eggs, the unborn.

Paradox: nest of sickness — the word for shelter and warmth bound by of to its opposite. Sibilance: eggs… nest… sickness hushes the stanza after the plosive beat of line 1. Hard end-stop.

Meaning & effect

The turtle has done what nature asks — the eggs are laid — and the place of safety has become the place of harm. Clarke does not say the eggs will die; she says where they lie, and lets nest of sickness do the predicting.

Giving the eggs their own For means the unborn are mourned as individuals before they exist: war's damage reaches into the next generation. The stanza ends on a falling, unstressed syllable — sick-ness — the sound of something failing.

Line 4
For the cormorant in his funeral silk,
Language & devices

Metaphor: funeral silk — the oil coating the bird's black feathers becomes mourning-dress. Connotation: silk is luxurious, smooth and glossy — exactly how oil looks on plumage, and grotesquely wrong for what it does. Pronoun: his — again the refusal of "it". Soft end-stop: the comma lets the image spread into the next two lines.

Meaning & effect

This is the war's most familiar image — the oiled seabird of the newspaper photographs Clarke worked from — and she makes it ceremonial: the bird is not merely dirty, he is already dressed for his own funeral, mourner and corpse at once.

The beauty of silk is the disturbing part: the poison is glossy, even handsome, and the line makes us see that something can look rich and be lethal. Choosing a cormorant, a bird few people love, extends the grief to the unloved.

Lines 5–6
the veil of iridescence on the sand, / the shadow on the sea.
Language & devices

Metaphor: the veil of iridescence on the sand — oil's rainbow film laid over the beach like a veil (the widow's veil, and the bride's). Lexis: iridescence — a precise, lovely word for oil's shimmer. Metaphor: the shadow on the sea — the slick as darkness on the water, with an echo of the biblical "shadow of death".

Apposition: two noun phrases added with no For and no verb, so the stain on sand and sea is listed as if it were a further victim. Sibilance: silk… iridescence… sand… shadow… sea. Hard end-stop.

Meaning & effect

The grief widens from the bird to his shore and then to his element: creature, beach, sea. Clarke mourns places as casualties — sand and sea get a line each, like the turtle and the eggs.

The veil continues the funeral (silk, then a veil), while iridescence again makes the damage beautiful to look at. The hissing consonants sound like something spreading and like a hush laid over the shore, and shadow ends the stanza in loss of light.

Line 7
For the ocean's lap with its mortal stain.
Language & devices

Polysemy: lap — the small sound of waves at the shore; a mother's lap; an animal lapping (the sea tonguing its own poison). Adjective: mortal — deadly, and also able to die; it sounds one letter away from "moral". Noun: stain — not a wound, which heals, but a mark that spreads, stays and implicates whoever made it.

Anaphora and Hard end-stop: this opens the only stanza in which every line both begins For and ends with a full stop.

Meaning & effect

The ocean is mourned as one victim among the rest, in a sentence the same shape as Ahmed's and the soldier's. The gentlest thing the sea does, lapping at the shore, and the most comforting human image, a lap, are both contaminated.

Mortal claims that the vast, seemingly endless sea can be killed, and the echo of "moral" turns pollution into guilt without anyone being accused. The line is the hinge from the natural world to the human one.

Line 8
For Ahmed at the closed border.
Language & devices

Proper noun: Ahmed — the only name in the poem and, apart from the line-opening Fors, its only capital letter. Synecdoche: one very common name stands for many people. Preposition: at — held at the border, not crossing it. Past participle: closed — someone closed it; no one is named.

Hard end-stop: eight syllables, the shortest human line; the two stresses of closed bor- shut it like a gate.

Meaning & effect

The first human in the poem is a civilian, not a soldier — a man stopped at a line someone drew on a map. Naming him gives him a person's dignity among the poem's types (the turtle, the soldier); the commonness of the name makes him every displaced person too.

He has no verb and no fate: he is simply at the border, waiting, and the reader waits with him. The stanza's sealed one-line sentences build the border into the form — each victim shut in a cell of syntax, unable to reach the next line.

Line 9
For the soldier in his uniform of fire.
Language & devices

Metaphor: uniform of fire — the soldier is clothed in flame, as uniforms are made of wool or cotton. Irony: a uniform should identify and protect its wearer; this one consumes him. Ambiguity: the soldier — no army, no side, no nationality. Hard end-stop.

Textual variant: Clarke's own notes quote in his uniform; some copies print "with his" (fire carried like kit, not worn).

Meaning & effect

Clarke's notes say this came from "a horrific photograph of a soldier burnt when his tank was bombed": the line turns that image into eight plain words. Fire replaces the uniform — what marks him as a soldier is what kills him — and the clothing motif (silk, veil) reaches a human body.

By not saying which side he fought for, Clarke makes the death simply a man's, mourned in the same sentence-shape as the ocean and Ahmed. In this stanza sea, civilian and combatant are equals.

Line 10
For the gunsmith and the armourer,
Language & devices

Anaphora: one For now covers two people — the list begins to double up. Lexis: gunsmith, armourer — old craft-words for those who make and maintain weapons. Parallelism: the gunsmith and the armourer — paired by and, each given his own the. Soft end-stop.

Meaning & effect

This is the poem's most surprising dedication: it mourns the makers of weapons alongside their victims. Clarke's grief refuses to sort people into innocent and guilty; those whose trade is war are also spent by it.

The old-fashioned words make the arms trade sound like a village craft, which keeps the men human — workers, not villains — while never letting us forget what they make.

Line 11
the boy fusilier who joined for the company,
Language & devices

Finite verb: joined is the only finite verb in the whole poem, and the boy its only agent — the one completed action in 'Lament' is a boy signing up. Juxtaposition: boy fusilier — a child set in front of a military title ("Fusilier" is the private's rank in British fusilier regiments).

Pun: the company — companionship, and a military company. Register: everyday idiom, left plain. The small for here means in exchange for, not dedicated to.

Meaning & effect

The line gives a reason for going to war, and it is tiny and human: he wanted friends. Clarke took such phrases from radio interviews with soldiers' mothers and left them unimproved — no "brave", no "tragic" — so the flatness carries the grief.

The pun turns the warm word cold behind the boy's back: he joined for company and was issued a Company. Setting a small for of motive beside the poem's great For of mourning prepares the double meaning of the last line.

Line 12
the farmer's sons, in it for the music.
Language & devices

Possessive: the farmer's sons — one farmer, several sons: one family's loss multiplied. Idiom: in it for the music — what you would say of someone joining a band; here the regimental band and the parade. Caesura: the comma after sons. Rhythm: in it for the — four unstressed syllables in a row, the flattest run in the poem, before music. Hard end-stop.

Meaning & effect

Like the boy, the farmer's sons went for something innocent — the music and show of soldiering. They come from the land, linking them to the poem's ruined earth, and the plural makes the loss a family's.

Clarke trusts the throwaway phrase to do the mourning: the lighter the reason, the heavier the cost. "The music" also hints at how war recruits — with bands and ceremony — which is why the poem refuses to be eloquent about these men.

Lines 13–14
For the hook-beaked turtles, / the dugong and the dolphin,
Language & devices

Plural: turtles — the single green turtle of line 1 has become many. Compound adjective: hook-beaked — the hawksbill turtle, named for its narrow, hooked beak; critically endangered. Lexis: dugong — the "sea cow", a gentle grazing mammal (the Gulf holds the world's second-largest population).

Alliteration: dugong and the dolphin — soft paired /d/. Asyndeton: creatures added by commas, with no chain of conjunctions.

Meaning & effect

The poem returns from people to sea-life, and the scale has grown: species now, not single animals. Clarke's choices are deliberately unglamorous — few readers could picture a dugong — so the grief is inclusive: every kind of life counts, known or unknown.

The dugong and the dolphin, paired by and exactly like the gunsmith and the armourer, gives sea-creatures the same grammar as the men four lines earlier.

Line 15
the whale struck dumb by the missile's thunder.
Language & devices

Idiom made literal: struck dumb — a phrase for shock made physical: the whale, which lives by sound, is silenced. Metaphor: the missile's thunder — nature's word for sky-noise now belongs to a weapon. Possessive: the missile owns the thunder; no one fires it.

Stress: whale struck dumb — three stressed syllables together, a cluster matched only by sun put out in line 19. Hard end-stop.

Meaning & effect

The largest creature in the list is silenced by the war's noise — the climax of a stanza that moves from small to large. A whale finds its way and its kind by sound, so struck dumb is a kind of death.

The image looks ahead to the last line: a voice destroyed by violence prepares for the ashes of language. And the stolen word thunder shows war taking over even nature's vocabulary.

Line 16
For the tern, the gull and the restless wader,
Language & devices

List: the tern, the gull and the restless wader — three birds in one line, the most crowded opening yet. Adjective: restless — the wader cannot settle, feed or rest on a fouled shore. Asyndeton with a final and.

Meaning & effect

The list is accelerating: line 1 gave one creature a whole line; line 16 fits three. The poem seems to be running out of room for everything it must mourn.

Restless is the key word: shorebirds that should wade and feed are kept moving, unable to stop on a shore that no longer supports them — a bird's version of Ahmed held at the border.

Line 17
the long migrations and the slow dying,
Language & devices

Parallelism: the long migrations and the slow dying — two adjective-noun pairs joined by and as if equal. Gerund: dying — a process, not a single event like "death". Long vowels: long… migrations… slow… dying stretch the line. Spondee: slow dy-.

Meaning & effect

Clarke sets one of nature's great achievements, migration over thousands of miles, against the death now waiting at its end. Slow dying is worse than death: oiled birds chill, starve or are poisoned over days.

The long vowels make the reader take the time the line describes. Migrations may also suggest people driven from their homes, though the poem leaves that unsaid.

Line 18
the veiled sun and the stink of anger.
Language & devices

Metaphor: the veiled sun — smoke from the burning wells drawn across the sun like a mourning veil (the veil of line 5, now in the sky). Synaesthesia: the stink of anger — an emotion given a smell. Register: stink, the lowest word in the poem, against elegiac veiled. Hard end-stop.

Meaning & effect

The mourning-veil has moved from the sand to the sun: the damage has reached the sky. Stink of anger fuses the real stench of burning oil with the rage that caused it, so the war's emotion becomes something you breathe.

The anger has no owner — no side, no leader — it simply hangs in the air like the smoke. And stink stops the poem becoming merely beautiful: this grief has a smell.

Lines 19–20
For the burnt earth and the sun put out, / the scalded ocean and the blazing well.
Language & devices

Imagery of the elements: earth (burnt earth), light (the sun put out), water (the scalded ocean), fire (the blazing well). Phrasal verb: put out — the casual words for snuffing a candle, used of the sun. Metaphor: scalded — burning on skin, applied to the sea.

Participles: burnt, scalded (done) against blazing (still going on). Stress: burnt earth… sun put out — five stresses in nine syllables, ending on three heavy monosyllables.

Meaning & effect

The last stanza widens the lament to the world's elements: earth, sun, sea and the fire itself. Clarke's own notes say the burning oil seemed to put out the sun, so the line is both apocalypse and plain report — the war has made an ancient image of the world's end literally true.

Put out makes the destruction horribly easy, a flick of the hand. The blazing well is the poem's nearest approach to naming oil, the fuel of the war and of the fire — and even here oil is not named.

Line 21
For vengeance, and the ashes of language.
Language & devices

Anaphora: the final For — like line 3, a one-line sentence closing its stanza, so the poem ends in the shape it began. Abstract nouns: vengeance, language — after creatures and elements, ideas. Ambiguity: For vengeance — dedication (vengeance mourned) or motive (all this done for vengeance).

Punctuation: vengeance, and — the only comma before and in the poem, a pause before the last name. Metaphor: the ashes of language. Dying fall: three stresses, a falling ending (lan-guage), then the full stop.

Meaning & effect

The last things mourned are not victims but what drove the war and what it left: vengeance, and language burnt like the wells. Clarke's gloss is "The ashes of language are the death of truth during war" — lies, propaganda and euphemism have reduced words to ash.

For vengeance can be heard as grief and as accusation, so the poem's only hint of a cause is folded into its rite. It ends by mourning the means of mourning; what survives is the bare act of naming, and then the full stop.

THE WHOLE POEM

The Whole Poem

Stepping back: what the poem is doing, first line to last

'Lament' is usually described as a sad catalogue: a list of the Gulf War's victims, human and animal, delivered with mounting grief. That description is accurate about the contents and wrong about the poem, because it misses what the poem withholds. The argument here: 'Lament' is built on a double refusal — it refuses to assert, and it refuses to accuse — and its power comes from performing, in grammar and ceremony, the only kind of speech it believes survives a war: naming without saying. The poem does not describe the death of honest language; it writes as if from inside it, and the form is the demonstration.

Start with what reading the poem actually feels like, line 1 to line 21. The title gives a genre-noun and stops. Then "For the green turtle" — and the ear understands at once that the title has not ended: Lament for. Every subsequent sentence re-attaches to that governing word, which means the reader is made to re-say "Lament" silently eleven times — the poem conscripts its reader into performing the rite, not observing it. This is the first sense in which the anaphora is the poem: it is not emphasis, it is liturgy, the structure of a litany of intercession — "For the sick… for the dying…" — in which a congregation offers up names. And a litany implies a hearer. The poem never names one. Prayers are said, in perfect order, into what may be an empty sky: that suspension — rite intact, addressee gone — is the poem's religious temperature, and one measure of what the war has burnt.

The sequence of the named is exact and means something. Two stanzas of sea-life first — turtle, eggs, cormorant, sand, sea — so that when the humans arrive in stanza 3 they arrive into a world already dying, not the other way round. Human suffering is not the context for environmental damage; environmental damage is the context for human suffering. Stanza 3 sets ocean, refugee and soldier as three grammatically identical, one-line, full-stopped sentences — the poem's strongest formal statement of its flattest claim: there is no hierarchy of grief here, a sea and a man take the same syntax. Ahmed, the only named being in the poem, stands at its threshold moment: the first human is not a combatant but a man stopped at a line someone drew. Then stanza 4, the poem's centre, does the hardest thing in it: it mourns the war's makers — gunsmith, armourer, fusilier, farmer's sons — in the same breath as its victims, because by the poem's logic they are its victims. After that the circle widens back out through species (stanza 5), flyways and atmosphere (stanza 6), to the elements themselves (stanza 7): earth, light, water, fire — creation's inventory, each item cancelled — and last of all the medium in which inventories are made: language.

Now the obvious objection, which any strong reading must meet head-on: a poem that ends by declaring language ash is self-refuting. Here is a poem — shapely, eloquent, anthologised, taught — whose final claim its own existence appears to disprove. If language were really ashes, 'Lament' could not have been written. The objection dissolves once you look at which language the poem has renounced. Go through all twenty-one lines looking for a statement — a main clause, something asserted of something — and you will not find one. The poem is eleven sentences with no predication in them: it never says the war is wrong, never says the turtle died, never says who set the fires. It has given up the assertive functions of language — the functions that reportage, propaganda, communiqués and euphemism share, the grammar in which a bombardment can be called a "surgical strike" — because in war those functions are the first corrupted. Clarke's own gloss is exact: "the ashes of language are the death of truth during war." What survives the fire is smaller and older: the capacity to name, and to set a name inside the dative of care — for. The poem is not self-refuting; it is self-exemplifying. It ends by mourning the language of saying in the only language left, the language of dedication.

The same withholding governs agency, and this is where the poem is most contestable. Its single finite verb is "joined"; its single agent is a boy; every act of destruction arrives as an agentless participle — closed, struck, veiled, burnt, put out, scalded (the one participle with a known doer, "laid", is the turtle's own act of creation). Nobody in 'Lament' does anything except enlist. One reading calls this the poem's deepest evenhandedness: grief refuses to become prosecution; at a funeral you do not read out the charge sheet. The other reading calls it evasion: the Gulf oil spill was not weather — it was a deliberate act, ordered by identifiable men, and a poem that mourns "the blazing well" without an arsonist converts a war crime into something like climate, to be grieved rather than judged. The defence, and it is a strong one, is that the poem does name the motive even as it withholds the men: "For vengeance". The last line files the accusation in the only grammar the poem allows itself — vengeance is not said to have caused anything (no clause could say so); it is simply set on the list, mourned-and-indicted in one word, the human faculty whose exercise fills the previous twenty lines. The charge is there; it has been folded into the rite.

And the rite itself is the answer to the poem's other great pressure: scale. A war's damage is uncountable, and the poem knows it — you can watch it running out of room, two griefs per stanza at the start, seven crammed into stanza 6, the singulars giving way to plurals — and a lesser poem would have answered scale with excess: piled adjectives, raised voice. Clarke answers it with ceremony and with terrible smallness of speech: "who joined for the company", "in it for the music" — the recruits' own idiom, or their mothers', lifted from radio interviews and left unimproved. The poem's tonal control is nowhere more severe: it will not translate a mother's flat phrase into poetry, because the flatness is the truth of it, and any eloquence added would be the first step back towards the language that ends in ashes. This is why calling the poem "sad" misses it. Sadness is an emotion the poem induces; the poem itself is doing something harder — holding grief, accusation, and a working ritual in a single unbroken posture, twenty-one lines at attention.

So the movement first line to last is best described not as a list but as a widening and a turning-inward at once: the circle of the mourned expands from one turtle to the four elements, while the poem's attention closes in on its own medium, until the two arrive together at the final line — the largest circle (everything, even abstraction) and the innermost point (the words this is written in). "For vengeance, and the ashes of language." — with the poem's one comma-before-"and", the drawn breath before the last name at a memorial, and then the full stop, after which there are no more words to be said. The lament ends because its medium has joined its subjects. What remains standing is the shape of the rite itself — seven equal stanzas, eleven dedications, order held all the way down — which is the poem's real, unstated claim: when truth has burnt, form is how grief keeps faith.

FORM & STRUCTURE

Form & Structure

How the poem is built, and why it matters

Form & genre

A free-verse lament shaped as a litany: 21 lines in seven unrhymed tercets. The whole poem is a list of dedications completing its one-word title — Lament / For….

Stanzas

Seven equal three-line units: sea-life (1–2); ocean, civilian and soldier as equals (3); the war's makers and recruits at the centre (4); sea-life again (5); birds and sky (6); the elements, vengeance and language (7).

Syntax

Eleven sentences, every one beginning For. No main clause anywhere, and only one finite verb: joined (line 11), at the poem's exact centre.

Metre

No fixed metre. Lines run from 6 to 12 syllables, mostly with three to five stresses; local effects carry the weight — the triple stress of whale struck dumb, the falling endings of five of the seven stanzas.

Rhyme

None. The chime rhyme would give is replaced by the tolling For; five lines end on the same weak -er syllable (border, armourer, thunder, wader, anger) — an unrhymed, dying echo.

Lineation & turns

Every line is end-stopped: eleven full stops, ten commas, no enjambment. Turns at line 7–8 (from the natural world to people) and at line 21 (from the world to the word).

The governing grammar: a title with no sentence attached

The title is not a label but the poem's grammatical head. Every stanza — in fact every sentence — completes the phrase "Lament / For…": Lament for the green turtle. Lament for Ahmed. Lament for vengeance. This is the traditional naming pattern of the genre (Dunbar's 'Lament for the Makaris', Lorca's Lament for Ignacio Sánchez Mejías), broken open: Clarke stops the title after its first word, so that the poem's whole body becomes the title's unfinished second half. Twenty-one lines try to complete the phrase "Lament for—", and none of them closes it.

The consequence is stark and easy to miss: the poem contains no main clause. It is eleven sentences long, and every sentence is a prepositional phrase — a dedication, not a statement. The eleven full stops fall after lines 2, 3, 6, 7, 8, 9, 12, 15, 18, 20 and 21, and each of the eleven sentences they close begins with For. Nothing in the poem is asserted; nothing is said about anything. The poem cannot say "war destroys" or "grief is unbearable", because assertion — the grammar of reportage and propaganda alike — is exactly what the last line declares burnt. What survives of language is the gesture of dedication: pointing grief at its objects, one by one.

Within this grammar there is exactly one finite verb: the boy fusilier who joined for the company (line 11). Every other verb-form is a participle. One of them, laid, has a known doer — the turtle, in the poem's single act of creation. All the acts of destruction arrive without one: closed, struck, veiled, burnt, put out, scalded — things done to the world by no named doer. No Saddam, no Bush, no army performs an action anywhere in the poem; even the missile appears only as a possessive, the missile's thunder. The one completed act in 'Lament', and its one grammatical agent, is a boy joining up in innocence. That is the poem's ethics compressed into syntax: agency belongs to the naive, damage arrives agentless — either a profound even-handedness or a deliberate refusal to prosecute, and the tension between those two readings runs through the whole poem.

The anaphora, mapped exactly

Eleven of the twenty-one lines begin For — Clarke's own count ("every verse, and 11 lines, begin with 'for'"). The distribution is uneven, and the unevenness is the argument:

Stanza Lines Lines beginning For Pattern
1 1–3 1, 3 two of three
2 4–6 4 opening line only
3 7–9 7, 8, 9 all three
4 10–12 10 opening line only
5 13–15 13 opening line only
6 16–18 16 opening line only
7 19–21 19, 21 two of three, including the last line

So the shape is 2 – 1 – 3 – 1 – 1 – 1 – 2. Three observations follow.

  • Every stanza restarts from the title. Whatever else varies, each tercet's first word re-sounds "Lament for—", so the reader silently supplies the title eleven times. The anaphora is not "repetition for emphasis"; it is the mechanism by which a one-word title governs a twenty-one-line poem.
  • The density peaks at stanza 3 — the pivot from nature to people. Ocean, man at the border, soldier: the only stanza in which every line begins For is also the only stanza in which every line ends with a full stop. Three self-contained, walled sentences: For the ocean's lap with its mortal stain. / For Ahmed at the closed border. / For the soldier in his uniform of fire. The stanza about a closed border is built of closed lines — each victim sealed in a grammatical cell, unable to reach the next line. Form performs border.
  • The frame: stanzas 1 and 7 have the same sentence-architecture. Each is a two-line For sentence followed by a one-line For sentence (lines 1–2 + 3; lines 19–20 + 21). The poem ends in the posture it began with — ritual returning to its opening shape — except that the opening's one-line sentence held eggs in a nest, and the closing one holds vengeance and ash. Only three stanzas end on a For line: 1, 3 and 7 — the frame and the pivot. Everywhere else the formula launches a stanza and lower-case lines absorb it.

Where the anaphora does not hold, the exceptions are pointed. Nine lines begin with the — continuations, each victim still definite, still known. One line begins with neither: in search of the breeding ground. (line 2). The line about searching is the only one that escapes the formula — syntax slipping off-pattern exactly where the turtle loses her map.

Finally, the two lower-case fors: joined for the company; in it for the music. The word that consecrates each victim reappears, small, inside the small print of motive — for meaning "in exchange for", "for the sake of". The elegy's word of dedication and the recruit's word of transaction are one word. That collision returns in the last line, where For vengeance can be read with either grammar — dedication or motive — and the poem needs both (see Difficult Moments).

Metre: scansion and what the substitutions do

Free verse, but with strong local shapes. Stressed syllables are in bold; the notation marks x (unstressed) and / (stressed).

Line Scansion What it does
1 For the green turtle with her pulsing burden, x x / / x x x / x / x A lift into the double stress green tur-, then two falling feet, pulsing burden, ending on an unstressed syllable: dedication, then weight.
2 in search of the breeding ground. x / x x / x / The shortest line of the stanza, three stresses, closing on a stressed monosyllable and a full stop: the search hitting its wall.
3 For her eggs laid in their nest of sickness. x x / / x x / x / x The spondee eggs laid sets the weight down as the eggs are; the stanza then sags to a falling ending, sickness — its last sound a syllable failing.
8 For Ahmed at the closed border. x / x x x / / x Eight syllables, the shortest human line; the name takes the first stress, the spondee closed bor- shuts the line like the border it names.
11 the boy fusilier who joined for the company, x / x x / x / x x / x x A loose, ambling four-stress line with a trailing ending — conversational, someone talking, not intoning. The poem's only finite verb takes an ordinary stress and no more: a boy's ordinary decision.
12 the farmer's sons, in it for the music. x / x / x x x x / x After the caesura, four unstressed syllables in a row (in it for the) — the flattest run in the poem — before music lands. Throwaway idiom scored as throwaway rhythm.
15 the whale struck dumb by the missile's thunder. x / / / x x / x / x Three stresses together, whale struck dumb — matched only by line 19's sun put out — then the falling fallout of missile's thunder. The line does to the voice what the blast does to the whale.
17 the long migrations and the slow dying, x / x / x x x / / x The stresses fall on the two adjectives of duration, and the spondee slow dy- drags; with the long vowels, the line takes longer to say than its syllables suggest — dying made durational.
19 For the burnt earth and the sun put out, x x / / x x / / / Five stresses in nine syllables, the densest line in the poem, ending on three hammered monosyllables: no unstressed syllable survives the line's end.
21 For vengeance, and the ashes of language. x / x x x / x x / x After line 19's pile-up, only three stresses: the mid-line pause, then a long subsiding curve to a falling ending — the poem's dying fall.

Five of the seven stanzas end on an unstressed syllable — sickness, music, thunder, anger, language — so the dying fall is the poem's structural signature. The two that end on a stress are the elemental ones: the sea., of fire.

End-stopping: hard and soft

Every one of the 21 lines is end-stopped — ten with commas, eleven with full stops; there is not a single enjambment. The two kinds of stop do different work. Hard end-stops (full stops) bring finality: each death is sealed, each victim treated as its own separate loss rather than blurred into the next, and the reader is halted and made to take it in before moving on. Soft end-stops (commas) bring accumulation: victims linked within a stanza, grief rolling forward, the listing effect that overwhelms. The interplay is a push and pull — continuous sorrow, interrupted by sharp and final pain — which is a precise description of the rhythm of mourning.

The alternation is distributed, not decorative: stanza 3 is all hard (the border); stanzas 5 and 6 are led by commas (the crowding lists); and the final line is hard — no more words to be said after language's ashes. And the absence of enjambment is itself a claim. Enjambment is syntax surviving the line-break — continuation, spill-over, life running past the end of the form. Clarke forbids it for twenty-one lines. Nothing here survives its line.

Stanza logic: the arch

The sequence is exact: sea creatures (stanzas 1–2) → the pivot where ocean, civilian and soldier stand as equals (3) → the makers and recruits of war at the exact centre (4) → sea creatures again (5) → birds and atmosphere (6) → the elements and the abstractions (7). The human matter is embedded in stanzas 3–4, walled in by the animal world on both sides — humanity surrounded by the nature it is burning. The poem's numerical centre, line 11 of 21, is the boy fusilier: the only finite verb, the only agent, at the midpoint.

The griefs also multiply as the poem goes on — roughly two in the first stanza, three in each of the next two, four in stanzas 4 and 5, seven crammed into stanza 6, six in the last — as if there is not enough time or space to lament everything the war has damaged. One item per line holds for the first three stanzas; from line 10 (the gunsmith and the armourer) lines begin to carry two or three.

The turns, then, are two: at lines 7–8, where the lament crosses from the sea to people and the first human arrives — the only being in the poem to bear a name; and at line 21, where the lament turns from the world to the word, from the casualties of war to the casualty that is the capacity to speak of them. Between those turns the poem does not develop an argument; it widens a circle — individual, species, element, meaning — until nothing stands outside it.

SOUND

Sound

What the poem does to the ear

The tolling word

For — a long, open vowel struck eleven times at the head of eleven sentences: a bell, a drumbeat, a held note.

Hush and hiss

Sibilance dominates stanzas 1–2: sickness, then silk… iridescence… sand… shadow… sea — the sound of something spreading, and of a shore being silenced.

Percussion

Hard /k/ and /d/ in stanza 5 — hook-beaked, dugong, dolphin, struck dumb — build the blast before thunder names it.

Dying fall

Long vowels slow stanza 6; the last line drops to three stresses and a falling ending, lan-guage, then silence.

The tolled vowel. Read aloud, the anaphora is a sound before it is a device: For is a long, open back vowel — the vowel of mourn and forlorn, and of the keening "aw" of a cry — struck eleven times at the head of eleven sentences. It works like a soft drumbeat, the steady beat of a funeral march; and unlike a drumbeat it is pitched — a held, singable note, the bugle's note in Clarke's own gloss of a lament as "a sad, military tune played on a bugle". The word tolls, and each toll opens a breath that the rest of the line spends.

Stanza 1: plosives fading into sibilance. The opening line beats with /p/ and /b/ — pulsing burden, breeding ground — the lip-consonants that come closest to a heartbeat. Then sibilance rises through pulsing and search to saturate line 3, her eggs laid in their nest of sickness. The move from plosive to sibilant mimics a heartbeat slowly fading: the life of line 1 hushed into the sickness of line 3. The stanza's sound-plot is its story.

Stanza 2: the hiss laid over everything. Silk… iridescence… sand… shadow… sea — the densest sibilance in the poem. Two effects at once, and a strong reading holds both: the hiss of something spreading (oil moving where it was never invited), and a hush — the sound of quieting, a finger to the lips, as the slick smothers birdsong and wave-noise alike. The stanza about a veil is voiced as a whisper; the sea's soundscape is being turned down.

Stanza 5: consonants as ordnance. The guttural /k/ of hook-beaked and struck, the drumming /d/ of dugong and the dolphin… struck dumb, and the thudding short u of struck dumb build the stanza's percussion before thunder names it. The triple stress of whale struck dumb lands inside this consonant-field: sound and stress detonate together, and the softest creatures in the poem — dugong, dolphin — carry its hardest consonants, as if the blast has entered their names.

Stanza 6: keening, then stench. The long migrations and the slow dying is built almost entirely of long vowels and diphthongs — the mouth cannot say it quickly; it is the poem's line of pure keening, sung grief. Then the register snaps: the stink of anger — short vowel, ugly /k/, a word from the gutter, not the elegy. The collision is deliberate: mourning's long vowels belong to lament, but what hangs in the air over the Gulf is not song, it is smell, and the line lets the war's actual atmosphere interrupt the genre's music. (The synaesthesia is analysed under Close Analysis.)

Paired phrases, swinging. From stanza 4 onwards and binds matched phrases — the gunsmith and the armourer, the dugong and the dolphin, the veiled sun and the stink of anger, the scalded ocean and the blazing well — so the litany swings in two-beat units, like call and response. Meanwhile five lines die away on the same weak -er syllable (border, armourer, thunder, wader, anger): no rhyme, but a muted echo running under the list.

The last line's diminuendo. After line 19's nine syllables carrying five stresses (burnt earth… sun put out) and line 20's paired stresses (scalded… blazing), line 21 drops to three stresses spread over ten syllables, with a falling ending: of language. fading away. Its one comma before and — the only one in the poem — is a drawn breath before the final name. The poem does not end with a burst of grief but with sound itself subsiding: a decrescendo into the full stop, the acoustic equivalent of ash after fire.

MOTIFS & SYMBOLS

Motifs & Symbols

Images that recur, and what they accumulate

Distinction, then the tracing: a motif recurs and accumulates; a symbol stands for something beyond itself. 'Lament' runs at least four motifs through its 21 lines — and behind all of them stands one governing symbol that the poem never names.

1. Fabric — silk, veil, uniform, shroud. The cloth motif enters at line 4 ("the cormorant in his funeral silk"), where oil is mourning-dress: the bird wears his own funeral. It spreads in line 5 to the land ("the veil of iridescence on the sand") — the veil, Victorian mourning-wear and bridal wear at once, laid over the beach. At line 9 it becomes human and lethal: the soldier's "uniform of fire" — the garment that should identify and protect him is the thing consuming him. And at line 18 the motif reaches the sky: "the veiled sun" — the same veil, now planetary, the oil-smoke drawing mourning-cloth across the one light everything lives by. Trace the scale: one bird's plumage → a beach → a man's body → the sun. The fabric motif measures the disaster's expansion, and it carries a constant irony: everything the war dresses, it dresses for a funeral.

2. Voice, sound and silence. The poem's second motif is acoustic, and it runs straight into the final line. The ocean has a voice — its "lap" (line 7), the smallest, most domestic water-sound. Music is a motive — the farmer's sons "in it for the music" (line 12), the regimental band, sound as war's false promise. Then sound becomes a weapon: "the whale struck dumb by the missile's thunder" (line 15) — the ocean's great singer silenced, and note the theft: "thunder", nature's own noise, is now the missile's possession; the war borrows nature's vocabulary to destroy nature's voices. By line 18 even the senses are scrambled — anger arrives as a "stink", emotion displaced into the wrong sense, as if the normal channels of expression are already down. And at line 21 the motif completes: "the ashes of language". Song promised, song silenced, speech burnt: the poem tracks the war's assault on every register of utterance, and ends by adding itself to the casualty list.

3. Fire and its residue. Fire enters on a single body — the "uniform of fire" (line 9) — and then runs the scale of stanza 7: "burnt earth", the sun "put out" (fire extinguished — the counter-image), "scalded ocean", "blazing well" (lines 19–20). Watch the grammar of the motif: blazing is a present participle — ongoing, unfinished — while burnt and scalded are past participles, damage already done; the stanza holds both tenses of catastrophe at once, still-happening and irreversible. Then the last line delivers fire's aftermath-noun: "ashes" (line 21). The motif's trajectory is combustion → residue; the poem ends after the fire, in what fire leaves. Against it runs water — lap, ocean, sea — until the two elements collapse into each other in "scalded ocean": the burn of boiling liquid done to the sea itself — water, the element that puts fire out, is now the thing burnt.

4. Motherhood and birth. The poem opens inside a reproductive emergency: "her pulsing burden… the breeding ground… her eggs… nest" (lines 1–3) — an entire vocabulary of birth, every term poisoned by its context ("nest of sickness"). It recurs in "the ocean's lap" (line 7), the mother's lap made mortal; in "the boy… the farmer's sons" (lines 11–12), where every soldier is implicitly somebody's child — and Clarke's sources here were literally the mothers, interviewed on radio; and in "the long migrations" (line 17), the journeys creatures make in order to breed. The motif inverts the elegy's usual consolation: laments traditionally set death against continuing life; here the continuing — eggs, nests, sons, migrations — is precisely what is being killed. War is figured throughout not as combat but as an attack on generation itself.

The governing symbol: oil, never named. Every motif above is oil seen without its name: the silk is oil, the veil is oil, the iridescence, the shadow, the stain, the scald, the blaze, the smoke that veils the sun — one substance behind a dozen appearances, and the word "oil" appears nowhere in the poem. This absence is the poem's most elegant structural fact. Oil is simultaneously the war's cause (the invasion grew out of disputes over oil and territory), its weapon (spilled and set alight), and its shroud (coating bird, beach and sky) — and Clarke treats it the way the poem treats every perpetrator: present everywhere, named never. It is a symbol in the strict sense — it stands for the whole system of greed and consequence the poem indicts — and its namelessness enacts the indictment: some things are too much the medium of the disaster to be seen as objects in it. Secondary symbols work inside its field: the sun (life-source, creation's first light) "put out"; the border (the human world's insistence on division, upheld even as the poison ignores it); ashes (what remains when meaning has been through fire).

THEMES

Themes

The ideas the poem is arguing about

01

War against the living world

Clarke's own summary is that "war can't be waged without grave damage to every aspect of life", and the poem argues it through order rather than statement. The first six lines belong to sea-creatures and their shore — turtle, eggs, cormorant, sand, sea — so when people arrive in stanza 3 they arrive in a world already dying; creatures (stanzas 5–6) and the elements (stanza 7) then close round the human stanzas from the other side. Human suffering becomes one episode inside an ecological catastrophe, not the other way round.

The detail insists the damage is to life itself, not to scenery: a pulsing burden, eggs in a nest of sickness, long migrations ending in slow dying, a whale struck dumb. The last stanza reaches the elements — burnt earth, the sun put out, the scalded ocean — so the casualty list ends with the conditions of life.

02

Grief without a hierarchy

'Lament' refuses to rank its dead. Stanza 3 gives the ocean, a man at a closed border and a soldier three identical one-line sentences: For the ocean's lap…, For Ahmed…, For the soldier…. Animals are given persons' pronouns (her, his), the soldier is given no side, and stanza 4 mourns the gunsmith and the armourer, the makers of weapons, in the same breath as their victims.

The equality is the poem's ethics: at a funeral nobody reads out a charge sheet. It is also a challenge to a reader used to sorting war's dead into ours and theirs, innocent and guilty, human and animal. One grammar for all of them — For… — makes every casualty count once, and count the same.

03

Generation and the poisoned future

The poem opens inside a mother's emergency — her pulsing burden… the breeding ground… her eggs — and keeps returning to birth and children: the ocean's lap, the boy fusilier, the farmer's sons, the long migrations that creatures make in order to breed. Clarke's sources for the soldiers were their mothers, speaking on the radio.

What war destroys, on this reading, is continuance: not only lives but the lives to come — eggs, sons, breeding grounds. Laments traditionally set death against life that goes on; here the going-on is what is being killed, which is why the poem offers no consolation.

04

The ashes of language: truth in wartime

Clarke glosses the last line herself: "The ashes of language are the death of truth during war" — propaganda, censorship and euphemism, a war fought with briefings as well as bombs. The poem's method answers that corruption. It is built from the reports that got through — photographs, mothers' words — and it asserts nothing: it has no main clause, only names set after For.

The theme runs through the poem's sounds as well: the whale struck dumb, thunder taken over by a missile, anger reduced to a stink. By putting language itself on the casualty list, Clarke implies that the last thing war destroys is our ability to tell the truth about it — and her plain naming is an attempt to keep that ability alive.

05

Vengeance and the missing culprit

Nobody in 'Lament' does anything except the boy who joined. The only other participle with a known doer is laid — the turtle's act of creation; every act of destruction arrives without one: closed, struck, veiled, burnt, put out, scalded. Oil, the war's cause and weapon, is never named. The poem can look as if it refuses to blame.

But blame is there, held down. The stink of anger hangs over stanza 6, and the last line puts vengeance on the list — mourned, by the grammar, but also, if For is heard as because of, named as the motive for everything before it. Because the anger is never shouted, the reader has to supply it, and the accusation lands harder.

06

Ritual against chaos

Faced with destruction beyond counting, Clarke answers with order: seven equal tercets, every line end-stopped, eleven sentences each beginning For. This is the shape of a litany, in which names are offered up one at a time, and of the old Welsh laments with their repeated openings. The ritual lets grief be specific and endless at once: each For gives one victim full attention, and the formula can go on for as long as there is something left to mourn.

Yet the rite has no addressee — no God, no "hear us" — and by the end its medium, language, is itself in ashes. What survives is the shape of the rite, held to the last full stop: grief keeping faith through form when nothing else can be trusted.

DIFFICULT MOMENTS

Difficult Moments

Where the poem is genuinely undecidable — and what to do about it

Cruxes

1. "For vengeance, and the ashes of language." — what is "For" doing in its own last line?

The difficulty. For twenty lines "For" has meant one thing: this lament is offered for — the dative of dedication. But English "for" has a second grammar, the grammar of motive and exchange ("for the sake of", "in return for"), and the poem has already used it twice, lowercase: "joined for the company", "in it for the music". When line 21 opens "For vengeance", both grammars are live. Reading A (dedication): vengeance is the last item mourned — the human faculty itself a casualty, pitied like the turtle; war has even ruined our anger. Reading B (motive): the line flickers into explanation — for vengeance all this happened; vengeance is not mourned but blamed, the war's cause smuggled onto its casualty list. Evidence for A: strict parallelism — every previous "For" is dative, and ritual repetition trains the reader to hear the eleventh as the first ten. Evidence for B: the two lowercase "for"s have already taught the motive-grammar inside this very poem; and "vengeance" is unlike every other item — not a creature or thing that can suffer, but an agent's reason. What a strong answer does: refuses to pick. The whole tragedy of the line is that in war the language of tribute and the language of transaction are the same word — the poem's formula of consecration is forced, at the last moment, to hold the war's motive inside it. Grief and accusation collapse into one preposition, and then the second half of the line tells you why no cleaner sentence was available: the language you would need for it is ash. Note also the comma — "vengeance, and the ashes" — the poem's only comma-before-"and": either a solemn pause before the final name, or the hinge of consequence (vengeance — and [therefore] ashes). Both, again.

2. "who joined for the company, / the farmer's sons, in it for the music." — is the flatness callous, tender, or ironic?

The difficulty. These are the poem's dead (or doomed) young men, and the poem describes their deaths' meaning in the language of a hobby: in it for the music, the idiom you would use of someone joining a pub band. Careless readers go two wrong ways: sentimental (the poem weeps over innocent boys) or ironic-superior (the poem mocks their naivety — they died for a band). The evidence cuts against both. Against mockery: Clarke sourced these phrases from radio interviews with the soldiers' mothers — the register is borrowed bereavement-speech, the way the families themselves talked, and the metre keeps it conversational (see the scansion of lines 11–12: the flattest stress-runs in the poem). A poem does not sneer in its sources' own words. Against sentiment: the lines refuse every available upgrade — no "brave", no "tragic", no elegiac vocabulary at all; the poem will not translate the mothers' flatness into poetry. What a strong answer does: names the technique — free indirect register, the vernacular of the bereaved incorporated unimproved — and reads the restraint as the poem's ethics in miniature. Understatement is the only register the poem trusts not to lie; eloquence about these boys would be recruitment's language ("the music" — the band, the parade — was the eloquence that got them killed). Add the pun the line quietly detonates: "the company" is companionship and a military unit — he joined for company and was issued a Company; the two meanings of the word are the two halves of his story, promise and machine. The flat register is where Clarke's power sits: the poem trusts the reader to supply the grief it declines to perform.

3. "For Ahmed at the closed border." — does the name individuate or tokenise?

The difficulty. Ahmed is the poem's only named being — turtle, cormorant, soldier, sons are all types with definite articles — and he is named with one of the commonest male names in the Arabic-speaking world. Reading A: the name is the poem's single act of full human recognition — everyone else is "the X", but a refugee is a person, with the kind of name that implies a family, a history, a face; his one line is the poem's moment of maximal dignity. Reading B (the uncomfortable one): a single, generic Arabic name — the Western newsroom's everyman-Arab — risks re-performing the anonymisation it protests; "Ahmed" as a name is close to "the refugee" as a category, and the poem gives him no verb, no face, no fate. Evidence for A: the capitalised name visibly breaks the definite-article system (it is the only capitalised word inside lines apart from the "For"s); his placement at the first human moment makes the civilian, not the soldier, the war's representative man. Evidence for B: the name's very commonness; the single line; the sourcing of the whole poem from Western media, which is where Clarke would have met him. What a strong answer does: holds the doubleness as the point — the name is deliberately both singular and countless; Clarke needs one man you could greet and a name ten thousand men answer to, because metonymy is the poem's entire method (one turtle for a species, one Ahmed for a displacement). Then it reads the line's form: hemmed in by full-stopped lines in the poem's only all-hard-stopped stanza, "at" (not "crossing", not "turned back from") holding him in arrested motion — the grammar builds the border it mourns, and the reader is left, like Ahmed, unable to get past the line's end.

4. "the sun put out" — hyperbole, or reportage?

The difficulty. Extinguishing the sun is the oldest apocalyptic hyperbole in the book — and in Kuwait in 1991 it happened: the smoke of six hundred burning wells turned midday dark ("pitch black at noon", as Carl Sagan later put it). So is line 19 the poem's most extreme figure or its most literal fact? Reading A (cosmic): the poem has left reportage for eschatology — un-creation, "Let there be light" reversed; the domestic phrasal verb "put out" (a candle, a lamp, a light at bedtime) makes the end of the world horribly easy, one breath. Reading B (documentary): the line is the plainest in the poem — it is what the photographs showed; Clarke, who built every image from media reports, is at her most factual precisely where she sounds most excessive. Evidence for A: the company the phrase keeps — "burnt earth", "scalded ocean" — a stanza systematically working through the elements; the Genesis resonance of ending with light and (next line but one) the word. Evidence for B: the verifiable smoke-darkness; Clarke's stated method of taking "all the details… from reports in the media". What a strong answer does: sees that the undecidability is historical, not verbal — the Gulf War closed the gap between apocalyptic rhetoric and weather report, so the line is unfalsifiable in both directions at once. And then connects that collapse to the final line: when hyperbole becomes literal, figurative language has lost its function — one more thing the war burnt. "The ashes of language" begins here, two lines early: the poem's most extravagant image is also its least invented, and there is no way of speaking that can keep those apart any more.

CLOSE ANALYSIS

Close Analysis

The moments that repay pressure, worked through

Quotation analysis

Ten moments chosen because they repay pressure — the famous set-pieces ("funeral silk", "the ashes of language") are treated at length elsewhere in this chapter.

1. "her pulsing burden" (l.1) — transferred epithet; pun; proleptic irony. The pulse belongs to the eggs (or to her own urgent blood) but is transferred to the "burden", so that the load itself beats — life felt as freight. "Burden" then opens twice more: the thing carried, and the archaic-technical sense of the refrain of a song — and this is the first line of a poem built entirely on a refrain ("For…"). The turtle carries her burden as the poem carries its own: the lament and the animal are doing the same labouring, rhythmic work of bearing something living towards ground that may not receive it. Intention/effect: Clarke fuses maternity, weight and song in two words, so the reader's first image already contains the poem's method — grief carried in repeating form.

2. "in search of the breeding ground." (l.2) — definite article; formula-break; terminal full stop. Not a breeding ground: the — green turtles return to the beach of their own hatching, one ground, non-negotiable, written into the body. The definite article makes the search unfalsifiable and therefore hopeless: there is no substitute to find. This is also the only line in the poem beginning with neither "For" nor "the" — the syntax itself off the map, searching — and the full stop ends the sentence where the search cannot end. Intention/effect: instinct meets the man-made in a single article; the reader feels the trap close grammatically before understanding it biologically.

3. "the veil of iridescence on the sand" (l.5) — metaphor; aestheticised toxicity. Oil-film genuinely is iridescent — rainbowed, shimmering, objectively lovely — and Clarke refuses to pretend otherwise. "Veil" holds bride and widow in one garment (silk in the previous line has already set a ceremony going, and the stanza cannot decide which ceremony it is). The horror is precisely the beauty: destruction that photographs well, poison you could mistake for ornament — an exact analogue for the war's own presentation, all tracer-light and precision-footage. Intention/effect: the reader is made complicit in finding the image beautiful, then made to notice what the beauty is made of; unease, not pathos, is the designed response.

4. "the ocean's lap with its mortal stain." (l.7) — polysemy stacked three deep. "Lap": the wave's smallest sound; the mother's lap (the poem's maternal motif reaching the sea); and the drinking animal's lap — the ocean tonguing its own poison. "Mortal": deadly; subject to death (the immortal-seeming ocean revealed as killable); and shadowed by "moral" — a stain of guilt, sin-language ("mortal stain" sounds close to "mortal sin"). "Stain" is the crucial noun: not a wound but a contamination — wounds heal, stains are permanent and, crucially, stains implicate whoever made them. Intention/effect: in nine words the sea becomes intimate, mortal and wronged, and the reader receives the guilt without any accuser being named.

5. "For Ahmed at the closed border." (l.8) — onomastics; prepositional arrest; participial deleted agent. The poem's only name (see Crux 3) — but press the small words too. "At" is the preposition of arrest: not crossing, not before, not turned back from — held at, durationless and permanent. "Closed" is a past participle with its agent deleted: someone closed it, no one is named — the poem's ethics of agentlessness at its most political, because a border, unlike a storm, always has a closer. Intention/effect: eight words perform bureaucratic finality; the reader waits with Ahmed in a line that cannot move, and the anger the line refuses to state accrues to the reader instead.

6. "the soldier in his uniform of fire." (l.9) — genitive metaphor; irony of issue. The "of" construction does the violence: a uniform made of fire, as uniforms are of wool or cotton — flame as standard issue, listed like kit. A uniform exists to identify, protect and make-uniform; this one destroys identity, consumes its wearer, and makes him uniform with every other burnt body — fire being the great equaliser of corpses. The variant some copies print, "with his", would only shift the horror from wearing to carrying. Intention/effect: Clarke converts the war's most unpublishable photograph into eight words that can be printed, and the reader's imagination is forced to develop the image the newspapers refused.

7. "who joined for the company," (l.11) — the poem's only finite verb; pun; borrowed register. All the grammar of agency in 'Lament' is concentrated here: one boy, one completed act, and the act is joining — affiliation, the least violent verb available. "The company" doubles: companionship (the loneliness of a boy who enlisted to belong) and the military unit that word becomes the moment he signs — the pun is the recruitment, the warm word turning into the cold one behind his back. The register is the family's own flat idiom, unimproved (see Crux 2). Intention/effect: the reader performs the double-take the boy could not — hearing, inside the friendly word, the machine that will spend him.

8. "the whale struck dumb by the missile's thunder." (l.15) — idiom literalised; appropriated lexicon; molossus. "Struck dumb" is dead metaphor for astonishment; Clarke reanimates it into physiology — underwater blasts can deafen and disorient whales and dolphins, whose whole world is acoustic. The possessive is the theft: the missile's thunder — ordnance has annexed nature's own word for sublime noise, so even the vocabulary of the sky now belongs to weapons. Three consecutive stresses ("whale struck dumb") detonate mid-line. Intention/effect: the ocean's largest voice is silenced by the war's borrowed one — and the reader is being prepared, six lines early, for what the poem will say about language itself.

9. "the long migrations and the slow dying," (l.17) — parallel syntax; gerund; quantitative metre. Two matched adjective-noun pairs, joined by "and" as if equivalent — and that false equivalence is the grief: an epic of navigation (Arctic-to-Africa flyways, species-memory older than any border) balanced against its new terminus. "Dying" as a gerund-noun is the masterstroke: not deaths (events, countable, over) but dying — a state, ongoing, possessed ("the slow dying") like a territory the birds now inhabit. The long vowels stretch the line's duration to match its subject. Intention/effect: the reader's voice must slow and lengthen — the poem makes you take the time that dying takes.

10. "the veiled sun and the stink of anger." (l.18) — synaesthesia; unowned emotion; register-collision. Anger has no smell; burning crude does — the line fuses them so that the atmosphere over the Gulf becomes an emotion you breathe. Crucially the anger is unowned: not Saddam's, not the coalition's, not the poet's — a free-floating rage hanging in the air like the smoke, which is the poem's agentlessness performed by weather. And "stink" — the lowest register in the poem, gutter-plain against elegiac "veiled" — refuses to perfume it. Intention/effect: the reader is denied the clean scapegoat and given nausea instead of blame; war's moral atmosphere is made physical, disgusting, and general.

CRITICAL LENSES

Critical Lenses

What each way of reading makes visible, and what it flattens

Critical lenses

Ecocritical. The lens this poem was practically written for — but push past "Clarke cares about nature". What the lens makes visible is the poem's structural biocentrism: the syntax grants a sea and a man identical sentences ("For the ocean's lap… For Ahmed…"), the pronoun system grants animals personal pronouns ("her pulsing burden", "his funeral silk" — the refusal of "it"), and the running order makes human suffering an episode inside an ecological catastrophe rather than the reverse (two stanzas of sea-life before any human appears). The poem also refuses the charismatic-species reflex: a cormorant (a bird fishermen hate), a dugong, a wader — the unloved mourned alongside the loved, grief without a favourites list. What the lens flattens: the war. Read purely ecocritically, 'Lament' becomes a pollution poem and loses "vengeance", Ahmed, the fusilier — the specifically human machinery of motive the last line indicts. The poem is not nature poetry with a war in it; it is a war poem that refuses to let "war" mean only humans.

Feminist. Makes visible the poem's maternal spine: it opens inside a female body's emergency ("her pulsing burden… the breeding ground… her eggs"), passes through the ocean's "lap" (the mother's lap made mortal), and mourns the combatants not as soldiers but as sons — "the boy", "the farmer's sons" — through phrases Clarke took from their mothers' radio interviews. The war's perspective in this poem is the perspective of those who bear and raise what war spends; its deepest definition of atrocity is the poisoning of generation itself (eggs, nests, breeding, migration — all reproductive acts). Male violence is present only as ownerless residue: agentless participles, a possessive missile. What it flattens: the poem's men are not only cyphers of a war-machine — gunsmith and armourer are mourned as workers, and the lens can reduce Clarke's inclusive grief to a gendered indictment the poem's evenhandedness pointedly withholds.

Postcolonial. Makes visible where the poem's knowledge comes from and who gets a name. A Welsh poet — from a small country with its own history of anglicisation, writing in the imperial language about a war conducted by Western powers in the Gulf — assembles her lament entirely from Western media: the one Arab in the poem has one line, no verb and a name that is also a category, while the detailed, tender particularity (joined for the company, in it for the music) is reserved for soldiers — very probably British — whose mothers Clarke heard interviewed on the radio. The lens sharpens the Ahmed crux: the poem's compassion crosses the border its information could not. It also notices "the closed border" as the colonial artefact par excellence — lines drawn by departed empires, upheld against the people who live there, ignored by the oil and smoke. What it flattens: the poem's genuine self-awareness — "the ashes of language" is, among other things, an admission that the reports the poem is built from are themselves burnt currency; the poem critiques its own sources from inside.

Marxist / materialist. Makes visible the commodity at the poem's centre and the class of its casualties. The war's cause, weapon and shroud is oil — the one substance never named, exactly as capital prefers to operate: everywhere effective, nowhere visible. The human dead are labour all the way down: the gunsmith and armourer (artisans of the arms economy, mourned as workers complicit without choice), the fusilier and the farmer's sons (rural recruits for whom the army is employment, company and a band — enlistment as economic fact dressed as adventure). No general, no minister, no shareholder appears; the poem mourns everyone the war-economy spends and no one it enriches. What it flattens: by deleting all agents, the poem also deletes the beneficiaries — a consistent Marxist reading wants the arms trade named and prosecuted, and Clarke's elegiac evenhandedness ("For the gunsmith…") grieves the system's instruments without indicting its owners. The lens calls that quietism; the poem would call it a funeral.

Historicist. Makes visible how precisely the poem is a document of the first television war watched live. 1991 was the war of pooled, censored, briefing-room coverage — "surgical strikes", "collateral damage", nose-camera footage with no bodies — and of a handful of images that escaped the management: the oiled cormorants, the burnt man in his vehicle. 'Lament' is built exclusively from that mediated seepage (Clarke says so), and its final line is a media-critique before it is a metaphysic: "the ashes of language" names what military euphemism and censorship had already done to public speech — Clarke's own gloss, "the death of truth during war". The poem's method — naming plainly what the coverage prettified or withheld — is counter-broadcasting: a litany against the communiqué. What it flattens: the poem's deliberate timelessness. Clarke strips away dates, nations and proper nouns (except Ahmed) precisely so the lament will fit the next war; a reading that chains it to 1991 mistakes the occasion for the subject — as the poem's continued life on exam syllabuses during later Gulf wars has demonstrated.

OTHER READINGS

Other Readings

Contested interpretations, and where each is weak

Alternative readings

1. The universal pacifist elegy

The poem deliberately erases sides: the soldier could be Iraqi or British, no nation is named, and Clarke's stripping of dates and places makes it a lament for war, applicable to any conflict (its afterlife on syllabuses through later wars supports this).

Evidence: the agentless participles (closed, struck, burnt, put out); the even-handed mourning of combatants and makers of arms (For the gunsmith and the armourer); the type-figures — the soldier, the boy fusilier.

Weakness: universality is bought with vagueness about a highly specific event. The spill and the fires were deliberate acts by an identifiable regime, the bombing a choice by an identifiable coalition, and a reading in which "everyone suffers, no one acts" turns crime into weather. The poem's one gesture towards cause, For vengeance, is left doing an enormous amount of unassisted work.

2. The ecocentric reading

This is primarily an environmental poem; the war is one instance of a general human assault on nature.

Evidence: the running order — animals first, last and framing the humans; roughly two-thirds of the lines given to creatures, sea and sky; the endangered-species precision (green turtle, hook-beaked turtles, dugong), taken from a Friends of the Earth list.

Weakness: stanzas 3–4 are irreducibly a war poem — borders, uniforms, fusiliers, armourers — and vengeance is a human motive with no ecological meaning. Read purely green, the poem loses its final line.

3. The media-critique reading

The poem's true subject is mediation: it is a poem about watching a war on television in Wales, assembled from photographs and radio (Clarke's own account), and its last line mourns the corruption of public language — censorship, euphemism, propaganda — more than speech itself.

Evidence: every image traceable to reportage; the ashes of language, glossed by Clarke as "the death of truth during war"; the poem's plain naming as counter-euphemism.

Weakness: nothing inside the text signals mediation — no screen, no newsprint, no camera. The reading is built on Clarke's notes, and it is fair to ask where the poem itself shows that it is second-hand.

4. The liturgical reading

The poem is a litany of intercession — "For the sick… for the dying…" — a prayer form with a congregation's rhythm and a priest's repetitions, performed for a world the war has unmade. Stanza 7 reverses Genesis (earth, light, waters, word), so the poem is scripture run backwards.

Evidence: the eleven For dedications; the ceremonial equality of all named; the un-creation imagery (the sun put out); the ending at language, the medium of "Let there be light".

Weakness: a litany has an addressee, and this poem conspicuously has none — no God, no "hear us". Prayer-shaped speech into silence may be the point, but then the reading is describing the ruin of liturgy, not liturgy.

5. The self-elegy for poetry

The final line turns the lament on itself: an elegy whose last casualty is the elegist's medium, ending in the confession that poetry cannot hold this.

Evidence: the ashes of language as the terminal phrase; the poem's renunciation of statement (no main clause anywhere); the dying-fall rhythm of the close.

Weakness: self-refuting if overstated — the poem exists, is eloquent and is taught; language demonstrably is not ash. The reading survives only in the softened form argued in The Whole Poem: assertive language is burnt, naming survives — which is no longer quite the despairing claim the reading wants to make.

6. The suppressed-rage reading

The lament is anger wearing ceremony: the diction hardens from pulsing to stink, anger and vengeance, and the ritual calm is a discipline clamped over fury — a protest poem in funeral dress.

Evidence: the stink of anger; For vengeance; the crowding of griefs (two in the first stanza, seven in the sixth) as control audibly strains.

Weakness: the form never actually breaks — no exclamation, no address, no rupture of the tercet or the formula. The anger is named twice but never voiced, and a reading that makes rage primary must explain why the poem's last sound is a diminuendo, not a raised voice.

REVISION NOTES

Revision Notes

The working notes, quotation by quotation

TITLE

Analysis
  • The title resonates with the poem in a multitude of ways as it encapsulates the poem’s purpose & tone, reflecting a deep // mournful song expressing grief for people, animals and environment lost during the 1990–91 Gulf War.
  • A Lament is both a passionate expression of mourning and sorrow which can be presented in the form of a song // poem // piece of music, tying into the poem’s elegiac form, or a complaint.
  • A lament captures both personal and public grief, beginning with an individual's sorrow branching towards universal mourning.
  • Reflective of the poem’s structure, Clarke opens the poem w/ singular losses to environmental damage resulting in widespread harm. Duality presents the poet mourning both single victims and the collective destruction caused by the Gulf War.
  • Private grieving: A lament provides a personal and raw expression of sorrow, indicating the poet’s full emotional transparency regarding the topic.
  • Public grief: Designed for community use to process collective crises. It twists personal sorrow into a shared experience of protest and pain, mirroring the poet voicing the complaints the media refuses to broadcast.
  • The title links to structure of the poem, using it to begin a list of lamented people // creatures // nature ([Lament] For…).
  • Allows poem to be read continually, permitting fluidity, travelling from one victim to another with destruction // suffering as a constant.
  • Connection between title & poem demonstrates the poet’s refusal to separate the act of naming from the act of mourning.
  • Simultaneously indicates elegiac form and beginning the elegy + consequently starting mourning // sorrowful tone
  • Having the title as a single word permits freedom to interpret what is lamented. Clarke provokes curiosity as the reader questions what is lamented, drawing them towards the poem. The poet answers it eleven times (each For) across seven stanzas, offering a broad scope of mourning, signaling the total destruction war creates.
  • The starkness permits multiple meanings for the reader to determine as the poem unfolds while implying the poem grieves over many things suggesting the encompassing damage war creates.
  • The lack of specificity upon which war acknowledges an inevitable impact, transcending a specific moment and discusses a universal impact. This opens Lament to be applied to any war // destruction, creating a timeless poem relevant to all losses.
  • Tone is established: Dignified and sorrowful, denies possibility of it being a partisan poem // triumphant war narrative.
  • Clarke ties in title to prevalent themes of war, the natural world and motherhood throughout the poem.
  • War and consequences: Traditionally associated with the aftermath of battle, Clarke titles the poem Lament to tie into the loss of soldiers and remembrance of war while expanding beyond the battlefield to include the natural world // civilians
  • Natural world: Poet laments both human loss and ecological destruction. She subverts the title's traditional association with human losses in battle by including victims in the natural world. Discussing both animal and terrestrial destruction under the same conditions, the poet captures the entirety of what is destroyed, mourning the natural world as she grieves human life.
  • Motherhood: A lament is deeply maternal with the title hinting towards maternal imagery w/ mothers of the boy soldiers and the pregnant turtle.

  • Despite the green turtle being an individual victim, utilising the rather than “a” allows Clarke to mourn the entire species rather than an anonymous turtle
  • Single green turtle is symbolic of countless others → metonymy
