  • Burden is ambivalent. Traditionally signals a negative weight on a person that cannot be shaken but undermined with turtle’s pregnancy being the main purpose assigned to her.
  • Illustrates duality of motherhood → Gift of life and weight of failure // responsibility
  • Eggs end up in a nest of sickness, presenting the mother turtle’s failure and the burden upon her.
  • The turtle’s fear of not being able to fulfill duties criticises war’s disruption in natural cycles.
  • ”Pulsing burden” → Transferred epithet
  • Turtle pulsing w/ urgency, Clarke’s transfer of this to the burden (unborn children) blurs line between mother and child + strengthens idea of mother’s responsibility, like if child dies she dies too
  • Being in search of a familiar place implies effort and uncertainty, showcasing the disruption the manmade disaster had upon the biological programming of animals.
  • Futile search evokes helplessness, permits reader to feel sorrow for the turtle.
  • Resonates with humankind (stanza 3) → Blurs line between nature and human: People search for place to raise children // displaced refugees seek safety (Ahmed at the closed border)
  • Endstopping sentence after search sketches how turtle assumes pointlessness of looking for a place that doesn’t exist. End of sentence mimics end of search.
  • Clarke keeps the sickness plaguing the nest ambiguous, paralleling the turtle’s lack of knowledge of what it is.
  • Puts reader into turtle’s shoes, equally confused.
  • Permits the poem to be used in multiple contexts where the sickness may not be oil.
  • Subverts typical interpretation of nest from warmth and safety to a cradle of death → Paradoxical
  • Hard endstop at the end of the stanza indicates finality, definitively sealing the egg’s future without negotiation. The poet aims to capture the helplessness of unborn creatures against the poison of mankind, evoking an emotional response from the reader.
  • Poet aims to force the reader to pause and absorb the impact of loss in a harshly conclusive manner without hesitation.
4 / 5 / 6

For the cormorant in his funeral silk, / the veil of iridescence on the sand, / the shadow on the sea.

Analysis
  • Alludes to deliberate oil spill into the Persian Gulf and its effect on nature with a cormorant coated in oil and its spreading contamination to the sand & sea. Based on photographs, Clarke describes seabirds doused in oil and the shadow on the sea as a spreading oil stain due to bombed wells.
  • Cormorant: A medium to large seabird with black plumage covering its body. Their feathers are not fully waterproofed, creating a vulnerability to oil spills as it’s absorbed rather than repelled, making a large number of them victims to an oil spill as they dive beneath the surface of the water to catch fish, often fatally.
  • The cormorant is widely disliked by fishermen and fish farmers. Clarke deliberately chooses them over a conventionally favoured bird, insisting all creatures should be mourned, rejecting biases against certain species.
  • Clarke further respects the bird through a masculine pronoun rather than it, providing him with dignity and individualism.
  • Ties cormorant into the soldier in his uniform of fire and the boy fusilier, suggesting equality in mourning and war’s destruction. Hierarchical perspective between human and animal is dissolved to indicate the poet’s constant belief of grieving all victims appropriately.
  • The cormorant metaphorically wearing funeral silk refers to traditional black clothing worn at a funeral, suggesting he is symbolically attending his own death. Literally, the poet describes the oil as a shiny coating over the bird, elevating environmental destruction into a ceremonial image to humanise the bird and invite the reader to mourn it as a person. The weight of the oil prevents the bird from flying, transforming it into a suffocating funeral shroud (used to wind around dead bodies before burial) that ultimately seals his fate.
  • Silk carries connotations of beauty and luxury associated with wealth, ceremony and elegance in stark contrast with oil. Clarke offers a different interpretation of oil as beauty, colliding with its toxic and repellent qualities. Oil has a sheen and smoothness comparable to silk, forcing the reader to see its elegant yet destructive qualities. The poet forces the reader to recognise the lack of a clear answer between good and bad, suggesting an unsettling truth.
  • Silk’s prominence in weddings ties into a veil of iridescence, suggesting a glorified death of the environment as well as a falsified and deceiving beauty.
  • The veil of iridescence extends the funeral imagery with a veil being symbolic of mourning.
  • Refers to oil spreading across sand, mirroring contamination of the Gulf War spill laying itself across the ocean like a mourning veil.
  • Scene extends the funeral metaphor from cormorant to the entirety of nature as if the world is mourning itself.
  • Veil further suggests concealment as oil physically covers sand, obscuring traces of the natural world.
  • Drags wedding connotations from silk. The poet glorifies death as people glorify war, using the same tone // attitude to showcase deaths as others would describe war. Creates a sense of unease and permits the reader to question whether it’s right to celebrate something as destructive as battle.
  • Soft endstop implies a slight pause, permitting continuation and creating the sense that the shadow is spreading similar to the oil.
  • The shadow on the sea metaphorically suggests a shadow of death and human destruction poisoning the natural world as well as foreshadowing the inevitable damage to the ocean. Adapting from the shadow of death, its foreboding nature captures the poet’s warning of war’s destruction.
  • Use of sibilance throughout stanza (silk // iridescence // sand // shadow // sea) allows a hissing quality, evoking an insidious sense and a spreading of evil. Also creates a quiet tone as if hushing // using a tarp (oil) to cover natural sound and life.
7 / 8 / 9

For the ocean’s lap with its mortal stain. / For Ahmed at the closed border. / For the soldier in his uniform of fire.

Analysis
  • The ocean’s lap evokes the gentle rippling sound of the water as it washes against the shore
  • The rhythmic motion of the sea creates a peaceful and reassuring sound, evoking a sense of calmness and serenity.
  • Lap evokes a sense of motherhood, describing safety and comfort, and strengthens maternal imagery expanding from the pregnant turtle. Clarke corrupts nurture and protection with oil’s mortal stain, suggesting mankind’s disruption to nature.
  • The mortal stain is physically the black coating of oil that brings death and destruction, literally staining and poisoning the land. Metaphorically, this evokes a blood stain as if the ocean has been mortal[ly] wounded and injured in a manner that will ultimately lead to death.
  • Moreover, the diction mortal suggests a temporary, finite, and impuissant (powerless, unable to take action) revealing the destruction caused by man, resulting in nature eventually perishing
  • A stain is not a wound, rather than breaking, it seeps and corrupts, suggesting the inability to be completely removed, paralleling an oil spill. The contrast between lap’s gentleness and the stain's corruption suggests war poisoning fundamental sources of comfort and safety, erasing comfort permanently.
  • Hard endstop after mortal stain closes line with finality suggesting the ocean’s wound is an incurable disease spreading to the shore. Mourning the ocean as a victim of war, Clarke establishes the ecological effects of the Gulf War’s destruction, mourning nature as she would a human casualty. She takes a radical position, insisting the natural world has an equal claim on grief.
  • Clarke moves to the human collateral damage of this war, encompassing everything and everyone.
  • The proper noun Ahmed introduces specificity to the generalised image of suffering, indicating individual tragedy. A name brings Ahmed individuality, acting as a human with an identity and history rather than a statistic or representing a category. Clarke insists his suffering is irreplaceable and acts as a voice for countless other refugees as an individual rather than an abstraction.
  • Highlights the toll of war takes, not only on the environment but on the lives of innocent people
  • The closed border is especially poignant as it symbolises the hopelessness and entrapment of refugees unable to escape the conflict that ravages both their homes and their futures.
  • The preposition of at indicates the inability to cross, unable to flee the horrors of war. Use of the implies a known and established sequence, chosen over “a”, the poet suggests routine entrapment.
  • The casual phrasing normalises injustice within war and simplistic refusal to grant a person safety, refusing to acknowledge their humanity as war does to countless innocent victims.
  • The ambiguity of Ahmed’s fate permits multiple interpretations and applications to voice other experiences of people turned away at borders.
  • The soldier brings the poem back to an ambiguous state contrasting the deliberate naming of Ahmed. His suffering originates from his role as a soldier, different to the citizens affected by the war.
  • The soldier burns in a metaphorical uniform of fire that transcends the literal image of a burning person to represent the inescapable destruction of war.
  • A uniform defines a soldier, allocating them to a place and group as well as serving as a garment of protection via either camouflage or design. The uniform burning signals the destruction of a soldier’s identity and cause, an ironic scene where the very thing that’s supposed to protect and identify him turns against him and consumes him whole. Being in close physical proximity, it prevents the soldier from escaping his fate, illustrating war’s destruction.
  • The poet alludes to a photograph of a soldier burnt when his tank was bombed. Clarke doesn’t invent the events of war but bases it off of real world images, warning the reader of the immediate risk of war.
  • Fire further links to broader imagery of burning destruction in the blazing well and burnt earth. The soldier’s burning body is a microcosm of the burning world, possibly foreshadowing the eventual outcome.
  • The word uniform carries irony in the sense of the reversal of protection and the uniform grieving // loss of three different victims of war, spanning from the natural world to innocent citizens and finally to soldiers
  • This stanza is the only one with all hard end-stops and every line beginning For, which emphasises the containment seen through the closed border.
  • Moreover, Ahmed is seemingly trapped in between a few juxtaposing elements:
  • The vast ocean coated with oil
  • The soldier burning alive
  • The contrast between fire and water indicates the duality of warfare on both man and nature, yet it’s simultaneously linked where the oil which the fire burns also poisons the sea.
  • The literary image of the border is conveyed through endstopped lines and isolation of stanzas, illustrating Ahmed’s hopelessness and inability to access others from physical separation.
  • This stanza develops the scope of Clarke’s lament where war is shown to not only destroy wildlife but everything it can. The ocean, refugee and soldier are placed in the same stanza as equals, suggesting the lack of hierarchy in suffering and war’s equal and universal devastation.
  • Intensifies hellish imagery of war where death is extremely visceral. The image of being burnt to death adds a layer of horror, suggesting the brutal, unrelenting nature of violence.
  • Shifts from the natural world to the human world, showing how the devastation of nature parallels the suffering of people caught in war
10 / 11 / 12

For the gunsmith and the armourer, / the boy fusilier who joined for the company, / the farmer’s sons, in it for the music.

Analysis
  • Clarke begins the stanza with a gunsmith and the armourer who furnish and maintain weapons and defence systems, being part of people who can profit financially from warfare.
  • Despite their contribution to war, Clarke insists that all should be mourned equally, a recurring idea throughout the poem. Deepens the sense of mourning of not just victims of war, but those who perhaps without choice become complicit in it by making weapons. The poet forgives those that take part in war, suggesting financial instability during wartime and the fight for survival and taking care of family outweighs moral choices.
  • Adds complexity and moral ambiguity to Clarke’s critique of war, it’s not only the soldiers and civilians who suffer but those whose livelihoods are tied to the production of violence. She suggests the lack of a definitive good and bad in war.
  • By mourning the gunsmith and armourer, the poet suggests that no one in a society at war is fully exempt from its horrors.
  • The next line creates an image of innocence and vulnerability through the description of a boy, with their naivety distancing them from brutal dictatorships and governments waging the war.
  • The poet’s portrayal of young men joining for the company and music indicates innocence and vulnerability. This shows their lack of driven motivation by political affiliation // propaganda being caught in conflict due to personal reasons. The gap between their motivations and the larger political forces enables the reader to feel sympathy towards the clueless soldiers, making their involvement tragic rather than provoking anger.
  • Use of boy reduces the soldier to a child, shattering the illusion of military heroism, revealing a human being inside the uniform. A child carrying a gun in a warzone seems ironic as his version of an adventure is twisted into a nightmarish scene of death and brutality.
  • Connected to poem’s maternal theme: Clarke took the boy + sons from radio interviews with their mothers.
  • boy fusilier is an ironic juxtaposition with the antiquity of military violence following something that carries heavy connotations of innocence.
  • joined → only finite verb in the whole poem; boy = only agent → the one completed act is a boy signing up
  • the company → pun: companionship + military unit (joined for friends, issued a Company)
  • The diction boy and sons reinforce the theme of lost potential, highlighting the youth of individuals with lives cut short by the war.
  • Choice of sons rather than son suggests a recurring pattern of young enlistments for naive reasons.
  • Regardless of survival, the war leaves a permanent indent in their mindset, being victims of the system and misguided reasons that led them to the war.
  • War corrupts the innocence that brought them there in the first place, an irreversible act of damage even if they survive the conflict itself.
  • Contrasting other stanzas, Clarke directly confronts the human cost of war on those who fight and fuel it as ordinary, often naive, humans tangled in a conflict beyond their control. As pawns in a game, the poet idealises them as citizens without a choice, being forced to accept duties against their morals to survive or given a falsified idea of war only to face its brutality with no way of backing out.
  • Though war is thought of as a conflict with two sides, Clarke’s choice to mourn the gunsmith, armourer and boy soldiers with other innocent victims without judgement indicates a universal experience of suffering regardless of what aspect war impacts them.
13 / 14 / 15

For the hook-beaked turtles, / the dugong and the dolphin, / the whale struck dumb by the missile’s thunder.

Analysis
  • The hook-beaked turtle is another name for the Hawksbill turtle, a critically endangered species
  • Choice of using hook leads to connotations with entrapment, suggesting that the turtles themselves are snared in the destruction surrounding them.
  • The shift from a singular turtle in stanza one escalates to many, mirroring the scale of the poem’s grief increasing from one lament to the next.
  • The reader moves from mourning a single animal to an entire species.
  • Similar to a snowball effect, overwhelms the reader in terms of destruction, revealing the true extent of devastation.
  • A dugong is a sea cow, similar to a manatee
  • Clarke draws attention to the diversity within the natural world, selecting more obscure species as they are often left out to give them a voice. Unfamiliarity acts as a reminder to the reader that war kills things that they haven’t recognised as a species.
  • Suggests universality of war’s harm, all forms of life regardless of popularity or uniqueness are at risk due to human callousness.
  • The whale is the largest marine animal and being the final and climactic image of the stanza, Clarke builds a crescendo of loss from small to large, mirroring the poem’s increasing emotional intensity.
  • Associated with wisdom, depth and peace, its silencing acts as a reminder of the ease of human destruction, silencing or killing the largest animal without deliberately intending to, and the consequent death of those qualities.
  • Being struck dumb, the poet literally describes the whale as speechless, being shocked into silence. Suggests the acoustic damage caused by underwater explosions. Relying on sound to communicate, this would disrupt and confuse the whale and dolphin, effectively silencing them or forcing them to travel directionlessly. Metaphorically, the whale’s peace is drowned by the missile's thunder, indicating the voices of reason being drowned out by the chaos of warfare
  • Two soft end-stops between the stanza emphasises a continuation of ideas and gentleness of life while ending with a hard end-stop after thunder mimics the ferocity and viciousness of human weapons.
16 / 17 / 18

For the tern, the gull and the restless wader, / the long migrations and the slow dying, / the veiled sun and the stink of anger.

Analysis
  • Tern and gull are seabirds, spending most of their time airborne, searching for food and relying on fish for survival
  • Terns are known for long migrations, introducing the theme of migration in the stanza
  • Waders are shorebirds which are often found wading along shorelines and mud flats to find food
  • The bird’s anxiousness suggests its unfamiliarity with this environment, unable to find safety and cannot stop moving, similar to refugees escaping war.
  • The restless wader suggests the struggle to find food to survive in a polluted habitat where water has become contaminated.
  • The long migrations initially refers to the disrupted migrations of seabirds due to the Gulf War’s environmental effect with burnt oil wells clouding the sky. Clarke mourns not only the deaths of the birds but the loss of a structured routine nature has developed over long periods of times.
  • Simultaneously, the migrations refer to the migrations of displaced refugees and stateless people such as Ahmed.
  • ”Long” suggests a physical distance and the endurance required for the journey where safety isn’t guaranteed.
  • The poet links the human and animal world, implying their similarities in attempting to find a safe end after a long arduous journey.
  • The slow dying refers to the gradual death of creatures affected by oil contamination due to a lack of food, inability to fly or those that die slowly due to poisoning. The poet enables the reader to feel sorrowful for the inescapable fate of the birds.
  • In the context of human victims, it refers to the death of people who have been displaced and died on the journey of trying to find shelter without adequate water. Clarke implies a painfully slow and aware death where people are helpless yet conscious of their impending death.
  • The personification of the veiled sun creates an image of a veneer made of smoke from the burning oil fields acting as a funeral veil
  • Symbolises the death of nature and offering a mournful tone, emphasising the theme of the death of the planet
  • The veiling // concealment of the sun diminishes its warmth and light, foreshadowing its death in the following stanza.
  • The stink of anger could literally refer to the smell of burning oil created by the environmental devastation in the Gulf War
19 / 20 / 21

For the burnt earth and the sun put out, / the scalded ocean and the blazing well. / For vengeance, and the ashes of language.

Analysis
  • Stanza opens with apocalyptic imagery with total environmental destruction at the centre of the first line, ascending war’s devastation to a cosmic level within a line.
  • A burnt earth literally refers to the Gulf War’s oil well fires. As a past participle (burnt), the poet suggests the earth’s total destruction has already happened beyond a repairable point. The lack of conditionality and prevention indicates the finality of the situation where the poet leaves no room for negotiation, a direct warning of the consequences of war.
  • The earth not existing eradicates all victims mentioned previously where its destruction crushes the medium of life.
  • The sun being put out captures the extinguishment of the ultimate source of life. Due to its simplicity, the poet suggests an astronomical amount of damage due to human carelessness. Paralleling snuffing out a candle, Clarke connects the destruction of the sun to an everyday task, contrasting the climactic point the poem has reached.
  • Escalation of the veiled sun from veiled obscurement to total extinguishment
  • The poet personifies the ocean with it being scalded, attributing a sense of suffering and vulnerability in a way the reader can relate (e.g. burning hand on stove)
  • Refers to theme of nature being a victim of human actions and inevitable consequences
  • The blazing well directly alludes to oil wells set on fire during the Gulf War, illustrating the magnitude of human destruction
  • Beyond extinguishing life on earth, the poet captures an image of wastefulness, an intentional move to pollute the environment partially understanding the consequences
  • Signifies human greed and personal benefit as underlying themes during conflict
  • The metaphorical ashes of language references the death of truth during war, suggesting damages beyond physical grasp. Clarke critiques media censorship obscuring truth from the public audience.
  • The inclusion of abstract concepts (language and vengeance) contrasts tangible imagery, broadening the scope of her laments.

Structural + General Analysis

Analysis
  • 7 stanzas of three lines (tercets)
  • 7 stanzas ↔ 7 days of creation? Stanza 7 undoes Genesis (earth, light, water, finally the word) → argue from imagery, not the number
  • Free verse
  • No fixed metrical (or rhythmic) structure
  • No set rhyme scheme
  • Rhyme suggests order, closure in a musically pleasant way; absence of rhyme removes chime // consolation (no resolution) — but form is strict (7 equal tercets, every line end-stopped) → ritual order containing chaos, not chaos
  • Each line is end-stopped with either a comma (soft) or a full stop (hard)
  • Lack of enjambment contributes to this slow and deliberate pace with each line standing on its own as a self-contained thought
  • Mimics the style and solemnity of a prayer or elegy, allowing the reader to pause and reflect on the gravity of each lamentation
  • Offers a sense of finality and mourning with each image or event carefully and respectfully acknowledge before moving onto the next
  • Measured rhythm enhances the poem’s tone of sorrow and reverence for the victims of environmental destruction and war
  • First three stanzas: One item/ image attributed to each line (line 10 already has two)
  • In further stanzas, this structure isn’t present, structure slowly falls as poem continues, expands to two subjects per line
  • As if Clarke doesn’t have enough time/space to lament all affected/destroyed by the war
  • The entire poem is built around a series of For phrases, expressing sorrow for different subjects
  • From endangered animals to the individuals involved in warfare
  • Anaphora: For opens 11 lines (1, 3, 4, 7, 8, 9, 10, 13, 16, 19, 21) + 2 lowercase mid-line fors (for the company, for the music) = 13
  • Creates a solemn, rhythmic quality that echoes the tolling of a funeral bell, acts as a soft drumbeat
  • Reflects steady beat of funeral march, reinforces elegiac form
  • The repetitive structure alongside the asyndetic nature of each lament reinforces the mournful tone, as each for introduces another casualty or loss to be grieved
  • The repetition invites contemplation, emphasising the sheer scale of destruction
  • Each toll marks a life, a species, or an aspect of the natural world devastated by the war
  • This effect is both hypnotic and haunting, mirroring the persistence of grief and the unrelenting nature of the damage cause
  • Clarke’s diction is lyrical, often carrying a musicality and emotional resonance, enhancing the elegiac tone of the poem
  • Heightens the poignancy of the subject matter, making the destruction made even more vivid and heartrending
  • Extensive sound patterning
  • Alliteration
  • Sibilance
  • Consonance
  • Assonance
  • The use of figurative language
  • Metaphor
  • A heavy lack of simile, which shows, that rather than merely being like something else, it has fundamentally altered the essence of the natural world
  • Emphasises the permanence of the damage, showing the irrevocable transformation
  • Personification
  • [Lament] For… Anaphoric
  • Follows a list-like structure: Catalogue of things harmed + acknowledgement of deaths
  • Encompasses all affected things w/ For… acting as a continuing list of destroyed beings
  • Acts as a list of grievances for animals/people/things
  • Cumulative effect (from anaphoric listing) continued w/ asyndeton
  • Tone travels from grief // mourning → Overt anger
  • Asyndeton (commas, no conjunction chains) ^^ effect of anger :
  • Constant pushing increases pace, introducing a rant-like feeling
  • Continues listing
  • Diction utilised per stanza
  • pulsing to dying
  • Author employs harsher diction combined with a lack of euphemisation Emphasises point of destruction
  • Intensity of content within stanzas escalates
  • Individual animals: Climactic point where natural and human worlds collapse
  • Final stanza breaks pattern of mourning creatures // people // environment to vengeance & language → Lack of available language to depict situation suggests inability to make sense // justify violence
  • the turtle + the cormorant — Stanza 1 + Stanza 2
  • Poem opens with smaller scale destruction, highlighting impacts upon singular animals
  • long migrations of the tern, the gull and the restless wader — Stanza 6
  • Migrating birds echo displaced people, showcasing the inevitable destruction of both nature and humanity → War’s grasp upon all possible things
  • slow dying + veiled sun // burnt earth + scalded ocean — Stanza 6 + 7 (67!!!!)
  • Reflection of wider environmental destruction → Poet expands to larger scale damage, underscoring wide effect + total demolition of environment
  • ashes of language — Stanza 7
  • Cumulation of her argument throughout the poem
  • Shifts from physical environmental damage to abstract loss of communication and obstruction of truth
  • Poet suggests the inability to articulate damage /find truth in language after complete destruction is the most devastating loss
  • Irreversible + people are unable to learn from mistakes due to lack of knowledge upon topic
  • Lines punctuated w/ comma and full stop
  • Permits reader to digest impact of lines // separates
  • End-stopped stanzas: Separates stanza by focus then ends it as a full stop, completes idea
  • Poet acts as a photographer compiling shots of a scene: End of the stanza almost completes the album the poet describes
  • Same general idea being captured
  • Punctuation controls pace of reading
  • End-stopping (full stops) forces the reader to pause fully → Complete understanding of
  • End-stopping (commas) enables the reader to pause & absorb while forming a feeling of endless harm
  • Hard end-stop: strong punctuation mark bringing reader to definitive pause
  • Full stop
  • Exclamation mark
  • Question mark
  • Soft end-stop: lighter // weak punctuation mark creating gentle pause, allows meaning to flow w/ fluidity b/w lines
  • Comma
  • Dash
  • Semi colon
  • Endstopped stanzas —> indicative of pause // completeness of idea
  • Author enables reader to have full bodied empathy + allows processing of discussion —> permitting processing slows the pace, detailing gruesomeness + almost spoon feeds the reader by forcing them to read at a specific pace to understand
  • Expanding idea of feeding the reader, clarke contrasts typical media censorship
  • The poem exposes new ideas, slower pace is like teaching reader what reality is
  • Endstopping contributes to slow + deliberate funereal rhythm (encapsulates what the poem discusses) —> reader pausing at the end of every line mimics steady + solemn beat of funeral march
  • Hard endstops create a sense of finality (reflection of death)
  • Ending a line in an endstop echoes the ending of a life —> ties into the theme of destruction in the poem. stanza moves from one point to another, ending with a hard endstop serves as a physical barrier to separate each victim the author depicts, forcing the reader to recognise each loss as individual rather than blurring deaths together —> poet ensures that each creature // person // environment thing is treated as its own separate loss + mourned appropriately by the reader by isolating images, forces reader to think about impacts before moving to next part
  • Bleak diction ties into idea of spoon feeding, author aims to not overcomplicate language as topic is difficult to grasp
  • Sheds light on deaths in a practical manner, utilising harshness to force reader to confront reality as opposed to being draped in euphemisms
  • Within stanza, soft endstops w/ commas
  • continuation of listing effect within stanza: breakdown from large idea into simpler ideas
  • Soft endstops
  • Soft endstops indicate continuation & reader is carried forward w/o pause —> reflective of how destruction bleeds into a multitude of aspects + continuation of list, this echoes oil spill where oil spread across the ocean without stopping
  • Lack of pause mirrors how war stops for nothing —> senseless destruction or something, indicates what poet is criticising
  • Soft endstops allow clarke to list multiple victims in quick succession into overwhelms reader w/ accumulating losses (ties back to cumulative grief in listing)
  • Prominent in stanza 5 // 6 // 7: the hook-beaked turtles, the dugong and the dolphin, the whale… combined w/ asyndeton to create flow
  • In first few stanzas, comma acts as detailing, increasing vivid descriptions to revive ashes of language
  • Soft endstops permit lyrical + songlike flow, fitting to elegiac form, hard endstops restrict full musicality (ensures the reader is able to grasp full impact rather than a melodic piece —> war is brutal, there is no sugarcoating) + bring rhythm to perspective as funeral march
  • Opposes definitive ending quality of hard endstops, soft endstops link victims together (within stanzas), capturing a full picture + its widespread effect harming all things, everything caught in destruction of war w/o fail
  • joining hands w/ each other, creates sense of togetherness + cohesion within period of chaos and destruction where humankind clashes w/ itself and nature
  • Universal impact
  • fluid movement b/w lines imply shared fate
  • Using both
  • Contrasting effects, kinda like a debate and a battle within itself, ties into two sides of war, disagreeing yet creating a cohesive piece to describe said situation (the poem not war)
  • Soft endstops, flowing lines, draw reader forward (combined w/ asyndeton), builds grief and momentum
  • Continuous effect where author creates recurring senseless destruction
  • Hard endstops —> decisive end that brings the reader to a halt, forces reflection, keeps rigid structure + pace
  • Creates steady beat of funeral march
  • Interplay creates push and pull effect
  • Reader is carried forth by soft endstops where recurring grief rolls over + is continued from one line to another then abruptly stopped to complete the idea, indicating the finality of death and the sudden end to lives war creates w/o warning
  • Mirrors process of mourning, continuous sorrow flowing interrupted by sharp, overwhelming pain forcing someone to reflect
  • Manipulation of hard and soft endstops is integral to poem’s emotional effect
  • Hard endstops enforce finality // separation // abruptness of death
  • Soft endstops create flow // accumulation
  • Forms distinctive funeral march like beat yet elegiac musicality to poem
  • relentless grief w/ moments of stillness to permit reader to process
  • Last line (For vengeance, and the ashes of language.) ends w/ hard endstop, definitive full stop signals absolute end of both poem and everything (animals // things // people // natural world + finally language)
  • Ending permits no escape or soft landing, no further soft endstop to drag + capture further emotions, indicates finality and the definitiveness of death (no undo button)
  • ties into idea of ashes of language, no more words to be said following last line
  • Reinforces poem’s central argument of war leading to complete and total destruction, full stop indicates no solution when war branches to every aspect of life
  • Note *litany* —> Add onto structure later (img 1)
  • Litany: Long repetitive list of complaints // problems
  • Long series of items
  • Freq used to describe a long list of negative things
  • A tedious recital or repetitive series
  • a litany of complaints
  • Repetitive —> Anaphora (For)
  • Lots to lament in a short space
  • The poet complains about senseless destruction, displacing people, slaughtering wildlife and destroying the environment. Consequences branch from physical items towards concepts of language
  • Poet laments all of it as a litany
  • Anaphora + cumulative list of victims
  • Poem also acts as a prayer for the unnamed: Litany gives voice to victims who cannot speak for themselves (animals, landscape and peoples voices drowned by media censorship —> ashes of language)
  • Functions as a prayer: Solemn, quiet and emotional appeal on behalf of the environmental and human casualties ;
  • Like a prayer interceding (intervene on behalf of another) for the helpless, the poem focuses on giving a voice to creatures and innocent people rather than political leaders
  • Clarke’s tone and diction begins to harden as you trail down the poem
  • The first stanza emphasises of green, pulsing, nest where sickness is not the norm, it stands out, offering a sense of life and vitality
  • By the penultimate stanza it points out stink, slow dying, anger which reveals to us the degradation of life, and the withering nature of everything

Lament

Analysis

Similar: wail // weeping

Similar: elegy // requiem // dirge

[Lament] For Ahmed at the closed border.

  • The one-word title
  • The start of a list of lamented people, events, creatures, and other things hurt in the war
  • A Lament is a song expressing grief for something lost or someone who has died
  • Noun
  • a passionate expression of grief or sorrow
  • his mother’s night-long laments for his father
  • a song, piece of music, or poem expressing grief or sorrow
  • the piper played a lament
  • a complaint
  • there were constant laments about the conditions of employment
  • The diction lament is understood to be tacitly (in a way that is understood or implied without being directly stated) present before each instance of the word For
  • [Lament] For the ocean’s lap with its mortal stain.
  • Clarke puts a slight twist to the traditional lament by painting her sorrow onto a broader canvas, focusing as much on the environmental cost as on the human cost of the Kuwait oil Disaster
  • Her theme beyond the expression of sorrow at the scale of destruction, is that human wars waged against one another are also waged against the natural world
  • Her usage of metonymy (individuals or small things to represent many)
  • Allows her reader to connect in a concrete way
Effect, style & response
  • Relevance to the poem
  • Establishes form as an elegy
  • Introduction of mournful tone
  • Structurally significant, allows the poem to list what the poet laments

“For the cormorant in his funeral silk, / the veil of iridescence on the sand, / the shadow on the sea.”

Analysis
  • Alludes to the oil deliberately spilled into the Persian Gulf by the occupying Iraqi army (Jan 1991)
  • A cormorant is a medium-to-large seabird, which is a reference to a photograph that Clarke saw in the newspaper, of one of these birds covered with oil
  • The diction funeral silk is a reference to the black clothes that are worn to a funeral, which evokes the shiny, viscous black coating of oil over the bird’s feathers
  • Almost like a shroud used to ritually wind around dead bodies before burial
  • The personification creates the visual image of a mourner dressed for a funeral after the death of his habitat/home
  • This funeral imagery is further developed in the next line as the oil has left a veil of iridescence on the sand reinforcing the poem’s tone of sorrow and loss
  • Black veils were traditionally worn by women at funerals up until the mid-twentieth century
  • Iridescent means luminous colours that seem to change when seen from different angles due to the way light interferes with the surface, both reflecting and refracting different wavelengths and is typical of the appearance of oil
  • Evokes how the oil has left a beautiful yet poisonous sheen
  • The shadow on the sea acts as a metaphor for death and the foreboding inevitability of death that is to come to the living animals
  • The extensive use of sibilance throughout this stanza Silk/irideSCenCE/Sand/SHadow/Sea allows a hissing quality which evokes an insidious sense of a spreading evil
  • This illustrates not only the physical damage, but the emotional toll it takes on the natural world

Analysis
  • The diction lap evokes the gentle rippling sound of the water as it washes against the shore
  • Yet the mortal stain is physically the black coating of oil that will bring death and destruction, as it in turn will literally stain and poison the land

  • Moreover, the diction mortal suggests a temporary, finite, and impuissant (powerless, unable to take action) revealing the destruction caused by man, even resulting in nature eventually perishing
  • Clarke moves to the human collateral damage of this war, which encompasses everything and everyone now

  • The closed border is especially poignant as it symbolises the hopelessness and entrapment of refugees unable to escape the conflict that ravages both their homes and their futures
  • This stanza is the only one all with hard end-stops and anaphorically emphasised through for which emphasises the containment seen through the closed border

  • The vast Ocean coated with oil

CONNECTIONS

Connections

How this poem pairs with the rest of the set

Comparison hooks

1. Report to Wordsworth — Boey Kim Cheng

Link. The closest pairing in the set: two eco-elegies that end by doubting their own medium as the sky fails. Boey's birds are few "in a sky slowing like a dying clock", "Poetry and piety have begun to fail", and "God is labouring to utter his last cry"; Clarke gives us the sun put out and the ashes of language. Both mourn nature and the tradition of mourning it.

Shared technique. Inherited elegiac machinery under strain, and the sea's creatures on the casualty list — Boey's Neptune "helpless as a beached whale", Clarke's whale struck dumb.

Difference. Boey speaks to someone ("You should be here") through a thicket of allusion (Proteus, Triton, Neptune) and names the culprit: "insatiate man moves in for the kill". Clarke has no addressee, almost no allusion and no culprit. Boey laments that the tradition cannot help; Clarke writes as if it is already ash and only the bare rite remains.

2. A Different History — Sujata Bhatt

Link. Both end at the same wound: language after violence. Bhatt asks "Which language / has not been the oppressor's tongue?"; Clarke ends with language itself in ashes. Conquest corrupts a language from within; war burns it down.

Shared technique. A turn from concrete particulars to an abstract close about language, inside a sacred frame — Bhatt's reverence for books ("without disturbing Sarasvati"), Clarke's litany.

Difference. Bhatt's poem holds a future: "the unborn grandchildren / grow to love that strange language". Clarke's unborn are eggs in their nest of sickness. Bhatt shows violence with a face — "the conqueror's face"; Clarke's violence has no face and no agent. Bhatt's is a history; Clarke's is a terminus.

3. The Chimney Sweeper — William Blake

Link. Both mourn the young, spent by institutions that speak the language of comfort, and both dress their victims for death. Blake's sweep says "They clothed me in the clothes of death / And taught me to sing the notes of woe"; Clarke's cormorant wears funeral silk, and her boy joined for the company.

Shared technique. The victim's plain idiom left uncorrected, so the reader must do the condemning — Blake's "They think they have done me no injury", Clarke's in it for the music.

Difference. Blake names the guilty outright — "God and his Priest and King, / Who make up a heaven of our misery"; Clarke names no one. Blake's child speaks for himself; Clarke's recruits never speak — their mothers do, offstage. Blake's frame is one city's trade in soot; Clarke's is a planet.

4. Sonnet 18 — William Shakespeare

Link. Two opposite faiths in language. Shakespeare is sure verse outlasts death: "So long lives this, and this gives life to thee." Clarke ends with the ashes of language. Both watch the sun fail — "the eye of heaven", "his gold complexion dimm'd" — against Clarke's veiled sun and the sun put out.

Shared technique. A closing turn to the poem's own medium: Shakespeare's "this" and "eternal lines", Clarke's language.

Difference. Shakespeare's sun dims by "chance or nature's changing course"; Clarke's is put out by war. Rhyme, a volta and a couplet that promises immortality, against unrhymed tercets that can only name the dead.

5. A Married State — Katherine Philips

Link. Two catalogues built on a repeated formula. Philips's "No blustering husbands to create your fears" leads a run of "No…" lines and "Few worldly crosses", listing what a single woman is spared; Clarke's For… lists what war has taken. One formula subtracts griefs; the other adds them.

Shared technique. Anaphora driving an end-stopped list that turns, at the close, to a summary in a new register — Philips's proverb "There's no such thing as leading apes in hell", Clarke's abstract ashes of language.

Difference. Philips counts the pangs of childbirth among the troubles a virgin escapes; Clarke mourns birth itself — a turtle's pulsing burden. Philips's is witty private counsel in heroic couplets, addressed to "Madam"; Clarke's is public grief, addressed to no one.

6. An Essay on Man — Alexander Pope

Link. Pope's man is "Great lord of all things, yet a prey to all", and 'Lament' shows both halves at once: humanity lording it over sea and sky until the sun put out, and humanity as prey — Ahmed at the border, the soldier in his uniform of fire. Pope's "Sole judge of truth, in endless error hurled" meets Clarke's gloss on her last line: "the death of truth during war".

Shared technique. Anaphora as argument: Pope's "In doubt to act or rest, / In doubt to deem himself a god or beast" piles up a condition as Clarke's For piles up losses.

Difference. Pope balances his paradoxes in couplets and contemplates "The glory, jest, and riddle of the world" with ironic poise; Clarke has no balance left, only consequences. Pope generalises about "man"; Clarke never uses the word, naming a boy, a gunsmith, Ahmed.

7. Hunting Snake — Judith Wright

Link. Both grant creatures the dignity of persons — Wright's snake is "he" throughout, as Clarke's turtle is her and her cormorant his — and both admire a dark creature lit by a sheen: Wright's "curves of diamond scale", Clarke's black funeral silk.

Shared technique. Exact, unsentimental attention to an animal's own business: Wright's snake "quested through the parting grass"; Clarke's turtle is in search of the breeding ground.

Difference. Wright's sheen is life — "Cold, dark and splendid", the snake leaves unharmed, and the watchers "went on". Clarke's sheen is oil, and in 'Lament' there is no going on. Wright, who campaigned to save the Great Barrier Reef from oil drilling, shows what attention spares; Clarke shows what its absence costs.

8. Before the Sun — Charles Mungoshi

Link. Two suns and two columns of smoke. Mungoshi's boy sends woodsmoke up "to the distant sky", perhaps "a sacrificial prayer", and shares his maize, one bite "for the sun" and one for himself. Clarke's smoke rises from the blazing well and veils the sun until it is put out. In one poem a child feeds the sun; in the other, war extinguishes it.

Shared technique. A ritual built on a repeated phrase with for at its heart, and an ending in residue — Mungoshi's cobs left as "two little skeletons", Clarke's ashes.

Difference. Mungoshi's rite is playful and answered: the sun winks back like an indulgent adult. Clarke's prayer has no one to hear it, and her residue is not what is left of a shared meal but what is left of a world.

Also worth setting beside it

Where I Come From (Brewster) — catalogue as memory against catalogue as obituary: "People are made of places", and Brewster's list ends with "A door in the mind" blowing open; Clarke's ends in ash. The Cockroach (Halligan) — one creature watched until it mirrors the watcher ("I thought I recognised myself"); Clarke's creatures mirror no one and matter for themselves. Love Armed (Behn) — who pays for a grand abstraction: Behn's Love sits "in Fantastic Triumph" while "Bleeding Hearts around him flowed"; Clarke sets vengeance on the casualty list it caused.

CONTEXT

Context

The world the poem came out of

The Poet: Seamus Heaney (1939–2013)

Seamus Heaney was born on 13 April 1939 at Mossbawn, the family farmhouse in the townland of Tamniaran near Castledawson, County Derry (Londonderry), Northern Ireland: the first of what would be nine children. At twelve he won a scholarship to St Columb's College, a Catholic boarding school in Derry, and he went on to read English at Queen's University Belfast, graduating in 1961 with First Class Honours. He taught in Belfast, joined the poets' workshop that Philip Hobsbaum ran there from 1963 (the 'Belfast Group'), and lectured at Queen's from 1966 to 1972, when he moved to the Irish Republic.

He became one of the most widely read poets of his time. In 1995 he won the Nobel Prize in Literature 'for works of lyrical beauty and ethical depth, which exalt everyday miracles and the living past': the citation could be a description of 'Follower'. He died in Dublin on 30 August 2013. His last words, texted to his wife Marie, were Noli timere: 'Don't be afraid'.

Mossbawn and Patrick Heaney

The Nobel Foundation's biography describes Mossbawn as 'a small farm of some fifty acres', and says that the father's 'real commitment was to cattle-dealing'. It also draws a contrast between the parents: Patrick Heaney was 'notably sparing of talk', while Margaret Kathleen Heaney (née McCann, 1911–1984), whose relations worked in the local linen mill, was 'notably ready to speak out'. In 1953 the family moved to a farm at Bellaghy, a few miles away.

Two facts change how the poem reads. First, a cattle dealer's son chose to remember his father at the plough: the poem selects the farm skill that most resembles the son's own craft of making lines. Second, Patrick Heaney was alive when 'Follower' was published in 1966; he died in October 1986, two years after his wife. Whatever the last stanza means, it is not about a dead man, and the poem never says the father is old: it says he keeps stumbling. The silent father and the son who talks are also the poem's own contrast: a man who speaks to his horses with a click, and a boy remembered as Yapping.

Death of a Naturalist (Faber, 1966)

'Follower' comes from Heaney's first full collection, Death of a Naturalist, published by Faber and Faber in 1966, when he was twenty-seven. The book made his name, and between 1966 and 1968 it won a run of prizes, among them the Eric Gregory Award, the Cholmondeley Award, the Somerset Maugham Award and the Geoffrey Faber Memorial Prize. Its poems come out of the farm childhood ('Death of a Naturalist', 'Blackberry-Picking', 'Churning Day', 'Mid-Term Break', about the death of his four-year-old brother Christopher in a road accident in 1953), and its recurring story is a child growing out of a world he loves into a more self-conscious adult identity.

The book opens with 'Digging', its partner poem. There the poet watches his father and grandfather dig, admits he has 'no spade to follow men like them', and decides to dig with his pen instead. The word follow is already there. In the essay 'Feeling into Words' (1974, collected in Preoccupations, 1980) Heaney called 'Digging' the first poem in which he thought 'my feel had got into words'. 'Follower' takes up the same problem with a different tool: the son cannot inherit the father's work, so he inherits it in writing.

The eldest son and the scholarship

In a farming family the eldest son would ordinarily be the one to take on the land. Heaney did not. The Nobel biography calls his departure for boarding school at twelve 'the decisive one', a move from 'the earth of farm labour' to 'the heaven of education'. Free grammar-school places for clever children from homes like his had only recently been opened up (the Education Act (Northern Ireland) of 1947 is usually credited), and Heaney's generation of Catholic farm children was among the first to go from the field to the university.

'Follower' never mentions school or books, but this departure is its buried subject. In the field the son is behind; by the last stanza he is ahead, in a life the father does not share, and the father is the one trailing in his wake. That is why the ending can carry guilt as well as tenderness. There is no hostility between father and son in the poem: the father carries the boy on his back, and the boy's dearest wish is to be like him. Nor does the son take over his father's work: the poem's whole point is that he could not and did not.

Working a horse-plough: the craft behind the images

The poem describes the job accurately. A pair of horses (the team) draws the plough while the ploughman walks behind, gripping its handles and guiding the horses with the reins. The share, which Heaney calls by its regional name, the sock, cuts the soil horizontally; an adjustable part of the plough (the wing, glossed variously as the share's side-blade or the board that turns the soil aside) lifts the cut strip and turns it over. A well-set plough in skilled hands turns the strip, the sod, over whole, its underside left smooth and shining by the steel, hence polished sod. At the end of the field, on the strip left for turning (the headrig, or headland), the team is wheeled round and brought back to cut the next furrow alongside the last. To keep the furrow straight the ploughman sights along it, and the boy's longing To close one eye copies exactly that gesture. The father's boots were hobnailed: their soles were studded with short, heavy-headed nails for grip and wear.

Heaney's childhood saw the last generation of this work. The small grey tractor designed by the County Down engineer Harry Ferguson, the TE20, went into production in 1946, and over the next decades tractors replaced horses on Irish farms. By the time the poem was published, a team of horses at the plough was already becoming a memory: the scene is both a father and a vanishing way of farming.

The words of the field

The ploughing vocabulary is regional, and some of it is very old. The Oxford English Dictionary records sock, 'a ploughshare', as a northern English and Scottish word, taken from Old French soc and generally thought to be of Celtic origin (Irish has soc). Headrig is Scots heid-rig, recorded from 1475 as 'the headrig, or headland, in a ploughed field'; rig is the Scots form of 'ridge'. These are the words of Ulster farming, where Scots settlers' speech, English and Irish overlap.

Heaney liked to read this layering in names. In his prose (collected in Preoccupations) he glossed Mossbawn itself: 'moss', a Scots word probably brought by the Planters; 'bawn', the English colonists' name for a fortified farmhouse; and, in the family's pronunciation, a hint of Irish bán, 'white', as in the white of bog-cotton. 'Follower' uses its field-words without explanation, as an insider does. The son who could not plough still speaks the plough's language, and that knowledge is part of the inheritance the poem shows.

Verse and the furrow

The English word verse comes from the Latin versus, from vertere, 'to turn': a turning, especially the turn of the plough at the end of a furrow, and so a furrow, a row, and a line of writing. The poem never says this, but its form acts it out: its one sentence that runs over a stanza break does so exactly at the headrig, where the team turns.

Heaney returned to the figure again and again. The first of his 'Glanmore Sonnets' (Field Work, 1979) opens 'Vowels ploughed into other: opened ground', and he called his selected poems Opened Ground: Poems 1966–1996 (1998). Writing about Patrick Kavanagh, the Monaghan farmer-poet whose work showed him that his own parish was a fit subject for poetry, Heaney spoke of 'the penalty of consciousness', the unease that comes when a way of life becomes literary material. 'Follower' is a small instance of that unease: the father's life becomes the son's material, and the son is honest enough to put himself in the picture as a nuisance.

The father poems after 'Follower'

Patrick Heaney stayed in his son's poetry for the rest of his career, in poems such as 'The Harvest Bow' (Field Work, 1979), where the father's hands plait a harvest bow in silence. After his death in 1986 the father returns throughout Seeing Things (1991). In 'Man and Boy' the piggyback from 'Follower' comes back: Heaney imagines being carried on his father's back like a 'witless elder rescued from the fire', the image of Aeneas carrying his old father Anchises out of burning Troy, the classical emblem of a son's devotion, here turned around so that the son is the one carried.

These later poems change how the end of 'Follower' sounds. In 1966 the father who will not go away was a living man. Read across the whole career, the line sounds like a promise the poetry kept: the father never did go away.

THE POEM

The Poem

Line by line, with the analysis alongside

Lines with a marker have analysis — click one, or just scroll.

Title
Follower
Language & devices

Title as a single noun with no article: Follower, not 'The Follower' or 'My Father'. An agent noun (one who follows) that names a role rather than a person, so it can attach to whoever fills the role. Polysemy: (1) one who walks behind; (2) a disciple or imitator of a master; (3) a successor, the next generation who 'follows' a father into his trade. The verb returns at a line-end in stanza 5 (follow), and the noun's sound already half-rhymes with the poem's key object, the furrow: f, a doubled liquid (ll / rr), -ow.

Meaning & effect

The poem is about the father, but the title names the son's position. Before a line is read, the speaker has defined himself by distance — secondary, behind, the one who comes after — and the poem will measure that distance exactly. Each sense of the word is live: the boy literally walks behind the plough; he is a would-be apprentice who copies the master's gestures; and he is the eldest son of a farming family who, in life, did not follow his father onto the land. The bare noun sounds modest and a little rueful, since a follower is never the leader. But it is also a riddle the last stanza solves: by the final line the father is the one walking behind, so the title has quietly changed hands. A further, more hopeful reading opens once the poem is finished: the son follows his father's craft in another medium, cutting lines of verse as carefully as furrows, so the title can name the poet's loyalty as well as his failure.

Line 1
the speaker remembers his father ploughing behind a team of horses
Language & devices

Declarative opening: possessive My father, plain past-tense verb worked, then the tool. Simple Anglo-Saxon diction, mostly monosyllables. The compound noun horse-plough puts two stresses together at the line-end, a heavy spondee. The preposition with suggests a partnership of man, animals and implement rather than a man merely using a tool. The comma lets the sentence run straight on into the description.

Meaning & effect

The poem opens like a caption under a photograph or a statement of record: who he was, and what he did. Worked is the key word, defining the father by labour before anything else, and the past tense already sets the scene in memory. Horse-plough dates that memory to the years before the tractor, so for a reader in 1966 the line was faintly elegiac: this was a skill on its way out. My father (not 'Dad') sets the emotional key: love expressed as respect, at a slight distance. The heavy double stress lands the plough solidly as the poem's first object, and plough will return as a rhyme-word in line 17, as the son's wish. The first line already holds the ambition the poem will measure.

Line 2
the father's shoulders swell, rounded like canvas filled by wind
Language & devices

Simile: the shoulders are compared to a full sail, the first of the poem's nautical images. Globed is a noun used as a verb (rounded into a globe), compact and physical. Three heavy monosyllables, full sail strung, end the line in a cluster of stresses (spondaic weight). Sibilance: shoulders… sail… strung. Strung means rigged and taut, but it is also a word for an instrument's strings (compare pluck, line 8). Synecdoche: the shoulders stand for the father's strength.

Meaning & effect

The father is seen from behind and below, at a small boy's eye level, as a broad curved back. Globed makes the shoulders huge and round, a whole world to the child (an association with Atlas, the giant who carries the globe on his shoulders, is possible, though nothing in the poem signals it). The sail simile turns effort into grace: a sail filled with wind is power that looks effortless, and the man becomes a vessel moving through the field as if through water. Strung adds tension, because ploughing pulls the body taut between the straining horses and the resisting earth. The three end-stresses slow the voice down so that we feel the weight. There is also a darker side to the image: a sail is driven by the wind, not in control of it, so the father may be strung between forces as well as mastering them. The picture is heroic, but it is also of a man bound to his work.

Line 3
his body taut between the plough's handles and the cut earth
Language & devices

Enjambment from line 2 (no punctuation after strung) completes the image. Between… and… places the body as the link between the two halves of the work. Technical nouns: shafts (the plough's long wooden members, its handles and beam; glossaries differ on the exact part) and furrow (the trench the plough cuts). Feminine ending: furrow ends on an unstressed syllable. Half-rhyme with plough (line 1). The line has only three strong beats (be-TWEEN the SHAFTS and the FUR-row), lighter than the lines on either side of it.

Meaning & effect

The father is fixed precisely in the working apparatus: suspended between the implement and the earth, he is the living connection that makes the plough work. The sail image completes itself, since a sail too is strung between fixed points, so craft and sea merge in one picture. The rhyme pairs plough with furrow, the tool with what it makes. That rhyme is only half a rhyme, though, and the line trails off on a soft unstressed syllable after the heavy line before. Furrow is also the poem's key word: the straight line the father cuts and, for a poet, the line of verse (the Latin versus, the root of 'verse', meant a turning, and so a furrow or a row; see Context). The son's word in stanza 5, follow, will take this rhyme slot and almost repeat its sound.

Line 4
the horses heave forward at a small click of his mouth
Language & devices

Strained is kinaesthetic imagery of effort against resistance. Onomatopoeia: clicking. Contrast between two big animals and one tiny sound. Hard /k/ sounds (clicking) close in the nasal ring of tongue. Full rhyme: tongue answers strung, and the full stop closes the stanza firmly.

Meaning & effect

The poem's first definition of mastery is economy. Two powerful horses straining against the plough obey a click of the tongue: no whip and no shout. Strained keeps the labour real, because the horses are pulling hard, and the father's gift is to direct great effort with the smallest signal, not to avoid effort. The clicking tongue is also the father's only 'speech' in the poem, a code without words that horses understand and a child can only admire. The Nobel Foundation's biography describes Patrick Heaney as 'notably sparing of talk', and the poem honours that silence by never giving him a word to say. This matters later, when the son's own tongue is heard Yapping in stanza 6. The full rhyme gives the first stanza a confident close: the picture is complete, and the man is in charge.

Line 5
a two-word verdict on his skill; he adjusts a blade
Language & devices

Minor sentence: An expert. Two words and a full stop, a verbless fragment that also makes a caesura after the third syllable. The Latinate noun expert comes from Latin expertus, 'tried, tested by experience'. Then the habitual modal would (what he always did). The precise verb set and the technical noun wing (a part of the plough, glossed as the share's side-blade or the part that turns the sod aside) follow.

Meaning & effect

The child's verdict comes first and the evidence after: the next three lines prove the two-word claim. The fragment is absolute, with no qualifying word, and it preserves the voice of a child's hero-worship inside the adult's poem. Expert is the only abstract praise the poem allows itself; everything else is shown in action. Its root fits well: an expert is someone tested by experience, whose knowledge comes from doing rather than from books, which quietly sets the father's kind of knowledge beside the son's later education. He would set the wing shifts into the habitual past, so this is not one remembered day but a ritual repeated season after season. Expertise, the line suggests, lives in small exact adjustments, not grand gestures. The full stop halting the rhythm after expert makes the child's awe audible as a pause.

Line 6
he fixes the shining steel-tipped ploughshare in place
Language & devices

Short, exact verb fit. Compound adjective steel-pointed. The dialect noun sock means a ploughshare (a northern English and Scots word, from Old French soc, generally thought to be of Celtic origin; compare Irish soc). A run of stresses, bright steel-point-, gives three heavy beats together. Plosives and dentals (b, t, p, k) and the visual image bright.

Meaning & effect

The language turns technical and the line becomes hard and bright, its consonants clicking together like metal parts fitting into place. Bright suggests a share scoured clean by use, so the shine is the record of work done. The specialist word sock (not the standard 'share') shows that the son knows his father's vocabulary from the inside: whatever else he failed to inherit, he inherited the words, and the poem is proof of it. The cluster of stresses slows the line so that we feel the weight of the steel. Steel-pointed gives the plough a weapon's edge, ploughing as a controlled violence against the ground. The very next line answers that hint with gentleness: the sod turns over without breaking.

Line 7
the turf turns over in one whole, unbroken strip
Language & devices

Imagery of smooth motion. Long, rounded vowels in rolled over. A negative used as praise, without breaking, which works like litotes: quality defined by what does not go wrong. Feminine ending breaking, half-rhyme with wing. End-stopped.

Meaning & effect

The proof of the father's skill is in the earth's response. The furrow-slice turns over in one unbroken strip, the mark of a well-set plough and a steady hand. The sound enacts the meaning: after line 6's clatter of consonants, this phrase rolls smoothly. Rolled keeps the sea in play (the turning sod is like a wave turning over, though the poem never says 'wave'). Without breaking is the poem's standard of perfection, wholeness, and it stands against everything that comes later: the son who stumbled and Fell, and the father who will stumble in his turn. At this point in the poem the phrase also describes the father himself: whole, steady, unbroken.

Line 8
at the turning-strip by the field's edge, one light tug
Language & devices

The dialect noun headrig is Scots heid-rig, recorded from 1475 ('the headrig, or headland, in a ploughed field'): the strip at the field's end where the team turns, and rig is the Scots form of 'ridge'. A single pluck is economy in one monosyllable, with a musical overtone (plucking a string; compare strung, line 2). Enjambment: the line ends in mid-phrase, the only point where a sentence runs across a stanza break.

Meaning & effect

The line brings us to the end of the field, the moment of the turn. Single repeats the lesson of the clicking tongue: one tug turns the whole team. Pluck is light, almost musical, as if the father played the reins like strings, so mastery here looks like artistry. Then the syntax refuses to stop, and a single pluck hangs over the white space of the stanza break. The reader has to turn the corner with the horses, and the form performs the action: the stanza turns where the plough turns. Readers often connect this with the root of 'verse', the Latin versus, a turning, as of the plough at the end of a furrow. Heaney's later work makes ploughing an open figure for writing, and this is the moment in 'Follower' where the figure is acted out rather than stated.

Line 9
on the lines swings the lathered pair about
Language & devices

The enjambed sentence lands across the stanza break, on the reins. A comma caesura follows. Juxtaposition of the father's tiny gesture with the sweating team. A cluster of stresses, team turned round, gives the turn its weight. Full rhyme: round / ground (line 11).

Meaning & effect

The turn is completed: the sentence crosses the gap between stanzas just as the horses wheel at the headrig and set off the other way. Sweating keeps the scene honest, because this is heavy labour and not a pastoral postcard. The contrast between one small pluck of the reins and the animals' straining bulk is the poem's whole idea of control in miniature. The three heavy stresses of team turned round make the wheeling feel physical and slow, a big body changing direction. The full rhyme with ground gives this turning stanza a firm frame, as if the furrow were squared off cleanly at the end.

Line 10
and they return to work; then his gaze
Language & devices

Back into the land: the preposition into suggests going into an element, not merely across a surface. A full stop mid-line (caesura), then enjambment leaves the father's eye hanging at the line-end. Synecdoche: eye stands for judgement. Half-rhyme: eye / exactly (stressed against unstressed).

Meaning & effect

The team goes back into the land as a boat goes back into the sea: the field is an element the man and horses enter and belong to. The mid-line full stop closes the turn neatly; then the focus jumps from the horses to the father's face, a cinematic cut from wide shot to close-up, isolated at the end of the line. The eye is where the real expertise lives (strength is in the shoulders, but skill is in the eye), and leaving it hanging makes the reader look, as the child looked. The pattern of large action followed by tiny precise action (the team turning, then the eye narrowing) repeats the pairing of horses and click in stanza 1. Back will return in stanza 4, as the father's back that carries the boy.

Line 11
squints and slants down towards the soil
Language & devices

Trochaic inversion: the line opens on a stress, Narrowed. Paired precise verbs, Narrowed and angled. A semantic field of measurement and geometry (narrowed, angled, mapping, exactly). Full rhyme: ground / round.

Meaning & effect

The father squints along the furrow, sighting a straight line, the gesture the boy will copy in line 18 (To close one eye). The verbs are geometrical, almost scientific: the ploughman works like a surveyor, or like a navigator taking a bearing with a sextant, a comparison that suits the poem's sea imagery. The stressed first syllable gives the narrowing a little jolt of concentration. The line ends on ground, the stubborn reality all this precision is aimed at. The tone is pure admiration: the child has watched so closely that he can record not just that his father looked, but how the eye changed shape.

Line 12
charting each furrow's course with precision
Language & devices

Metaphor: Mapping, ploughing as cartography, lines drawn on the land. The adverb exactly is the stanza's last word and a feminine ending. A falling rhythm (MAP-ping the FUR-row ex-ACT-ly) with only three strong beats. Half-rhyme: exactly / eye. The line is end-stopped and closes the father's half of the poem (three stanzas, twelve lines).

Meaning & effect

Mapping turns ploughing into a kind of writing on the land: the father draws straight lines on a blank field. For a poet the image is irresistible, since the field becomes the page and the furrow the line. Exactly is the father's standard, and it becomes the son's standard as a writer: the whole poem tries to describe him exactly. There is a quiet irony in the line, though: the line about exactness is itself rhythmically loose, and its rhyme (eye / exactly) is inexact, as if the son's lines cannot quite match the father's furrows. With this full stop the poem's first half ends, and the father's mastery is complete; from here on the poem belongs to the son.

Line 13
the boy totters along in the track of his studded boots
Language & devices

The first-person I enters for the first time, after twelve lines: exactly halfway. The verb stumbled sets the son's clumsiness against the father's verbs of control (set, fit, turned). Hobnailed means boots with short, heavy-headed nails studding the soles. Metaphor: wake, the trail of disturbed water behind a ship, continues the nautical strand. A fairly regular iambic tetrameter.

Meaning & effect

The son enters only at the halfway point, and he enters falling behind. The father has been all verbs of control; the son's first verb is stumbled. Hobnailed wake is a brilliant compression: the father's studded boots print a churned track in the soil as a ship leaves a wake on water, and the boy is tossed about in it like a small boat behind a big one. The idiom 'in someone's wake' (following, left behind) is part of the meaning. So the boy follows in his father's footsteps in the most literal sense, and fails even at that: the footsteps are too big for him. Some readers also hear the other 'wake', the Irish vigil over the dead. It is a different word, so this is a pun the reader brings, not one the line spells out, but it lets a shadow of the father's death into the poem very early.

Line 14
now and then tumbling onto the shiny turned earth
Language & devices

The line opens on a stress, Fell (an initial inversion), so the fall happens at the very start of the line. Repetition: sometimes (then Sometimes, line 15). Polished sod is the turned furrow-slice, left smooth and shiny by the steel. The semicolon balances this line against the next.

Meaning & effect

The verb lands first, and the rhythm itself falls. The polished sod is the father's finished work, smooth and gleaming, and the boy falls onto it: the follower cannot keep his feet on his father's masterpiece, and perhaps spoils it. Polished makes the earth something crafted and finished, like a shoe or a piece of furniture, the product of an artist's care. Sometimes softens the confession (not always), and the semicolon holds the sentence open for its kinder second half. Falling and being carried are set side by side, so the father who makes the boy feel small is also the one who lifts him.

Line 15
at times his father carries him piggyback
Language & devices

Anaphora: Sometimes answers sometimes in line 14. Active voice, father as subject and son as object (he rode me), with an unusual transitive use of rode: the father 'rides' the boy, meaning he carries him. Back echoes line 10. Enjambment runs into line 16.

Meaning & effect

This is the most tender moment in the poem: the expert stoops to lift the nuisance onto his back for a piggyback. The repeated sometimes pairs failure with comfort (sometimes he fell, sometimes he was carried), and the pairing is the father's kindness built into the syntax. Grammatically the boy is the object: he does nothing and is simply carried, which shows his dependence. The odd verb makes the father both rider and horse: he does the riding, yet he also bears the weight like his team. This is the poem's only moment of physical contact between father and son, and it is the image the last stanza turns inside out.

Line 16
the boy bobbing up and down with each heavy step
Language & devices

Rhythmic mimesis: a falling-then-rising rhythm (DIP-ping and RI-sing to his PLOD) rocks like a walk. Paired present participles, Dipping and rising, are nautical imagery (a boat on a swell). Plod is a slow, heavy, steady walk. Full rhyme: plod / sod. End-stopped.

Meaning & effect

The line's rhythm rocks the reader the way the boy is rocked on his father's back: we feel the walk. Dipping and rising carries on the sea image, so the boy rides his father like a small boat on a swell, and the father is both ship and sea. Plod is deliberately unheroic: not a stride but a heavy, patient, reliable gait. The honest word is itself a form of love, and it keeps the hero human. The full rhyme closes the stanza securely; this is the only stanza that ends on comfort, the child safe and held. What the boy feels in his body here, the father's rhythm, is perhaps the deepest thing he inherits, and the poem reproduces it as metre.

Line 17
the child longed to become a ploughman himself
Language & devices

A plain declarative of desire. The infinitive phrase grow up and plough runs adulthood and the trade together. A spondee, grow up, comes after a pyrrhic (i WANT-ed to GROW UP and PLOUGH). Plough returns as an end-word from line 1. Half-rhyme: plough / follow (line 19).

Meaning & effect

The child's ambition is stated with complete simplicity: to grow up meant to plough, because to the boy adulthood and his father's trade are one thing. The spondee leans hard on grow up, giving the wish its urgency. The return of plough to the end of the line ties the son's wish to the father's fact in line 1. But in line 1 plough rhymed with furrow; here it will rhyme with follow. The rhyme scheme tells the story of the ambition before the next lines admit it: where the father produced furrows, the son produced only following. Heaney, the eldest son, did not take on the farm, so the wish recorded here went unfulfilled, at least in the form the boy imagined.

Line 18
to copy the one-eyed squint and the braced arm
Language & devices

Two infinitives of imitation, To close one eye and the braced arm (stiffen), set side by side without a conjunction (asyndeton). A comma caesura after eye. Monosyllables throughout. An echo of line 11 (the narrowed eye): gestures copied. The rhythm shifts after the comma (STIFF-en my ARM).

Meaning & effect

To the boy, being a ploughman means copying two gestures he has watched: the closed eye that sights the furrow and the braced arm that holds the plough steady. It is a child's imitation, the posture without the skill, like copying the shape of handwriting without knowing what the words say. The line moves us because it shows how closely he watched: he knows exactly what his father's body does, even if he cannot do it. Stiffen also hints at how a child imagines manhood: as rigidity, effort, holding firm. A further possibility is that one closed eye means half-sight: the boy saw only part of his father, and the adult poem is an attempt to see him whole.

Line 19
but all he managed was to trail after him
Language & devices

A flat, colloquial self-judgement, All I ever did. The title-word follow stands at the line-end. Pure trochaic tetrameter (ALL i EV-er DID was FOL-low), the only line in the poem that falls from start to finish. Feminine ending. Half-rhyme with plough. Hyperbole in ever.

Meaning & effect

This is the son's verdict on himself: nothing but following. The rhythm reverses, and the poem's usual rising beat turns falling for one line, as if the line itself trails along behind. Ever stretches the admission over the whole of childhood, and an adult might hear in it a sigh about a whole life spent in someone else's track. The tone is rueful, even comic in its bluntness. Follow now explains the title, and it occupies the rhyme slot furrow had in line 3: the father made furrows, and the son followed them. Yet there is hidden pride in the line too. Following is how apprentices learn, and the poem, cut as carefully as any furrow, is the evidence that the following was not wasted.

Line 20
in the big man's shade, all over the farm
Language & devices

Metaphor and symbol: broad shadow. A spondee, broad shad-, after two light syllables (a pyrrhic). Round the farm suggests circling and limits. Full rhyme: farm / arm. End-stopped.

Meaning & effect

The father's shadow is literally big (he is a broad man) and symbolically overwhelming, since to live in someone's shadow is to be overshadowed and eclipsed. But a shadow also shelters, giving shade from the sun, so the image holds protection and limitation at once: the boy is safe there, and unseen. Round the farm suggests endless circling inside a bounded space, the farm as the whole world of childhood, never outside his father's shade. The full rhyme closes the son's section firmly: this was the whole of childhood. And the broad shadow is exactly what the last stanza turns around, because the father who once fell across the son now falls in behind him.

Line 21
he admits he was a pest, forever losing his footing
Language & devices

A noun of adult self-judgement, nuisance. An asyndetic list of present participles, tripping, falling, running on into Yapping (line 22); the commas act as caesuras. Feminine ending falling, half-rhyme with stumbling. Anaphora: I opens stanzas 4, 5 and 6.

Meaning & effect

The adult speaker sums up the child bluntly: a nuisance, the word an exasperated grown-up might use of a child under his feet.
