The list of -ing words piles up restless, uncontrolled movement, the opposite of the father's single, exact actions; the participles are continuous, so the nuisance was ongoing. The tone could be rueful (he winces at the child he was) or fond (he smiles at him); the word does not decide. The pattern of I opening the son's three stanzas (I stumbled, I wanted, I was) makes this half of the poem a series of confessions. Here the word is still turned on the boy alone; within two lines the poem will look for its echo in the father.

Line 22
forever chattering like a pup; then the present breaks in
Language & devices

Onomatopoeia: Yapping (a small dog). A full stop mid-line (caesura), then the volta: But today. This is the shortest line, at seven syllables, and it opens on trochees. Enjambment after today.

Meaning & effect

Yapping makes the boy a little dog at a working man's heels: noisy, irritating, useless. It is also language, the son's tongue set against the father's click. There is an irony buried here: the yapping boy grows up to be the poet, the one in the family who works with words. Then, after the full stop, two words switch the poem from past to present after twenty-one and a half lines of memory. The turn comes late and suddenly, in mid-line, like a thought that interrupts the speaker. The shortness of the line makes it abrupt, as though the rhythm itself loses its footing at the point of change, and today is left hanging at the line-end, waiting for what it will reveal.

Line 23
now the roles reverse: the father is the unsteady one
Language & devices

Cleft sentence (the 'it is X who…' pattern), which throws emphasis onto the reversed subject, the father. Present continuous: keeps stumbling (repeated, ongoing). Verbal echo: stumbled (line 13) becomes stumbling. Feminine ending, half-rhyme with falling.

Meaning & effect

This is the reversal: the verb that belonged to the boy now belongs to the father. The cleft construction puts the father in the spotlight with a note of surprise, as if to say it is he, of all people. Keeps makes the stumbling a pattern rather than a single slip. Crucially, the poem does not say why he stumbles. Old age is one inference, since years have passed, but the poem never calls him old or says he depends on his son. The stumbling can also be figurative: the father as a memory that trails after the son, the old way of life out of step in the son's educated world, or a conscience the son cannot shake off. Whichever it is, the expert has been given the child's clumsiness, and the precise echo of stumbled makes the reversal feel exact, almost designed, like a furrow ploughed back the other way.

Line 24
he trails his son and refuses to leave
Language & devices

A spatial reversal: the line opens by placing the father at the speaker's back. A comma pause. The modal will not expresses refusal (volitional will, not just the future). Idiom: go away, what one says to a pest. Full rhyme: away / today, the most emphatic close in the poem. Nine syllables with crowded, irregular stresses (WILL NOT GO a-WAY): the line will not scan smoothly. End-stopped on the poem's last full stop.

Meaning & effect

The father now follows. Will not go away is the poem's most open phrase. It can sound impatient, the adult irritated as the father may once have been by the yapping boy; haunted, a memory that will not leave; guilty, because the son who did not follow cannot escape his father's example; or loving, he will always be with me. The modal matters: will not means refuses to, so the persistence is the father's own choice, his will, as strong as ever. The full rhyme seals the stanza, so the presence sounds fixed and permanent, while the bumpy rhythm makes the line itself stumble. And the poem is its own proof: the father who will not go away has been kept in it for good. Read after Patrick Heaney's death in 1986, the line also takes on a ghostly sense, one the poem could not have intended in 1966 but cannot now shake off.

THE WHOLE POEM

The Whole Poem

Stepping back: what the poem is doing, first line to last

'Follower' is built like the work it describes. It goes up the field one way and comes back down the other, so that by the last furrow everything has been turned over: the leader follows, the expert stumbles, the past gives way to today. The poem's argument is not simply that the father was a hero and the son a disappointment. It is that what passes from father to son is not the trade but the standard, and that this inheritance is a debt that can be neither repaid nor left behind. The father will not go away because the son has become, in another medium, the thing he admired.

The title states the son's position before the father appears: secondary, behind, the one who comes after. Then the first line states the father's position as plain fact: My father worked. No adjectives, no feelings; the poem's love will be shown as attention, not declared. The first three stanzas are an argument by demonstration. At their centre stands a two-word verdict, An expert., and everything around it is evidence: the body (shoulders globed), the voice (his clicking tongue), the hands (set the wing, the bright steel-pointed sock), the earth's response (rolled over without breaking), the turn at the headrig, and finally the eye (Narrowed and angled). Each image pairs force with lightness. The shoulders are huge, but they belong to a sail, which is power that looks effortless; the horses strain, but they are steered by a click; the whole sweating team wheels round on a single pluck of the reins. Mastery, in this poem, is great effort made to look easy, and the child's admiration is above all admiration for economy.

The poem does more than describe that economy: it performs it. The only sentence that runs across a stanza break does so exactly at the headrig, so the reader has to turn the corner with the horses, and the stanza turns where the plough turns. The Latin versus, from which 'verse' descends, meant a turning, and so a furrow and a line; whether or not Heaney had the etymology in mind, the poem shows that a line of verse can be cut like a furrow. The section closes on exactly, the father's standard, which becomes the poem's. Even here there is a small confession. The line about exactness falls loosely, and its rhyme (eye against exactly) does not quite match. The son's furrows are not as straight as his father's, and the poem lets us hear it.

Only at the halfway mark does the son appear, and he appears falling behind: I stumbled. Where the father had verbs of control, the son has verbs of accident: stumbled, Fell. The images that glorified the father now measure the boy's smallness. The ship's wake becomes the churned track of hobnailed boots, too big to walk in, and the polished sod, the father's finished work, is what the boy slips on. Yet stanza 4 is also where the poem stops the father from being merely a monument. Sometimes, the poem says, he rode me on his back: the expert stoops to carry the nuisance, and the rhythm of Dipping and rising lets us feel the walk from the child's perch. The word plod is deliberately unheroic, and it makes the hero human, slow, patient and kind. The boy's helplessness is answered by the father's strength, and that exchange is the hinge on which the ending will turn.

Stanza 5 states the desire and its failure in one breath. He wanted to grow up and plough: to the boy, adulthood and the father's trade are the same thing, and he imagines it as two copied gestures, To close one eye and a stiffened arm. Then comes the flat verdict, All I ever did, in the poem's only wholly falling line, and its last word, follow, takes the rhyme slot that furrow held in the first stanza. The rhyme scheme tells the story: where the father produced furrows, the son produced following. The broad shadow gathers the poem's double feeling into one image, because a shadow both shelters and eclipses. The boy is safe in his father's shade and invisible in it.

The last stanza begins with the harshest word the son uses: he was a nuisance, Yapping like a pup at a working man's heels. Then, after a full stop in mid-line, the poem turns. But today: after twenty-one and a half lines of past tense, the present arrives, and every position is reversed. The father keeps stumbling, the son's own verb from line 13; he is behind; and he will not go away.

The strongest objection is that this ending is cold: an impatient adult complaining about an ageing father who has become a burden, so that the reversal undoes the tribute that came before. Elmer Andrews, among the poem's critics, notes how unusually frankly it admits that family ties can be a burden as well as a support, and some readers hear nothing but exasperation in the last line. The poem's own words resist that reading in three ways. First, it never says the father is old or dependent. It transfers to him the child's verbs, stumbling, following, refusing to leave, so the son is recognising his childhood self in the father, not passing judgement on a stranger. Second, will not expresses will, not mere futurity: the father's persistence is a refusal, as forceful as the hand that turned the team. Third, the words of exasperation are the words the son has already used of himself. He was the nuisance; now he is the one with a follower he cannot shake off, and the question the poem leaves is whether he will carry this follower as patiently as he was once carried. The impatience, if it is there, is honest, and the honesty is what makes the earlier love believable. James Simmons, who was dismissive of much of Heaney's first book, singled 'Follower' out for exactly this outspokenness.

There is a final reason the father will not go away: the poem itself. The son who could not cut a furrow has cut twenty-four lines in six even quatrains, held together by rhyme and four-beat rhythm, and in them the father works for ever at the plough. The last turn of the poem is a ploughman's turn. The son now walks in front, but the line he cuts runs alongside his father's, and the father is still there, just behind him, in every line. 'Follower' does not settle whether that presence is a comfort, a haunting or a reproach. It insists, with the full chime of today against away, that it is permanent.

FORM & STRUCTURE

Form & Structure

How the poem is built, and why it matters

Form & genre

Six quatrains, twenty-four lines: a first-person lyric of memory in three movements. The father works (stanzas 1–3), the child follows (4–5), and the present arrives (6). There is no dialogue and no named place or date: one remembering voice in plain words, with an ending that turns the whole memory around.

Stanza plan

Twelve lines for the father, twelve for the son, and of the son's twelve only the last two and a half belong to today. The father fills the first half of the poem as completely as he filled the field.

Metre

A loose four-beat line with an iambic (da-DUM) tendency rather than strict iambic tetrameter. Sixteen lines have eight syllables, seven have nine, and one has seven. Some lines carry only three strong beats, some crowd four or five stresses together, and line 19 is wholly trochaic.

Rhyme

ABAB in every stanza: five full rhymes and seven half-rhymes. Plough is used as a rhyme-word twice, matched first with furrow and then with follow. Six lines end on an unstressed (feminine) syllable.

Syntax

Short, plain sentences: one verbless fragment (An expert.), one sentence that runs across a stanza break (lines 8–10), and one cleft sentence in the last stanza. Every stanza except the second ends on a full stop.

Turns

There are two. A physical turn comes at the headrig, where the sentence wheels across the stanza break with the horses. A turn in time comes with the volta, But today, in the middle of line 22.

Stanza logic

The poem is laid out like a field. The first half (stanzas 1–3, twelve lines) belongs entirely to the father. It moves from the whole man to the smallest organ of his skill: the body (shoulders), the voice (clicking tongue), the hands (set, fit), the earth's response (without breaking), the turn at the headrig and, last, the eye. The second half (stanzas 4–6, twelve lines) belongs to the son. It moves from what he did (stumbled, Fell, was carried) to what he wanted, then to what he was (a nuisance), and in its last two and a half lines to what has happened since. The pronouns mark the division: He and his govern the first half, while I opens each of stanzas 4, 5 and 6 (I stumbled, I wanted, I was). The son's half therefore reads as a sequence of confessions.

The proportions matter. The father gets twelve lines of mastery, the son's childhood nine and a half, and the present two and a half. The poem's subject shrinks as it moves from the expert to the nuisance to the single today. Yet the last and shortest movement overturns everything before it, just as a few seconds at the headrig turn the whole team.

Metre: a four-beat line that stumbles

The poem is often labelled iambic tetrameter, but that label is only approximate. The ear hears a four-beat walking pulse (the plod) with an iambic tendency, constantly varied. Lines run from seven to nine syllables; some carry only three strong stresses, some pile them up, and a few reverse direction altogether. The variations are where the meaning is. In the table, x is an unstressed syllable, / a stressed one, and ‖ a full-stop pause.

Line Stress pattern Where it bites What the variation does
1 x / x / x x / / horse-plough Two stresses together at the line-end set the plough down heavily, the poem's first solid object.
2 x / x / x x / / / full sail strung Three heavy monosyllables: the strain and fullness of the sail-like back.
3 x / x / x x / x furrow Only three beats and a soft feminine close: the line slackens after the effort of line 2.
5 x / x ‖ x x / x / An expert. The full stop after the third syllable halts the metre: awe heard as a pause.
6 x / x / / / x / bright steel-pointed Three stresses in a row: the weight and hardness of steel.
9 x / x / x / / / team turned round Stresses pile up as the heavy team wheels at the headrig.
11 / x x / x x x / Narrowed The line opens on a stress: a jolt of concentration.
12 / x x / x x / x exactly A falling rhythm with three beats: the line about precision is itself loose.
14 / / x x x / x / Fell The line falls at its first syllable, as the boy does.
16 / x x / x x x / Dipping and rising Down, then up: the rocking walk felt from the father's back.
17 x / x x / / x / grow up Two light syllables, then two heavy ones: the wish pressed hard.
19 / x / x / x / x follow Four trochees, the only wholly falling line: the line itself trails behind.
20 x x / / x / x / broad shadow Light, light, then heavy, heavy: the father's bulk looms over the boy.
22 / x / x ‖ x x / But today Seven syllables, the shortest line: the rhythm loses its footing at the turn.
24 x / x x / / / x / will not go away Crowded stresses in a nine-syllable line: the last line will not scan smoothly, stumbling and persisting at once.

Two patterns stand out. First, the father's lines gather stresses on the objects and actions of the work (horse-plough, full sail strung, bright steel-pointed, team turned round), so the verse feels the weight he handles. Second, the son's lines tend to fall: they open on a stress (Fell, Dipping, All), end on an unstressed syllable, or both. The single wholly trochaic line, 19, is the son's verdict on himself, and its falling rhythm trails after the beat as he trailed after his father. In the last stanza the metre itself stumbles: a line of nine syllables, then one of seven, then two more of nine, so the father's new unsteadiness can be heard in the verse.

Rhyme, worked out

Stanza A rhyme (lines 1 and 3) B rhyme (lines 2 and 4)
1 plough / furrow: half (stressed against unstressed) strung / tongue: full
2 wing / breaking: half (on the unstressed -ing) sock / pluck: half (consonance on /k/)
3 round / ground: full eye / exactly: half (stressed against unstressed)
4 wake / back: half (consonance on /k/) sod / plod: full
5 plough / follow: half (an echo of stanza 1) arm / farm: full
6 falling / stumbling: half (both feminine) today / away: full

Every stanza keeps its ABAB shape, but only five of the twelve pairs rhyme fully, and every stanza except the second contains exactly one full pair. The full rhymes fall on strong, plain monosyllables (strung/tongue, round/ground, sod/plod, arm/farm, today/away). The half-rhymes are of two kinds: a stressed syllable matched with an unstressed one (plough/furrow, eye/exactly, plough/follow), or a match of final consonants only (sock/pluck, wake/back). The effect is of a close match that is never quite perfect, which is a fair description of a son's imitation of his father. Stanza 2, the stanza of technical words, is the only one with no full rhyme at all: there the exact word (sock, headrig) matters more than the chime.

The most telling pair is the one the poem repeats. Plough is a rhyme-word twice. In stanza 1 it rhymes with furrow: the tool with what it makes. In stanza 5 the son's wish to plough rhymes with follow, which is what he actually did. The rhyme scheme tells the story before the sentences do: the father produced furrows, and the son produced following. Furrow and follow are near-twins in sound, differing only in the doubled consonant (rr against ll), so the son's word sounds like a slightly mis-made copy of the father's.

Six lines end on an unstressed, 'feminine' syllable: furrow, breaking, exactly, follow, falling, stumbling. Each leaves a weak syllable trailing after the last beat, a small follower at the end of the line. In the final stanza both A-rhymes are feminine, so the falling-away sound gathers where the father stumbles. Then the poem closes on its most emphatic full rhyme, today against away, as if the present and the father's refusal to leave were sealed together.

Lineation, enjambment and caesura

In the father's stanzas, line-ends usually coincide with complete operations: he sets the wing, he fits the sock, the sod rolls over, each in its own line, as if the verse were laying out the job step by step. Enjambment is saved for moments of movement or suspension:

  • the body strung across lines 2–3;
  • the turn at the headrig across lines 8–9, the only sentence that crosses a stanza break;
  • the father's eye left hanging at the end of line 10;
  • the rocking piggyback across lines 15–16;
  • today left hanging at the end of line 22.

Lines 10 and 22 share a design. Each has a full stop in the middle, after which a new subject begins at the end of the line and runs over into the next: first the father's eye, then But today. The poem uses the same device for its two great shifts of attention, the first narrowing in on the father's skill and the second turning from the past to the present.

The son's stanzas are more broken. Commas cut line 18 in two and chop line 21 into a list, and a full stop splits line 22. Where the father's sentences flowed through the turn, the son's movements are jerky and interrupted, tripping, falling. The syntax acts out the difference in grace.

Syntax and tense

The father's half uses the habitual past (would set), so the ploughing is not one remembered day but a ritual repeated over years. Its single verbless fragment, An expert., is the child's absolute verdict. Its one long sentence, from the headrig to back into the land, is the poem's longest unbroken action, continuous like the plough. The son's half opens three times on I and a past verb, the grammar of confession. The final sentence is a cleft construction (the 'it is X who…' pattern), which throws all the emphasis onto the father and carries a note of surprise. Its verbs are the present continuous keeps stumbling (ongoing, repeated) and the modal will not (refusal). The shift from past to present tense is the volta.

The two turns

The headrig turn and the volta answer each other. At the headrig the team turns and comes back down the field alongside the furrow it has just cut. At But today the poem turns and comes back over its own material: the child's stumbled returns as the father's stumbling, following becomes being followed, and the boy behind becomes the man in front. The whole poem copies the structure of a ploughed field, with lines laid side by side and running in opposite directions. The last stanza is the return furrow.

SOUND

Sound

What the poem does to the ear

Consonants

Hard /k/ sounds return through the rhyme-sounds sock/pluck and wake/back, echoing the father's clicking. Plosives p and b recur (plough, pluck, plod, polished, back, broad), and s-sounds hiss through stanza 1.

Vowels

Long, rounded vowels fill the father's stanzas (shoulders, globed, rolled, over; plough, round, ground). They give way to short vowels and -ing endings in the son's.

Rhythm

A walking four-beat pulse, the plod, which strains, rocks and finally stumbles (see Form & Structure).

Onomatopoeia

Three signal-sounds: clicking and pluck for the father, Yapping for the child.

Stanza 1 is full of breath and hiss: shoulders, sail, strung, shafts, horses, strained. The s-sounds bind man, sail and team into one moving apparatus, and the stanza sounds like wind in canvas and effort under strain. Against that soft background, clicking is a sharp signal, and the poem keeps the click going underneath its rhymes. Two of the half-rhymes are pure /k/ consonance, sock / pluck and wake / back, and all four words name the father's doings: the share he fits, the tug he gives, the track he leaves, the back that carries the boy. Wherever the father acts, the line tends to end on his click.

A second family of sounds binds tool, gesture and gait together: plough, pluck, plod, with polished close by. The man who plods behind the plough turns it with a pluck, and the shared pl- makes them one person in sound. When the boy says he wanted to grow up and plough, the cluster comes back in his mouth: he can say the word, even if he cannot do the work.

The father's stanzas are rich in long, rounded vowels: the /əʊ/ of shoulders, globed and rolled over, the /aʊ/ of plough, round and ground. They are as rounded as the shoulders and the turning sod they describe, and they make the father's world sound full and whole, unbroken like the sod. The son's stanzas turn to short vowels and the unstressed -ing endings of participles: Dipping and rising, then tripping, falling, Yapping, stumbling. These are the sounds of small, repeated, unfinished movements. Several of them fall at line-ends as feminine endings, so the weak syllable trails after the beat like the boy after the man. By the last stanza the round vowels have almost gone. Only go keeps one: an echo of the father's sound in the very phrase that says he will not leave.

Onomatopoeia carries the poem's contrast between two kinds of voice. The father's sounds are signals that work: a click that sets two horses straining, a pluck that turns the team. The child's sound is noise that achieves nothing: Yapping, a pup at a working man's heels. The irony is that the yapper grows up to be the one in the family who works with words. This poem is his voice at last doing what the father's click did, directing a heavy, living material with exactness.

Last, the sound of the ending. Will not go away is a run of heavy monosyllables that slows the voice almost to a halt, so the refusal is heard as weight. Then the open vowel of away chimes fully with today. The last line stumbles in its rhythm and lands on the poem's firmest rhyme: unsteady, and permanent.

MOTIFS & SYMBOLS

Motifs & Symbols

Images that recur, and what they accumulate

Motifs and symbols

1. Following and being behind

The title names the motif, and the poem traces it through the son's whole life. First it is physical: the boy stumbled in the father's hobnailed wake, the track of boot-prints left in the soil, and the idiom 'in someone's wake' (following, left behind) is part of the meaning. Then it becomes imitation. He copies gestures (To close one eye), and the summary All I ever did turns the whole of childhood into following. Then it becomes eclipse: his broad shadow, where to follow is to live in someone's shade, sheltered and unseen. Finally the motif changes owner, and the father is the one behind, who keeps stumbling at his son's back. The motif grows from a boy's walk into a life's relationship, and its last appearance turns it inside out.

2. The sea in the field

A strand of nautical imagery runs through a poem set entirely on dry land: the full sail of the shoulders, strung like rigging; the sod that rolled over like a wave; the team going back into the land as a boat goes back to sea; the boy in the wake; the piggyback Dipping and rising like a small boat on a swell. These images make the father a ship or its captain, a power moving with grace through a heavy element, and they make the field as alive as water. They also build a relationship: the boy first bobs helplessly in the father's wake, then rides on him as on a ship. In the final stanza the sea has gone completely: no sail, no wave, no wake. The father has lost his element.

3. The eye

Skill in this poem lives in the eye. The father's eye is isolated at a line-end, then Narrowed and angled, then Mapping. The eye that keeps the furrow straight is the father's intelligence, the part that stands for the whole. The boy's ambition is to copy it, To close one eye, and the poem itself is the work of another eye, the child's, which watched closely enough to remember exactly how his father's face changed. In the last stanza the looking has stopped. The father is behind, out of sight, felt rather than seen, and the watcher has become the one who is followed.

4. Breaking and stumbling

The poem's standard of perfection is wholeness: the sod turns over without breaking. Everything else in the poem is measured against that. The boy stumbled and Fell, and the last stanza's list (tripping, falling) piles up the opposite of the unbroken sod. Then the breaking reaches the father, who keeps stumbling. The motif carries a sense of time: what was whole at the start (the sod, the father) cannot stay whole, and the poem's own rhythm stumbles in its last line.

5. Tongue and voice

The father has a tongue but no words. His clicking tongue is a signal his horses obey, and the Nobel biography's description of Patrick Heaney as 'notably sparing of talk' fits a poem that never lets him speak. The child's tongue makes noise to no purpose: Yapping. Between these two tongues lies the poem itself, the son's voice grown up, doing in words what the father did with a click: controlling a heavy, living material with small, exact signals. The motif becomes the poem's quiet claim about inheritance. The son did not get the plough; he got a tongue, and learned to use it like his father.

THEMES

Themes

The ideas the poem is arguing about

01

Inheritance: the standard, not the trade

'Follower' asks what a son inherits from a father whose skill he cannot follow, and its answer is precise. He does not inherit the plough: the wish to grow up and plough ends in following. He inherits the vocabulary, used as an insider uses it, without explanation: wing, sock, headrig, sod. He inherits the habit of exact attention: the boy recorded how the eye Narrowed and angled and what the arm did. Above all he inherits the standard, exactly, and the poem is that inheritance made visible: twenty-four lines cut as carefully as furrows.

Heaney's companion poem 'Digging', which opens the same book, makes the exchange explicit: the son has 'no spade to follow men like them', so he will dig with his pen. 'Follower' never says so; it simply shows the craft passing into a new medium. But inheritance here is also a debt. The father who will not go away is a standard the son can never finish meeting, and the poem ends with the debt still open.

02

Craft and mastery

Ploughing is presented as an art and the ploughman as an artist. The father's work is a sequence of exact operations: he would set the wing, fit the bright steel-pointed sock, turn the team at the headrig and sight along the furrow. His mastery is economy. Two straining horses obey his clicking tongue; the sweating team turns on a single pluck. The proof is in the material, the sod that rolled over without breaking, and the metaphor of Mapping makes the work a kind of writing on the land.

The poem refuses to treat farm work as unskilled. It gives that work the precision of technical language and pays the craftsman the tribute of getting his words right. The same respect makes the comparison with the poet's own craft possible, because both trades are judged by one standard: exactly.

03

Love without words

The love in this poem is never stated. It appears as attention, in the child's minute observation of every setting and gesture, and in one moment of touch: rode me on his back, Dipping and rising to the father's walk. The father speaks only in clicks. The son is the talker, remembered as Yapping, and the poem is his attempt to say in words what the father showed in action.

There is no hostility here. The father's patience in carrying the boy who gets under his feet is the poem's quiet proof of love, and it gives the last stanza its moral weight: the son who was carried must now decide how to bear a follower of his own.

04

Time and the reversal of roles

Twenty-one and a half lines of past tense are followed by But today. The poem is built to deliver one reversal, and it does so with words it has already used. The child stumbled; now the father keeps stumbling. The boy followed; now the father is behind. The plough turns the soil over, and time turns the relationship over: what was strong becomes unsteady, and what was small takes the lead.

The poem presents this universal experience (children outgrow and overtake their parents) without naming age, illness or decline. Instead it offers the reversal as a mirror: the son now sees in his father the clumsy child he was, so the change feels less like a judgement than a recognition.

05

Leaving the land

Heaney was the eldest son of a farming family, and he left the farm for a scholarship at twelve. The poem never mentions school or books, but this departure is its buried subject. In the field the son is behind; by the end he is ahead, in a life the father does not share, and the father trails after him. Alan Peacock reads the father's halting gait in the last stanza as the measure of the son's departure from his father's tradition, and Elmer Andrews reads the poem as marking a boundary between an unreflective rural life and the self-conscious world of literature.

Guilt is never stated. It lives in the image of a father left behind who will not leave, and in the son's harsh words about himself. To write about the farm at all is already to stand outside it, and to pay what Heaney, writing about Patrick Kavanagh, called 'the penalty of consciousness'.

06

Memory that will not go away

The last line is finally about memory. The father exists in the present only in the son's experience (today), and the modal will not gives him a will of his own. The past does not release us, and the people who made us walk behind us for the rest of our lives. Whether this persistence is comfort, haunting, burden or conscience, the poem refuses to decide.

The poem also enacts what it describes. A memory that would not go away became a poem, and the poem keeps the father at the plough permanently. Read after Patrick Heaney's death in 1986, the line gains a further sense: the father who will not go away is the father the later poems kept meeting.

DIFFICULT MOMENTS

Difficult Moments

Where the poem is genuinely undecidable — and what to do about it

Cruxes

1. What exactly has been reversed in the last stanza?

The difficulty. The last stanza says the father keeps stumbling behind the son, but not why or how. Many readers assume old age and dependence; the poem names neither.

Competing readings. (a) Literal: years have passed, the father has aged, and his body is now unsteady. Evidence: the time-word today, the present continuous keeps, a verb of physical clumsiness. (b) Figurative: the father is a memory or a conscience that trails the son through adult life. Evidence: will not go away sounds like a thought one cannot shake off, and the father is behind like the past. (c) Social: the son has moved into a world of education and words where the father is the clumsy outsider, so the expert of the field becomes a beginner in the son's world. Evidence: the poem's whole structure of expertise turned the other way round. (d) Retrospective: Patrick Heaney was alive in 1966 and died in 1986, and a reader now may hear a ghost.

What a strong answer does. It notices that the poem transfers the child's exact words (stumbling, following, being a nuisance) to the father, so the reversal is above all a mirror: whatever the cause, the son now sees in his father the child he was. It holds the literal and figurative senses together rather than choosing between them, and it does not treat 'old age' or 'dependence' as if the poem stated them.

2. will not go away: exasperation, haunting or devotion?

The difficulty. The last phrase is what one says of a pest, but it could equally be what one says of a love that lasts.

Competing readings. Exasperation: this is the idiom of irritation, and the son has just called himself a nuisance, so the roles have swapped, irritation included; the modal will not hardens the tone. Haunting or guilt: the son who left the land cannot escape the father's example, and the father follows him as a reproach. Devotion: the father's loyalty means he goes on following because he loves, and the full rhyme of today with away seals his presence as permanent. Elmer Andrews takes the poem as unusually frank in showing family as a burden as well as a support, which allows both the exasperated and the devoted readings at once.

What a strong answer does. It hears more than one tone and shows which words produce each: the colloquial idiom (impatience), the volitional will (the father's will, not just the future), the echo of nuisance, and a rhythm that stumbles before closing on a full rhyme. It sees that the poem's honesty about impatience is what makes its love believable.

3. Is the son a failure?

The difficulty. The son judges himself harshly (All I ever did, a nuisance, Yapping), yet he is the one who made the poem.

Competing readings. (a) Plain confession: he failed to inherit the craft and the farm, and says so. (b) Adult irony: the self-mockery is affectionate hindsight and comic exaggeration (ever, always). (c) Hidden success: following is how apprentices learn, and the poem, made with care in rhymed quatrains, proves that he inherited the standard in another medium. The 'yapper' became a poet.

What a strong answer does. It sets the son's words about himself against what the poem does. The gap between the confession and the craftsmanship is part of the meaning: the poem's lines contradict the speaker's verdict on himself.

4. Who is the follower?

The difficulty. The title is a singular noun, but by the end it fits two people.

Competing readings. The boy: the literal follower in the furrow and the would-be successor. The father: he follows the son in the last stanza. The poet: a follower in the sense of a disciple, carrying his father's craft into words, or (as Bradley Skeen argues) keeping a lost tradition alive by writing about it. Even the poem follows the father's pattern, laying its lines side by side like furrows.

What a strong answer does. It treats the title as something the poem changes: a label for the son at the start and for the father at the end, so the title itself performs the reversal. It also notes the missing article ('Follower', not 'The Follower'), which lets the noun float between the two men.

5. Hero or man: does the poem idealise the father?

The difficulty. Stanzas 1–3 read like hero-worship: the sail, the expert, the exact eye. Is the portrait a child's myth?

Competing readings. Idealised: the child's-eye view enlarges the father (globed shoulders, a broad shadow), the nautical imagery makes him a captain, and the whole first half works like a monument. John Boly reads the poem as a kind of eulogy and funerary monument. Realistic: the poem keeps the labour honest (strained, sweating, plod) and records the father's patience as well as his power. Boly too sees the last lines as deliberately breaking the idealised, timeless image.

What a strong answer does. It separates the child's view (preserved in An expert.) from the adult's frame (the hindsight of nuisance and today), and shows that the poem needs both. The idealised father is real to the child, and the stumbling father is real to the man.

CLOSE ANALYSIS

Close Analysis

The moments that repay pressure, worked through

Quotation analysis

1. globed like a full sail

Coined verb; nautical simile; stress cluster.

A noun becomes a verb: globed makes the shoulders rounded and enormous, a world seen from a small boy's height. The simile then turns muscle into canvas. A sail full of wind is power that looks effortless, and the comparison gives the labouring father grace: he moves through the field like a ship through water. The stresses gather at the end of the line (full sail strung), so the voice slows under the weight, and strung adds tension, a body rigged taut between plough and earth. The image begins the poem's strand of sea-imagery (wake, dipping and rising), which makes the farm an element and the father its master.

Intention and effect: Heaney opens with the child's-eye view at its most heroic, so the reader feels the scale of the man the son must measure himself against.

2. his clicking tongue

Onomatopoeia; contrast; sound-signal.

Two powerful horses strained, and what directs them is the smallest sound a person can make. The /k/ clicks are audible in the word itself, and the line defines mastery as economy: maximum effect from minimum signal. It is also the father's only 'speech' in the poem. He talks to animals in a code without words, and the son, the poem's talker, is defined against this by his Yapping. The poem never gives the father a sentence to say.

Intention and effect: the father's authority is shown as quiet competence, not force, and the motif of two tongues (clicking and yapping) begins.

3. An expert.

Minor sentence; caesura; Latinate diction.

A two-word verdict, then a full stop: no verb, no qualification, the voice of a child's hero-worship preserved in the adult's poem. Expert is the only abstract praise the poem allows. Everything around it is demonstration, and the lines that follow are the evidence. The word's Latin root (expertus, 'tested by experience') suits a skill learned in the field rather than from books, and quietly sets the father's knowledge beside the son's later education. The full stop also stops the metre, so the awe is heard as a pause.

Intention and effect: the bluntness makes the admiration feel absolute and unarguable, which is exactly how it felt to the child.

4. bright steel-pointed sock and without breaking

Technical and dialect diction; stress cluster; contrast of sound.

The specialist word sock (a northern English and Scots word for a ploughshare, from Old French soc) shows the son speaking his father's language from the inside. The cluster of stresses (bright steel-point-) and the hard consonants make the line clank like metal fitting metal, and steel-pointed gives the share a weapon's edge. The next line answers with smoothness: the sod rolled over without breaking, in long vowels and an unbroken phrase. Force is in the tool; gentleness is in the result. The unbroken sod is the poem's image of perfect skill, and its standard of wholeness is what the son, and later the father, will fail to keep.

Intention and effect: the reader hears the difference between effort and ease, and learns what 'expert' means in the father's world: power so well controlled that the earth turns over whole.

5. a single pluck

Enjambment across the stanza break; juxtaposition; musical connotation.

At the headrig the father turns the whole sweating team with one tug of the reins: the lesson of the clicking tongue again. Pluck is light, almost musical (strings are plucked, and the father's body was strung), so mastery here looks like artistry. Then the sentence runs over the white space between stanzas, and the reader turns the corner with the horses: the stanza turns where the plough turns. The English verse comes from Latin versus, a turning (of the plough), a furrow, a line, so this is the moment where ploughing and poetry become one action.

Intention and effect: Heaney makes the form perform the content, proving in the poem's structure that a line of verse can be turned like a furrow.

6. Mapping and exactly

Metaphor; semantic field of precision; feminine ending.

After Narrowed and angled, the father's eye is Mapping the furrow: ploughing as cartography, lines drawn on a blank field. For a poet the image is irresistible, since the field becomes the page. Exactly is the father's standard, and it becomes the son's: the whole poem tries to describe him exactly. Yet the line about precision falls loosely in rhythm and ends on a weak syllable, and its rhyme with eye is inexact.

Intention and effect: the father's exactness is set up as the measure of everything, while the verse quietly admits that the son's lines cannot quite match it.

7. his hobnailed wake

Metaphor; compound adjective; idiom.

The father's studded boots leave a churned track in the soil as a ship leaves a wake on water, and the boy stumbled in it like a small boat behind a big one. The idiom 'in someone's wake' (following, left behind) is part of the meaning, and so is the literal sense. He is following in his father's footsteps and cannot even manage those, because the prints are too big for him. Hobnailed sounds heavy and hard, even a little intimidating. The son's first appearance in the poem is a stumble.

Intention and effect: the son introduces himself through his failure to keep up, so the poem's admiration is immediately paired with inadequacy.

8. rode me on his back

Repetition; rhythmic mimesis; tender reversal.

Sometimes he fell, and Sometimes he was carried: the repeated word pairs the boy's failure with the father's kindness. The verb is unusual, because the father 'rides' the boy in the sense of carrying him, as if the man were also the horse. The next line rocks (Dipping and rising), so the reader feels the walk from the child's perch, and the father's gait is a plod: slow, heavy, reliable. This is the only physical contact in the poem, and its tenderness answers the boy's helplessness with the father's strength.

Intention and effect: the moment humanises the hero and creates the image the last stanza inverts, when the burden falls on the other side.

9. To close one eye

Infinitive of imitation; echo; monosyllables.

The boy's ambition is not a career but two gestures copied from watching: the closed eye that sights the furrow and the braced arm that steers. He imitates the posture without the skill, like a child copying the shape of handwriting without knowing the words. The echo of the father's narrowed eye from stanza 3 shows how closely he watched, and the plain monosyllables are the plainness of a simple, wholehearted want.

Intention and effect: the line is touching because it shows love as imitation, and painful because imitation is all it is.

10. his broad shadow

Symbol; spondee; double meaning.

The father's shadow is literally big (he is a broad man), and the two heavy stresses make it loom. But a shadow is two things at once: shade that shelters and darkness that eclipses. To live in someone's shadow is to be protected and overshadowed together, safe and unseen. Round the farm adds circling and limits, the farm as the boundary of the boy's world. The image gathers the poem's mixed feelings into one figure, and the last stanza turns it round, because the man who cast the shadow is now behind.

Intention and effect: the reader feels both the comfort and the cost of growing up in a great man's company.

11. But today

Volta; caesura; enjambment.

After a nuisance, the participles tripping, falling and the sharp animal noise Yapping, a full stop falls in mid-line and two words turn the poem from past to present. The turn comes late (after twenty-one and a half lines of memory) and suddenly, in the shortest line of the poem, as if the rhythm loses its footing at the moment of change. Today is left hanging at the end of the line, with the present still waiting to be revealed.

Intention and effect: the abruptness makes the reversal feel like a realisation rather than an argument, something the speaker sees all at once.

12. will not go away

Verbal echo; cleft sentence; modal of refusal; full rhyme.

The father keeps stumbling, the child's own verb from line 13, given to him in a cleft sentence that throws the emphasis onto the father with a note of surprise (it is he, of all people). The poem does not say why: age, memory and conscience all fit, and none is named. Then comes the idiom one uses of a pest, with the modal of refusal. Will not means refuses to, so the persistence is the father's own will. The rhythm stumbles through a crowded nine-syllable line, and then the full rhyme with today seals the ending.

Intention and effect: Heaney ends on an image that is impatient, guilty and loving at once, and its frankness is what makes the earlier admiration believable.

CRITICAL LENSES

Critical Lenses

What each way of reading makes visible, and what it flattens

Critical lenses

Formalist

A formalist reading attends to how the poem's shape carries its meaning, and 'Follower' rewards it at every level. The poem is laid out like a ploughed field: twelve lines going up the field with the father, twelve coming back with the son. Its one sentence that crosses a stanza break does so at the headrig, where the team turns. Its rhyme scheme narrates the story (plough rhymes with furrow, then with follow), its feminine endings trail like followers, and its last stanza turns back over its own words like a return furrow. On this reading the poem is an ars poetica, a poem about the making of poems: proof that a line can be cut like a furrow, by a son who claims he could never plough.

What it flattens: the human relationship. A purely formal reading can make the father a pretext for craft, and lose the poem's raw feelings: tenderness, inadequacy, the impatience of will not go away.

Psychoanalytic

This lens sees a son defining himself against a powerful father. The father is all body and authority (globed shoulders, a broad shadow that both shelters and eclipses); the son is small, noisy and falling, and he wants not just to farm but to be the father (To close one eye). The ending reads as the father internalised. The figure who will not go away is a voice within the son's mind, the standard he carries everywhere, close to what psychoanalysis calls the superego (the internalised parent who judges). The reversal, with the son in front and the father behind, is the son's attempt to step out of the shadow, and the last line admits that he cannot.

What it flattens: the love. The poem shows no rivalry, only devotion and patience on both sides, and a psychoanalytic reading can turn the piggyback into a power struggle that the text does not support.

Marxist / materialist

A materialist lens looks at labour, skill and class. The poem gives a farmer's skill the dignity of precise language (An expert, set the wing, Mapping), refusing the snobbery that treats manual work as unskilled. It also records a change in how farming was done: the horse-plough belonged to a world the tractor was replacing, so the father's expertise was becoming obsolete even as it was praised. And the son's path, from the farm to education to writing, is a story of social mobility in which the next generation leaves manual labour for the professions and the father is left behind.

What it flattens: the poem's intimacy. The father is not a type of the rural worker but a particular man who carried his son, and this lens has little to say about the poem's sound, which is where much of its feeling lives.

Historicist and postcolonial

A historicist reading places the poem in Catholic rural Ulster in the 1940s: the end of horse-ploughing, and the start of free grammar-school places that allowed sons like Heaney to leave the land. The vocabulary carries the region's layered history. Sock came into English through Old French and is probably Celtic in origin; headrig is Scots, the speech of the Planters' descendants; and the whole poem is in English. Heaney himself read the same layering in the name of his family's farm, Mossbawn. A postcolonial reader might see the father Mapping the furrow as a native's mark on ground that colonial maps had renamed, and note that the son's chosen tongue is the language of the old colonisers.

What it flattens: the poem's surface politics are almost nil. It was written before the Troubles, names no place, and is about one family; pressing the colonial reading too hard turns a ploughman into an emblem he never was.

Gender

The poem's world is entirely male: a father, a son, a team of horses, and a farm with no mother in it. Masculinity is defined by size, strength, silence and control (shoulders, his clicking tongue), and the boy fails on every count: small, noisy, falling. Yet the son grows into a man of words, so the poem quietly values the tongue as well as the arm and suggests another kind of manhood. A feminist critic might also notice who is absent. Heaney's mother, 'notably ready to speak out' in the Nobel biography's phrase, has no place here, and inheritance is imagined entirely through the male line and the field.

What it flattens: the gentleness. The father who carries the boy is not only a model of hard masculinity, and the poem's tenderness is part of its idea of what a man is.

Ecocritical

An ecocritical lens sees a working partnership between people, animals and land. The father steers his team with a click rather than a whip, and turns the soil over without breaking it: a craft that cooperates with its material. The team goes back into the land as if into an element. The age of the tractor that followed changed that relationship, so the poem preserves a disappearing closeness to the earth.

What it flattens: the poem is not an idyll. The horses strain and sweat, the labour is hard, and the poem's real subject is the human relationship, not the land.

OTHER READINGS

Other Readings

Contested interpretations, and where each is weak

Alternative readings

1. An elegy written in advance

'Follower' can be read as a memorial that fixes the father at his best, at the plough, for ever. John Boly reads the poem as a kind of eulogy and funerary monument, whose last lines deliberately break the idealised, timeless image of the father. Readers also find a funeral hidden in the vocabulary: the wake, the sod, and a father who will not leave, like a ghost.

Evidence: the past tense of stanzas 1–5; the monumental first half; wake and sod; the line's later life after Patrick Heaney's death in 1986.

Weakness: in 1966 the father was alive, and the last stanza is in the present tense: he keeps stumbling. The funeral puns are a reader's associations (the 'wake' kept for the dead is a different word from a ship's wake), and the ending is about a living relationship, not a grave. Boly's own comparison of the lurching father to a zombie has not been taken up by other critics.

2. A poem about writing poems

In this reading the furrow is the line, the field is the page, the headrig is the line-break, and exactly is the poet's standard. The son who could not plough turns out to be a ploughman of verse. The Latin root of 'verse' (versus, a turning, a furrow) and Heaney's later images of ploughing as writing support it.

Evidence: the enjambment across the stanza break exactly at the turn; Mapping; the poem's own careful quatrains; 'Digging' in the same book, where the pen replaces the spade.

Weakness: 'Follower' never mentions writing, and the reading can turn the father into a metaphor for the son's career and lose the person. It also struggles with the last stanza, which is about the father's presence, not the poet's craft.

3. The son's departure from tradition

Here the father stands for a whole way of life (rural, manual, traditional), and the son is the one who left it. Alan Peacock reads the father's halting gait in the last stanza as the measure of Heaney's departure from his father's tradition, a widely shared view. Elmer Andrews sees the poem marking the border between an unreflective rural life and the self-conscious world of literature, and Bradley Skeen calls it a lament for a lost tradition that the son keeps alive by writing about it.

Evidence: the horse-plough, already passing by 1966; the son's failure to grow up and plough; the father now behind, out of step in the son's world; Heaney's own biography (the scholarship at twelve).

Weakness: it makes the father an emblem. The poem's details are personal (the piggyback, the click, the eye), and nothing in the text mentions education, the city or modernity: those come from the biography.

4. The resentful son

Some readers hear a son's hostility in the poem: the father as an overbearing figure whose shadow blots the boy out, and a last line of pure exasperation. Elmer Andrews notes how frankly the poem admits that family relationships can be a burden as well as sustaining.

Evidence: the broad shadow; the son's harsh words about himself (a nuisance, Yapping), which may echo what he was told as a child; the idiom go away.

Weakness: there is no cruelty anywhere in the poem. The father carries the boy, the boy longs to be like him, and the admiration is total, so reading the father as harsh or abusive is a misreading. Whatever impatience the ending holds is the son's, and it is set against the father's patience in stanza 4.

5. The ageing parent and the dutiful child

This is the plainest reading of the ending: the strong father has become old and frail, and the son now looks after him, as the father once looked after the son.

Evidence: the time-word today; the physical verb in keeps stumbling; the reversal of the piggyback image; the common experience of children caring for ageing parents.

Weakness: the poem does not say that the father is old, ill or dependent, or that the son cares for him. It says he is behind and will not go away, which sounds more like a presence than a patient. Patrick Heaney lived another twenty years after the poem was published. The literal reading is possible, but it closes down meanings the poem keeps open.

REVISION NOTES

Revision Notes

The working notes, quotation by quotation

Title

Follower

Analysis
  • No article → names a role, not a person → can change hands
  • Literal: boy walking behind the plough
  • Disciple / imitator of a master
  • Successor → eldest son expected to 'follow' into the farm (Heaney didn't)
  • Negative side: secondary, little agency → 'living in someone's shadow'
  • By the last line → the father is the follower
Effect, style & response
  • Title = riddle solved in the last stanza
  • Hopeful sense: poet 'follows' the father's craft in another medium (lines ≈ furrows)
  • Sound: follow ≈ furrow (f + ll/rr + -ow)

Overview

Analysis
  • Memory → admiration → role reversal
  • St 1–3: father's skill (body, voice, hands, eye)
  • St 4–5: son stumbling, carried, wanting, following
  • St 6: confession → But today → reversal
  • Father now keeps stumbling behind the son
    • Poem never says 'old' or 'dependent' → cause left open
Effect, style & response
  • Love shown as attention, never stated
  • Ending ambiguous: affection / frustration / guilt / memory

Context

Analysis
  • Seamus Heaney 1939–2013; born Mossbawn, Co. Derry; eldest of 9
  • Farm ≈ 50 acres; father Patrick = farmer + cattle dealer
    • Nobel bio: 'real commitment' = cattle-dealing; 'notably sparing of talk'
  • Death of a Naturalist (Faber, 1966): 1st collection
    • childhood, rural life, family, growing into adult identity
  • Scholarship at 12 → St Columb's → Queen's (First, 1961) → never took over farm
  • Father alive in 1966 (died Oct 1986)
  • Last generation of horse-ploughing (Ferguson TE20 tractor, 1946)
Effect, style & response
  • Accurate farm detail → authenticity + tribute
  • 'Digging' (same book): pen replaces spade → 'no spade to follow men like them'
  • Nobel Prize 1995

Structure

Analysis
  • 6 quatrains → 12 lines father / 12 son (last 2½ = now)
  • Lines 7–9 syllables, mostly 8 → even on the page, like furrows
  • Loose four-beat line, iambic tendency (not strict iambic tetrameter)
    • rhythm 'stumbles': spondees, trochees, anapaests
  • Enjambment + caesura modulate rhythm
  • I opens st 4, 5, 6 → anaphora → confessions
Effect, style & response
  • Steady form ≈ father's steady skill
  • Poem laid out like a field: up one way, back the other
  • Last stanza = the return furrow

Rhyme

Analysis
  • ABAB; 5 full: strung/tongue, round/ground, sod/plod, arm/farm, today/away
  • 7 half: plough/furrow, wing/breaking, sock/pluck, eye/exactly, wake/back, plough/follow, falling/stumbling
  • Feminine endings: furrow, breaking, exactly, follow, falling, stumbling
  • plough rhymes with furrow (st 1) → follow (st 5)
Effect, style & response
  • Close match, never perfect → son's imitation never exact
  • Rhyme tells the story: father makes furrows, son only follows
  • Final full rhyme today/away → presence sealed
1–4

globed like a full sail

Analysis
  • Plain opening → My father worked: labour defines him
  • horse-plough → pre-tractor; already vanishing by 1966
  • Simile full sail → power + grace; nautical imagery begins
    • sail → wake → dipping and rising
  • globed → round, muscular; huge to a child (Atlas? association only)
  • strung → taut, rigged → tension of the work
  • Father = link Between the shafts and the furrow
  • clicking tongue → onomatopoeia; control with tiny effort
Effect, style & response
  • Child's-eye view: from behind, from below
  • Sibilance: shoulders / sail / strung / shafts / strained → wind, effort
  • strained → kinaesthetic; labour kept real

5–8

An expert.

Analysis
  • Minor sentence + caesura → absolute verdict; hero-worship
  • Then the evidence → set the wing, sock, headrig = technical / dialect words
    • sock = ploughshare (N. English / Scots; Old French soc, prob. Celtic)
    • headrig = Scots heid-rig, headland where the team turns (rig = ridge)
  • Monosyllabic verbs set / fit / pluck → precise, economical

  • Son knows the father's words → he did inherit something

a single pluck

Analysis
  • Only enjambment across a stanza break → at the headrig
    • sentence turns where the plough turns

Effect, style & response
  • verse < Latin versus = a turning (of the plough), furrow, line

His eye

Analysis
  • Synecdoche: shoulders = strength; eye = skill, judgement
  • Semantic field: narrowed / angled / mapping / exactly → precision, cartography
  • Trochaic openings (Narrowed, Mapping) → concentration
  • Sighting along the furrow (one eye) → copied by the boy in st 5

his hobnailed wake

Analysis

  • wake = trail behind a ship → left behind
  • Literally following in his footsteps → prints too big for him
  • polished sod → steel leaves turned soil shiny → father's 'artwork'
Effect, style & response
  • Fell stressed at line-start → rhythm falls

rode me on his back

Analysis
  • sometimes repeated → falling ↔ carried; father there for him
  • Piggyback → only physical contact; tenderness
  • Active verb, boy = object → dependence

  • plod → slow, steady, reliable
Effect, style & response
  • Dipping and rising → falling-rising rhythm; boat on a swell

his broad shadow

Analysis
  • grow up and plough → to the boy, adulthood = father's trade

  • Heart of the poem: past desire vs present understanding
  • plough/follow replaces plough/furrow
  • Tone: rueful, self-mocking; adult hindsight
  • Hidden pride: the poem's own craft → he followed in another field
21–22

Yapping

Analysis
  • a nuisance → blunt adult hindsight (rue? fond smile?)
  • Asyndetic list tripping, falling → restless, constant
  • Yapping → onomatopoeia; small dog at the heels
  • Line 22 = shortest line (7 syllables)
  • Full stop → volta But today (mid-line) → past to present
Effect, style & response
  • Yapping tongue vs clicking tongue → two kinds of language
  • Irony: the 'yapper' becomes the poet
  • Turn arrives like a sudden thought
22–24

But today

Analysis
  • Roles reversed: father now follows, keeps stumbling
  • stumbled (l. 13) → stumbling → verbal echo = mirror
  • Cleft sentence → spotlight on the father
  • will not go away → modal will = refuses
  • Poem does NOT say the father is old or dependent → open
Effect, style & response
  • Readings: ageing (literal) / memory, haunting / guilt (didn't follow into farming) / father out of step in son's world / love (always with him)
  • Tone: frustration and/or affection → frankness makes the love believable
  • Rhythm stumbles (9 syllables, crowded stresses); full rhyme today/away seals it
  • After 1986 (father's death) → ghostly echo

Sound

Analysis
  • /k/ clicks: clicking → rhymes sock/pluck, wake/back (all father's actions)
  • pl- cluster: plough, pluck, plod (+ polished)
  • Sibilance st 1 → wind in a sail; breath, effort
  • Long round vowels for the father: shoulders, globed, rolled over; plough, round, ground
  • Last stanza: round vowels nearly gone → only go keeps one
Effect, style & response
  • -ing endings pile up in the son's stanzas (dipping, tripping, falling, stumbling) → unfinished motion
  • will not go away → slow heavy monosyllables → refusal in sound

Big ideas

Analysis
  • Inheritance: the standard, not the trade
  • Craft = art; mastery = economy
  • Love without words
  • Time reverses roles → ploughing 'turns over' the relationship
  • Guilt of the son who left the land
  • Memory that will not go away
Effect, style & response
  • 'Follower' ↔ 'Digging': pen for spade
  • Links: 'Storyteller' (craft handed on), 'Before the Sun' (boy wants adult work), 'The Cockroach' (watcher turns inward), 'Sonnet 18' (lines that outlast time)
CONNECTIONS

Connections

How this poem pairs with the rest of the set

Comparison hooks

With 'Storyteller' (Liz Lochhead)

Link: both poems watch an older figure practise a craft and ask how it passes to the next generation. For Lochhead's storyteller, telling the stories 'was her work', a craft 'like spinning'; Heaney's father is An expert at the plough. Shared technique: a craft described as an art, and a tongue at work. Her 'tongue clacked' while hands stitched; his clicking tongue drives the team. Both poems end with the older generation carried into the younger: her stories hang in 'the sleeping heads of the children' until they fly again, and his father will not go away. Difference: Lochhead's inheritance succeeds, because the craft becomes the children's and the stories fly. Heaney's son fails to inherit the father's craft and carries him instead as a presence, half burden and half blessing.

With 'Before the Sun' (Charles Mungoshi)

Link: a boy and adult work. Mungoshi's boy splits a big log with 'the sharp axe', because 'when you are fourteen' big logs are what you want; Heaney's boy wanted to grow up and plough. Shared technique: a grown-up presence seen by a child (a sun that 'winks / like a grown-up'; a father seen from below, globed), in plain first-person speech. Difference: Mungoshi's boy can do the work, and does it joyfully in the present tense, sharing his roasted maize with the sun bite for bite. Heaney's boy can only follow, and his poem looks back from adulthood towards a reversal that Mungoshi's morning never reaches. Mungoshi writes free verse in short, breathless lines; Heaney's rhymed quatrains are as ordered as furrows.

With 'The Cockroach' (Kevin Halligan)

Link: the watcher and the watched. Halligan's speaker begins 'I watched a giant cockroach'; Heaney's spends three stanzas watching his father. Both poems turn at the end on the watcher himself: Halligan's speaker 'thought I recognised myself', and Heaney's finds the man he once watched now following him. Shared technique: a late turn that collapses the distance between observer and observed, so that the final line changes everything before it. Difference: Halligan's insect is a stranger whose aimless 'crooked rings' become a mirror of the speaker's own restlessness. Heaney's father is the most familiar person in the speaker's world, and the mirror is time: the son sees the child he was in the father who now trails behind him.

With 'Sonnet 18' (William Shakespeare)

Link: lines that keep a person against time. Shakespeare promises that the beloved will live 'When in eternal lines to time thou grow'st', since 'So long lives this, and this gives life to thee'. Heaney's lines are close kin to furrows ('verse' from versus), and they keep the father ploughing for ever. Shared technique: a volta that turns the poem on a 'But' (Shakespeare's 'But thy eternal summer shall not fade'; Heaney's But today), and a shadow image: Death will not brag that the beloved 'wander'st in his shade', while Heaney's boy lives in his father's broad shadow. Difference: Shakespeare's 'But' defeats time, and Heaney's admits it. In Sonnet 18 the beloved never fades; in 'Follower' the expert stumbles, and the consolation is not that he is unchanged but that he will not go away.

With 'Where I Come From' (Elizabeth Brewster)

Link: 'People are made of places', and Heaney's speaker is made of a farm and a father. Both poems look back from an adult life elsewhere at a rural childhood carried in the mind. Brewster's people 'carry woods in their minds', with 'wooden farmhouses, old'; Heaney's father walks behind him and will not go away. Shared technique: concrete physical detail of country life (her hens 'clucking aimlessly'; his hobnailed wake and polished sod), and a final movement in which the past breaks into the present ('A door in the mind' blows open; But today). Difference: Brewster's memory is of a place and its seasons, and it arrives like weather, bracing and refreshing. Heaney's is of a person, a relationship with obligations, which is why it can feel like a burden as well as a gift.

With 'A Different History' (Sujata Bhatt)

Link: what a later generation inherits, and what it makes of an inheritance it did not choose. Bhatt asks which language has not been 'the oppressor's tongue', and ends with 'the unborn grandchildren' who 'grow to love that strange language'. Heaney's poem is by a son who took up the tongue (English verse) rather than the plough, in an Ulster where farm-words carry Scots and Celtic history (sock, headrig). Shared technique: reverence for a craft and its objects (Bhatt's books, handled gently because they are sacred; Heaney's lovingly named plough-parts), and a turn into reflection on what changes across generations. Difference: Bhatt's inheritance is collective and political (a country, a language, a conquest); Heaney's belongs to one family, and its politics are left almost entirely implicit.

With 'Carpet-weavers, Morocco' (Carol Rumens)

Link: children and craft. Rumens's children are hard at work in 'the school of days', weaving a carpet whose colours pass from 'all-that-will-be' into 'the frame of all-that-was'. Heaney's child longs to work and can only follow. Shared technique: a skilled craft described lovingly and exactly (knots and colours; wing and sock), with time folded into the image: the carpet freezes the future into the past, and the poem's past gives way to today. Difference: Rumens's children are the workers, and her poem holds a question about their labour. Heaney's child is the useless one, carried by the worker, and the question his poem asks is about inheritance rather than exploitation.

Storyteller

Liz Lochhead · 1981

A kitchen storyteller's talk is counted as work — breath spun into the strongest thread, lost at dawn, then roosting in the sleeping children until night lets it fly.

30
Form
