ContextThe PoemThe Whole PoemForm & StructureSoundMotifs & SymbolsThemesDifficult MomentsClose AnalysisCritical LensesOther ReadingsRevision NotesConnections
CONTEXT

Context

The world the poem came out of

The Poet: Liz Lochhead (b. 1947)

Elizabeth Anne Lochhead was born on 26 December 1947 in Lanarkshire — the Scottish Poetry Library says Motherwell; Wikipedia gives Craigneuk, a former mining village on the edge of Motherwell — and in 1952 her family moved to a council house in the mining village of Newarthill. She studied at Glasgow School of Art from 1965 to 1970, began writing poems there, and earned her living teaching art in secondary schools (in Bristol, Glasgow and Cumbernauld) while she wrote. Her first collection, Memo for Spring (1972), followed a win in a BBC Radio Scotland poetry competition in 1971.

She became one of the most public voices in Scottish writing: a performer of her own work and of revue (with Tom Leonard and Alasdair Gray), a playwright (Mary Queen of Scots Got Her Head Chopped Off, 1987), and a translator of classics into Scots (a Tartuffe; a Medea that won the Saltire Society's Scottish Book of the Year in 2001). She was Glasgow's Poet Laureate from 2005 and Scotland's national poet, the Makar, from her appointment on 19 January 2011 — succeeding her friend Edwin Morgan — until 2016, when Jackie Kay followed her. She received the Queen's Gold Medal for Poetry in 2015. Robert Crawford (Identifying Poets, 1993) praised the “kaleidoscopic pace and liveliness” of her Scots diction; Anne Varty described her work as that of “one woman speaking to many” — a fair description of a poem about a woman holding a room with her voice. Lochhead is well known as a feminist, and once remarked that feminism is “like the hoovering”: you just have to keep doing it — a joke that sets housework and women's other work side by side, much as this poem does.

The Grimm Sisters (1981)

'Storyteller' is the opening poem of The Grimm Sisters, published in London by Next Editions in association with Faber and Faber in 1981 (the Scottish Poetry Library's bibliography) and gathered three years later into Dreaming Frankenstein & Collected Poems (Polygon, 1984). Dates of 1978 or 1979 circulate online — one study site says the poems were finished in 1978 — but 1981 is the publication date the bibliographies support.

The title swaps the Brothers Grimm into the feminine. PoetryProf sums up the book well: its poems follow the paths of well-known fairy tales, but “the viewpoint is female” and the tone “often ironic”. Elsewhere in the collection 'Rapunzstiltskin' fuses two Grimm tales, 'Tam Lin's Lady' retells a Border ballad from the woman's side, and 'The Grim Sisters' plays on the title's pun. As the first poem, 'Storyteller' does something different from the rest: it does not rewrite a tale; it restores the teller — the woman through whose voice the tales passed before men wrote them down.

The Brothers Grimm and their tellers

Jacob (1785–1863) and Wilhelm Grimm (1786–1859) published Kinder- und Hausmärchen ('Children's and Household Tales') in two volumes (1812 and 1815) and revised it through seven editions to 1857, Wilhelm in particular polishing, moralising and Christianising the tales as he went. The collection was presented as the voice of the German folk, but most of their informants were educated young women from middle-class families in and around Kassel — the Wild sisters (Dortchen Wild later married Wilhelm) and the Hassenpflug sisters, of French Huguenot descent — along with a few men and some printed sources. None was named on the title page.

The most famous exception is Dorothea Viehmann (1755–1815), a tailor's wife from Niederzwehren near Kassel, also of Huguenot descent, who supplied many of the tales in the second volume. Wilhelm's preface praised her, unnamed, as a countrywoman who told her tales vividly and repeated them without altering them, and Ludwig Emil Grimm's portrait of her in the second edition (1819) fixed the image of the old peasant 'tale-wife'. Lochhead's storyteller is not identified with Viehmann or with any real woman: the poem names no one, and nothing in the sources consulted for this chapter makes the link. Her details — delft, clogs, flat fields, a Scots-sounding idiom — make her a composite, the archetype of the female teller rather than a portrait of one historical woman.

Spinning, spinning rooms and 'spinning a yarn'

Until mechanisation, spinning was the defining women's labour of Europe: 'spinster' first meant simply a woman who spins, and 'the distaff side' still means the female line of a family. In many regions women gathered on winter evenings to spin together — the German Spinnstube or spinning room — and these gatherings were a natural setting for songs, gossip and tales. Scotland had its own version, the 'rocking' (a 'rock' is a distaff): Burns, in his 'Epistle to J. Lapraik' (1785), remembers how at Fasten-e'en ‘we had a rockin’ to ‘ca' the crack’ — to chat — while they worked at their stockings.

The link between spinning and telling runs through the fairy-tale tradition itself: Rumpelstiltskin spins straw into gold, Sleeping Beauty pricks her finger on a spindle, and the frontispiece of Perrault's tales (1697) shows an old woman with her distaff by the fire, telling stories to children, beneath the label Contes de ma mère l'Oye — 'Mother Goose tales'. Behind them stand the Fates of Greek myth, who spin, measure and cut the thread of life. English remembers the connection in idioms: to spin a yarn (originally sailors' slang), to lose the thread. Walter Benjamin's essay 'The Storyteller' (1936) argued that storytelling flourished among people busy with rhythmic handwork such as spinning and weaving, and that a story sinks deepest into a listener who forgets himself in the work — very close to the poem's sewing, half-listening women and its sleeping children.

Feminist re-visions of the fairy tale

The Grimm Sisters belongs to a decade in which women writers went back to the fairy tales. Anne Sexton's Transformations (1971) retold seventeen Grimm tales in sardonic free verse, narrated by ‘a middle-aged witch, me’; Angela Carter's The Bloody Chamber (1979) rewrote Bluebeard, Beauty and the Beast and Red Riding Hood from inside, giving their heroines desire and agency. Adrienne Rich's essay 'When We Dead Awaken: Writing as Re-Vision' (1971–72) gave the movement its key word: re-vision, the act of “entering an old text” from “a new critical direction”.

Lochhead's opening poem makes a distinctive contribution to that project. Instead of correcting what the tales say about women, it corrects who is credited with the tales: it moves the woman from inside the story (stepmother, witch, drudge) to the teller's chair — and insists that what she does there is work.

The kitchen, the dresser and the dawn

The poem's objects are precise. A dresser is the shelved kitchen cupboard on which a household displayed its plates; delftware is tin-glazed earthenware, originally from Delft in the Netherlands, and in Scots 'delf' came to mean any crockery. Scouring meant scrubbing wood or metal with sand, soda or ash; patchwork and darning were the thrift crafts of households that could not afford new cloth. Clogs — wooden-soled shoes — were the footwear of field and mill workers across northern Europe, the Netherlands and northern England among them.

Put together, these details do not locate a single village. A Scots-sounding kitchen (delf, sloven, shiftless) sits beside a Low Countries or north German dawn of clogs and flat fields — the landscape of the Grimms' own tales. The setting is deliberately once-upon-a-time: a composite peasant world in which the storyteller can stand for every woman who told tales by a fire.

THE POEM

The Poem

Line by line, with the analysis alongside

Storyteller

This poem is still in copyright, so its words are not reproduced here: each line shows a short summary. Read it alongside your anthology or the exam paper, or use Add the text to paste it in from your own copy (it stays on this device).

TStoryteller
1she takes her seat — no capital letter, no name
2by a table scrubbed clean
3in a kitchen already brushed tidy
4by shelves of chipped blue-and-white Dutch-style crockery.
5The last scraps of light are hoarded away like food.
6Nobody could call the tales pointless,
7because while her voice rattled on
8one hand, or four women's hands, kept sewing;
9grain was scraped from its casing;
10scraps of cloth were joined into a quilt;
11or worn socks were mended.
12Nobody would ever smear her as lazy.
13Whether her housekeeping was slack or immaculate,
14whether her broth was thin or good —
15telling tales was her job: the central claim.
16A simile: it resembled making thread,
17drawing nothing but air into one unbreakable strand —
18the strand completed. Then, every evening,
19she kept us in suspense, breath stopped,
20for a conclusion we had long memorised.
21Then, as dawn broke,
22while the women roused themselves to light the hearth,
23while a farm-worker groped for wooden shoes,
24while pale, colourless light spread across level land,
25the tales melted away in the spiral of the ear —
26yet they (the turn)
27roosted head-down, like bats,
28inside the dreaming children's minds,
29until they took wing once more
30in the night that belongs to the teller(s).

Lines with a marker have analysis — click one, or just scroll.

Title
Storyteller
Language & devices

Title as a bare noun: no article, no name, no possessive. Storyteller reads like a trade or a job description (compare 'Weaver', 'Blacksmith'), and the compound joins the thing made to its maker. The word comes back, pluralised and without an apostrophe, as storytellers in the last line, so title and ending frame the poem. The poem opens Lochhead's collection The Grimm Sisters (1981), whose own title turns the Brothers Grimm into women.

Meaning & effect

The title gives the woman a role before it gives her anything else, and she never receives a name: the poem's argument in one word is that storytelling is an occupation, a skill practised and valued like any other. At the head of a book called The Grimm Sisters, it also points to who did the telling behind the most famous fairy-tale collection in Europe — the tellers, many of them women, whose tales the brothers wrote down and published under their own names. By the final line the singular role has widened to storytellers: what survives is the office, handed on, not the individual who first held it.

Line 1
sat down
Language & devices

Lower-case opening: the poem begins without a capital letter, on a pronoun with no antecedent — we are never told who she is. Three monosyllables, evenly and heavily stressed. In medias res: the poem begins as if a story were already under way and the listener already knew the woman.

Meaning & effect

The missing capital makes the opening feel like a continuation rather than a start — as though the speaker were picking up a tale everyone in the room knows, about someone who needs no introduction. Sitting down marks a double change of state: the end of the day's chores and the beginning of the evening's other work. PoetryProf compares the moment to Scheherazade or a teacher taking her chair: the teller's authority begins when she sits. The anonymity is pointed, too: like most of the women whose tales reached print, she is never named.

Lines 2–3
scoured table … swept kitchen
Language & devices

Parallel prepositional phrases (at the…, in the…) move the eye outward from table to room. The past participles scoured and swept describe finished labour without saying who did it. Sibilance runs from sat through scoured to swept.

Meaning & effect

The setting is built out of housework already done: scouring (scrubbing with sand or soda) and sweeping are the hard, daily, unseen jobs of a poor household. Only when they are finished can the telling begin, so the stanza's order — labour, then story — is the order of the woman's day. The agentless participles quietly raise the question the whole poem asks: whose work counts, and who gets the credit? PoetryProf hears a faint Cinderella in the swept kitchen, the drudge at the hearth — apt for a book about the women inside the tales.

Line 4
cracked delft
Language & devices

Concrete detail: a dresser (a kitchen cupboard with open shelves for displaying plates) holding delft — blue-and-white tin-glazed earthenware named after Delft in the Netherlands; in Scots, 'delf' came to mean ordinary crockery. Plosives in cracked delft (k, t, d) harden the line after the soft sibilants. The first full stop closes the opening sentence.

Meaning & effect

The only decorative things in the room are damaged — a mark of poverty, but also of care, since the cracked plates are kept and displayed rather than thrown out. They anticipate the stories themselves: old, worn by handling, imperfect, still treasured and still in daily use. The Dutch name also begins the poem's composite setting (delft here, clogs and flat fields at dawn): a kitchen that could be Scottish or anywhere in the northern European peasant world of the fairy tales.

Line 5
every last crumb of daylight
Language & devices

Metaphor: daylight imagined as food — crumb, and the idiom salted away (stored up, hoarded; from preserving meat or fish in salt). Hyperbole of thrift in every last. Agentless passive: no hoarder is named. The stanza's longest line, ending on a lilting anapaestic fall. Sentence-initial And, the connective of spoken narrative.

Meaning & effect

In a household this poor, even daylight is rationed like bread: every scrap has been used for work, and now it is put away. The idiom cuts two ways — the light is used up, and it is also preserved, kept in store — which anticipates the ending, where the stories too are stored, unseen, in the children. Darkness is not a loss here but the start of the storyteller's time. The line also tells us that the poem will think in terms of a domestic economy: what is spent, what is saved, what is worth keeping.

Line 6
No one could say
Language & devices

Litotes: nobody could call the stories useless — praise by denying an accusation. useless is the poem's first abstract, evaluative word. The definite article in the stories implies a known repertoire. A falling rhythm (/ x x / x / x x / x) that the first line of the next stanza will repeat exactly.

Meaning & effect

The poem turns from description to argument. It anticipates a hostile voice — practical, thrifty, suspicious of idleness — that would call storytelling a waste of time, and it answers that voice in its own terms. The praise is deliberately grudging: not 'the stories were wonderful' but 'nobody could call them useless'. That is how a hard-working community actually expresses approval, and it makes the defence more convincing than enthusiasm would be.

Lines 7–8
the tongue clacked
Language & devices

Causal for introduces the evidence. Synecdoche: the tongue for the teller, fingers for the women working — people reduced to their working parts. Onomatopoeia: clacked, a hard, wooden sound (PoetryProf links it to the noise of weaving). Alliteration on f in five or forty fingers; the line keeps a regular trochaic beat (/ x / x / x /), like a needle going in and out.

Meaning & effect

The stories are first justified by what happens while they are told: as the teller talks, her listeners' hands keep sewing. Clacked is double-edged — it is the verb for a gossip's tongue, the kind of word used to belittle women's talk — but here it becomes the sound of a tool in use, keeping time with the needles. Five or forty is a teller's offhand arithmetic: one hand, or four women's worth of fingers; a couple of listeners or a crowd. The number does not matter, only the pairing of voice and work. Note the tongue, not 'her tongue': the poem describes a function as much as a person.

Lines 9–11
grated from the husk
Language & devices

An asyndetic list of chores in three agentless passives (was grated, was pieced, was done). Alliteration: patchwork / pieced, darning / done. The lines shrink, then settle on a firm full stop that closes the stanza. or offers alternatives: a typical evening, not one particular night.

Meaning & effect

The list is a catalogue of women's making-do: husking or grating grain, piecing scraps of cloth into patchwork, darning worn clothes. Each turns waste or raw material into something of use — and each is also a figure for how a tale is made, pieced together from inherited scraps and mended where it has worn thin. The passives erase the workers: the work simply gets done, by no one in particular, which is exactly the invisibility the poem sets out to correct. The stanza ends with the jobs finished and the stories credited with helping to finish them.

Line 12
slander her shiftless
Language & devices

Ellipsis: the sentence has no main verb — '[There was] never the one to…' — an idiom that sounds spoken, almost proverbial. slander is a strong, quasi-legal word (a false and damaging accusation); shiftless means lazy, lacking initiative or resource. Sibilance on slander… shiftless. The line repeats line 6's rhythm exactly, and like it ends on a '-less' word.

Meaning & effect

The second defence moves from the stories to the woman: nobody ever accused her of laziness. The weight of slander shows how serious that charge would be in a community that measures a woman by her industry. The echo of useless in shiftless makes the two accusations sound like one voice — the voice that judges women by what they lack. The crabbed, elliptical syntax also starts to sound like an older speaker talking, as if the storyteller's own idiom were seeping into the verse.

Lines 13–14
sloven or spotless
Language & devices

Two antitheses: sloven or spotless (housekeeping) and Dishwater or tasty (cooking). Inversion and ellipsis: a verbless sentence that the reader must rebuild — 'no matter whether [she was] a daily sloven or spotless, [or whether] her soup was dishwater or tasty'. Alliteration and sibilance: sloven… spotless, then soup. Dishwater is a noun used as an adjective — a blunt, homely insult for thin soup.

Meaning & effect

These lines exempt the storyteller from the two standards by which every other woman in this world is judged: a clean house and a good table. Slack or immaculate, thin soup or tasty, it made no difference — nobody called her shiftless, because her real work lay elsewhere. This is the poem's boldest move: it values a woman as one would value an artist, for her art. The scrambled word order makes us reconstruct the sense like a listener following a teller's run-on speech, and the unglamorous Dishwater keeps the portrait honest: this is no idealised peasant kitchen.

Line 15
To tell the stories
Language & devices

A plain declarative sentence, almost all monosyllables, in regular iambic tetrameter (x / x / x / x /) — the poem's one regular iambic line. End-stopped, and placed at the hinge of the poem: the fifteenth of thirty lines, closing the first half. An infinitive as subject; the sentence ends on the stressed work.

Meaning & effect

This is the poem's thesis, stated with the flat certainty of a proverb. Two stanzas of defence end not with 'storytelling was as good as work' but with an outright claim: it was her work — her job, her contribution. The word answers both accusations, useless and shiftless. Against a tradition in which women's talk was dismissed as chatter and women's unpaid labour went uncounted, the line insists that cultural labour is labour. The regular metre makes it sound like something everyone has always known, which is exactly the authority the poem wants for it.

Lines 16–18
like spinning … single strongest
Language & devices

Simile: storytelling was like spinning — the poem's governing comparison, playing on the idiom 'to spin a yarn'. Paradox: gathering air into the strongest thread. Superlative: single strongest. Enjambment: the adjectives hang at the line-end and the noun thread arrives only on the next line, closed by a full stop — a hard caesura.

Meaning & effect

Having called storytelling work, the poem now says what kind: spinning, for centuries the defining female craft (hence 'spinster', first meaning a woman who spins, and 'the distaff side' for the female line). A spinner draws out loose fibres and twists them into one continuous strand; the storyteller does the same with air — breath, words, almost nothing — and makes the strongest thing the community owns, the narrative thread that holds it together. The line-break enacts the craft: the thread is drawn across the gap and finished on the next line. Spinning also outranks the stitching and darning of stanza 2, because it makes the thread those jobs use. Read as a portrait of Lochhead's own art, it is a definition of a poem's line: breath gathered into one strong strand (an 'air' can even be a tune).

Lines 18–20
Night in … knew by heart
Language & devices

Night in clips the idiom 'night in, night out' — ellipsis that compresses habit into two words. The first-person plural enters for the only time: us, we. Habitual she'd ('she would') and causative have us waiting. Enjambment across held / breath makes the reader hold the breath at the line-break. Paradox: suspense over an ending already known by heart.

Meaning & effect

The speaker is suddenly revealed as one of the listening children, remembering from adulthood: the poem is a memory of being held by a voice. The storyteller's power is physical — she makes her audience stop breathing, and the lineation makes us do the same. The paradox is the heart of oral culture: everyone knew how the story ended, and the suspense was real anyway, because the pleasure lay in the telling, the ritual and the shared moment rather than in surprise — like a child who wants the same bedtime story told the same way every night. By heart means memorised, but it also says where the stories live.

Line 21
first light
Language & devices

A short line opening the last stanza, which is a single sentence of ten lines. Sentence-initial And echoes line 5, so the night is framed between the last of the daylight and the first. first light answers every last crumb.

Meaning & effect

The clock turns: the night of telling is over and the working day returns. Light in this poem is not hope or knowledge but the medium of labour, so its return means the stories must retreat. Grammatically the line opens a long sentence whose main verb is held back for four lines, so the poem itself starts to build suspense: the form has learned its technique from the woman it describes.

Lines 22–24
felt for clogs
Language & devices

Anaphora and tricolon: three clauses beginning as, each delaying the main verb. Reflexive verb: stirred themselves. Synecdoche: the peasant's feet. Alliteration on f: fire, feet felt for, flat fields. Drained, monochrome imagery in thin grey light; washed joins the poem's cleaning verbs (scoured, swept).

Meaning & effect

Dawn is painted in three strokes: the women rousing themselves to rebuild the fire (their day begins, again, with labour), a worker's feet groping half-asleep for wooden shoes, and a weak grey light spreading over level fields. The images are generic and continental — clogs, flat land, a singular peasant — the world of folk tale rather than one documented village. Daylight here is thin, colourless and watery (compare the Dishwater soup): the poem reverses the usual values of light and dark, making the day meagre and the night rich. The repeated as slows time to the pace of bodies waking one by one.

Line 25
whorl of the ear
Language & devices

The main clause arrives at last: the stories dissolved. Dissolved is a metaphor of melting into liquid — salt into water, a dream at waking. whorl is a pun: the spiral of the outer ear, and, in its oldest sense, the small weighted wheel on a spindle that keeps it turning. A rocking, anapaestic rhythm (x / x x / x x / x x /).

Meaning & effect

At first this sounds like loss: daylight dissolves the stories as it dissolves dreams. But the pun completes the spinning simile — the thread spun by the teller's tongue is wound onto the 'whorl' of the listener's ear, so listening finishes the craft. And what dissolves is not destroyed: it is still there, invisibly, in solution. The stories are absorbed rather than consciously remembered; they become part of the listener. The apparent defeat is the beginning of survival.

Lines 26–28
but … sleeping heads
Language & devices

Volta: but, on the poem's shortest line (two syllables), turns the sentence from loss to survival. Implied metaphor: the stories become bats, never named, roosting upside down. The reflexive hung themselves echoes stirred themselves (line 22) and gives the stories a will of their own — personification shading into zoomorphism. Synecdoche: sleeping heads. The speaker now says the children, not us.

Meaning & effect

The stories do not die with the night; they roost. Bats are an exact emblem for oral tales: creatures of the dark that find their way by sound, invisible by day, hanging in the roof-space above the very children they now live in. As the women stir themselves awake, the stories put themselves to sleep — a handover between day and night. Being upside down suggests the inverted logic of dreams, and perhaps of fairy tales themselves, where the youngest child wins and the poor become royal. The reflexive verb carries a faint Grimm darkness ('hanged themselves'), but the stress falls on independence: the stories choose their own resting place and no longer need the teller. The shift from us to the children lets the speaker stand outside now, watching a new generation receive what she once received.

Lines 29–30
flew again … storytellers night
Language & devices

flew completes the unnamed bat metaphor; again makes the ending cyclical. The poem closes on night, echoing Night in (line 18). storytellers is printed without an apostrophe in the anthology text — an ambiguity: the storyteller's night (hers), the storytellers' night (every teller's), or a compound like 'market day'. The title word returns in the last line.

Meaning & effect

The cycle closes and reopens: night returns, and with it the stories, flying free of the heads that kept them. Ending on night rather than on the teller or the children confirms darkness as the generative time. The missing apostrophe is the poem's last act of handing on: the night may belong to her, or to all storytellers — including the children who heard her and the poet who is now telling us. The poem is itself the proof: the stories she told are flying again, here, in Lochhead's words.

THE WHOLE POEM

The Whole Poem

Stepping back: what the poem is doing, first line to last

The argument

'Storyteller' is an argument dressed as a memory. It sets out to win a case — that a woman's storytelling is work — and wins it in the language of the people who would deny it: the language of thrift, use and industry. Then, having won, it leaves that language behind. The stories end the poem not as tools that helped the sewing along but as living, wilful creatures that roost and fly on their own terms. The poem travels from a kitchen economy, in which everything is scoured, salted, grated, pieced and counted, to a natural history of the imagination; and it makes that journey in the shape of a told tale — dusk, night, dawn, night again — so that it demonstrates the craft it is defending.

Stanza 1: a world measured in work

The opening is all economy. The woman is introduced without a capital or a name, and the room around her is made of finished labour: a scoured table, a swept kitchen, plates kept on the dresser although they are cracked. Nothing is wasted, not even light: every last crumb of daylight is salted away, stored like food against hard times. The participles and the passive voice keep the workers invisible — no one is said to have scrubbed, swept or saved — and that invisibility is the poem's real subject. This is a world where women's work is everywhere and credited nowhere, and the storyteller sits down at the exact point where the countable work stops.

Stanza 2: the defence on the accuser's terms

The second stanza opens by imagining the charge against her: that the stories were useless. The answer is shrewdly practical. Nobody could say so, because while the tongue clacked the hands of the listeners stitched, grated, pieced and darned. Lochhead does not yet claim that stories are valuable in themselves; she claims that they kept the work going. The grammar enacts the claim: tongue and fingers share one sentence, one rhythm, one function. Even the insult buried in clacked — the verb for a gossip's tongue — is turned into the sound of a tool in use. The stanza closes on finished chores, with the stories given a share of the credit.

Stanza 3: from defence to definition

The third stanza is the poem's hinge, and it moves in three steps. First it defends the woman herself: nobody would slander her shiftless, whether her house was slovenly or spotless, her soup Dishwater or tasty. She alone is exempt from the domestic standards by which every other woman is judged. Second, the defence collapses into a verdict at the exact midpoint: telling the stories was her work. Not like work, not as good as work — work. Third, the poem says what kind of work, and here the tone changes from argument to wonder: telling was like spinning, gathering air into the single strongest thread. The comparison is chosen with care. Spinning is the archetypal female craft, and it is the craft the others depend on, since stitching and darning need the thread it makes. The storyteller does not merely accompany the household's work; she produces its most necessary material, out of nothing but breath.

Then the poem lets slip who is speaking. Night in — night in, night out — she'd have us waiting, breath held, for an ending everyone knew by heart. The speaker was one of the children. The suspense was real although everyone knew the ending, because the value of the tale lay in the telling and the shared ritual, not in news. The case for storytelling is now being made not by argument but by evidence: the speaker's own remembered body, holding its breath.

Stanza 4: loss and survival

The final stanza is a single long sentence that performs the storyteller's craft. Three clauses beginning as hold back the main verb while dawn arrives: the women rouse themselves to build the fire, the peasant's feet grope for clogs, a thin grey light spreads over flat fields. The day is meagre and watery — the same thin grey as the dishwater soup — and its arrival seems to defeat the night: the stories dissolved. Then comes the two-syllable turn, but, and the most memorable image in the poem. The stories hang themselves upside down in the sleeping heads of the children, like bats, until they fly again in the storytellers night.

The bats answer everything the poem has argued. They are not useful. They do not grate corn or darn socks. They belong to the dark, find their way by sound, and keep their own hours; they need no teller to keep them alive. The reflexive hung themselves gives the stories a will of their own, just as the women stirred themselves to work: one group wakes, the other sleeps, and the household is handed from day to night. And the speaker who was one of us now says the children, standing outside the scene as an adult — one of those in whom the stories survived. The poem we are reading is the proof: the stories are flying again, here, in another teller's voice.

The strongest objection

The strongest objection is that the poem concedes too much. By defending stories because they kept the needles moving, and by calling telling work, it seems to accept the very work-ethic that dismissed women's talk in the first place: art must earn its keep. A second objection is nostalgia — the poem paints a timeless, placeless peasantry of delft and clogs, an archetype as manufactured as the Grimms' own image of the peasant tale-wife.

Both objections describe real features of the poem, and both are answered by its shape. The language of use is tactical: Lochhead meets the hostile voice in its own currency (No one could say), wins, and then moves beyond it into a final image that no utilitarian could value — bats in the dark, stories flying because they want to. The argument for usefulness is the poem's way in, not its conclusion. As for nostalgia, the poem's honesty keeps getting in the way of idyll: the delft is cracked, the soup may be dishwater, the dawn is grey and cold, the day begins in labour. And its composite setting is deliberate. A poem about stories is itself told as a story — an unnamed she, a once-upon-a-time kitchen, a fairy-tale logic of creatures and flight. It does not pretend to document one village. It honours the woman who stands behind all the villages, and it shows her art outliving her, which is the only kind of credit the oral tradition ever gave.

FORM & STRUCTURE

Form & Structure

How the poem is built, and why it matters

Form & genre

Free verse: no rhyme scheme, no fixed metre, no regular stanza length. A portrait poem of a single unnamed figure that is also a defence (stanzas 2–3 argue a case), a memory (the speaker was one of the listeners) and, as the opening poem of The Grimm Sisters, a frame for the collection.

Stanzas

Thirty lines in four stanzas of 5, 6, 9 and 10 lines — each longer than the last. No lines are indented. Each stanza is also a stretch of time: dusk, the evening's work, the night's telling, dawn and the return of night.

Sentences

Nine sentences. Stanzas 2 and 4 are each a single flowing sentence; stanza 3 breaks into five, several of them short, end-stopped verdicts. The final stanza is one ten-line sentence whose main verb is held back for four lines.

Metre

No regular metre, but pockets of strong pattern: a trochaic beat in lines 8–9, an identical falling rhythm in lines 6 and 12, regular iambic tetrameter in line 15, and a rocking anapaestic line at 25.

Voice & tense

Third person (she, the women, the children) with one brief break into the first-person plural (us, we, lines 19–20). Past tense, much of it habitual (she'd have us waiting): this happened night after night.

Turns

A shift at lines 15–16 from argument to celebration (verdict, then simile), and a volta at line 26, the poem's shortest line, where but turns loss into survival.

A shape that grows

The stanzas lengthen steadily — five lines, six, nine, ten — and the growth suits a poem whose central image is a thread being drawn out and a story gathering force as it goes. The four stanzas also make a complete cycle of time. Stanza 1 is dusk: the chores done, the last of the light put away. Stanza 2 is the working evening, voice and fingers going together. Stanza 3 moves into the night's telling and the held breath of the audience. Stanza 4 runs from dawn to the following night, so the poem ends where the next telling begins. The structure is circular: it starts with daylight being salted away and ends on night, with the title word returning in the last line. Nothing is resolved because nothing needs to be; the cycle is the point.

The argument's order

Inside that cycle, the poem argues in a clear sequence. Description (stanza 1) gives way to defence (stanza 2: the stories were not useless, because the work went on while they were told), then to a second defence of the woman herself (lines 12–14: she was never called shiftless, whatever her housekeeping). The defence ends in a verdict, her work, at line 15 — the fifteenth of thirty lines, closing the poem's first half. Everything after it is demonstration rather than argument: the simile of spinning, the remembered suspense, the stories' survival. The poem stops defending the storyteller and starts showing what she does.

Metre and rhythm

Lochhead's free verse is not shapeless; its rhythms change with what is being described.

Line Stress pattern What it does
6 (No one could say) / x x / x / x x / x a falling rhythm for the imagined accusation, ending on the unstressed -less of useless
8 (five or forty fingers) / x / x / x / a regular trochaic beat, like a chant or a needle going in and out
9 (grated from the husk) / x / x / x / the same beat: the list of chores keeps time with the work
11 (darning) x x / x x / an anapaestic run that settles the stanza on its closing stress
12 (slander her shiftless) / x x / x / x x / x exactly the pattern of line 6, so the two accusations — useless, shiftless — sound like one voice
15 (her work) x / x / x / x / the poem's only regular iambic line, giving the thesis the ring of a proverb
18 (Night in) / / / three stresses split by a full stop: the thread is finished, the night begins
25 (whorl of the ear) x / x x / x x / x x / a rocking, lullaby rhythm as the stories melt into sleep
26 (but) x / the shortest line — two syllables — and the turn

Line 24, by contrast, is heavy: of its nine syllables, as many as seven can take a stress (thin, grey, light, washed, the first of over, flat, fields), so the dawn light spreads slowly and flatly across the line. Lines lengthen for the big tableaux — line 5 (twelve or thirteen syllables, the longest), line 13, line 22, line 25 — and shrink to two or three syllables at the hinges: the opening, Night in, and the two-syllable volta.

Rhyme, and the one that matters

There is no rhyme scheme, and the poem's music is the music of speech: stress, alliteration, the repeated -less of useless, shiftless and spotless. The single full chime is structural. Light and night recur through the poem — daylight (line 5), Night in (18), first light (21), grey light (24), night (30) — and the last stanza's first and last lines end on exactly that rhyme, light and night. The final sentence travels from one to the other, and the chime makes the return of the storytelling night feel inevitable.

Syntax: who does what

The grammar carries the poem's argument about invisible labour. Stanza 1 uses past participles with no agent (scoured, swept) and a passive (salted away); stanza 2 lists chores in three agentless passives (was grated, was pieced, was done). Work is everywhere and the workers are nowhere — exactly the condition the poem protests. The only active agents in the first two stanzas are she and parts of bodies: the tongue and fingers. In the last stanza the agents change: the women stirred themselves, the peasant's feet feel for clogs, the light washes over the fields — and then the stories themselves become the subject, with reflexive and active verbs: they dissolved, hung themselves, flew. By the end the stories are the poem's most independent actors.

Stanza 3 bends word order in the manner of speech. Line 12 has no main verb ('[There was] never the one to…'); lines 13–14 form a verbless sentence that the reader has to rebuild ('no matter whether [she was] a sloven or spotless…'). The effect is twofold: the reader works like a listener following a run-on speaker, and the voice starts to sound like an older Scots speaker rather than the printed page. Sentence-initial And (lines 5 and 21) is the connective of oral narrative — events simply follow one another, as in a told tale.

The last stanza is a periodic sentence. Three clauses beginning as delay the main clause for four lines; the main clause (the stories dissolved) seems to end the story; but reverses it. The sentence has the shape of a tale — setting, apparent loss, reversal, resolution — so the poem builds suspense in exactly the way it says the storyteller did.

Lineation and enjambment

Lochhead's line-breaks are placed for meaning. single strongest / thread draws the thread across the gap and completes it on the next line, as a spinner draws out fibre. held / breath makes the reader pause, breath held, at the line-end. Line 26 ends on a bare pronoun, leaving the stories suspended in white space before they hung. Short lines act as hinges: the opening line, Night in, first light, the two-syllable but, flew again. Long lines carry the tableaux. The alternation of short and long is the rhythm of a speaking voice drawing breath.

Punctuation and capitals

The poem opens without a capital letter, on an unexplained she: no name, no introduction, as if the tale were already under way. Capitals otherwise appear only at the start of sentences — with one exception in the anthology text, Dishwater at the start of line 14, mid-sentence, which gives the homely insult a proverbial weight. Punctuation is sparse; the long final sentence runs ten lines without a comma. Most striking, the last line prints storytellers with no apostrophe, so the night may be the storyteller's (hers), the storytellers' (every teller's), or simply a kind of night, like 'market day'. Some websites print storyteller's; the anthology text does not, and the open form suits a poem about a role passed from one teller to the next.

Turns

There are two. The first comes at lines 15–16, where argument turns into celebration: the verdict (her work) is followed at once by the simile (like spinning), and the tone moves from defence to wonder. The second, the volta proper, is line 26: but, alone with one pronoun on the poem's shortest line, turns the last sentence from the stories' dissolving to their survival. Placing the conjunction on its own suspends the reader in the gap — the poem's own held breath.

SOUND

Sound

What the poem does to the ear

Sibilance

Stanza 1 is hushed with s-sounds — sat, scoured, swept, salted — a room going quiet before a performance. Stanza 3 gathers a second wave: slander, shiftless, sloven, spotless, soup, stories, spinning, single strongest — the whisper of a wheel turning. The poem closes softly on sleeping and storytellers.

Plosives

Hard k, t, d and p sounds cluster around objects and tools: cracked delft, clacked, crumb, corn, husk, pieced, darning, done, clogs. These are the sounds of the material world of kitchen and field, knocking against the soft sibilance of voice and breath.

F-alliteration

five or forty fingers (line 8), then the dawn's fire, feet felt for and flat fields (lines 22–24), and finally flew (line 29). One consonant travels from working hands to the hearth and the fields, and ends in flight.

The '-less' words

useless (line 6), shiftless (line 12), spotless (line 13): three words built on the same suffix, the vocabulary of a community that measures people by what they lack. The poem answers them with a word that lacks nothing: work.

Sound as argument

The most telling sound-pattern is the st-cluster that runs through the poem like the thread it describes: stories (lines 6, 15, 25), stitched (8), strongest (17), stirred (22), storytellers (30). The sound binds the stories to stitching and to strength, so the poem's claim — telling is a kind of making, and the strongest kind — is made in the ear as well as in the argument. It also links the storyteller's work to the women's: the stories are told while fingers stitched, and they dissolve as the women stirred.

Clacked is the poem's one clear onomatopoeia: a hard, wooden double click. It is the sound of a busy tongue, and of needles or a loom, and Lochhead lets the two meanings sit together — talk and handwork keeping one rhythm. The trochaic beat of lines 8–9 (/ x / x / x /) carries the same idea: the list of chores is spoken to the tempo of the work.

The softening at the end

The final stanza changes the poem's sound-world. After the hard consonants of chores and clogs, the stories dissolved in the whorl of the ear, a phrase of liquid l and r sounds and open vowels; whorl even sounds like 'whirl', the turning of a spindle. The rhythm of line 25 rocks in anapaests (x / x x / x x / x x /) like a lullaby. Then the sounds grow softer still: the nasals of hung, down, children, again and the long vowels of sleeping and flew hum like breathing in sleep. The last word, night, is a long open vowel that the stanza's first line has already prepared — light and night frame the final sentence — so the poem ends on a sound of return rather than closure.

Silence and breath

Some of the poem's most important sounds are pauses. The enjambment at held / breath makes the reader stop, mid-phrase, at the line-end, as the children stopped breathing. The full stop inside line 18, between the finished thread and Night in, is a hard caesura: one act ends, another begins. And the two-syllable line 26 is almost all white space: a breath held before the stories come back to life. A poem about the spoken voice uses silence as part of its music, exactly as a good teller does.

MOTIFS & SYMBOLS

Motifs & Symbols

Images that recur, and what they accumulate

Thread and textile

The poem's textile vocabulary grows in status as it goes. In stanza 2 it is the vocabulary of chores: fingers stitched, patchwork was pieced, darning was done — the thrift crafts of a household mending what it cannot replace. At line 16 it becomes a figure for art: telling stories was like spinning, gathering air into the single strongest thread. Spinning is the craft the others depend on (stitching and darning need thread), so the storyteller is promoted from accompanist to supplier. In line 25 the motif completes itself in a pun: whorl, the spiral of the ear and the weighted wheel of a spindle, so the listener's ear becomes the spindle on which the teller's thread is wound. From chore to art to transmission: by the end, thread is what passes from one generation to the next.

Light and dark

Light in this poem is scarce and poor. It is rationed like bread — every last crumb of daylight is salted away (line 5) — and when it returns at first light (line 21) it is thin grey light (line 24), watery and colourless, the medium of labour. Night, by contrast, is abundance: Night in (line 18) is the time of the stories, and the poem's last word is night. Lochhead reverses the usual symbolism in which light means knowledge and darkness ignorance; here darkness is where imagination is fed and the day is what has to be endured. The motif is bound together by sound: light and night recur five times, and the last stanza opens on the one and closes on the other.

Food, salt and dissolving

The opening treats daylight as food — crumb, salted away — and the household's economy is an economy of scarcity: grain grated from the husk, soup that may be Dishwater. Salt matters because it preserves; to salt something away is to store it against hard times. When the stories dissolved at dawn (line 25), the image quietly recalls salt dissolving in water: gone from sight but still present, still flavouring what it has dissolved into. The motif turns the stories into both nourishment (what feeds a poor household that has little else) and preserved store (what is kept, invisibly, in the children for later use).

The working body

Lochhead rarely shows whole people. She shows parts of bodies at work: the tongue that clacked (line 7), five or forty fingers (line 8), the held breath of the listeners (lines 19–20), the ending known by heart (line 20), the peasant's feet feeling for clogs (line 23), the ear (line 25), the sleeping heads (line 28). The synecdoche does two jobs. It makes storytelling one bodily labour among others — the tongue is a tool, like the fingers. And it maps the path of a story: out of the teller's tongue, into the listener's ear, held in the breath and the heart, stored in the head, and finally released into flight.

Cleaning and washing

The poem opens on cleaned surfaces — a scoured table, a swept kitchen — and its middle stanza turns cleanliness into a measure of women: sloven or spotless. The storyteller is excused from that measure. At dawn the cleaning returns in a new form: thin grey light is said to have washed over the fields, as if the day were scrubbing away the night. Read together, the cleaning words chart a pressure the poem resists: the day's work wipes things clean, but the stories survive the wash, hidden in the children's heads, ready to fly again.

THEMES

Themes

The ideas the poem is arguing about

01

Storytelling as women's work

The poem's central claim, stated at its midpoint, is that telling the stories was her work. Lochhead earns the claim in stages. First the stories are shown to accompany labour: while the tongue clacked, the listeners' fingers stitched, grain was grated from the husk, patchwork was pieced. Then the claim hardens: telling was not merely the soundtrack to work, it was work. Finally it is given a craft: like spinning, the archetypal female labour.

The poem thus refuses the old opposition between women's 'idle' talk and real, productive labour. The word clacked belongs to the vocabulary used to belittle women's speech, and the poem reclaims it as the sound of a tool. Set at the head of a book that reclaims the Grimms' tales for the women who told them, the theme has a cultural edge: a vast inheritance of stories was produced by women's unpaid, uncredited work.

02

How women are judged

The poem is precise about the standards by which a woman in this world is measured: industry (shiftless is a slander), cleanliness (sloven or spotless), cooking (Dishwater or tasty). The opening stanza's scoured and swept surfaces show those standards being met. The storyteller is the one woman exempt from them: whatever her house or her soup, no one called her lazy, because her real work lay elsewhere.

The exemption is both a tribute and a critique. It honours the storyteller as an artist, valued for her art; and it exposes, by contrast, how every other woman is valued — by surfaces and soup. The '-less' words (useless, shiftless, spotless) are the language of that measuring, and the poem replaces them with a word of positive worth: work.

03

Oral tradition and the handing-on of stories

The poem dramatises how a culture without books keeps its stories. The tales are a known repertoire (the stories), told night after night (Night in), with endings the audience knows by heart. Transmission is bodily and almost involuntary: the stories pass from tongue to ear, dissolve in the whorl of the ear, and lodge in the sleeping heads of the children, beneath awareness, until they can be told again.

The poem is also evidence of its own theme. The speaker was one of the listeners — she'd have us waiting — and is now an adult telling us about it; by the last stanza she speaks of the children from outside, as one of the generation in whom the stories survived. The closing storytellers, without an apostrophe, makes the role plural: the night belongs to whoever tells next.

04

Night, imagination and survival

The poem inverts the usual values of light and dark. Day is scarce and grey: daylight is hoarded in crumb-sized portions, and dawn brings only thin grey light and the return of labour. Night is the time of plenty, imagination and community. At dawn the stories seem to be lost — the stories dissolved — but the volta (but) reveals that they are only sleeping, hung like bats until night lets them fly again.

The theme is survival rather than permanence. The stories are not fixed in a book; they dissolve and re-form, vanish and return. Lochhead's image of survival is cyclical and alive — creatures that roost and fly — rather than monumental.

05

Art and use

The middle stanzas answer an accusation that art is useless. Lochhead first answers it on its own terms (the work got done while the stories were told), then transcends it (the telling was work, and it made the single strongest thread). But the final image goes further: bats are not useful, and the stories that hang and fly by their own will are valuable simply because they live. The poem uses the language of usefulness to win its case and then shows that the case was never really about use.

06

Who gets the credit

The grammar of the poem is full of unnamed workers: agentless passives (was grated, was pieced, was done), participles (scoured, swept), synecdoches (the tongue, fingers, feet), and a heroine who is only she. This is the anonymity of folk culture, in which nobody signs the work — and, the book's title reminds us, the anonymity that let the Brothers Grimm publish a collection gathered largely from women tellers under their own names. The poem does not supply a name; it supplies a title, Storyteller, and an argument that the work deserves the credit, whoever did it.

DIFFICULT MOMENTS

Difficult Moments

Where the poem is genuinely undecidable — and what to do about it

Cruxes

1. Does the poem defend stories for being useful — or against the idea that they must be?

The difficulty. Stanza 2 justifies the stories by what got done while they were told: No one could say they were useless, because the sewing, grating and darning went on. Stanza 3 then calls telling her work. Is Lochhead accepting the terms of the work-ethic that dismissed women's talk — art must earn its keep — or arguing against them?

Competing readings. A concession: the defence is conducted entirely in productive terms; even the praise is grudging litotes, and the climactic claim is that storytelling counts because it is labour. A materialist reader might say the poem accepts that a woman's worth must be measured in output and simply adds a new output to the list. A tactic, then a transcendence: the poem meets the hostile voice in its own currency and wins, then moves beyond it — the simile makes something out of air, and the final image of bats, which do nothing useful at all, values the stories simply because they live. A redefinition: the poem neither concedes nor escapes but enlarges what counts as work, in the spirit of 1970s feminist arguments that women's unpaid labour, domestic and cultural, is real labour.

What a strong answer does. It traces the poem's movement — practical defence, verdict, simile, image — rather than freezing one stage. It hears the grudging tone of the early defence as a community's voice, not the poet's last word, and it lets the ending's 'useless' bats be the final answer, without pretending the earlier stanzas avoid the accuser's language.

2. Who is she — and where is this kitchen?

The difficulty. The storyteller has no name, and the poem begins with a lower-case pronoun. The setting pulls in different directions: a Scots-sounding idiom (Never the one to, sloven, shiftless) and a dresser of delft, but also clogs, flat fields and a generic peasant, the landscape of the Low Countries or the Grimms' Germany.

Competing readings. A remembered individual: the speaker was one of us; the details (cracked plates, possibly thin soup) feel personal, and the poem reads as a memory of a particular woman. A Grimm informant: the book's title, and the peasant world of clogs and fields, point toward the Grimms' tellers — above all Dorothea Viehmann, the countrywoman from near Kassel whose portrait became the image of the tale-wife. But nothing in the poem or in Lochhead's sources consulted here makes that identification, and the Grimms' real informants were mostly educated young women in Kassel, not peasants at all. A composite archetype: the title, the anonymity and the mixed geography make her every woman who told tales by a fire.

What a strong answer does. It holds the personal and the archetypal together: the poem offers the texture of real memory (us, the soup) while withholding name and place, so that one woman can stand for a whole tradition. It does not claim a specific model the evidence does not support.

3. At dawn, are the stories lost or saved?

The difficulty. the stories dissolved sounds like defeat — daylight dissolving dreams. Then the stories hung themselves, a phrase with a dark echo ('hanged themselves'), and roost upside down like bats. Is the ending consoling, elegiac or uncanny?

Competing readings. Elegy: the whole poem is in the past tense; the world of delft and clogs is gone, and flew again may be a hope rather than a fact. Survival: what dissolves is absorbed, not destroyed; the volta but reverses the loss; bats sleep by day and fly by night, so again makes the survival cyclical and certain. The uncanny: bats are gothic creatures, the reflexive verb has a shadow of death, and the stories lodge in children's heads beyond anyone's control — fitting for Grimm tales, which are full of wolves, witches and cruelty.

What a strong answer does. It reads dissolved and but together, sees the darkness of the image as part of the tales' power rather than a contradiction of the consolation, and notices that survival depends on night: the stories live only when they are told again.

4. Whose night is it?

The difficulty. The last line prints storytellers with no apostrophe in the anthology text (some websites silently add one, giving 'storyteller's').

Competing readings. Singular possessive: her night — the tribute ends with the night belonging to the woman the poem has defended. Plural possessive: the storytellers' night — every teller's, including the children who will grow up to tell, and the poet who is telling us now. Compound noun: a 'storytellers night', like 'market day' — a fixture of the calendar, a communal institution rather than anyone's property.

What a strong answer does. It works from the printed form, shows how each reading changes the ending, and connects the openness to the poem's central idea: the storyteller's role is not owned but handed on. The ambiguity is best read as the poem's final act of transmission, the singular Storyteller of the title becoming plural at the close.

CLOSE ANALYSIS

Close Analysis

The moments that repay pressure, worked through

Quotation analysis

1. every last crumb of daylight — salted away (line 5)

Techniques: metaphor (light as food), idiom, hyperbole of thrift, agentless passive, sentence-initial And.

Daylight is imagined as bread, used down to every last crumb, and then salted away — the idiom for hoarding, from preserving meat or fish in salt. The image makes poverty concrete without self-pity: in this household even the light is rationed. But the idiom also means 'saved for later', so the line contains the poem's whole pattern in miniature: something apparently used up is in fact preserved.

Intention and effect: Lochhead makes nightfall a beginning rather than an ending, and teaches us to read later disappearances — the stories dissolving at dawn — as storage rather than loss.

2. the tongue clacked (line 7)

Techniques: synecdoche, onomatopoeia, definite article, reclaimed pejorative.

The teller is reduced to her working organ, as her listeners are reduced to fingers: storytelling becomes one bodily labour among others. Clacked is a hard, wooden sound — needles, a loom, a busy tongue — and it is also the verb for a gossip's chatter, the kind of word used to dismiss women's talk. Lochhead keeps the insult and changes its meaning: the clacking tongue keeps time with the work.

Intention and effect: the reader hears women's speech re-valued from within the very vocabulary that belittled it.

3. slander her shiftless — sloven or spotless (lines 12–13)

Techniques: ellipsis, inversion, sibilance, antithesis, the repeated '-less' suffix.

Line 12 has no main verb; line 13 begins a sentence that has to be rebuilt by the reader. The scrambled syntax sounds like an older speaker talking, and the antitheses set out the standards — industry, cleanliness, good soup — by which women in this world are judged. Slander is a strong word: to call a woman shiftless is to damage her. The storyteller alone is exempt, whatever her housekeeping.

Intention and effect: the poem praises a woman as one would praise an artist, and in doing so exposes the narrow scale on which every other woman is weighed.

4. her work (line 15)

Techniques: plain declarative, monosyllables, regular iambic tetrameter, end-stopping, placement at the poem's hinge.

After two stanzas of qualified defence, the poem states its thesis without qualification. Not 'like work' — work. The line is the poem's one regular iambic line and sits fifteenth of thirty, closing the first half, so it has the weight of a proverb and the position of a verdict. work answers both useless and shiftless.

Intention and effect: the reader is given the claim as if it were common knowledge — the authority of a saying, applied to a truth that tradition did not say.

5. like spinning — single strongest — thread (lines 16–18)

Techniques: simile, paradox, superlative, enjambment, caesura.

Spinning is the archetypal female craft ('spinster', 'distaff side'), the craft of the Fates, and the source of the idiom 'to spin a yarn'. The storyteller spins from air — breath, words — and makes the single strongest thread, the narrative line that holds a community together. The enjambment draws the thread across the line-break, and the full stop after thread snaps it off, finished.

Intention and effect: storytelling is promoted from accompaniment to the most fundamental craft of the house — and, read as Lochhead's own art, the image defines a poem's line: breath gathered into one strong strand.

6. held / breath — knew by heart (lines 19–20)

Techniques: enjambment, first-person plural, habitual modal, paradox, idiom.

The only appearance of us and we reveals the speaker as one of the listening children. The line-break after held makes the reader pause, mid-phrase, as the children did. The paradox — suspense over an ending everyone knew — captures the nature of oral storytelling: the pleasure is in the telling and the shared ritual, not in novelty.

Intention and effect: the poem's argument becomes testimony; the remembered body of the speaker is the evidence that the stories worked.

7. felt for clogs — thin grey light (lines 23–24)

Techniques: anaphora (as… as… as…), synecdoche, alliteration, monochrome imagery, delayed main verb.

Dawn arrives in three slow strokes, each clause beginning as, each delaying the sentence's main verb. A worker's feet grope half-asleep for wooden shoes; a weak, colourless light spreads over level land. The day is meagre and watery, the same grey as Dishwater.

Intention and effect: the delayed syntax builds suspense, and the drained palette reverses the usual symbolism of light — the day is what must be endured, the night what nourishes.

8. whorl of the ear (line 25)

Techniques: pun, metaphor (dissolved), anapaestic rhythm.

The main clause finally arrives and seems to announce defeat: the stories dissolved. But whorl means both the spiral of the ear and, in its oldest sense, the small wheel on a spindle that keeps it turning; the spinning simile is completed as the teller's thread is wound onto the listener's ear. What dissolves is not destroyed but absorbed.

Intention and effect: transmission is shown as bodily and unconscious — the stories become part of the listener rather than something she remembers.

9. hung themselves — sleeping heads — storytellers night (lines 27–30)

Techniques: implied metaphor (bats, never named), reflexive verb, synecdoche, cyclical again, ambiguity of the missing apostrophe.

The stories roost like bats in the children's heads: nocturnal, invisible by day, finding their way by sound. The reflexive verb echoes the women who stirred themselves at dawn, so one group wakes as the other sleeps. The faint echo of 'hanged' adds a Grimm shadow. Then they flew again, and the poem ends on night — the night that belongs to the storyteller, or to all storytellers.

Intention and effect: the ending turns survival into a living cycle, and the open apostrophe hands the role on — to the children, and to the poet whose poem is the stories flying again.

CRITICAL LENSES

Critical Lenses

What each way of reading makes visible, and what it flattens

Critical lenses

1. Feminist

What it makes visible. The poem's three feminist gestures: it names women's cultural labour as work (her work); it frees one woman from the domestic standards by which all women are judged (sloven or spotless, Dishwater or tasty); and it makes the handing-on of stories a line of women and children, from the teller to us to the children. At the head of The Grimm Sisters, it also restores the teller to a tradition that men wrote down and signed. It belongs to the 1970s project Adrienne Rich called re-vision, alongside Sexton's Transformations and Carter's The Bloody Chamber — but where they rewrote the tales, this poem rewrites the credit.

What it flattens. The poem's women are not only victims of an unfair measure; the community's voice is grudgingly approving (No one could say), and the storyteller holds real power over her audience. A purely protest reading can miss the poem's warmth and its pleasure in the craft.

2. Materialist

What it makes visible. The poem is about value and production: what counts as useless, what counts as work. It is precise about the economy of a poor household — rationed light, grated grain, patchwork, darning, thin soup — and about the labour that keeps it running. Storytelling appears as a form of social reproduction: the community remakes its shared culture nightly, as it remakes its clothes. The anonymous passives show labour without workers, the condition of unpaid domestic work.

What it flattens. The poem's final image escapes economics altogether: bats are not productive. A materialist reading risks treating the stories as only another commodity, when the ending insists on their freedom.

3. Formalist

What it makes visible. How much the form performs: stanzas that lengthen like a drawn-out thread; a thesis placed at the hinge in the poem's only regular iambic line; enjambments that draw out a thread (single strongest / thread) and hold a breath (held / breath); a last stanza built as a periodic sentence with suspense, loss and reversal; a final light/night chime. The poem tells its story in the way it says stories were told.

What it flattens. History. A formalist reading can say how the poem works but not why its subject — a woman's anonymous voice behind a famous male-authored collection — matters, nor why the book's title is a pun.

4. Psychoanalytic

What it makes visible. The stories end in the sleeping heads of the children, the place of dreams. Bruno Bettelheim's The Uses of Enchantment (1976) argued that fairy tales do their work on a child's unconscious, helping children master fears they cannot name; Lochhead's bats, roosting unseen in the dark of the sleeping mind and flying at night, are an image of that hidden work. The upside down posture suits the inverted logic of dream, and the eerie echo of 'hanged themselves' suits the dark material of the tales.

What it flattens. The social world: the kitchen, the women's work and the question of credit, which are the poem's main concerns for three stanzas out of four.

5. Historicist

What it makes visible. The real history behind the archetype. The Grimms presented their tales as the voice of the folk and made the countrywoman Dorothea Viehmann its emblem, though most of their informants were educated young women in Kassel. Spinning really was where tales were told: in German spinning rooms, in Scottish 'rockings', in Perrault's frontispiece of an old woman spinning by the fire. Walter Benjamin's 'The Storyteller' (1936) tied storytelling to the rhythm of handwork, as this poem does.

What it flattens. The poem is not a document. Its setting is composite and its woman unnamed; historicist detail can tempt a reader to pin her down (to Viehmann, say) where the poem deliberately does not.

6. Reader-response

What it makes visible. The poem makes its reader behave like its listeners. We are thrown into a scene with an unexplained she; we have to rebuild the scrambled syntax of stanza 3; we pause, breath held, at a line-break; we wait four lines for the main verb of the final sentence. And many readers, like the children, know the ending already — the fairy tales are part of their own childhoods — which makes the paradox of suspense by heart our own.

What it flattens. Reader-response can make the poem about us. The poem is careful to keep its focus on her: her work, her night.

OTHER READINGS

Other Readings

Contested interpretations, and where each is weak

Other readings

1. A portrait of the poet's own art

The storyteller is Lochhead's model for herself: a woman who holds a room with her voice. Lochhead is well known as a performer of her own poems, and the poem defines poetry as voiced craft — air spun into a strong thread — absorbed by listeners rather than possessed by readers.

Evidence: the spinning simile as a definition of the poetic line; the speaker who was one of us and is now the teller; free verse shaped to sound like speech; the plural storytellers at the end.

Weakness: the poem's attention is on the woman and her community, not on the poet. To read it mainly as self-portrait risks repeating the very move it criticises — giving the credit to the writer rather than the teller.

2. An elegy for a vanished oral culture

The poem mourns a world that has gone: kitchens of scoured tables and cracked delft, women sewing by voice-light, children who learned their culture by ear. The past tense governs everything, and flew again may be the poet's hope rather than a fact.

Evidence: the habitual past (she'd have us waiting); the archaic, peasant details (clogs, the dresser, the peasant); the thin, grey dawn that dissolves the stories.

Weakness: the poem refuses elegy at its turn. but and again insist on survival, and the poem itself — a grown listener retelling the scene — is evidence that the stories did fly again.

3. A frame for The Grimm Sisters: reclaiming the tales

As the collection's opening poem, 'Storyteller' sets up the book's project: to give the fairy tales back to the women who told them, after men had collected, edited and signed them. The unnamed she is the source from which the book's other voices descend.

Evidence: the title of the book; the anonymity of the teller; the agentless passives of women's work; the insistence on her work.

Weakness: the poem itself never mentions the Grimms, books or writing; the reclamation is implied by context, and a reader with only the anthology page in front of them has to infer it.

4. A darker reading

The ending is not simply comforting. Stories that hung themselves upside down in sleeping heads, flying out at night, are uncanny — closer to the Grimms' wolves and witches than to nursery comfort. The tales have a life the children cannot control.

Evidence: the echo of 'hanged themselves'; the bat image, with its gothic associations; the sleeping heads, where the stories act unseen.

Weakness: the poem's tone throughout is affectionate and its final movement is release (flew); the dark undertone is real but secondary.

5. A Scottish, vernacular reading

The poem's idiom is Scots-inflected — delft (in Scots, 'delf' is crockery), sloven, shiftless, Night in, the proverb-like Never the one to — and its central figure belongs to a culture whose ballads and tales were carried largely by women's voices. Lochhead, a Makar who writes and performs in Scots, writes as an heir of that tradition.

Evidence: the spoken syntax of stanza 3; the vernacular words; the kitchen with its dresser of delf.

Weakness: the setting deliberately reaches beyond Scotland — clogs, flat fields, a generic peasant — into the continental world of the Grimms. The poem is Scottish in voice but universal in scene.

CONNECTIONS

Connections

How this poem pairs with the rest of the set

Comparison hooks

With 'Follower' (Seamus Heaney)

Link: a child watches an adult practise a craft with awe, and the poem becomes the record of that watching. Heaney's father is ‘An expert’ at the plough; Lochhead's storyteller spins the single strongest thread. Both poems are about what passes down the generations. Shared technique: synecdoche of the working body (Heaney's father's shoulders and eye, Lochhead's tongue, fingers and ear), and a final reversal of roles — Heaney's son now leads with the father stumbling behind; Lochhead's listener has grown into a teller, speaking of the children. Difference: Heaney's inheritance is a burden — the father who ‘will not go away’ — and the craft was never learned; Lochhead's inheritance is a release, stories that flew again, and the craft has passed on.

With 'Carpet-weavers, Morocco' (Carol Rumens)

Link: women's and children's work with thread, and craft as a way a culture carries itself forward. Shared technique: textile imagery that becomes a figure for time and transmission — Rumens's ‘flickering knots’ and the carpet that ‘will travel’, Lochhead's spinning and whorl. Difference: Rumens's children are workers at ‘the loom’, their craft producing a commodity that leaves them behind; Lochhead's children are listeners, and what the women make (stories) stays with them, roosting in their heads. Rumens's future is the carpet's; Lochhead's is the children's.

With 'Sonnet 18' (William Shakespeare)

Link: both poems claim that something made of words survives the death of what it praises. Shared technique: breath as the medium of survival — Shakespeare's poem lives ‘So long as men can breathe’; Lochhead's stories are spun from air and depend on held breath. Difference: Shakespeare's survival is fixed, written and signed — ‘eternal lines’ by a named author for a named beloved; Lochhead's is oral, anonymous and cyclical: the stories dissolve each dawn and fly again each night, and nobody owns them.

With 'A Married State' (Katherine Philips)

Link: both poems weigh how women's lives are measured by domestic roles. Philips reads misery in ‘wives' careful faces’; Lochhead's storyteller might be sloven or spotless, her soup Dishwater or tasty. Shared technique: antithesis as a weighing-scale (married and virgin states; sloven and spotless). Difference: Philips escapes the measure by refusing marriage altogether; Lochhead's woman escapes it from inside the household, through the value of her art — no one could call her shiftless, because telling was her work.

With 'A Different History' (Sujata Bhatt)

Link: both poems ask how a culture survives through language — Bhatt through reverence for books (it is a sin to be ‘rude to a book’) and the inherited ‘oppressor's tongue’; Lochhead through the unwritten tongue that clacked. Shared technique: a closing turn to a future generation — Bhatt's ‘unborn grandchildren’ who grow to love a strange language, Lochhead's sleeping heads of the children. Difference: Bhatt's inheritance comes through conquest and print, and her ending is uneasy; Lochhead's comes through a woman's voice and is celebrated.

With 'Where I Come From' (Elizabeth Brewster)

Link: what is absorbed in childhood is carried for life. ‘People are made of places’, Brewster says, and her people ‘carry woods in their minds’; Lochhead's children carry stories in their heads. Shared technique: the mind as a container that keeps its contents out of sight until something releases them — Brewster's ‘door in the mind’ that blows open, Lochhead's stories that fly again at night. Difference: Brewster's inheritance is a landscape and is entirely personal; Lochhead's is a body of tales shared by a community and handed on deliberately, by a teller.

With 'Hunting Snake' (Judith Wright)

Link: both poems turn on a held breath. Wright's walkers ‘froze half-through a pace’ and then took ‘a deeper breath of day’; Lochhead's listeners wait, held / breath, for the ending. Shared technique: a speaking we and suspense built into the line — Wright's long-delayed release, Lochhead's enjambments and periodic last sentence. Difference: Wright's suspense is caused by real danger and ends in daylight; Lochhead's is created by art, and its release belongs to the night.

Up before the sun, a boy turns a chore into a feast and the feast into a rite — and when the late guest only winks, he eats its share too.
