CONTEXT

Context

The world the poem came out of

The Poet: Charles Mungoshi (1947–2019)

Charles Lovemore Mungoshi was born on 2 December 1947 at Manyene, near Chivhu, in what was then Southern Rhodesia, into a farming family, and grew up in that rural district of the central highveld. He went to school at St Augustine's Mission, Penhalonga, then worked for the Forestry Commission and for the book firm Textbook Sales before becoming an editor at the Literature Bureau (1975–81). After independence he spent about five years at Zimbabwe Publishing House, was writer in residence at the University of Zimbabwe (1985–87), and from 1987 worked as a freelance writer, scriptwriter and editor. He also acted in Zimbabwean television drama; his wife, the actress Jesesi Mungoshi, played the title role in the film Neria (1993). He died in Harare on 16 February 2019, aged 71.

He wrote in both Shona and English. In 1975 he published two novels, Waiting for the Rain (English, Heinemann) and Ndiko Kupindana Kwamazuva (Shona, Mambo Press), and both won International PEN awards. His story collections include Coming of the Dry Season (1972), The Setting Sun and the Rolling World (1987) and Walking Still (1997); the last two each won the Commonwealth Writers' Prize for the Africa region (1988 and 1998). His work was banned for a time by the Rhodesian regime. He is usually thought of as a prose writer first, and that matters for this poem: it is a storyteller's poem, built from a sequence of small events.

The Milkman Doesn't Only Deliver Milk (1981)

'Before the Sun' comes from Mungoshi's only collection of poems, The Milkman Doesn't Only Deliver Milk. Memory Chirere, a Zimbabwean writer and lecturer at the University of Zimbabwe, gives the first edition as the Poetry Society of Zimbabwe, 1981 — the year after independence (18 April 1980) — and a revised second edition from Baobab Books, Harare. Sources disagree about the date of that edition: most give 1998, while Chirere's reference list and Poetry International's copyright line give 1988. Poetry International prints the poem from the Baobab edition. Because that edition was revised, the poem's own first printing cannot be dated more exactly from these sources.

Chirere calls it the least celebrated of Mungoshi's books, and Mungoshi himself was modest about poetry: in an interview with the scholar Flora Veit-Wild he described it as “a sideline, a mere finger exercise”. Chirere reads that phrase as a clue to method, not a dismissal: the poems were where Mungoshi practised compressing language to great precision. 'Before the Sun' fits. It has almost no decoration, and its effects come from exact observation, line-breaks and saying very little.

Compression: Bashō, haiku and Shona work-songs

Chirere records that Mungoshi admired the seventeenth-century Japanese poet Matsuo Bashō, and he argues that Mungoshi's shortest poems have “the multi-dimensional feel” of “far-eastern Haiku or Zen philosophy”; he also compares Mungoshi's poems about objects with late Thomas Hardy. Haiku give one moment of attention, in the present, with the season marked and the comment left out, and a “cutting” word that stops the poem mid-flight. That is a useful lens here: the season is marked (dew, a forecast storm, fresh maize), the poem stays in the present tense, the one-word line arc stops the sentence in the air, and the meaning of the smoke is left open. It is an analogy, not a claim that the poem is written as haiku.

Chirere also connects Mungoshi's short narrative verse to Shona working songs such as the rapoko (finger-millet) threshing song, whose job is to make work feel like play and play feel like work. He describes the free verse as “short, almost hesitant, cascading lines”, with a speaker who observes without being seen. Both descriptions fit this poem closely: a chore turns into a game, and the speaker does not even appear as “I” until line 32.

The real morning: firewood, green maize and the rains

Everything in the poem is ordinary rural work. In a homestead that cooks on wood, splitting logs and lighting the fire is a daily early-morning job, often given to older children. The maize is roasted on the cob over the fire. Chirere calls the cobs “green mealies”, the Southern African English term for fresh maize picked before the grain dries and hardens, roasted whole over the coals and eaten straight off the cob. When the kernels are bitten away, what is left is the pale, ridged core: the poem's skeletons is an exact picture before it is a symbol.

The details fit together. Zimbabwe's rains fall roughly from November to March, and a typical rainy-season day starts hot and clear and builds to an afternoon storm: the poem's first stanza forecasts exactly that. Dew on the grass means the sun is not yet up to dry it. Maize planted with the first rains is ready to eat green from about February, before the main harvest of dry grain from around April. In many rural homes the first green cobs also come at the end of the lean months before harvest, which may be part of why the boy can call two cobs a feast — though the poem itself never mentions hunger.

The speaker's age comes in sideways, as a rule of life: when you are fourteen. If the speaker is close to the poet (born December 1947), a fourteenth year would fall around 1961–62, in colonial Rhodesia. The poem gives no date, though, and its “I” need not be Mungoshi.

The sky and the sacred: what the smoke can and cannot carry

The smoke that rises to the distant sky is called a signal of some unclear kind, or else a sacrificial prayer. Two religious traditions make that second reading available. In Shona religion, as it is usually described, the high God, Mwari (also called Musikavanhu, “creator of people”, and Nyadenga, a name tied to the sky), is generally approached through the ancestral spirits, the vadzimu. Offerings to them (kupira) are usually of beer or snuff, and ceremonies asking for rain (mukwerera) are held around the start of the rains. Mungoshi was also educated at a Christian mission school, and in the Bible the smoke of a burnt offering rises to God: after the Flood “the LORD smelled a sweet savour” (Genesis 8:21), and a psalm asks that prayer rise “as incense” and that lifted hands be “the evening sacrifice” (Psalm 141:2).

What can be claimed is limited. The poem names no god, ancestor, shrine or ceremony. The usual accounts of Shona offerings describe beer and snuff, not smoke, and the boy's fire is a cooking fire, not an altar. sacrificial prayer is the speaker's own tentative second guess, set beside the practical signal and the shrug of some sort. So the religious meaning is a possibility the poem opens, not a rite it describes. It is supported mainly by the ending, where food really is offered to a power in the sky and then eaten. Chirere reads the poem not as ritual but as pastoral communion: the rising sun is “the boy's terrestrial playmate”.

Childhood, Rhodesia and Zimbabwe: before and after 1980

Childhood runs through Mungoshi's writing. Waiting for the Rain (1975) is set in a rural family in a time of drought, as a son prepares to leave home to study abroad, and is about the gap that education opens between him and the people who raised him. After independence he wrote for children: Stories from a Shona Childhood (1989) and One Day Long Ago: More Stories from a Shona Childhood (1991), and the children's stories won a Noma Award (1992). Seasons and the sun recur in his titles (Coming of the Dry Season, Waiting for the Rain, The Setting Sun and the Rolling World). Here, unusually, the sun is not drought or ending but company. Chirere's summary of the childhood poems is that they look back on rural innocence from a distance with nostalgia, but are “never sentimental”: they admit that growing up is hard. In this poem the deflating words do that work: unlike sawdust, just winks, just two little skeletons.

On politics, the evidence points to restraint. Chirere notes that Mungoshi's poetry is usually seen as rarely making socio-political statements, and argues that its politics are “implicit rather than explicit” in some poems ('Neighbours', 'After the Rain', 'Home'). 'Before the Sun' is not one of the poems he reads that way. Nothing colonial appears in it: no white farmer, school, church, money or war. A reader may notice that a book published the year after independence offers a black Zimbabwean childhood as complete in itself, needing no outside frame, but there is no evidence that Mungoshi meant this poem as a political statement. Its subject is a boy, a fire, two cobs and the sun.

THE POEM

The Poem

Line by line, with the analysis alongside

Before the Sun

This poem is still in copyright, so its words are not reproduced here: each line shows a short summary. Read it alongside your anthology or the exam paper, or use Add the text to paste it in from your own copy (it stays on this device).

TBefore the Sun
1a vivid, deep-coloured dawn sky (no verb)
2foretelling hot weather soon
3and, once midday has passed,
4a downpour to come.
5glinting splinters of wood
6leap off the keen blade
7travelling a way across open space,
8[one word: the curve of their flight]
9and, after what feels like forever,
10come to rest, falling like rain
11onto grass still wet from the night.

13but at the age of fourteen
14[two words: large logs, now plural]
15are exactly what one craves.
16the timber releases

19won't set off a sneeze.
20the fire lifts a slender smoke-twist
21which, after a while, rises straight
22and widens like a flute's bell
23toward the far-off heavens: perhaps a message
24of an unspecified kind,
25or an offering made in worship.
26the burning timber fizzes,
27embers leap upward (a capital opens the clause).

29at last appears
30over the eastern horizon, like a
31guest arriving late to a banquet
32the speaker has a pair of corn cobs
33prepared for its arrival.
34he invites the sun to join him
35in eating the fire-cooked corn
36but it merely gives a wink
37the way an adult would.
38so he starts without it, with large
39turn-taking mouthfuls:
40a bite on the sun's behalf,

Lines with a marker have analysis — click one, or just scroll.

Title
Before the Sun
Language & devices

The Preposition Before has two senses held together (Ambiguity): earlier than (the boy is up before sunrise) and in front of, in the presence of, as one stands before a king or an altar. The Definite article makes it the sun, the one sun everyone shares. The title names no boy, meal, place or season: only the sun and a relation to it. It is also literally true of the poem's layout. The sun is not mentioned in the text until line 28, so the first twenty-seven lines really do happen before the sun. The poem's last word returns to sun (Circular structure).

Meaning & effect

The title sets up both the comedy and the seriousness of the poem. In the time sense it is a small boast: the boy has beaten the sun to the day, so when the sun arrives his work is done and his food is ready, and the sun is the latecomer. In the presence sense, everything he does — the fire, the smoke climbing to the sky, the portion set aside — is done in front of a great power, almost as a performance or an offering. The poem keeps both senses alive: a race the boy wins and a ceremony he performs. By the end he is no longer before the sun but sitting in its light, and the movement between those two prepositions is the shape of the whole morning.

Line 1
Intense blue
Language & devices

A Noun phrase with no verb; the whole first sentence (lines 1–4) has no main verb at all (Minor sentence). The adjective Intense is usually used of heat, feeling or concentration, not colour, so the blue is made strong, saturated, almost pressing. Visual imagery of colour comes before any person, place or pronoun: the poem starts In medias res.

Meaning & effect

The poem begins with perception, not story: before we know who is looking, we are given what is seen. Intense makes this a fierce, clear morning rather than a soft dawn, and it already hints at the heat to come. A sky can only look blue to someone who is outside and looking up, so the speaker is already awake and outdoors; the title's Before has already happened. Without a verb, the morning is a state rather than an event: it simply is, and the reader is placed inside it.

Lines 2–4
early heat
Language & devices

Personification: the morning is promising, like a person giving a pledge (and also in the weaker sense of “showing signs of”). The lines are a forecast (Prolepsis): the whole day is mapped before it happens, heat first and then heavy rain. There is still no main verb; the Participle promising carries the sentence to the stanza's full stop. A comma after afternoon delays the last two words. later is the first of three (lines 3, 9, 21).

Meaning & effect

The speaker reads the sky like a farmer reading the weather: competently, without fuss. The forecast is the ordinary rainy-season pattern on the highveld — a hot morning, a storm in the afternoon — and in a farming world, with maize in the fields, rain is good news. So the opening is hopeful. But it also frames the poem: the bright morning sits inside a longer day that the poem will never reach, since it ends while the morning is still young. heavy is the stanza's one weighty word, a slight shadow over the brightness. The personified, promising morning also introduces the poem's basic premise: nature behaves like someone who talks to the boy, which prepares for the sun as a guest.

Lines 5–7
bright chips … sharp axe
Language & devices

The Definite articles (The, the sharp axe) present the scene as familiar. Paired adjectives give light and edge: bright, sharp. Enjambment holds back the verb fly. The chips are the grammatical subject and the axe is only where they fly from: the person swinging it is left out (Ellipsis). Hard sounds — the /b/, /ch/, /sh/ and /ks/ of bright chips and sharp axe — make the work audible. for some distance is a deliberately vague measure, the first of three somes (lines 7, 24, 30), and through the air is a redundant phrase that lengthens the line.

Meaning & effect

The work begins without a worker. The boy is so absorbed in what he is watching that he disappears from his own sentence, which is how real concentration feels. bright is exact: freshly split wood is pale and catches the early light, so the chips flash as they fly. Treating the chips as a spectacle turns the chore into something worth watching. The vague some distance is how a watcher sees, not a measurer: what matters is the flight, and the extra, unhurried phrase through the air lets the line take its time, as the chips do.

Line 8
arc,
Language & devices

A One-word line, the shortest in the poem, with white space on both sides. arc is used as a Verb (to move in a curve): a noun from geometry turned into an action. It is the middle term of three verbs, fly … arc … settle. The comma keeps the sentence suspended rather than ending it, and Enjambment runs into and out of it.

Meaning & effect

The line does what it says. The chip reaches the top of its curve and seems to hang there, and the reader's eye hangs with it on a single word. Mungoshi breaks the sentence at its highest point, so one flight becomes three moments: launch, peak, landing. The word comes from geometry, the language of clean, perfect shapes, so a scrap of firewood is given the dignity of a mathematical curve. The line is the poem's clearest statement of its method: one exact word, placed in space, instead of description. It works rather like the “cut” in the haiku Mungoshi admired, holding a single image still.

Line 9
eternities later
Language & devices

Hyperbole: a chip falls in about a second, yet lands eternities later. The plural eternities, rather than the cliché “an eternity”, multiplies the exaggeration. The line slows narrative time (Time dilation). The casual connective and and the trailing comma keep the sentence drifting. later echoes line 3.

Meaning & effect

This is the poem's psychological centre: deep attention stretches time. To the absorbed fourteen-year-old, the second of the chip's fall really does seem endless, so the exaggeration is accurate to the experience rather than boastful. eternities is a grand, strange word in a poem of plain words, and it brings in a sense of time beyond human measure that quietly prepares the religious language of line 25. It also contrasts with the first stanza: there, a whole day is squeezed into four lines; here, one second is stretched to eternity. Time in this poem is measured by attention, not by clocks.

Lines 10–11
in showers
Language & devices

The Phrasal verb settle down is gentle and domestic — what birds or children do at night — and contrasts with fly. Metaphor: the chips fall in showers, like rain. dewy marks early-morning moisture. Sibilance and longer vowels (settle, showers, grass) soften the stanza after its hard opening. The stanza's single sentence ends here.

Meaning & effect

The stanza enacts a complete movement: a sharp launch, a suspended peak, a soft landing. settle down gives the chips a kind of life, as if they rest after flying. showers makes the boy's chopping a small private weather: the axe makes a rain of wood before the sky delivers the heavy rain it has promised, so the boy's work echoes the rhythm of the day. dewy is a time-stamp, since the dew is still on the grass and the sun has not risen to dry it. The beauty here is found in debris — chips that will simply be burned.

Line 12
a big log
Language & devices

A blunt Declarative sentence of five monosyllables, ending in a Colon that sets up what follows. The Register drops from the lyrical second stanza to flat fact. big is the first of three uses (lines 12, 14, 38).

Meaning & effect

After the slow-motion beauty of the chips comes a plain statement, which is exactly how a boy sizes up a job: no bark, grain or weight, just big. The bluntness is comic and honest. The colon poses a problem — the log is big, so what? — that the next lines answer. The line also quietly puts a person back into the scene: someone is standing over the log, measuring it by eye.

Lines 13–15
when you are fourteen
Language & devices

The Conjunction but turns an apparent difficulty into the attraction. The shift to the Second person you turns a private feeling into a general rule, and that rule is how the speaker's age is given: when you are fourteen. Repetition with a change of number — a big log becomes big logs — widens one task into an appetite. Line 14 is just two words, set apart. The word order puts big logs first and what you want after, so the logs are emphasised.

Meaning & effect

This is the funniest and truest moment in the poem: at fourteen, the difficulty is the point. A big log tests your strength and measures how grown-up you are becoming, so the boy does not put up with the chore — he wants it to be hard. you makes the feeling universal; anyone who has been fourteen recognises it. It also reveals a voice that can stand outside fourteen and generalise about it, the clearest hint that an older poet is shaping the memory. The age is stated as a law of life rather than a fact about I, so the poem tells us who the speaker is by telling us what he wants.

Lines 16–17
nose-cleansing odour
Language & devices

Olfactory imagery: the poem moves from sight to smell. The hyphenated Compound adjective nose-cleansing, which sounds coined, describes an effect on the body rather than a scent. There is a contrast of Diction: sweet is pleasant and lyrical, odour neutral and almost clinical. The wood is again the subject; the boy is still absent. Enjambment after gives off.

Meaning & effect

Smell is the most bodily sense, and Mungoshi describes it by what it does: it clears your nose. The wood is generous — it gives off its scent — and clean. Whether this is the smell of freshly split timber or of the first burning, even the fuel is a pleasure; nothing in this morning is drudgery. The functional, made-up compound is typical of the poem's taste for exact, useful words over pretty ones.

Lines 18–19
(unlike sawdust)
Language & devices

A Parenthesis, the poem's only brackets, holding a negative comparison, unlike sawdust. The impersonal Pronoun one is formal and detached, while the contraction doesn't is colloquial. Bathos: the poem moves from sweet to sneezing.

Meaning & effect

A deliberate deflation. After the sweetness, the speaker adds a practical, almost scientific aside: this smell, unlike the dust from a saw, won't make you sneeze. It keeps the poem honest — this is the “never sentimental” quality Chirere finds in Mungoshi's childhood poems — and it sounds like someone who knows wood well enough to compare kinds of work, perhaps the older voice again. The brackets mark the remark as an aside, as if the speaker leans in, says it and steps back. The detached one returns, transformed, as the counting word of the final chant.

Lines 20–22
a thin spiral
Language & devices

Ellipsis: the lighting of the fire is never shown; between stanzas the wood is simply burning. The Phrasal verb sends up implies sending something to someone (a flare, a message, a petition). A precise visual sequence: thin spiral → straightens → flutes out. flutes out turns a noun into a verb: the smoke widens like the bell of a flute, or forms a fluted column, and the word also carries music. Sibilance links sends, spiral, smoke, straightens. later appears again.

Meaning & effect

Mungoshi lets the gap between stanzas tell part of the story: the fire has been lit without comment. The smoke is observed exactly — a curl, then a straight column as the fire steadies in still morning air, then spreading higher up. sends up turns smoke into communication: something is being dispatched upward. flutes out adds shape and sound to a silent image, and the column joining the boy's fire to the sky prepares the question of what the smoke means.

Lines 23–25
a signal … sacrificial prayer
Language & devices

A Colon after the distant sky introduces an interpretation. Two alternatives are joined by or and neither is chosen: the practical signal and the religious sacrificial prayer (Juxtaposition of registers). The hedge of some sort (the second some) shrugs. Sibilance runs through sky, signal, sort, sacrificial. Three short lines fall down the page; distant puts the destination far off.

Meaning & effect

This is the poem's interpretive centre, and it falls at the exact middle of the poem (lines 23–24 of 46). The speaker sees the smoke as possibly a message and possibly an offering to God or the gods, and refuses to choose; the shrug of some sort undercuts any solemnity. Both readings share one assumption: the smoke is addressed to someone, so the sky is imagined as a listener. sacrificial prayer is the poem's only openly religious phrase. It draws on an idea common to many traditions — smoke rising to heaven — but names no god and no rite. It also looks ahead: at the end, food really is offered to a power in the sky, and then eaten.

Lines 26–27
hisses … sparks fly
Language & devices

The shortest stanza, two lines of Parallelism: article, noun, verb, twice. Onomatopoeia in hisses. Repetition of fly from line 6, as chips become sparks. The second line begins with a capital although it follows a comma. It is the only line in the poem that is capitalised without beginning a sentence, so the two clauses stand side by side as equals. Both are in the simple present: short, complete statements.

Meaning & effect

The fire takes hold in two lines: sound, then light. The bare, matching clauses sound like a formula or a chant, and the poem slows into something like ceremony. fly links the two halves of the boy's work: the axe made chips fly, and now the fire makes sparks fly. This is the poem's hinge. Everything before it is preparation and everything after it is the guest and the meal, and Mungoshi gives the turning point the least space, so the turn happens as quickly as a fire catching.

Lines 28–29
shows up
Language & devices

The first mention of the sun in the poem, twenty-eight lines in. The sentence opens with And, as an oral storyteller's sentences do. The Adverb finally signals impatience. shows up is a colloquial Idiom, used of people who turn up (late) to a gathering, not of stars. Personification begins.

Meaning & effect

The sunrise is told as if a friend had turned up late. finally carries the boy's mock-complaint: he has been working for some time and the sun is behind schedule. The casual idiom cuts the sun down to human size; the most powerful thing in the sky is treated as a slack guest. The title's first meaning is completed here: the boy has been, quite literally, before the sun.

Lines 30–31
some latecomer
Language & devices

Simile: the sun is like some / latecomer, the poem's first like, arriving at a feast. Internal rhyme: East (mid-line) chimes with feast (line-end), the poem's one close rhyme. The capital on East makes the direction proper, slightly formal. some (the third) is casual and dismissive. Enjambment after some delays the comparison for a beat.

Meaning & effect

The comparison makes sunrise a social occasion and the boy's breakfast a feast: two cobs of maize promoted to a banquet. Calling the sun some latecomer is mock-scornful but affectionate, since you only complain about lateness when you were expecting the guest. The rare rhyme lands as the guest arrives, so the language gives a small flourish of welcome. feast may also carry the real specialness of fresh green maize after the lean months, but the tone is play: the boy has a feast because he has decided it is one.

Lines 32–33
two cobs of maize
Language & devices

The first I in the poem, at line 32 of 46, in the same sentence as the sun's arrival. The colloquial I have got is childlike, with a touch of pride. The number is exact: two. ready is a host's word, and the sun is still it. There is no comma after feast, so the sun's arrival and the boy's readiness run together in one breath.

Meaning & effect

The speaker names himself only as company arrives: the I appears when there is someone to be “I” in front of. Two cobs means one each, so he planned a share for the guest before the guest appeared. That recasts the log, the fire and the smoke as preparations for a visit. I have got is the pride of a host who is ready on time when the guest is not. The sun is still it here; it becomes a person in the next stanza, when it is spoken to.

Lines 34–35
come share
Language & devices

The verb tell (not “ask” or “beg”) is confident, even bossy. share is placed at the line-end by Enjambment, and the word order that follows (with me before its object) is slightly formal. roasted is a Participle used as an adjective: the cobs have been cooked on the fire. The boy speaks to the sun in reported speech, a kind of Apostrophe.

Meaning & effect

The boy speaks to the sun as an equal, almost a junior: no prayer, no awe, just an invitation from host to guest. This is a different relationship with the sky from the sacrificial prayer of stanza 5 — friendship rather than worship, sharing rather than giving something up. share sits at the end of its line as the poem's key moral word, because the meal becomes a feast only when it is shared.

Lines 36–37
just winks
Language & devices

Personification is completed: the sun winks. The Adverb just means “merely” (the first of two; compare line 45). A second Simile (a grown-up) brings in the only adult in the poem. A wink is a one-eyed gesture of shared understanding, and it is also a good picture of the sun's first glint over the horizon, or of an eye half-closed against it. The stanza ends on a short line and a full stop.

Meaning & effect

The sun's answer is perfect: it neither accepts nor refuses, but acknowledges the game, as an amused adult winks at a child's pretend party. just carries a small disappointment — the sun only winks; it will not sit down and eat — but the boy takes it cheerfully. The wink sets the limit of the poem's closeness to nature: the world plays along, kindly, from a distance. It is also the only grown-up in the poem. No parent or elder appears, and the sun takes that role: benign, knowing, uninvolved.

Lines 38–39
So I go ahead
Language & devices

So is a logical connective: the wink is taken as permission. The idiom go ahead is what a host does when a guest is delayed. big returns for the third time, isolated at the line-end by Enjambment. alternate is the word that turns eating into a structure. A Colon presents the ritual that follows.

Meaning & effect

The boy reads the wink as “carry on” and starts, politely, by the rules of hospitality. big ties the bites to the big logs: the same fourteen-year-old appetite, now for pleasure instead of work. alternate is the key word. Eating becomes an ordered game, the kind of rule children invent, and a pattern repeated on purpose like this is also the shape of a ritual.

Lines 40–43
for the sun
Language & devices

Repetition and Parallelism across four short lines, in the counting formula of a children's sharing game (“one for you, one for me”). one and sun share a vowel (Assonance, almost an Internal rhyme); me stays outside that sound. The second pair adds This, a pointing (Deictic) word, as if a cob is held up. The lines alternate as the bites do. A full stop ends the first pair and a colon the second.

Meaning & effect

Form becomes action: the lines take turns, as the eaters do. The formula is a child's — the way children divide sweets — so the scene is play. But the measured, repeated pattern also sounds like a chant or a liturgy, an offering portioned out in words, and the poem holds both: here a game and a rite are the same gesture. The shift to This one shows the boy warming to the game, more emphatic and theatrical. The cool, impersonal one of line 19 has become the warm counting word of a shared meal. And of course the sun cannot eat, so the boy eats every bite: the sharing is entirely imaginative, generous in spirit and comic in fact.

Lines 44–45
two little skeletons
Language & devices

till lets the ritual run to its natural end. Metaphor: the stripped cobs are skeletons, ridged and pale like bone. little is the poem's only diminutive, reversing the three bigs. just (the second) means “only”. two returns from line 32.

Meaning & effect

The meal ends in an image of death, and the poem will not be simply cheerful. The picture is accurate first — a gnawed cob does look like a small spine — and comic. But skeletons brings mortality into a poem that has had none: everything eaten leaves remains. little cancels the poem's bigs, so the appetite for big logs and big bites ends in something small, and just deflates once more. Whether this is gentle humour, a shadow of transience, or the proper remains of a completed offering is the poem's main crux, and Mungoshi, as with the smoke, does not say.

Line 46
lying in full sunlight.
Language & devices

The final words return to the title's noun, sun (Circular structure). The preposition has changed: the title's Before has become in. sun ends four lines of the poem (28, 40, 42, 46) and is its last word. The last sentence runs from the chant, through a colon, straight into this image, with no comment in between.

Meaning & effect

The boy began before the sun and ends in it: the morning is over, the light has arrived, the shared feast is finished. The skeletons lie in open daylight, a picture of something used up, and perhaps the start of the hot day forecast in line 2. The sun that winked is now simply the light falling on what is left; the playmate has become the impartial day. The poem ends on an image, not a comment, leaving the reader to weigh the joy against the bones.

THE WHOLE POEM

The Whole Poem

Stepping back: what the poem is doing, first line to last

The argument of the poem

'Before the Sun' can look like a charming snapshot: a boy splits a log, lights a fire, roasts two cobs of maize and invites the sun to breakfast. Read closely, it is a poem about what attention does to an ordinary chore — it turns work into play, play into something like a rite, and a meagre breakfast into a feast. It is also about the limits of that transformation, which the poem marks every time with a shrug, a bracket or the word just. Its joy convinces because it is never naive. Each moment of enchantment is followed by a small deflation, and the poem ends by admitting that what was enjoyed has been used up.

Before anyone is there

The poem starts with perception and no perceiver. Intense blue morning has no verb and no I; the first sentence runs for four lines without a main verb, so the morning is a state the reader is placed inside rather than an event that happens. Yet the morning is already a speaker of sorts, promising heat and then rain, and the boy reads it like a farmer. Two things are set up at once. Nature is something that talks, which prepares for the sun as a guest. And the day is bigger than the poem: the forecast reaches into an afternoon that the poem never gets to, so the bright morning is enclosed, from the start, inside a day that will move on.

The chips stanza shows what attention does to time. The worker vanishes from his own sentence — the chips fly from the sharp axe, with no arm, no swing, no I — because he is absorbed in what he sees. The sentence breaks at the top of the flight on the single word arc, and the landing comes eternities later. The hyperbole is precise rather than boastful: to a fourteen-year-old wholly inside the moment, one second really is endless. The chips land in showers on dewy grass, so the boy's axe makes a small private weather before the sky delivers the rain it promised. Already the chore is a spectacle.

Work becomes appetite

The third stanza converts difficulty into desire: it is a big log — but at fourteen big logs are exactly what you want. This is the poem's comic truth about growing up: the hard version of the job is the attractive one, because what you can split measures what you are becoming. Memory Chirere links Mungoshi's short verse to Shona work-songs that make work feel like play and play feel like work, and this stanza does that in miniature. The switch to you also lets an older voice show through: only someone past fourteen can generalise about being fourteen.

Then comes the first deflation. The wood's sweet nose-cleansing odour is followed by a bracketed, almost scientific aside, (unlike sawdust), noting that it won't make you sneeze. The poem will not let sweetness stand unqualified. This is what Chirere means when he calls Mungoshi's childhood poems nostalgic but “never sentimental”: the poem stays loyal to the actual texture of the morning, sneezes included.

The smoke at the centre

The fire is lit off-stage, between stanzas; we see only its smoke, which sends up a spiral that straightens and flutes out to the distant sky. At the exact centre of the poem (lines 23–24 of 46) the speaker interprets it: a signal, of some sort, or a sacrificial prayer. This is the poem's furthest reach toward the sacred, and the shrug of some sort stops it from becoming solemn. Both alternatives imagine the sky as a listener; neither is chosen. Shona and Biblical traditions can both support the second reading, but the poem names no god or rite. Its subject is the way an ordinary act can look like worship, not a ceremony it secretly records. The two-line fire stanza that follows, in which the wood hisses and sparks fly, has the bare, matched rhythm of a chant: the hinge between preparation and meal, given the least space in the poem.

The guest arrives

The sun is not mentioned until line 28, so the poem has literally happened before the sun. When it shows up it is demoted to a slack guest, some latecomer to a feast, and the poem's one close rhyme (East … feast) greets its arrival. Only now does I appear, at line 32: the speaker becomes a self at the moment he has company. I have got two cobs is the pride of a host who is ready when the guest is not, and it recasts everything before it — log, fire, smoke — as preparation for a visit.

He tell[s] the sun to come and share: the tone is friendship, not supplication, a different relation to the sky from the sacrificial prayer. And the sun's reply is the second deflation: it just winks, like a grown-up. The wink acknowledges the game without joining it, as an amused adult humours a child. Nature plays along, kindly, from a distance — the limit of the poem's communion, stated without complaint.

The rite, and what is left

So the boy goes ahead with big alternate bites, and the poem's lines alternate with him: one for the sun, one for himself, then again with a pointing This. The formula is a child's sharing-game and also the shape of a liturgy; here play and ritual are the same gesture, and the detached pronoun one of line 19 has become the warm counting word of a meal. Since the sun cannot eat, the boy eats every bite. The generosity is entirely imaginative, and comic in fact.

The ending is the final deflation. The cobs are just two little skeletons. just shrinks, little cancels the poem's three bigs, and skeletons brings the first image of death into a poem that has had none. The picture is first of all exact (a gnawed cob does look like a small spine) and funny; but it admits that whatever is consumed leaves remains, and the poem's last word returns to the sun. The boy who began before the sun now sits in its full light, with the morning — and the feast — over.

The strongest objection

The strongest objection is that the poem is slight: a pleasant anecdote, or a piece of nostalgia that makes a hard rural childhood pretty. The reply is in its construction and its restraint. It is built more carefully than its casual voice suggests: the sun withheld for twenty-seven lines, the I withheld until the sun arrives, the smoke placed at the exact centre, one turned from pronoun to number, big reversed into little, chips falling in showers before the rain. And it refuses sentiment exactly where sentiment is easiest — after the sweet smell, after the invitation, after the feast. A second objection pulls the other way: that the poem is a disguised Shona rite and the boy is really worshipping. That reading has real support (the smoke, the offering, the portioning chant), but it has to ignore the poem's own shrug — of some sort — and the wink that declines the offering. The better account is the poem's own: a morning attended to this fully is a feast, a game and very nearly a prayer, and it is also, by the last line, eaten.

FORM & STRUCTURE

Form & Structure

How the poem is built, and why it matters

Form & genre

Free verse: 46 lines in nine stanzas, with no metre, no rhyme scheme and no regular stanza shape. In genre it is a dawn poem, a childhood lyric and a small narrative of work, and in its last stanza it becomes a kind of ritual chant. It can also be read as a reversed aubade: the traditional dawn poem resents the sunrise (Donne's “Busy old fool, unruly sun”), while this one waits for the sun as a guest.

Stanzas

Nine stanzas of 4, 7, 4, 4, 6, 2, 6, 4 and 9 lines. Each stanza is a single sentence except the last, which has two. The shortest stanza (two lines, the fire catching) is the hinge; the longest (nine lines, the shared meal) is the ending.

Lines & rhythm

Very short lines, mostly two to five words: the one-word line arc (line 8) and the two-word big logs (line 14) are the extremes. There is no metre. Rhythm comes from stress clusters, line-breaks and repetition, and from the counting chant of lines 40–43.

Rhyme & echo

No rhyme scheme. One close rhyme, East (mid-line 30) with feast (end of line 31), arrives with the sun. Three line-endings far apart rhyme fully: air (7), prayer (25), share (34). Other echoes come from repeated words: sun ends four lines; big ×3; some ×3; later ×3; fly ×2; just ×2.

Syntax & punctuation

Ten sentences. The first has no main verb. There are four colons (lines 12, 23, 39, 43), one pair of brackets (line 18), and one oddity: The sparks fly begins with a capital after a comma (line 27).

Voice & tense

First-person, present tense throughout: there is no simple past and no “I remember” frame. No person appears in stanzas 1–2; a generalising you comes in stanza 3 and an impersonal one in stanza 4; I is withheld until line 32, the stanza in which the sun arrives.

Two halves: before the sun, and with it

The poem is built in two unequal parts, and the title names the first. Stanzas 1–6 (lines 1–27) contain no mention of the sun at all: they are sky, chips, log, smell, smoke and fire — the boy's work, done in the half-light. Stanzas 7–9 (lines 28–46) begin when the sun arrives and are taken up with the guest and the meal. Structurally, then, the poem does exactly what its title says. Twenty-seven lines happen before the sun, and the last nineteen happen in its presence. The final word, sun, closes the frame the title opened, and the change of preposition from Before to in measures the morning's passing.

One sentence, one act of attention

Because each stanza (apart from the last) is one sentence, each reads as a single act of noticing, and its length is however long the noticing takes. The chips stanza is the longest sentence (seven lines) because the flight is being slowed down: launch, arc, eternities, landing. The log stanza and the smell stanza are four lines each, quick judgements. The smoke stanza runs to six lines as the column climbs and the speaker interprets it. The fire stanza is two lines because a fire catching is sudden. The poem's shape is the shape of a mind moving from one absorption to the next. Memory Chirere describes Mungoshi's free verse as “short, almost hesitant, cascading lines”, and the stanza-sentences do cascade, especially in stanza 5, where three short lines tumble down the page to the poem's two interpretations of the smoke.

The last stanza breaks the pattern. It has two sentences: the first states the rule (alternate bites, ending in a full stop at line 41), and the second repeats it with more emphasis (This one), then runs through a colon into the ending. Giving the final ritual two sentences lets it be stated and then performed, and the colon at line 43 joins the chant directly to its result: the counting leads straight to the skeletons.

Lineation: short lines and white space

The short lines are a way of controlling the reader's speed. Three places show it clearly.

  • arc (line 8). A one-word line with white space on both sides: the eye stops on the word as the chip pauses at the top of its curve. It is the middle verb of three (fly → arc → settle), cut out and held up, so the sentence is suspended at its highest point.
  • big logs (line 14). Two heavy stressed words alone on a line, the boy's desire set out like a slogan. The line-break isolates the object of the wanting before the verb arrives on the next line.
  • like some / latecomer (lines 30–31). The break after some delays the comparison for a beat, like a comic pause before a punchline.

Enjambment elsewhere does similar work. The break between chips and fly holds the verb back so the chips hang in the air. The break after big (line 38) leaves the word alone at the line-end, recalling the big log, before alternate arrives. The break after till the cobs delays skeletons so that the metaphor lands as a small surprise. Almost every line runs on into the next, which gives the poem the feel of a voice thinking as it goes, and makes the few end-stopped lines (the full stops at the ends of stanzas) feel like moments of settling.

Rhythm in key lines

There is no metre to scan, but the stresses in key lines are worth counting, because the poem's rhythm changes with its subject.

Fragment Stress pattern Effect
Intense blue morning x / / / x three stresses crowded together: a strong, full opening, as heavy as the colour
bright chips / / two stresses side by side (a spondee): hard and quick, like the axe-blow
arc / a single stress surrounded by silence: the pause at the top of the flight
eternities later x / x x / x few stresses among many light syllables: the line drifts and lengthens, as the moment does
big logs / / two heavy stresses: the weight of what he wants
wood hisses / sparks fly / / x / / matched clusters of stress: the fire stanza as a chant
one for the sun / x x / the falling-rising beat of a counting rhyme
two little skeletons / / x / x x stresses then a falling run of light syllables: the poem's energy runs down

The pattern across the poem moves from heavy, clustered stresses (the sky, the axe, the logs, the fire) to the light, sing-song beat of the counting chant and then the dying fall of skeletons. The rhythm traces the morning: effort, then play, then ending.

Rhyme and echo, worked out

The poem has no rhyme scheme, and it is sometimes said to contain only one rhyme. That is not quite right. There is one close rhyme, East … feast, and it falls exactly where the sun arrives: East sits in the middle of line 30 and feast ends line 31, so it is an internal rhyme across a line-break rather than a rhyme on two line-ends. In a poem otherwise without nearby rhymes, the language gives a small chime of welcome at the guest's entrance.

There is also a widely spaced chain of full rhymes on line-endings: air (line 7, the chips' flight), prayer (line 25, the smoke's meaning) and share (line 34, the invitation). They are eighteen and nine lines apart, so the ear may not register them, and they may not be planned. But they join the poem's three upward or outward movements: the chips into the air, the smoke into the sky as prayer, the meal held out to the sun to share.

Beyond rhyme, the poem's music is repetition. sun ends four lines (28, 40, 42, 46). one sounds like sun, so the counting word contains the guest's sound, while me stays outside it. big comes three times, and is cancelled at the end by little. some comes three times (some distance, some sort, some / latecomer) — a habit of loose, unpretentious measuring. later also comes three times, linking three scales of time: the afternoon, the chip's eternities, and the smoke straightening. fly comes twice, chips then sparks, and just twice, at the wink and at the skeletons.

Punctuation: colons, brackets and one capital

The colon is the poem's characteristic mark. It appears four times, and each time it presents something for inspection: the log (big log:), the meaning of the smoke (the distant sky:), the ritual (alternate bites:) and the result of the ritual (for me: → the skeletons). The colon is a mark of display, which suits a poem that holds objects up to look at them rather than explaining them.

The brackets of (unlike sawdust) are the poem's only parenthesis, and they mark an aside: a practical comparison that sounds like an older, knowledgeable voice stepping in and out again. The capital on The sparks fly, after the comma that follows The wood hisses, is the one place where a line begins with a capital without beginning a sentence. The effect is to make the two clauses equal and separate, like two lines of a chant.

Pronouns and tense: where the speaker appears

The poem's pronouns are an architecture of their own. Stanzas 1–2 contain no person at all. The chips fly from the sharp axe, and nobody swings it. Stanza 3 brings in a generalising you (when you are fourteen), stanza 4 the formal one (make one sneeze), and stanzas 5–6 go back to impersonal subjects (It, The wood, The sparks). The first I comes at line 32, in the sentence where the sun arrives, and me follows (lines 35, 41, 43). The speaker becomes a self at the moment he has company. Meanwhile one changes job: the detached pronoun of line 19 becomes the counting number of lines 40–43.

The present tense throughout is the poem's boldest formal decision. A remembered childhood is told without the frame of memory, so the reader is inside the fourteen-year-old's morning rather than looking back at it with an adult (compare the past tense and the adult present of Heaney's 'Follower'). Only two moments hint at an older voice: the generalisation when you are fourteen, which only someone past fourteen can make, and the knowledgeable bracket (unlike sawdust).

The turn

If the poem has a volta, it is line 28, when the sun appears, where the poem turns from work to company. The six stanzas of preparation give way to three stanzas of hospitality, and with that turn comes the first simile, the first rhyme and the first I. The two-line fire stanza just before it is the hinge: the moment the fire catches, the guest is due. A smaller, later turn comes in the final two lines, where the game stops and the image of skeletons lets time and loss into the poem. The poem never comments on that last turn. It sets down the image and stops.

SOUND

Sound

What the poem does to the ear

Sound in free verse

With no metre or rhyme scheme, the poem's sound comes from consonant patterns, a few vowel echoes, repetition, and the rhythm of its very short lines.

Key patterns

Sharp-to-soft consonants in stanza 2; sibilance running from axe to fire; onomatopoeia in hisses; one close rhyme (East … feast); the counting chant of one and sun.

Stanza 2: sharp to soft

The chips stanza is a single sound-movement from hard to soft. It opens on short, clipped sounds: bright chips and sharp axe pack plosive /b/ and /p/, the affricate /ch/, the fricative /sh/ and the cluster /ks/ around short vowels. They are as edged as the tool, and they make the blow audible. In the middle, arc stands alone, a single open vowel closed by /k/, a hard sound held in silence. The stanza ends in softer, longer sounds: settle, showers and dewy grass bring in the hushed /sh/, the voiced /z/ of showers, and long vowels in down, dewy and grass. The reader hears the chips fly and land, and the softening matches settle down: the stanza itself comes to rest.

Sibilance from axe to fire

One sound, /s/, runs through every stage of the morning and changes its job each time. It is sharp in the axe (sharp, axe); soft in the landing (settle, showers, grass); curling upward in the smoke, where sends, spiral, smoke and straightens link the whole rising movement; and literally audible when the wood hisses. Then sacrificial and signal take it up into the sky. The consonant carries the poem from cutting to burning to prayer.

The fire couplet

The two lines of the fire stanza (wood hisses, sparks fly) are two tiny sound-pictures. The first is fricative — the /s/ and /z/ of hisses are the hiss of damp wood. The second is abrupt: sparks wraps /sp/ and /ks/ around one short vowel, the sound of a spark cracking, and fly opens into a long vowel as the spark rises. Matching syntax and stress (article, noun, verb) give the pair the ring of a chant.

flutes out

The long /oo/ of flutes makes the mouth round and open as the word is said, so the sound shapes itself like the widening column of smoke. It is the one musical instrument in the poem, and it gives a silent image a sound.

The welcome rhyme and the long /ee/

The single close rhyme, East … feast, arrives with the sun, so the language greets the guest with a small chime. It also gathers a long /ee/ sound that has been running quietly through the poem: heat (line 2), fourteen, sneeze, then East and feast, and finally me at the ends of lines 41 and 43. The vowel that announced the day's heat ends up in the boy's own pronoun.

The counting chant

one for the sun, then the boy's own share, repeated with This one — the four lines alternate in length and stress as the bites alternate between eaters. The rhythm is a counting-out rhyme (the falling-rising beat of one for the sun), which gives the passage its innocence. It is also call-and-response, like an antiphon in church, which gives it its solemnity. one and sun share a vowel, so the counting word echoes the guest, while me is outside the echo. The boy is bound to the sun in sound and separate from it in fact: he eats every bite.

The dying fall

The last lines lose energy in sound as the meal ends. just two little skeletons begins with stresses and then runs down through light syllables (skel-e-tons), and the final words are short and plain. The poem does not end on a strong beat or a chime but on a quiet fall, like a fire burning down.

MOTIFS & SYMBOLS

Motifs & Symbols

Images that recur, and what they accumulate

Motifs and symbols

1. The sun: absent host, late guest, impartial light

The sun is in the title and then disappears for twenty-seven lines. The first stanzas are lit by a sky that is Intense blue before sunrise, with dew still on the grass. When the sun does come (line 28) it is cut down to human size, a guest who shows up at last, some latecomer to a feast. It is spoken to (I tell the sun), it answers like an adult (just winks), and it is given a share in the chant (for the sun). Then, in the last line, it is no longer a person but simply light: the cobs lie in it. Across the poem the sun moves from absence, to guest, to playmate (Chirere calls it “the boy's terrestrial playmate”), and finally to the impartial day that falls on what is left. What it gathers is the poem's attitude to nature: intimate, playful, and not quite equal.

2. Fire and smoke: the upward offering

The fire is never lit on the page, but it fills the middle of the poem. It begins as wood that gives off a sweet smell, becomes smoke that sends up a thin spiral and flutes out to the distant sky, and then hisses and throws sparks. The verbs make the fire an act of sending: something goes up from the boy to the sky. The speaker names the possibility outright — a sacrificial prayer — and then hedges it. The motif returns in a different form at the end, where the roasted maize is portioned out for the sun. Fire and smoke carry the poem's religious undertone: the offering rising and the offering shared.

3. Big and little: the scale of a fourteen-year-old

a big log, big logs, big alternate bites: three times the poem measures things by size, and size is what the boy values. The big log is a test he wants, the big bites a pleasure he has earned. The single reversal comes in the last stanza: two little skeletons. The appetite for bigness ends in littleness, and that one diminutive gives the ending its quiet ache. The motif tracks growing up: at fourteen you want everything big, and the poem lets the reader see, without the boy saying so, that consuming things makes them small.

4. Rain and water: the weather of the day

Rain is forecast in the first stanza (heavy rain after a hot morning); the chips fall in showers; the grass is dewy. The boy's axe makes a miniature rainfall before the sky makes the real one, so his work echoes the day's own rhythm. In a farming world, with maize in the fields, promised rain is good news, so the motif keeps the poem hopeful. It also reminds us that the morning is enclosed in a larger cycle: the dew will dry, the heat will come, the storm will break, and the poem ends before any of it happens.

5. Time: later, eternities, finally, till

The poem is full of small time-words: later three times (the afternoon, the chip's fall, the smoke straightening), eternities, finally, till. They show time behaving elastically. The first stanza compresses a whole day into four lines, the second stretches a second into eternities, the sun is finally there, and the chant goes on till the cobs are bare. Time is measured by the boy's attention and appetite, not by a clock. The last of the time-words, till, marks the one limit attention cannot stretch: the end of the food, and of the morning.

THEMES

Themes

The ideas the poem is arguing about

01

Childhood and absorbed attention

The poem's central achievement is psychological accuracy about a child's attention. The boy is so absorbed that he disappears from his own sentences (the chips fly from the sharp axe, with no one holding it); a falling chip lands eternities later; each stanza is one sentence, one act of noticing, before the mind moves to the next. The present tense keeps us inside the moment rather than looking back on it. Mungoshi does not describe childhood from outside; he reproduces how it feels from inside: totally engaged, elastic in time, needing no one.

That the speaker is fourteen matters. when you are fourteen stands at the threshold between child and adult. The boy wants difficulty (big logs), takes pride in being ready, and organises a game with rules. Yet he still lives in a world where the sun can be invited to breakfast. The poem catches the last stage of childhood, when competence and imagination briefly coexist.

02

Work made into play — and play into ritual

The boy is doing real, heavy, early-morning work — splitting a log, making a fire, cooking — and the poem has no word of complaint in it. Difficulty becomes appetite (wanting big logs is the poem's version of a work-song), the chips are a spectacle, and the cooking ends in a game. Memory Chirere links Mungoshi's verse to Shona working songs, like the rapoko threshing song, which make work feel like play and play feel like work; this poem does the same thing at the level of form. The game then becomes something like a rite: alternate bites, a repeated formula, a portion set aside for the sun. The poem's point is not that the chore is secretly sacred, but that the same gestures can be work, play and ritual at once, depending on how they are done.

03

Kinship with the natural world — and its limits

Nature in the poem is company. The morning is promising, the wood gives off a smell that clears the head, the smoke goes up like a message, and the sun is complained about, invited and humoured like a friend. The relationship is social, not worshipful (the boy tell[s] the sun to come) and not exploitative. But the poem is clear-eyed about the limits: the sun just winks, like a grown-up indulging a child, and the boy eats both shares. The closeness is real but one-sided, and the child accepts it without disappointment. This is why the poem is warm about nature without being naive.

04

The sacred inside the ordinary

Religious language enters only once, and hedged: the smoke is a signal of some sort or a sacrificial prayer. Yet the poem's sequence has the shape of an offering: a fire is built, smoke rises to the sky, a power is invited, food is portioned out to it and then eaten. Shona and Biblical traditions both make that pattern recognisable, but the poem names no god or ceremony and twice declines to confirm the religious reading (the shrug of some sort; the wink). The theme is not that the boy is worshipping. It is that close, loving attention to ordinary things comes very near to reverence, and the poem will not say where one becomes the other.

05

Hospitality and sharing

The boy prepares two cobs before his guest arrives, invites it to share, and divides the meal with scrupulous fairness: one for the sun, one for himself. Sharing is the poem's moral centre. It turns two cobs into a feast and a solitary breakfast into a social occasion. The generosity is wholly imaginative (the sun cannot eat, so the boy eats it all), which makes it comic, but the impulse is real: even alone, the child sets a place for someone else. Read against the season of green maize, which often comes at the end of lean months, the impulse to share may be more generous still, though the poem never mentions scarcity.

06

Time, transience and the end of the morning

The poem is framed by a day it never reaches: the forecast heat and heavy rain. Inside that frame, time stretches (eternities) and then runs out (till). The ending — two little skeletons lying in the sun — is the poem's one image of death: the meal used up, the morning over, the guest who winked now simply the light falling on remains. Nothing is said about loss, and the restraint is the point. The poem is a small, complete happiness that knows it is temporary, and it closes, as it opened, with the sun.

DIFFICULT MOMENTS

Difficult Moments

Where the poem is genuinely undecidable — and what to do about it

Cruxes

1. What is the smoke — a signal, or a sacrificial prayer?

The difficulty. At the poem's exact centre (lines 23–25) the smoke reaching the distant sky is called a signal, of some sort, or a sacrificial prayer. It is the only openly religious phrase in the poem, and the speaker refuses to choose between it and a practical reading. How much religious weight can it bear, and from which religion?

Competing readings. Religious: sends up and flutes out make the smoke a dispatch to the sky. In Shona religion, as usually described, the high God Mwari (also Nyadenga, a name tied to the sky) is approached through the ancestral spirits, and offerings are made to them. In the Bible the smoke of burnt offerings rises to God. The ending supports this reading: food is portioned out for the sun in a repeated formula, then eaten, which is the pattern of many offerings. Secular: the smoke is just smoke from a cooking fire; a signal is the sort of thing smoke on a hillside can be, and of some sort is a boy's shrug. The poem names no god, ancestor or ceremony, and the usual accounts of Shona offerings describe beer and snuff, not smoke. Both at once: the two options share one assumption — that the smoke is addressed to someone — so the sky is imagined as a listener either way.

What a strong answer does. It keeps the speaker's hesitation in view rather than resolving it. The religious reading is available, and the ending strengthens it, but the poem presents it as a possibility the boy entertains, not a rite he performs. It also avoids claiming a specific Shona ceremony the text does not show. The interesting point is that the same column of smoke can be practical, playful and devout at once, and Mungoshi will not say which.

2. What does the sun's wink mean?

The difficulty. Invited to share the maize, the sun just winks like a grown-up. A wink can mean many things, and just suggests some disappointment.

Competing readings. Indulgence: the sun humours the boy as a kind adult humours a child's game — acknowledging it, enjoying it, not joining in. Permission: the boy reads the wink as “go ahead”, and the next line begins So I go ahead. Refusal: just means “merely”; the sun declines the offering, and the communion with nature is one-sided. Literal light: a wink is also how the first glint of a rising sun looks, or how an eye half-closes against it, so the personification grows out of an exact visual fact. Complicity: a wink shares a secret; the sun and the boy both know the sun cannot eat, and the game goes on anyway.

What a strong answer does. It sees that the wink is perfect precisely because it is all of these at once: affectionate, permissive and non-committal. It notes that the sun is the poem's only grown-up — no parent or elder appears — and that the boy's response is cheerful, not hurt. The limit of the relationship is stated without complaint, which is why the poem is warm about nature without being naive.

3. How dark is the ending?

The difficulty. The meal ends with the cobs just two little skeletons, and the last word is sun. Is this a cheerful image of a meal finished, or a shadow of death across a happy poem?

Competing readings. Not dark: a gnawed cob genuinely looks like a small spine; little is affectionate, and the image is funny — the boy has eaten the sun's share too. Quietly elegiac: little cancels the poem's three bigs, just deflates, and skeletons brings death into a poem that had none. The bones lie in the open light, the morning is over, and the hot day forecast in line 2 is about to begin. Ritually complete: if the sharing was an offering, then the offering has been consumed, as offerings often are by those who make them, and the bare cobs are the proper remains of a rite done right. Growing up: at fourteen the boy is near the end of the time when the sun can be a playmate; the remains point to what is used up and cannot return.

What a strong answer does. It holds the humour and the shadow together, and shows how the language produces both: an accurate picture (skeletons for cobs) that also carries mortality, and a diminutive that reverses the poem's scale. It connects the ending to the poem's habit of deflation (unlike sawdust, just winks) and to its opening forecast, which reminded us from the start that the morning would not last. Mungoshi, as with the smoke, places the image and withdraws.

4. Who is speaking — a fourteen-year-old, or an adult remembering?

The difficulty. The poem is in the present tense, with no “I remember” and no adult frame. Yet it was written by a man in his thirties or later, and the speaker's age is given as a general rule: when you are fourteen.

Competing readings. A child's present: the present tense, the absorbed attention (eternities later), the bluntness (a big log) and the games all belong to a fourteen-year-old living the morning now. An adult's memory in disguise: only someone past fourteen can generalise about being fourteen, and the knowledgeable bracket (unlike sawdust) sounds like a grown-up comparing kinds of woodwork. Mungoshi worked for the Forestry Commission after leaving school, and it is tempting, though unprovable, to hear that adult experience in the aside. Chirere reads the childhood poems as looking back on rural innocence from a distance. Both: the poem is a remembered morning written as if it were happening, with the adult showing through at two small seams and then withdrawing.

What a strong answer does. It recognises the present tense as a choice that keeps the reader inside the boy's experience, and finds the two places where an older voice shows through. It does not over-read biography. The effect matters more than the source: the poem gives a child's morning without the consolations or regrets of hindsight. The only adult judgement it allows is the quiet weight of the ending.

CLOSE ANALYSIS

Close Analysis

The moments that repay pressure, worked through

Close analysis

Ten moments that repay pressure, in the order of the poem. Quotations are kept to short fragments.

1. Intense blue (line 1)

Adjective of pressure; verbless opening. Intense belongs to heat, feeling and concentration more than to colour, so the first word gives the morning force rather than prettiness: a deep, saturated sky with heat already behind it. The whole first sentence has no main verb, so the morning is a condition the reader is placed in, not an event. No person, place or pronoun is given. Intention and effect: Mungoshi puts perception before story, and the reader sees the morning before knowing who is seeing it — as the absorbed boy does.

2. arc (line 8)

One-word line; noun used as verb; white space. The chip's flight is broken into three verbs, and the middle one is set alone on its line, so the reader's eye pauses where the chip pauses, at the top of its curve. arc comes from geometry, the language of perfect shapes, and a scrap of firewood is lifted into that language. The comma keeps the sentence open, the movement unfinished. Intention and effect: the line is the poem's method in one word — exact naming, placed in space, instead of description — and it makes the reader experience a split second as a held moment.

3. eternities later (line 9)

Hyperbole; plural; time dilation. A chip falls in about a second; the poem says eternities, and the plural makes it stranger than the cliché “an eternity”. To a fourteen-year-old wholly absorbed, the fall really does seem endless, so the exaggeration is truthful about attention. The grand word also brings a sense of time beyond human measure into a poem of plain words. Intention and effect: the reader feels time stretch, and the poem establishes that its clock is the child's attention: a day compressed into four lines, a second stretched to eternity.

4. when you are fourteen (line 13)

Second person; generalisation; the stated age. The age arrives as a rule of life rather than a fact about I. but turns the problem of the big log into the attraction: at fourteen, difficulty is what you want, because what you can split measures what you are becoming. you universalises it, and it also lets an older voice show through, since only someone past fourteen can say it. Intention and effect: the reader smiles in recognition, and the poem defines its speaker by his appetite, a boy on the edge of adulthood who turns a chore into a challenge.

5. (unlike sawdust) (line 18)

Parenthesis; bathos; practical comparison. Straight after the sweet nose-cleansing odour, the speaker adds a bracketed aside comparing the smell to sawdust, which, unlike it, would make you sneeze. The brackets mark it as a remark from slightly outside the scene, and the impersonal one in the next line sounds grown-up. Intention and effect: the deflation keeps sweetness from becoming sentimentality — Chirere's “never sentimental” is earned in lines like this — and the reader trusts the poem's pleasure because it is so matter-of-fact.

6. sacrificial prayer (line 25)

Alternatives joined by “or”; register shift; hedge. The smoke is offered two meanings, a signal, of some sort, and the religious one, and neither is chosen. sacrificial is the poem's heaviest word before skeletons, and the shrug of some sort keeps it light. Both readings imagine the sky as a listener. Intention and effect: placed at the poem's exact centre, the phrase opens the possibility of the sacred and then leaves it open, preparing the ending's portioned offering without turning the boy's breakfast into a ceremony.

7. some latecomer (lines 30–31)

Simile; personification; internal rhyme. The sun shows up like a guest late to a feast. some is casually dismissive, the idiom cuts the sun down to human size, and the poem's one close rhyme (East … feast) chimes as it arrives. Two cobs become a banquet in a single word. Intention and effect: the comedy of a boy grumbling at the sun's lateness hides a real reversal of scale: the boy, up first, is host, and the greatest power in the sky is the one who has to catch up.

8. two cobs of maize (line 32)

First-person pronoun withheld until now; exact number; host's pride. I appears for the first time at line 32 of 46, in the same sentence as the sun's arrival. I have got is childish and proud. Two cobs means one each, planned before the guest arrived, so the earlier work turns out to have been preparation for a visit. Intention and effect: the speaker becomes a self only when he has company, and the reader sees that the whole solitary morning was secretly hospitable.

9. just winks (line 36)

Personification; deflating adverb; simile. Asked to share, the sun just winks like a grown-up. The wink acknowledges the game without joining it, as an amused adult humours a child; just registers a small, cheerful disappointment. A wink is also a good picture of the rising sun's first glint. Intention and effect: the poem's closeness to nature is given its limit — the world plays along kindly, at a distance — and the sun becomes the only adult in a childhood poem with no parents in it.

10. two little skeletons (line 45)

Metaphor; diminutive; deflation. The gnawed cobs look like small bony spines, which is accurate and funny. But little reverses the poem's three bigs, just shrinks them further, and skeletons is the first image of death in the poem. The last word then returns to the sun. Intention and effect: the feast ends in remains, and the reader is left to hold the joy of the morning against its using-up, with no comment from the poet. It is the same suspension as the smoke: an image placed, and a meaning left open.

CRITICAL LENSES

Critical Lenses

What each way of reading makes visible, and what it flattens

Critical lenses

1. Formalist

What it makes visible. How much the poem's effects depend on placement. A formalist reading notices the sun withheld for twenty-seven lines (so the poem is literally “before the sun”); the one-word line arc stopping the sentence at the top of the chip's flight; the I delayed until the guest arrives; the smoke's two meanings set at the exact centre of the 46 lines; the close rhyme East … feast marking the sun's entrance; and one turned from impersonal pronoun (line 19) into counting word (lines 40–43). The plainness is engineered.

What it flattens. The poem's human warmth and its world: a formalist account can make the boy into a set of devices and forget that the details (green maize, firewood, the afternoon storm) are real and particular.

2. Ecocritical

What it makes visible. A relation with nature that is neither scenic nor exploitative but social. The morning promising, the generous wood, the smoke sent upward, the sun teased, invited and humoured: the natural world is a companion, and the boy's work (cutting, burning, cooking) is part of a cycle of dew, heat and rain. Chirere's sense that nature and man commune in the poem fits this lens. Set beside the damaged nature of 'Report to Wordsworth' or 'Lament', this is the set's most intact natural world.

What it flattens. The poem's honesty about limits. The sun just winks and the boy eats both shares; the communion is imagined, and the poem knows it. An ecocritical reading can also pass over the fact that the boy is felling and burning wood, which the poem treats as simply part of life.

3. Postcolonial

What it makes visible. What is absent. A rural African childhood in Rhodesia is presented without any colonial frame: no white farmer, school, church, money, law or war. The poem asks for no explanation and offers its world as complete. The collection first appeared in 1981, the year after independence, from a writer whose early work had been banned for a time by the Rhodesian regime. Chirere argues that Mungoshi's politics, where present, are “implicit rather than explicit”.

What it flattens. The evidence. The poem itself contains no political reference, Chirere does not read this poem politically, and there is no sign that Mungoshi meant it as a statement. Reading absence as resistance can make every quiet poem a protest. The safer claim is that the poem's self-sufficiency can be read as significant in its moment, not that it was designed to be.

4. Materialist

What it makes visible. The facts under the lyricism: a fourteen-year-old up before dawn doing heavy household work, splitting wood and cooking his own breakfast of two cobs, in a season that often follows the lean months before harvest. A materialist reader asks whether the poem's joy disguises labour and scarcity — a child taught to want the chore (big logs) he cannot avoid. The contrast with Blake's chimney sweeper and Rumens's carpet-weavers is sharp.

What it flattens. The boy's own experience. The poem reports how the work felt, and it felt like pleasure and pride; overriding that with an adult economic judgement would be a different falsification. The boy is not exploited by anyone in the poem, and nothing suggests he is hungry.

5. Psychoanalytic and developmental

What it makes visible. A mind at the edge of adolescence. The wish for big things, the pride of being ready first, the invented rules (alternate bites), and the imaginative game of feeding an adult figure who cannot eat all suggest a child practising independence and hospitality, rehearsing an adult role while still playing. The sun as a grown-up who winks is a benign parental figure, present but not intrusive, and no actual parent appears. The ending's skeletons can be read as the first awareness of loss arriving inside play.

What it flattens. The poem's lightness. Reading the sun as a displaced father, or the skeletons as a death-wish, imposes a depth the plain, comic surface does not invite; the poem's insight is in what it shows, not in what it hides.

OTHER READINGS

Other Readings

Contested interpretations, and where each is weak

Other readings

1. A celebration of childhood

The poem is a hymn to a childhood morning: physical work enjoyed, every sense open, and an imagination free enough to invite the sun to breakfast. The ending is simply the cheerful debris of a good meal.

Evidence: the absence of complaint; the pleasure in big logs; the comedy of some latecomer; the game of one for the sun; Chirere's sense of the childhood poems as recalling rural innocence.

Weakness: it has to ignore the deflations (unlike sawdust, just winks, just two little skeletons) and the forecast that encloses the morning in a day that will move on.

2. An elegy in the present tense

The poem was written by an adult about a world he had left: the present tense is a technique for refusing to let the memory be past, and its ache lies in what it does not say.

Evidence: the generalising when you are fourteen, which only someone older can say; the knowing bracket (unlike sawdust); the ending's skeletons; Chirere's view that Mungoshi looks back on rural childhood with nostalgia but is “never sentimental”.

Weakness: nothing in the poem mourns; the tone is playful throughout, and reading it as elegy can import a sadness the text only glances at.

3. A rite performed without being named

The poem records a ritual: a fire built, smoke sent to the sky, a power invited, food portioned out to it and consumed. The boy prays in the shape his culture (Shona or Christian) has given him, without calling it prayer.

Evidence: sends up, flutes out, sacrificial prayer; the formula of the chant; the portion for the sun; the parallel, chant-like fire couplet.

Weakness: the poem itself hedges (of some sort), names no god or ceremony, and lets the sun decline the offering with a wink. The ritual is at most a resemblance the poem notices.

4. A poem of attention in the manner of haiku

Following Mungoshi's admiration for Bashō, the poem is a sequence of exact images with commentary removed, set in a marked season, cut by the isolated arc, and ending on a bare object rather than a conclusion. Its subject is attention itself.

Evidence: the one-sentence stanzas; the present tense; the season-markers (dew, forecast storm, fresh maize); the refusal to explain the smoke or the skeletons; Chirere's comparison with “far-eastern Haiku or Zen philosophy”.

Weakness: the poem is also a story with a plot, a joke and a host-and-guest drama, closer to Shona narrative song than to haiku. The haiku frame is an analogy, not a form.

5. Scarcity made into generosity

Two cobs of green maize, possibly at the end of the lean months before harvest, are a small meal. The boy's answer to having little is to invite a guest and call it a feast.

Evidence: the exact count, two cobs; the cobs eaten to the bone; the season implied by fresh maize and rain.

Weakness: the poem never mentions hunger, the boy's bites are big, and his tone is plenty, not want. This reading depends on outside knowledge of the agricultural calendar, not on the text.

6. A small poem

Some readers find the poem slight: a pleasant vignette that risks nothing and resolves nothing.

Evidence: its plain diction; its lack of argument or conclusion; Mungoshi's own description of poetry as “a sideline, a mere finger exercise”.

Weakness: the apparent artlessness is built: the sun withheld for twenty-seven lines, the I delayed until the guest arrives, the smoke at the exact centre, one transformed, big reversed into little, showers anticipating rain. Mungoshi's “finger exercise” is, by his own account, practice in precision.
