CONNECTIONS

Connections

How this poem pairs with the rest of the set

Connections

1. Seamus Heaney, 'Follower'

Link. The closest pairing: rural childhood, physical work and the wish to be bigger. Mungoshi's boy wants big logs; Heaney's wants to “grow up and plough”. Both poems are also interested in an adult's one-eyed look: Heaney's boy wants “To close one eye” like his ploughing father, and Mungoshi's sun winks like a grown-up.

Shared technique. Precise detail of a craft (the axe and chips; the plough and furrow) and an ending image the poet does not explain.

Difference. Heaney writes in the past tense with an adult frame and turns the relationship round at the end (the father “will not go away”); Mungoshi stays in the present and offers no verdict. Heaney's child is “a nuisance” in a master's shadow; Mungoshi's boy is competent, alone and in charge, and the only “grown-up” is the sun.

2. Judith Wright, 'Hunting Snake'

Link. A moment of suspended time in an encounter with the natural world, under the sun. Wright's walkers “froze half-through a pace”; Mungoshi's chip lands eternities later.

Shared technique. Time dilation and close visual attention (Wright's snake, its “curves of diamond scale” glazed by sun; Mungoshi's thin spiral of smoke), followed by an unexplained return to ordinary life — Wright's “deeper breath of day”, Mungoshi's eaten cobs.

Difference. Wright's encounter is awe and fear before a creature that ignores the humans; Mungoshi's is friendship with a sun that answers with a wink. Wright's ending releases tension; Mungoshi's adds a quiet shadow.

3. William Shakespeare, Sonnet 18

Link. The two great suns of the selection. Shakespeare's sun is “the eye of heaven”, sometimes “too hot”, its “gold complexion dimm'd”; Mungoshi's is a late guest who winks — the old figure of the sun as an eye, made intimate and comic.

Shared technique. Personification of the sun and an awareness of transience (“every fair from fair sometime declines”; two little skeletons).

Difference. Shakespeare argues against time and claims victory through verse (“So long lives this”); Mungoshi lets the morning end without argument, setting down the remains in the light.

4. Carol Rumens, 'Carpet-weavers, Morocco'

Link. Children, work and the sacred. Rumens's children weave “the garden of Islam” for a mosque where it will be “heaped with prayer”; Mungoshi's boy sends up smoke that may be a sacrificial prayer.

Shared technique. The present tense, used to hold children inside a moment of work, and a link between ordinary labour and worship.

Difference. Rumens's children are watched from outside, labourers for others, taught only by “the school of days”; Mungoshi's boy speaks for himself, works for himself, and turns his chore into a game. The pairing sharpens the question of when children's work is a pleasure and when it is a cost.

5. William Blake, 'The Chimney Sweeper' (Songs of Experience)

Link. Two children at work in the early part of the day. Blake's is “A little black thing” in the snow, sent out while his parents pray; Mungoshi's is warm, fed and unsupervised beside his own fire.

Shared technique. A child's voice and a sharp, simple image of what the child has or lacks, with religion in the background (Blake's “God and his priest and king”; Mungoshi's sacrificial prayer).

Difference. Blake's ballad is bitterly ironic about adults who exploit a child's happiness; Mungoshi's free verse has no irony and no exploiting adult. Both poems are about what a child is owed, and they answer completely differently.

6. Gillian Clarke, 'Lament'

Link. The sun and the natural world under opposite conditions. Clarke mourns “the burnt earth” and “the sun put out” after the Gulf War; Mungoshi's sun rises on an untouched morning and is invited to breakfast.

Shared technique. A sequence of separate images rather than an argument, each given its own short unit (Clarke's “For…” lines; Mungoshi's one-sentence stanzas).

Difference. Clarke's fire is the “blazing well” of war; Mungoshi's is a cooking fire whose smoke may be prayer. One poem is elegy for a destroyed world, the other a record of an intact one.

7. Elizabeth Brewster, 'Where I Come From'

Link. “People are made of places.” Mungoshi's speaker is made of one hillside, one season and one hour, and the poem's exactness about that place is where its meaning comes from.

Shared technique. Sensory detail of a rural home (Brewster's “acres of pine woods” and its weather; Mungoshi's dew, smoke and storm).

Difference. Brewster generalises about places and the minds they shape; Mungoshi never generalises except once (when you are fourteen) and stays inside a single morning.

CONTEXT

Context

The world the poem came out of

The Poet: Katherine Philips (1632–1664)

Katherine Fowler was born in early January 1632 in the London parish of St Mary Woolchurch Haw (John Aubrey gives her baptism as 11 January), the only daughter of John Fowler, a London merchant, and Katherine Oxenbridge. She grew up in a Puritan household and from the age of eight attended Mrs Salmon's school in Hackney, one of the few places where a girl could get a serious education. After her father's death her mother married twice more; the third husband, in late 1646 or early 1647, was Sir Richard Phillipps of Picton Castle, Pembrokeshire, and Katherine's world moved to west Wales. In August 1648, aged sixteen, she married James Philips of Cardigan Priory, a kinsman of her stepfather.

As "Orinda" she became the most admired woman poet of her generation, writing above all about friendship, especially between women, for a circle that used pastoral names: her husband was "Antenor", Anne Owen "Lucasia", Mary Aubrey "Rosania", her correspondent Sir Charles Cotterell "Poliarchus". Her translation of Corneille's Pompey was staged at the Smock Alley theatre in Dublin in February 1663, often described as the first play by a woman produced in a British or Irish public theatre. An unauthorised edition of her Poems, printed for Richard Marriott, was advertised in January 1664; she protested that she had not sanctioned it. She died of smallpox in London on 22 June 1664, aged thirty-two, and was buried at St Benet Sherehog. Henry Herringman's folio of 1667 called her "the Matchless Orinda". 'A Married State' is in neither edition.

One leaf in a girl's hand (c. 1646–48)

The poem survives in one manuscript only: an untitled copy in Philips's own hand on a single cropped folio leaf, once folded like a letter, now in the National Library of Wales among the papers of the Owen family of Orielton, Pembrokeshire — the family of Anne Owen, the friend she later called "Lucasia". The leaf is signed "C. Fowler", her maiden name. Claudia Limbert, who first printed the poem complete (English Literary Renaissance, 1986), describes the hand as "less sure, more childish" than Philips's later fair copies and dates it between her mother's remarriage (December 1646) and her own wedding (August 1648): the author was fourteen to sixteen, and unmarried.

The same leaf carries a short poem beginning 'No blooming youth', which prefers "the beauty of the mind" and a husband of "sence", and a mock prose "receipt" (recipe) for curing lovesickness whose ingredients include "the spirits of reason" and "the Powder of experiance". Limbert hears in all three the voice of "a pragmatic young woman of good humor", and reads the leaf as the earliest evidence of Philips moving away from the Puritanism of her upbringing. Extracts were first printed in Ronald Lockley's Orielton (1977); after Limbert's article the poem appeared in Kissing the Rod (1988), the anthology of seventeenth-century women's verse, and in Patrick Thomas's Collected Works (1990, poem 130). The title 'A Married State' is editorial, taken from the first line.

Thirteen shared lines

In 1993 Limbert and John H. O'Neill showed that the poem shares thirteen of its sixteen lines with an anonymous 62-line poem addressed to a lady, beginning "Madam / I cannot but Congratulate": the catalogue of literary manuscripts (CELM) describes the sixteen-line text as made up of that poem's lines 13–16, 43–44, 48–50 and 59–62. They called the relationship "composite authorship" ('Composite Authorship: Katherine Philips and an Antimarital Satire', Papers of the Bibliographical Society of America, 1993). Copying, cutting and adapting other people's verse was a normal part of manuscript culture, and the leaf compresses a long satire to a quarter of its length.

This changes what can be claimed. The poem's arguments and many of its phrases may not be the girl's invention, and nothing about it should be read as autobiography. What is visibly hers is the selection and the shape — a sixteen-line case moving from diagnosis to alternative to verdict to command — and the decision to write it out and sign it with her own name.

Wales, war and her own marriage

The leaf belongs to the years of the Civil Wars. The first war ended in 1646 with the king's defeat. In 1648 Pembrokeshire, where the family now lived, became a centre of the Second Civil War when the commanders of its Parliamentarian garrisons declared for the king, and Cromwell besieged Pembroke Castle from May to July; Charles I was executed in January 1649. A poem in which a woman is crown'd, freed, told to Suppress a rebell and to Turn… apostate uses words that were loaded everywhere in England at that moment, whether or not the girl intended the parallel.

James Philips was a Parliamentarian who served as a justice of the peace in Cardiganshire and sat in the 1653 ("Barebones") Parliament; one contemporary called him a man "in with all Goverments, but thrived by none". Katherine was a royalist, and later wrote a poem on the execution of Charles I. Older biographies, and still the Poetry Foundation's, give his birth as 1594, making him fifty-four to her sixteen, and Limbert repeated the figure in 1986; Warren Chernaik's entry in the Oxford Dictionary of National Biography gives his age at the marriage as twenty-four, on the evidence of the marriage record, and the large gap is now discounted. Either way the poem was written before the wedding and is not a portrait of him. Their son Hector died in infancy in 1655 (her epitaph speaks of a child "in less than six weeks, dead"); a daughter, Katherine, born in April 1656, survived and married Lewis Wogan of Boulston.

The married state in law, church and childbed

In law, marriage changed what a woman was. Under the common-law doctrine of coverture an unmarried adult woman (feme sole) could own property, make contracts and sue; a wife (feme covert) was "covered" by her husband's legal person, her goods and earnings became his, and she could not normally contract or sue in her own name. The Lawes Resolutions of Womens Rights (1632), published the year Philips was born, likened the wife to a small stream running into the Thames: "the poor rivulet looseth her name… it beareth no sway; it possesseth nothing during coverture."

The Prayer Book service that had defined marriage for a century (Parliament replaced it with the Directory for Public Worship in 1645) called matrimony "an honourable estate, instituted of God in paradise, in the time of man's innocency"; it gave as marriage's purposes "the procreation of children" and "a remedy against sin" for those without "the gift of continency", and it asked the bride, "Wilt thou obey him, and serve him…?" Against that background the poem's words are exact: a state, what it affords, a wife who must please, cares that Attend on a husband, a single woman inocent, wild nature suppressed rather than licensed. Childbirth was the other fact of the married state. Historians estimate the risk of dying at around one or more in every hundred births in seventeenth-century England, mounting over a normal run of pregnancies, and roughly one baby in six died in its first year. Pangs that extort your tears is not hyperbole.

St Paul's case for staying single

The poem's argument has a respectable source: St Paul's advice in 1 Corinthians 7, the chief passage of scripture that ranks the single life above marriage. In the King James Version (1611) Paul writes, "I would have you without carefulness", and explains: "There is difference also between a wife and a virgin. The unmarried woman careth for the things of the Lord… but she that is married careth for the things of the world, how she may please her husband." He wants the unmarried to "attend upon the Lord without distraction" (vv. 32–35), warns that those who marry "shall have trouble in the flesh" (v. 28), and judges that a widow "is happier if she so abide" (v. 40).

1 Corinthians 7 (KJV) 'A Married State'
"without carefulness" wifes Carefull faces; all the cares
"how she may please her husband" so hard to please
"a wife and a virgin" A married state / A virgin state
"the things of the world" worldly crosses
"attend upon the Lord without distraction" distract your prayers; Attend on matrymony
"happier if she so abide" allways happy
"if they cannot contain, let them marry: for it is better to marry than to burn" (v. 9) Suppress wild nature if she dare rebell

The last row is where the poem leaves its authority behind. Paul lets those who cannot master desire marry; the poem allows nobody that exit. Elsewhere it keeps Paul's frame: by ending its catalogue on prayers it makes the one argument against marriage that no Protestant could call impious.

Anti-marriage satire, and the apes in hell

Warnings against marriage were an old genre, often called molestiae nuptiarum ("the troubles of marriage"): Juvenal's sixth satire; the treatise on marriage attributed to Theophrastus that St Jerome preserved in Against Jovinian; the anthology ("Valerie and Theofraste") that Jankyn reads aloud to Chaucer's Wife of Bath. Almost all were written by men to warn men off wives. The anonymous satire behind this poem belongs to the same family but warns a woman off husbands, and the sixteen lines look forward to Mary Astell's Some Reflections upon Marriage (1700) and Lady Mary Chudleigh's 'To the Ladies' (1703): "Wife and servant are the same, / But only differ in the name."

The final line answers a proverb: a woman who died unmarried would "lead apes in hell", usually explained as her punishment for having no children to lead to heaven. Shakespeare's two most marriage-resistant heroines quote it. Beatrice will "lead his apes into hell" (Much Ado About Nothing, 2.1); Katherina complains that because her father favours her sister she must "lead apes in hell" (The Taming of the Shrew, 2.1). Both end their plays married. Philips's speaker simply denies that the punishment exists.

Friendship, 'apostasy' and the funeral of a friendship

The leaf was written years before the friendship poems that made Philips famous, but its vocabulary returns in them. Her later poems treat friendship between women as a sacred bond — 'Friendship's Mystery, To My Dearest Lucasia' declares "There's a religion in our love" — and they use the language of faith for its betrayal. When Mary Aubrey ("Rosania") married in 1652, Philips wrote 'On Rosania's Apostacy, and Lucasia's Friendship', and another poem to an unfaithful friend opens "Lovely apostate! what was my offence?" When Anne Owen ("Lucasia") married Marcus Trevor in 1662, Philips wrote to Cotterell from Dublin that "there are few Friendships in the World Marriage-proof", and that "We may generally conclude the Marriage of a Friend to be the Funeral of a Friendship."

Whether her circle was a formal "Society of Friendship", as Edmund Gosse claimed, or a looser network of friends, is disputed. Read back from the later poems, Turn, turn apostate to love's Levity looks like the first form of a lifelong idea: that the bond between women is the true faith and marriage the defection. The girl who copied it could not have known how literally she would come to mean it.

16There's no such thing as leading Apes in hell.

Lines with a marker have analysis — click one, or just scroll.

Title
A Married State
Language & devices

Editorial title: the only manuscript, Philips's own copy, is untitled; the poem is known by the words of its first line, so the heading is a quotation of the opening rather than a label she chose. Indefinite article: A makes the subject generic: any marriage, not hers or yours. Polysemy: State means a condition of life, a legal status, the Prayer Book's "holy estate of matrimony", an estate in property, and a state in the political sense. Participle: Married names something done to a person and then fixed as a condition.

Meaning & effect

The title promises a description and delivers a verdict, because the phrase comes from a line that goes straight on to say how little this condition affords. The weight falls on State. Marriage is presented not as a feeling or a relationship but as a status a woman enters and then lives inside, which is exactly how law and church treated it. The generic A closes off the easy reply ("but my marriage is happy") before it can be made, and line 2 closes it again. The title also hides half the poem. The poem compares two states, married and virgin, and recommends the second, so a reader expecting a portrait of marriage gets a case against it. Because the heading is editorial, it names the matter in dispute the way a legal brief does: the condition the poem argues against.

Line 1
A married state affords but little ease:
Language & devices

Aphorism: a general truth stated as fact, with no I and no example. Verb: affords means yields or provides; it also carries the sense of what one can pay for, so marriage becomes a provider judged by its return. Litotes: but little ease rather than "no ease". Diction: ease in the period means freedom from pain, care and anxiety as well as rest. Iambic pentameter: perfectly regular. Colon: the line ends as a proposition does before its proof.

Meaning & effect

The poem opens with a verdict, not a story: marriage gives women very little peace of mind. Its force is its coolness. A complaint would invite sympathy or dismissal; an axiom in perfect metre invites agreement, and the line sounds as if it reports a known fact rather than offers an opinion. Affords quietly turns marriage into an account to be balanced: what does this state provide for the person who enters it? The answer, but little, is more damaging than "none", because a measured claim is harder to refute than an absolute one. The colon promises evidence, and the next three lines supply it. A girl of fourteen to sixteen, not yet married, speaks with the composure of a judge, and the poem never apologises for it.

Line 2
The best of husbands are so hard to please
Language & devices

Superlative: The best of husbands — the claim is made about the finest case, not the worst. Concession used as attack: granting that good husbands exist. Intensifier: so hard; in speech both words take stress, so the effort is audible. Embedded rhyme: ease / please — the wife's word sits inside the husband's. Biblical echo: 1 Corinthians 7:34, where the married woman "careth… how she may please her husband".

Meaning & effect

This is the poem's sharpest tactical move. Philips does not say husbands are cruel, a claim that one kind man would answer; she says even the best of them are hard to please, which makes the problem the arrangement, not the individual. If the ideal husband still demands constant effort, then any marriage is a life spent satisfying someone else, and the standard is never met once and for all. The wife does not even appear in the sentence, only the person she must please. The rhyme makes the point in sound: please swallows ease, as the husband's satisfaction is made out of the wife's peace. Set beside Paul's words, the line takes scripture's neutral description of married life and shows it to be a complaint.

Line 3
This in wifes Carefull faces you may spell,
Language & devices

Demonstrative: This points back to line 2 as the thing to be proved. Metaphor: faces as texts. Verb: spell means to read letter by letter, to make out with effort. Diction: Carefull means full of care — anxious, burdened (Paul's "carefulness") — not cautious. Second person: you enters for the first time. Trochaic inversion: THIS in, then stresses crowd onto wifes Carefull.

Meaning & effect

Having made her claim, the speaker produces evidence, and it is something anyone can see: the faces of married women. Spell is precise. The truth is not hidden, but it has to be read slowly and attentively, as a child spells out a word, which implies that most people look at wives without reading them. You may spell turns the addressee from a listener into a witness: she is asked to test the claim against her own observation rather than take it on trust. The care written on these faces is the first appearance of the poem's key idea; line 11 will name all the cares the single woman escapes. The heavy stresses on wifes Carefull make the line itself look burdened before it eases into you may spell.

Line 4
Tho they desemble their misfortunes well
Language & devices

Concessive conjunction: Tho (though). Verb: desemble (dissemble) — to hide true feelings behind a false appearance. Euphemism: misfortunes names suffering as bad luck, nobody's fault. End-weight: well closes the line on a stress. Iambic pentameter: perfectly regular — a composed line about composure.

Meaning & effect

The line meets the obvious objection, that many wives look content, and turns it into more evidence: they look content because they are good at hiding what they feel. That makes the argument hard to answer, since cheerfulness now proves the case as well as gloom does; a sceptic would call the claim unfalsifiable. It also records a real expectation, that a good wife does not complain, and well carries a dry admiration for how skilfully the act is kept up. Misfortunes is tactful: no husband is blamed, and suffering becomes simply what marriage brings. Philips wrote this before her own wedding, so the speaker is an observer reading other women, not a wife confessing her own act; her authority comes from close looking. The smooth metre is itself a kind of dissembling: nothing in the sound betrays strain.

Line 5
A virgin state is crown'd with much content,
Language & devices

Parallelism: A virgin state answers A married state word for word and position for position. Metaphor: crown'd — the single woman is royal, and behind the word lies the old Christian image of a special crown for virgins. Antithesis: much content against but little ease; a verb of honour (crown'd) against a verb of supply (affords). Alliteration: hard /k/ in crown'd… content. Turn: the poem's first change of direction.

Meaning & effect

The poem turns to its alternative and builds it as a mirror of line 1. Marriage affords a little; virginity is crown'd with much. The crown makes the unmarried woman a sovereign rather than a subject, which matters when the first state handed a wife's legal person to her husband. Content is a quieter word than joy: it means being satisfied with one's condition, which is exactly what the Carefull wives are not. The parallel syntax does the persuading. By setting the two lives side by side as two states, the poem makes choosing between them look like a rational comparison rather than an act of defiance.

Line 6
It's allways happy as it's inocent
Language & devices

Adverb: allways admits no exception. Ambiguity: as can mean "because" or "to the same degree that". Diction: inocent means free from guilt and, at its Latin root (in-nocens), harmless, doing no hurt. Contraction: It's… it's makes the line quick and conversational after the ceremonial crown'd. Light rhyme: the stressed content rhymes with the unstressed last syllable of inocent.

Meaning & effect

The virgin state is happy because it is innocent, or happy in exactly the degree that it is innocent; either way the line ties happiness to a moral condition rather than to luck. Its implication is pointed: if the single life is happy because innocent, marriage must involve some loss of innocence. The poem has already shown what kind: not chiefly sexual, but the daily dissembling of line 4, a life of keeping up appearances. The Latin root adds a second sense, a life that neither does harm nor suffers it, and the next four lines list the harms it escapes. The Prayer Book said marriage was instituted "in the time of man's innocency"; this line hands innocence to the woman who stays single. The breezy contractions make the claim sound too obvious to need argument.

Line 7
No Blustering husbands to create your fears,
Language & devices

Anaphora: No… begins a three-line run. Ellipsis: a verbless phrase, understood as "[there are] no…". Adjective: Blustering — of wind, blowing in violent gusts; of people, loud, bullying, full of empty threat. Plural: husbands — the type again, not one man. Infinitive of purpose: to create your fears, as if fear were the husband's function. Elision: ten syllables only if Blustering is said "blust'ring"; otherwise the word's bluster overfills the line.

Meaning & effect

The first freedom of the virgin state is freedom from a husband's temper. Blustering makes male anger frightening and slightly ridiculous at once: weather and noise, alarming but full of air. Create says the fears did not exist until he made them; they answer no real danger, only his moods. The grammar of the whole catalogue is telling: each harm comes with to and an infinitive, as though husbands, childbirth and children existed in order to cause suffering. And each harm lands on your, so the poem now speaks directly about its reader's future. Every No is a promise: none of this, if you stay single.

Line 8
No pangs of child birth to extort your tears,
Language & devices

Anaphora: second No. Diction: pangs is the standard word for the pains of labour, as in the King James Bible's "the pangs of a woman that travaileth" (Isaiah 21:3). Verb: extort — to wrest or wring out by force or threat (Latin extorquere, "to twist out"). Metaphor: tears are taken as an extortioner takes money. Plosives: pangs, child birth, extort.

Meaning & effect

The second freedom is freedom from childbirth, and this is the darkest line in the poem. In the 1640s labour carried a real risk of death, and pangs names it in the Bible's own vocabulary. Extort is the striking choice. Tears are not shed or caused but extorted, forced out of someone who has no choice, so childbirth becomes something done to the woman rather than a blessing she receives. The line quietly refuses the consolation her culture offered for these pains, that they were Eve's punishment to be borne with patience. Its plain, regular rhythm makes it sound like a statement of fact rather than a cry, which is more disturbing.

Line 9
No children's crys for to offend your ears,
Language & devices

Anaphora: third and last No. Archaism: for to is an older infinitive marker, familiar from the King James Bible ("what went ye out for to see?"), and it fills the metre. Verb: offend — hurt or displease; offend your ears is an idiom for an unpleasant noise. Triplet: ears is the third rhyme on one sound (fears / tears / ears). Bathos: the scale drops from mortal danger to noise.

Meaning & effect

After the risk of death comes the sound of crying children, and the drop in seriousness is deliberate. The anticlimax is funny, and it stops the catalogue becoming a lament: the poem will not let its reader settle into pity. But the descent also makes an argument. The married woman is besieged at every level, from terror (fears) to pain (tears) to daily irritation (ears), and the list follows the order of a married life: husband, labour, children. A reader may find the line callous. Its point, though, is not that children are unlovable but that they are one more claim on a woman who already has no time of her own. Counting children among the burdens is the poem's boldest departure from the marriage service, which named "the procreation of children" as marriage's first purpose.

Line 10
Few worldly crosses to distract your prayers
Language & devices

Broken anaphora: Few, not No. Diction: worldly — of this world rather than the spirit; crosses — trials, afflictions, with Christ's cross behind the word. Verb: distract — pull apart, draw away; Paul wants the unmarried to "attend upon the Lord without distraction" (1 Corinthians 7:35). Near-rhyme: prayers stretches the fears / tears / ears sound to a fourth line, imperfectly. Climax: the catalogue ends on prayers.

Meaning & effect

Two things change here. First, the pattern breaks: the single life has few troubles, not none. The concession makes the speaker more credible, because she is not selling a paradise. Second, the catalogue climaxes not on comfort or freedom but on prayers: the deepest cost of marriage, in the poem's argument, is spiritual, since its worries crowd out a woman's attention to God. That is St Paul's own case for the single life, and borrowing it gives the poem an authority no one could call irreligious. Worldly crosses is exact: troubles that look like the crosses a Christian is told to bear, but which belong to the world and sanctify nothing. The imperfect rhyme makes this line sound slightly out of step with the three before it, like a concession added to a list.

Line 11
Thus are you freed from all the cares that do
Language & devices

Logical connective: Thus marks the conclusion of the proof. Inversion: Thus are you freed puts the verb before the subject, formal and oratorical. Verb: freed — released from bonds. Absolute: all the cares. Echo: cares returns to Carefull (line 3). Enjambment: the line ends on the weak auxiliary do, so the sentence spills into line 12. Trochaic opening: THUS are.

Meaning & effect

The case is closed: the virgin state frees a woman from every care that marriage brings. Freed is the key word, stronger than "spared" or "safer": marriage is cast as bondage and the single life as release. In the 1640s, when freedom and liberty were the slogans of a civil war, the word carried weight even in a private poem. Cares completes a ring begun with Carefull faces: what could be read in wives' faces is now named as what the single woman escapes. This is the only line in the poem that runs on without a pause, and it ends on the weakest possible word, so the cares overflow into the next line as they overflow a wife's days.

Line 12
Attend on matrymony and a husband too.
Language & devices

Alexandrine: twelve syllables and six stresses, the only line longer than pentameter. Verb: Attend on — wait on as servants do, accompany as a retinue; it inverts Paul's "attend upon the Lord". Personification: the cares are matrimony's attendants. Bathos: and a husband too is tacked on after the abstraction. Etymology: matrymony comes from Latin matrimonium, from mater, mother — the institution is named for motherhood, and the husband comes last.

Meaning & effect

This is the poem's best joke and one of its most serious claims. The cares are pictured as matrimony's servants, following it wherever it goes, and then, almost as an afterthought, comes and a husband too, as though he were one more item in the train. The line is overloaded: it is the only line with an extra foot, and the extra weight arrives exactly with the husband, so the line about the burdens of marriage drags under its own burden. The verb points two ways. The cares Attend on matrimony, and the wife is the one who must attend on the husband; the Prayer Book bride promised to "obey him, and serve him". Paul wanted the unmarried free to "attend upon the Lord"; here the married woman attends on matrimony instead. The full stop, the first in the poem, ends the case.

Line 13
Therefore, madam, be advised by me:
Language & devices

Logical connective: Therefore introduces the application, as at the end of a sermon or syllogism. Direct address: madam, the poem's only vocative. Imperative: be advised. First person: me, the only first-person word in the poem. Caesura: two commas, the only doubly punctuated line. Metrical irregularity: nine syllables as now spoken (ten if advised is sounded "advisèd"), opening on two falling words, THERE-fore, MA-dam.

Meaning & effect

The poem turns from proof to advice, and for the first time the speaker appears. Everything before has been impersonal; now a young woman steps forward and claims the right to counsel another, in a world where parents, guardians and family interests normally decided whom a gentlewoman married. By me is the boldest phrase in the poem: the case against marriage had scriptural cover, but a girl setting her own judgement against family and custom did not. The commas slow the line to a formal pace, and its broken rhythm marks the change of voice. Madam is courteous and slightly distant, the address of a letter to a lady; the longer anonymous poem with which this one shares thirteen lines also opens "Madam", so the form is a verse letter of counsel.

Line 14
Turn, turn apostate to love's Levity.
Language & devices

Epizeuxis: Turn, turn — immediate repetition, urgent. Spondee: two stresses open the line. Religious diction: Turn is the verb of conversion; apostate means one who abandons a faith (Greek apostasia, defection or revolt). Personification / Capitalisation: Levity — lightness, frivolity, inconstancy, the opposite of gravity. Light rhyme: the strong me is answered by the weak last syllable of Levity.

Meaning & effect

The command is to renounce love as one would renounce a false religion. Love is imagined as a faith with worshippers, and the speaker as a missionary for unbelief, which turns the whole tradition of love poetry, where the lover is a devotee and the beloved a saint, upside down. Levity is the charge against that religion: love is not grave and sacred but light, frivolous and changeable. The grammar is briefly slippery, because Turn… to sounds like converting towards something; apostate to means a renegade from it, and once the line is complete the sense is clear: abandon love's lightness. The doubled Turn, turn is the poem's most urgent moment, as if the speaker were taking her friend by the arm. Even the rhyme is light, landing on an unstressed syllable.

Line 15
Suppress wild nature if she dare rebell,
Language & devices

Imperative: Suppress — the verb for putting down an uprising. Personification: wild nature is female (she), a rebel. Conditional: if she dare rebell — a challenge. Political diction: Suppress, rebell. Spondee: WILD NA- swells the line before regular iambs return (she DARE re-BELL), as though order were restored inside the line.

Meaning & effect

This is the most honest line in the poem, because it admits the cost. The single life will not be effortless: desire (wild nature) will rise, and the woman must put it down by force, as a ruler suppresses a revolt. The poem's political vocabulary comes together here. The woman crown'd in line 5 must now govern her own territory, and her own body is the province that may rebel. The image contains an irony: the "rebel" is the impulse towards the most conventional choice of all, marriage, while the unconventional choice is cast as lawful order. This is also where Philips parts company with St Paul. Paul allowed that those who "cannot contain" should marry, since "it is better to marry than to burn"; the poem gives no such permission.

Line 16
There's no such thing as leading Apes in hell.
Language & devices

Allusion: the proverb that women who die unmarried will "lead apes in hell" (Shakespeare's Beatrice and Katherina both cite it). Colloquialism: There's no such thing — plain speech. Bathos: religious and political language gives way to a common saying. Negation: the last no recalls the No… catalogue and abolishes the threat. Iambic pentameter: perfectly regular. Rhyme: rebell / hell repeats the sound of spell / well (lines 3–4).

Meaning & effect

The poem ends by removing the last threat used to push women into marriage: the folk belief that a woman who died a virgin would be punished by leading apes in hell — on the usual explanation, because she had no children to lead to heaven. Philips does not argue with the superstition or take offence at it; she says it does not exist, in the plainest words of the poem, and stops. The deflation is funny, and it is also an argument about power: the sanction that keeps women marrying turns out to be a story, not a law of God. The proverb's assumption, that a childless woman must be given something to lead, is thrown out with the apes. Yet the last word is hell: the poem ends on a punishment, even one it denies. The regular metre and the return of the -ell rhyme from line 3 make the close sound settled, and the poem ends as confidently as it began.

THE WHOLE POEM

The Whole Poem

Stepping back: what the poem is doing, first line to last

'A Married State' is a case at law conducted in sixteen lines. It weighs two conditions a woman might live in, a married state and a virgin state, finds the first wanting even at its best, and ends by telling its reader to choose the second and stop fearing the consequences. The conclusion was not new; warnings against marriage were an old genre. What is remarkable is the method. The poem never complains. It argues, in the most reasonable verse form English had, with the signposts of a proof (This, Tho, Thus, Therefore), and it takes the authorities its world used to defend marriage — law, scripture, the Prayer Book, popular proverb — and turns each one round. Its boldest move comes near the end: at the one point where St Paul, the poem's quiet authority, allowed an exit into marriage, it refuses the exit.

The opening is a verdict delivered without heat. A married state affords but little ease has no I, no example, no grievance; it is an axiom in perfect iambic pentameter, and a colon then promises proof. Affords frames marriage as an account to be balanced, and but little is cannier than "none", because a measured claim is harder to refute. Line 2 is the poem's masterstroke of concession. By choosing The best of husbands, Philips makes the problem the arrangement rather than the man: if the ideal husband is still so hard to please, any marriage is a life spent pleasing someone else. The rhyme says so in sound, since please swallows ease. The evidence follows, and it is visible to anyone who looks: wifes Carefull faces, which you may spell like a text. Line 4 then closes the trap. If wives look content, it is because they desemble their misfortunes well. A sceptic will call this unfalsifiable; the poem's answer is that a wife's composure is part of what marriage demands, and that the evidence must therefore be read, not merely seen.

Line 5 builds the alternative as a mirror. A virgin state answers A married state position for position; affords becomes crown'd, little becomes much, anxious ease becomes content. The parallel turns a choice that would look like defiance into a comparison between two states, and the crown makes the single woman a sovereign where the wife, in law, was absorbed into her husband's person. Line 6 ties happiness to innocence, with the barbed implication that marriage costs innocence — the daily dissembling of line 4. Then comes the catalogue. No Blustering husbands, No pangs of child birth, No children's crys: a husband's temper, the danger of labour, the noise of children, in the order a married life brings them and on a falling scale from fear to pain to irritation. Each harm arrives with an infinitive of purpose (to create, to extort, for to offend), as if suffering were the function of each thing, and each lands on your. Extort is the darkest word in the poem: tears forced out by violence, childbirth as something done to a woman. Then the pattern breaks. Line 10 says Few, not No, and ends not on comfort but on prayers. The concession buys credibility, and the climax reveals the poem's deepest claim, which is Paul's: marriage is a distraction from God, and its troubles are worldly crosses that sanctify nothing.

The verdict is given in two lines. Thus are you freed — the vocabulary of release, in a decade when freedom was a war cry — from all the cares that do / Attend on matrymony and a husband too. The only enjambment in the poem lets the cares spill over the line-end, and the only alexandrine lets the husband arrive as an afterthought, an extra foot dragging the line. The joke is also an inversion of scripture: Paul wanted the unmarried to "attend upon the Lord"; the married woman attends on matrimony, and the bride of the Prayer Book promised to "serve him". At the first full stop the case is closed.

Only now does the speaker appear. Therefore, madam, be advised by me is the single first-person phrase in the poem, and it is its real audacity: a girl of fourteen to sixteen, in a world where families arranged marriages, claims the right to counsel another woman against one. The command that follows is religious: Turn, turn apostate to love's Levity. Love becomes a false faith, light and inconstant, and the urgent doubled verb is the poem's most passionate moment. Then the cost is admitted. Suppress wild nature if she dare rebell concedes that desire will rise and must be put down like a revolt; the crowned woman of line 5 has a rebellious province to govern, and its rebel, ironically, is the impulse towards the most conventional choice of all. Here Philips parts company with Paul, who said that those who "cannot contain" should marry, since "it is better to marry than to burn". The poem allows no such exit. Its last line removes the last threat instead: There's no such thing as leading Apes in hell. The proverbial punishment for dying unmarried is not refuted but declared non-existent, in the plainest words and the most regular metre in the poem, and the -ell rhyme of lines 3–4 returns to close the frame.

The strongest objection is that none of this is serious. The poem is juvenilia, thirteen of its lines also occur in someone else's anonymous satire, and its author married within two years and stayed married until her death; its real point, on this view, is its jokes. But the objection mistakes where the poem's seriousness lies. Its claims do not depend on its author's life: coverture, the dangers of childbirth, the expectation that a wife please and serve were facts, and the poem states them accurately. Borrowing is not the opposite of authorship in a manuscript culture, either: the sixteen lines are a deliberate reduction of a sixty-two-line satire to one ordered case, and whoever wrote the phrases, the shape — diagnosis, alternative, verdict, command — belongs to the person who cut it, who then signed it. And the jokes fall precisely on the gravest claims: that marriage makes a woman an attendant (line 12), and that the sanctions enforcing it are fictions (line 16). Wit is how the poem makes those claims sayable, not proof that it does not mean them.

The poem's real subject, then, is authority: who decides how a woman should live. It begins with the impersonal authority of a maxim, borrows Paul's, sets aside the Prayer Book's, abolishes the proverb's, and arrives at be advised by me. A girl who was herself about to be married claims, in the voice of public reason, the right to tell another woman not to be. That claim, more than the case against marriage, is what makes the poem startling.

FORM & STRUCTURE

Form & Structure

How the poem is built, and why it matters

Form & genre

A verse letter of counsel in heroic couplets: sixteen lines of rhymed iambic pentameter addressed to madam. It belongs to the old genre of warnings against marriage (molestiae nuptiarum), here turned to warn a woman off husbands, and it is built as an argument rather than a lyric.

The text

The only manuscript is Philips's untitled autograph (c. 1646–48), so the title is editorial. This chapter prints the text Jack's class uses, which keeps the manuscript spellings (wifes, Carefull, desemble, allways, inocent, crys, matrymony, rebell) with some editorial apostrophes and punctuation. Limbert's transcription of the leaf has "Turn turn", "loves Levity" and "Theres", and the manuscript catalogue gives the first line as "A marryd state". Modernised printings read wives' careful, dissemble, crowned, always, innocent, cries, matrimony, rebel; PoetryProf's text misprints Therefore in line 13 as "Thus".

Four movements

Lines 1–4: the case against marriage (axiom, then evidence). Lines 5–10: the case for the virgin state (axiom, then catalogue). Lines 11–12: the verdict (Thus). Lines 13–16: the advice (Therefore), ending by refuting a threat. 4 + 6 + 2 + 4.

Metre

Iambic pentameter, mostly very regular. Three lines break the measure: line 7 (eleven syllables unless Blustering is elided), line 12 (twelve syllables, an alexandrine, the only one), and line 13 (nine syllables, or ten with "advisèd", opening on two falling words).

Rhyme

aabbccdddd eeffgg. Seven couplets and, at lines 7–10, a triplet (fears / tears / ears) stretched to a fourth line by a near-rhyme (prayers). The last couplet (rebell / hell) repeats the sound of lines 3–4 (spell / well).

Punctuation & lineation

No full stop until line 12: the whole case runs as one sweep, lightly punctuated in the manner of manuscript verse. The advice then comes in two short sentences (13–14, 15–16). Only lines 11–12 are enjambed; only lines 13–14 have pauses inside the line.

The form is not a container for the argument; it is the argument's credential. Closed couplets in pentameter were becoming, in the 1640s, the measure of polished public verse (Waller and Denham were making it fashionable), and a generation later they would be the voice of Dryden and Pope. Each couplet clicks shut like a proposition proved. A girl writing against marriage in this measure is claiming the register of reason rather than of complaint, and the poem's few irregularities are placed where the argument needs them.

A proof in four movements

The poem moves like a syllogism, and its connectives are the signposts: This (evidence for line 2), Tho (the objection answered), Thus (the conclusion), Therefore (the application). The two halves of the case open with matching axioms, A married state… (1) and A virgin state… (5), each followed by its evidence: four lines on what marriage costs, six on what the single life escapes. The verdict takes two lines and the advice four. The proportions matter. The case for the virgin state is the longest section, but it is made almost entirely of negatives (No… No… No… Few): the poem describes the good life by what is absent from it, which is rhetorically safe (it never has to say what a single woman does with her days) and also its most exposed point.

The one formal surprise inside the scheme, the triplet with its near-rhyme at lines 7–10, falls at the centre of the catalogue, where the grievances accumulate. A couplet poem trains the ear to expect closure every two lines; here the same sound keeps returning, and the form stops closing exactly where the troubles stop ending.

Scansion

Stresses in capitals; feet divided by |.

Line Scansion What it does
1 a MAR- | -ried STATE | af-FORDS | but LIT- | -tle EASE Perfectly regular. The axiom arrives with total composure; the colon then opens the proof.
2 the BEST | of HUS- | -bands are | SO HARD | to PLEASE Pyrrhic then spondee in natural speech: the stresses pile up on so hard, and the effort of pleasing is audible.
3 THIS in | WIFES CARE- | -full FA- | -ces YOU | may SPELL Initial trochee on the pointing This, then a spondee on wifes Carefull: the line is weighted with care.
4 tho THEY | de-SEM- | -ble THEIR | mis-FOR- | -tunes WELL Perfectly regular. A composed line about composure: nothing in the sound betrays the strain it describes.
5 a VIR- | -gin STATE | is CROWN'D | with MUCH | con-TENT Regular, and a mirror of line 1 stress for stress: the alternative is built to the same measure.
7 no BLUST'- | -ring HUS- | -bands to | cre-ATE | your FEARS Elision needed. Unelided, Blustering gives eleven syllables: the husband's bluster overfills the line.
10 FEW WORLD- | -ly CROSS- | -es to | dis-TRACT | your PRAYERS Spondee on Few worldly: after three light Nos the line opens heavily, marking the change from No to Few.
11 THUS are | you FREED | from ALL | the CARES | that DO Trochaic opening for the conclusion; the line ends on the weak auxiliary do, forcing the only enjambment.
12 at-TEND | on MA- | -try-MO- | -ny AND | a HUS- | -band TOO Alexandrine: six feet. The line about matrimony's burdens is overloaded, and the extra weight arrives with a husband too.
13 THERE-fore, | MA-dam, | be ad- | VISED by | ME Irregular: nine syllables (ten with "advisèd"), two falling feet, two commas. The metre breaks where the voice turns personal.
14 TURN, TURN | a-POS- | -tate to | LOVE'S LEV- | -i-TY Spondee, pyrrhic, spondee: the urgent command jolts the rhythm; the final stress falls on a weak syllable for the rhyme with me.
15 sup-PRESS | WILD NA- | -ture if | she DARE | re-BELL Spondee on wild nature: the rebel swells the line; regular iambs at the end restore order, as the verb demands.
16 there's NO | such THING | as LEAD- | -ing APES | in HELL Perfectly regular. Plain speech in perfect metre: the threat is dismissed with complete calm.

The pattern is clear. The case (1–6) is almost perfectly regular, as befits a demonstration. Disturbance gathers in the catalogue (7, 10), peaks in the verdict's overloaded line (12), and breaks at the turn to direct address (13–15). The last line returns to perfect order.

Rhyme

Lines Rhyme words Scheme Note
1–2 ease / please aa Full, and embedded: please contains ease.
3–4 spell / well bb Full; the sound returns at 15–16.
5–6 content / inocent cc Light rhyme: stressed -tent against an unstressed -cent.
7–9 fears / tears / ears ddd Triplet: the couplet pattern fails to close.
10 prayers d (near) Near-rhyme to modern ears; pronunciation of these vowels was shifting in the seventeenth century, so it may have sounded closer then.
11–12 do / too ee Full, but on a weak auxiliary, which forces the run-on.
13–14 me / Levity ff Light rhyme: a stressed pronoun against a weak final syllable.
15–16 rebell / hell gg Full; repeats bb, framing the poem.

Two things stand out. The poem's rhymes are tight where it argues (ease/please, spell/well) and loosen where it concedes or exhorts (prayers, Levity). And the matching -ell rhymes link the beginning of the evidence to the end of the advice: what you may spell in wives' faces is set against the hell the poem abolishes.

Syntax, voice and punctuation

The case is impersonal. Wifes and they are third person; you first appears as a general reader (you may spell), then becomes specific in the catalogue, where four lines end on your (fears, tears, ears, prayers) and the second person is the target of every harm. The catalogue is verbless: No Blustering husbands to create your fears means "[you will have] no blustering husbands…", and each phrase hangs on an infinitive of purpose, which makes every harm sound intended. The first person appears once, at the hinge: be advised by me.

Punctuation is light, as in manuscript verse. Lines 2, 4, 6 and 10 end without any stop, and there is no full stop until line 12, so the whole case runs as one breath, from axiom to verdict. Then the advice comes in two crisp two-line sentences. The only pauses inside a line are in lines 13–14 (Therefore, madam, and Turn, turn), exactly where the speaker turns to address her reader.

The turns

There are three. Line 5 is the argumentative turn, from the married state to the virgin state, marked by the parallel phrasing rather than by a conjunction. Line 10 is a small swerve inside the catalogue, Few for No, where the poem concedes and then climaxes on prayers. Line 13 is the main turn, from proof to command, from general to personal, from third person to first, and it is the most metrically disturbed line in the poem.

The borrowed lines and the shape

Because thirteen of the sixteen lines also occur in an anonymous 62-line satire, the shape described here — four movements, a proof that turns to advice — is partly the result of cutting. That makes the structure more, not less, revealing: it shows what the person who made the sixteen-line version chose to keep. She kept the opening axiom and its evidence, the catalogue, the verdict and the command, and finished on the proverb. (The questions this raises are discussed under Difficult Moments.)

SOUND

Sound

What the poem does to the ear

ease / please

The first rhyme is embedded: please contains ease. The wife's peace sits literally inside the husband's pleasure, and the long /iː/ lets both words linger.

The -ell frame

spell / well (3–4) and rebell / hell (15–16) share one sound. The evidence read in wives' faces and the punishment the poem abolishes chime across the whole poem.

Fears, tears, ears… prayers

Three full rhymes on one sound, then a fourth that nearly rhymes. The chime keeps returning as the troubles do, and the imperfect prayers sounds like the list's one concession.

Plosives at the points of force

Blustering, pangs of child birth, extort, crosses, Suppress: hard consonants gather where the poem names violence and effort.

Light rhymes

content / inocent and me / Levity rhyme a stressed syllable with an unstressed one. The rhyme on Levity is itself light.

Plain cadence at the close

Line 16 is almost all monosyllables in regular iambs: conversation, after the Latinate apostate and Levity.

The opening four lines are hushed by sibilance — state, so, spell, desemble, misfortunes — and soft in their vowels, which suits a diagnosis delivered quietly, almost confidentially, about something wives do not say aloud. The sound hardens in the virgin state: crown'd with much content opens with a firm /k/ and ends on the clipped -tent, and the same consonant runs through the poem's key words, Carefull, crown'd, content, crosses, cares. Care and crown begin with one sound: the poem's two states are distinguished by what follows it.

The catalogue is where the poem becomes physical. Blustering is close to onomatopoeia, a gust of /bl/ and /st/; pangs of child birth packs plosives and a heavy cluster into three words, and extort hisses and then snaps shut on /t/, the sound of something being wrung out. Against these, crys and ears are open and long, and the anticlimax of line 9 is audible as well as logical. The No that opens lines 7–9 is a soft, unstressed syllable, so the change to Few in line 10, which takes stress, can be heard as well as read.

In the verdict the sound slows. Thus are you freed from all the cares that do is all monosyllables until the weak do, which cannot end anything, and the alexandrine that follows drags its six beats to a husband too, a long vowel on the last word. Then the voice changes. Therefore, madam, breaks into two falling words fenced off by commas; Turn, turn brings two stresses into collision, the hardest jolt in the poem. Suppress returns to sibilance, a hiss of control, before wild nature swells with long vowels (/aɪ/, /eɪ/) and the rebellion is put down by the clipped rebell.

The final line is the quietest. There's no such thing as leading Apes in hell is said in the rhythm of ordinary speech, with only the long /eɪ/ of Apes and the /l/ of leading and hell to bind it. The last no picks up the three Nos of the catalogue, and the closing hell rhymes with the spell of line 3: the poem ends on the sound it used to introduce its evidence.

MOTIFS & SYMBOLS

Motifs & Symbols

Images that recur, and what they accumulate

Motifs and symbols

1. The state: condition, status, kingdom

The poem's governing noun appears twice, once for each life: A married state (1), A virgin state (5). At first it means simply a condition. But the second state is crown'd, and from then on the word gathers political meaning: the single woman is freed (11), and at the end she must Suppress a rebell (15). By the close, the two states have become rival constitutions. In one the woman is a subject who must please and Attend on a ruler; in the other she is a crowned sovereign, with the duty every sovereign has of governing her own territory, which here means her own desire. The motif accumulates from description to politics, and its last stage admits that self-rule has a price.

2. Care, pleasing and attendance

A chain of words makes married life a form of service. Husbands are so hard to please (2); wives' faces are Carefull (3); the single woman is freed from all the cares (11) that Attend on matrymony and a husband too (12). Please and care are St Paul's words for the married woman's divided mind, and Attend on is the verb of servants waiting on a household; behind it stands the Prayer Book bride who promised to "obey him, and serve him". The chain moves from the wife's obligation (please), to its mark on her (careful faces), to its personification (cares as attendants), and the single life is defined as release from the whole retinue.

3. Faces, reading and performance

The poem is preoccupied with the gap between what is shown and what is true. Wives' faces must be read slowly (you may spell, 3) because wives desemble their misfortunes well (4); the virgin state is happy because inocent (6), free of the need to pretend. The speaker sets herself up as a reader of appearances and asks madam to become one too (be advised, 13). The motif ends with a story told to frighten girls: the apes in hell (16), an appearance with nothing behind it. The poem has moved from reading a mask to exposing a fiction.

4. Borrowed religion

Religious vocabulary runs from start to finish, and it changes direction as it goes. It first honours the single life (crown'd, inocent, 5–6), then names marriage's spiritual cost (worldly crosses, prayers, 10; Attend on, 12, inverting "attend upon the Lord"), then treats love itself as a false religion (Turn, turn apostate, 14), and finally abolishes a false hell (16). Faith is the poem's licence: it lets a girl argue against marriage without sounding impious. But it is also its target, because the one sanction it dismisses outright is a religious one.

5. Noise and the besieged body

The catalogue makes marriage a series of assaults on the body through the senses: Blustering husbands (noise and weather, 7), pangs that extort your tears (pain, 8), crys that offend your ears (sound, 9). Each rhyme word is a part or product of the body under pressure: fears, tears, ears. Against this stands the silence of prayers (10). In line 15 the body reappears as an insurgent of its own: wild nature is the one force inside the woman herself, and the poem's remedy for it is suppression.

THEMES

Themes

The ideas the poem is arguing about

01

Marriage as an institution, not a relationship

The poem's most disciplined choice is that it never attacks a husband. The title's A and the plural husbands keep the subject general, and line 2 concedes the strongest counter-example in advance: The best of husbands are so hard to please. The complaint is therefore structural. Marriage is a state that affords a woman little, an arrangement in which one person's occupation is pleasing another, and no amount of individual kindness can change that.

This was close to a legal description. Under coverture a wife's legal person was absorbed into her husband's, and the Prayer Book bride promised to "obey him, and serve him". The poem's diction tracks that reality: please, Carefull, cares that Attend on the husband. It makes the case without heat, which is what makes it hard to dismiss: it reads as a description of a condition, not a grievance against a man.

02

Freedom, sovereignty and self-government

The single woman is crown'd (5) and freed (11): the poem's vocabulary for the alternative to marriage is the vocabulary of rule and liberty, used in years when England was fighting over exactly those words. Marriage makes a woman a subject; the virgin state makes her her own sovereign.

But sovereignty has to be exercised. Suppress wild nature if she dare rebell (15) admits that the crowned woman must govern a rebellious province, her own desire. The poem's idea of freedom is therefore not the absence of restraint but self-rule, and it is honest about the cost. It also contains an irony: in this poem the rebel is the urge to do the conventional thing, and the unconventional life is cast as lawful order.

03

Faith turned against custom

The poem's case is religious before it is social. Its catalogue climaxes on prayers (10), its troubles are worldly crosses, its key words — care, please, distract, attend — come from St Paul's argument for the single life in 1 Corinthians 7, and its command is framed as a conversion: Turn, turn apostate. A Protestant culture that had abolished convents and made marriage the norm for women still read Paul every Sunday, and the poem uses his authority against the custom.

It is not simply pious, though. At the point where Paul allowed marriage to those who "cannot contain", the poem refuses the exit (Suppress wild nature), and its last line dismisses a religious threat outright: There's no such thing as leading Apes in hell. Faith is both the poem's licence and something it is willing to correct.

04

What women hide: the face, the body and the cost

The poem's evidence is what wives conceal. Their faces carry care that must be spelled out, and they desemble their misfortunes well (4): contentment is part of the work marriage demands. The catalogue then names what lies behind the composed face: a husband's temper, the pangs of child birth that extort your tears, the endless claims of children. Extort is the key word, making childbirth something taken from a woman by force at a time when it carried a real risk of death.

The poem's method suits this theme. It speaks in a calm voice and in near-perfect metre about suffering that cannot be spoken of, so the form itself mimics the composure it exposes.

05

Wit, reason and the right to advise

Therefore, madam, be advised by me (13) is the poem's boldest claim: a girl of fourteen to sixteen, in a world where families arranged marriages, sets her own judgement against custom. What makes the claim stick is the manner. The heroic couplet, the proof-like connectives (This, Thus, Therefore), the impersonal opening — all are the signs of public reason, not private complaint.

So is the wit. The tacked-on and a husband too, which overloads the poem's only alexandrine; the bathos of crying children after the danger of childbirth; the deadpan dismissal of the apes. Each joke falls on a serious claim and makes it sayable. A bitter poem would have been easy to dismiss as the grievance of an unhappy woman; a witty one cannot be.

06

Love's levity and reason's cure

The poem treats love not as a sacred passion but as love's Levity (14): light, frivolous, inconstant, a false religion to be renounced. Reason is the remedy, and wild nature is to be governed. The same leaf on which Philips copied the poem carries a mock recipe for curing lovesickness with "the spirits of reason" and "the Powder of experiance", and a poem preferring "the beauty of the mind". The theme is less hatred of marriage than a young writer's refusal to be governed by feeling.

DIFFICULT MOMENTS

Difficult Moments

Where the poem is genuinely undecidable — and what to do about it

Cruxes

1. How much of this poem is Philips's?

The difficulty. The poem survives only in Philips's teenage hand, signed "C. Fowler", but thirteen of its sixteen lines also occur in an anonymous 62-line satire beginning "Madam / I cannot but Congratulate" (as lines 13–16, 43–44, 48–50 and 59–62). Limbert and O'Neill (1993) call this "composite authorship". Editions printed before 1993, including Thomas's Collected Works, present the poem as wholly hers.

Competing readings. (a) An extract. On this view the girl copied the best lines of a circulating satire, and the poem's arguments and phrasing are someone else's; claims about Philips's own views, let alone her feelings about her marriage, rest on sand. (b) An adaptation. Reducing sixty-two lines to sixteen is itself composition: the shape — axiom, evidence, alternative, verdict, command — exists only in her version, and she signed it. (c) A finer question of which lines. The catalogue entry does not say which three lines lack a counterpart. The line numbers it gives fall neatly onto the poem's own units (1–4, 5–6, 7–9, 13–16), which would leave lines 10–12 — the Few… prayers concession and the alexandrine — as the unmatched lines; but that is an inference from the numbers, not a reported finding, and should be held lightly.

What a strong answer does. It treats the speaker as the poem's voice rather than as Katherine Philips's diary, and credits the poem's design — its order, compression and close — to the version on the page. It avoids biographical claims ("she wrote this about her husband"), and notices that the question sharpens the poem's interest: a girl chose these lines, in this order, to keep.

2. Who is madam, and how seriously is she being advised?

The difficulty. The addressee is never named. Madam could be a friend, a neighbour, a younger girl, or a conventional figure; the longer anonymous satire also opens "Madam", so the address may be part of the genre. The tone also hovers between counsel and a game.

Competing readings. (a) Real counsel. The poem names real conditions — coverture, the danger of childbirth, the duty to please — and its by me is an act of advice between women, in a world where marriages were arranged for them. (b) A coterie game. It is a witty piece in an established satirical genre, written in a copybook alongside a mock recipe for lovesickness; its jokes (the dragging husband, the apes) signal play, and its author married within two years. (c) Both at once. The wit is how something risky remains sayable. The two best jokes fall on the two gravest claims: that a wife is an attendant (12) and that the threat enforcing marriage is a fiction (16).

What a strong answer does. It does not need to identify madam. It reads her as the poem's implied reader — a young unmarried gentlewoman being asked to look at wives' faces herself (you may spell) — and takes the third position, showing how the jokes carry the argument rather than cancelling it.

3. Turn, turn apostate to love's Levity: renouncing what?

The difficulty. The grammar wobbles. Turn… to sounds like converting towards something, while apostate to means a renegade from it. And is Levity the false god itself (love is mere lightness), or a quality of love the reader is told to abandon (renounce love, which is light)?

Competing readings. (a) Renounce love. Love is a false religion, and its defining quality is levity: unserious, inconstant, weightless. The command overturns the whole tradition of love poetry, where the lover is a devout worshipper. (b) Renounce frivolity, not feeling. Levity names a light, giddy kind of love, the infatuation that leads girls into marriage, rather than all love; the companion poem on the same leaf, preferring "the beauty of the mind" and a husband of "sence", supports a pragmatic rather than ascetic reading. (c) Read forward. In Philips's later friendship poems, "apostate" is the word for a friend who leaves the faith of friendship by marrying ('On Rosania's Apostacy'); here the same word urges apostasy from love. The reading is suggestive but anachronistic: those poems came years later.

What a strong answer does. It notes the momentary double-take and settles the sense from the line as a whole (abandon love's lightness), then weighs (a) against (b) using wild nature in line 15, which shows that the poem expects desire itself, not just giddiness, to resist. It uses the later "apostasy" poems as an echo, not as the key.

4. Suppress wild nature: liberation or a new confinement?

The difficulty. The poem promises freedom (freed, 11), then ends by demanding self-suppression (15). Is the single life it recommends liberty, or a different kind of discipline?

Competing readings. (a) Feminist liberation. Self-government replaces government by a husband; the crowned woman rules herself, and suppression is the price of sovereignty that any ruler pays. (b) Ascetic confinement. The bargain is bleak: freedom from a husband is bought by denying one's own body, and the poem's ideal looks less like liberty than like the convent life Protestant England had abolished. (c) A departure from Paul. Paul allowed that those who "cannot contain" should marry — "it is better to marry than to burn" — and the Prayer Book called marriage a "remedy against sin" for those without "the gift of continency". The poem denies the need for that remedy, which makes the line a claim about women's capacity for self-command, not only a renunciation.

What a strong answer does. It sees the honesty: the poem names the cost of its own advice. It notices the irony that the rebel is the impulse towards convention, and that the metre itself swells on wild nature and is brought back to order by the line's end. It can hold (a) and (b) together: the poem's freedom is real, and it is not free.

5. The last line: triumph or residue?

The difficulty. There's no such thing as leading Apes in hell could be the poem's victory or an anticlimax, and its final word is hell.

Competing readings. (a) Triumph. The last sanction against staying single is dismissed with a shrug, in the plainest words and the most regular metre in the poem; the threat is not refuted but declared non-existent, which is the right way to treat a bogey. (b) Residue. A poem recommending the single life ends by naming the place of punishment, straight after conceding that wild nature will rebel; the joke leaves an echo. (c) A limit. The line abolishes an imaginary hell, but says nothing about the real social costs of remaining unmarried — money, dependence, contempt — which the poem never mentions.

What a strong answer does. It reads the line as the end of an argument about authority: law, scripture and custom have been weighed, and the folk threat is the one authority simply thrown out. It hears the return of the No catalogue in no such thing, and the -ell rhyme closing the frame begun at spell / well, and it can admit what the poem leaves unsaid.

CLOSE ANALYSIS

Close Analysis

The moments that repay pressure, worked through

Quotation analysis

Twelve moments, in order, chosen because each repays close pressure.

1. A married state affords but little ease: (1)

Aphorism; litotes; commercial verb; regular pentameter; colon. The poem opens on a maxim, not an anecdote, and the regular metre gives it the authority of common knowledge. Affords means provides or yields, and it brings with it the sense of affordability: marriage is assessed by what it returns to the person who enters it. But little is calculated understatement, harder to refute than "none". The colon presents the line as a proposition awaiting proof. Intention and effect: the reader is put in the position of a juror hearing a case stated, not a friend hearing a complaint, and is invited to agree before any evidence is given.

2. The best of husbands are so hard to please (2)

Superlative; concession; embedded rhyme; biblical echo. By choosing the best case, Philips makes the problem the institution, not the man. The wife is absent from her own sentence; only the husband and his pleasure appear. Please swallows the ease of line 1, so the rhyme acts out the transfer, and Paul's "how she may please her husband" is turned from description into complaint. Intention and effect: the counter-argument ("but some husbands are kind") is disarmed before it can be made, and the reader realises the claim is about a structure.

3. This in wifes Carefull faces you may spell, (3)

Demonstrative; metaphor of reading; trochaic inversion; second person. The face is a text, spell means to decipher letter by letter, and Carefull means full of care. The stresses crowd onto wifes Carefull, weighting the line. You may spell makes the addressee a witness. Intention and effect: the poem shifts authority from the speaker to the reader's own eyes; the evidence is in plain sight, but only for those who read carefully.

4. Tho they desemble their misfortunes well (4)

Concession; verb of disguise; euphemism; regular metre. The objection that wives look happy is converted into evidence: they are skilled at hiding. Misfortunes blames no one, and well is dry praise for the performance. Intention and effect: the line makes the case almost unanswerable, and its own smooth metre performs the composure it describes, so that the reader hears a calm surface over what it hides.

5. A virgin state is crown'd with much content, (5)

Parallelism; royal metaphor; antithesis; alliteration. The line mirrors line 1 position for position: virgin for married, crown'd for affords, much for little, content for ease. The crown suggests sovereignty and the old Christian crown of virgins. Intention and effect: framing the choice as a comparison between two states makes the unconventional option look like the rational one, and the image lifts the single woman from subject to ruler.

6. It's allways happy as it's inocent (6)

Ambiguous conjunction; etymology; contraction; light rhyme. As means because or in proportion as; either way happiness depends on innocence. Inocent at its root means harmless, doing no hurt. The breezy contractions make a large claim sound obvious. Intention and effect: the implication — that marriage costs innocence, through the dissembling of line 4 — is left for the reader to draw, and the Prayer Book's claim that marriage began "in the time of man's innocency" is quietly reversed.

7. No Blustering husbands to create your fears, (7)

Anaphora; ellipsis; weather diction; infinitive of purpose. Blustering makes male anger both alarming and ridiculous, noise and wind; create says the fears are manufactured by his moods. The verbless phrase with its infinitive makes fear sound like a husband's function. Intention and effect: the first item of the catalogue belittles the husband even as it names the threat, and your puts the reader's own future in the line.

8. No pangs of child birth to extort your tears, (8)

Biblical diction; violent verb; plosives; plain rhythm. Pangs is the Bible's word for the pains of labour; extort, from the Latin for "twist out", makes tears something taken by force. In the 1640s childbirth carried a real risk of death. Intention and effect: the plainest line holds the darkest fact, and the verb refuses the consolation that such suffering was holy; the reader feels violence where the culture offered blessing.

9. No children's crys for to offend your ears, / Few worldly crosses to distract your prayers (9–10)

Bathos; archaism; broken anaphora; near-rhyme; climax. After the danger of death, the noise of children: the scale drops from fear to tears to ears. Then Few replaces No, and the list ends on prayers, with worldly crosses and distract echoing Paul's wish for a life "without distraction". Intention and effect: the comic drop keeps pity at bay, the concession makes the speaker credible, and the climax reveals the deepest claim — marriage is a spiritual distraction — which no one could call irreligious.

10. Thus are you freed from all the cares that do / Attend on matrymony and a husband too. (11–12)

Conclusion; enjambment; personification; alexandrine; bathos. Freed names marriage as bondage; the cares become matrimony's retinue; Attend on inverts Paul's "attend upon the Lord"; and the husband arrives last, an afterthought that adds the line's extra foot. The only enjambment lets the cares overflow the line. Intention and effect: form becomes the joke: the line about marriage's burden is itself overburdened, and the reader laughs at the moment the verdict is delivered.

11. Therefore, madam, be advised by me: / Turn, turn apostate to love's Levity. (13–14)

Connective; vocative; first person; caesura; epizeuxis; religious diction; light rhyme. The case becomes counsel, and the speaker appears for the only time. The doubled Turn is the verb of conversion, apostate the word for a renegade from a faith, and Levity the charge against love: lightness and inconstancy. The weak rhyme of me with Levity is appropriately light. Intention and effect: the impersonal voice becomes an urgent personal plea, and love is demoted from sacred passion to a frivolous cult the reader is told to leave.

12. Suppress wild nature if she dare rebell, / There's no such thing as leading Apes in hell. (15–16)

Political diction; personification; spondee; proverb; bathos; regular metre. Desire is a female rebel to be put down; the metre swells on wild nature and is brought back to order by she dare rebell. Then the proverbial punishment for dying unmarried is dismissed in plain speech and perfect iambs, and the -ell rhyme recalls spell / well. Intention and effect: the poem names the cost of its advice and, unlike St Paul, allows no exit through marriage; then it removes the last threat with a shrug, leaving the reader with calm confidence and a final word, hell, that keeps the danger in view.

CRITICAL LENSES

Critical Lenses

What each way of reading makes visible, and what it flattens

Critical lenses

Feminist

The lens under which the poem looks most radical. It makes visible a woman's analysis of marriage as an institution that costs women: the duty to please (2), the mask of contentment (4), legal and practical subordination (the state that affords little), the mortal risk of childbirth (8), and the claim of one woman to advise another against the order arranged for her (be advised by me, 13). It places the poem in a line that runs to Mary Astell's Some Reflections upon Marriage (1700) and Lady Mary Chudleigh's "Wife and servant are the same". What it flattens: the poem's class (it speaks to gentlewomen with families to keep them), its religious frame (the climax is prayers, not independence), and its ending in self-suppression, which some feminist readers find a bleak substitute for liberty. It also risks treating as a manifesto what is partly an adaptation of someone else's satire.

Historicist

Puts the poem in 1646–48: a defeated king, a Second Civil War breaking out in the poet's own Pembrokeshire, a Parliament that had abolished the Prayer Book, and the law of coverture. Under this lens state, crown'd, freed, rebell and Suppress carry the charge of the decade, and madam faces a choice between two constitutions. It also shows what the poem answers: the Prayer Book's "honourable estate… in the time of man's innocency" and its "remedy against sin". What it flattens: intention. Nothing shows the girl meant a political allegory, and the vocabulary may be shared with the anonymous satire she adapted; the lens can turn a witty counsel poem into a pamphlet.

Theological

Reads the poem as a versified 1 Corinthians 7: care, please, distraction, attend, wife and virgin, happiness in remaining single. On this view Philips is less a rebel than a conservative, reviving the Christian preference for celibacy that Protestant England, having closed the convents, had quietly dropped; the catalogue's climax on prayers is sincere. What it makes visible: the poem's licence to speak, and the precise point where it outruns Paul (Suppress wild nature against "better to marry than to burn"). What it flattens: the wit, and the last line, where a religious threat is dismissed as folklore.

Formalist
