Shows the argument built into the verse: closed couplets as the sound of reason; a near-perfectly regular demonstration (1–6) disturbed in the catalogue (7–10), overloaded in the alexandrine (12), broken at the turn (13–15) and restored in the last line (16). It hears the embedded rhyme of ease in please, the triplet that refuses closure at the centre, the light rhymes on inocent and Levity, and the -ell frame. What it flattens: everything outside the text, including the question of what the girl adapted and why the poem never says what a single woman will actually do.

Textual and material

Asks what kind of object the poem is: an untitled autograph leaf, folded like a letter, in a girl's unformed hand, sharing its paper with a poem on the "beauty of the mind" and a mock recipe for lovesickness, kept among a friend's family papers, sharing thirteen lines with an anonymous satire, and unprinted until the twentieth century. This lens makes visible the culture of manuscript copying, where selecting and reshaping verse was a form of authorship, and it explains the title (editorial), the spelling, and the address to madam. What it flattens: the poem's voice and argument, which matter however the lines came to be on the page.

Queer / "Sapphic-Platonic"

Harriette Andreadis's term for Philips's friendship poetry captures her later work's passionate, quasi-religious bonds between women ("There's a religion in our love") and her treatment of friends' marriages as apostasy. Read through it, Turn, turn apostate to love's Levity is a first sketch of a life organised around women rather than husbands. What it flattens: chronology and evidence. The poem was written years before those friendships, says nothing about what the reader should turn to, and its stated alternative is prayer and self-command, not another bond.

OTHER READINGS

Other Readings

Contested interpretations, and where each is weak

Other readings

1. The proto-feminist protest

The poem is one of the earliest arguments in English by a woman that marriage is bad for women as a class and that the single life is a legitimate, better choice. Evidence: The best of husbands (an institutional complaint); the dissembling wives; extort your tears; freed; be advised by me. Weakness: the alternative is defined almost wholly by negatives; its highest good is prayers; it ends in self-suppression; and thirteen of its lines are shared with an anonymous satire, so it is risky to treat it as a personal manifesto.

2. Pauline counsel

A devout, conservative poem: St Paul's case for celibacy in verse, with the vocabulary of 1 Corinthians 7 almost intact. Evidence: Carefull, please, distract your prayers, Attend on, A virgin state, allways happy. Weakness: it departs from Paul at the decisive point, refusing his concession that those who cannot contain should marry, and it ends by laughing at a religious threat. Piety is its licence, not its whole meaning.

3. A coterie game

A clever young woman's exercise in a fashionable satirical genre, written for friends and not meant as policy; its author married within two years. Evidence: the jokes (and a husband too, the crying children, the apes); the mock recipe for lovesickness on the same leaf; Limbert's sense of "a pragmatic young woman of good humor". Weakness: the jokes fall on serious claims, and the facts it states — about wives' duty, childbirth and the law — were accurate. Play is the manner, not proof of insincerity.

4. A girl's dread of her own marriage

Written by a teenager whose mother had just married for the third time, months or a year before her own arranged wedding, the poem voices fear of what is coming. Evidence: the dating of the leaf (between December 1646 and August 1648); the urgency of Turn, turn; the speaker's close reading of wives' faces. Weakness: it is advice to madam, not a confession; much of it is shared with an anonymous poem; and the old claim of a husband thirty-eight years her senior, which used to anchor this reading, rests on a disputed birth date (the ODNB gives his age as twenty-four).

5. A political allegory

In the years of the Civil Wars, a poem about two states, a crown'd sovereign, a people freed, and a rebell to be suppressed reads as a constitutional argument in domestic form: who governs whom? Evidence: the cluster of political words and the date. Weakness: nothing in the poem points to public events, and the vocabulary is the ordinary language of self-government; the allegory is a resonance a reader brings, not a code the poem asks to be cracked.

6. The sceptic's reading

The poem is a brilliant piece of rhetoric that proves less than it claims. Evidence: line 4 makes the case unfalsifiable (happy wives are only dissembling); the good life is described only by what it lacks; the cost of the single life is reduced to desire, ignoring money and dependence. Weakness: the poem itself concedes (Few, Suppress), and its job is persuasion of one reader, not proof; its honesty about cost is unusual in advice of any kind.

REVISION NOTES

Revision Notes

The working notes, quotation by quotation

Title

"A Married State"

Analysis
  • Title editorial: MS untitled → taken from line 1
  • A = generic → any marriage = the institution
  • State = condition / legal status / "holy estate of matrimony" / polity
  • Half the poem = the other state → title names what it argues against
Effect, style & response
  • Reads like a legal heading → a case, not a complaint
1

affords but little ease

Analysis
  • Aphorism → opinion disguised as fact
  • affords = yields / provides → marriage as an account judged by its return
  • Litotes but little → harder to refute than "none"
  • ease = freedom from care / anxiety, not just rest
  • Perfect iambic pentameter + colon → proposition, then proof
2

The best of husbands

Analysis
  • Superlative + concession → even the best → problem = system, not man
  • so hard to please → wife's job = pleasing; wife absent from sentence
  • Rhyme ease / please → please swallows ease
  • Echo 1 Cor 7:34: married woman "careth… how she may please her husband"
3–4

wifes Carefull faces

Analysis
  • Faces = texts → spell = read letter by letter, decipher
  • Carefull = full of care, anxious (Paul's "carefulness") ≠ cautious
  • you may spell → reader made a witness
  • desemble = disguise feelings → contentment = performance
  • misfortunes → euphemism, nobody blamed
Effect, style & response
  • Unfalsifiable trap: happy face = good dissembler
  • Smooth metre of l. 4 = composure itself
  • Written before her marriage → observer, not confessing wife
5–6

crown'd with much content

Analysis
  • Exact parallel with l. 1: married → virgin, affords → crown'd, little → much, ease → content
  • crown'd → sovereign not subject; old Christian crown of virgins
  • allways happy as it's inocent → as = because / to the degree that
  • inocent = guiltless; Latin root = harmless
  • Implies marriage costs innocence → the dissembling of l. 4
  • Reverses Prayer Book: marriage made "in the time of man's innocency"
7

Blustering husbands

Analysis
  • Anaphora No… begins
  • Blustering = stormy wind / loud empty threats → frightening + ridiculous
  • create your fears → fears manufactured by his moods
  • Infinitive of purpose → harm sounds like husband's function
  • your → reader's own future
8

extort your tears

Analysis
  • pangs = Bible's word for labour pains
  • extort = wring out by force (Latin "twist out") → childbirth as violence
  • Real risk of death in childbirth, 1640s
  • Refuses consolation that the suffering is holy (Eve's curse)
Effect, style & response
  • Darkest line, plainest rhythm → stated as fact
9–10

No… No… No… Few

Analysis
  • Descending tricolon: fears → tears → ears (terror → pain → irritation)
  • = order of a married life: husband → labour → children
  • Bathos l. 9 → humour blocks pity
  • for to = archaic infinitive (KJV "for to see")
  • Few, not No → concession → credibility
  • Climax on prayers → marriage = spiritual distraction (1 Cor 7:35 "without distraction")
  • worldly crosses → troubles that sanctify nothing
11–12

and a husband too

Analysis
  • Thus → verdict; freed → marriage = bondage
  • cares closes ring with Carefull (l. 3)
  • Only enjambment (do / Attend) → cares spill over
  • Alexandrine l. 12 → 12 syllables, extra foot = the husband → line drags
  • Attend on = serve → inverts Paul's "attend upon the Lord"; bride vowed to "obey him, and serve him"
  • matrymony ← Latin mater (mother)
  • First full stop of the poem → case closed
13

be advised by me

Analysis
  • Therefore → application, like a sermon / syllogism
  • madam = only vocative; verse letter of counsel
  • me = only first-person word → boldest claim
  • Two commas + irregular metre (9 syllables) → voice turns personal
Effect, style & response
  • A girl of 14–16 advising against arranged marriage
14

Turn, turn apostate

Analysis
  • Epizeuxis + spondee → urgency, grabbing her arm
  • Turn = conversion; apostate = renegade from a faith (Greek: defection, revolt)
  • Love = false religion → inverts love poetry's devotion
  • Levity = lightness, frivolity, inconstancy (opposite of gravity)
  • Light rhyme me / Levity
15

Suppress wild nature

Analysis
  • Political verbs Suppress, rebell → self as kingdom
  • wild nature… she = desire personified as female rebel
  • Admits the cost → honest
  • Irony: the "rebel" = urge towards convention (marriage)
  • Departs from Paul: "better to marry than to burn" → no such exit here
  • Spondee WILD NA-, regular iambs restore order
16

leading Apes in hell

Analysis
  • Proverb: unmarried women "lead apes in hell" (no children to lead to heaven)
  • Shakespeare: Beatrice (Much Ado), Katherina (Shrew)
  • There's no such thing → denial, not argument → threat = story
  • Last no echoes the No… catalogue
  • Plain speech, perfect metre; rebell / hell echoes spell / well
Effect, style & response
  • Triumph… but last word = hell

Structure

Analysis
  • 16 lines, heroic couplets (iambic pentameter)
  • 4 + 6 + 2 + 4: case against → case for → Thus verdict → Therefore advice
  • Connectives This, Tho, Thus, Therefore → a proof
  • Rhyme aabbccdddd eeffgg → triplet ll. 7–9 + near-rhyme prayers
  • No full stop till l. 12 → case in one breath
  • Turns: l. 5 (states), l. 10 (Few), l. 13 (advice)

Context & dates

Analysis
  • Written c. 1646–48, aged 14–16, before her marriage (Aug 1648)
  • Only copy: her own hand, signed "C. Fowler", Orielton papers, NLW
  • Not printed in 1664 or 1667; first printed 1977 / 1986
  • 13 of 16 lines shared with an anonymous 62-line satire ("Madam / I cannot but Congratulate")
  • Husband James Philips: 24 at marriage (ODNB); old claim of 54 discounted
  • Civil Wars: Pembroke besieged 1648; Charles I executed Jan 1649

Law, church, Paul

Analysis
  • Coverture: wife = feme covert → no property, contracts, lawsuits in own name
  • Prayer Book: "obey him, and serve him"; "remedy against sin"
  • 1 Cor 7: "carefulness", "please her husband", "without distraction", "better to marry than to burn"
  • Genre: molestiae nuptiarum (anti-marriage satire), usually men warning men → here a woman warned off husbands
CONNECTIONS

Connections

How this poem pairs with the rest of the set

Comparison hooks

1. Behn, 'Song: Love Armed' (01)

Link: Two seventeenth-century women on love as a false god. Behn's lovers "set him up a Deity"; Philips tells madam to Turn, turn apostate to love's Levity. The vocabulary overlaps: Behn's Love did "Fresh pains… Create" and took "sighs and tears" and "Fears"; Philips's husbands create your fears and childbirth will extort your tears.

Shared technique: Patterned syntax turns complaint into a case (Behn's "From me… From thee…", Philips's No… No… No…), and both arguments turn on "Thus": "Thus thou and I, the God have armed" against Thus are you freed.

Difference: Behn writes from inside desire, after the harm is done; Philips writes from outside, advising escape before it begins. Freedom in Behn belongs to the indifferent beloved ("the Victor is, and free"); in Philips it belongs to the woman who never marries. Behn's song is the form of feeling; Philips's couplets are the form of argument.

2. Blake, 'The Chimney Sweeper' (Songs of Experience) (03)

Link: Both expose suffering hidden behind a cheerful face, and an institution that uses the cheerfulness as its alibi. The sweep: "because I am happy and dance and sing, / They think they have done me no injury". Philips's wives desemble their misfortunes well. Both poems ask the reader to read through the happy surface.

Shared technique: Religious language turned on its users. Blake's parents praise "God and his priest and king, / Who make up a heaven of our misery"; Philips takes Paul's words and the vocabulary of faith (crosses, prayers, apostate) against marriage, and dismisses a folk hell.

Difference: Blake's victim is a child who cannot escape; Philips's addressee is a young woman who still can, and the poem is advice, not lament. Blake's voice is angry; Philips's is cool, witty and strategic.

3. Pope, 'An Essay on Man' (12)

Link: Two arguments about the human condition in heroic couplets, both opening on a maxim ("Know then thyself, presume not God to scan"; A married state affords but little ease) and both using the word state: Pope's man is "Placed on this isthmus of a middle state".

Shared technique: Antithesis held in closed couplets, and the drama of reason against passion. Pope's man is "Chaos of thought and passion, all confused"; Philips orders Suppress wild nature if she dare rebell. Pope later mocked the "needless Alexandrine" that "drags its slow length along"; Philips's line 12 is an alexandrine that drags on purpose, with the husband as its extra foot.

Difference: Pope surveys humanity from above, with balanced paradox and no remedy; Philips addresses one reader and gives a command. His couplets describe a riddle; hers make a case.

4. Shakespeare, Sonnet 18 ('Shall I Compare Thee…?') (14)

Link: Both are short, rhymed pentameter arguments that end in a confident couplet, and both use legal and commercial language: "summer's lease hath all too short a date", "possession of that fair thou ow'st"; marriage affords but little ease. Sonnet 18 also follows the seventeen sonnets in which the speaker urges a young man to marry and have children, and it is the first to drop the call for children and rely on verse alone to outlast time. Philips urges a woman not to marry and counts children's crys among the burdens.

Shared technique: Weather as a figure for what threatens: "Rough winds do shake the darling buds of May" and Blustering husbands. Both poems also personify nature: Shakespeare's "nature's changing course", Philips's wild nature that may rebell.

Difference: Shakespeare's poem praises a beloved and promises permanence ("So long lives this, and this gives life to thee"); Philips's treats love as Levity, light and impermanent, and its only promise is release.

5. Clarke, 'Lament' (07)

Link: Both are catalogue poems built on repeated openings. Clarke's "For the green turtle…" mourns casualties; Philips's No Blustering husbands… No pangs… No children's crys lists harms escaped.

Shared technique: Anaphora with a significant break. Philips's pattern swerves to Few and climaxes on prayers; Clarke's litany ends on "For vengeance, and the ashes of language", where the final item turns abstract.

Difference: Clarke's list grieves for harm done to others and assigns no remedy; Philips's list is persuasion, aimed at one reader's future (your fears, your tears), and ends in a command.

6. Bhatt, 'A Different History' (02)

Link: Both examine customs enforced by sacred language. Bhatt's India makes it "a sin / to be rude to a book"; Philips's world threatens unmarried women with apes in hell. Both ask how people come to love what was imposed on them: Bhatt's "unborn grandchildren / grow to love that strange language"; Philips's wives keep up the face of contentment.

Shared technique: Using the oppressor's own terms. Bhatt asks "Which language / has not been the oppressor's tongue?"; Philips argues against marriage in the language of the Bible and the measure of public reason.

Difference: Bhatt accepts a mixed inheritance with irony and some tenderness; Philips refuses the inherited role outright and dismisses the sanction with There's no such thing.

7. Heaney, 'Follower' (08)

Link: Both concern the role a young person is expected to inherit. Heaney's boy wanted to "grow up and plough", following his father; Philips urges a young woman to refuse the life prepared for her.

Shared technique: A turn late in the poem that changes the relationship between generations: Heaney's father now "keeps stumbling / Behind me"; Philips's speaker suddenly steps forward (be advised by me).

Difference: Heaney's son fails to take up the role and carries guilt about it; Philips's addressee is told to decline the role and feel none, because the role itself is the problem.

An Essay on Man

Alexander Pope · 1733

The opening of Epistle II: forbidden to scan God, man turns to study himself — and finds a creature so evenly divided that the only exact definition is a contradiction, the glory, jest, and riddle of the world.

CONTEXT

Context

The world the poem came out of

The Poet: Alexander Pope (1688–1744)

Pope was born in London on 21 May 1688, the son of a Catholic linen merchant, in the year the "Glorious Revolution" drove out England's last Catholic king. For the rest of his life the law treated people like him as suspects. Catholics could not go to university, vote or hold public office, and a statute forbade them to live within ten miles of London, so around 1700 the family moved to Binfield in Windsor Forest. After a few years at small Catholic schools Pope was largely self-taught. He read his way through Latin, Greek, French and Italian literature without ever entering the institutions that certified learning.

At about twelve he contracted tuberculosis of the spine (Pott's disease). He never grew taller than about four and a half feet, his back was bent, and he lived with constant pain and headaches. Samuel Johnson records that in later life Pope had to be laced each morning into a "bodice made of stiff canvas" before he could hold himself upright. In the Epistle to Dr Arbuthnot (1735) Pope called his existence "this long disease, my life".

He became the dominant poet of his age anyway. After An Essay on Criticism (1711) and The Rape of the Lock (1712–14) came his translations of Homer's Iliad (1715–20) and Odyssey (1725–26, with two collaborators). Sold by subscription, they made him financially independent and paid for the villa at Twickenham (from 1719), with its celebrated garden and grotto. The Dunciad (1728) made him the most feared satirist in England and gave him a standing army of enemies. He died at Twickenham on 30 May 1744. The man who wrote Great lord of all things, but a prey to all was a celebrated outsider in a frail body, though the passage speaks of "man", not of Pope, and should not be read as confession.

An Essay on Man (1733–34)

The Essay is a philosophical poem in four epistles, or verse letters. Pope's own headings give each its subject: the nature and state of man "with respect to the Universe" (I), "with respect to Himself, as an Individual" (II), "with respect to Society" (III) and "with respect to Happiness" (IV). Epistle I appeared in February 1733, Epistle II (which opens with this extract) about April, Epistle III later that year, and Epistle IV in January 1734. Later editions headed the poem "Written in the year 1732". It was planned as the opening book of a much larger system of ethics in verse, which Pope never finished.

Its aim is stated in Epistle I: "But vindicate the ways of God to Man", a deliberate echo of Milton's promise in Paradise Lost to "justifie the wayes of God to men". The poem is a theodicy, an argument that the universe is well designed even though humans, seeing only a part of it, complain of disorder and evil.

The friend addressed is Henry St John, Viscount Bolingbroke (1678–1751), the brilliant Tory minister of Queen Anne's reign, a Jacobite exile for a time, and later Pope's close friend and philosophical mentor. How much Bolingbroke supplied is disputed. Pope's friend Joseph Spence recorded him saying "how much, or rather how wholly he was obliged to Lord Bolingbroke for the thoughts and reasonings in his moral work", and that he had received "seven or eight sheets" from him. Lord Bathurst later told the critic Hugh Blair that Pope had merely put Bolingbroke's prose into verse. When Boswell read Blair's account to Johnson he replied, "Depend upon it, sir, this is too strongly stated."

In "The Design", a short preface first printed when the four epistles were collected in Pope's Works (1735), Pope calls the poem "a general map of man" and says he chose "verse, and even rhyme" for two reasons. Precepts so written "strike the reader more strongly at first, and are more easily retained by him afterwards", and he "could express them more shortly this way than in prose itself". He hoped its merit lay "in steering betwixt the extremes of doctrines seemingly opposite", which is a fair description of what the eighteen lines of this extract do.

Published in Disguise

Pope had spent five years making enemies with The Dunciad, and he expected anything under his name to be savaged. So the Essay came out anonymously, "Printed for J. Wilford", a bookseller not associated with him, although his usual publisher, Lawton Gilliver, had bought the right to print each epistle for £50 an epistle. Johnson records that Pope's name "and that of his friend to whom the work is inscribed, were in the first editions carefully suppressed". The first edition addresses Bolingbroke as "Laelius", after the Roman statesman famous for friendship; later editions read "Awake, my St John!" A note "To the Reader" even claimed that the author would "vie with no man in these epistles, particularly with the noted author of two lately published", meaning Edward Young, whose two verse Epistles to Mr Pope had appeared in 1730.

The ruse worked. The poem, wrote Johnson, quoting Warburton, "was given to every man except him only who could write it". Pope sent advance copies to writers he had offended, "that they might defeat their own enmity by praises which they could not afterwards decently retract". By 1734 he had owned the work.

Pope kept revising. The short preface to Epistle II explains that the epistles were issued separately so that the author "might profit of its judgment on the parts" (the public's judgement). His manuscript began "Learn we ourselves, not God presume to scan". In the first edition line 2 read "The only science of mankind is man", and line 8 read "To deem himself a part of God or beast", so the famous run of three In doubts is a revision. The anthology prints a modernised text of the final version, with spellings such as Placed, reasoning and hurled in full and lighter punctuation than Pope's (he printed "in doubt to act, or rest;"). There is one verbal difference. Line 16 in the anthology reads but a prey to all, where Pope's own text reads "yet a prey to all". The sense is the same: here but means "and yet".

Where the Extract Sits

The eighteen lines are the first paragraph of Epistle II, and they only make full sense from both sides. Epistle I ends by insisting that what looks like disorder is our failure of vision: "All discord, harmony not understood; / All partial evil, universal good: / And, spite of pride, in erring reason's spite, / One truth is clear, Whatever is, is right." It had already told the reader to "Know thy own point", to accept "this due degree / Of blindness, weakness" that heaven allots. The next words of the poem are Know then thyself.

Pope's marginal summary labels the extract exactly: "The business of man not to pry into God, but to study himself. His middle nature…" What follows the extract is a mocking survey of human achievement: "Go, wondrous creature! mount where science guides, / Go, measure earth, weigh air, and state the tides". It ends "Then drop into thyself, and be a fool!" Even Newton, Pope adds, could explain the comets but not "one movement of his mind". Then, at line 53, comes the constructive argument: "Two principles in human nature reign; / Self-love, to urge, and reason, to restrain". The passions are the wind and reason the compass card that shows the course: "On life's vast ocean diversely we sail, / Reason the card, but passion is the gale".

William Warburton, the commentator Pope endorsed, insisted that the dark picture has a positive purpose. Pope gives "this sublime description of man for the very contrary purpose to what sceptics are wont to employ such kind of paintings, namely, not to deter men from the search, but to excite them to the discovery of truth". On lines 11–14 he adds that although man is "abused by himself, he has it still in his own power to disabuse himself". The bleakness is real, but it is the opening move of an argument, not its conclusion.

The Great Chain of Being

Behind a middle state lies the oldest map of the universe in European thought, the Great Chain of Being. Everything that exists, in this picture, is ranked on a single ladder. At the top is God; then the orders of angels (pure spirit); then man; then animals, plants and finally lifeless matter. Every possible rung is filled, and each creature differs only slightly from the next. Man is the one link that is both spirit and matter. He has a rational soul like the angels and a body and appetites like the animals, which is why older writers called him a "middle nature".

Epistle I had drawn the Chain in full: "Vast chain of being! which from God began, / Natures ethereal, human, angel, man, / Beast, bird, fish, insect, what no eye can see, / No glass can reach; from infinite to thee, / From thee to nothing." Its moral is that no link can be moved: "From Nature's chain whatever link you strike, / Tenth or ten thousandth, breaks the chain alike." To wish to be higher than man is therefore to wish creation broken, the "pride" the extract keeps returning to. Epistle I also mocks the proud belief that everything was made for us: asked what the heavens and earth are for, "Pride answers, ''Tis for mine!'" The historian Arthur O. Lovejoy's classic study The Great Chain of Being (1936) made Pope's Essay one of its chief exhibits.

The picture was under new pressure in 1733. Newton (died 1727) had shown that the heavens obey mathematical laws, and Pope had written his epitaph ("God said, Let Newton be! and all was light"). An age that had just learnt to measure the planets could easily believe it might measure God too. The command presume not God to scan is aimed at exactly that confidence. A few lines after the extract Pope imagines angels watching Newton "unfold all Nature's law" and showing him off "as we show an ape".

Sceptics, Stoics and "Know Thyself"

"Know thyself" (gnōthi seauton) was inscribed at the temple of Apollo at Delphi, the most famous oracle of the ancient world. Socrates made it the first task of philosophy. In Plato's Phaedrus he refuses to waste time explaining myths: "I must first know myself, as the Delphian inscription says." He asks whether he is "a monster more complicated and swollen with passion than the serpent Typho, or a creature of a gentler and simpler sort, to whom Nature has given a diviner and lowlier destiny". That is the shape of Pope's lines 1–2 and 8 two thousand years earlier. The French moralist Pierre Charron (Of Wisdom, 1601) had put line 2 in prose: "The true science and true study of man is man." So had Pascal, in the English translation Pope's editors cite: "The study of man is the proper employment and exercise of mankind."

Sceptics. Followers of Pyrrho of Elis (c. 360–270 BC) held that nothing can be known for certain. The wise therefore suspend judgement on everything and find peace in not deciding. Montaigne revived the attitude in the 1500s ("What do I know?").

Stoics. Followers of Zeno, who taught in the Painted Porch (Stoa) at Athens around 300 BC, and later of Epictetus, Seneca and Marcus Aurelius, held that virtue is the only good. The wise man, ruled entirely by reason, is unmoved by pain, passion or fortune and needs nothing outside himself. Christian moralists called this self-sufficiency pride. Pope's own verdict comes later in Epistle II: "In lazy apathy let stoics boast / Their virtue fixed; 'tis fixed as in a frost … But strength of mind is exercise, not rest."

Lines 5–6 compress a diagnosis from Pascal. The philosophers, he argued, saw only half of man. Those who saw his greatness fell into pride, and those who saw his weakness into despair or idleness; "they could not escape either pride or sloth" (ils n'ont pu fuir ou l'orgueil ou la paresse). His English translation also supplied line 5's thought: "We have an idea of truth, not to be effaced by all the wiles of the sceptic." Pascal's cure is Christian revelation. Pope's man is simply barred from both errors because he is genuinely both things.

Sources and Reception

Pope's editors, from Joseph Warton in the eighteenth century to Whitwell Elwin in 1871, traced line after line of the extract to Blaise Pascal's Pensées. Pope could read them in French or in Basil Kennett's English version (second edition, 1727). There man is "a chimæra… What a confused chaos! What a subject of contradiction!", "A professed judge of all things, and yet a feeble worm of the earth; the great depositary and guardian of truth, and yet a mere huddle of uncertainty; the glory and the scandal of the universe." Pascal's man even "hangs": "He will find himself hanging, in the material scale, between the two vast abysses of infinite and nothing." The difference matters as much as the borrowing. Pascal piles up the contradictions to drive the reader to God: "Know then, proud man, what a paradox you are to yourself… Listen to God" (Connaissez donc, superbe, quel paradoxe vous êtes à vous-même… Écoutez Dieu). Pope keeps the first half of that and forbids the second, since his first line tells man not to scan God. Elwin called the passage "a partial and distorted copy from Pascal", who "overcharged the evil to exalt the remedy", whereas "Pope had not any remedy to suggest."

Montaigne is in the background too. He wrote that "Presumption is our natural and original disease", and imagined the Delphic god telling man he is "the investigator without knowledge, the magistrate without jurisdiction, and, after all, the fool of the farce". Pope declared in 1733 that he loved "to pour out all myself, as plain / As downright Shippen, or as old Montaigne".

The poem was an international success and an international scandal. The Swiss professor Jean-Pierre de Crousaz, reading it in French translations, attacked it in 1737–38 as fatalistic "natural religion" that had no need of revelation. (Johnson translated one of his attacks, and remarked that he could not determine whether anyone had discovered the true meaning of in doubt to act or rest.) William Warburton answered Crousaz in a series of letters from late 1738. Pope wrote to thank him: "you have made my system as clear as I ought to have done, and could not." Voltaire called it "the most beautiful, the most useful, the most sublime didactic poem that has ever been written in any language". After the Lisbon earthquake of 1755 he attacked the optimism of "all is well" (tout est bien) in his poem on the disaster and in Candide (1759). Rousseau defended the Essay to him in 1756, and Kant quoted it in his Universal Natural History (1755). Johnson (Life of Pope, 1781) was severe: "Never was penury of knowledge and vulgarity of sentiment so happily disguised. The reader feels his mind full, though he learns nothing."

THE POEM

The Poem

Line by line, with the analysis alongside

An Essay on Man
TAn Essay on Man
1Know then thyself, presume not God to scan;
2The proper study of mankind is man.
3Placed on this isthmus of a middle state,
4A being darkly wise, and rudely great:
5With too much knowledge for the sceptic side,
6With too much weakness for the stoic’s pride,
7He hangs between; in doubt to act or rest,
8In doubt to deem himself a god or beast,
9In doubt his mind or body to prefer,
10Born but to die, and reasoning but to err;
11Alike in ignorance, his reason such,
12Whether he thinks too little or too much:
13Chaos of thought and passion, all confused;
14Still by himself abused or disabused;
15Created half to rise and half to fall,
16Great lord of all things, but a prey to all;
17Sole judge of truth, in endless error hurled:
18The glory, jest, and riddle of the world!

Lines with a marker have analysis — click one, or just scroll.

Title
An Essay on Man
Language & devices
  • Extract marker: the anthology heads the passage from An Essay on Man. "From" matters: these are the first eighteen lines of Epistle II of a four-epistle poem, a unit Pope's own marginal summary treats as one step ("The business of man not to pry into God, but to study himself. His middle nature…").
  • Genre word: "Essay" comes from French essai, "attempt, trial" (Montaigne's word for his explorations of himself). Pope had used it before (An Essay on Criticism, 1711), and it recalls Locke's Essay Concerning Human Understanding (1690), the period's great book on the limits of the mind.
  • Generic noun: "Man" means the human species, a category in the singular, the way a naturalist might write "on the horse". "An" is modest: one essay, an attempt.
  • Epistle: Epistle II first appeared, anonymously, about April 1733 as An Essay on Man. In Epistles to a Friend. A verse letter explains the second person of line 1.
Meaning & effect

The title promises a treatise, a general account of what a human being is. The extract shows that the subject resists exactly that kind of definition: an "essay", a trial, turns out to be the right word for an inquiry that ends on riddle. The word "from" also tells the reader to take these lines as a step in an argument. The then of line 1 points back to Epistle I, so the passage opens mid-case, as a conclusion drawn from what came before and the start of what comes next.

Line 1
Know then thyself, presume not God to scan;
Language & devices
  • Imperatives, one positive and one negative: Know and presume not, balanced across the Caesura after thyself.
  • Allusion: Know… thyself is the Delphic maxim gnōthi seauton, inscribed at Apollo's temple at Delphi and adopted by Socrates as the first business of philosophy.
  • Connective then means "therefore". It draws the conclusion of Epistle I, which ended "Whatever is, is right".
  • Chiasmus: Know (verb), thyself (object) | God (object), scan (verb). The two objects meet at the caesura; the two verbs of knowing stand at the ends.
  • Diction: presume means to dare beyond one's right. scan means to examine minutely or judge by a standard. It is also the word for measuring the metre of verse, and the line scans perfectly. Its Latin root, scandere, means "to climb".
  • Trochaic inversion: Know seizes the first stress, so the command lands before the metre settles.
  • Revision: Pope's manuscript read "Learn we ourselves, not God presume to scan", a polite first-person plural. The final line turns it into a direct command in the Delphic formula.
  • Source: Pascal had written "Know then, proud man, what a paradox you are to yourself" (Connaissez donc, superbe, quel paradoxe vous êtes à vous-même), going on to "Listen to God". Pope keeps the self-knowledge and forbids the God-scanning.
Meaning & effect

The whole passage starts on a hinge. Left of the comma is the inquiry Pope permits; right of it is the inquiry he forbids, so a door opens and a door shuts in one line. Pope does not deny that God exists or is good. He forbids man to scan him, to measure and judge God's ways like a line of verse, because that is presumption, the overreaching the whole of Epistle I has just condemned. then makes the command sound logical rather than arbitrary: the universe is beyond our sight, so turn the instrument round and look at the one thing in range. The irony the next seventeen lines deliver is that the permitted object will prove almost as hard to scan as the forbidden one.

Line 2
The proper study of mankind is man.
Language & devices
  • Aphorism: a complete, quotable proposition in ten syllables, ending in the passage's only full stop.
  • Polyptoton: mankind… man. The same root narrows from the whole species to the single specimen, and the student and the thing studied are the same creature.
  • Rhyme scan / man: the forbidden activity is paired with the permitted object.
  • Diction: proper means fitting, suited to our rank, and (Latin proprius) "one's own".
  • Syntax: an eight-syllable subject holds back its predicate to the last two syllables, is man. No comma breaks the line, which runs in one breath and snaps shut on the definition.
  • Revision: the first edition (1733) read "The only science of mankind is man". Pope's change turns an exclusive "science" (in its old sense, any body of knowledge) into a "proper study".
  • Source: Charron (1601): "The true science and true study of man is man"; Pascal, in the English Pope's editors cite: "The study of man is the proper employment and exercise of mankind."
Meaning & effect

Line 2 gives the reason for line 1's redirection: inquiry should begin where it belongs. Its shape (X is man) sounds final and self-evident, and that confidence is the set-up for the joke the passage then plays: the "study" is announced as a programme, and the next sixteen lines report that its subject is a mass of contradictions. The polyptoton hides a trap. If mankind studies man, the investigator is the specimen, and the study can never get outside its object. proper also concedes a limit: not the highest study, but the one fitted to our station. The revision from "only Science" makes that humility exact.

Line 3
Placed on this isthmus of a middle state,
Language & devices
  • Past participle Placed: passive and agentless, though the agent is obviously God. Its stressed first syllable inverts the opening foot.
  • Metaphor isthmus: a narrow neck of land between two seas, joining two larger land masses.
  • Demonstrative this, as if pointing at the ground under our feet.
  • middle state: man's rank in the Great Chain of Being, the only creature that is both spirit (shared with angels) and body (shared with animals). state means condition and also rank.
  • Literary source: Abraham Cowley's ode 'Life and Fame' had called life a 'Vain, weak-built isthmus' rising 'betwixt two eternities' (traced by Joseph Warton).
  • Suspended syntax: the sentence starting here does not reach its main verb, hangs, until line 7.
Meaning & effect

Placed carries the theological premise quietly. Man did not choose his position, he was put there, so complaining about it (the error Epistle I attacked) misunderstands the arrangement. The isthmus is exact on several levels at once. It joins: man is where the spiritual and material halves of creation touch. It separates: there is sea on either side. It is narrow and exposed: a place to stand precariously between expanses you cannot see across. Cowley's isthmus stood between two eternities of time; Pope moves it into the order of being, so the danger becomes one of rank rather than mortality. The grammar does what the image says: we are Placed in mid-sentence and kept waiting four lines for the subject.

Line 4
A being darkly wise, and rudely great:
Language & devices
  • Two Oxymorons balanced across the Caesura after wise: darkly wise / rudely great.
  • Parallelism: adverb plus adjective, twice.
  • darkly means dimly, obscurely, as in poor light (cf. 1 Corinthians 13:12, "through a glass, darkly"), not "sinisterly".
  • rudely means roughly, crudely, unfinished (Latin rudis, raw, unworked), not "impolitely".
  • Abstract noun A being: the vocabulary of the Chain ("Vast chain of being!" in Epistle I), classifying man as one item in creation's inventory.
  • Colon: opens onto the explanation in lines 5–6.
Meaning & effect

Pope grants man his two great claims, wisdom and greatness, and qualifies each in the same breath: wise, but in the dark; great, but rough-hewn. Nothing is denied and everything is diminished. This is the passage's method in miniature, concession followed by limit, and the balanced halves make the qualification sound like a measurement rather than an insult. A being holds the subject at arm's length. The reader told in line 1 to know thyself is now shown a specimen in a catalogue, which is what self-study turns out to require.

Lines 5–6
With too much knowledge for the sceptic side, / With too much weakness for the stoic’s pride,
Language & devices
  • Anaphora With too much… / With too much and exact Syntactic parallelism across the couplet.
  • Antithesis: knowledge / weakness; sceptic / stoic.
  • sceptic: the ancient Sceptics (Pyrrho and his followers) held that nothing can be known for certain, so the wise suspend judgement on everything and find peace in not deciding. side means a party in a dispute.
  • stoic: the Stoics (Zeno, Epictetus, Seneca) held that the wise man, ruled by reason alone, is unmoved by pain, passion or fortune and needs nothing outside himself. pride names what Christian critics saw in that claim.
  • Rhyme side / pride: both words name stances, not doctrines.
  • Excess: both disqualifications come from "too much", not too little.
  • Source: Pascal, in the 1727 English: "We have an idea of truth, not to be effaced by all the wiles of the sceptic."
Meaning & effect

The couplet explains darkly wise, and rudely great by closing the two great ancient escape routes from the human condition. Man cannot be a consistent sceptic, because he knows too much to doubt everything (he cannot seriously doubt that he exists, or that fire burns). He cannot be a stoic either, because he is too weak to rise above pain, appetite and grief. The symmetry is the argument. The same middle position that gives him too much knowledge for one school gives him too much weakness for the other, so he fails both tests by being too much of two things at once. The perfectly matched lines make the double exclusion feel like proof. Calling stoicism pride also ties it to the presumption warned against in line 1.

Line 7
He hangs between; in doubt to act or rest,
Language & devices
  • Main clause at last: subject He and verb hangs arrive four lines after Placed.
  • Verb hangs: suspended, without footing. It is also what the beam of a pair of scales does.
  • Caesura: the semicolon after between is the heaviest mid-line pause in the passage.
  • Anaphora begins: in doubt, the first of three.
  • Antithesis: act or rest.
  • Pronoun shift: thyself (line 1) has become He.
  • Source: Pascal's man "will find himself hanging, in the material scale, between the two vast abysses of infinite and nothing" (1727 English).
Meaning & effect

After four lines of description the sentence finally lets man do something, and what he does is hang. hangs is the least active verb Pope could have chosen, and the semicolon leaves between dangling in mid-line, so the reader is held in the pause the word describes. between takes no object, because the objects are everything already named: wisdom and darkness, greatness and roughness, scepticism and stoicism. The first doubt is the most practical: whether to do something or nothing. The ordinary paralysis of a day sits underneath the grander doubts that follow. act or rest is also the hardest phrase in the passage to pin down. Johnson doubted whether anyone had found its true meaning; Warburton heard in rest the passive calm of the Stoics, which Pope rejects later in the epistle ("strength of mind is exercise, not rest"). Notice too that the reader commanded to know thyself is now watching him, as if self-knowledge can only proceed by treating oneself as a third person.

Lines 8–9
In doubt to deem himself a god or beast, / In doubt his mind or body to prefer,
Language & devices
  • Anaphora: In doubt… In doubt now takes the line openings. With line 7 it forms a Tricolon of doubts: act/rest, god/beast, mind/body.
  • Antithesis: god or beast; mind or body.
  • deem means judge or consider. Reflexive himself: the doubt is about self-assessment.
  • Allusion: Aristotle's Politics says a man who needs no community is no part of a city, being either "a beast or a god". Pascal: "Man is neither angel nor brute".
  • Inversion (hyperbaton): his mind or body to prefer puts the object before the verb.
  • Revision: the first edition read "To deem himself a part of God or beast". Line 8's In doubt, the middle one of the three, was added later, and "a part of God" (which can sound as if man were a fragment of the divine) became the plainer a god.
  • Source: Pascal, in the 1727 English: "Shall he be equal to God, or shall he not be superior to the beasts?"
Meaning & effect

The doubts widen and then turn inward. Line 8 is cosmic: man cannot tell which end of the Chain he belongs to, the half that shares in the divine (reason, soul) or the half that shares with animals (appetite, mortality). Warburton read it as a doubt whether the soul is mortal or immortal. The reflexive himself makes it a crisis of self-judgement, since he is the one doing the deeming and he cannot decide. Line 9 brings the question inside his own skin: which part of himself should he value? The inverted word order makes the line stumble, with the verb, prefer, postponed to the end as though the choice keeps being put off. The three doubts descend from what to do, to what to be, to what to value in oneself: from the world, to the cosmos, to the self.

Line 10
Born but to die, and reasoning but to err;
Language & devices
  • Parallelism across the Caesura: participle, but to, infinitive, twice.
  • but means only, merely here, not "however".
  • Antithesis: Born / die; reasoning / err.
  • Monosyllables and Trochaic inversion: Born but to die opens on a heavy stress.
  • Metre: the anthology's reasoning must be said as two syllables (Pope printed reas'ning) for the line to scan as pentameter.
Meaning & effect

Line 10 answers line 9's doubt by disposing of both options: the body exists to die, the mind exists to err. but to makes the end sound like the purpose. It is not merely that we die and make mistakes, but that this is what birth and reason are for. This is the bleakest formulation in the passage, and its neatness is half its force: two identical halves, a life's sentence in ten syllables. The "only" is meant to sting rather than to be literal. Warburton, the commentator Pope endorsed, glossed it as "though we reason to err, yet we comprehend some few truths". The line states the weakness at full strength because the passage is building a case against pride, not pronouncing a final sentence. A Christian reader may object to what it leaves out. Elwin protested that man "is not born only to die, but death has the present life on one side of it, and immortality on the other".

Lines 11–12
Alike in ignorance, his reason such, / Whether he thinks too little or too much:
Language & devices
  • Ellipsis: his reason such means "his reason [is] such [that he is] alike in ignorance". The verb is missing.
  • Inversion: the result, Alike in ignorance, comes before its cause.
  • Antithesis: too little or too much.
  • Repetition: too much returns from lines 5–6.
  • Rhyme such / much: the flattest pair in the passage, two vague words of quantity.
  • Colon: opens the final catalogue.
  • Source: Pascal, in the 1727 English: "If we think too little of a thing or too much, our head turns giddy, and we are at a loss to find out our way to truth."
Meaning & effect

Unpacked, the couplet says that man's reason is so made that he ends equally ignorant whether he thinks too little or too much. Warburton's gloss: reason's sphere is so narrow that "the too immoderate use of it is attended with the same ignorance that proceeds from the not using it at all". This goes further than line 10. It is not just that reason errs, but that more thought is no cure: there is no right dose. The person who thinks too little stays ignorant through idleness, the person who thinks too much through over-subtle speculation, and they finish level. The dull rhyme lands like a shrug, measurement failing in vague quantities. The colon then opens six lines that no longer argue at all; they simply list.

Line 13
Chaos of thought and passion, all confused;
Language & devices
  • Apposition: from here to the end there is no main verb. Man is defined by noun phrases set beside He.
  • Trochaic inversion: Chaos opens on a stress.
  • Antithesis: thought and passion, reason and feeling.
  • confused, from Latin confundere, "pour together": mixed so that the parts cannot be separated.
  • Allusion: Chaos is the formless state before creation (the "without form, and void" of Genesis; Milton's Chaos). Pope's source in Pascal reads "What a confused chaos!" in the 1727 English translation.
Meaning & effect

The noun is enormous. In a poem about an ordered creation, man alone is called Chaos, the condition of matter before God sorted it. Pope then pins the chaos to a precise mixture: thought and passion poured together so that neither works alone. This is exactly the problem Epistle II goes on to tackle. Within forty lines Pope announces "Two principles in human nature reign; / Self-love, to urge, and reason, to restrain", so the chaos is the disorder the rest of the epistle sets out to arrange. Read in isolation the line sounds like despair; in its place it is a diagnosis.

Line 14
Still by himself abused or disabused;
Language & devices
  • Still means always, continually, not "nevertheless".
  • Archaic sense: abused means deceived, misled (the period's usual sense); disabused means undeceived, freed from a false belief.
  • Polyptoton and internal Rhyme: abused / disabused, one root with and without its negating prefix, both chiming with confused.
  • Reflexive by himself: deceiver and deceived are the same person.
  • Passive voice; this is the last pronoun of the passage.
  • Metre: or DIS-a-BUSED puts a beat on the prefix, so the metre stresses the very syllable that reverses the meaning.
Meaning & effect

Glossed correctly, the line describes an endless cycle: man fools himself, catches himself out, then fools himself again. No outside villain is needed. The same mind does the deceiving and the undeceiving, so there is no stable point from which he simply sees clearly. The near-identical words make the point by sound: abused and disabused differ only by a prefix, as if error and correction were one thing wearing opposite signs. It is also the last time the passage gives man a pronoun. After himself he becomes a list of titles.

Line 15
Created half to rise and half to fall,
Language & devices
  • Past participle Created: a maker is implied again (compare Placed, line 3).
  • Parallelism and Antithesis: half to rise and half to fall, balanced like a fraction across the unpunctuated caesura.
  • Biblical resonance: fall recalls the Fall of Genesis 3; rise recalls spiritual ascent and resurrection.
  • Metre: perfectly regular iambic pentameter, matching the line's sense of a fixed law.
Meaning & effect

The Chain is restated as arithmetic. Man is not sometimes rising and sometimes falling; he is built from both tendencies in equal measure. Created does two things. It removes blame, since this is the design, not a fault that crept in, and it removes any hope of escape, since you cannot climb out of your own specification. In a Christian poem fall cannot be innocent: it carries Adam's Fall, and rise answers it with salvation. The even halves make the doubleness sound like a law of nature.

Line 16
Great lord of all things, but a prey to all;
Language & devices
  • Antithesis: lord / prey.
  • Parallelism (not chiasmus): lord of all things / prey to all, noun + preposition + all in each half.
  • Balanced half-lines: the only line split exactly in the middle, five syllables either side of the comma.
  • Repetition: all twice, rhyming back to fall.
  • Conjunction but means "and yet": it reverses the first half without cancelling it. Unlike the two buts of line 10, it does not mean "only". (Pope's own text reads "yet"; the anthology prints but.)
  • Biblical diction: lord of all things recalls man's dominion over creation (Genesis 1:28; Psalm 8, "thou hast put all things under his feet").
  • Metaphor prey: hunting vocabulary, man as quarry.
  • Rhythm: a heavy first half, Great lord of all things, with up to four stresses in five syllables, against a light, quick second half, but a prey to all.
Meaning & effect

Man's relation to the world runs in two directions at once: he rules everything, and anything can destroy him, whether disease, weather, animals, accident or his own passions. The doubled all makes the line airtight, because the same totality is both his kingdom and his predator and there is no safe remainder. prey drops him back among the animals, the hunted rather than the hunter, which answers line 8's god or beast with both at once. The exact central caesura makes the line a perfect balance, and the rhythm tips it: the title is weighty, the fall quick and light. The lordship is real, and it is no protection.

Line 17
Sole judge of truth, in endless error hurled:
Language & devices
  • Antithesis: judge of truth / endless error.
  • Chiasmus: judge, truth | error, hurled. The opposed domains, truth and error, meet at the caesura; the outer words contrast a seated judge with a body flung through space.
  • Sole: the only one, with no higher court to appeal to.
  • Passive participle hurled: violent and involuntary. It is Milton's verb for Satan's fall ("Hurld headlong flaming from th' Ethereal Skie").
  • Assonance and Alliteration: endless error. error also brings back line 10's rhyme-word, err.
  • Colon: hands the verdict to line 18.
  • Source: Pascal, in the 1727 English: "the great depositary and guardian of truth, and yet a mere huddle of uncertainty".
Meaning & effect

Man is the only judge of truth available. Having been forbidden to scan God, he has nobody else to ask, and this sole judge is being flung endlessly through error. Judging is an act of stillness and authority; being hurled is helpless motion. The two halves cannot both hold, so the line pictures a judge whose bench is falling. endless removes the hope that error might simply run out, and the colon makes the next line a sentence passed on the judge himself.

Line 18
The glory, jest, and riddle of the world!
Language & devices
  • Tricolon: three nouns after fifteen lines of pairs.
  • glory means splendour, honour (Psalm 8: man "crowned… with glory and honour"); jest means a joke, a laughing-stock; riddle means a puzzle that will not come out.
  • Caesura: two commas, the only line with two marked pauses. They fall after the third and fourth syllables, so jest stands alone between them, the only word in the passage isolated by punctuation on both sides.
  • Exclamation: the passage's only exclamation mark ends the sentence that began at line 3.
  • Rhyme hurled / world: the last word is world, not "man".
  • Source: Pascal's Pensées call man "gloire et rebut de l'univers" (glory and refuse of the universe), in the 1727 English "the glory and the scandal of the universe".
Meaning & effect

The verdict refuses to be a verdict. After fifteen lines of balanced pairs, Pope breaks his own pattern with three terms instead of two, as if man cannot even be summed up as a pair. The order rises, drops and suspends: glory (what we may be proud of), jest (what we may be laughed at for), riddle (what cannot be settled either way). The comparison with Pascal shows the tone. Pascal's man is the glory and the refuse of the universe, a believer's disgust; Pope swaps refuse for jest, the satirist's word, and adds riddle, so the ending is comic and baffled rather than revolted. The exclamation mark holds wonder and exasperation together. The final word places the creature we were told to study inside the larger spectacle of creation, and a riddle, unlike a sentence, invites another attempt. The very next line of the poem is "Go, wondrous creature!"

THE WHOLE POEM

The Whole Poem

Stepping back: what the poem is doing, first line to last

The passage obeys its own first line. Forbidden to scan God, it scans man, with every measuring instrument the heroic couplet possesses: balance, antithesis, the half-line set against the half-line. The reading it gets is a contradiction. Pope's achievement is to make that failure exact. The more precisely man is measured, the more clearly he refuses to come out as a single quantity. So the extract is neither a lament for human weakness nor a hymn to human greatness. It demonstrates that the "proper study" begins with the student discovering how much of himself he cannot see.

The hinge (lines 1–2)

Know then thyself, presume not God to scan opens a door and shuts one in the same ten syllables. Left of the comma is the Delphic command that began Greek philosophy; right of it is a prohibition. then means "therefore": Epistle I has just argued that the universe looks disordered only because we see a fragment of it, so the sensible conclusion is to turn the instrument round. presume names the sin, overreaching, and scan names the activity: to examine minutely, and also to measure verse. The line forbids scanning and scans perfectly. Line 2 then states the programme in the passage's only sentence of untroubled confidence: The proper study of mankind is man. It has no internal pause and moves straight to its last word. It sounds like the opening of a research project. Everything after it is the research report, and the report is unsettling.

Placing the specimen (lines 3–6)

The second sentence begins with Placed, a participle with no agent named. Someone put man here, and complaining about the placing would repeat the presumption of line 1. this isthmus of a middle state locates him on the Great Chain of Being, the ranked ladder of creation, at the one rung that is both spirit and matter. An isthmus is exact. It joins two land masses, it separates two seas, and it is narrow enough to be dangerous. Then Pope grants man his two great claims and qualifies each as he grants it: darkly wise, and rudely great, wise but in poor light, great but roughly made. Lines 5–6 close antiquity's two famous escape routes. Man has too much knowledge to be a true sceptic who doubts everything, and too much weakness for the Stoic's pride in being untouched by pain. Notice that both disqualifications come from excess. He is not too little for either philosophy; he is too much of two things at once.

The subject arrives, and hangs (lines 7–12)

After four lines of description the subject finally appears, and his one action is hangs. The semicolon after between leaves the word dangling in mid-line, and the grammar mirrors the image: He is suspended between four lines of description before him and eleven after. Three doubts follow, each widening the gap. What to do: to act or rest. What to be: a god or beast. What to value in himself: his mind or body. Then line 10 removes the grounds for choosing: Born but to die, and reasoning but to err. Body and mind are each reduced to their failure, and but to makes the failure sound like the purpose. Lines 11–12 go further still. Thinking more is no cure: man is Alike in ignorance whether he thinks too little or too much. The flattest rhyme in the passage, such/much, lands where reason runs out.

The verbs go (lines 13–17)

From line 13 there is no main verb. Man is no longer allowed to do anything; he is renamed, six times. Chaos of thought and passion, all confused puts him back in the state of matter before Creation sorted it. Still by himself abused or disabused describes an endless cycle of self-deception (in 1733 abused meant "deceived") and self-correction, with no outside villain. Created half to rise and half to fall makes the doubleness part of the design. Then the passage awards him two titles and snatches each back within the line. He is Great lord of all things, but a prey to all, a balance split exactly down the middle. He is Sole judge of truth, in endless error hurled, a judge whose bench is falling. The participles are passive throughout (Placed, Born, Created, hurled), so even the grammar treats him as something acted upon.

The verdict that will not balance (line 18)

After fifteen lines of pairs, the last line gives three terms: The glory, jest, and riddle of the world! The form breaks its own habit, as if man cannot be summed up even as a contradiction between two things. The order rises, drops and suspends. glory is what we may be proud of, jest what we may be laughed at for, and riddle what neither pride nor laughter settles. Pope's source, Pascal, had called man the "glory and refuse" of the universe, a believer's disgust designed to drive the reader to God. Pope keeps the glory, replaces refuse with the satirist's word jest, and adds riddle. The exclamation mark holds wonder and exasperation together, and the last word is not "man" but world. The student told to study himself ends by seeing himself as one strange item in a spectacle he cannot see whole.

The strongest objection

Pope's critics have put the case against the passage in two forms. Johnson thought the philosophy was common sense in fine clothes: "Never was penury of knowledge and vulgarity of sentiment so happily disguised. The reader feels his mind full, though he learns nothing." Whitwell Elwin, editing Pope in 1871, made the sharper charge. The passage is "a partial and distorted copy from Pascal", and Pascal "overcharged the evil to exalt the remedy", the Christian gospel, whereas "Pope had not any remedy to suggest." On this view the extract is either despair without hope or rhetoric without content: Pascal's indictment of man with Pascal's cure removed.

The answer

The objection misreads the extract's job. First, it is the opening of an argument, not its end. Pope's marginal summary calls it "His middle nature", and thirty-five lines later he begins the constructive case: "Two principles in human nature reign; / Self-love, to urge, and reason, to restrain". Warburton, whom Pope endorsed, saw the purpose: the dark description is offered "not to deter men from the search, but to excite them to the discovery of truth". Second, the extract does contain a remedy, and it sits in line 1. Pope substitutes humility for grace. To know that you cannot scan God, and that your own reason misleads you, is the self-knowledge the Delphic command asked for. Third, the tone is not despairing. jest and riddle are comic, puzzled words, and the very next line of the poem is "Go, wondrous creature!" A riddle, unlike a sentence of condemnation, invites another attempt.

As for Johnson, the ideas may be old, but the poem does not merely state them; it acts them out. The subject that hangs between its modifiers, the verbs that vanish, the antitheses that speed up to one per line, the exact central split of Great lord of all things, but a prey to all, the pattern of pairs broken by the last line: these are not decoration on the argument. They are the argument, carried out on the reader's ear. The study of man is "proper" because it is the one study whose failure teaches you something true, namely what kind of creature is doing the studying.

FORM & STRUCTURE

Form & Structure

How the poem is built, and why it matters

Form & genre

Eighteen lines, nine heroic couplets, forming the first verse paragraph of Epistle II of a philosophical poem in verse letters. The genre is didactic (teaching) verse: a public voice, general nouns, no "I". It argues; it does not confide.

Metre

Iambic pentameter: ten syllables, five beats, the rising pattern da-DUM. It is regular enough that every departure is audible. Lines 1, 3, 10, 12, 13 and 14 open on a stressed syllable, and reasoning must be said as two syllables (Pope printed "reas'ning").

Rhyme

Nine rhyming couplets, AA BB CC and so on: scan/man, state/great, side/pride, rest/beast, prefer/err, such/much, confused/disabused, fall/all, hurled/world. All are masculine (the rhyme falls on a stressed final syllable). Only rest/beast is imperfect to a modern ear.

Syntax

Two sentences. Lines 1–2 hold a command and its reason, ending in the passage's only full stop. Lines 3–18 are a single sixteen-line sentence ending in its only exclamation mark, and its one main clause is He hangs between (line 7).

Caesura

Nine lines have a punctuated mid-line pause (1, 4, 7, 10, 11, 13, 16, 17, and line 18, which has two). The other nine either pivot on an unpunctuated or or and, or run whole. Every line ends on a punctuation mark, so nothing is strictly enjambed.

The heroic couplet: a form built for weighing

A heroic couplet is a pair of rhyming iambic pentameter lines. It is "closed" when the sense and the syntax finish with the rhyme, so that each couplet lands like a small, complete proposition. Dryden made it the standard form for serious English argument and Pope perfected it. The form offers balance at two levels. Line answers line across the rhyme, and inside each line the caesura (a pause, usually marked by punctuation) divides the ten syllables into two halves that can be set against each other. A writer can therefore weigh this against that twice over, in the couplet and in the half-line.

Pope said in "The Design" that he chose "verse, and even rhyme" because precepts so written "strike the reader more strongly at first, and are more easily retained by him afterwards". Line 2 proves the point, since it is one of the most quoted lines in English. The irony of the extract is that a machine designed to weigh and settle is turned on a creature who will not settle. Couplet after couplet clicks shut on a judgement, and each judgement is that no judgement holds. The form's confidence and the content's uncertainty pull against each other, and that tension is the passage's main effect.

Four movements

  1. Lines 1–2: the command and its reason. The only couplet that is a complete sentence. It is the one moment of settled statement, sealed by the full stop.
  2. Lines 3–6: placement and description. The second sentence begins, but its subject does not arrive. In turn we get a participle (Placed…), a noun phrase (A being…) and two parallel phrases (With too much…), all describing a man who has not yet been named.
  3. Lines 7–12: the main clause and the doubts. He hangs between at last; then the three In doubt phrases; then reason's double failure in lines 10–12, closed by a colon.
  4. Lines 13–18: the catalogue. Six lines with no main verb, one contradiction per line, ending in the three-part verdict of line 18.

The movement runs from instruction to description to pure paradox, and the imperative of line 1 never returns. Pope commands once, then spends sixteen lines showing why the command is so hard to obey.

Metre: the key lines scanned

Capitals mark stressed syllables, · marks the division between feet, and ‖ marks the caesura.

Line Scansion What the variation does
1 KNOW then · thy SELF, ‖ pre SUME · not GOD · to SCAN Inverted (trochaic) first foot: the command lands before the metre settles, then four regular iambs restore order at once.
2 the PROP · er STUD · y OF · man KIND · is MAN Fully regular, with only a light beat on of and no punctuated pause. The line runs in one breath to man: certainty sounds seamless.
3 PLACED on · this IS · thmus OF · a MID · dle STATE The stress falls on the passive Placed, on what was done to him rather than anything he does.
7 he HANGS · be TWEEN; ‖ in DOUBT · to ACT · or REST The feet are regular, but the heaviest pause in the passage falls after the fourth syllable. The line hangs where it says hangs between.
10 BORN but · to DIE, ‖ and REAS · 'ning BUT · to ERR Inverted opening on Born, with reasoning squeezed to two syllables. The halves are built alike, so the second blow repeats the first.
13 CHA os · of THOUGHT · and PAS · sion, ‖ ALL · con FUSED Inverted opening on Chaos. A late caesura, after the seventh syllable, leaves all confused as a short, sagging tail.
14 STILL by · him SELF · a BUSED · or DIS · a BUSED The beat lands on dis, the syllable that reverses the meaning.
16 GREAT LORD of ALL THINGS, ‖ but a PREY to ALL The only exact 5 ‖ 5 split. Up to four strong syllables are crowded into the first half, and two quick light ones (but a) follow the pause: the title is heavy, the fall fast.
18 the GLO · ry, ‖ JEST, ‖ and RID · dle OF · the WORLD Regular feet, but pauses after the third and fourth syllables isolate jest. Then comes an unbroken run of six syllables to world.

Rhyme, couplet by couplet

  • scan / man (aa): the forbidden act is rhymed with the permitted object. The first rhyme already contains the whole programme.
  • state / great (bb): position against claim. great is qualified by rudely before the rhyme lands.
  • side / pride (cc): both rhyme-words name stances (a party in a dispute; a vice), not doctrines.
  • rest / beast (dd): the one rhyme that does not quite close to a modern ear, and it falls on the doubting couplet. Whether the vowels were closer in 1733 is uncertain.
  • prefer / err (ee): the choice and the mistake. Line 9's preference is answered by line 10's error.
  • such / much (ff): the flattest pair in the passage, two vague words of quantity, placed where reason runs out.
  • confused / disabused (gg): line 14 also contains abused, so three -used words fall within two lines. abused and disabused are one word with and without its negating prefix: the rhyme pattern itself goes round in a circle.
  • fall / all (hh): the Fall and the totality. all has already sounded inside line 16, so the line rhymes with itself.
  • hurled / world (ii): violent, helpless motion joined to the whole of creation.

The rhyme-words trace the argument. The passage opens by pairing scan with man, examining a creature, and closes by pairing hurled with world, that creature flung across the universe he was meant to study.

Syntax: where the subject is, and what it does

The grammatical subject of the long second sentence is a single word, He, and it does not appear until line 7. Before it come four lines of description (3–6); after it come eleven lines of phrases that rename or describe it (7–18). The subject is literally suspended between its own modifiers, so the grammar does what the main verb says: He hangs between.

Count the finite verbs (verbs with a subject and a tense). There are only five in eighteen lines: Know and presume (1, commands), is (2), hangs (7) and thinks (12). Man is the subject of just two of them, and thinks sits inside a subordinate Whether… clause. Line 11 has lost even its verb: his reason such means "his reason [being] such [that]…", a compressed construction called an ellipsis (words left out that the reader must supply).

From line 13 there is no verb at all, only apposition: noun phrases set beside He to rename him. Chaos of thought and passion, Great lord of all things, Sole judge of truth, The glory, jest, and riddle of the world each give him another name. The participles describing him are past participles, things done to him: Placed, Born, confused, abused, disabused, Created, hurled. The only active participle in the passage, reasoning, is but to err.

The pronouns fade in the same way. Man is thyself (1), then He, himself, his, he (7–14), and after himself in line 14 he has no pronoun at all. A passage that begins by addressing you ends with the noun world. As the sentence proceeds, man loses first his actions, then his person.

The figures of balance

  • Antithesis: opposed ideas set in matching grammatical form. There are about fifteen pairs (thyself/God, wise/great qualified by darkly/rudely, sceptic/stoic, act/rest, god/beast, mind/body, born/die, reasoning/err, too little/too much, thought/passion, abused/disabused, rise/fall, lord/prey, truth/error). Early on one opposition fills a couplet; from line 13 there is one per line, six lines running.
  • Parallelism: the same grammatical shape repeated, as in lines 5–6 (With too much [noun] for the [adjective] [noun]) and line 10 (participle + but to + verb, twice).
  • Chiasmus: a crossed ABBA pattern. In line 1, Know… thyself / God… scan puts verb and object, then object and verb, so the two objects of knowing meet at the comma. In line 17, judge of truth / error hurled sets the judge and the hurled body at the outer edges and truth against error in the centre.
  • Anaphora: a phrase repeated at the start of successive units. With too much (5–6), and in doubt three times (7–9). The first in doubt begins in mid-line, after the semicolon; the next two begin lines. The phrase takes over the line as the doubt takes over the man. Line 8's In doubt was a revision; the first edition read "To deem himself a part of God or beast".
  • Tricolon: a sequence of three. There are two: the three doubts (act/rest, god/beast, mind/body) and the three nouns of line 18.
  • Zeugma: one word "yoked" (Greek zeugma) to two others, usually in different senses. It is Pope's trademark elsewhere, as in The Rape of the Lock's "Or stain her honour, or her new brocade". Here Pope deliberately avoids it. Every pair keeps its words in the same sense, so the contradictions lie in man, not in a pun. The nearest thing is zeugma in its older, broader sense, one verb serving many phrases: the single verb hangs governs everything that follows it.

Caesura and the balanced half-line

Pope places most pauses after the fourth or sixth syllable, the standard positions in Augustan verse (lines 1, 4, 7, 10, 11, 17). Three lines break the habit, each for a reason. Line 16 splits exactly in half, 5 ‖ 5, the most perfect balance in the passage, for its most total reversal: lord of everything, prey to everything. Line 13 pauses late, after the seventh syllable, so the verdict all confused is a short, collapsing tail. Line 18 breaks into three, 3 ‖ 1 ‖ 6.

Several unpunctuated lines still divide sharply on a conjunction: a god | or beast (8), too little | or too much (12), abused | or disabused (14), half to rise | and half to fall (15). Pope himself printed commas in some of these ("act, or rest", "abused, or disabused", "rise, and half to fall"). The anthology's modern punctuation removes them, so in the anthology text the balance is carried by the syntax alone.

Punctuation and pace

There is one full stop (line 2) and one exclamation mark (line 18). Between them the marks are commas, semicolons and colons, which suspend rather than close. Each colon opens onto something larger: line 4's onto the explanation of lines 5–6, line 12's onto the catalogue, and line 17's onto the verdict. Because every line ends on punctuation, the sixteen-line sentence is built by accumulation, unit added to unit, not by flowing enjambment. It piles up the way the contradictions do.

The turns

Four hinges organise the passage. At line 3 command gives way to description. At line 7 the main verb finally arrives, and it is hangs. At line 13, after the colon, argument gives way to catalogue. At line 18 the pairs give way to three. The last turn is the decisive one. Seventeen lines have tried to define man by balancing two terms; the final line breaks the form's own habit, as if the creature cannot be summed up even as a pair.

SOUND

Sound

What the poem does to the ear

The couplet's click

Each couplet closes on a full masculine rhyme, so every pair of lines sounds like a conclusion arriving. What these conclusions keep concluding is that nothing can be concluded: the sound of certainty applied to uncertainty.

Rhythm

Regular iambic pentameter, so the few heavy or inverted openings (Know, Placed, Born, Chaos) are heard at once. Each falls on a command, a passive placing, a mortality or a disorder.

Soft half, hard half (line 1)

Know then thyself runs on soft, continuous sounds, n, th, s, f. presume not God to scan is full of stopped consonants: p, t, g, d, t, k. The permitted inquiry sounds easy; the forbidden one sounds hard-edged, a door closing on scan.

The hum of line 2

mankind is man is built on nasal consonants (m, n, n, m, n), and the line has no internal pause, so it is spoken in one breath and ends on its strongest syllable. Its smoothness is the source of its authority.

The sound of doubt and excess

The anaphora in doubt… In doubt… In doubt restarts three times from the same sound without moving forward, the audible shape of indecision, and line 8 adds a d alliteration in doubt to deem. too much sounds three times (5, 6, 12), and too little or too much is clipped and repetitive: t, t, l, t. Every repeated sound in the passage is a repetition of an amount or a doubt.

Plosives in line 10

Born but to die, and reasoning but to err is packed with b, t and d, hard stopped sounds with no liquids to soften them. Its two halves share a rhythm, so the second lands like a repeated blow.

Flat rhyme, circling rhyme

such / much is the dullest pair in the passage: two short, colourless syllables where reason runs out. confused, abused and disabused put three buzzing -used endings into two lines. abused or disabused chimes with itself, and the metre puts a beat on dis, so the ear hears the same word turned inside out, a sound that goes round in a circle, like the self-deception it describes.

Weight and speed (line 16)

Great lord of all things is slow: long vowels, liquid l and r, stresses crowded together. After the comma, but a prey to all runs fast, two light syllables tumbling into prey. The lordship sounds heavy; the fall is quick.

The judge and the fall (line 17)

Sole judge of truth uses long, grave vowels (o, u). Then endless error hurled runs a sequence of short e sounds into rolling r and l, and error echoes line 10's err. The line moves from stillness into a tumble.

The last line

glory, riddle and world are all full of liquid l and r sounds, so the line rolls. jest is the one word without them: short, sibilant, ending on a hard t, and isolated between two commas. The joke-word sounds different from everything around it. The final rhyme hurled / world shares the dark central vowel and the -rld cluster. The passage that began with the bright, open -an of scan / man ends on a sound that rolls and does not close cleanly.

MOTIFS & SYMBOLS

Motifs & Symbols

Images that recur, and what they accumulate

Pope's extract has no story and no concrete scene, so its motifs are clusters of words, a vocabulary that returns and gathers meaning as the argument goes on.

1. Measuring

It begins with scan: to examine minutely, and to count the beats of a line of verse. Then the words of quantity multiply: middle, too much (5, 6), too little or too much (12), half… half (15), all… all (16), Sole (17), endless (17). Man is weighed and calculated, and the answer never comes out. He is too much for one philosophy, too much for the other, equally ignorant at either dose of thinking, exactly half one thing and half another. By the end the measurements are infinite (endless) or total (all), and measurement turns into riddle. The motif turns the age's confidence in calculation, the Newtonian dream of measuring everything, back on the measurer.

2. Up and down

The Great Chain of Being is vertical, and the passage keeps moving on that axis. presume is the upward overreach; scan comes from Latin scandere, "to climb".
