Line 8 names the top and bottom of man's neighbourhood, a god or beast. Line 15 makes the motion itself his design, half to rise and half to fall, and fall cannot be innocent in a Christian poem: it carries Adam's Fall. Then come the extremes, Great lord against prey, the seated judge hurled, and finally glory, the word for heavenly splendour. Man is never allowed to stay at any height. His characteristic position is in between, and his characteristic motion is a drop.

3. Between

isthmus, middle state, side, He hangs between, and the hinge-word or five times (act or rest, god or beast, mind or body, too little or too much, abused or disabused). This is the vocabulary of position, and it turns every question about man into a choice he cannot make. The isthmus is its image: a strip of land that both joins and separates, a place you cross but cannot settle. The ors are its grammar. The motif peaks at line 7, where between has no object; the objects are everything around it.

4. The self as its own object

thyself (1), himself (8), by himself (14): the reflexive pronoun keeps returning, because the study of man is an inquiry in which investigator and specimen are the same person. The polyptoton mankind… man (2) states it, and Still by himself abused or disabused shows its cost: the deceiver and the deceived, the corrector and the corrected, are one mind. Pope also keeps the specimen at arm's length (A being, He), as if self-knowledge required treating oneself as a third person. After line 14 the reflexive disappears with the pronouns.

5. The hidden maker

God is named once, in the command not to scan him. Yet he is everywhere in the grammar. Placed, Born, Created are passive participles whose agent is never named but is obviously present. The motif ends in glory, the word Scripture uses for God's own splendour, here given to man. The maker cannot be examined, but his handiwork is the whole subject. The design is felt in every line, which is why complaint about it would be presumption.

THEMES

Themes

The ideas the poem is arguing about

01

The limits of human knowledge

The passage opens with a prohibition, presume not God to scan, and spends seventeen lines showing why it is wise. Man is darkly wise, wise as if in poor light. He reasons but to err, and he is Alike in ignorance whether he thinks too little or too much. That last point is the most radical: it is not that we know too little and should learn more, but that reason's range is fixed, and pushing it harder produces a different ignorance of the same size.

Pope wrote in the decade after Newton, when the heavens had just been reduced to mathematics. The theme is a warning attached to that confidence. Measure the planets by all means, but the instrument has limits, and the first thing to measure is the measurer.

02

Self-knowledge: the proper study

Know then thyself takes the Delphic maxim that began Greek philosophy and makes it the only licensed inquiry. The proper study of mankind is man is the programme. proper means fitting to our rank and also our own. The theme is ironic in a productive way: the study yields not a portrait but a list of contradictions, and the self turns out to be its own deceiver (Still by himself abused or disabused).

Yet the theme is not defeatist. To know that one is The glory, jest, and riddle of the world is real knowledge, the kind Socrates meant: knowing what you are includes knowing what you cannot settle about yourself.

03

Man's middle place

this isthmus of a middle state puts man on the Great Chain of Being, between the angels (pure spirit) and the animals (body and appetite). He shares in both, and the passage tracks the consequences: he cannot decide whether to deem himself a god or beast. He is Created half to rise and half to fall, and he is both lord and prey. The middle is honourable, since man is the link that joins the two halves of creation, and unstable, since he belongs wholly to neither.

The theme also deflates human self-importance. Epistle I mocks the proud belief that the universe exists for us, and the extract places man not at the centre of creation but at a joint in it.

04

Pride and presumption

The vocabulary is theological: presume, pride, fall, hurled (Milton's verb for Satan's expulsion). The sin under attack is the one that destroyed Satan and Adam, wanting a knowledge and a status not one's own. Even the Stoic ideal of self-sufficiency is filed as the stoic's pride. The grand titles man gives himself, Great lord of all things, Sole judge of truth, are each cut down in the same line.

Pope does not condemn man for being weak. He condemns the refusal to accept the terms of that weakness, and the passage's balanced half-lines repeatedly perform the correction: claim, then limit.

05

Reason and passion, mind and body

In doubt his mind or body to prefer and Chaos of thought and passion, all confused name the conflict that the rest of Epistle II takes up. confused keeps its Latin sense of "poured together": thought and passion are not two neat compartments but a mixture. Line 10 disposes of both halves of a person, the body Born but to die, the mind reasoning but to err.

In context this chaos is a problem stated in order to be worked on. Pope's next step is "Two principles in human nature reign; / Self-love, to urge, and reason, to restrain", with passion the gale and reason the compass. The extract shows the disorder before the ordering begins.

06

Paradox, and the tone of wonder

Contradiction is not a fault in man but his definition: wise in the dark, great but unfinished, lord and prey, judge and wanderer. The final tricolon refuses even a two-term contradiction: glory, jest, riddle. The tone is the theme's real argument. Pascal, Pope's source, used the same contradictions to drive his reader to despair of himself and so to God. Pope's jest and his exclamation mark make the ending comic and astonished rather than disgusted, and the next line of the poem, "Go, wondrous creature!", confirms that the riddle is also a marvel.

DIFFICULT MOMENTS

Difficult Moments

Where the poem is genuinely undecidable — and what to do about it

Cruxes

1. The proper study of mankind is man: a programme or a retreat?

The difficulty. The line is quoted everywhere as a humanist slogan, a celebration of studying human beings. In the poem it follows a prohibition, and what follows it is a list of human failures.

Competing readings. (a) Programme: the line launches a new science of human nature. Charron had said "The true science and true study of man is man", and the age of Locke wanted to audit the mind before trusting it. (b) Retreat: having been forbidden to scan God, we fall back on the only object within range. Elwin pointed out that Pascal, who wrote that "The study of man is the proper employment and exercise of mankind", meant studying man instead of mathematics, never instead of God. (c) Irony: the confident announcement sets up a study whose result is riddle.

What a strong answer does. It takes proper seriously, fitting to our rank rather than the highest study, and notices the first-edition reading, "The only science of mankind is man": Pope softened an exclusive claim into a humble one. The line is both programme and limit, and the passage tests it at once.

2. What does in doubt to act or rest mean?

The difficulty. The other two doubts are clear (god or beast, mind or body). This one is vague, and Johnson, translating Crousaz's attack on the poem, said he could not determine whether anyone had discovered its true meaning.

Competing readings. (a) Practical: whether to do something or nothing, the daily paralysis beneath the grand doubts. (b) Philosophical: Warburton heard rest as the Stoics' passive calm, which Pope rejects later in Epistle II ("strength of mind is exercise, not rest"). (c) Elwin's version: whether to commit to an active belief or sink into inert scepticism, which picks up the sceptic side of line 5.

What a strong answer does. It lets the vagueness work. Placed straight after He hangs between, the doubt about acting is itself a form of hanging, and the three doubts move from doing, to being, to valuing. Readings (b) and (c) show the line answering lines 5–6: the sceptic rests in suspended judgement, the Stoic rests in apathy, and man can settle into neither.

3. presume not God to scan: piety or deism?

The difficulty. The line sounds like Christian humility, yet the poem's first great critic, Crousaz (1737–38), called it fatalistic "natural religion", a religion of reason that needs no revelation.

Competing readings. (a) Orthodox: this is the angel's advice to Adam in Milton, and Job's question whether man "by searching" can "find out God". It is humility before mystery. (b) Deist: the extract mentions no Christ, grace, soul or afterlife. Born but to die leaves out what a Christian would add, and Elwin protested that man "is not born only to die". Pascal's same contradictions end in "Listen to God"; Pope forbids the inquiry and offers no Saviour. The first edition's "a part of God" in line 8 could sound pantheist. (c) Strategic: Pope, a Catholic in a Protestant country, wrote a theodicy broad enough for any believer, and Warburton defended it as orthodox.

What a strong answer does. It notices what is present and what is absent. God is everywhere in the grammar (Placed, Created) but never approached, and the passage's "remedy" is humility, not grace. That is why it could be praised as pious and attacked as deist.

4. What tone is the last line?

The difficulty. The glory, jest, and riddle of the world! can be read as awe, contempt or comedy, and the exclamation mark fits all three.

Competing readings. (a) Awe: glory is the word Psalm 8 uses for man "crowned… with glory", and the next line is "Go, wondrous creature!" (b) Contempt: jest is the operative word; the passage has earned exasperation, and riddle means no answer. (c) Comic mastery: the satirist's flourish. Pope replaces Pascal's "refuse" with jest, trading disgust for laughter.

What a strong answer does. It argues that the line is built not to resolve. The tricolon breaks the pattern of pairs, the words rise, drop and suspend, and the comparison with Pascal shows which way the tone leans: away from revulsion, towards amused wonder. A line about irresolvability would be poorly served by a single resolved tone.

CLOSE ANALYSIS

Close Analysis

The moments that repay pressure, worked through

Quotation analysis

1. Know then thyself, presume not God to scan;

Two imperatives across a caesura; Delphic allusion; chiasmus; pun on scan.

A door opens and a door shuts in one line. The permitted half is the Delphic maxim; the forbidden half names the sin, presumption. The pattern crosses (verb, object | object, verb), so thyself and God, the two possible objects of knowledge, meet at the comma, while Know and scan, the two verbs of knowing, stand at the edges. scan means to examine minutely and to measure verse, and the line scans perfectly.

Intention and effect: Pope fences the founding command of philosophy at once, so the reader starts with a limit. The tidy form makes the restriction feel reasonable rather than arbitrary.

2. The proper study of mankind is man.

Aphorism; polyptoton; only full stop; no punctuated caesura.

A complete thesis in ten syllables, its subject held back until the last two, is man. mankind… man narrows the species to the specimen, and the student and the thing studied become one. proper means fitting and also our own.

Intention and effect: the line sounds self-evident, which is the set-up for what follows. The passage's most confident sentence introduces a study whose result is a riddle.

3. Placed on this isthmus of a middle state,

Agentless passive participle; metaphor; the Great Chain of Being.

Placed implies a placer who is never named. isthmus is exact: a narrow neck of land that joins two land masses and separates two seas. Man is the joint between spirit and matter, honoured by the position and endangered by it. The sentence then makes us wait four lines for its subject.

Intention and effect: the reader feels the precariousness, and the passive verb quietly forbids complaint: we did not choose our station.

4. A being darkly wise, and rudely great:

Two oxymorons balanced across the caesura; false friends.

darkly means dimly, as in "through a glass, darkly"; rudely means roughly made, unfinished (Latin rudis, raw). Each great claim is granted and diminished in the same breath.

Intention and effect: this is the method of the whole passage in miniature, concession followed by limit, delivered with a balance that makes the qualification sound like a measurement rather than an insult.

5. With too much knowledge for the sceptic side, / With too much weakness for the stoic's pride,

Anaphora; exact parallelism; antithesis of the two ancient schools.

The sceptic suspends judgement on everything; the Stoic claims to be untouched by pain and passion. Man fails both tests by excess. He knows too much to doubt everything, and he is too weak to be invulnerable. pride files Stoicism under the sin of line 1.

Intention and effect: the matching lines make the double exclusion feel like a proof. Antiquity's two great answers to the human condition are closed.

6. He hangs between; in doubt to act or rest,

Delayed main clause; the heaviest caesura; start of the in doubt anaphora.

The subject arrives after four lines of description, and his one action is to hang. The semicolon leaves between dangling, and the grammar matches it: He is suspended between his own modifiers. in doubt then repeats three times, moving from mid-line to line-openings as the doubt takes over.

Intention and effect: the reader is held in the pause the word describes. Indecision becomes something we hear and feel, not just something we are told.

7. Born but to die, and reasoning but to err;

Parallel halves; but meaning "only"; antithesis; plosives.

Body and mind are each reduced to their failure, and but to makes death and error sound like the purposes of birth and reason. The two halves share a rhythm, so the second blow repeats the first.

Intention and effect: the bleakest line, stated at full strength because the passage is building a case against pride. Warburton softened it: as we enjoy "some small portion of life", so "we comprehend some few truths".

8. Still by himself abused or disabused;

Archaic sense; polyptoton; reflexive; metrical stress on dis.

abused meant "deceived", disabused "undeceived", and Still means always. Man fools himself, catches himself out and fools himself again, with no outside deceiver. The two words differ only by a prefix, and the metre stresses it.

Intention and effect: a strikingly modern idea of the self as its own deceiver. The sound circles as the mind does.

9. Great lord of all things, but a prey to all; / Sole judge of truth, in endless error hurled:

Antithesis; exact 5 ‖ 5 balance; chiasmus; Miltonic verb.

Each line grants a title and takes it back. The doubled all makes line 16 airtight: the same totality is his kingdom and his predator. Line 17's judge is hurled, Milton's word for Satan's fall, so a seated authority becomes a body in flight. Having been forbidden to scan God, man is the Sole judge left, and he is falling.

Intention and effect: the comic timing of satire, set up and knocked down in ten syllables, and a frightening idea: there is no higher court to appeal to.

10. The glory, jest, and riddle of the world!

Tricolon breaking the pattern of pairs; two caesuras; the only exclamation; final word world.

After fifteen pairs, three terms: what we are proud of, what we are laughed at for, and what settles neither. jest stands alone between two commas. Pascal's "glory and refuse" becomes glory and joke, and riddle is added.

Intention and effect: the form breaks to prove the point that man cannot be summed up even as a pair. The tone leans to amused wonder, and the next line, "Go, wondrous creature!", confirms it.

CRITICAL LENSES

Critical Lenses

What each way of reading makes visible, and what it flattens

Critical lenses

Formalist

It makes visible how much of the argument is carried by the machinery. The subject He is suspended between modifiers as the verb says hangs between. The finite verbs vanish after line 12 and the pronouns after line 14. The antitheses accelerate to one per line, line 16 splits exactly in half, and the tricolon of line 18 breaks the pattern of pairs. This lens best answers Johnson's charge that the thought is commonplace: the poem does not just state an old idea, it acts it out. It flattens the theology and the history. The forms mean what they mean because Pope's readers believed in a ranked, designed creation.

Historicist

It makes visible a poem written in the decade after Newton, when measurement seemed limitless and Pope had just written Newton's epitaph. presume not God to scan is aimed at that confidence, and the passage's own measuring words (too much, half, all) turn calculation back on the calculator. It also places the author: a Catholic barred from university and office, self-taught, publishing anonymously to dodge enemies. The lens risks reducing a general account of humanity to a period document; the extract has lasted precisely because its paradoxes are not tied to 1733.

Theological

It makes visible the Christian vocabulary (presume, pride, fall, Created, glory) and the poem's purpose as a theodicy, a defence of God's design. It also shows the striking absences: no Christ, grace or afterlife. Read beside Pascal, whose identical contradictions end in "Listen to God", Pope's lines remove the cure and keep the diagnosis, which is why Crousaz accused the poem of deism and Elwin complained that "Pope had not any remedy to suggest". The lens can flatten the wit, treating jest as if it were Pascal's "refuse".

Psychoanalytic

It makes visible a divided self: Chaos of thought and passion, all confused, a mind by himself abused or disabused, unable to choose between mind or body. Self-deception without an outside deceiver anticipates later ideas of the unconscious, and the shift from thyself to He looks like a mind that can only examine itself by stepping outside itself. The lens is anachronistic. Pope's "passions" are not repressed drives, and the rest of Epistle II proposes not analysis but balance: self-love urging, reason restraining.

Feminist

It makes visible the generic masculine: mankind, man, He, himself, lord. The universal human being is grammatically male, and the "middle state" between god and beast is described as if it were a man's position. Set beside Katherine Philips, whose A Married State weighs women's legal and bodily lot in the same couplet form, Pope's state of man looks like a view from a particular place. The lens can misrepresent the eighteenth-century convention, in which man meant humankind, and the extract makes no claim about women at all.

Ecocritical

It makes visible the Great Chain as an ecology of ranks, and man's double place in nature: Great lord of all things, with Genesis's dominion over creation, but a prey to all, hunted, vulnerable, one link among many. Epistle I mocks the pride that thinks the universe was made for us. Read today, after Boey's insatiate man moves in for the kill, lord of all things sounds like a warning. The lens risks importing modern environmental worries into a poem whose hierarchy is fixed and God-given, not a web to be protected.

OTHER READINGS

Other Readings

Contested interpretations, and where each is weak

Alternative readings

1. The problem stated, not the verdict

Evidence: Pope's marginal summary labels the extract "His middle nature", the first step of an argument. Thirty-five lines later comes the constructive case ("Two principles in human nature reign; / Self-love, to urge, and reason, to restrain"). Warburton says the dark picture is drawn "not to deter men from the search, but to excite them to the discovery of truth". The next line, "Go, wondrous creature!", is a challenge, not an epitaph.

Weakness: the anthology prints these eighteen lines alone, and they must stand on their own. Their eloquence goes into the indictment, not the cure.

2. A Pascalian picture of fallen man, minus the cure

Evidence: line after line comes from Pascal: the "confused chaos", the "judge of all things", the "glory and the scandal of the universe". Elwin called it "a partial and distorted copy" that keeps Pascal's despair and drops his remedy. Born but to die omits the resurrection a Christian would add.

Weakness: the tone is not Pascal's. jest replaces Pascal's "refuse", the ending is comic and astonished rather than disgusted, and line 1 makes humility, not despair, the response.

3. Satire: mock-heroic anthropology

Evidence: the author of The Dunciad sets up grand titles (Great lord of all things, Sole judge of truth) and knocks each down in the same line. jest is a satirist's word, and the exclamation can be heard as a flourish.

Weakness: the satire has no target but everyone, the poet included, and the passage's seriousness about knowledge and God is not a joke. Satire is one register among several, not the whole.

4. A humanist celebration of range

Evidence: The proper study of mankind is man became a humanist slogan. Man contains glory and is lord of all things, a creature whose very contradictions make him the most interesting object in creation.

Weakness: the line is framed by a prohibition and followed by error, ignorance and chaos. The first edition's "only science" became the humbler "proper study". The celebration is real but always qualified.

5. A deist poem in Christian dress

Evidence: Crousaz attacked the Essay as natural religion without revelation. Its framework came from Bolingbroke, a freethinker, and the extract never mentions Christ, grace or the soul. The first edition's "a part of God" sounds pantheist.

Weakness: Pope was a practising Catholic, Warburton defended the poem's orthodoxy and Pope endorsed the defence, and presume not God to scan is a commonplace of Christian humility (Job, Milton's Raphael).

6. A disabled poet's body in the argument

Evidence: Pope stood about four and a half feet tall, was in constant pain from spinal tuberculosis and called his life "this long disease". rudely great, his mind or body to prefer and a prey to all had a personal meaning for him.

Weakness: the passage speaks of "man", not of Pope, and its terms come from Pascal and the Chain of Being. Biography may explain the force of the physical vocabulary, but it cannot be its meaning.

REVISION NOTES

Revision Notes

The working notes, quotation by quotation

Title

"An Essay on Man"

Analysis
  • Essay = attempt, trial (French essai, Montaigne's word) → modest, provisional
    • Echoes Locke's Essay Concerning Human Understanding (1690): limits of the mind
  • Man = humankind (generic), not the male sex
  • Extract = first 18 lines of Epistle II (of four verse letters)
    • Pope's own summary: man's business is not to pry into God but to study himself

Context

Analysis
  • Alexander Pope (1688–1744): defining poet of the Augustan age (c. 1700–1750: reason, order, balance, wit)
  • Catholic in Protestant England → penal laws: no university, no public office, not allowed within 10 miles of London
    • Largely self-taught
  • Spinal tuberculosis (Pott's disease) from c. 12 → c. 4 ft 6 in, constant pain; "this long disease, my life"
  • Homer translations → financial independence, villa at Twickenham
  • An Essay on Man (1733–34): four epistles, addressed to Lord Bolingbroke
    • Aim: to "vindicate the ways of God to Man" (echo of Milton) = a theodicy
    • Published anonymously → enemies praised it before knowing it was his
  • Epistle I ended: "Whatever is, is right" → extract turns from the universe to man himself

Great Chain of Being

Analysis
  • God → angels → man → animals → plants → matter
  • Man = the only link that is both spirit (like angels) and body (like beasts)
    • → middle state, a god or beast
  • Remove one link → the whole chain breaks → wishing to be higher = pride
1

Know then thyself

Analysis
  • Imperative + allusion: gnōthi seauton, inscribed at Apollo's temple at Delphi; Socrates' first task of philosophy
  • then = therefore → follows from Epistle I
  • Two commands across the caesura: Know (allowed) vs presume not (forbidden)
  • scan = examine minutely + measure metre (the line scans perfectly)
    • Latin scandere = to climb → overreaching
  • presume = the sin of overreaching (Satan, Adam)
2

The proper study of mankind is man

Analysis
  • Aphorism: complete thesis in 10 syllables; perfect iambic pentameter
    • Only full stop in the passage; no mid-line pause → sounds final, seamless
  • Polyptoton mankind… man → student = specimen
  • proper = fitting to our rank + our own
  • First edition: "The only science of mankind is man" → humbler revision
  • Irony: confident programme → the study produces a riddle
3–4

isthmus of a middle state

Analysis
  • Metaphor: isthmus = narrow neck of land between two seas
    • Joins (spirit + matter) and separates; narrow, precarious
  • Placed = passive; God the unnamed placer → we didn't choose our station
  • Oxymorons darkly wise (dimly, as through a glass) / rudely great (roughly made, Latin rudis), not "rude"
    • Each claim granted then limited
5–6

sceptic side / stoic's pride

Analysis
  • Anaphora With too much… + exact parallelism
  • Sceptics: nothing can be known → suspend judgement
  • Stoics: wise man unmoved by pain/passion → self-sufficient
  • Man disqualified from both by excess: too much knowledge / too much weakness
  • pride → links Stoicism to the sin of line 1
7–9

He hangs between

Analysis
  • Main clause arrives at last (subject He delayed 4 lines)
    • He literally hangs between descriptions (4 lines before, 11 after)
  • hangs = suspended, no footing; semicolon = longest pause → line itself hangs
  • Anaphora in doubt ×3 → tricolon of doubts: act/rest → god/beast → mind/body
    • Doing → being → valuing
  • act or rest is debated (Johnson unsure); maybe action vs Stoic calm
10

Born but to die

Analysis
  • but = only, merely (not "however")
  • Parallelism: body → death; mind → error
  • but to sounds like a purpose → bleakest line
  • Plosives b/t/d → blow repeated
  • Warburton: as we enjoy some life, "we comprehend some few truths"
11–14

too little or too much

Analysis
  • Ellipsis: his reason [is] such that he is equally ignorant either way → no right dose of thinking
  • Flat rhyme such / much
  • Chaos = before Creation; confused = poured together (Latin)
  • After line 12: no main verb → man only renamed, never acts
  • abused = deceived; disabused = undeceived; Still = always
    • Self-deception cycle, no outside villain
15–17

Great lord of all things

Analysis
  • half to rise and half to fall → built from both; fall = Adam's Fall
  • Great lord of all things, but a prey to all: exact 5|5 balance, all doubled
    • Anthology but; Pope's text "yet" (same sense)
  • Sole judge of truth, in endless error hurled → judge flung; hurled = Satan's fall (Milton)
  • Passive participles throughout (Placed, Born, Created, hurled) → man acted upon
18

The glory, jest, and riddle of the world!

Analysis
  • Tricolon after ~15 pairs → breaks the pattern: man can't be summed up even as a pair
    • Not "balanced": two commas isolate jest
  • glory (pride) → jest (laughter) → riddle (unsolved)
  • Pascal: "gloire et rebut" (glory and refuse) → Pope swaps refuse for jest → comic wonder, not disgust
  • Only exclamation: awe + exasperation
  • Ends on world, not man; next line: "Go, wondrous creature!"

Structure

Analysis
  • 9 heroic couplets (rhyming iambic pentameter), all end-stopped
  • Couplet + caesura = balance at two levels → perfect for a two-sided creature
    • Irony: form of order, content of chaos
  • 2 sentences: 1–2 command/thesis; 3–18 one long sentence
  • Command → description → pure paradox

Themes

Analysis
  • Human paradox: contradiction = man's definition, a condition to accept
  • Limits of knowledge: God can't be scanned; reason errs
  • Man's middle place: not the centre of creation (anti-anthropocentric)
  • Pride and presumption
  • Reason vs passion (rest of Epistle II: self-love urges, reason restrains)
  • Extract = problem stated, not the final verdict
CONNECTIONS

Connections

How this poem pairs with the rest of the set

Comparison hooks

With 'A Married State' (Katherine Philips)

Link: the set's two poems in heroic couplets, about ninety years apart, both weighing a human state. Philips sets 'A married state' against 'A virgin state'; Pope places man in a middle state. Shared technique: balance, antithesis and epigram, and but meaning "only": Philips's marriage 'affords but little ease', Pope's man is Born but to die. Both end on a single line that sums up and dismisses, Philips's 'leading apes in hell', Pope's riddle of the world. Difference: Philips uses the couplet's authority to argue a woman's practical case from the margins and reaches a firm conclusion; Pope, at the centre of literary power, uses it to show that no conclusion about man will hold, and breaks the pattern of pairs in his last line.

With 'The Cockroach' (Kevin Halligan)

Link: a study of aimlessness that becomes self-knowledge. Halligan's insect 'looked uncertain where to go'; Pope's man is in doubt to act or rest. Shared technique: a creature described from outside until the description turns back on the describer. Halligan ends 'I thought I recognised myself'; Pope begins Know then thyself. Difference: Pope announces the programme and generalises (mankind); Halligan performs it privately, through one small creature, and ends in a hesitant first person, 'I don't know', where Pope ends with a confident exclamation about the unknowable.

With 'Song: Love Armed' (Aphra Behn)

Link: the war between passion and reason. Behn shows a human passion made into a tyrant god; Pope's man is Chaos of thought and passion. Shared technique: the same rhyme. Behn's Love hurls fire 'in sport' and rhymes 'hurled' with 'the Amorous World'; Pope ends in endless error hurled: / The glory, jest, and riddle of the world! Both also name Pride (the stoic's pride; 'his Pride and Cruelty'). Difference: in Behn the lovers make a god who then rules them; in Pope man is forbidden even to scan God and is himself the thing hurled.

With 'The Chimney Sweeper' (William Blake)

Link: the order of things and who pays for it. Pope's Essay argues that "Whatever is, is right", that every link of the Chain belongs in a good design. Blake's child is a link in a social order run by 'God and his priest and king', who 'make up a heaven of our misery'. Shared technique: religious vocabulary under pressure (Created, glory; 'praise God'). Difference: Pope forbids man to question the design (presume not God to scan); Blake's poem exists to question it, and his child sees through the adults who justify his suffering.

With 'Report to Wordsworth' (Boey Kim Cheng)

Link: man's place in nature. Pope's man is Great lord of all things, but a prey to all; Boey's 'insatiate man moves in for the kill', a lord who has turned predator. Shared technique: classical and divine order invoked to measure human conduct, and a closing rhymed couplet ('sky' / 'cry'). Difference: Pope's universe is intact and God beyond scanning; in Boey the sea-gods are 'entombed' and 'God is labouring to utter his last cry'. The chain of being Pope trusts has broken.

With 'Shall I Compare Thee…?' (Sonnet 18, William Shakespeare)

Link: human limitation in iambic pentameter, ending on a couplet verdict. Shared technique: generic man: Shakespeare's 'So long as men can breathe or eyes can see', Pope's mankind. Difference: Shakespeare's couplet resolves triumphantly, verse defeating death; Pope's man is Born but to die, and his final couplet refuses to resolve, ending on riddle.

With 'Hunting Snake' (Judith Wright)

Link: human beings measured against an animal. Wright's walkers 'froze half-through a pace', caught between movement and stillness, which is Pope's in doubt to act or rest made physical. Shared technique: the language of prey and hunting (a prey to all; the snake's 'fierce intent'). Difference: Wright's snake is undivided and wholly itself, 'Cold, dark and splendid', and the humans, briefly, are its awed audience, not lord of all things; Pope's man is all division and never stops talking about himself.

Carpet-weavers, Morocco

Carol Rumens · 1987

The carpet is given a journey, a purpose and a future; the children who knot it get only more knotting — and the instant in which all-that-will-be becomes all-that-was.

12
