CONTEXT

Context

The world the poem came out of

The Poet: Carol Rumens (1944–2026)

Carol Rumens was born Carol-Ann Lumley on 10 December 1944 in Forest Hill, south London. She won a scholarship to grammar school, read Philosophy at London University (leaving before she finished the degree) and in 1965 married David Rumens; they had two daughters and divorced in 1985. Her first collection, A Strange Girl in Bright Colours, appeared in 1973, and more than a dozen followed, alongside plays, a novel (Plato Park, 1987), translations from Russian and anthologies, among them Making for the Open: The Chatto Book of Post-Feminist Poetry 1964–1984 (1985). She was poetry editor at Quarto (1982–84) and the Literary Review (1984–88), held writing and teaching posts at Kent, Queen's University Belfast, University College Cork and Stockholm University, and later taught creative writing at Hull and at Bangor. She won the Prudence Farmer Award (1981), a share of the Alice Hunt Bartlett Award for Unplayed Music and a Cholmondeley Award (1984), and was elected a Fellow of the Royal Society of Literature in 1984.

From 2007 she wrote the Guardian's weekly ‘Poem of the week’ column — close readings of other poets' work — and kept it going until her death on 25 April 2026, aged 81. She has often been compared to Philip Larkin, and the plain, level, end-stopped sentences of this poem show why. Her later work turns increasingly to foreign places, languages and customs; Ben Wilkinson's British Council essay on her picks out other cultures' customs as a recurring source of her inspiration.

*Selected Poems* (1987): first publication

‘Carpet-weavers, Morocco’ was first collected in Rumens's Selected Poems (Chatto & Windus, 1987): it does not appear in any of her earlier books. No earlier magazine printing, exact date of composition or account of the occasion behind it has been found, so the safe date is ‘by 1987’.

It has since become a school text, and it is in Cambridge's Songs of Ourselves anthology (2005), the source of this set selection. The poem contains no ‘I’, no date and no place-name beyond the title, so what it records is a scene, not an anecdote: we are never told who is watching, or when.

Children at the looms: Morocco's carpet workshops

Hand-knotted carpets were one of the trades in which child labour drew international attention. In 1978 the London-based Anti-Slavery Society published a report, Child Labour in Morocco's Carpet Industry, on children's work in Moroccan carpet workshops. The problem outlasted it. In January 2001 the Christian Science Monitor (Nicolas Pelham) found about fifty children, some of them about six or younger, weaving in a back room of the Congress Palace in Fes; one six-year-old worked ten hours a day for $14 a month, paid to the child's mother, and a UNICEF officer described girls of five or six who stand all day at the loom. Morocco then admitted to 538,000 child workers under 13.

The employers' defence, reported in the same article, is the usual one: small hands weave better, and the work teaches a trade in a country of high unemployment. It is a justification, not a finding. Morocco's Labour Code of 2003 (in force from 2004) raised the minimum working age to 15. Rumens's poem dates from the years when this was being investigated and publicised. Nothing shows that she knew the report, and the poem names no workshop, wage or employer; but these facts show what the scene she describes meant at the time, and why hard at work and the school of days are not neutral phrases.

How a knotted carpet is made

A pile carpet is built on an upright loom. Warp threads are stretched vertically between two beams; the weaver ties a short length of coloured wool around a pair of neighbouring warps, cuts it, and works across the width in a row; then weft threads are passed through and beaten down with a heavy comb, locking the row in place under the next. Moroccan pile carpets are usually tied with the symmetrical (Turkish) knot. Because the carpet is made from the bottom up, the design rises with the work — lower border first, top border last — and on a fixed upright loom, where the finished part is not rolled away, the weavers sit on a plank or bench that is raised as the weaving climbs. So the bench will be raised is plain workshop fact before it is anything else, and the tree-tops of a garden design really are woven last.

Moroccan weaving has two broad traditions: rural Amazigh (Berber) rugs, woven by women in villages, often in geometric designs, and the workshop carpets of cities such as Rabat, more densely knotted and often floral. The poem's bench, its several children at one loom and its pictorial garden suggest a workshop, but Rumens names no town and no style.

Prayer, the mosque and the garden

Muslim prayer must be made in a clean place, and its movements — standing, bowing, kneeling and prostration with the forehead to the ground — are one reason mosque floors are carpeted; the niche design of a prayer rug recalls the mihrab, the niche in a mosque wall that marks the direction of Mecca. The Qur'an's word for paradise, al-janna, means ‘the garden’, and it repeatedly promises the faithful ‘gardens under which rivers flow’ (2:25, in a common translation). Persian ‘garden carpets’ of the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries map a formal garden seen from above — water channels dividing beds of trees and flowers — and are often read as images of paradise.

Historians of Islamic gardens, D. Fairchild Ruggles among them, caution against reading every garden, or every garden design, as a literal picture of paradise. Rumens's phrase the garden of Islam is her own, not a technical term: it gathers the carpet's trees and flowers, the paradise they evoke, and the faith — perhaps the wider Muslim world — that the carpet will serve.

Watching without a verdict: the tradition the poem works in

English poetry about child labour has a famous model in the set: Blake's ‘The Chimney Sweeper’ (Songs of Experience, 1794), which lets the child speak and names ‘God and his priest and king’ as those who make ‘a heaven of our misery’. Rumens takes the opposite course — no first person, no adjective of judgement, no named employer: an impersonal, observational lyric that arranges facts and lets tense and grammar carry the weight.

Its forms are documentary ones: the caption of the title (trade, comma, country), the photograph's attention to surfaces, the report's plain sentences, each line a complete statement. A British reader of the 1980s would bring a Western frame — television, the tourist market, the imported carpet — and the poem quietly builds that frame into its own similes.

THE POEM

The Poem

Line by line, with the analysis alongside

Carpet-weavers, Morocco

This poem is still in copyright, so its words are not reproduced here: each line shows a short summary. Read it alongside your anthology or the exam paper, or use Add the text to paste it in from your own copy (it stays on this device).

TCarpet-weavers, Morocco
1young workers at the weaving frame of somewhere else entirely
2hair plaited and glossy-dark; clothes vividly coloured
3graded in size, they would sound like a set of bells
4eyes fixed on the shimmering knots, as if at a screen
5the paradise pattern rises, so their seat must go up too
6next, they'll thread red branchwork through the highest foliage
7the finished rug will leave on a trader's lorry
8mosque attendants will unroll it across the floor
9thick and yielding, it'll sink beneath the worshippers' weight
10back in the workshop: still labouring, time their only teacher
11the hues of the future leap off their fingertips (runs on)…
12…and set solid, locked within the finished past

Lines with a marker have analysis — click one, or just scroll.

Title
Carpet-weavers, Morocco
Language & devices

The title is a Caption: occupation, comma, place — the format of the label under a photograph, a museum exhibit or a travel-book plate. The Compound noun Carpet-weavers names people by their product and their trade, with no article, no number, no age and no names. The comma sets the job beside the country without a verb, so nothing is yet said about them: Morocco is a location, not a world.

Meaning & effect

The title promises documentary neutrality — workers, located — and the poem keeps that promise in its tone while breaking it in its first three words, where the weavers turn out to be The children. That gap between weavers and children is the poem's subject. The caption form also places the reader where a visitor to an exhibition stands, looking at people labelled by what they make; the poem will later show the cost of that position (the would of line 3, the television of line 4).

Line 1
young workers at the weaving frame of somewhere else entirely
Language & devices

The Definite article presents The children as already there in front of us, not introduced. Polysemy: loom is the weaving frame and also the verb to loom, to rise up large and threatening (PoetryProf notes the frightening connotation). Ambiguity: another world has no stated referent. The line is one plain Declarative sentence in the simple present, closed by a full stop — the pattern of the first ten lines.

Meaning & effect

The line holds three worlds at once. The carpet on the loom shows another world, a garden of paradise; the children live in a world apart from the reader's, of work rather than school; and to a British reader Morocco is the kind of place people call another world, a phrase that can make it exotic. Rumens does not choose, and the flat statement makes the ambiguity sound like a fact. The first line also corrects the title: before we see a weaver we see a child.

Line 2
hair plaited and glossy-dark; clothes vividly coloured
Language & devices

Visual imagery in two balanced halves either side of a Caesura, Their braids answering their dresses (Parallelism). Alliteration on b (braids, black, bright) and the Contrast of black hair with bright cloth. oiled implies grooming: someone has prepared these children for the day. The only verb is are, so the line is pure description. It is the poem's one perfectly regular line of Iambic pentameter: five stresses in strict alternation.

Meaning & effect

Rumens makes the children particular — cared-for, dressed, individual — so that they cannot dissolve into a statistic about child labour. But the details are a painter's or a photographer's: colour, sheen, arrangement. The children are seen, not heard, and they do nothing. The line's balance and its neat metre make the scene attractive, and the poem goes on to ask what it means to find working children attractive.

Line 3
graded in size, they would sound like a set of bells
Language & devices

The Conditional would — the only one in the poem — makes the image hypothetical. An Implied metaphor shading into Synaesthesia (sight turned into sound): children graded by height become a set of chimes or bells. assorted is a word for goods — assorted sizes, assorted colours. melodious and the m and l sounds make the line itself lilt.

Meaning & effect

The poem's most beautiful image is marked as imaginary: no chime sounds; it is a fancy in the onlooker's head, and would is the one place the unseen observer's imagination shows. Rumens lets herself turn the children into music and flags that she has done it. The image also carries its own warning: chimes are instruments, arranged and struck by someone else and valued for the order they make, and assorted sorts children like stock. Harmony and use arrive in a single line.

Line 4
eyes fixed on the shimmering knots, as if at a screen
Language & devices

Simile: like television is a modern comparison from the observer's world, not the children's. flickering fits both a screen and fast fingers, the coloured tufts appearing and vanishing. The children's first action Verb is watch, not tie or weave. Irony: television is passive consumption, but they are producing an image. The line ends on the falling, unstressed syllables of television, the only line that does not end on a stress.

Meaning & effect

The simile measures the distance between the reader's childhood, in which television is what children do instead of working, and this one. It is also an exact picture of skilled repetitive work: the hands go on and the eyes follow, absorbed or detached. Read generously, they are as engrossed as any child; read bleakly, they are hypnotised. Either way the work seems to happen by itself while they look on — the first sign that the poem gives the making to the material rather than to the makers.

Line 5
the paradise pattern rises, so their seat must go up too
Language & devices

Metaphor: the carpet's pattern is the garden of Islam, and it grows — an organic verb for knotting. The garden evokes the Qur'an's paradise (al-janna, the garden) and perhaps the faith itself spreading. The main clause brings the first Future tense and an Agentless passive: the bench will be raised, by whom we are never told. It is literal too: at an upright loom the weavers' seat is raised as the carpet rises.

Meaning & effect

The sacred and the practical share one sentence: paradise grows, furniture is adjusted. The children's labour is credited to the garden, which grows as if unaided, and their only advancement in the poem is that their bench goes up with the product — they rise, but only inside the workshop and only because the work requires it. PoetryProf also reads a figurative raising — the children lifted in others' eyes by fine work, with a pun on raising the benchmark. The missing agent matters: whoever owns the workshop is never named.

Line 6
next, they'll thread red branchwork through the highest foliage
Language & devices

Then continues the sequence, still in the future (will lace). lace means to thread delicately, as in lace-making, and also to tie tight. Metaphor: veins are a leaf's veins and blood vessels, so the woven trees are alive. The Compound words dark-rose and tree-tops crowd the stresses together — six beats, three in a row (DARK-ROSE VEINS) — and the line slows, as dense as the pile. Rose is both a garden flower and a dye colour.

Meaning & effect

The loom's logic and the design's coincide: carpets are woven upward and trees grow upward, so the children reach the tree-tops last, at the top of the frame. They will climb a garden they cannot enter. This is the children's only future verb in the poem, and it promises more work, higher up the same frame; PoetryProf hears the insistent will either as a strong sense of purpose or as a sign that they have no choice. veins gives the carpet life and raises the question of whose life is in it; PoetryProf calls the idea that the children weave in their life's blood ‘too much of a stretch’, preferring the time and devotion they give. The luxury of the line's sound is the luxury of the product.

Line 7
the finished rug will leave on a trader's lorry
Language & devices

A new subject, The carpet: the children vanish for the whole of stanza 3. will travel gives the object a verb normally used of people (Personification). In the merchant's truck the trader appears only as a Possessive attached to a vehicle. truck is modern and commercial, a hard monosyllable after the tree-tops: a deliberate drop in Register.

Meaning & effect

Here the poem's politics are done by grammar. The product gets movement, a route and a destination; the makers stay where they are. The one adult who turns the children's work into money is barely present — no name, no action, only ownership — which is how a supply chain looks from inside a workshop. The reader follows the carpet out of the room, as the market does.

Line 8
mosque attendants will unroll it across the floor
Language & devices

The Pronoun It makes the carpet the protagonist. Passive voice with a named agent, by the servants of the mosque — the only passive in the poem that says who acts. spread means unrolled, laid out. servants is a dignified title for mosque attendants and a word for people who serve. Consonance: truck and mosque end on the same /k/; Sibilance (spread, servants, mosque) softens the sound.

Meaning & effect

Trade hands the carpet to worship in consecutive lines with no seam between them: one journey, not two worlds. The mosque and its servants are treated with respect — the poem does not sneer at faith. servants adds another link to a chain of hands (children, merchant, attendants, worshippers), all serving something, and only the first link is children.

Line 9
thick and yielding, it'll sink beneath the worshippers' weight
Language & devices

Fronted Tactile imagery: Deep and soft is the thickness of a good pile, and the language of someone running a hand over a carpet before buying it. Polysemy: give means to yield under weight and to bestow (PoetryProf). Metaphor: heaped with prayer makes worship physical, the weight of kneeling bodies; heaped is a word for piled goods. Long vowels and p sounds (deep, heaped, prayer) give the stanza its slowest close.

Meaning & effect

This is the carpet's purpose: to cushion worshippers who kneel and press their foreheads to the floor. The children's labour becomes the softness under other people's devotion — a gift, in the second sense of give. Yet heaped measures prayer by bulk, as a market measures goods. The poem neither places the children among those who pray nor excludes them; it moves on. The whole stanza is in the future: the carpet's life lies ahead of it.

Line 10
back in the workshop: still labouring, time their only teacher
Language & devices

Repetition: The children are repeats the opening of line 1, a Framing device that returns the poem to the present tense. The Idiom hard at work is the praise-phrase for a diligent pupil. The Metaphor the school of days unpicks the compound schooldays into a school made of days, and echoes the idiom the school of life (PoetryProf).

Meaning & effect

After the carpet's journey to the mosque the children are exactly where they were nine lines earlier: the carpet has a story, they have a condition. the school of days says two things at once — they are being taught a real craft by apprenticeship, and their only school is the passing of working days. The approving idiom, applied to child labour, carries commendation and accusation together, and the poem lets both stand.

Lines 11–12
the hues of the future leap off their fingertips (runs on)… / …and set solid, locked within the finished past
Language & devices

The poem's only Enjambment: fly ends line 11 and the sentence runs on into freeze. Fronting: the phrase about their fingers comes first, so the verb lands on the very edge of the line. The Hyphenated compounds all-that-will-be and all-that-was turn clauses into nouns, so future and past become things. Antithesis of fly and freeze; Alliteration on f (from, fingers, fly, freeze, frame). frame is the loom's frame, a picture frame and a film's freeze-frame. A Paradox about time.

Meaning & effect

The closing paradox: as each knot is tied, the future — the colours of the pattern still to come — leaves the fingers and at once becomes the past, fixed in the woven part held by the frame. There is no lasting present, only the instant of the knot, which is the tense the children have lived in all along. The line-break acts this out: the colours cross the one boundary the poem allows and are caught by the first word on the other side. Rumens leaves open what is frozen — the pattern, the children's own futures turned into an object others will own, or a permanence that will outlast them — and ends on the past, with a full stop.

THE WHOLE POEM

The Whole Poem

Stepping back: what the poem is doing, first line to last

‘Carpet-weavers, Morocco’ is usually read as a choice between two verdicts: a quiet protest against child labour, or a celebration of craft and faith that the protest reading ignores. The better account is that the poem withholds verdicts so that its grammar can deliver something harder to argue with: a distribution of time. Tense by tense, the carpet is given a future — a journey, a destination, a use — while the children who make it are given the present and a single future verb, which promises more of the same work; and in the final sentence even that present turns out to be no more than the instant in which their future becomes the carpet's past. The poem does not say this is wrong. It makes it visible, row by row, the way a carpet makes its pattern visible.

The method is announced by the gap between title and first line. The title is a caption — trade, comma, country — the label under a photograph or an exhibit; the first line corrects it. The weavers are The children, and they are at the loom of another world: the world in the pattern, the garden of paradise they are knotting; the world they live in apart from the childhood the reader assumes; and the world a visitor sees when looking at Morocco from outside. Rumens does not choose, and a plain declarative sentence closed by a full stop makes the ambiguity sound like a fact.

Stanza one then does what a camera does. Line 2 is all surface — braids, oil, black, bright — arranged in two balanced halves, and it is the poem's one perfectly regular line of iambic pentameter: the children are composed, in both senses. Line 3 goes further and turns them into music, graded by height into a melodious chime. But this is the one line governed by would. The chime is hypothetical, a fancy in the onlooker's head; the poem's prettiest image is the only one it marks as invented, and in marking it Rumens admits that somebody is standing in this workshop turning children into art. The image confesses its cost as well: a chime is a set of instruments, arranged and struck by another hand, and assorted is a word for goods.

Stanza two moves the eye from the children to the work, and quietly takes the work away from them. They watch their knots like television — the reader's emblem of a child's leisure laid over a child's labour, and an exact picture of the trance of skilled repetition, when the hands work and the eyes follow. Then the making passes to the pattern: the garden of Islam grows, as if by itself, and the only thing done in answer is that the bench will be raised — by nobody, since the passive has no agent and no employer appears anywhere in the poem. The bench rises because the carpet rises; the children's one advancement is a piece of furniture adjusted to the product. The future tense has arrived, and it belongs to the design. Next they will work the canopy of the woven trees, the last and highest part: a garden they will climb but never enter.

Stanza three is where the argument is made, and it is made without the children. Every verb is future and every subject is the carpet: it will travel, be spread, give. The object acquires everything its makers lack — movement, a destination, a community, a purpose — and the adults who handle it are glimpsed only as a possessive (the merchant's truck) and as the agent of a passive (the servants of the mosque). Commerce and worship sit in consecutive lines with no seam; their end-words, truck and mosque, even close on the same /k/. The stanza ends in the poem's softest line, the carpet yielding when heaped with prayer, where give means both to sink under weight and to bestow. The children's work becomes the floor beneath other people's devotion. The poem neither mocks that devotion nor places the children within it; it simply moves on.

Stanza four returns to the opening words — The children are — and finds the children where they were, hard at work. Nine lines of narrative have happened to the carpet and none to them. The phrase that places them, the school of days, unpicks schooldays into a school made of days, and the praise-word for a diligent pupil is attached to labour, so that commendation and accusation arrive together. Then the last sentence — the only one longer than a line — turns the poem's tense-pattern into a paradox. From their fingers the colours of all-that-will-be fly, and the verb sits on the very edge of the line, the poem's only run-on: for one moment something crosses a boundary. The next word is freeze. The future leaves the hands and lands as the past, held in the frame — the loom's frame, a picture frame, a film's freeze-frame. The sentence has no present except the instant of the knot, which is exactly the tense the children have been given throughout.

The strongest objection comes from two sides at once. PoetryProf argues that the child-labour reading is too quick: the children belong to a community whose work will be honoured in a mosque; the school of days can echo the proud school of life; fly suggests escape and possibility, and the ending is ‘magical’. From the other side a postcolonial reader can say that the poem is too comfortable: a British poet finds other people's working children beautiful, gives them braids and heights but no thoughts, never declares her own position, and makes from their labour an object — the poem — as portable and decorative as the carpet.

Both objections describe something real, and the poem's design answers both. Against the first: the celebration is there, and the poem lets it be fully felt — the craft is skilled, the faith is treated with dignity, give is generous — but the grammar keeps a ledger that celebration cannot erase. The carpet gets the future tense and the children do not; the colours fly only into a freeze. Against the second: the poem has already confessed. The would of line 3 marks its aestheticising as the onlooker's, and the television simile casts the reader as a viewer of a screen, consuming the image of children who are producing one. The missing ‘I’ is not innocence. It is a refusal to make these children an occasion for an observer's feelings, combined with enough grammatical evidence that the reader cannot leave the room unjudged.

What the poem finally says is not that the children are victims, or artists, but that making turns time into objects, and that it matters whose time is spent. A carpet, like a poem, outlives the moment of its making and travels to people who will never meet its makers. Rumens builds her poem like the carpet — twelve sealed rows, a single thread allowed to cross — so that its paradox applies to her own lines too: they also fix a moment of other people's lives into a frame that others will own.

FORM & STRUCTURE

Form & Structure

How the poem is built, and why it matters

Form & genre

Twelve lines in four unrhymed tercets (three-line stanzas) of equal shape. An observational lyric with no speaker: no ‘I’, no addressee, no question, no exclamation, no verdict. Its nearest relatives are documentary forms — the caption, the photograph, the report — that record without comment.

Line & metre

No fixed metre. A long, level line of 10–13 syllables, most lines carrying four or five strong stresses: a loose pentameter (PoetryProf's description). Eleven of the twelve lines open on a light, unstressed word, so the movement is steadily rising; the exception is line 9, which opens on the stressed Deep. Only line 2 is perfectly regular iambic pentameter.

Rhyme

None, full or half, and no scheme. A few faint end-echoes stand in for it: truck and mosque (lines 7–8) close on the same /k/; raised and days (5, 10) share a vowel and a final z; bright and chime (2–3) share a long i.

Syntax & punctuation

Eleven sentences in twelve lines. Lines 1–10 are each one complete sentence ending in a full stop; lines 11–12 form the only sentence longer than a line. The poem has just three commas (lines 2, 5 and 9) and no colon, semicolon, dash, question mark or exclamation mark.

Enjambment

Exactly one. Line 11 ends on the verb fly, unpunctuated, and runs into freeze. Every other line is end-stopped.

Tense

Present (lines 1–5) → future (5–9, will five times) → present (10–12). Line 3's would is the only conditional. There is no past-tense verb: the past appears only as the hyphenated noun all-that-was.

Four tercets, four movements

The stanzas divide the poem's attention cleanly, and their order is the argument. Stanza 1 (lines 1–3) looks at the children: where they are, how they look, how they are arranged. Stanza 2 (4–6) looks at the work: their eyes on the knots, the pattern growing, the bench rising, the tree-tops still to come. Stanza 3 (7–9) follows the finished carpet out of the room — truck, mosque, prayer — and the children are not in it: no children, no they, no their. Stanza 4 (10–12) comes back to the workshop with the poem's opening words and ends on the paradox about time.

So the shape is an envelope: children, work, carpet, children. The outer stanzas are in the present and begin the same way (The children are); the inner ones carry the poem forward into the future and away from the makers. The carpet's journey sits at the centre, held between the children on either side, as the finished part of a carpet is held in its frame.

Three-line stanzas suit the subject. They read as bands of pattern: four equal blocks, twelve lines, a grid as regular as rows of knots (PoetryProf likens the careful end-stopping to the regularity of carpet design). A three-line unit also cannot fall into two balanced halves, so no stanza settles into a neat either/or; each moves on from its first line instead of answering it. Twelve lines is the length of Blake's ‘The Chimney Sweeper’, the set's other poem about a child working for adults' comfort and worship — and short enough that every line must carry a whole idea.

The turns

There is no single volta, but there are two quiet shifts and one return. The first is the comma in line 5: As the garden of Islam grows is still present tense, and the main clause after the comma is the first future verb. The tense turns at the moment the pattern starts to grow, as if the future belongs to the product. The second shift is line 7, where the grammatical subject changes from the children to The carpet. The return is line 10, which repeats the opening words: after nine lines in which the carpet has travelled to a mosque and been knelt on, the children are where they were. The final sentence then turns from scene to idea — from what the children do to what their doing does to time.

Metre: a level line and its exceptions

Rumens writes a long line that never settles into a pattern, so the reader feels steadiness without song — the rhythm of a report, or of captions read aloud. Against that level surface small disturbances show, and they fall on the lines that matter. (x = unstressed, / = stressed, \ = secondary stress.)

Line Syllables / beats Stress pattern What it does
2 10 / 5 x / x / x / x / x / The one perfectly regular pentameter, balanced on its comma (braids … dresses). The children are composed — metrically as well as visually.
3 13 / 5 x x / x / x / x x / x x / Double light syllables (as-SORT-ed, me-LO-di-ous) give a rocking lilt: the line sounds like the chime it imagines.
4 12 / 4 x / x / x x / x / x \ x Ends on the unstressed tail of television — the only line that does not end on a stress. It trails off, like attention drifting to a screen.
6 12 / 6 x x x / x / / / x x / \ Three stresses in a row (DARK-ROSE VEINS) and a compound to close: the densest line, thick as the pile it describes.
8 11 / 3 x x x / x x / x x x / Only three strong stresses among the passive's small words (it will be… by the… of the…): the lightest line, as unemphatic as its grammar.
9 10 / 5 / x / x x / x / x / The only line that begins on a stress — the hand pressing the pile.
11 13 / 5 x x / x x / x x / x x / / The longest line; two stresses collide at its end (…BE FLY), loading the edge just before the break.
12 10 / 4 x / x x x / x / x / Contracts to ten syllables and settles toward iambic order: the line about freezing into a frame is itself the poem's nearest approach, after line 2, to fixed metre.

The three ten-syllable lines are the children's appearance (2), the carpet's softness (9) and the frozen past (12): the three moments at which something is presented as finished.

Sentences as rows: end-stopping

Each of lines 1–10 is a complete sentence ending in a full stop, and most follow the plainest English pattern, subject–verb–complement: The children are…, They watch…, The carpet will travel…. The effect is of separate statements laid side by side, each finished before the next begins — like a row of knots tied across the width and beaten down before the next row starts. Nothing is subordinated to anything else, so nothing is said to cause anything else: the poem never says because or but. The reader has to make the connections — between the merchant's truck and the children's bench, between the soft carpet and the hard work — and that is where the poem's judgement happens.

The few departures from the pattern mark the shifts. Line 5 is the only sentence before the end built from a subordinate and a main clause, and its comma is the hinge from present to future. Line 9 fronts its adjectives, so that touch (Deep and soft) comes before use. Line 2's comma balances two halves, braids against dresses. These three commas are the only internal punctuation in the poem.

The single enjambment

After eleven closed lines, line 11 does not stop. Its last word is fly, and with no punctuation the colours cross the line-break — the only thing in the poem that crosses a boundary. The first word on the other side is freeze. The enjambment acts out the paradox: the flight is the run-on, and the arrest is the next word. PoetryProf notes the energy the open line-end gives the ending; that energy lasts exactly one line-break.

The sentence also runs future-first and past-last, so its word order performs the passage it describes, and it shrinks as it goes. Line 11 is the longest in the poem (13 syllables), line 12 one of the shortest (10); all-that-will-be has four syllables, all-that-was three. Time contracts as it passes through the children's fingers.

Tense: the poem's hidden structure

Stanza Verbs Tense Grammatical subjects
1 are · are · would make present; one conditional the children; their braids; their heights
2 watch · grows · will be raised · will lace present → future they; the garden; the bench; they
3 will travel · will be spread · will give future only the carpet; it; it
4 are · fly · freeze present the children; the colours

The future arrives in the middle of line 5, as the garden grows: the tense belongs to the design first. The children receive a single future verb, they will lace, and it promises more of the same work, higher up the same frame. In stanza 3 the future belongs wholly to the carpet, the subject of every verb — it will travel, be spread, give — while the makers drop out of the grammar. Stanza 4 returns them to the present, and in the closing sentence future and past are no longer tenses at all but hyphenated nouns: things that can fly and be frozen. PoetryProf hears the insistent will either as purpose or as compulsion; the grammar supports both, since a future that can be stated this confidently is a future already decided.

The closing paradox about time

The last sentence puts the poem's only verbs of motion and stillness side by side, both in the present: the colours fly and freeze. Between all-that-will-be and all-that-was there is no lasting present — only the instant at the fingertips in which a knot is tied and a colour leaves the future to be fixed in the past. That is the paradox: making does not so much happen in time as convert it, and the present tense the children have been given throughout turns out to be no more than that instant.

It also explains why the poem can be so sure of the future. The design is already known — in line 6 the poem can say exactly what the children will weave next — so all-that-will-be is as settled as all-that-was. For the carpet, the future is a journey. For the children, it is the next row.

Title and frame

The title is a caption — trade, comma, place — and the first line corrects it: the weavers are The children. The poem is bound at both ends by hyphens. The title's Carpet-weavers fastens people to their product; the last two lines fasten whole clauses into single words; in between, dark-rose and tree-tops knot the design together. The final image of form is the frame: the loom that holds the carpet, the picture-frame around a scene, and the shape of the poem itself, which has held these children in twelve fixed lines.

SOUND

Sound

What the poem does to the ear

Rhyme

None. The only end-echoes are faint: truck / mosque (/k/), raised / days (long a + z), bright / chime (long i).

Rhythm

Level, rising and end-stopped: eleven full stops, eleven silences. The one missing pause is after fly.

Signature sound

The f-chain of the ending: from, fingers, fly, freeze, frame.

Stanza 1: the pleasure of the picture

The first stanza is the poem's most enjoyable to say, and that is part of its point. Line 2 runs on bright plosive b's — braids, black, bright — in strict iambic alternation, so the description sounds as neat as the children look. Line 3 moves to liquids and nasals: the m's of make and melodious close on the m of chime, and the long i of heights rings with chime (and with bright at the end of the line before). It is music describing music, and it is the line governed by would. Rumens lets the sound be lovely at exactly the moment she marks the loveliness as an onlooker's fancy.

Stanza 2: work and density

Line 4 is quicker and thinner: short vowels in flickering, the k of flickering and like, the t's of knots and television, and the short o shared by watch and knots. It sounds like many small, identical actions, and it trails away on the soft, unstressed end of television. Line 5 is threaded with z sounds (as, Islam, grows, raised). Then a long a runs from raised into lace and veins, and line 6 piles up its stresses — dark-rose veins — before closing on the hard t's of tree-tops. The sound thickens as the pattern does.

Stanza 3: from commerce to worship

A hard /k/ marks the stages of the carpet's journey: carpet, truck, mosque. Truck lands as a blunt, closed monosyllable after the tree-tops. Line 8 softens into sibilance — spread, servants, mosque — and line 9 into long vowels and gentle p's: Deep, heaped, prayer. The long ee of deep and heaped is the sound of sinking into pile. Across three lines the consonants relax as the carpet passes from trade to devotion, doing tonal work the poem refuses to do in statement — while the shared /k/ of truck and mosque keeps the two places in one chain.

Stanza 4: the f-chain

The children are returns with the steady beats of hard at work and the long vowels of school of days. Then the ending turns on one consonant: From, fingers, fly, freeze, frame — five f-words in two lines, giving the source (fingers), the motion (fly), the arrest (freeze) and the enclosure (frame). Fly and freeze begin almost identically, f and then a liquid or r, for two opposite actions, so that escape and capture sound like versions of one word. The long ee of freeze recalls deep and heaped: the carpet's softness and the children's frozen colours share a vowel.

The closing compounds echo each other too. all-that-will-be and all-that-was share their first two syllables and differ only at the verb, so the ear hears future and past as near-twins, one small sound apart. The poem's last sound is the short, closed was; its first line ended on world. It begins on a place and ends on a tense.

Silence

The poem's most constant sound is the pause. Eleven full stops make eleven silences, each line completed and set down before the next begins, at the slow, level pace of someone recording what they see. Against that, the single unpunctuated line-end after fly is heard as much as seen: the one place where the voice is not allowed to rest — and it lasts only until freeze.

MOTIFS & SYMBOLS

Motifs & Symbols

Images that recur, and what they accumulate

Motifs and symbols

1. Another world, and the garden

The poem's first noun phrase, another world, is left open, and the poem fills it three ways. By line 5 it is the world in the pattern: the garden of Islam, the Qur'anic paradise (al-janna, ‘the garden’) knotted into wool, which grows as if alive and acquires dark-rose veins in its tree-tops. By stanza 3 it is the world the carpet will enter — the mosque, the worshippers, the prayer. And all along it is the world of the workshop, apart from the reader's idea of childhood.

The garden gathers the poem's central irony. The children make paradise row by row, and the poem never places them in it: they will reach the tree-tops only as weavers. The garden climbs, they climb with it on a raised bench, and then the garden leaves on a truck.

2. Watching, screens and the frame

Someone is looking throughout, though no one says ‘I’. The look first shows in the conditional would of line 3, where an onlooker imagines the children as a chime. In line 4 the children themselves watch — their own knots, like television — and the simile brings in the onlooker's world of screens, where images flicker and children are viewers, not workers. The motif ends in freeze and frame: a freeze-frame, the moment a moving picture stops and is held.

A thread of film language — flickering, television, freeze, frame — runs through a poem about hand-weaving. It implicates the reader, who is also watching children on a page and is shown, in the end, a frame.

3. Height and rising

Vertical movement accumulates. The children have assorted heights (3); the garden grows and the bench will be raised (5); they will reach the tree-tops (6); the carpet will be heaped with prayer (9); the colours fly (11). Everything rises — but the children rise only because the product does. The bench is lifted to keep them level with the work, so their one ascent in the poem is a piece of furniture adjusted to the carpet (PoetryProf also hears a figurative raising: the children lifted in others' estimation by fine work). The motif ends with the one upward movement that looks free, the flying colours, and stops it at once with freeze.

4. Hands and the chain of service

The poem passes the carpet through a chain of hands. The children's fingers tie the knots (4) and lace the veins (6); the merchant is implied only in the possessive of the merchant's truck (7); the servants of the mosque spread it (8); the worshippers press it with their bodies (9); and the poem ends back where the chain began, at the children's fingers. Every link serves something — trade, a mosque, God — and only the first link is children.

The motif also tracks who gets credit for acting. The children act (watch, lace); the bench is raised by no one; the merchant does nothing but own; the servants act on the carpet; and in the last sentence the colours themselves are the subject of fly and freeze. The makers' hands are where everything starts, and the grammar keeps moving the credit elsewhere.

5. Colour passing from children to carpet

Line 2 gives the children their colours: braids oiled and black, dresses bright. After that the colour in the poem belongs to the carpet — the dark-rose of the woven veins, and finally the colours of all-that-will-be, which leave the children's fingers and become the carpet's fixed past. The brightness moves from the children into the object.

Veins makes the transfer bodily: the woven garden has a circulation. PoetryProf asks whether the children are weaving their life's blood into the carpet and calls the idea ‘too much of a stretch’, preferring the time and devotion they give. Either way, the colour that was theirs in line 2 is the carpet's by line 12.

THEMES

Themes

The ideas the poem is arguing about

01

Child labour, seen without a verdict

The poem's subject is children doing skilled adult work, and its method is to describe it without one word of judgement. The evidence of harm is all in the grammar and the idioms: the children are hard at work — the praise-phrase for a diligent pupil — in the school of days, a school made only of working days; the bench is raised by an agent the poem never names; the only adult with a stake in their labour appears as a possessive, the merchant's truck. There is no employer, wage, hour or complaint anywhere in the poem.

Yet the poem also refuses to make the children pitiable. They are cared for (oiled braids), dressed in colour, absorbed in work they do well. Rumens keeps the full picture — the craft is real, the ordinary childhood is missing — and leaves the reader to put the two together. That restraint is a stance, not neutrality: a verdict the reader assembles is harder to dismiss than one delivered.

02

The object outruns its makers

Tense carries this theme. The carpet is given a future: it will travel, will be spread, will give. It gets a vehicle, a destination, a community and a use. The children are given the present, one future verb that promises more work (they will lace), and in stanza 3 no place in the poem at all. Stanza 4 finds them exactly where line 1 left them.

The theme reaches beyond Morocco. Anything made by hand — a carpet, a garment, a poem — leaves its makers and goes to people who will never meet them. The poem makes that ordinary fact visible, and asks what it means when the makers are children.

03

Faith, trade and the chain of hands

The carpet's route runs from workshop to truck to mosque in consecutive lines with no seam, and the poem's vocabulary mixes the two worlds: assorted and heaped are words for goods, set beside the garden of Islam, servants and prayer. Commerce and worship are not opposed here; they are stages of one journey.

The poem treats the faith with respect. The mosque's servants are dignified, the carpet's purpose is generous — it will give, cushioning those who kneel — and nothing sneers. The question it leaves is about placement, not belief: the children make the floor of other people's devotion, and the poem neither includes them among the worshippers nor shuts them out. It simply moves on.

04

Time turned into objects

The last sentence makes weaving a way of converting time: all-that-will-be flies from the children's fingers and freezes into all-that-was. The future becomes the past in the instant of the knot, with no lasting present between. As a claim about making, this is true of all craft: every knot fixes something that could have been otherwise.

But it lands on children. What leaves their fingers is, on one reading, their own future — their days, spent and fixed into an object someone else will own; on another, a permanence that will outlast them. The whole tense pattern prepares the paradox: the children live in the present, and the present turns out to be only the moment in which their time becomes the carpet's.

05

Beauty and the watcher's eye

The poem is beautiful, and it knows that beauty is part of the problem. Its loveliest lines — the braids and dresses, the melodious chime, the dark-rose veins, the Deep and soft pile — are the ones that make the scene attractive to an outsider. Rumens marks the most aestheticising image with the poem's only conditional, would, and brings the observer's culture into the simile like television.

So the poem examines its own looking. The reader stands where a visitor or a customer stands, admiring craft and children together, and the grammar keeps reminding them what they are admiring. There is no ‘I’, but the act of watching is everywhere.

06

Craft, skill and learning

What the children do is difficult and valuable, and the poem respects it: they knot a design so fine it can be said to grow, and they will lace its highest veins. The school of days can be heard straight — a real apprenticeship in a craft learned through daily practice, the proud school of life that PoetryProf hears in it — and bitterly, as the only school these children get. The poem holds both at once: skill gained, childhood spent.

DIFFICULT MOMENTS

Difficult Moments

Where the poem is genuinely undecidable — and what to do about it

Cruxes

1. the loom of another world — whose world?

The difficulty. The first line gives another world no referent, and loom can be a noun or a verb.

Competing readings. (a) The world in the pattern: the carpet depicts a garden of paradise, so the children sit at the loom that makes another world — confirmed by the garden of Islam grows four lines later. (b) The world the children inhabit: apart from the reader's idea of childhood, a world of work instead of school, which the closing school of days supports. (c) The outsider's phrase: to a British reader of the 1980s Morocco is the kind of place people call ‘another world’, so the phrase may record — and expose — an exoticising view. (d) The verb: to loom is to rise up threateningly. PoetryProf notes the frightening connotation, then asks for the literal sense first; on this reading the adult world of labour bears down on the children.

What a strong answer does. It refuses to pick one and shows how the poem activates each in turn: the garden in stanza 2, the separate childhood in stanza 4, the outsider's eye in the television simile. The plain declarative sentence makes the ambiguity sound like a fact, which is how the whole poem works.

2. a melodious chime — admiration or complicity?

The difficulty. The poem's prettiest image turns working children into music. Is Rumens celebrating them, or showing how easily an onlooker turns children into a picture?

Competing readings. (a) Tender admiration: the children's graded heights look harmonious, and the image honours their order and grace. (b) Self-exposure: would — the only conditional in the poem — marks the chime as imagined, so the one place an onlooker's mind shows is the moment of aestheticising, and the poem confesses it. (c) Critique: a chime is a set of instruments, graded, arranged and struck by someone else, and assorted is a word for stock. The image contains the use it seems to celebrate.

What a strong answer does. It notices that the conditional and the stock-word sit inside the beautiful line, so admiration and its cost arrive together. The image is both a real response and a test of the reader's response.

3. the school of days — deprivation or education?

The difficulty. Line 10 returns to the poem's opening words and fixes the children in place with two phrases, hard at work and the school of days, that can sound proud or bitter.

Competing readings. (a) Deprivation: there is no school, only days; the children's education is the passing of working time, and hard at work — praise for a pupil — becomes an accusation. (b) Education: a craft is being learned by apprenticeship, and school of days echoes the proud school of life (PoetryProf), honouring learning that does not happen in classrooms. (c) Time as the teacher: whatever the children learn, the subject is time itself — which prepares the closing paradox.

What a strong answer does. It reads the line against line 1 — nine lines of the carpet's progress and none of theirs — and lets the commendation and the complaint stand together, as the idiom does. The repetition is the evidence: their situation has continuation but no story.

4. The ending — what is frozen, and is fly an escape?

The difficulty. The last sentence is a paradox, and its subject, the colours of all-that-will-be, is deliberately unspecified. Whose future flies, and what does the freeze mean?

Competing readings. (a) The pattern: the carpet's colours, waiting in the future of the design, become fixed past the instant they are knotted — a general truth about making. (b) The children's futures: their days and possibilities leave their fingers and are frozen into an object others will own; on this reading it is the coldest line in the poem. (c) Permanence and agency: PoetryProf hears fly as escape or possibility, calls the ending ‘magical’, and notes that the children, passive watchers at the start, end up responsible for everything that was and will be; the carpet will carry their work long after them. (d) Determinism: the design is already known — line 6 can say what they will weave next — so all-that-will-be is as settled as all-that-was.

What a strong answer does. It ties the meaning to the form. The colours fly over the poem's only enjambment and are caught by the next word, freeze: the flight is real but lasts one line-break. A strong reading lets the magic and the arrest coexist — the children do make something lasting, and what lasts is fixed in a frame they stay behind.

CLOSE ANALYSIS

Close Analysis

The moments that repay pressure, worked through

Quotation analysis

1. The title against The children and another world

Techniques: caption title; compound noun; correction; polysemy; ambiguity.

The title has the shape of a label under a photograph: a trade, a comma, a country. Carpet-weavers names people by their product, with no age, number or name. The poem's first three words replace the label — the weavers are The children — and the definite article presents them as already in front of us. Then loom doubles as the weaving frame and a looming threat (PoetryProf notes the frightening connotation), and another world takes three referents: the paradise garden in the design, the separate world of children who work instead of going to school, and the outsider's phrase for a faraway country.

Intention and effect: Rumens lets the reader see the scene as a market or a museum would — workers, located — and corrects that view at once, so every later description of skill is shadowed by the word children. The plain, end-stopped sentence makes three meanings sound like one fact: the children make one world, live in another, and are seen from a third.

2. braids are oiled and black

Techniques: visual imagery; alliteration; parallel clauses around a caesura; regular iambic pentameter.

Line 2 gives four concrete details in two balanced halves, braids answered by dresses, with b-alliteration (braids, black, bright). oiled implies care — someone prepared these children this morning — so they cannot dissolve into a statistic. But the only verb is are: they are described, not doing. It is the poem's one perfectly regular pentameter.

Intention and effect: The children are made individual and attractive in the same breath — composed, in both senses. The line's neatness is part of what the poem examines: how easily working children become a pleasing picture.

3. a melodious chime

Techniques: conditional; synaesthesia; implied metaphor; diction of goods.

would is the only conditional in the poem: no chime sounds, and the image is an onlooker's fancy. Height becomes sound, and children graded by size become a set of bells. The adjective assorted, earlier in the line, is a shop word — assorted sizes, assorted colours.

Intention and effect: The poem's loveliest image is the only one it marks as invented, so the one moment an observer's mind shows is the moment of turning children into art. The image carries its own warning: instruments are arranged and struck by someone else, and assorted sorts children like stock.

4. like television

Techniques: simile; irony; shift of register; feminine ending.

The comparison comes from the observer's world, not the children's. flickering fits a screen and fast fingers. The children's first action is watch — not tie or weave — and the line ends on the trailing, unstressed end of television.

Intention and effect: Television is what children in the reader's culture do instead of working; the simile measures the distance without comment. It also catches the trance of skilled repetition — hands working, eyes following — and reverses the usual roles: these viewers are producing an image, while the reader watching them is the one consuming it.

5. the bench will be raised

Techniques: agentless passive; first future tense; literal detail with figurative force; organic metaphor.

At an upright loom the weavers' plank is raised as the carpet climbs, so this is plain workshop fact. But the passive names no agent, and no employer appears anywhere in the poem. The clause follows the garden of Islam grows, whose organic verb credits the work to the design.

Intention and effect: The children's one advancement in the poem is a piece of furniture adjusted to the product: they rise only because the carpet does. PoetryProf adds a figurative raising — the children lifted in others' eyes by fine work — but the grammar keeps the authority over them invisible.

6. dark-rose veins

Techniques: metaphor; compound words; stress cluster; double-edged verb.

veins belong to a leaf and to a body, so the woven garden lives and circulates. lace means to thread delicately and to tie tight. Three stresses in a row (DARK-ROSE VEINS) make this the densest line in the poem. And they will lace is the children's only future verb: more work, at the top of the frame.

Intention and effect: The children will reach the tree-tops of a garden they can never enter. veins raises a question the poem does not ask — whose life is in the carpet? PoetryProf calls the life's-blood reading ‘too much of a stretch’ and prefers the time and devotion given; either way, the carpet comes alive as the makers move out of view.

7. the merchant's truck

Techniques: change of grammatical subject; personification; possessive; register shift; consonance.

Stanza 3 opens with The carpet, and the children vanish for three lines. The carpet will travel — a verb for people. The merchant, the one adult who turns the children's work into money, exists only as a possessive attached to a vehicle. truck is hard, modern and commercial after the tree-tops, and shares its /k/ with mosque at the end of the next line.

Intention and effect: The politics are done by grammar: the product gets a route, a destination and a verb of freedom; the makers stay put. The merchant's near-absence is how a supply chain looks from the workshop floor — and from the room where the carpet ends up.

8. it will give … heaped with prayer

Techniques: polysemy; tactile imagery; metaphor; fronted adjectives.

Deep and soft is the touch of a fine pile, the language of a hand run over a carpet before buying. give means both to yield under weight and to bestow (PoetryProf's double reading). heaped with prayer makes worship physical — the weight of kneeling bodies — in a word used for piled goods.

Intention and effect: The carpet's purpose is generous and the poem respects it: the children's work becomes the softness beneath other people's devotion. But heaped measures prayer by bulk, and the poem neither places the children among the worshippers nor excludes them. It moves on, and the silence is the reader's to fill.

9. the school of days

Techniques: repetition and framing; idiom; metaphor.

The children are repeats the opening of line 1: after nine lines of the carpet's journey, they are where they were. hard at work is the praise-phrase for a diligent pupil. the school of days unpicks schooldays into a school made of days, and echoes the school of life (PoetryProf).

Intention and effect: Praise and accusation arrive in the same words. The children are learning a real craft, and their only school is the passing of working time. The return to the present tense confirms that their situation has continuation but no story.

10. all-that-will-be fly … freeze

Techniques: the poem's only enjambment; hyphenated compounds; paradox; antithesis; f-alliteration.

The colours fly across the poem's only open line-end and are caught by the next word, freeze. The compounds turn clauses into nouns, so future and past become materials. frame is the loom, a picture-frame and a film's freeze-frame. fingers, fly, freeze and frame chain the sentence on one sound.

Intention and effect: As each knot is tied, the future becomes the past with no lasting present between — the instant the children have lived in all along. Rumens leaves open what is frozen: the pattern, the children's own futures turned into an object others will own, or a permanence that will outlast them. PoetryProf finds the moment ‘magical’; the form allows that magic exactly one line-break before it stops.

CRITICAL LENSES

Critical Lenses

What each way of reading makes visible, and what it flattens

Critical lenses

Formalist

What it makes visible. The poem as a mechanism. Eleven end-stopped lines and one enjambment, falling on fly and landing on freeze. One conditional, on the one aestheticising image. One agentless passive, on the one act of authority. A stanza entirely in the future in which the children do not appear. No past-tense verb, and the past admitted only as a noun in the last line. Each formal fact corresponds to something the poem declines to say aloud, which is how a poem with no stated argument makes one.

What it flattens. Why any of it matters — the children, Morocco, the trade. A purely formal reading can admire the carpet and forget the weavers, repeating the very danger the poem dramatises.

Marxist / materialist

What it makes visible. The carpet as a commodity. As it travels, the labour in it disappears: the product takes over the verbs (The carpet will travel), the garden grows as if by itself, and the merchant is reduced to a possessive — ownership without action. assorted and heaped are market words. The children's time is converted into a saleable object, all-that-will-be into all-that-was. The poem stages what Marx called the fetishism of commodities: a made thing that seems to have a life of its own, while the people who made it drop out of view.

What it flattens. The faith and the craft. The carpet's destination is a mosque, not a showroom, and give is generous; a materialist reading can turn devotion into mere disguise and miss the poem's respect for both the skill and the prayer.

Postcolonial

What it makes visible. The observer's position. A British poet looks at Moroccan children, finds them lovely, and gives them braids, heights and fingers but no thoughts or speech. another world can be an exoticising phrase; like television brings in the West's frame of reference; the reader becomes a consumer of the image, as of the carpet. The absent ‘I’ can be read as evasion: a gaze that never has to account for itself.

What it flattens. The poem's self-awareness. would marks the aestheticising as the onlooker's; the television simile turns the eye back on the viewer's own culture; and the refusal to speak for the children is arguably more respectful than putting words in their mouths. PoetryProf's warning against equating Morocco with poverty cuts against a reading that sees only victims.

Feminist

What it makes visible. The weavers are almost certainly girls — the braids and dresses suggest it, and Moroccan carpet weaving has long been women's and girls' work. Textile craft is one of the oldest forms of women's labour to be prized as art in the object and ignored in the maker. Once finished, the carpet passes into public worlds of trade and worship, the merchant and the mosque, and the makers stay inside.

What it flattens. The poem never says ‘girls’; its stated focus is childhood (The children), and a gender reading has to infer what the poem leaves implicit.

Historicist

What it makes visible. The poem's moment. It was written by 1987, in the years when child labour in carpet-making was being investigated — the Anti-Slavery Society published Child Labour in Morocco's Carpet Industry in 1978 — and long before Morocco raised its minimum working age to 15 (2003). A British reader then would know the imported carpet and the campaign against how it was made; the poem answers that context by withholding the campaign's rhetoric.

What it flattens. The poem names no date, report or law, and its closing paradox about time is meant to reach beyond any decade. Read only historically, a meditation sounds like a documentary.

Reader-response

What it makes visible. The reader's position is built in. We watch, as the children watch their knots and as viewers watch television; we may own a carpet like this one; and because the poem never tells us what to feel, the judgement we form is ours. The discomfort many readers feel is evidence of the poem working.

What it flattens. It can make the poem about the reader's feelings — exactly what the absent ‘I’ refuses to do with the observer's.

OTHER READINGS

Other Readings

Contested interpretations, and where each is weak

Other readings

1. A protest poem by implication

The poem indicts child labour through grammar instead of statement.

Evidence: hard at work in the school of days (there is no school); the agentless bench will be raised; the merchant's truck (someone profits, unseen); stanza 3's future tense, which belongs only to the carpet; and the closing image of the children's futures frozen into someone else's object.

Weakness: it has to ignore what the poem plainly honours — the skill, the care in the oiled braids, the dignity of the mosque, the generosity of give — and it cannot explain why there is not one word of complaint.

2. A celebration of craft and devotion

PoetryProf argues that the language resists the quick reading of the poem as a critique of forced child labour: the children's work may be a genuine act of religious significance and devotion, and Morocco should not be equated with poverty.

Evidence: the garden of Islam grows; the dignity of the servants of the mosque; give as bestowal; the school of days as the proud school of life; the ‘magical’ ending in which the colours fly.

Weakness: it must read hard at work and the school of days against their grain, and it cannot account for the tense pattern — the carpet's journey while the children stay — or for a word like assorted.

3. The poem as a postcolonial problem

The poem itself is complicit: a British poet turns other people's working children into twelve beautiful lines for a British readership.

Evidence: the children are given exteriors and no inner lives; the connoisseur's vocabulary (Deep and soft, assorted); the phrase another world; no ‘I’ to account for the looking.

Weakness: the poem marks its own aestheticising with would, turns the screen-simile back on the viewer's culture, and refuses to speak for the children — so the reading accuses the poem of a blindness it openly displays.

4. A poem about making poems

‘Text’ and ‘textile’ share a Latin root, texere, to weave. The poem is twelve tight rows, made one at a time, that freeze a moment of other lives into a frame — and it too will travel, be spread out in classrooms, and outlive the people in it.

Evidence: the stanzas as bands of pattern; end-stopped lines as rows; frame as picture-frame and poem-shape; the last sentence's paradox, true of all making.

Weakness: it can turn the children into a metaphor for the poet — the very appropriation the poem guards against — and the poem never mentions writing.

5. A future already decided

The future in the poem is not open: the bench will be raised, they will lace the tree-tops, the carpet will travel — all predictable, because the design and the trade are fixed. So all-that-will-be is as settled as all-that-was.

Evidence: the confident will, five times; line 6 knowing exactly what the children will weave next; PoetryProf's sense that will may mean they have no choice.

Weakness: it overrides fly, the poem's one word of release, and the reading of the ending as possibility; determinism is a pattern in the grammar, not something the poem states.

6. The children as true makers

The children are not victims but the poem's artists: passive watchers at the start, they end as the source of everything. PoetryProf notes that they finish responsible for all that was and all that will be.

Evidence: the closing sentence begins with their fingers; the colours are their creation; the carpet's whole future depends on their present.

Weakness: the grammar keeps giving the agency away — the garden grows, the bench will be raised, and the colours, not the children, are the subject of fly and freeze — and the poem never shows the children choosing anything.

REVISION NOTES

Revision Notes

The working notes, quotation by quotation

Title

Carpet-weavers, Morocco

Analysis
  • Caption format: trade + comma + place → photo caption / museum label
  • Names people by their product → no ages, names or number
  • Line 1 corrects it: The children → gap between weavers and children = the poem's subject
  • PoetryProf: title makes no mention of children → first line a surprise
Effect, style & response
  • Reader placed like a visitor looking at a labelled exhibit

Context: Rumens + the poem

Analysis
  • Carol Rumens (1944–2026): b. Forest Hill, south London; d. 25 April 2026
  • Poet, critic, novelist, translator (Russian); Guardian 'Poem of the week' 2007–2026
  • First collected in Selected Poems (Chatto & Windus, 1987) → date = 'by 1987'
  • Compared to Larkin → plain, level, end-stopped statements
  • Later work → foreign places, languages, customs
  • No 'I' in the poem → the observer is never shown

Context: carpets + child labour

Analysis
  • Upright loom: vertical warps, knots tied in rows, woven bottom → top
    • Bench raised as the carpet grows → the bench will be raised = literal
    • Tree-tops of a garden design = woven last
  • Anti-Slavery Society report: Child Labour in Morocco's Carpet Industry (1978)
  • Christian Science Monitor, 2001: ~50 children at looms in Fes, some ~6 or younger; 10 hrs/day for $14 a month
  • 'Small hands weave better' = employers' excuse, not a fact
  • Morocco Labour Code 2003 → minimum working age 15
  • Rural Amazigh (Berber) rugs vs urban workshop carpets (e.g. Rabat) → poem suggests a workshop; names no town

Context: the garden of Islam

Analysis
  • Qur'an: paradise = al-janna = 'the garden' → 'gardens under which rivers flow'
  • Garden carpets: formal garden seen from above (trees, flowers, water channels)
  • Prayer = standing, bowing, kneeling, prostration → why mosque floors are carpeted
  • Prayer-rug niche ↔ mihrab (direction of Mecca)
  • the garden of Islam = Rumens's own phrase: design + paradise + the faith

Structure + overview

Analysis
  • 12 lines, 4 unrhymed tercets; loose pentameter (10–13 syllables)
    • Only line 2 perfectly regular iambic pentameter
  • 11 sentences: lines 1–10 each one end-stopped sentence
  • Only one enjambment: 11 → 12, on fly
  • Stanzas: children (1) → work (2) → carpet's journey (3) → children again (4)
    • Envelope: The children are opens lines 1 + 10
  • Tense: present → future (stanza 3 all future, children absent) → present
    • No past-tense verb; past only as a noun: all-that-was
  • Form as carpet: tercets = bands; end-stopped lines = rows of knots beaten down
Effect, style & response
  • Report/caption style → no verdict → reader does the judging
1

the loom of another world

Analysis
  • loom = weaving frame + verb to loom (threatening) — PoetryProf
  • another world → 3 readings:
    • the world in the pattern (paradise garden)
    • a world apart from normal childhood (work, not school)
    • the outsider's 'other world' (exoticising Morocco)
  • Plain declarative + full stop → ambiguity sounds like fact
2

oiled and black

Analysis
  • Visual imagery; b-alliteration (braids, black, bright)
  • oiled → cared for, prepared by someone → real children, not a statistic
  • Balanced halves around the comma; only perfectly regular pentameter
  • But: described, not doing → painter's / photographer's eye → children composed
3

a melodious chime

Analysis
  • would = only conditional → imagined; the observer's fancy shows here
  • Synaesthesia: heights → sound; graded like a set of bells
  • Instruments = played by someone else → harmony + use
  • assorted = shop word (assorted sizes)
Effect, style & response
  • Prettiest image = the one marked as invented → poem confesses its own aestheticising
4

like television

Analysis
  • Simile from the reader's world → TV = what children do instead of work
  • Irony: viewers consume images; these children produce one
  • flickering → screen + fast fingers → trance of repetitive work (absorbed or hypnotised)
  • First action verb = watch, not weave
  • Starts film vocabulary: flickering → television → freeze → frame
5–6

the bench will be raised

Analysis
  • the garden of Islam grows → organic verb → design grows 'by itself'
  • First future tense, after the comma

  • Literal: bench raised as the carpet rises
    • PoetryProf: also raised in others' eyes; 'raising the benchmark'

7–8

the merchant's truck

Analysis
  • New subject: The carpet → children vanish for all of stanza 3

9

heaped with prayer

Analysis
  • Deep and soft → tactile; buyer's language; only line starting on a stress
  • give → yield under weight + bestow (PoetryProf: polysemic)
  • heaped → bulk-goods word → devotion measured like goods
  • Kneeling + prostration → children's work = floor beneath others' devotion

the school of days

Analysis
  • Repeats The children are (line 1) → frame; nothing has changed for them

all-that-will-be → all-that-was

Analysis

Themes

CONNECTIONS

Connections

How this poem pairs with the rest of the set

Comparison hooks

With 'The Chimney Sweeper' (William Blake)

Link: children working for adults' comfort and worship, in two poems of exactly twelve lines. Blake's sweep, ‘A little black thing’ in the snow, works while his parents praise ‘God and his priest and king’; Rumens's children weave a carpet that will be heaped with prayer.

Shared technique: religious language fastened to child labour, and children heard as music — Blake's ‘notes of woe’, Rumens's melodious chime. Both poems also show adults who believe no harm is done: Blake's parents think they have ‘done me no injury’; Rumens's mosque receives a carpet whose making is never mentioned.

Difference: Blake gives the poem to the child, who names the guilty and accuses them of making ‘a heaven of our misery’. Rumens gives her children no voice, names no one, and lets tense and grammar carry the charge. Blake's rhymes deliver a verdict; Rumens's unrhymed, end-stopped lines withhold one.

With 'Before the Sun' (Charles Mungoshi)

Link: a child at work, and things flying from working hands. Mungoshi's boy splits a log before sunrise and loves it — at fourteen, big logs ‘are what you want’.

Shared technique: a stretched instant of time and a sacred note. Mungoshi's ‘bright chips’ ‘fly from the sharp axe’ and settle ‘eternities later’; Rumens's colours fly from the children's fingers and freeze into the past. His smoke rises like ‘a sacrificial prayer’; her carpet is heaped with prayer.

Difference: Mungoshi's boy works for his family's day and his own pleasure, and the poem lives inside his senses and desires. Rumens's children have braids, heights and fingers but no thoughts: the poem never enters them. His work feels like freedom; theirs is the school of days.

With 'Storyteller' (Liz Lochhead)

Link: women's and children's hands, and textile craft as an image of art. Lochhead's storyteller talks while ‘five or forty fingers stitched’, and telling ‘was like spinning’; Rumens's children knot a garden.

Shared technique: the thread as a figure for making that outlasts its moment, and the same verb at the end. Lochhead's stories, kept in ‘the sleeping heads of the children’, wait ‘till they flew again’; Rumens's colours fly — and freeze.

Difference: direction and ownership. Lochhead's craft passes into the children and lives on in them; Rumens's passes out of the children into an object that leaves on the merchant's truck. Storytelling ‘was her work’ and is valued by the household around her; the weavers' work is valued only in the finished carpet, far away.

With 'Follower' (Seamus Heaney)

Link: manual skill watched closely, and childhood measured against work. Heaney's father is ‘An expert’, ‘Mapping the furrow exactly’, while the boy is a stumbling nuisance behind him.

Shared technique: exact technical detail of a craft — the plough's wing and sock; the knots, the raised bench, the tree-tops woven last — and an ending that turns on time: Heaney's father now stumbles behind him and ‘will not go away’; Rumens's future freezes into the past.

Difference: the roles are inverted. Heaney's child longs to work and cannot; Rumens's children are the experts, and there is no adult master anywhere in the poem. Heaney looks back through memory with an ‘I’; Rumens looks on in the present, with none.

With 'Hunting Snake' (Judith Wright)

Link: intense, wordless watching that ends without a stated conclusion. Wright's walkers ‘froze half-through a pace’ to watch the snake pass; Rumens's colours freeze into a frame.

Shared technique: a single moment held still, and a strong sense of season and time — Wright's ‘late season's grace’, Rumens's all-that-will-be and all-that-was.

Difference: Wright's watchers are a ‘we’, part of the scene and shaken by it; Rumens's observer never appears. Wright's subject is a creature moving freely past; Rumens's is children held in place while their work moves on.

With 'Where I Come From' (Elizabeth Brewster)

Link: how places and work make people. Brewster begins ‘People are made of places’ and lists ‘the smell of work’ among what city people carry; Rumens's children are made by their place of work, where the loom is their school.

Shared technique: a calm, observational voice building a world from concrete details — Brewster's ‘battered schoolhouses’, Rumens's school of days.

Difference: Brewster's speaker knows her place from inside and carries it in her mind wherever she goes; Rumens's children are seen only from outside, and what they make is carried away from their place while they stay.

Shall I compare thee…? The comparison is made, summer loses on every count, and the beloved’s beauty is moved off nature’s short lease into the one property time cannot take back: this poem.

CONTEXT

Context

The world the poem came out of

The Poet: William Shakespeare (1564–1616)

Shakespeare was baptised in Holy Trinity Church, Stratford-upon-Avon, on 26 April 1564, the son of John Shakespeare, a glover and wool-dealer who rose to be the town's bailiff, and Mary Arden. He married Anne Hathaway in 1582; their children were Susanna (born 1583) and the twins Hamnet and Judith (1585). Hamnet died in 1596, aged eleven. By 1592 Shakespeare was established in London as an actor and playwright, and from 1594 he was a leading member and sharer of the Lord Chamberlain's Men, the company for which he wrote most of his plays. He put his earnings into property: New Place, one of the largest houses in Stratford, in 1597, and a share in the lease of Stratford tithes in 1605. He died on 23 April 1616.

Besides the plays he wrote two long narrative poems, Venus and Adonis (1593) and The Rape of Lucrece (1594), both dedicated to the young Henry Wriothesley, third Earl of Southampton: the only works he is known to have dedicated himself. The 154 sonnets are his largest body of non-dramatic verse.

Two titles: 'Sonnet 18' and 'Shall I Compare Thee…?'

The 1609 edition prints the sonnets numbered and untitled; nothing shows that Shakespeare gave any of them a title. 'Sonnet 18' therefore names a form and a position (this is the eighteenth poem in the sequence), and it is the title Cambridge's 0475 syllabus uses for the 2026–2028 selection from Songs of Ourselves Volume 1. Many anthologies title the poem from its first words instead. When Cambridge set it in June 2015 and November 2016, from Jo Phillips's anthology Poems Deep and Dangerous, the papers printed it as 'Shall I Compare Thee…?'.
