The two names point in different directions. The number places the poem in an argument with the seventeen sonnets before it; the first-line title isolates it as a free-standing love lyric and makes its opening question its identity.

Written in the 1590s, printed in 1609

Nobody knows exactly when Sonnet 18 was written. In Palladis Tamia (1598) Francis Meres praised Shakespeare's "sugred Sonnets among his priuate friends", so sonnets by him were circulating in manuscript by then, and versions of two (138 and 144) were printed in The Passionate Pilgrim in 1599. Most scholars place the bulk of the early-numbered sonnets in the 1590s, some perhaps revised later. The poem is therefore well over four centuries old, and it has been in print since 1609.

Those years included long closures of the London playhouses because of plague, for most of the time between mid-1592 and 1594. With the theatres shut, writing poems for patrons was one of the few ways a playwright could earn, and Venus and Adonis and Lucrece both belong to this period. Some critics link the start of the sonnets to the same years, though that cannot be proved for Sonnet 18.

The sonnets were entered for publication by Thomas Thorpe on 20 May 1609 and printed by George Eld as SHAKE-SPEARES SONNETS. Neuer before Imprinted. Thorpe's dedication to the mysterious "Mr. W. H.", "the onlie begetter of these insuing sonnets", wishes him "that eternitie promised by our ever-living poet", so the promise this sonnet makes was already the volume's selling point. Whether Shakespeare authorised the publication is disputed: Katherine Duncan-Jones argued that he did; many scholars think Thorpe acted without him.

The sequence: a young man, and seventeen sonnets about children

The 154 sonnets fall into two large groups. Sonnets 1–126 are mostly addressed to, or concern, a young man (critics call him the "Fair Youth"); 127–152 mostly concern a woman (the "Dark Lady"); 153–154 are two short Cupid poems. The young man has never been identified. Southampton and William Herbert, Earl of Pembroke, are the usual candidates, and he may be a composite or a fiction.

Sonnets 1–17, the "procreation sonnets", all urge him to marry and have children so that his beauty survives him ("From fairest creatures we desire increase", Sonnet 1). Sonnet 18 reuses their vocabulary. Sonnet 13 says he holds his beauty "in lease"; Sonnet 14 foresees beauty's "doom and date"; Sonnet 15 first offers the poet's verse as a remedy ("I engraft you new"); Sonnet 16 retreats, calling it "my barren rhyme" beside "the lines of life" that children would be; Sonnet 17 settles for both: "You should live twice, in it and in my rhyme." Sonnet 18 is the first poem in the sequence that never mentions a child: verse alone will do it. Sonnet 19 continues in the new confidence: "My love shall in my verse ever live young."

The sonnet and the art of praise

The sonnet (Italian sonetto, "little sound") was perfected by Petrarch (1304–1374) in poems to Laura and brought into English by Sir Thomas Wyatt and Henry Howard, Earl of Surrey, whose poems were printed in Tottel's Miscellany (1557). Surrey developed the pattern Shakespeare uses: three quatrains and a couplet, rhyming ABAB CDCD EFEF GG. In the 1590s sonnet sequences became a fashion, set off by the printing of Sidney's Astrophil and Stella in 1591 and followed by Daniel's Delia (1592), Drayton's Idea's Mirror (1594) and Spenser's Amoretti (1595).

Petrarchan praise works by comparison: the beloved's eyes are stars or suns, her lips coral, her cheeks roses. Shakespeare mocks the method in Sonnet 130 ("My mistress' eyes are nothing like the sun"). Sonnet 18 takes a middle course: it tests the stock comparison and outbids it, the move rhetoricians call outdoing, praising someone by showing they surpass the usual standard. Elizabethan grammar-school rhetoric drilled pupils in set exercises of praise and comparison, and the octave reads like one, carried out with unusual exactness.

Verse that outlasts time: the eternising tradition

The boast that poetry outlives monuments and death is one of the oldest in European verse. Horace's Odes 3.30 begins "Exegi monumentum aere perennius" ("I have finished a monument more lasting than bronze") and claims "non omnis moriar" ("I shall not wholly die"). Ovid ends the Metamorphoses (book 15) by declaring that he has completed a work which neither Jove's anger, fire, sword nor devouring time can destroy; the poem's last word is vivam, "I shall live". Shakespeare knew Ovid in Latin and in Arthur Golding's English translation (1567).

Elizabethan sonneteers turned the boast from the poet to the beloved. In Spenser's Amoretti 75 (1595) the poet writes his lady's name on the sand, the waves wash it away, and he promises: "My verse your virtues rare shall eternize". Shakespeare returns to the claim again and again: Sonnet 55 ("Not marble nor the gilded monuments / Of princes shall outlive this powerful rhyme"), 60, 63 ("His beauty shall in these black lines be seen") and 65. Sonnet 18 is its first full statement in the sequence. What is distinctive is how little of the beloved the poem preserves. Horace and Ovid name themselves; Spenser's lady at least has a name, if only in the sand; Sonnet 18's beloved is only thee.

Words the Elizabethans heard: humours, leases, the calendar

Humours. Elizabethan medicine, following Galen, held that the body contains four humours (blood, phlegm, yellow bile and black bile). A person's complexion was their particular mixture; a temperate person had them in balance (temperament comes from Latin temperare, to mix in due proportion). temperate (line 2) and complexion (line 6) belong to one vocabulary, and the poem uses it to say that the beloved is in balance where the sun is not.

Leases and owning. A lease granted the use of land or a house for a fixed term in return for rent; when the term ran out, the property went back to its owner. Owe often meant own: in The Tempest Prospero accuses Ferdinand of usurping "the name thou ow'st not". So lease, date, possession and ow’st would have sounded to Shakespeare's readers like the language of tenancy and title.

The calendar. England kept the Julian calendar until 1752, ten days behind the Gregorian calendar that much of Catholic Europe adopted in 1582, so Shakespeare's May ended around what we call 10 June, and Midsummer Day was 24 June. the darling buds of May could be early summer's own buds. Historians also record a run of cold, wet summers and failed harvests in 1594–97, though no one can say whether that weather lies behind the poem.

The psalm. Psalm 23, with its "valley of the shadow of death", was read in church from the Book of Common Prayer psalter, so his shade (line 11) carried its echo.

The poem since 1609: gender, editors and readers

Sonnet 18 never says whether the beloved is a man or a woman: the only gendered pronouns belong to the sun and to death (his gold complexion, his shade). The young man comes from the sequence around it; Sonnet 20 calls him "the master-mistress of my passion". When John Benson reprinted the sonnets in his Poems of 1640 he rearranged and merged them, gave them titles, and altered some pronouns so that poems to the young man could read as addressed to a woman. Edmond Malone's edition of 1780 restored the 1609 order and text.

The poem has since become one of the most quoted in English and a favourite reading at weddings. That is a little ironic: it follows seventeen sonnets urging marriage, it is the first to stop doing so, and it never mentions love, marriage or the beloved's body. Its fame owes something to its plainness. Nearly every word is still current, and the couplet makes a claim that every new reader appears to confirm.

THE POEM

The Poem

Line by line, with the analysis alongside

Sonnet 18
TSonnet 18
1Shall I compare thee to a summer’s day?
2Thou art more lovely and more temperate:
3Rough winds do shake the darling buds of May,
4And summer’s lease hath all too short a date;
5Sometime too hot the eye of heaven shines,
6And often is his gold complexion dimm’d;
7And every fair from fair sometime declines,
8By chance or nature’s changing course untrimm’d;
9But thy eternal summer shall not fade,
10Nor lose possession of that fair thou ow’st;
11Nor shall death brag thou wander’st in his shade,
12When in eternal lines to time thou grow’st:
13So long as men can breathe or eyes can see,
14So long lives this, and this gives life to thee.

Lines with a marker have analysis — click one, or just scroll.

Title
Sonnet 18
Language & devices

Two titles circulate, and neither is Shakespeare's. The 1609 Quarto prints the sonnets numbered and untitled, so 'Sonnet 18' is a Genre label plus a position in a sequence; it is the title Cambridge's 2026–28 syllabus uses. Many anthologies, including the one Cambridge set in 2015 and 2016, title the poem from its first words instead: 'Shall I Compare Thee…?', a Rhetorical question cut off by an Ellipsis before the comparison is named. Sonnet comes from Italian sonetto, "little sound" or "little song": the label promises fourteen lines, a love subject and a turn.

Meaning & effect

The number is not neutral. Eighteen is the first poem after the seventeen "procreation sonnets", which urge a young man to have children so that his beauty survives him, and it is the first that never mentions a child. The plain title therefore quietly announces a new argument: verse, not offspring, will preserve him. The first-line title does something different. It turns the opening question into the poem's identity and, with its ellipsis, leaves the comparison hanging, as if the poet has not yet decided. Neither title names the beloved, and the poem never will: a first hint of its oddest feature, that the person it promises to make immortal is never described. A numbered sonnet is also an entry in a series, like a line in a ledger, which suits a poem that turns out to be full of leases, possession and debt.

Line 1
Shall I compare thee to a summer’s day?
Language & devices

Rhetorical question in the form of Dubitatio: the speaker pretends to hesitate over how to speak. The Modal verb Shall is deliberative ("should I?"), and I, on the metrical beat, is the only first-person pronoun in the poem. Direct address: thee is the singular, intimate second person (Sonnets 15–17 had called the young man "you"). a summer’s day is the stock comparison of love poetry; the indefinite article makes it generic, and a day is short by definition. Regular Iambic pentameter, closed by the question mark.

Meaning & effect

The poem begins by stopping to choose its words, and that hesitation is already a compliment: the usual praise may not be good enough. The question is real in form but rhetorical in effect, since line 2 answers it at once, so the reader watches a mind test a comparison rather than receiving a ready-made one. The comparison offered carries its own defeat: a summer's day is beautiful, but it is one day, and it ends. Shall I also puts the speaker in charge of the act of comparing. This is a question about how to write as much as about the beloved, and the poem's real subject, what writing can do, is present from the first words. Read in sequence, after seventeen sonnets repeating one argument, the question sounds like a fresh start: what else might praise do? A gentler reading hears a lover asking permission, may I compare you?, courtship as tact.

Line 2
Thou art more lovely and more temperate:
Language & devices

The answer is two Comparative adjectives, more lovely and more temperate, doubled by more… more. lovely means beautiful and worthy of love: it is the nearest the poem comes to the word love. temperate has three senses at once: of weather, mild, neither too hot nor too cold; of the body, having the four humours in balance (Elizabethan medicine); of character, moderate and self-governed (the virtue of temperance). The sense may pull stress onto Thou (an initial inversion: you, unlike summer). The Colon presents what follows as evidence; the rhyme falls on the light last syllable of temperate.

Meaning & effect

He answers his own question by comparing anyway: comparatives cannot work without the comparison the first line pretended to doubt. The two adjectives praise different things, lovely a degree of beauty and temperate a kind of beauty, and the second is the poem's key word. Every fault the octave finds in summer will be an extreme or a lapse (too rough, too short, too hot, too dim); temperate names their opposite, the balance that never swings. It is a cool, almost moral compliment, praising steadiness rather than dazzle, and steadiness is exactly what can later be stretched into eternal. The colon turns the line into a thesis awaiting proof, so the love poem is set up as an argument, which is why the octave reads like evidence presented in order.

Line 3
Rough winds do shake the darling buds of May,
Language & devices

Spondee: Rough winds puts two stresses together before the line settles into regular iambs. The violent verb shake, with the emphatic auxiliary do, meets the tender darling, an endearment ("little dear") and the only one in the poem, spent on flowers. buds are beauty not yet opened. Alliteration on the soft plosives of darling buds follows the harsh Rough. May: under the Julian calendar England still used, May ran later in the season than ours (to about our 10 June), and Midsummer Day was 24 June, so May could count as the start of summer.

Meaning & effect

The first count against summer: it is violent, and the beauty it holds is attacked from outside. By calling the buds darling the poet makes us feel the shaking as harm done to something loved and small; the tenderness he never spends on the beloved goes to the flowers summer damages. Buds are promise rather than fulfilment, so summer is shown spoiling its own future before it blooms. If May belongs to summer, these are summer's own buds and the season wrecks what it should bring to flower; even if May is spring, the beauty is shaken before summer has properly begun. The metre plays the gust: two heavy beats, then the smooth run of the darling buds of May. The image also has a history in the sequence (Sonnet 1 pictured the young man as a bud that buries its own content), so the line's fear is for youth itself.

Line 4
And summer’s lease hath all too short a date;
Language & devices

Legal metaphor: a lease lets someone use property for a fixed term, after which it returns to the owner; date is that term and its end (the date of expiry). Personification: summer is a tenant. The intensifier all too short is a complaint, not a description. Archaic hath. The line ends on the hard consonant of date; the semicolon closes the first quatrain. The rhyme pairs temperate with date: the beloved's balance against summer's deadline.

Meaning & effect

The second count: summer is brief, and the reason is a contract. Summer does not own its season; it rents it, and the end is written into the agreement from the start. That changes transience from bad luck into law: the end of summer is not an accident but a term. The legal word opens the poem's hidden argument about ownership (if summer is only a tenant, who can hold beauty outright?), and line 10 will answer with possession. all too short is the lover's voice breaking into the case: even the full term would not be enough. In the sequence the line performs a transfer. Sonnet 13 had said the young man held his own beauty "in lease", and Sonnet 14 had foreseen beauty's "doom and date"; here the lease and the date belong to summer, and the young man is about to be offered something better than tenancy.

Line 5
Sometime too hot the eye of heaven shines,
Language & devices

Trochaic inversion: Sometime takes the first stress, meaning sometimes, at times. too hot names an excess, the opposite of temperate. Metaphor and Periphrasis: the eye of heaven is the sun, a grand, old figure (Spenser's Faerie Queene, 1590, has "the great eye of heaven", Shakespeare's Richard II "the searching eye of heaven"). Personification makes the sun a watching face. Inversion: the adverbial phrase comes first, delaying the subject.

Meaning & effect

The third count: when summer's sun does shine, it overdoes it. This failing is excess; the next line's is deficiency, and together they define temperate by its opposites: summer is never in balance. The periphrasis raises the stakes of the comparison. The beloved is now being measured against the sun, the eye of heaven, not merely a day, and still wins: the poem's hyperbole is climbing. Sometime keeps the fault intermittent. The sun does not always scorch, which is the point: you cannot rely on it. And eye plants the poem's ending. Heaven's eye will fail, but in line 13 human eyes keep the poem alive, so the sun is quietly being replaced as the source of the beloved's light.

Line 6
And often is his gold complexion dimm’d;
Language & devices

The frequency rises: Sometime becomes often. Inversion: often is his gold complexion dimm’d puts the verb before its subject. Personification: the sun has a face, his gold complexion. complexion means skin colouring and also, in humoural medicine, a person's mixture of humours, their temperament. gold is the sun's colour, the colour of wealth, and the colour of the fair beauty poets praised. The passive dimm’d names no agent (the clouds go unmentioned). The rhyme pairs dimm’d with untrimm’d, two participles of damage.

Meaning & effect

The fourth count is the opposite of the third: too often the sun is clouded, so summer is both too much and too little and never temperate. complexion ties the line back to line 2. The beloved is balanced in his humours, while the sun's face keeps changing colour, so the beloved beats the sun at its own kind of beauty. The passive verb makes the loss happen without anyone doing it, which is how the next two lines describe all decline. gold makes the sun the most precious beauty nature has, and even that is unreliable. The personification also gives the sun a human face that loses its colour: an image of ageing slipped into a line about weather.

Line 7
And every fair from fair sometime declines,
Language & devices

The scope widens to a Generalisation: every. Polyptoton in fair from fair: the first fair is a noun meaning a beautiful thing or person, the second the abstract noun beauty (a common Elizabethan use). sometime now means at some time, eventually, and the metre stresses its second syllable (some-TIME), unlike line 5. declines means sinks or falls away, as the sun declines from noon. Polysyndeton: And… And… And (lines 4, 6, 7) piles up the case.

Meaning & effect

The case against summer becomes a law about everything: every beautiful thing, in the end, loses its beauty. The repetition stages the separation, splitting the word fair from itself as beauty is split from what was beautiful. every fair now includes the beloved, which is what makes the turn necessary: if all beauty declines, his will too, unless something intervenes. The shift in sometime is the line's quiet horror. In line 5 summer's bad days came now and then; here decline comes at some time, not occasionally but certainly. declines keeps the sun of lines 5–6 in view, so the sun's daily fall becomes the image of all beauty's fall. Some readers also hear fair as fine weather, which keeps the line inside the summer it is generalising from.

Line 8
By chance or nature’s changing course untrimm’d;
Language & devices

Two agents of loss: chance (accident, illness, misfortune) and nature’s changing course (ordinary change: ageing, the turning seasons). Alliteration on chance… changing course. Polysemy in untrimm’d: stripped of trim, that is finery or ornament; or, in the nautical sense Robert Jungman has drawn attention to, out of trim, like a ship whose sails are not set to a changing wind. Syntax: untrimm’d most naturally describes every fair (stripped of beauty by chance or nature), though it can be read with course. The semicolon closes the octave.

Meaning & effect

The octave ends by naming the two ways beauty is lost, suddenly by accident or slowly by nature's ordinary change, and between them they leave nothing out. That is the strongest case for decay the poem can make, and it is made deliberately strong so that the turn will mean something. untrimm’d pictures beauty as ornament or rigging: what is lost is the finish, and the thing is left bare (Sonnet 1 had called the young man "the world's fresh ornament"). The sailing sense fits course and changing: beauty as a ship that drifts once the wind shifts and no one adjusts the sails. Eight lines in, the beloved has not been mentioned since line 2. More than half the poem has been about what he is not.

Line 9
But thy eternal summer shall not fade,
Language & devices

Volta: But turns the poem at line 9, where an Italian sonnet turns. Paradox: eternal summer, a season that never ends. thy falls on a beat (contrastive stress: your summer, not nature's). The Modal verb shall not is the language of promise or prophecy, the first of three negations (shall not, Nor, Nor). fade is soft and gradual after the octave's violence. Hyperbole.

Meaning & effect

The turn: the beloved is exempt from everything the octave proved. The trick is that the poem now gives him a summer of his own, his youth and prime, so the comparison was not refused but improved: he is a summer without a lease. shall not is not hope but guarantee; the speaker talks like a prophet, or like someone with the power to make it so. The paradox cannot be true in nature, where every summer ends, so the line raises the question how? and holds the answer back until line 12. fade is a gentle verb, as though the poet, having seen off storms and scorching, now faces the quietest threat of all, ordinary wearing-away. The exuberance of the claim is the line's emotional charge: having proved that everything fades, the speaker simply says not you.

Line 10
Nor lose possession of that fair thou ow’st;
Language & devices

Legal diction: possession (lawful holding, ownership) answers line 4's lease. that fair means that beauty, picking up line 7. ow’st means ownest: in Shakespeare's English owe often meant own (Prospero says Ferdinand usurps "the name thou ow'st not"), with the modern sense owe audible behind it (Pun; Mark Howell reads the beauty as a debt to be paid back). Anaphora: Nor begins lines 10 and 11. The 1609 Quarto spells lose as "loose", an ordinary spelling then.

Meaning & effect

The beloved will keep his beauty as owner, not tenant: the poem turns summer's lease into possession. It answers line 7 almost word for word (every fair declines from fair; you will not lose that fair), so the sestet replies to the octave point by point. The own/owe double sense is the line's crux. If ow’st means own, his beauty is his property and cannot be repossessed. If it also means owe, his beauty is a loan from nature that must be repaid at death; the earlier sonnets said as much ("Nature's bequest gives nothing but doth lend", Sonnet 4) and insisted the only repayment was a child. Here the poem lets us hear the debt and cancels it: you will not have to give it back.

Line 11
Nor shall death brag thou wander’st in his shade,
Language & devices

Personification: death boasts, and brag is a blunt, almost comic monosyllable: death as a show-off. Allusion: his shade recalls Psalm 23's "valley of the shadow of death" (familiar from the Prayer Book psalter) and the classical shades, the ghosts of the dead who drift through the underworld; wander’st is their aimless movement. Nor continues the Anaphora. Metrically death falls on an off-beat, though in speech shall death brag is three heavy words together.

Meaning & effect

The third denial reaches the last threat: death will not be able to boast that it has you. The poem meets death with contempt rather than terror, cutting him down to a braggart whose boast will be false. The promise has a careful limit: it is death's brag that is denied, not death itself, so the body will still die; what death cannot do is claim him. his shade makes death's realm the opposite of the octave's summer and sun, a place of shadow where the beloved would be one more ghost among ghosts. The psalm's speaker walks through the valley of the shadow of death unafraid because God is with him; here the protector is the poem. The image of wandering also answers line 8's changing course: the dead drift, while the beloved, in the next line, will grow.

Line 12
When in eternal lines to time thou grow’st:
Language & devices

When means since or as long as: the condition. eternal repeats line 9. Pun on lines: lines of verse; a line of descent (the children Sonnets 1–17 demanded); and the lines time draws on a face (Sonnet 19: "draw no lines there with thine antique pen"). to time thou grow’st: to grow to is to become joined to something, as a graft grows into the tree it is set in (Sonnet 15: "I engraft you new"). Metaphor of grafting; Paradox of growing as time passes. The colon opens onto the couplet.

Meaning & effect

The mechanism is revealed: the beloved escapes time by being written into it. Instead of being worn down by time he grows into it, attached like a graft that lives off the stock it is joined to, so the more time passes, the more he grows. lines holds the sequence's whole change of mind in one word. The earlier sonnets wanted his line of descent; the line that will carry him now is verse. It also reverses ageing: instead of time writing lines on his face, the poet writes lines that keep him young. The repeated eternal welds the beloved's summer (line 9) to the poem's lines (line 12), so his eternity is the poem's and the two cannot be separated. to time can mean for all time or in step with time; either way, time stops being the enemy and becomes the medium.

Line 13
So long as men can breathe or eyes can see,
Language & devices

Conditional: So long as gives both a duration and a condition. Anaphora: So long begins lines 13 and 14. Synecdoche: men for humanity, eyes for readers. Two verbs: breathe (to be alive; and breath is what a poem is spoken on) and see (to read). Perfectly regular Iambic pentameter made entirely of monosyllables. eyes answers the eye of heaven (line 5). The couplet is printed indented.

Meaning & effect

The promise gets its terms: the beloved will live as long as there are living readers. This is a human eternity, not "for ever" but "as long as people exist", a hyperbole that is also a precise condition. The two verbs name the two ways a poem lives, spoken on someone's breath and read by someone's eyes, so the line describes the act the reader is performing at that moment. Human eyes take over from the sun: heaven's eye dims, but readers' eyes keep the beloved's summer lit. The plain monosyllables make the claim sound simple and certain. Yet So long as is also a limit (if there are no more readers, the promise lapses), and that honesty inside the boast is part of what makes the ending moving rather than merely proud.

Line 14
So long lives this, and this gives life to thee.
Language & devices

Deixis: the Demonstrative this, used twice, is the poem pointing at itself. Chiasmus: lives this / this gives life (verb then noun, noun then verb). Polyptoton: lives… life. A Caesura at the comma balances the two halves. All monosyllables, with the strong verbs lives and gives on off-beats, so the line is heavy and slow. Present tense (lives, gives) after the sestet's future shall. The last word, thee, echoes the thee of line 1; the final rhyme pairs see with thee.

Meaning & effect

The poem names itself as the giver of life: as long as there are readers, this lives, and it gives the beloved life. The grammar enacts the claim. this is the subject of both clauses and thee the object at the end, the one who receives; the I of line 1 has disappeared, and the agent now is the poem. gives life is the language of birth, so what the earlier sonnets begged the young man to do for a child is done for him by the poem. The present tense makes every reading the moment the promise comes true, which is why the ending feels self-proving: it is true as you read it. The irony sits in the same words. What is kept alive is thee, a pronoun without a face or a name, while the thing that most certainly survives is this.

THE WHOLE POEM

The Whole Poem

Stepping back: what the poem is doing, first line to last

Sonnet 18 is usually read as the purest compliment in English, but its shape is an argument, and the argument is about ownership. A summer's day is beautiful but rented; the beloved's beauty, the poem claims, can be owned outright, on one condition, which turns out to be the poem itself. The sonnet asks whether it should compare, compares anyway, wins the comparison on every count, and then moves its beloved out of nature, where everything is held on lease, into verse, where possession is permanent. The cost of the move is the poem's quiet strangeness: the beloved it makes immortal is the one thing in it we never see.

The opening question is a feint. Shall I compare thee to a summer’s day? sounds hesitant, but the hesitation is a compliment (the commonest praise in love poetry may not be good enough), and line 2 answers at once with two comparatives, more lovely and more temperate. The poet who doubted comparison is already comparing. The second adjective sets the terms of everything that follows. temperate means mild weather, a body whose humours are in balance and a character in control of itself; it praises not intensity but evenness. The colon after it presents the rest of the octave as evidence.

The evidence is arranged as a case. Summer is violent: Rough winds do shake the darling buds of May, the two hard stresses of Rough winds hitting the line before it settles. It is brief, and the brevity is contractual: summer’s lease hath all too short a date. It overdoes things, Sometime too hot the eye of heaven shines, and then fails to do them at all: often is his gold complexion dimm’d. Each count is an extreme or a lapse, the opposite of temperate, and the hyperbole climbs as it goes; by line 5 the beloved is being measured against the sun. Then the case becomes a law. And every fair from fair sometime declines, / By chance or nature’s changing course untrimm’d: every beautiful thing loses its beauty, by accident or by the ordinary turning of time, and between them chance and nature leave no exit. sometime, which meant sometimes in line 5, now means at some time, inevitably. The beloved, included in every fair, has not been mentioned for six lines.

That silence makes the turn possible. But thy eternal summer shall not fade: the But at line 9 swings the poem from nature to the beloved, and the paradox of eternal summer shows that the comparison was never really refused. The beloved is a summer after all, only one without a lease. The sestet then answers the octave point by point. Summer's beauty fades; his shall not fade. Every fair declines from fair; he will not lose possession of that fair thou ow’st. Behind all decline stands death; death will not brag thou wander’st in his shade. The legal word answers the legal word, possession for lease, and the double sense of ow’st, own and owe, lets us hear the debt nature might call in before the poem cancels it. Even death's defeat is phrased with care: what is denied is his boast, not his power over the body.

Only at line 12 do we learn how: When in eternal lines to time thou grow’st. The repeated eternal welds the beloved's summer to the poem's lines, and the pun on lines gives away the poem's place in Shakespeare's sequence. For seventeen sonnets the poet urged the young man to preserve himself through a line of descent, children who would copy his face; now the line that will carry him is verse. to time thou grow’st completes the reversal. To grow to something is to be grafted onto it, and a graft lives off the stock it is set in: instead of being worn down by time, the beloved grows by it. Time stops being the enemy and becomes the medium.

The couplet states the terms and points at the instrument. So long as men can breathe or eyes can see is hyperbole, but it is also a precise condition: a poem lives on the breath that speaks it and the eyes that read it, so the line describes what the reader is doing at that moment. So long lives this, and this gives life to thee then gives the poem itself the last word. this is the subject of both clauses; thee is the object at the end, the one who receives; the I of line 1 has disappeared. The verbs are present tense after the sestet's future shall, so the promise is not deferred: it comes true whenever the poem is read. That is the source of the ending's famous confidence. It is a claim that every reader appears to confirm.

The strongest objection is that this is hardly a love poem at all. It never uses the word love; it says nothing about the speaker's feelings or the relationship; it does not describe the beloved (no face, no voice, not one physical detail); and in its last line it praises itself. On this view the young man is merely the occasion for a poem about poetry, and four centuries later what survives is the art, not the person.

The objection is right about the facts and wrong about the feeling. The poem's love lies in what it chooses to give. A Petrarchan lover talks about his own suffering; this one says I once and then gets out of the way, spending fourteen lines on the beloved's survival and none on his own reward. The exuberance is real (having proved that everything fades, he says not you three times over), and so is the commitment, staked on the one thing a poet can actually guarantee. The blankness of the beloved is the price of that guarantee, and also its generosity: a thee without features is one that every reader can fill, which is why the poem is still read at weddings. Even the conditional So long as is part of the love, an honest admission that eternity depends on other people. The last two words are to thee. The poem knows it is the thing that lives; it insists that the life was meant for someone else.

FORM & STRUCTURE

Form & Structure

How the poem is built, and why it matters

Form & genre

An English (Shakespearean) sonnet: fourteen lines of iambic pentameter in three quatrains and a couplet, rhyming ABAB CDCD EFEF GG. It is a sonnet of praise and also an eternising sonnet, one that promises its subject life through verse. As in the 1609 Quarto, it is printed as one block with the couplet indented.

Quatrains & couplet

Q1 (1–4): the question, the answer and two counts against summer. Q2 (5–8): two more counts and a law that all beauty declines. Q3 (9–12): the turn, three denials and the means. Couplet (13–14): the terms and the instrument. Each quatrain closes on a semicolon or a colon.

Metre

Iambic pentameter, ten syllables in every line (every and wander'st are spoken as two syllables, ow'st and grow'st as one). The pattern is very regular, so the departures stand out: the spondee Rough winds (3), the trochee Sometime (5), the stressed thy (9), the demoted death (11) and the heavy last line.

Rhyme

Seven sounds: day/May, temperate/date, shines/declines, dimm’d/untrimm’d, fade/shade, ow’st/grow’st, see/thee. All are full rhymes except temperate/date, which rhymes on the light last syllable of temperate, a normal licence of the period.

Turns

The main turn is But at line 9 (summer → the beloved), where an Italian sonnet turns. The couplet makes a second, smaller shift (the beloved → the poem, this).

Lineation & punctuation

Every line ends on punctuation, so there is no enjambment, though the sense runs on across 7–8, 9–10, 11–12 and 13–14. Only line 1 ends with a question mark and only line 14 with a full stop: in modern pointing, lines 2–14 are one long sentence of linked clauses.

Words

114 words, 93 of them monosyllables. Sixteen of the 21 longer words are in the octave, five in lines 9–12, none in the couplet.

Text & editions

The 1609 Quarto uses old spellings (louely, Maie, vntrim'd, loose for lose, wandr'st, breath for breathe) and lighter pointing. Modern editions punctuate differently. The text Cambridge printed in 2015 and 2016 (from Poems Deep and Dangerous) has date:, By chance, or Nature's changing course, untrimm'd;, thou owest;, Death, thou growest; and a comma after breathe. No variant changes a word.

The argument, step by step

The sonnet is built as a case and its answer, and the rhyme units mark the stages.

Lines Move Key words What it sets up
1–2 Question, then answer Shall I compare…?; more lovely and more temperate The thesis; temperate becomes the standard
3–4 Counts 1–2: violence, brevity Rough winds; lease… date The property argument (lease → possession)
5–6 Counts 3–4: excess, deficiency too hot; dimm’d temperate defined by its opposites; the eye that readers will replace
7–8 The law of decline and its two agents every fair from fair; chance or nature’s changing course Includes the beloved, so a turn is needed
9 Turn: exemption But thy eternal summer shall not fade Answers fading and brevity (3–4)
10 Denial Nor lose possession of that fair Answers 7 (fair from fair) and 4 (lease)
11 Denial Nor shall death brag Answers the end that every count implies
12 The means eternal lines… grow’st Answers 8: time becomes growth
13–14 Terms and instrument So long as…; this gives life to thee The poem as the agent of life

The proportions are as revealing as the order. Eight lines go to summer and decay, four to the beloved, two to the poem. The four lines on the beloved are almost entirely negative (shall not, Nor, Nor), so he is defined by what will not happen to him rather than by anything he is, and the only positive verb he receives, grow’st, depends on eternal lines. Each quatrain is a closed step, and the couplet, set apart by its indentation and its new rhyme, states the verdict.

The sestet answers the octave point by point. Fading and brevity (3–4) are met by shall not fade. The law that every fair from fair sometime declines (7) is met almost word for word by Nor lose possession of that fair. Summer's lease (4) is replaced by possession (10). The death implied by all decline is denied its brag (11). And nature’s changing course (8), the process of time, is turned into growth: to time thou grow’st (12). The structure is that of a reply to a charge, item by item.

Scansion

Stresses are in capitals, with feet marked by |.

Line Scansion What it does
1 shall I | com-PARE | thee TO | a SUM- | mer's DAY (x / | x / | x / | x / | x /) Regular. The beat falls on I, the only first-person pronoun in the poem; to is promoted, and a reader may lean on thee instead, tilting the line towards the beloved.
2 THOU art | more LOVE- | ly AND | more TEM- | per-ATE (/ x | x / | x / | x / | x /) The sense pulls the first stress onto Thou (you, unlike summer): an initial inversion, or a hovering stress if read regularly. The last syllable of temperate is promoted to carry the rhyme with date.
3 ROUGH WINDS | do SHAKE | the DAR- | ling BUDS | of MAY (/ / | x / | x / | x / | x /) Spondee: two stresses collide at the gust, then four smooth iambs carry the buds. The rhythm is the wind striking and passing.
5 SOME-time | too HOT | the EYE | of HEAV- | en SHINES (/ x | x / | x / | x / | x /) Initial trochee: Sometime leads, so the sun's excess arrives as something occasional and unpredictable.
7 and EV- | 'ry FAIR | from FAIR | some-TIME | de-CLINES (x / | x / | x / | x / | x /) Regular, with every as two syllables. Both fairs take beats; sometime is now stressed on its second syllable as its meaning shifts from at times to in time.
9 but THY | e-TER- | nal SUM- | mer SHALL | not FADE (x / | x / | x / | x / | x /) Contrastive stress on thy (your summer, not nature's). shall takes the beat, making the promise metrically certain, while the sense presses on not as well.
11 nor SHALL | death BRAG | thou WAN- | der'st IN | his SHADE (x / | x / | x / | x / | x /) death falls on an off-beat, metrically demoted, though spoken naturally shall death brag is three heavy syllables: the swagger the line mocks.
12 when IN | e-TER- | nal LINES | to TIME | thou GROW'ST (x / | x / | x / | x / | x /) Regular; the beats fall on the key words: eternal, lines, time, grow'st.
13 so LONG | as MEN | can BREATHE | or EYES | can SEE (x / | x / | x / | x / | x /) Ten monosyllables in perfect iambs: the plainest line in the poem for its largest claim.
14 so LONG | lives THIS, | and THIS | gives LIFE | to THEE (x / | x / | x / | x / | x /) Regular in pattern but heavy in speech: lives and gives are strong verbs on off-beats, so almost every syllable carries weight and the last line slows to a close. The comma after this is the pivot of the chiasmus.

The regularity is itself expressive. A poem praising the temperate is metrically temperate: almost every line keeps its five beats without strain, every line ends on a stress, and the few substitutions fall on the moments of violence (3), unpredictability (5) and contrast (9). The diction moves the same way. The octave holds sixteen of the poem's twenty-one words of more than one syllable (compare, temperate, complexion, declines, untrimm'd…); lines 9–12 hold five; the couplet none. The claim grows larger as the language grows plainer.

Rhyme, pair by pair

  • day / May: both A-rhymes belong to summer, the comparison and the month it falls in.
  • temperate / date: the beloved's virtue rhymed against summer's deadline, the two halves of the argument in one sound. The rhyme lands on the light last syllable of temperate against the hard monosyllable date, so for now the deadline sounds the stronger.
  • shines / declines: the sun's shining yoked to its decline, brightness and fall in one chime.
  • dimm’d / untrimm’d: two past participles of damage, so the octave ends on what has been done to beauty.
  • fade / shade: the two dangers the sestet denies, rhymed together.
  • ow’st / grow’st: the only rhymes whose subject is the beloved: owning and growing, possession and increase.
  • see / thee: reading and the beloved. To see the poem is to have thee, and the final rhyme word repeats the thee of line 1.

One vowel threads the scheme. The long /eɪ/ of day returns in May, date, fade and shade, so the sound of the opening summer comes back in the rhyme words of loss at the very moment the sestet denies them. The couplet's /iː/ breaks out of it.

Syntax, punctuation and lineation

Every line ends on punctuation, so each line is a complete unit of sense. That is part of why so many have become proverbial (the darling buds of May, summer’s lease, the eye of heaven), a fitting fate for a poem that claims its lines will last. Yet the syntax runs across pairs of lines where the argument needs it: the law of decline needs line 8 to name its agents, the denials of 9–11 share one grammar, the condition When in eternal lines completes line 11, and the couplet is one sentence split by its anaphora.

The heavier stops mark the logic. The colon after temperate presents evidence; the semicolons after date, dimm’d, untrimm’d and ow’st (in this text) separate counts and denials like items in a list; the colon after grow’st opens onto the conclusion.

The tenses move with the argument. The octave is in the general present (do shake, hath, shines, declines), the tense of laws that always hold. The sestet switches to the future of promise: shall not fade, Nor shall death brag. The couplet returns to the present, lives and gives, so the promised future is fulfilled in the present of every reading.

The pronouns track who matters. I appears once, in the first three words. The beloved is addressed seven times (thee, Thou, thy, thou, thou, thou, thee), beginning and ending the poem. In the last line the grammatical subject is neither of them but this, the poem, which takes over the act of giving life.

The turn, and the second turn

The But of line 9 falls exactly where a Petrarchan sonnet turns between octave and sestet, so this English sonnet has an Italian shape inside it: eight lines of case, six of answer. The rhyme scheme still divides 4 + 4 + 4 + 2, so the sestet itself has two parts, the denials (9–12) and the couplet (13–14). The couplet does not reverse anything. It changes the subject, from thee to this, and reveals what the whole promise rests on. Some readers therefore treat the couplet as the poem's real turn; it is better described as a second hinge, from the beloved to the poem.

The 1609 text and modern texts

The 1609 Quarto, SHAKE-SPEARES SONNETS, prints the poem as number 18, untitled, with its couplet indented (as all the couplets are), in old spelling (louely, Maie, vntrim'd, loose, wandr'st, breath) and with lighter punctuation than modern editions. Its loose was simply a spelling of lose, though it lets a modern eye glimpse loosen; its breath is the period's spelling of breathe. Every modern text is an editor's modernisation, and they differ in pointing. The version given here has a colon after temperate, semicolons after date, dimm’d, untrimm’d and ow’st, a lower-case death, and a colon after grow’st. The version Cambridge printed on its 2015 and 2016 papers, taken from Jo Phillips's anthology Poems Deep and Dangerous, capitalises Nature's and Death, sets chance and Nature's changing course off with commas, spells out owest and growest (still spoken as one syllable each for the metre), and adds a comma after breathe. No variant changes a word, and none changes the argument; the capitals simply make visible the personifications that are there anyway.

SOUND

Sound

What the poem does to the ear

Sound patterns

The gust and the buds. Line 3 opens with two heavy stresses, Rough winds, on a rolling /r/ and a breathy /f/: the end of Rough is a puff of air. Then the consonants soften into voiced plosives, the /d/ and /b/ of darling buds, and the line ends on the open vowel and soft nasal of May. Harshness meets tenderness in the mouth as it does in the image.

A short date said slowly. all too short a date lengthens the very phrase that complains of shortness: the long vowels of all, too and short hold the voice, and then the line stops dead on the /t/ of date. The lease runs on and then ends abruptly, which is exactly what a lease does.

Heat, then dimming. Sometime too hot the eye of heaven shines is breathy with /h/ (hot, heaven) and open vowels. Line 6 closes on dimm’d, where the lips shut on /m/ and the /d/ cuts the sound off; its rhyme, untrimm’d, repeats the same muffled ending, so the octave closes twice on the sound of something shut off.

fair from fair. The /f/ alliteration and the exact repetition make the ear hear one word returning slightly changed: beauty heard slipping away from the beautiful thing.

chance or nature’s changing course. The repeated /tʃ/ of chance… changing and the hard /k/ of course give the line a clattering, unsettled sound, change audible in the consonants.

The vowel of day. The poem's first rhyme sound, the long /eɪ/ of day, runs through May and date and returns in the rhyme words fade and shade. The sound that opened on summer comes back in the two words of loss, at the very moment the sestet denies them.

Denial and swagger. The nasal /n/ of Nor… Nor gives lines 10–11 a flat, firm sound, like an objection entered twice. death brag packs the plosives /d/, /b/ and /g/ into two blunt syllables, so the boast sounds like what it is, before the line softens into the hushed /ʃ/ of his shade.

Smooth lines. Line 12 runs on liquids and long vowels, eternal lines to time thou grow’st, the smoothest sound in the sestet for the moment the beloved escapes.

The couplet's breath. Lines 13–14 are twenty monosyllables, mostly with long, open vowels (so, long, breathe, eyes, see, life, thee) and few hard clusters, so they are the easiest lines in the poem to say: a couplet about breathing that is effortless to breathe. The /l/ of long… lives… life threads the word life through the line before it arrives. The /iː/ of breathe… see… thee binds the conditions of reading to the beloved. The sibilants of So… see… this… this hush the close. The repeated So long gives the couplet the cadence of an oath, and the comma after this in line 14 balances the chiasmus on a single pause.

see / thee. The last rhyme joins the act of reading to the person read about: to see the poem is to have thee. It ends on an open vowel that could be held indefinitely, and thee echoes the thee of line 1, so the poem closes on the sound it began with.

MOTIFS & SYMBOLS

Motifs & Symbols

Images that recur, and what they accumulate

Motifs and symbols

1. Summer and its sun

Summer is the poem's measuring-rod, and it changes status as the poem goes on. In line 1 it is a standard of beauty, a summer’s day. In line 4 it is a tenant, holding its season on a lease. In lines 5–6 it becomes the sun, the eye of heaven with his gold complexion: the grandest beauty nature has, and still unreliable, too hot or dimm’d. In line 9 it returns transformed: thy eternal summer. The motif's journey is the poem's argument in miniature. Summer is not discarded but transferred, from nature, where it ends, to the beloved, where it will not. The sun's fall is implied in declines (7), and its work as the source of light is taken over by readers' eyes (13).

2. "Fair": beauty as a possession

The word for beauty is used three times as a noun: every fair from fair (7) and that fair thou ow’st (10). As a noun, beauty becomes a thing, something that can be separated from its owner, lost, owned or owed. Around it gather the poem's other words for beauty: lovely (2), darling (3), gold (6) and the trim implied by untrimm’d (8). None of them describes the beloved's body. Beauty in this poem is a property rather than a picture, which is why it can be moved from nature into verse.

3. Lease, possession and debt

A vocabulary of property runs beneath the imagery. The lease and date of line 4 make summer a tenant on a fixed term; possession and ow’st (10) give the beloved title to his beauty, or a debt for it; death's brag (11) is a claim to him that will fail. The motif ends in a gift: this gives life to thee (14). The sequence of ideas (rent, own, owe, claim, give) traces the poem's movement from a world where beauty is borrowed to one where it is given outright.

4. Eyes and lines

Seeing and writing come together at the end. The first eye in the poem is the sun's, the eye of heaven (5), and it fails: too hot, often dimmed. The second belongs to readers: eyes can see (13). Between them stand the eternal lines (12), verse to be seen, and also a line of descent and the lines time draws on a face. this (14) is the thing those eyes are looking at. The motif replaces nature's unreliable eye with human ones and makes reading the light by which the beloved lives.

5. Growth and the shade

The poem's natural cycle runs from bud to shadow and then back to growth. buds (3) are beauty not yet open, already shaken; declines (7), untrimm’d (8) and fade (9) are the stages of loss; his shade (11) is death's realm, where the dead wander. Then the verb reverses: to time thou grow’st (12), the beloved growing, grafted onto time, and the couplet ends in breath and life (breathe, lives, life). The motif turns the ordinary direction of time inside out. In nature, growth leads to decay; in the poem, decay is answered by growth.

THEMES

Themes

The ideas the poem is arguing about

01

Poetry against time

The poem's central claim is that verse can do what nature cannot: keep a person's beauty from ending. The octave builds the case for decay as thoroughly as it can. Summer is shaken by Rough winds, rented on a short lease, too hot or dimm’d, and every fair from fair sometime declines, so the turn at line 9 has something real to defeat. The sestet's answer is not a cure found in nature but a change of medium: the beloved survives When in eternal lines to time thou grow’st. The pun on lines carries the whole argument, replacing the line of descent that Sonnets 1–17 demanded with lines of verse.

The claim is also limited with care. The poem promises that death will not brag, not that the beloved will not die, and the eternity lasts only So long as men can breathe or eyes can see. Poetry here is not magic but a process that needs living readers. That is why the ending feels both triumphant and true: the couplet's present tense (So long lives this) is fulfilled every time the poem is read.

02

Love as praise and promise

This is a love poem without the word love (only lovely), without a description of the beloved, and without any account of the relationship. Its love is expressed instead as two acts, praise and a guarantee. The praise is extravagant: the beloved outshines summer and the sun itself, the eye of heaven. The promise is more extravagant still: thy eternal summer shall not fade. The speaker's commitment is total and his tone exuberant. Having proved that everything beautiful fades, he simply declares not you, three times over (shall not… Nor… Nor).

What makes the love moving is its generosity. The speaker says I once and then disappears; nothing in the poem concerns his feelings, his suffering or his reward, which is very unlike the complaining lovers of the Petrarchan tradition (or Behn's speaker in 'Love Armed'). Love here means wanting the other person to last, and spending all one's skill to make it happen. The hyperbole is a lover's, but the gift is a poet's: what he can give is not a body, a marriage or a child, but this.

03

Nature on trial

Nature is the standard source of praise in love poetry, and Sonnet 18 puts it on trial and finds it wanting. Summer is violent (Rough winds do shake), brief (all too short a date), excessive (too hot) and unreliable (often is his gold complexion dimm’d). Line 7 turns the complaint into a law: everything beautiful declines By chance or nature’s changing course. Nature's beauty is real, but it is held on terms it cannot keep.

The poem thus joins the Renaissance argument about art and nature and sides with art: what is made in words outlasts what is born. Yet the poem cannot do without nature. Its only images of beauty are natural (buds, sunlight, gold, summer), and the beloved's immortality is described as an eternal summer, nature with its flaws removed. Art does not replace nature here so much as perfect it: the poem keeps summer's beauty and cancels its lease.

04

Ownership, debt and the terms of life

Beneath the flowers runs a vocabulary of property. Summer holds its season on a lease with a fixed date; the beloved will not lose possession of the beauty he ow’st (owns); death's brag is a claim to him that will not stand. Time in this poem works like a contract, with terms and an expiry, and the sestet's achievement is to change the beloved's title from tenancy to ownership. Critics such as Christopher Thurman have traced how often the sonnets think about love through borrowing, lending and debt, and this poem is a compact example.

The double sense of ow’st complicates the triumph. If the beloved owns his beauty, he cannot be evicted from it; if he owes it, as Sonnet 4 says ("Nature's bequest gives nothing but doth lend"), it is a loan that death will call in. The procreation sonnets said the only way to repay it was a child. Sonnet 18 offers a different settlement: the debt is cancelled because the beauty is transferred into the poem, where no landlord can reclaim it.

05

Balance and constancy

The quality the poem prizes most is not intensity but evenness. temperate (mild, balanced in humour, self-governed) is the beloved's defining virtue, and every fault of summer is a lack of it: too rough, too short, too hot, too dim, present Sometime and often but never steadily. eternal is simply temperateness without end, constancy stretched to infinity.

The form embodies the virtue it praises. The pentameter is unusually regular; every line ends on punctuation; each quatrain is a closed unit; the argument proceeds in order and the couplet resolves it. The poem is itself temperate (even, balanced, controlled) in a way summer is not, which is part of why its claim to last feels earned. It is a strange compliment by modern standards, since we do not usually call a beloved moderate, but in Elizabethan terms balance was the condition of health, virtue and lasting beauty.

06

Who is made immortal?

The poem promises to keep thee alive, but what it most certainly preserves is itself. The beloved is never named and never described: no face, no voice, no age, not one physical detail. The only things given positive content are summer, which loses, and the poem, this, which in the last line becomes the grammatical subject of both clauses while the beloved is the object at the end. The poet, too, vanishes after Shall I.

Read one way, this is the poem's genius: by leaving the beloved blank, it lets every reader fill thee with their own beloved, which is why it is still read at weddings four centuries later. Read another way, it is the poem's quiet irony: the young man is immortal only as an addressee, and the true survivor is the art. The poem keeps both readings open, and its last two words, to thee, insist that the gift was meant for him.

DIFFICULT MOMENTS

Difficult Moments

Where the poem is genuinely undecidable — and what to do about it

Cruxes

1. Does the poem compare, or refuse to compare?

The difficulty. Line 1 asks whether to compare the beloved to a summer's day, and the usual reading is that the answer is no, you are better. But line 2 is a comparison (more lovely and more temperate), the octave carries the comparison out point by point, and line 9 gives the beloved thy eternal summer, as if he were a summer after all.

Competing readings. (a) The poem rejects the comparison: summer is too flawed to be worthy, so the beloved is placed above nature altogether. (b) The poem outdoes the comparison, the classic rhetorical move of praising someone by showing they surpass the standard: he is like summer, only better, and comparing is the means of praise. (c) The poem transforms the comparison: line 9 shows that the beloved is a summer, but an eternal one, so the comparison is kept and only its flaws are removed, and what makes the difference is the poem.

What a strong answer does. It notices that Shall I compare…? is a question about method, which the poem answers in practice: it compares relentlessly, and the result is not "unlike summer" but "summer without a lease". That reading explains why summer appears in lines 1, 4 and 9, and why the turn depends on it.

2. untrimm’d: what is lost, and what is it attached to?

The difficulty. Line 8 ends on a word with several possible meanings and an uncertain grammatical home.

Competing readings. On meaning: (a) stripped of trim, that is finery or ornament, so beauty is a decoration that chance or time strips away (Sonnet 1 had called the young man "the world's fresh ornament"); (b) out of trim, the nautical sense Robert Jungman has drawn attention to: a ship whose sails are not adjusted to nature’s changing course drifts; (c) some readers hear a lamp left untrimmed and guttering, prompted by the rhyme with dimm’d. On grammar: untrimm’d most naturally describes every fair (every beauty is stripped by chance or by nature's course), but it can also be read with course, making nature's course itself untrimmed: unchecked, uncorrected, going its own way.

What a strong answer does. It does not choose one sense as the only right one. The ornament reading makes beauty superficial and removable; the sailing reading makes it a balance that a changing wind upsets, which suits the poem's praise of the temperate. Holding both shows how the octave's last word gathers up its earlier faults: things done to beauty from outside, and a loss of balance within.

3. ow’st: owning or owing?

The difficulty. In Elizabethan English ow’st means ownest, and editors gloss it so. But the modern sense, owe, sits very close, in a poem already full of leases.

Competing readings. (a) Own: the beloved holds his beauty as property and will not lose possession of it, the exact answer to summer's lease (4). (b) Owe: Mark Howell reads the beauty as a debt that must be paid back to nature; the procreation sonnets had said as much ("Nature's bequest gives nothing but doth lend", Sonnet 4) and insisted the payment was a child. (c) Both: the line lets us hear the debt and then cancels it, so he keeps what he owes.

What a strong answer does. It argues that the pun is not a slip but the point: Sonnet 18 moves the beloved's beauty from the condition of a loan to that of a possession, and the double word holds both conditions at the moment of transfer. Howell also suggests a pun on fair and fare, the payment owed for life's journey, which sharpens the debt reading.

4. Eternity, or another lease? The conditional couplet

The difficulty. The sestet promises an eternal summer and eternal lines, but the couplet adds a condition: So long as men can breathe or eyes can see.

Competing readings. (a) Hyperbole: "as long as humanity exists" means for ever, and the condition is only a grand way of saying so. (b) Honesty: the poem admits that its eternity depends on readers, and so is itself a kind of lease, held from the human race rather than from nature. (c) Self-fulfilment: the condition describes exactly what a reader is doing (breathing the words, seeing the lines), so every reading renews the promise, and the present tense lives comes true each time.

What a strong answer does. It weighs the boast against the condition rather than ignoring either. The ending is confident because the poem has in fact been read for four centuries, and moving because the poet knew it might not be: the promise is a lover's faith in other people, not a magic spell.

5. Who is made immortal?

The difficulty. The poem promises to keep thee alive but tells us nothing about the beloved: no name, face, age or voice. The only thing given life and agency at the end is this.

Competing readings. (a) The beloved: the poem preserves him as the one it speaks to, and thee is its last word. (b) The poem: the beloved is the occasion and the real subject is poetry's power; the poet says I once and lets the poem take the grammatical subject of the final line. (c) Anyone: by leaving the beloved blank, the poem lets every reader put their own beloved in his place, which is why it is read at weddings.

What a strong answer does. It sees that all three readings rest on one fact, that the beloved is never described, and asks what that blankness does. It can be read as generosity, as irony, or as both: the poem knows that it is what survives, and still insists, in its last two words, that the life it carries is to thee.

CLOSE ANALYSIS

Close Analysis

The moments that repay pressure, worked through

Quotation analysis

Twelve moments, in the poem's order: what each phrase does, and why it is there.

1. Shall I compare thee to a summer’s day? (1) — dubitatio; modal verb; direct address. The speaker stops to choose his words before he starts: the commonest compliment in love poetry may not be good enough. Shall I is deliberative, and I, the only first-person pronoun in the poem, takes the beat; thee is the intimate singular. The comparison chosen contains its own defeat, since a summer’s day is a single day. Intention and effect: Shakespeare makes the reader watch a mind testing a comparison, so the praise arrives as the result of thought rather than routine, and the poem's subject, how to praise, is set before what to praise.

2. more lovely and more temperate (2) — comparatives; polysemy. The answer compares anyway. lovely praises degree; temperate praises kind: mild like good weather, balanced in the humours, self-governed. Intention and effect: by making the key virtue evenness rather than brilliance, Shakespeare sets the standard every count against summer will fail, and prepares a quality, constancy, that can be stretched into eternal.

3. Rough winds do shake the darling buds of May (3) — spondee; juxtaposition of shake and darling. The metre takes the gust (ROUGH WINDS) and then smooths into the buds. darling, the poem's only endearment, goes to flowers not yet open. Intention and effect: summer is shown damaging its own future, and the tenderness makes the harm felt; the beloved's beauty, by implication, needs protecting from a world that shakes what it loves.

4. summer’s lease hath all too short a date (4) — legal metaphor; personification. Summer is a tenant whose term is fixed in advance, and date is both the duration and the expiry. all too short is the lover's complaint breaking into the case. Intention and effect: transience becomes a contract rather than an accident, which opens the poem's argument about ownership: if summer only rents beauty, someone must be able to own it, and line 10 says who.

5. the eye of heaven… his gold complexion dimm’d (5–6) — periphrasis; personification; humoural double sense. The sun is a face that is too hot one day and dimm’d the next: excess, then deficiency, never balance. complexion means both colouring and the mixture of humours, so the sun is shown to be intemperate in the medical sense. Intention and effect: the comparison escalates to the sun itself and the beloved still wins; the hyperbole is earned by argument, not merely asserted.

6. every fair from fair sometime declines (7) — generalisation; polyptoton; shift of sense. The complaint becomes a law; fair is split from itself; sometime changes from now and then to eventually. Intention and effect: by including every beauty, the beloved's too, Shakespeare makes the turn necessary rather than decorative: without something new, the beloved will decline like everything else.

7. By chance or nature’s changing course untrimm’d (8) — two agents; polysemy. Accident and ordinary change cover every way beauty can be lost, and untrimm’d means stripped of ornament or, in the sailing sense, set adrift by a changing wind. Intention and effect: the octave closes on the strongest case for decay it can make, so the reply has a real opponent.

8. But thy eternal summer shall not fade (9) — volta; paradox; modal of promise. The turn gives the beloved a summer of his own, without its lease, and shall not is a guarantee. Intention and effect: the exuberance is the point. Having proved that all beauty fades, the speaker simply says not yours, and the paradox makes us ask how, which the poem holds back for three lines.

9. Nor lose possession of that fair thou ow’st (10) — legal diction; pun on own/owe. possession answers lease, and that fair answers every fair from fair. Intention and effect: the sestet rebuts the octave point by point, like a reply to a charge, and the double sense lets us hear beauty as a debt to nature before the poem cancels it.

10. Nor shall death brag thou wander’st in his shade (11) — personification; allusion to Psalm 23 and the classical shades. Death is reduced to a braggart, and the beloved will not be one more ghost wandering in the dark. Intention and effect: contempt replaces fear, but the promise is carefully limited to death's boast, not his power over the body, which keeps the poem truthful.

11. When in eternal lines to time thou grow’st (12) — pun on lines; grafting metaphor; repetition of eternal. Lines of verse replace the line of descent that Sonnets 1–17 demanded, and to grow to time is to be grafted onto it. Intention and effect: time stops being the enemy and becomes the medium in which the beloved grows, while the repeated eternal welds his summer to the poem's lines.

12. So long as men can breathe or eyes can see, / So long lives this, and this gives life to thee. (13–14) — conditional; anaphora; deixis; chiasmus; monosyllables. The beloved lives as long as there are readers to speak and see the poem; this, twice, is the poem naming itself as the giver of life; the twenty plain words end on thee. Intention and effect: the present tense makes the promise come true in every reading, so the ending proves itself, while the grammar quietly admits what survives most surely: not a face, but this.

CRITICAL LENSES

Critical Lenses

What each way of reading makes visible, and what it flattens

Critical lenses

1. Formalist

What it makes visible. The poem as a machine for argument: a question, four counts against summer, a law of decline, a turn at line 9, three denials answering the octave point by point, and a couplet that states the terms. It notices the details that do the work (the spondee of Rough winds, the shift in sometime, the pun on lines, the chiasmus of the last line, the monosyllabic couplet) and shows how the regular, end-stopped form embodies the temperate balance it praises.

What it flattens. Admiration for the machine can hide the poem's strangeness: a structure this well made can distract from the fact that the person it praises never appears in it. Reading the poem alone also cuts it off from the sequence that gives lines its double sense.

2. Historicist

What it makes visible. The world the words come from: Galenic humours behind temperate and complexion; Elizabethan leases behind lease, date and possession; a Julian-calendar May; the Prayer Book psalm behind his shade; the 1590s sonnet vogue, and plague years when poems for patrons mattered more than plays. Thorpe's 1609 dedication, wishing "that eternitie promised by our ever-living poet", shows the poem's promise already being sold.

What it flattens. The date of Sonnet 18 is unknown, so links to particular events (plague, bad harvests, Hamnet Shakespeare's death) are possibilities, not facts, and the poem's power does not depend on them.

3. Materialist: love in the language of property

What it makes visible. A love poem that thinks in terms of tenure. Beauty is rented (summer), owned or owed (the beloved), claimed (death's brag) and finally given (gives life). Critics such as Christopher Thurman have traced the sonnets' habit of thinking about love through lending and debt; here the beloved's beauty is moved from leasehold to freehold, and grow’st even carries a faint sense of value increasing over time.

What it flattens. The tenderness and wonder. darling buds and eternal summer are not only transactions, and reading every word as money misses the poem's delight.

4. Queer and gender criticism

What it makes visible. In the sequence the beloved is a young man (Sonnet 20's "master-mistress"), and the poem is one man's unembarrassed praise of another's beauty. Sonnet 18 itself has no pronoun for the beloved's sex, only his for the sun and death, and its reception shows readers adjusting it: Benson's 1640 edition altered some pronouns in the sequence, and the poem is now a staple of weddings. The lens asks what that neutrality has hidden and what it has made possible.

What it flattens. The poem's own text does not settle the beloved's sex, and reading it only through the sequence can overwrite what makes it so widely usable.

5. Reader-response

What it makes visible. The poem makes its reader the mechanism of its promise: So long as men can breathe or eyes can see describes the very act of reading, and this lives whenever someone reads it. The blank beloved invites readers to supply their own thee. Meaning here is something the reader completes, and the poem says so.

What it flattens. The original address to a particular person, and the poem's historical strangeness: making it about us can erase the young man it was written for.

6. Ecocritical

What it makes visible. Nature as a foil to be outdone. Summer is rough, brief, excessive and dim, and the poem sides with art against it. Read beside Boey's 'Report to Wordsworth' or Clarke's 'Lament', the confidence that nature is merely imperfect, not damaged, belongs to a world that could take the seasons for granted.

What it flattens. The poem is not really about nature; it uses nature as the standard of praise. It also depends on nature for every image of beauty it has, so its victory over summer is a tribute to summer too.

OTHER READINGS

Other Readings

Contested interpretations, and where each is weak

Other readings

1. A love poem of praise and promise

The default reading: a lover finds the conventional comparison too weak, outdoes it, and offers a guarantee instead of a compliment.

Evidence: the comparatives of line 2, the exuberant thy eternal summer shall not fade, the three denials, and the gift in the last line, this gives life to thee.

Weakness: it has to explain why a love poem never says love, never describes the beloved and ends by praising itself.

2. A poem about poetry

The real subject is the power of verse: eight lines dismantle nature, four make a claim, and two name the poem as the agent.

Evidence: eternal lines, the doubled this, and the vanishing I: the poet steps aside and the poem holds the final sentence.

Weakness: the poem's power is put at the beloved's service; the last word is thee, not this.

3. A move in the sequence: verse instead of children

After seventeen sonnets urging the young man to marry and have children, Sonnet 18 is the first that never mentions a child, and it keeps the earlier poems' vocabulary while changing its meaning.

Evidence: lease (Sonnet 13's "hold in lease"), date (14's "doom and date"), grow’st (15's "I engraft you new"), lines (16's "lines of life"), and the pun on lines as lineage.

Weakness: the order of the 1609 sonnets may not be Shakespeare's own, and the poem works fully on its own, as anthologies print it.

4. The sceptical reading: the vanishing beloved

The poem promises immortality and then gives its subject no features at all; four centuries later nobody knows who he was. What survives is the poem.

Evidence: no physical detail; thee only a pronoun; the poem as grammatical subject at the end; Sonnet 17's worry that future readers would not believe a description.

Weakness: Renaissance praise often idealises rather than describes, and the blankness is also the poem's generosity, since it lets any reader fill thee.

5. A patron's poem

If the young man was a nobleman and the poet a writer in need of support, the poem can be read as an offer: I can give you what no one else can, permanence.

Evidence: the language of property and title; the eternising boast as something a poet could trade; Thorpe's dedication promising "eternitie".

Weakness: nothing in Sonnet 18, or in the record, shows it was written for a patron; the reading is speculation and can make the poem merely calculating.

6. A consolation against death

The poem can be read as written against mortality itself: death personified, mocked and denied his boast.

Evidence: Nor shall death brag; the echo of Psalm 23's "shadow of death"; the procreation sonnets' fear of the young man dying without trace.

Weakness: the tone is triumphant rather than grieving, and attempts to tie the poem to the plague years or to Hamnet Shakespeare's death (1596) founder on its unknown date.

REVISION NOTES

Revision Notes

The working notes, quotation by quotation

Title

'Sonnet 18' / 'Shall I Compare Thee…?'

Analysis
  • 1609 Quarto: numbered, no titles
  • 18 = first sonnet after the procreation sonnets (1–17) → first with no child
  • Syllabus 2026–28: 'Sonnet 18'; 2015/16 papers (other anthology): 'Shall I Compare Thee…?'
  • First-line title: question + ellipsis → comparison left hanging
Effect, style & response
  • Neither title names the beloved; nor does the poem
1

Shall I compare thee to a summer’s day?

Analysis
  • Rhetorical question / dubitatio: feigned hesitation over how to praise
  • Modal Shall → deliberating; the only I in the poem (on the beat)
  • thee = intimate singular (15–17 used "you")
  • a summer’s day = stock compliment; a day is short → comparison carries its own defeat
Effect, style & response
  • Reader watches a mind test a comparison → argument, not declaration
2

more lovely and more temperate

Analysis
  • Comparatives more… more → he compares after all
  • lovely = nearest word to love in the poem
  • temperate: mild weather / balanced humours / self-controlled → key word
  • Colon → thesis; evidence follows
Effect, style & response
  • Praises steadiness, not dazzle → sets up eternal
3

Rough winds do shake the darling buds of May

Analysis
  • Spondee Rough winds → gust in the metre, then smooth iambs
  • shake (violent) vs darling (tender): only endearment in the poem, given to buds
  • buds = beauty unopened → summer damages its own future
  • May = early summer (Julian calendar; Midsummer 24 June)
Effect, style & response
  • Loved and fragile → harm felt, not just seen
4

summer’s lease hath all too short a date

Analysis
  • Legal metaphor: lease = rented for a fixed term; date = term + expiry
  • Summer = tenant, not owner → brevity is a contract, not bad luck
  • all too short = lover's complaint
  • Echoes Sonnet 13 "hold in lease", 14 "doom and date"
Effect, style & response
  • Opens the property argument → answered by possession (10)
5–6

the eye of heaven / gold complexion dimm’d

Analysis
  • Trochee Sometime; too hot = excess; dimm’d = deficiency → never temperate
  • Periphrasis the eye of heaven = sun; personified face
  • complexion = skin colour + humoural temperament → links to temperate
  • Passive dimm’d: no agent
Effect, style & response
  • Hyperbole climbs: beloved beats the sun itself
  • eye → eyes can see (13): readers replace the sun
7

every fair from fair sometime declines

Analysis
  • Generalisation: every → law of all beauty, incl. the beloved
  • fair from fair = beautiful thing / beauty itself; word split from itself
  • sometime now = eventually (l.5 = sometimes); stress on -TIME
  • declines = the sun's descent
Effect, style & response
  • Intermittent → inevitable: makes the turn necessary
8

By chance or nature’s changing course untrimm’d

Analysis
  • Two agents: chance (accident) + nature's course (ageing, seasons) → nothing escapes
  • untrimm’d = stripped of trim/ornament OR sails out of trim (nautical)
  • Alliteration ch / ch / c
  • Octave ends: beloved absent since l.2
Effect, style & response
  • Strongest possible case for decay → the turn means more
9

But thy eternal summer shall not fade

Analysis
  • Volta But at l.9 (Italian position)
  • Paradox eternal summer; thy stressed → your summer
  • Comparison not refused but upgraded: summer without a lease
  • shall not = guarantee/prophecy; first of three negatives
Effect, style & response
  • Exuberant certainty: "not you"
10

Nor lose possession of that fair thou ow’st

Analysis
  • possession answers lease (4): tenant → owner
  • that fair answers every fair from fair (7) → point-by-point rebuttal
  • ow’st = own (Elizabethan) + owe → beauty as a debt to nature (Sonnet 4)
Effect, style & response
  • Debt heard, then cancelled
11

Nor shall death brag thou wander’st in his shade

Analysis
  • Death personified as a braggart → mocked, not feared
  • shade = shadow of death (Psalm 23) + classical ghosts (shades) wandering
  • Only death's brag denied: the body still dies
Effect, style & response
  • Contempt for death; the poem replaces the psalm's protecting God
12

eternal lines / to time thou grow’st

Analysis
  • lines = verse / lineage (1–17's children) / wrinkles (Sonnet 19)
  • grow to = be grafted onto (Sonnet 15 "I engraft you new")
  • eternal repeated (9, 12) → beloved's eternity = the poem's
  • Paradox: he grows as time passes
Effect, style & response
  • Time: enemy → medium
13–14

So long lives this, and this gives life to thee

Analysis
  • Conditional So long as → eternity on human terms (readers)
