  • breathe (speak) + see (read) = how a poem lives
  • Deixis this ×2 = the poem; chiasmus lives / this / this / life
  • All 20 words monosyllables; present tense → true at every reading
  • Last word thee (= l.1)
Effect, style & response
  • Self-proving ending, but what survives is this, not a face

Form & structure

Analysis
  • Shakespearean sonnet: 3 quatrains + couplet, ABAB CDCD EFEF GG, iambic pentameter
  • Q1 + Q2 = case against summer (4 counts + 1 law); Q3 = 3 denials + the means; couplet = terms
  • Every line end-stopped; each quatrain closed
  • Turns: l.9 (summer → beloved); couplet (beloved → poem)
Effect, style & response
  • Form = argument; regularity embodies temperate

Sound & metre

Analysis
  • Spondee l.3; trochee l.5; death demoted l.11; heavy l.14
  • Same vowel in day / May / date / fade / shade → light and its loss
  • see / thee rhyme → reading = the beloved
  • /l/ in long… lives… life
Effect, style & response
  • Couplet's plain monosyllables = oath-like certainty

Context: the sequence

Analysis
  • 1609 Quarto (Thorpe); 1–126 young man; 127–152 woman; 153–154 Cupid poems
  • 1–17 procreation sonnets: marry, have children
  • 18 = first with no child → verse alone
  • Probably 1590s (Meres 1598: "sugred Sonnets"); printed 1609 → 400+ years old
Effect, style & response
  • The poem as a change of argument, not just a compliment

Context: verse that outlasts time

Analysis
  • Horace, Odes 3.30: monument "more lasting than bronze"
  • Ovid, Metamorphoses 15: last word vivam, "I shall live"
  • Spenser, Amoretti 75: "My verse your virtues rare shall eternize"
  • Shakespeare again: 55 "Not marble…", 63, 65
Effect, style & response
  • Classical poets immortalise themselves; 18 → the beloved (unnamed)

Ironies

Analysis
  • Doubts comparison → compares throughout (eternal summer)
  • Beloved never described: no face, name, body
  • I once; this = subject at the end → poem praises itself
  • No word love; no marriage, despite its use at weddings
Effect, style & response
  • Generosity (any reader fills thee) or self-regard (the art survives)?
CONNECTIONS

Connections

How this poem pairs with the rest of the set

Comparison hooks

1. Boey Kim Cheng, 'Report to Wordsworth' (05)

Link: Two sonnets about what poetry can do against loss, each ending in a couplet about seeing. Shakespeare trusts verse to defeat time; Boey's speaker reports that "Poetry and piety have begun to fail". Shakespeare's sun, the eye of heaven, is merely unreliable; Boey's sky ends in catastrophe: "O see the wound widening in the sky".

Shared technique: Both use the Shakespearean rhyme pattern (ABAB CDCD EFEF GG, with half-rhymes in Boey) and a closing couplet that calls on sight (eyes can see; "O see"). Both personify nature and the heavens.

Difference: Shakespeare's nature is imperfect and art perfects it; Boey's is destroyed by "insatiate man", and the speaker calls on a dead poet for help that cannot come. One couplet guarantees life; the other hears God "utter his last cry".

2. Kevin Halligan, 'The Cockroach' (06)

Link: Two sonnets that end by fusing the speaker's subject with something else. Shakespeare's poem becomes the beloved's life (this gives life to thee); Halligan's speaker finds himself in the insect: "I thought I recognised myself".

Shared technique: Iambic pentameter, a sonnet's argument, and a last line that changes how the whole poem reads.

Difference: Sonnet 18's couplet is the most confident resolution in the set; Halligan withholds a couplet altogether (ABAB CDCD EFGEGF) and ends on "I don't know" and a guess. Shakespeare's I appears once and vanishes into the poem; Halligan's "I" begins as a detached watcher and ends as the subject.

3. Aphra Behn, 'Song: Love Armed' (01)

Link: Two love lyrics working inside the Petrarchan tradition of praising the beloved by comparison. Behn's beloved has "Bright Eyes" from which Love takes "his fire"; Shakespeare's beloved is set against the sun itself, the eye of heaven.

Shared technique: An argument organised around pronouns that ends on the long /iː/ of the beloved's pronoun: Behn's "thee… free", Shakespeare's see… thee.

Difference: Behn's love wounds the speaker ("my poor Heart alone is harmed") and leaves the beloved "the Victor… and free"; Shakespeare's speaker hardly mentions himself, and love is a gift rather than a wound. Behn's ending is a complaint; Shakespeare's is a guarantee.

4. Katherine Philips, 'A Married State' (11)

Link: Both poems turn away from marriage and children as the answer to a life. Sonnets 1–17 urged the young man to marry and father children; Sonnet 18 is the first to stop, and offers verse instead. Philips urges a woman to stay single, spared childbirth's pains that "extort your tears".

Shared technique: Rhymed iambic pentameter carrying an argument to a decisive close: Philips's poem is all couplets, and Shakespeare's argument ends on one.

Difference: Philips argues with dry wit ("A married state affords but little ease"); Shakespeare is rapturous, and his alternative to children is not freedom but poetry.

5. Carol Rumens, 'Carpet-weavers, Morocco' (13)

Link: Both are about making something that outlasts its makers' moment. Rumens's weavers knot "all-that-will-be" into a pattern that will "freeze" into "all-that-was"; Shakespeare's beloved grow’st into eternal lines.

Shared technique: The made object becomes the image of time, a carpet's pattern and a poem's lines, and both poems use future and present tenses to fix what is passing.

Difference: Shakespeare's art is meant to preserve a person; Rumens's preserves a pattern, while the children who made it stay in "the school of days" and the carpet leaves without them. Both end up keeping the art more surely than the people: Shakespeare calls this a triumph; Rumens leaves it uneasy.

6. Seamus Heaney, 'Follower' (08)

Link: Lineage and time. The sonnets before 18 wanted the young man to live on in a son; Heaney's son wanted to "grow up and plough" like his father, and ends with the father "stumbling / Behind me".

Shared technique: Both endings reverse the direction of time: Shakespeare's beloved grows (grow’st) instead of declining; in Heaney the follower becomes the one followed.

Difference: Shakespeare's permanence is a gift; Heaney's is a weight, a father who "will not go away". Shakespeare replaces family with art; Heaney shows inheritance as something you cannot put down.

7. Alexander Pope, 'An Essay on Man' (12)

Link: Both ask what a human being is in time. Pope's man is "Born but to die, and reasoning but to err"; Shakespeare's beloved is born to decline like every fair, unless verse intervenes.

Shared technique: Iambic pentameter, antithesis and paradox (Pope's "darkly wise, and rudely great", Shakespeare's eternal summer) and the authority of rhyme.

Difference: Pope ends on unresolved paradox, "The glory, jest, and riddle of the world!"; Shakespeare resolves his in a couplet that claims victory over death.

A hunting snake that never notices its watchers stops them dead, and the poem's quiet event is the blow that, this time, nobody strikes.

CONTEXT

Context

The world the poem came out of

The Poet: Judith Wright (1915–2000)

Judith Arundell Wright was born on 31 May 1915 at Armidale, on the New England tableland of northern New South Wales, the eldest child of Phillip Wright, a grazier, and his first wife, Ethel. She grew up on her family's sheep country. After her mother's early death and her father's remarriage (1929) she boarded at New England Girls' School, then studied philosophy, English, psychology and history at the University of Sydney. When the Second World War began she went home to help on her father's station during the labour shortage, and the landscape of that return fed her first book, The Moving Image (1946), which made her name.

From 1950 she lived at Mount Tamborine in south-east Queensland with the philosopher and novelist Jack McKinney. Their daughter Meredith was born in 1950, they married in 1962, and McKinney died in 1966. Wright began losing her hearing in her twenties and was completely deaf by the early 1990s. She spent her last decades near Braidwood, NSW, and died in Canberra on 25 June 2000, aged 85, shortly after joining a march in Canberra for reconciliation between non-Indigenous and Aboriginal Australians. Her honours include the Queen's Gold Medal for Poetry (1991).

The conservationist and campaigner

Wright's activism was not a sideline to the poetry. She was a founding member of the Wildlife Preservation Society of Queensland (founded 1962) with the naturalist David Fleay, the artist Kathleen McArthur and Brian Clouston, and she was its president from 1964 to 1976. The society campaigned against oil drilling on the Great Barrier Reef and sand mining on Queensland's islands and beaches, including Fraser Island (K'gari). Wright told the Reef story in The Coral Battleground (1977).

She was equally committed to Aboriginal land rights. She was a founding member of the Aboriginal Treaty Committee (formed in 1979 with H. C. “Nugget” Coombs) and described its work in We Call for a Treaty (1985). The Cry for the Dead (1981) is her history of the dispossession of Aboriginal people in the region her own family had settled. She was a close friend of the Aboriginal poet Oodgeroo Noonuccal (then Kath Walker), to whom her poem 'Two Dreamtimes' is addressed. Wright knew her family's land had been taken from its first owners, and much of her later writing is a public reckoning with that inheritance.

Date and first publication

'Hunting Snake' is harder to date than most poems in the set. PoetryProf dates it to 1964, which places it in Wright's Tamborine Mountain years and the early life of the Wildlife Preservation Society. Its first collection could not be confirmed in this research. It is not in The Other Half (1966), and it does not appear among the indexed contents of Five Senses: Selected Poems (1963). Some websites name a Wright collection called Hunting Snake, but no such book appears among her dated collections, and the reference is probably to the poem itself. The safest statement is “c. 1964, middle period”. The poem is set in the Cambridge anthology Songs of Ourselves Volume 1 for the 2026–2028 examinations.

If the date is right, the poem was written while Wright was helping to build Queensland's first serious wildlife-preservation campaign. A poem about letting a dangerous animal pass unharmed came from someone organising, at that moment, to stop the killing of wild things.

'The Killer' (1947): the snake she killed first

Wright had written this encounter before. 'The Killer' first appeared in the journal Southerly in December 1947 and was reprinted in Woman to Man (1949), and later in Five Senses (1963) and both Collected Poems (1971, 1994). In its 28 lines a speaker goes down to a creek to rest and drink, is surprised by a black snake, and lashes out and kills it. The title can point at the venomous snake or at the human who kills it. The critic Andrew Taylor (Reading Australian Poetry, 1987) reads the poem as guilt: less guilt at killing an innocent creature than at failing to recognise that the enemy lay within herself, and so killing the creature outside instead.

'Hunting Snake' returns to the same scene, a sunlit day, a sudden meeting and a great black snake, and reverses the outcome: the walkers freeze, watch, and let it go. Read side by side, the two titles mirror each other ('The Killer' leaves open who kills, 'Hunting Snake' who hunts), and the later poem reads as an answer to the earlier one. This is a critical reading, not something Wright is recorded as saying.

The great black snake: natural history

Wright names no species. In eastern Australia, though, a “black snake” usually means the red-bellied black snake (Pseudechis porphyriacus), and the details fit it: a large, glossy black snake with red or pink lower sides, common from south-east Queensland down through New England and the coast, often near water, and active by day. It eats mainly frogs, as well as lizards, small mammals and other snakes. It is venomous and a bite needs treatment, but it is shy rather than aggressive. Wright gives it what it needs, real caution, and spares it terror.

Two details are exact. A snake hunts by scent: the forked tongue flicks out, collects chemical traces from the ground and air, and carries them to a sensing organ in the roof of the mouth (the vomeronasal or Jacobson's organ). That is how it follows a trail with its tongue flickering. And snakes are ectotherms, taking their body heat from their surroundings. A mild, sunny late-autumn day is when a snake can still bask, warm up and hunt before winter slows it down, so the late season's grace that comforts the walkers may also be the snake's last good hunting weather. The poem never uses the words venom, poison, bite or danger. To an Australian reader none of them needs saying.

Serpent, sublime and Lawrence's 'Snake'

Three traditions stand behind the poem. The first is imported. In Genesis 3 the serpent is the tempter, cursed to crawl on its belly, and European settlers carried that meaning to a continent full of venomous snakes. The second was already in Australia. In many Aboriginal cultures a great serpent (often called the Rainbow Serpent in English, with many local names) is a creator being linked to water and life. The poem does not depict it, but Wright's refusal of the Genesis reflex was made in a country where an older, opposite reading of the snake existed.

The third is the sublime. Edmund Burke's Philosophical Enquiry into the Origin of Our Ideas of the Sublime and Beautiful (1757) argued that power and danger, felt at a safe distance, produce what he called “a sort of delightful horror”. The poem's sequence of frozen stride, lost breath and suspended thought, followed by a deeper breath, fits that account, and PoetryProf links the poem to Burke and the Romantics. The closest poem in English is D. H. Lawrence's 'Snake' (Birds, Beasts and Flowers, 1923). A man at his water-trough in Sicily admires a drinking snake, then obeys the voices of “my accursed human education” and throws a log at it, and is left with “a pettiness” to expiate. Wright's walkers feel the same awe and throw nothing.

THE POEM

The Poem

Line by line, with the analysis alongside

Hunting Snake

This poem is still in copyright, so its words are not reproduced here: each line shows a short summary. Read it alongside your anthology or the exam paper, or use Add the text to paste it in from your own copy (it stays on this device).

THunting Snake
1basking in sunlight, in the kindly lateness of the year
2beneath the mildest heaven of the fall
3the two are strolling, then stop dead mid-stride
4a huge dark serpent swings swiftly past them
5its head held low, its tongue testing the ground for scent
6it hunts onward, the stems opening before it
7sunlight gives its gem-like skin a shining coat
8the watchers' breathing stops as it goes by
9which path it traced, which little creature
10ran, still alive, from its savage purpose
11they hardly considered; motionless, they stayed put
12their gaze travelled along with it as it moved
13chilly, shadowy and magnificent, it vanished
14among stems that concealed its quarry
15they breathe in the daylight more fully than before
16a glance between them; then they walk on

Lines with a marker have analysis — click one, or just scroll.

Title
Hunting Snake
Language & devices

A two-word Noun phrase with no article, which reads like a field-guide label or the caption of a painting. Its first word is grammatically Ambiguous. As a Participial adjective, Hunting describes a snake that is hunting, which is what the poem shows. As a Gerund with Snake as its object (as in “duck hunting”), it names the hunting of snakes. Each reading puts a different creature in the role of hunter.

Meaning & effect

The title puts the snake's purpose first, and the poem keeps faith with it: from its first appearance to its last the animal is hunting, and it never once attends to the people. The second sense names the outcome the poem refuses. Settler Australians routinely killed snakes on sight, and Wright had written that version herself in 'The Killer' (1947), where a speaker kills a black snake at a creek (see Context). A third sense builds as you read. The walkers are tracking too, because their eyes follow the snake the way it follows its prey, so the title also names the chain of attention the poem describes. Wright chooses the first sense and lets the other two hang over it.

Line 1
Sun-warmed … late season's grace
Language & devices

The Compound adjective Sun-warmed opens a Periodic sentence: two lines of setting before the subject we arrives in line 3. The Demonstrative before late season puts the speaker inside the moment. late season means late autumn. grace is a Pun (or Polysemy): gracefulness, a favour freely given (the religious sense), and a period of grace, a reprieve before winter. Sibilance runs through the line (Sun, this, season's, grace), and the two heavy opening syllables slow its start.

Meaning & effect

The poem begins in comfort, and the comfort is exact: a last mild spell before the cold, felt as a gift rather than something earned. grace makes the day feel granted, which prepares the sense that what follows is a privilege, a sighting the walkers are allowed. late quietly signals an ending, since the year is running down, and that matters later for an animal that has to feed before winter. Sun-warmed also states, without comment, the one thing the walkers share with the snake: the people enjoy the sun, and the cold-blooded snake depends on it to move at all.

Line 2
gentlest sky
Language & devices

A second adverbial phrase lengthens the delay. The Superlative gentlest goes one step past “gentle”. The line opens with a Trochaic inversion (UN-der), so it eases in rather than striding. Its sounds are soft liquids and nasals (n, m, l), with almost no hard stops. The sky is given human mildness, a light touch of Pathetic fallacy.

Meaning & effect

Not just a mild sky but the mildest: Wright stacks up warmth, grace and gentleness so that nature first appears kindly and protective, unlike the stock picture of a harsh Australian bush (PoetryProf makes this contrast). Two lines in, there is still no subject or verb, and the syntax lingers the way the walkers do. It is the last moment in the poem when the walkers' world is the subject. From line 4 the world belongs to the snake.

Line 3
froze half-through a pace
Language & devices

The subject at last is the First-person plural we. The poem never says “I”. Two verbs sit either side of a Caesura in a Juxtaposition of motion and its stopping. froze is a Metaphor that turns temperature into sudden stillness. half-through a pace is precise Kinaesthetic imagery: a stride interrupted with one foot still lifted. A full stop ends the sentence mid-stanza. The metre stays regular, but the three heavy syllables of froze half-through slow the second half of the line.

Meaning & effect

The long, easy sentence ends in an arrest. The walkers stop part-way through a step, caught by their bodies before their minds know why. The cause is not named until line 4, so the reaction comes before its explanation. That order is Wright's point: awe and fear arrive as physical events, not thoughts. froze is a startling verb in a poem so full of warmth. The warm-blooded people turn cold and still while the cold-blooded snake moves fluidly, a reversal the poem completes with Cold in line 13. we makes the reaction shared and simultaneous: two people stopping as one. The plural also hints that this could be anyone.

Line 4
The great black snake
Language & devices

The snake gets a whole line and a whole sentence to itself. great black snake is three stressed monosyllables in a row, with a Spondee in the second foot, and the hard Plosives g, b and k make the phrase heavy and slow. The Definite article The treats it as a known presence of this country, not “a snake”. reeling is a fluid Present participle, suggesting whirling and swaying, and a line paying out from a reel. The last word tells us it is passing them, not coming at them.

Meaning & effect

The cause arrives after the effect. Wright names the animal in plain, weighty words for size, colour and kind, then releases it into motion, and the sound does the same: hard consonants give way to the liquid r and l of reeling. The verb catches a snake's sinuous side-to-side movement and its speed. It may also hint at the dizziness of the watchers, who are the ones reeling inside. Most importantly, from its first moment the snake is passing by. It has no interest in the people at all, and the poem never suggests an attack.

Line 5
Head down, tongue flickering
Language & devices

Two Absolute phrases present the head and tongue before the pronoun he (line 6), so the snake is built up from close-up details, as if through a lens. flickering is quick Kinaesthetic imagery, and trail is hunting vocabulary. This is the poem's most irregular line: four stresses packed at the start (HEAD DOWN, TONGUE FLICK-) followed by a rush of light syllables. It has nine syllables unless flickering is clipped to two.

Meaning & effect

This is a naturalist's description. A snake hunts by scent, flicking its forked tongue to collect chemical traces from the ground (see Context), so tongue flickering on a trail is exact. Head down shows complete absorption: the snake is reading the ground, not watching the watchers. The metre flickers too, a heavy, held-down start and then quick light taps, like the tongue's rapid touches. The poem slows down to look closely just as the walkers do.

Line 6
quested … the parting grass
Language & devices

The pronoun he gives the snake a gender and a self. The humans never become individuals. quested is elevated diction: its Connotations are the knight's quest, a noble search (from Latin quaerere, to seek), and in older hunting usage hounds “quest” when they cast about for a scent. In the parting grass, the Present participle and a touch of Personification make the grass open ahead of him, as a crowd parts for royalty. The line is perfectly regular Iambic tetrameter and ends on a semicolon.

Meaning & effect

The verb raises the hunt to something heroic and purposeful, and it is also technically exact for an animal following a scent. The grass parting makes the landscape cooperate: the snake belongs here and the land makes way for it, while the walkers have been reduced to stillness. The smooth, regular line suits the effortless movement. The snake moves through its own domain while the people are visitors standing on its edge.

Line 7
diamond scale
Language & devices

glazed is a Metaphor: sunlight as a glassy coating, like the glaze on pottery. curves gives the body's sinuous shape. diamond scale combines a Connotation of gems (brilliant, precious, the hardest stone) with accuracy, since snake scales really are diamond-shaped, and the singular scale makes the skin sound like a material, like mail armour. This is Visual imagery of shine. sun returns from line 1, where it warmed the walkers, and here it gilds the snake.

Meaning & effect

The poem's most beautiful image makes the snake precious rather than repellent. Its vocabulary is jewellery and craft, so the snake becomes an object of value, almost a made thing, and the inherited picture of the serpent as sly tempter has no room to form. diamond keeps hardness inside the beauty: splendour and danger in one word. The same sun touches walkers and snake alike, but only the snake shines.

Line 8
we lost breath to watch
Language & devices

lost breath is a compressed Idiom (“we lost breath”, not “we lost our breath”), which makes it a bare bodily fact. The infinitive clause that follows gives the cause. There is a small Stress clash: the metre wants “and WE lost BREATH”, but speech says “we LOST BREATH”, so two heavy syllables collide where the breath stops. A full stop closes the stanza. (Some printings read see for watch; PoetryProf's text and most others read watch.)

Meaning & effect

The stanza gives three lines to the snake and one clause to the humans, and that clause is a loss. As with the frozen stride, awe is registered by the body: the walkers stop breathing. watch names their only action in the poem, which is watching. pass repeats the line-4 point that the snake is passing through, not stopping. The breath lost here is taken back, deeper, in line 15, and the poem's emotional arc lies between those two breaths.

Lines 9–10
what small food / fled living
Language & devices

Two fronted Noun clauses (indirect questions, with no question marks) are placed before their verb, which arrives only in line 11: Inversion or Hyperbaton. Anaphora repeats What… what. The Enjambment at small food / fled living holds the prey as mere food at the line-end, then the next line restores it as a living, fleeing creature. In fierce intent, an Abstract noun becomes the thing the prey flees from. Alliteration links fled and fierce.

Meaning & effect

The poem turns to the snake's hidden world, its route and its prey, which the walkers cannot see. small food is the predator's view: a frog or lizard reduced to a meal. fled living insists on the prey's life at the moment it is threatened, so for the length of a line-break a living animal is only food. fierce intent is the poem's strongest statement of the snake's will: it is not drifting but wanting. Because the verb is delayed, the reader spends two lines on these questions before learning the walkers scarcely thought about them. The poem thinks what its people did not.

Line 11
we scarcely thought
Language & devices

This is Paralipsis (also called apophasis): the poem raises the prey and then says the walkers hardly considered it. scarcely is an Understatement. The semicolon is a mid-line Caesura. The second half is an Inversion that puts still before its verb (for “as we stood still”), and still is Ambiguous: motionless, and also “even now, continuing”. The foot after the semicolon is a Trochaic substitution (STILL as), so the stress lands on stillness. Consonance on st (still, stood) makes the phrase hard to say quickly.

Meaning & effect

The walkers' minds are suspended along with their bodies, and thought gives way to pure attention. scarcely is honest, almost a confession: the wonder depends on not thinking about the death the snake is pursuing. Wright neither condemns nor excuses this. She records it. The second half of the line returns to stillness, and its clustered consonants make the line itself stand still.

Line 12
our eyes went
Language & devices

went is repeated in two senses, an Antanaclasis: the eyes “go” figuratively (the gaze follows) and the snake goes literally. eyes works as a Synecdoche, the part of the walkers that leaves while their bodies stay. The line is built of soft sounds (w, h, s, n) with almost no hard consonants, so it glides. A full stop closes the third stanza.

Meaning & effect

This is the stanza's paradox: standing completely still, the walkers are carried off, because their attention travels with the snake. It is the closest they come to joining it. The repeated verb makes the line follow itself, acting out the watching of something moving away. The people have become pure eyes, and their only movement is the movement of looking.

Line 13
Cold, dark and splendid
Language & devices

A Tricolon of adjectives comes before the pronoun (Inversion), opening with a Spondee (COLD, DARK) slowed by a comma. The order rises to a Climax. Cold means cold-blooded, unfeeling, deathly. dark means black, mysterious, menacing. splendid means magnificent, and comes from Latin splendere, to shine, so dark and splendid is close to an Oxymoron: dark yet shining, which is exact for a glossy black snake. gone is stative: the snake has already vanished when it is described. The Enjambment after gone leaves the word alone at the line-end.

Meaning & effect

This is the poem's one explicit judgement of the snake, delivered as it disappears. The first two adjectives are the ones a frightened settler might use, and Wright does not deny them. She adds a third that changes their moral weight: coldness and darkness become part of the splendour, not grounds for killing. Because the description arrives with gone, the snake is defined by its after-image. The line-break lets it vanish before the sentence says where it went.

Line 14
hid his prey
Language & devices

The line opens with a Trochaic inversion on its first word. the grass returns from line 6 in a Contrast: grass that parted to let the snake through now hid its prey. hid his prey is Ambiguous. It may mean hidden from the snake, which would not protect the prey from a hunter working by scent, or hidden from the walkers and from us. Alliteration links hid his. The full stop ends the snake's part of the poem.

Meaning & effect

The snake leaves through the same grass it entered, which now works as a curtain. The kill is never shown: the grass hides it from the walkers and from the reader, so the hunt continues without witnesses. The snake's last word in the poem is prey. Its hunt is its whole story, and the poem's final image of the animal is purpose carrying on out of sight.

Line 15
a deeper breath
Language & devices

An Echo and Antithesis with line 8: lost breath becomes deeper breath. The Comparative deeper implies “deeper than before”. In breath of day the Metaphor makes the day itself air to be breathed in, and day answers the snake's dark. The line is perfectly regular Iambic tetrameter, so the metre steadies as the breathing does. day completes the inner rhyme with prey.

Meaning & effect

Breathing is restored, and deepened. The encounter has enlarged the walkers' sense of being alive, and their first act afterwards is again bodily. day stands against dark: the snake goes into darkness, into the grass and the kill, while the people breathe the daylight more fully. The rhyme sets the snake's prey beside the humans' day, the death hidden in the grass next to the life breathed in.

Line 16
each other … went on
Language & devices

Lines 15–16 form a Tricolon of verbs (took, looked, went on), which answers line 13's three adjectives. The Reciprocal pronoun each other is the first point at which we divides into two people. The diction is the plainest in the poem, with no adjective, no image and no figure, a deliberate Anticlimax. The line opens with a trochee (LOOKED at). on closes the Envelope rhyme begun by gone in line 13.

Meaning & effect

The ending is plain on purpose: a shared look, and the walk resumes. What passes in that look (relief, wonder, leftover fear) is left unsaid, and the poem trusts the silence. each other turns the joint we into two people facing one another, so the encounter ends in human connection. went on rhymes with the snake's gone, pairing the snake's departure with the humans' continuing: two lives going separate ways. Against Wright's own 'The Killer', the plainness carries the moral. Nobody strikes, and simply going on is the act that matters.

THE WHOLE POEM

The Whole Poem

Stepping back: what the poem is doing, first line to last

'Hunting Snake' looks like the simplest poem in the set: two people on an autumn walk see a large black snake, stop, watch it pass, and walk on. Its sixteen lines contain no argument and no stated lesson. But the poem is built on a sharp asymmetry. The snake never notices the people, and the people cannot stop noticing the snake. Wright measures, almost entirely through the body, what it does to human beings to meet something magnificent that is not about them at all. Read against her own earlier snake poem, 'The Killer' (1947), and against the settler reflex of killing snakes on sight, the poem's real event is something that does not happen: nobody strikes.

The first stanza sets a trap of comfort. The long opening sentence delays its subject through two lines of warmth, a late season's grace and an autumn's gentlest sky, so that the reader settles as the walkers do. When the subject finally arrives, it brings two verbs at once, one of motion and one of arrest, and the sentence and the stride stop together, half-through a pace. The order is the first sign of Wright's method: the reaction comes before its cause. Only in line 4 do we learn why the walkers froze, and the snake gets that line to itself, a whole sentence, three heavy stresses in great black snake, then the fluid release of reeling. From the first moment the snake goes by. It is passing them, not coming at them.

The second stanza is the poem's long look. Wright builds the snake out of close-up detail before she names it as he: the head held low, the tongue flicking on a scent trail, the hunting verb quested, grass parting for it, sun glazing its scales into diamond. The description is both exact natural history (snakes do read the ground with the tongue) and a deliberate act of valuing. The diction of quest and jewellery makes the animal noble and precious rather than sinister, and the inherited Christian picture of the serpent as tempter never gets a foothold. The grammar does the same work. The snake has three full lines and all the active verbs. The humans get one clause, introduced by and, and its verb is a loss: we lost breath. Awe arrives as a physical event, the stopped breath, and the people in the poem are reduced to a shared bodily reaction.

The third stanza turns from what can be seen to what cannot. The snake has a whole hidden world of route and prey (What track, what small food), and the line-break before fled living holds a living animal for one beat as nothing but food. Then comes the poem's most honest phrase. The walkers scarcely thought about any of it. Wright places the questions before the verb that dismisses them, so the reader thinks what the walkers did not. Rapture, she admits, depends on a suspension of moral attention, on not thinking about the frog or lizard that is about to die. The stanza ends in a paradox of stillness and motion: the walkers stand still, yet our eyes went with the snake. Their bodies stay, and their attention leaves with the animal.

The last stanza delivers the poem's single judgement as the snake disappears. Cold, dark and splendid lets the two adjectives a frightened settler would use stand, then adds a third that changes their moral weight. Coldness and darkness become part of the splendour, not reasons to kill. Even splendid holds the paradox together, since at root it means shining, and a glossy black snake is dark and bright at once. The snake is already gone when it is described, and it vanishes where the grass hid his prey, so the kill happens out of sight and the hunt continues without witnesses. Then the humans return as grammatical subjects with three verbs in a row. They take a deeper breath of day, look at each other, and go on. The breath lost in line 8 is recovered, and recovered deeper. For the first time the joint we divides into two people who can look at one another.

The form tracks all of this. Three stanzas of alternating rhyme pull the ear forward while the snake moves; the last stanza switches to enclosed rhyme, which closes back on itself. Each of its rhyme pairs joins the snake's world to the humans' world: the snake's gone rhymes with the walkers' went on, and its prey with their day. The parting of ways is written into the sound. The language goes plain in the last line, with no adjective and no image, as if the beauty had belonged to the encounter and not to the world the walkers return to.

The strongest objection is that the poem aestheticises a killer. It makes a predator gorgeous, looks away from the victim, and buys its sublime moment with inattention, since the grass that conceals the kill hides it from us too. On this view the poem is a pretty picture with a death edited out. The answer is that Wright does not edit it out. She puts it in. fled living insists on the prey's life, fierce intent names the snake's will to kill, and we scarcely thought records the walkers' looking-away as a fact, almost a confession. The poem does not pretend nature is gentle. Its gentlest sky hangs over a hunt. What it refuses is the human urge to intervene, judge or destroy. In Wright's 'The Killer' a speaker meets a black snake at a creek and kills it; in Lawrence's 'Snake' a man admires a snake and then throws a log at it. Here the walkers feel the same awe and do nothing, and in a country that killed snakes by reflex, doing nothing is the moral act.

So the poem's plainness is its point. A writer who spent her life campaigning to stop the destruction of wild places wrote a poem in which the whole drama is looking properly and letting be. The snake goes on hunting, the people go on walking, and the poem holds the two lives side by side in a single rhyme without letting either one take the other.

FORM & STRUCTURE

Form & Structure

How the poem is built, and why it matters

Form & genre

A short narrative lyric of a single encounter: sixteen lines in four quatrains, told in the past tense by a plural we. It belongs to the tradition of the nature encounter and the sublime (compare Lawrence's 'Snake'), but in miniature: there is no argument and no stated lesson, only a sequence of observed events.

Stanzas

Four quatrains, each a stage of the encounter. 1, the walk and the sighting (lines 1–4). 2, the snake seen close (5–8). 3, its unseen hunt and the walkers' absorption (9–12). 4, its disappearance and their recovery (13–16). Every stanza ends with a full stop.

Metre

Iambic tetrameter: four beats and, in fifteen lines, eight syllables. Line 5 has nine unless flickering is clipped. Every line ends on a stressed syllable (masculine endings), and fifteen of the sixteen end-words are monosyllables (the exception is intent).

Rhyme

ABAB CDCD EFEF, then GHHG. Twelve lines of cross-rhyme give way to an envelope (enclosed) rhyme in the last stanza, as the snake disappears. All the rhymes are full except food / stood, a slant (eye) rhyme.

A form that moves, then closes

The first three stanzas use alternating rhyme, and alternating rhyme reaches forward: each rhyme jumps over a line to find its partner, so the ear is pulled continually on. That suits stanzas 1–3, which are about something in motion, the snake reeling, questing and passing. Then the last stanza changes pattern, which PoetryProf identifies as the shift from ABAB to ABBA.

Line End word Letter Rhyme quality
1 grace A full (grace / pace)
2 sky B full (sky / by)
3 pace A
4 by B
5 trail C full (trail / scale)
6 grass D full (grass / pass)
7 scale C
8 pass D
9 food E slant: same spelling and final consonant, different vowel (food / stood)
10 intent F full (intent / went)
11 stood E
12 went F
13 gone G full in British and Australian speech (gone / on)
14 prey H full (prey / day)
15 day H
16 on G

Enclosed rhyme turns back on itself, and the outer pair closes around the inner one. Two things make this more than a change of pattern.

  • Each rhyme pair joins the snake's world to the humans'. Lines 13–14 belong to the snake and lines 15–16 to the walkers, and the rhymes cross that boundary. The snake's gone rhymes with the humans' went on, and the snake's prey rhymes with the humans' day. At the poem's close the death in the grass and the breath of daylight are bound together by sound, and so are the animal's departure and the people's continuing.
  • The ending is delayed. In stanzas 1–3 every rhyme returns after one line. In stanza 4 the first rhyme-sound (gone) waits three lines for its partner, so the poem's final word completes a sound left hanging since the snake vanished. The stanza clicks shut on the poem's last syllable.

The single imperfect rhyme is worth noticing. food and stood look identical but do not sound alike, and they pair the prey with the motionless watchers in the very sentence that admits they scarcely thought about it. It may be chance, but the one rhyme that fails to chime falls on the poem's one moral blind spot.

Metre and where it breaks

The tetrameter is very regular, which is why its departures register. (Stress marks: / stressed, x unstressed.)

Line Fragment Pattern What the variation does
1 Sun-warmed / / a heavy, settled opening: the walkers at ease
2 under the… / x x / trochaic first foot, so the line eases in rather than striding
3 froze half-through / (/) / regular metre, but a run of heavy syllables after the caesura slows the line as the walkers halt
4 great black snake / / / three stresses in a row (spondee): the snake's arrival has weight, then reeling releases it
5 Head down, tongue flick- / / / / x x x / the poem's one nine-syllable line: four stresses piled up, then a light rush, like the tongue's flicker
8 we lost breath metre x / x /, speech x / / metre and speech clash on the two heavy syllables where breath stops
11 still as we stood / x x / trochaic substitution straight after the semicolon, so the beat lands on stillness
13 Cold, dark / / spondaic opening for the poem's one judgement
15 (whole line) x / x / x / x / perfectly regular: the metre steadies as the breathing does
16 looked at / x trochaic opening, so the humans' first new action takes the first beat

The irregular line (5) is the first close-up of the snake, and the most regular lines (6, 15) are the snake's easy movement and the humans' recovered breath. Wright saves metrical disturbance for the moments of greatest intensity: the arrival, the close look, the halt, the verdict.

Sentence shapes

The poem has six sentences, and their shapes tell the story.

Sentence Lines Shape
1 1–3 periodic: two lines of setting before we arrives, then two verbs either side of a comma, moving and stopping
2 4 one line, one clause: the snake given a whole sentence to itself
3 5–8 long and cumulative: body details, then he, then sun on his scales; the humans get only the last clause, and it is a loss of breath
4 9–12 inverted: two indirect questions placed before the verb that dismisses them (we scarcely thought), then a semicolon and the stillness
5 13–14 three adjectives before the pronoun; the snake is defined as it vanishes
6 15–16 three verbs in a row (took, looked, went on): the humans become active subjects again

The full stop at line 3 is the only mid-stanza stop in stanzas 1–3. It falls exactly where the walkers stop, so the walk and the sentence end together. The final stanza divides cleanly in two, two lines of snake and two of humans, which is the structural form of the poem's parting of ways. Stanza 2 is the most telling. Three lines belong to the snake, and the humans enter only at the end, through and, as an afterthought to their own story.

The plural we and the frozen stride

There is no I anywhere. The walkers are never named, described or told apart, and they do everything together: they walk, freeze, lose breath, stand, watch, breathe. The snake, by contrast, is he nine times in nine lines (6–14) and has a head, a tongue, curves, scales, a track, an intent and a prey. The animal is the poem's only individual; the humans are a joint reaction. Only at the very end does each other split the we into two people who can look at one another.

The freeze in line 3 sets up a structure of suspension. From froze to stood (line 11), the humans perform no voluntary act, and between their two verbs of motion, walked (3) and went on (16), they essentially stop being agents. Their stillness frames the snake's movement the way the stanzas frame a moving image. Every quatrain is sealed by a full stop, but inside the stanzas the lines run on (gone / into the grass), so the poem gives continuous motion in four still frames.

Enjambment and the two key line-breaks

  • small food / fled living (9–10): the break holds the prey as nothing but food for one beat, then restores its life.
  • gone / into (13–14): the snake is simply gone at the line-end, before the next line says where. The break performs the disappearance before the sentence explains it.

The turn and the ending

The volta comes at line 15. Its first word, We, takes the sentence back from the snake, and the rhyme scheme turns at the same moment: day answers prey where the earlier stanzas would have answered gone. The ending is anti-climactic on purpose. After splendid, diamond and fierce intent, the last line is the plainest in the poem: seven words, six of them monosyllables, with no adjective and no image. The language goes flat the moment the snake is out of sight, as if the beauty belonged to the encounter rather than to the world. Even so, went on supplies the rhyme that closes the whole form. The plainest words do the final structural work.

SOUND

Sound

What the poem does to the ear

Sound palette

The poem opens soft, with sibilants, liquids and long open vowels. It hardens with plosives the moment the snake appears, and the final stanza is the heaviest in hard consonants (PoetryProf notes its gutturals, dentals and plosives) before the last line goes plain.

Rhyme sounds

All the rhymes are masculine and nearly all are full. The exception is the slant rhyme food / stood. The long “ay” vowel of the first rhyme (grace / pace) returns in stanza 2 (trail / scale) and again in the last stanza (prey / day).

Rhythm

Regular four-beat lines whose few disturbances (lines 4, 5, 8, 11, 13) fall exactly on the moments of greatest intensity. See Form & Structure.

The opening hush. Lines 1–2 are built on s sounds and open vowels: Sun-warmed, season's grace, gentlest sky. There is hardly a hard stop in them. The sound is warm, slow and unthreatening, the acoustic version of gentlest. Wright makes the reader relax so the next sounds can startle.

The snake arrives in plosives. great black snake gives three stressed syllables in a row with hard g, b and k, the heaviest cluster in the poem so far, landing just after the walkers froze. The line then releases into the liquid r and l of reeling, and the sound goes from hard to flowing: first the shock of the thing, then its motion.

The flicker. In Head down, tongue flickering quick d, t and ck taps are separated by short vowels, and the line moves in small rapid touches, the way a tongue samples scent. The run of light syllables after flick- makes the tongue dart.

The rustle and the sheen. quested and the parting grass are thick with st, th, rt and ss sounds, a dry, brushing texture that suits a body moving through grass. The next line, sun glazed his curves, goes smooth: the buzzing z of glazed, the long vowels, the liquid l of scale. After the ticking of line 5 the sound itself seems to shine.

Breath and flight. In lost breath the stopped st runs straight into the plosive b, so the reader's own mouth checks for a moment. Stanza 3 brings in the fricative f: fled living, fierce intent. It is the breathy sound of escape, and it links the prey's flight to the hunter's will.

The line that stands still. still as we stood packs two st clusters into four words, and they cannot be said quickly. The line holds the mouth where the walkers are held. By contrast our eyes went glides on w, h and vowels, with almost nothing hard in it. The gaze moves smoothly while the body stays put.

The verdict. Cold, dark opens the last stanza with two hard, stressed monosyllables separated by a comma (k, d, k), each landing like a judgement entered. splendid then opens out through its liquid l and nasal n. The hard sounds continue through the stanza (grass, hid, took, deeper, breath), which gives the close a firmer, heavier sound than the dreamlike middle.

The plain close. The last line has almost no patterning: no alliteration, no sibilant run, mostly short vowels. It is the sound of the ordinary world resuming. Its one acoustic event is the rhyme on, which answers gone three lines back, so the stanza and the poem shut on a sound the ear had almost stopped waiting for.

MOTIFS & SYMBOLS

Motifs & Symbols

Images that recur, and what they accumulate

Motifs & symbols

1. Sun, shine and dark

The poem's first word is Sun-warmed, and the warmth belongs to the walkers. In line 7 the same sun moves to the snake (sun glazed his curves), and there it does more than warm: it makes the body glitter like diamond. Light passes from the people to the animal, and the snake becomes the bright thing in the scene. At the end of the poem light and darkness meet in one creature: dark and splendid, where splendid at root means shining. The glossy black snake is literally both. When it leaves, the humans are left with day, breathing in the plain daylight more deeply. Through the motif the poem argues that darkness and brilliance are not opposites in nature, whatever the moral tradition says.

2. Breath

Breath measures the encounter. It is lost at the centre of the poem (we lost breath, line 8) and taken back near the end, deeper (line 15). Between those two points the walkers barely live as agents: they cannot think, cannot move, and can only watch. The motif makes awe physiological. You stop breathing when something takes your breath away, and the poem means it literally. It also gives the ending its positive claim: the encounter does not change the world, but it changes how fully the walkers inhabit it, in a breath of day that the snake, which lives on in the dark grass, has made deeper.

3. Grass

The grass is the snake's element and the poem's curtain. In stanza 2 it is parting, opening ahead of the snake as if making way for royalty. In stanza 4 it hides: it hid his prey, closing over the hunt and the kill. Same noun, opposite offices, eight lines apart: the grass first reveals the snake to the walkers and then conceals what the snake is doing. It marks the boundary of human knowledge. We see what the snake allows to show above the grass, and the life-and-death business below it (the small food, the fierce intent) stays out of sight.

4. Going and staying still

The verb went occurs four times, and who owns it tells the story. The snake went reeling by (line 4). In line 12 the verb comes twice, first for the eyes (our eyes went) and then again for the snake: the eyes borrow it for a moment, but only to follow him. The humans get it for themselves only in the last line, went on, once the snake has finished using it. Against this the poem sets a cluster of stillness words, all belonging to the walkers: froze, still, stood. The pattern shows motion as the snake's property. The humans can resume moving only after the moving thing has gone.

5. Watching (eyes, thought, the look)

The walkers' one activity is looking: to watch him pass, our eyes went, and finally the look they give each other. The snake, Head down, never looks back. Watching is set against thinking, since they scarcely thought, so the poem's kind of attention is pre-verbal and total, not analytical. The motif ends by turning: the eyes that followed the snake turn to the other human, and the last look in the poem is shared between people. Attention that began fixed on the wild ends in recognition between the two who saw it.

THEMES

Themes

The ideas the poem is arguing about

01

Awe as a bodily event

The poem's distinction is that it renders awe as a sequence of physical events rather than an emotion described. The body halts before the mind knows why (froze half-through a pace). Breathing stops (we lost breath). Thought switches off (we scarcely thought). Attention becomes involuntary (our eyes went with him). Then, once the snake has gone, breathing comes back deeper. Wright never uses the words fear, wonder or awe. She records what the body does and lets the reader name it.

This is the pattern of the Burkean sublime, power felt at a safe distance as “a sort of delightful horror”, and the snake's indifference supplies the safety. The poem goes further than the theory, though. The after-effect is not exaltation but a quiet enlargement of ordinary life: a breath of day taken more fully, a look exchanged, a walk resumed.

02

A world not about us

The snake never notices the walkers. It is Head down, reading a scent trail, driven by its own fierce intent. It goes by, and it leaves without registering that they exist. What stops them is not menace but irrelevance: the discovery of something magnificent moving through the world for purposes that have nothing to do with them. The grammar makes the same point. The snake is he, with nine masculine pronouns in nine lines (6–14), and it gets the active verbs (quested, followed). The humans are an unnamed we whose verbs are reactions (froze, lost, scarcely thought, stood).

Being ignored by the sublime is stranger than being threatened by it. The poem removes people from the centre of the scene and finds that the scene is richer without them there.

03

The hunt, and what goes unthought

Beneath the beauty is a killing. Stanza 3 raises the prey (what small food, fled living) and says the walkers scarcely thought about it. In stanza 4 the grass hid his prey, so the death happens off-stage, concealed in the same breath as the poem's grandest description. The walkers' rapture depends on not thinking about the small animal that is about to die, and Wright says so plainly.

She neither condemns the snake nor sentimentalises the prey. Predation is simply part of what makes the snake splendid: fierce intent is admired, not deplored. The honesty lies in recording the suspension of moral attention rather than hiding it. Nature here is not gentle, and the gentlest sky of line 2 does not cover the whole scene.

04

Restraint: the blow not struck

Read against Wright's 'The Killer' (1947), where a speaker kills a black snake at a creek, and against the settler habit of killing snakes on sight, the poem's real event is a non-event. The walkers do nothing. They freeze, watch, and let the animal go about its life. The title's second sense, the hunting of snakes, is the action the poem declines.

This restraint is quiet but deliberate, and it carries Wright's conservationist ethic: looking properly at a creature is the first step towards not destroying it. The final line's plain went on is the moral act. The walkers simply continue, and so does the snake.

05

The inherited serpent, refused

European culture reads the snake through Genesis: the tempter, the enemy, the thing to be crushed. Wright lets two of the inherited adjectives stand (Cold, dark) and then adds splendid, which does not deny them but strips them of their moral force. The jewellery of glazed and diamond scale turns a “sinister” body into something precious, and the chivalric quested turns a predator into a questing knight.

There is no simile anywhere in the poem: the snake is never “like” anything. Wright describes the animal on its own terms instead of translating it into human ones, and that refusal to domesticate it is itself an argument about how to see.

DIFFICULT MOMENTS

Difficult Moments

Where the poem is genuinely undecidable — and what to do about it

Cruxes

1. Who is hunting?

The difficulty. The title is grammatically double. Hunting can describe the snake (a snake that hunts) or name an activity of which the snake is the object (the hunting of snakes). The poem never settles which, and a third candidate emerges as it goes on: the watchers themselves.

Competing readings. The snake hunts. This is the plain sense and the poem supports it everywhere: the tongue flickering on the trail, the verb quested, the fierce intent, the small food that flees, the prey in the grass. PoetryProf's reading is that the snake is the hunter, not the hunted. Snakes are hunted. This second sense names what settler Australians did by reflex and what Wright's own speaker does in 'The Killer' (1947). Here the title points to the violence the poem withholds. The humans hunt with their eyes. The walkers track the snake as it tracks its prey (our eyes went with him), so the poem shows a chain of attention: prey, hunter, watchers.

What a strong answer does. It keeps the first sense primary, since that is what happens, and then shows how the poem uses the other two. The second sense gives the restraint its meaning (no one hunts the snake), and the third shows that human looking is itself a kind of pursuit, which the poem ends by turning away from as the walkers look at each other instead.

2. we scarcely thought: honesty or complicity?

The difficulty. Stanza 3 raises the prey's fate in two careful clauses, then says the walkers hardly considered it. In stanza 4 the grass hid his prey. Is the poem admitting a moral blind spot, or committing one?

Competing readings. Complicity. The sublime is bought by looking away. The walkers' wonder needs them not to think about the frog or lizard about to die. The poem's grandest description (Cold, dark and splendid) sits beside the hidden kill, and the grass hides the death from the reader too. Honesty. Wright puts the prey in. fled living insists on its life, fierce intent names the will to kill, and scarcely is an exact admission rather than a cover-up. The poem records the suspension of moral attention as part of what awe is. Ecological realism. Predation is not a moral failure to be noticed or judged. It is how the snake lives, and admiring the hunter is not the same as approving cruelty.

What a strong answer does. It notices the paralipsis, the poem raising exactly what it says the walkers did not think about, and argues that the poem is more aware than its people. The reader is made to think what the walkers scarcely thought. It can grant the force of the complicity reading while showing that Wright exposes the looking-away instead of performing it.

3. Fear or wonder?

The difficulty. The poem never names an emotion. The walkers freeze, lose breath, stop thinking and later breathe deeper, and every one of these can signal terror or rapture.

Competing readings. Fear. froze suggests the freeze response to a predator. Australian black snakes are venomous. Cold and dark carry menace, and the deeper breath reads as relief at a danger passed. Wonder. The diction is admiring: grace, quested, glazed, diamond, splendid. The snake goes by and never threatens them, and the walkers' eyes go with it willingly. Both, which is the sublime. Burke's “delightful horror” is fear felt at a safe distance turning into a kind of delight. The poem's sequence fits that account, and the snake's indifference provides the safety.

What a strong answer does. It shows that the refusal to name the emotion is deliberate. Physical reactions come before categories, so the reader feels the mixture instead of being told about it. It locates the fear (the freeze, Cold, dark) and the wonder (diamond, splendid) in particular words, and it notices that the one evaluative line places splendid last.

4. What changes at the end?

The difficulty. The last line is the plainest in the poem: a look exchanged, and the walk resumed. Has the encounter changed anything?

Competing readings. Nothing. They went on. No lesson or revelation is stated, and the flatness is Wright refusing to claim a transformation that did not happen. Everything, unstated. a deeper breath of day records an enlargement of life, and the look at each other holds something too large for words. The plainness is tact, not emptiness. A parting of ways. The rhyme gone / on pairs the snake's exit with the humans' continuing: two lives proceed separately, and nobody has taken anything from anybody. The change is a non-event, the absence of the blow that 'The Killer' strikes.

What a strong answer does. It reads the ending through its form as well as its words: the envelope rhyme closing the stanza, breath returning deeper, each other splitting the we for the first time. It also treats the understatement as the poem's claim. What has changed is how fully the walkers live in an ordinary day, and that a dangerous creature is still alive.

CLOSE ANALYSIS

Close Analysis

The moments that repay pressure, worked through

Quotation analysis

1. froze half-through a pace (line 3)

Techniques. Metaphor (froze), kinaesthetic imagery, caesura, end-stopped sentence mid-stanza.

The walkers are arrested mid-stride, one foot off the ground, and the comma before the phrase splits the line between moving and stopping. The verb is temperature turned into stillness. In a poem that begins Sun-warmed, warm-blooded people suddenly go cold and motionless, while the cold-blooded snake will move fluidly. The cause is not named until the next line, so the body reacts before the mind or the reader knows why.

Intention and effect. Wright presents awe and fear as physical facts, faster than thought. The reader's own momentum through the long first sentence is halted at the same point.

2. The great black snake (line 4)

Techniques. Three stressed monosyllables (spondee), plosive consonants, definite article, present participle.

Size, colour, kind: the animal is named in the plainest, heaviest words, g, b and k packed into three beats, then let loose in the liquid reeling, a word for swaying, whirling and unwinding like a line from a reel. The treats it as a known presence of the country, not a stray “a snake”. And it is passing them.

Intention and effect. The sound performs the shock of the sighting and then the fluency of the creature. From the first moment the poem establishes that the snake is passing, not attacking.

3. tongue flickering on the trail (line 5)

Techniques. Absolute phrase, kinaesthetic imagery, hunting vocabulary, metrical irregularity.

This is natural history set to rhythm. Snakes hunt by scent, collecting traces on the forked tongue, and the line packs four stresses at its start before a run of light syllables, so it moves like the tongue's quick touches. The lowered head shows the snake's attention is on the ground, not on the people.

Intention and effect. Exactness is a form of respect: Wright looks at the animal as it really is, absorbed in its own work, and the people are already irrelevant to it.

4. quested … the parting grass (line 6)

Techniques. Elevated diction and connotation, personification of the grass, regular iambic tetrameter.

quested brings the knight's quest into a snake's hunt and is also apt in an older hunting sense, for hounds casting for a scent. The grass parting ahead of him is the landscape making way, as a crowd parts for royalty. The perfectly regular line moves as smoothly as the snake does.

Intention and effect. The snake is ennobled and placed at home. This is its domain, and the humans are visitors standing still at its edge.

5. sun glazed … diamond scale (line 7)

Techniques. Metaphor, visual imagery, the semantic field of jewellery and craft, repeated sun.

Sunlight becomes glaze, a glassy coat of the kind fired onto pottery, and the scales become diamond, brilliant, precious and the hardest stone. The image is also accurate, since snake scales are diamond-shaped. The sun that warmed the walkers in line 1 now gilds the snake.

Intention and effect. Wright re-codes the serpent. The vocabulary of value and art leaves no room for the Genesis tempter, and diamond keeps hardness, and so danger, inside the beauty.

6. what small food / fled living (lines 9–10)

Techniques. Enjambment, fronted noun clause (inversion), alliteration with fierce.

The line-break holds the prey at the line-end as nothing but food, the predator's view of it. Then the next line begins fled living and restores its life and fear. The clause is one of two indirect questions placed before the verb that dismisses them.

Intention and effect. For one beat the reader shares the snake's view and then the prey's. The poem quietly brings in the death that the walkers do not think about.

7. we scarcely thought (line 11)

Techniques. Paralipsis, understatement, mid-line caesura (semicolon).

Having spent two lines on the snake's route and prey, the poem says the walkers hardly considered them. scarcely is precise and honest: thought did not vanish entirely, but it was overwhelmed. After the semicolon the line returns to stillness (still, stood).

Intention and effect. Awe suspends judgement, and Wright records that suspension as part of the experience, making the reader think what her walkers did not.

8. Cold, dark and splendid (line 13)

Techniques. Tricolon with climax, spondaic opening, inversion (adjectives before the pronoun), near-oxymoron.

Cold (cold-blooded, unfeeling) and dark (black, mysterious, menacing) are the inherited settler adjectives, and Wright lets them stand. splendid, whose Latin root means shining, comes last and changes their weight, and dark and splendid is exact for a glossy black body. The description arrives as the snake is already gone.

Intention and effect. This is the poem's one judgement, and it is a verdict of splendour. Coldness and darkness become part of the snake's magnificence, not grounds for killing it.

9. a deeper breath of day (line 15)

Techniques. Echo and antithesis with lost breath (line 8), comparative, metaphor, perfectly regular metre.

The breath taken away at the poem's centre returns, and returns deeper. The day becomes something breathed in, its light set against the snake's dark. The line is the most regular in the poem, so its rhythm steadies with the walkers' breathing. Its rhyme partner is prey.

Intention and effect. The encounter leaves the walkers more alive, not changed in belief but living more fully. The rhyme sets the hidden death beside the breath of life.

10. each other … went on (line 16)

Techniques. Reciprocal pronoun, tricolon of verbs (took, looked, went on), plain diction (anticlimax), closing envelope rhyme with gone.

The joint we splits for the first time into two people who can look at one another, and the poem's last verb is simply continuing. There is no adjective, no image and no stated lesson. on completes the rhyme left open by the snake's gone.

Intention and effect. The poem trusts the silence of that look. The plain ending is the moral event: unlike the speaker of 'The Killer', no one strikes, and two lives go their separate ways.

CRITICAL LENSES

Critical Lenses

What each way of reading makes visible, and what it flattens

Critical lenses

1. Ecocritical

What it makes visible. The poem is a model of the attention ecocriticism values. It looks exactly at a living animal (tongue on the scent trail, head down, scales in the sun), grants it its own purposes (fierce intent) and its own pronoun (he), and lets it go. Nature is not scenery, symbol or threat. It is a life going on independently of us. The poem's central act, doing nothing, is the ethic Wright spent her public life arguing for as a founder of the Wildlife Preservation Society of Queensland: see properly, then leave alone. Even predation is accepted as part of the snake's splendour, not edited into a gentler nature.

What it flattens. Ecocriticism can make the poem sound like a manifesto, and it is not one. There is no message about conservation in the text, and the walkers do not reflect, resolve or campaign. The lens also has difficulty with the poem's aestheticising language (diamond, glazed), which treats the animal as a precious object to be admired, close to the human-centred gaze the lens criticises.

2. Formalist

What it makes visible. The poem's meaning sits in its mechanics. Twelve lines of alternating rhyme are followed by an envelope rhyme exactly as the snake disappears. Each final rhyme pair joins a snake-word to a human-word (gone / on, prey / day). The snake is he nine times and the humans an undifferentiated we. The stress clashes fall on the moments of shock. The single slant rhyme (food / stood) falls on the prey. The last line drops every adjective the poem has been spending. None of this is stated, and all of it is meaning.

What it flattens. Reading only the mechanism can lose the poem's context: its place in Wright's career, its answer to 'The Killer', and the settler habit of killing snakes. These change what the restraint means.

3. Postcolonial / settler-colonial

What it makes visible. The Genesis serpent arrived with the colonists, and the reflex to kill snakes came with it. Wright, a pastoralist's daughter who spent decades campaigning for Aboriginal land rights and a treaty, refuses the imported reading of the animal in the plainest way: she calls it splendid. Read as a parable of settler presence, the poem shows two people walking through country and meeting a creature wholly at home in it, sovereign and indifferent to them. They take nothing and pass through. The snake belongs; the people are visitors.

What it flattens. Nothing in the poem refers to Aboriginal people, colonial history or land, and pressing it into allegory risks making the snake stand for something, which the poem refuses. This reading depends on biography and should stay a resonance, not a decoding.

4. Psychoanalytic

What it makes visible. Andrew Taylor read Wright's earlier 'The Killer' as guilt at failing to recognise the enemy within and killing the creature outside instead. Through that lens 'Hunting Snake' is the same confrontation resolved differently. The cold, dark thing is encountered, acknowledged as splendid, and allowed to live, a reconciliation with what had been projected outward and destroyed. The suspension of thought (we scarcely thought) fits a state in which the controlling ego gives way to pure perception.

What it flattens. It turns a real animal into a figure of the psyche, the very translation the poem resists with its exact natural history. It also depends heavily on reading the two poems as a pair.

5. Reader-response

What it makes visible. The poem works on the reader's body as well as the walkers'. The long first sentence lulls, the halt at pace stops the reader too, and the clustered sounds of still as we stood are hard to say quickly. Because emotions are never named, the reader must supply them. Fear and wonder are left for each reader to weigh, and the final look between the walkers is left blank, to be filled in.

What it flattens. Reader-response can make the poem's indeterminacy sound total, but Wright does steer us. The one evaluative line ends on splendid, and the diction of grace, quested and diamond tilts the reader firmly towards admiration.

OTHER READINGS

Other Readings

Contested interpretations, and where each is weak

Other readings

1. A precise account of the sublime

The poem records an encounter with something beautiful and dangerous that overwhelms ordinary perception and leaves the observers more alive. Its distinction is accuracy: the sublime is rendered as a sequence of bodily events, not an emotion described.

Evidence. The frozen stride, lost breath, we scarcely thought, eyes that follow involuntarily, and finally a deeper breath of day. The snake's indifference supplies the safe distance that Burke's “delightful horror” requires. PoetryProf links the poem to Burke and the Romantic sublime.

Weakness. The classic sublime is vast (mountains, storms, the sea), and this is a snake in the grass. The poem's after-effect is not exaltation but a quiet return to ordinary life, which the label can overstate.

2. An answer to 'The Killer'

Wright had already written this meeting. In 'The Killer' (1947) a speaker surprised by a black snake at a creek kills it. 'Hunting Snake' revisits the scene and reverses the outcome, so it is a self-correction in which stillness is the achievement.

Evidence. The same animal and the same sunlit setting, an ambiguous title in both cases (who is the killer, who is hunting), and a final stanza whose plainness makes not striking the event.

Weakness. Wright is not recorded as linking the two poems, and they are probably about seventeen years apart. The pairing is the critic's construction, and the later poem stands complete without it.

3. The aestheticised predator

A sceptical reading holds that the poem makes a killer beautiful and buys its rapture by looking away from the victim. The grass that hid his prey hides the death from the reader as well.

Evidence. The prey is reduced to small food. we scarcely thought admits the inattention. The grandest description (Cold, dark and splendid) comes just as the kill happens out of sight.

Weakness. Wright puts the prey in (fled living) and the will to kill (fierce intent), and the admission in scarcely exposes the looking-away. The poem seems more aware of the cost than this reading allows.

4. A parable of settler presence

Two people pass through country where a creature is entirely at home, sovereign and indifferent to them. For once they take nothing.

Evidence. The snake's ease (the parting grass), the humans' stillness and plural anonymity, went on as what visitors do, and Wright's lifelong reckoning with her pastoral family's inheritance of Aboriginal land.

Weakness. The poem contains no reference to history, land ownership or Aboriginal people. The reading is imported from biography, and it risks turning a real snake into a symbol.

5. Just a snake

The plainest reading: there is no symbol at all. The poem is a snake, hunting, in autumn, seen exactly, and its refusal to make the animal mean something is the point.

Evidence. There is no simile, so the snake is never likened to anything. The details are exact natural history (the tongue, the scent trail, basking-season warmth), no moral is drawn, and the ending is plain.

Weakness. Language is never neutral. quested, diamond and splendid are evaluative choices, and the title's double grammar invites more than description.

Revision Notes

The working notes, quotation by quotation

  • snake = hunter, not hunted (PoetryProf)

Context

Analysis
  • Judith Wright (1915–2000), b. Armidale, New England tableland NSW; pastoral family

  • settler reflex: kill snakes on sight; Genesis serpent = evil

late season's grace

Analysis
  • atmosphere: warm, gentle, peaceful → calm before the encounter

Effect, style & response

  • Sun-warmed: humans enjoy the sun; cold-blooded snake needs it

froze half-through a pace

Analysis

great black snake

Analysis

tongue flickering · quested

Analysis

  • Head down → absorbed; ignores humans

  • the parting grass → nature makes way; snake belongs here
7–8

diamond scale

Analysis
  • glazed, diamond → jewellery/craft vocab → precious, not sinister
  • reverses the Eden serpent

we scarcely thought

Analysis
  • small food / fled living → enjambment: prey = food, then alive

Cold, dark and splendid

Analysis
  • tricolon, climax: cold (ectotherm, unfeeling) · dark (black, mystery) · splendid (magnificent; Latin “shining”)

a deeper breath of day

Analysis
  • grass hid his prey → kill offstage
