Effect, style & response
  • nobody strikes → restraint = the moral act

Structure

Analysis
  • 16 lines, 4 quatrains; iambic tetrameter (8 syllables; l.5 = 9)
  • ABAB CDCD EFEF → GHHG (envelope rhyme) as the snake vanishes
  • gone / on (snake leaves / humans go on); prey / day (death / life)
  • only slant rhyme: food / stood
  • every stanza end-stopped; 6 sentences
  • no simile; no I; snake = he ×9 (ll.6–14)

Themes

Analysis
  • sublime: awe as bodily event (freeze → breath lost → thought stops → deeper breath)
  • nature's indifference: snake never notices them
  • predation unthought: prey hidden in the grass
  • restraint: the blow not struck (vs 'The Killer'; Lawrence's 'Snake')
  • inherited serpent symbol refused
CONNECTIONS

Connections

How this poem pairs with the rest of the set

Comparison hooks

1. The Cockroach — Kevin Halligan

Link. The set's other poem built entirely on watching a single creature. Both even open with the same word for a step. Halligan's cockroach starts to pace and Wright's walkers freeze half-through a pace. In both, the watching is the action.

Shared technique. Plain past-tense narration of observed movement, with verbs carrying the meaning. The cockroach paces, skirts and jogs in crooked rings; the snake goes reeling, quested and was gone. Both poems end in understatement.

Difference. Halligan's creature loses its purpose (uncertain where to go), and the watcher ends by recognising himself in it: I recognised myself. Wright's snake is nothing but purpose (fierce intent), and the watchers recognise nothing of themselves. The snake stays wholly other. Halligan finds the human in the animal; Wright finds what is not human, and honours it.

2. Report to Wordsworth — Boey Kim Cheng

Link. Nature intact against nature destroyed. Boey's Nature has been laid waste, and his sea-gods are entombed in the waste / we dump. Wright's snake is magnificent, healthy and in no danger, even from the people who meet it.

Shared technique. Both work through an implied we that includes the reader: Boey's we dump, Wright's watchers. Both set human behaviour against a natural power.

Difference. In Boey insatiate man is the predator who moves in for the kill. In Wright the only kill belongs to the snake, and the humans conspicuously do not move in. Boey's poem mourns what human appetite has done; Wright's quietly shows the alternative, restraint, and her conservation campaigns supply the link between the two.

3. Lament — Gillian Clarke

Link. Two poems about creatures and their sheen. Clarke's war-poisoned birds wear funeral silk and the veil of iridescence on the sand is an oil slick. Wright's living snake shines because sun glazed his curves.

Shared technique. Visual imagery of glossy surfaces, and close attention to particular animals named by their behaviour (Clarke's turtle in search of the breeding ground, Wright's snake on its trail).

Difference. In Clarke the shine is death, a beautiful surface laid on by human violence. In Wright it is life, natural and the snake's own. Clarke catalogues casualties; Wright records a creature that humans, for once, leave untouched.

4. An Essay on Man — Alexander Pope

Link. Two answers to what kind of creature a human being is. Pope's man hangs in doubt whether to count himself a god or beast, darkly wise, and rudely great. Wright's walkers meet a creature with no such doubt, single-minded and wholly itself.

Shared technique. Both define the human against the rest of creation. Pope does it by abstract antithesis, Wright by the asymmetry of pronouns and verbs: the active, individual he against a passive, plural we.

Difference. Pope argues in heroic couplets and states the paradox. Wright's tetrameter quatrains state nothing, and the vertigo of human smallness is produced in the reader rather than described. Pope's man is the centre of a riddle; Wright's people are, for sixteen lines, on the edge of somebody else's story.

5. Follower — Seamus Heaney

Link. Close, admiring observation of something more skilled than the watcher. Heaney's father at the plough is An expert, and Wright's snake works its scent trail with the same total competence. In both poems the onlooker's eyes follow the master.

Shared technique. Precise technical detail as a form of praise (Heaney's plough-work, Wright's tongue and trail), and a plain, withholding final line.

Difference. Heaney's son stumbles in his father's hob-nailed wake and wants to become him. In the end the roles reverse, and the father is the one who will not go away. Wright's snake never acknowledges its followers and does go away. The walkers have no wish to be like it, only to let it be.

6. Before the Sun — Charles Mungoshi

Link. Two sunlit encounters between people and the natural world, each turning an ordinary moment into something like a rite. Mungoshi's boy shares his breakfast with the sun in a private morning ritual; Wright's walkers take a deeper breath of day.

Shared technique. A single short episode, observed sensuously, that ends without a stated moral.

Difference. Mungoshi's nature is companionable and responsive: the boy and the sun share a meal and a world. Wright's nature is splendid and indifferent, and the snake does not know the walkers exist. Together the two poems frame the set's range, from nature as intimate to nature as wholly other.

Synthesis

All fifteen at once

The paper sets one poem at a time, but the best answers know what is distinctive about it — and that is easiest to see against the others. Threads that run through several poems first, then the whole set side by side: read along a row.

01

Power, and who pays for it

Each of these poems locates a beneficiary and a bill, and refuses to let them be the same person. The interesting move is always the accounting: who is enriched, who is spent, and whether the poem says so outright.

Song: Love Armedthe lover is spent; the beloved goes free The Chimney-Sweeperthe parents rise to church on the child's labour A Different Historythe conqueror's tongue, paid for in the soul A Married Statethe wife pays in tears; the husband is merely hard to please Carpet-weavers, Moroccochildren knot the carpet that merchant and mosque will use Lamentthe war's bill is presented in turtles and boys
02

Inheritance, not choice

The speakers do not decide who they are. Place, language, family and history have already decided, and the poem is the discovery of that — sometimes as a gift, sometimes as a sentence, often as both.

Where I Come FromPeople are made of places A Different Historythe grandchildren inherit the language, and love it Followerthe son inherits the father — as a figure he cannot shake off Carpet-weavers, Moroccochildren born into a pattern they did not design Storytellerthe stories pass into the sleeping children's heads The Chimney-Sweeperthe child is dressed in the clothes of death
03

Institutions and their alibis

Church, state, empire, marriage and war all arrive with an explanation ready. The poems are interested in the gap between the explanation and the damage — and in how normal the damage looks.

The Chimney-SweeperGod and his priest and king A Different Historycolonial education as cultural cropping A Married Statemarriage itself — even The best of husbands fail Lamentthe gunsmith, the armourer, and the company Song: Love Armedthe lovers set him up a Deity by mutual agreement Carpet-weavers, Moroccocommerce and faith share the same carpet
04

Nature: casualty, mirror or mystery

Nature is never scenery here. It is a casualty, a witness, the thing that formed the speaker, a guest at breakfast, or something wholly indifferent to us — and the poems measure what it costs, or gives, to be near it.

Report to Wordsworththe sea-gods entombed in the waste / we dump Lamentthe scalded ocean and the blazing well Where I Come Fromthe mind keeps the weather of its landscape Hunting Snakean animal that never notices the people it awes Before the Suna boy who shares his breakfast with the sun A Different Historythe tree the paper came from must not be offended
05

Form turned against itself

Several poems adopt a form with an established promise — the love sonnet, the song, the nursery rhyme, the wedding-poem's couplets — then make the form say something it was never built to say.

The Cockroacha sonnet that withholds its own resolving couplet Report to Wordsworththe sonnet as a casualty report The Chimney-Sweepera nursery-rhyme lilt that delivers an indictment Song: Love Armeda stage song whose dance-metre delivers a verdict A Married Statethe heroic couplet, voice of public reason, turned against marriage Sonnet 18a love sonnet that ends by praising itself
06

Watching, and being implicated

Many of these poems begin with a speaker at a safe distance and end with the distance gone. Track the pronouns and you can date the collapse almost to the word.

The CockroachI watched becomes I recognised myself Report to Wordsworththe waste / we dump — the poet is inside the we Song: Love ArmedThus thou and I, the God have armed Hunting Snaketwo watchers frozen mid-step, then let go Followerthe boy who watched his father is now the one being followed The Chimney-Sweeperthe observer's question hands the poem to the child
07

Time, and what outlasts it

Summer fades, mornings end, fathers age, carpets are finished and nights run out. Each poem pits something against time — verse, story, ritual, memory, pattern — and each is honest about what it costs.

Sonnet 18verse against death: So long as men can breathe Carpet-weavers, Moroccothe future knotted into the past as the weaving is done Storytellerstories that outlive the night that told them Followera past that will not go away Before the Sunone ordinary morning made into a rite An Essay on Manman Born but to die, and reasoning but to err
08

Work, craft and skill

A surprising number of these poems are about work done with the hands — and about how a poem can honour, envy, imitate or indict it.

Followerploughing as mastery: An expert Storytellerstory-telling counted as work, alongside stitching and darning Carpet-weavers, Moroccosmall fingers at the loom Before the Sunthe axe, the fire, the roasting maize The Chimney-Sweepera trade advertised by a child's street-cry Where I Come Fromthe city's smell of work
09

What a human being is

Underneath their subjects, several poems ask the oldest question: what kind of creature are we? Their answers range from Pope's balanced paradox to a man finding himself in an insect.

An Essay on ManThe glory, jest, and riddle of the world! The Cockroacha man who recognises himself in vermin Hunting Snakehumans reduced to held breath before an animal Report to Wordsworthinsatiate man moves in for the kill Song: Love Armedlovers who build the god that rules them
10

Women's lives, women's voices

Three centuries apart, these poems are written from inside the lives women were expected to lead — desire, marriage, housework, story — and they argue with the roles as they describe them.

A Married Statethe virgin state as a crown Song: Love Armeda woman's desire Enough to undo the Amorous World Storytellera woman judged sloven or spotless, honoured for her stories Carpet-weavers, Moroccogirls at the loom whose work will travel without them
11

Childhood

Children appear as workers, listeners, followers and celebrants. What each poem lets a child see — and what it sees that the child cannot — is where the meaning lies.

The Chimney-Sweepera child sold into soot, still singing Before the Suna fourteen-year-old's private morning ritual Followera small boy stumbling in his father's wake Carpet-weavers, Moroccochildren at work in the school of days Storytellerchildren listening, then dreaming the stories

The set at a glance

PoemFormWrittenEra / movementCentral argumentKey themesTalks to
Aphra BehnSong: Love ArmedTwo octaves, ababcdcd efefgfgf; iambic tetrameter; written to be sungSung 1676 (opening Abdelazer); printed 1677; reprinted 1684 as 'Love Arm'd'RestorationLove's tyranny is home-made: two lovers arm the god and set him up a Deity, and only the one who desires more pays.Love as manufactured power · Unequal desire: who pays · A woman's desire at full scale · Love as a false religion · Private passion, public tyrannyThe set's poem about a power its victims build: it shares Philips's view of love as a creed to renounce, Blake's god made out of misery, Bhatt's love for a strange conqueror and Pope's creature who makes what unmakes him, and it answers Shakespeare's serene lover with one who wins the record but not the love.
Sujata BhattA Different HistoryFree verse in two parts, 18 + 11 linesIn print Jan–Feb 1987 (PN Review 53); collected in Brunizem, 1988Post-colonialWhere it is a sin to be rude to a book, the grandchildren grow to love the tongue that cropped their ancestors' souls — and the poem that asks how it happens is written in that tongue.Language as vessel and weapon · Colonial violence and its namelessness · The sacred in everyday practice · Inheritance across generations · Love without absolutionThe set's poem about language itself: what a conquered people inherits and why it comes to love it. It speaks to Brewster's people formed by place, Heaney's son who cannot shake off his father, Lochhead's stories passed into sleeping heads, Rumens's children weaving a pattern they did not design, and Clarke's lament that ends in the ashes of language.
William BlakeThe Chimney-SweeperThree quatrains; couplets then cross-rhyme (AABB CACA DEDE); loose four-beat linesDrafted c. 1793; published 1794RomanticA child's happiness is used against him twice — as the pretext for putting him to work and as the proof that no harm was done — while God and his priest and king make heaven out of what it costs.Exploitation of children · Religion and power · Self-deception · Innocence and experienceThe set's sharpest poem about who pays for other people's comfort and piety: it speaks to Rumens's child weavers, Mungoshi's free working boy, Heaney's son following his father's work, and Pope's confident order of things.
Elizabeth BrewsterWhere I Come FromFree verse; three stanzas of 11, 8 and 2 lines; a dropped line at the first break; one closing rhymeProbably 1950s; collected 1977 (Sometimes I Think of Moving)Modern CanadianPlaces make people, but not equally: the city leaves a smell that drops from them, home is carried in their minds — and in the last two lines home proves it by blowing back in, uninvited and cold.Place and identity · City and country · Involuntary memory · Endurance and renewal · Climate and the mindThe set's poem of origins: it shares Boey's smog-choked flowers, Heaney's past that will not go away, Mungoshi's rural senses and Bhatt's unchosen inheritance, but makes place an inner climate rather than a scene.
Boey Kim ChengReport to WordsworthShakespearean sonnet, ABAB CDCD EFEF GG; loose iambic pentameter; one sentence-chain from report to prayerPublished 1992 (Another Place)Contemporary SingaporeanA modern poet files a damage report with Wordsworth in Wordsworth's own words: the Nature his sonnets trusted, the pagan gods he hoped to glimpse and the poetry and piety that served her are listed as casualties, and the last cry is still being laboured towards.Environmental destruction and greed · Loss of the sacred · Complicity · The failing power of poetry · Inheritance of a literary traditionThe set's poem about a whole tradition under threat: it answers Wordsworth the way Bhatt answers English, mourns as Clarke's 'Lament' mourns, implicates its speaker as 'The Cockroach' does, and reverses the confidence of Shakespeare's and Pope's claims for poetry and order.
Kevin HalliganThe CockroachHybrid sonnet: Shakespearean octave, Italian-style sestet, no couplet (ABAB CDCD EFGEGF)Undated; in print by 2005 (Songs of Ourselves)ContemporaryA man watches an insect lose its purpose and, in the last four words, stops being able to watch from outside.Restlessness and purpose · Projection and self-recognition · Guilt and deserving · Not knowingThe set's sharpest study of watching and projection: it answers Wright's unknowable snake, Pope's creature 'in doubt to act or rest', Heaney's role-reversing follower and Shakespeare's confident couplet with a sonnet that cannot reach one.
Gillian ClarkeLamentSeven unrhymed tercets; free-verse litany, every line end-stoppedc. 1991, during the Gulf War; collected by 1997ContemporaryA prayer with no god in it: eleven dedications beginning For mourn turtle, refugee, soldier and sea without ranking them — until language itself joins the dead.War against the living world · Grief without a hierarchy · The poisoned future · Truth and language in wartimeThe set's widest casualty list: it shares Boey's grief for a failing natural world, Bhatt's and Shakespeare's concern with what language can survive, and Blake's and Behn's question of who pays for a grand cause, while refusing, unlike them, to name a culprit.
Seamus HeaneyFollowerSix quatrains, ABAB (mostly half-rhyme); loose four-beat linesPublished 1966 (Death of a Naturalist)Modern IrishWhat a son inherits from a father whose craft he cannot follow is the standard, not the trade — and the debt cannot be left behind: the expert who led now follows, and will not go away.Inheritance · Craft and mastery · Father and son · Time and role reversal · MemoryThe set's central poem of inheritance and craft: it speaks to Lochhead's storyteller and Mungoshi's working boy about what children take from adult work, to Halligan and Shakespeare about watchers, time and lines that last, and to Brewster and Bhatt about what a place and a tongue hand down.
Liz LochheadStorytellerFree verse, 30 lines in four stanzas (5/6/9/10)1981Modern ScottishA woman's storytelling is counted as work — breath spun into the strongest thread — and the stories outlive each dawn, roosting in the children until night lets them fly.Storytelling as women's work · Oral tradition and transmission · How women are judged · Night, imagination and survivalIt pairs most closely with the set's poems of watched and inherited craft (Follower, Carpet-weavers) and of women judged by domestic roles (A Married State), and answers Sonnet 18's written, signed permanence with an oral, anonymous, cyclical survival.
Charles MungoshiBefore the SunFree verse: 46 lines in nine irregular stanzas (4-7-4-4-6-2-6-4-9)Published 1981 (The Milkman Doesn't Only Deliver Milk)Modern ZimbabweanA boy up before the sun turns a chore into a feast and the feast into a rite — but every enchantment is qualified, and the shared meal ends as two little skeletons in the light.Childhood and absorbed attention · Work made into play and ritual · Kinship with nature, and its limits · The sacred in the ordinary · TransienceThe set's warmest childhood poem: a free, competent working child to set against Blake's sweep and Rumens's weavers, a present-tense morning against Heaney's remembered fields, and a friendly sun beside Shakespeare's 'eye of heaven' and Clarke's 'sun put out'.
Katherine PhilipsA Married State16 lines of heroic couplets; a triplet plus near-rhyme (ll. 7–10); one alexandrine (l. 12)c. 1646–48 (autograph leaf, before her marriage); first printed 1977/1986Civil WarTwo states weighed like a legal case: marriage affords but little ease even with the best of husbands, the single life is crown'd — and the last line abolishes the hell that frightened women into marrying.Marriage as an institution · Freedom and self-government · Faith turned against custom · Women's hidden suffering · Wit and the right to adviseThe set's coolest argument about an institution: it shares Blake's eye for suffering hidden behind a cheerful face, Behn's view of love as a false god, Pope's heroic couplets and reasoning voice, and Shakespeare's legal diction, but it alone tells its reader to refuse the life laid out for her.
Alexander PopeAn Essay on ManExtract: nine heroic couplets (iambic pentameter), all end-stoppedWritten 1732; Epistle II published c. April 1733AugustanForbidden to scan God, man studies himself and finds a creature so evenly divided that the only exact definition is a contradiction: the glory, jest, and riddle of the world.Limits of knowledge · Self-knowledge · Man's middle place · Pride and presumption · Reason and passionThe set's most systematic answer to what a human being is: its couplets talk to Philips's, its self-recognition to Halligan's cockroach, its trusted design to Blake's and Boey's broken ones.
Carol RumensCarpet-weavers, MoroccoFour unrhymed tercets; eleven end-stopped lines, one enjambmentBy 1987 (first collected in Selected Poems, 1987)Modern BritishThe carpet is given a journey, a purpose and a future; the children who knot it get only more knotting — and the instant in which all-that-will-be becomes all-that-was.Child labour · Craft and commerce · Faith · Time and making · The observer's gazeThe set's coolest poem about children's work and adults' worship: it answers Blake's accusing sweep with silence, gives Mungoshi's happy working boy a voiceless counterpart, and turns Lochhead's thread of story into a traded thing.
William ShakespeareSonnet 18Shakespearean sonnet: three quatrains and a couplet, ABAB CDCD EFEF GG, iambic pentameterProbably 1590s; printed 1609ElizabethanSummer only rents its beauty; the poem promises the beloved outright possession of his, and in the couplet makes this, the poem itself, the thing that lives and gives life.Poetry against time · Love as praise and promise · Nature found wanting · Beauty, ownership and debtThe set's oldest poem and its most confident claim for art: every poem here that weighs what outlasts time (stories, carpets, memory, a dead poet's verse) answers its couplet, and the set's later sonnets, Halligan's and Boey's, refuse its resolution.
Judith WrightHunting SnakeFour quatrains of iambic tetrameter; ABAB CDCD EFEF, then envelope rhyme GHHGc. 1964 (first collection unconfirmed)Modern AustralianAwe arrives as a bodily event (a frozen stride, a lost breath, suspended thought) before a creature that never notices its watchers, and the poem's quiet event is the violence that does not happen.Awe and the sublime · Nature's indifference · Predation unthought · RestraintThe set's purest encounter with an animal: against Halligan's man who finds himself in a cockroach, Boey's and Clarke's ruined nature and Mungoshi's companionable sun, it offers nature that is magnificent, intact and wholly indifferent to us.
Reference

Techniques, by family

The vocabulary the analysis above depends on. Naming a device earns nothing on its own — the marks are in what you say it does.

Basic 6

Metaphor

Directly compares two different things without using like or as.

  • Life is a roller coaster
  • He is a shining star
  • Her heart is gold
  • Her heart of gold was broken

metaphorical, metaphorically

Extended metaphor

A metaphor that extends

  • The Tyger by William Blake is, at its core, an extended metaphor of the industrial revolution.

Simile

Indirectly compares two different things using like or as

  • He ran like the wind
  • His eyes sparkled like stars

Hyperbole

Metaphor to do with exaggeration

  • I will love you for a million years.
  • His abs of steel could not be penetrated.

hyperbolic, hyperbolically

Onomatopoeia

A word that sounds like something

  • Bang
  • Boom
  • Buzz
  • Sizzle

Symbolism

The use of words or images to symbolise specific ideas or feelings

  • He handed her a red rose and she knew at the moment how he felt.
  • The mirror broke and he knew that things would not be good from there on.
  • Jeff saw a crow next to a black cat on a Friday afternoon.

symbolic, symbolise

Personification 5

Personification

Metaphorically giving human qualities to something nonhuman

  • The sun smiled at us
  • The wind whispered secrets
  • Time waits for no one
  • The business ran and of breath and died

personify

Anthropomorphism

Literally attributing human characteristics, emotions and behaviours to non-human things (think Toy Story, Alice in Wonderland, Zootopia, Tom & Jerry)

  • My cat stood up suddenly to lecture me about taxes

anthropomorphic

Pathetic fallacy

Attributing human emotions to nature & weather (specific form of personification)

  • The rain wept
  • The clouds seemed sullen
  • The rocks seemed indifferent 9

Zoomorphism

Personification but for animals - attributes animal characteristics to non-animals

  • Will barked at us after he was stripped naked.
  • She meowed like a furry

Chremamorphism

Objectifying humans or animals

  • Be a rock
  • Iron heart
  • Man of steel
  • He wore a rock-like expression.

Contrast 5

Juxtaposition

A general contrast arising from two words/phrases that are near each other

  • For some people, it's the age of light, while for others, it's the age of darkness.

juxtapose

Oxymoron

A pair of contrasting words right next to each other

  • Deafening silence
  • Organised chaos
  • Boiling ice

oxymoronic

Antithesis

A contrast of ideas - think yin & yang

  • As the antithesis to the introverted and gloomy Batman, the Joker seems friendly and extroverted but is actually evil.
  • Good vs evil
  • Light vs darkness
  • naivety vs scepticism

antithetical

Foil

A contrast of characters

  • Batman vs Joker (also an antithesis)

Mostly interior to an antithesis, given that the contrast between characters is only significant if it represents some contrast in idea

Paradox

Contrasting, contradictory statements (two things that can’t be true simultaneously)

  • All animals are equal, but some animals are more equal than others

paradoxical

Repetition 14

Repetition

The repetition of a word or phrase

  • In order to improve my writing, I must practice, practice, practice.

repeated

Parallelism

Any case where the construction/structure of a sentence is repeated, even if they are far apart

  • I have a dream speech opens many verses with the titular I have a dream

Anaphora

Repetition of a sentence structure at the start of a sentence or clause

  • Be bold. Be brief. Be gone.
  • We will fight for our rights. We will fight for our freedom. We will fight for our justice.

Epiphora

Anaphora but at the end of a sentence or clause

  • See no evil, hear no evil, speak no evil

Rhyme

Repetition of a sound at the end of each word

  • His palms are sweaty, knees weak, arms are heavy. There’s vomit on his sweater already, mom’s spaghetti.

rhyming

Alliteration

Repetition of a letter at the start of each word

  • Tony the Tiger took the train to town.
  • Madam memory is a great and subtle dissembler.

alliterative

Sibilance

The repetition of ‘s’ sounds (pissing -th, sh and z sounds also count)

  • That slithery, suspicious sibling of his.

sibilant

Assonance

The repetition of vowel sounds → euphonic effect

  • It was raining in Spain.
  • The round flower

Consonance

The repetition of consonant sounds → dissonant/cacophonic effect

  • He struck a streak of bad luck.

Diacope

A repetition that is separated by a few words

  • Every unhappy family is unhappy in its own way.
  • To be or not to be
  • The wheels on the bus goes round and round
  • A penny saved is a penny earned

Polysyndeton

The repetition of conjunctions

  • And I came and I saw and I conquered
  • → confusion / circularity

Asyndeton

The omission of conjunctions → repeated commas/punctuation

  • I came, I saw, I conquered
  • → assertiveness / briskness / out of breath

Motif

A repeated or recurring symbol

  • Bright light is used multiple times in Romeo & Juliet

Theme

A repeated idea

Diction 12

Diction

Word choice

Assign adjective: childlike, formal/informal, lighthearted/solemn, meaningless, passive-aggressive, intimate, distant

Ethos

Appeal to authority

  • Do it because I’m your dad

Pathos

Appeal to emotion

  • Do it because I just want the best for you

Logos

Appeal to logic

  • Do it because, if you don’t, you may regret it later on in life

Modality

Imperative

Command

  • Die D

Monosyllable

One syllable word(s)

  • Go to die
  • Monosyllabic diction

monosyllabic

Dialogue

An exchange of words by one or more characters

Assign adjective: childlike, formal/informal, lighthearted/solemn, meaningless, passive-aggressive, intimate, distant

Dialect

A local/regional expression of language

  • Howdy! G’day sur.
  • You got dat phat bunda still

Assign adjective: local/native, lower/middle/upper class, foreign

Colloquialism

Informal, everyday language/slang

  • Wanna, y’all, gonna, swag, rizz

Ambiguity/omission

The intentional lack of detail to create a greyish atmosphere or a sense of mystery, or some relation to fragmented memory

  • It was on this poignant day - afternoon, to be precise, since I’ve already had lunch - that I met the detective, looked into his eyes, felt his blistered hands.
  • They departed, the gods, on the day of the strange tide.

ambiguous ***intentionally omitted

Aphorism

A pithy statement that contains a general truth

  • A chain is only as strong as its weakest link
  • A penny saved is a penny earned

Novel 14

Climax

The culmination (most intense or exciting part) in a story.

  • In Shakespeare's play Romeo and Juliet, Romeo finds out that Juliet is dead and makes the decision to kill himself in her tomb. Juliet then sees her lover dead and makes the decision to kill herself as well.

climactic, culminate, reaches fever-pitch, reaches a boiling point

Anticlimax

A disappointing end to an exciting or impressive series of events.

  • At the end of the novel, when the two characters are on top of a ferris wheel gazing over their hometown, they don't kiss and, instead, go home and never confess their love for each other.

anticlimactic

Bathos

Anticlimactic effect created by a build up and then collapse in expectations (serious to ridiculous)

  • The answer to the ultimate question of life, the universe and everything is… 42!

bathetic

Narrative stance

First person: personal + opinionated → we feel closer to the narrator

  • I died
  • Second person: direct + commanding → we feel closer to ourselves
  • You died
  • Third person (limited): limited to one character’s perspective - closer to a character

Multiple perspectives

When the perspective of the narrator shifts from one character to another

  • For example, when chapter 1 of book X starts with narrator Bob, but switches to narrator Jess in chapter 5
  • Atonement, Half of a Yellow Sun

Unreliable narrator

A narrator who may be biassed or are unreliable in telling the story objectively

  • A good example of an unreliable narrator is when the narrator is a child
  • Briony in Atonement

Author surrogate

When the characters are subtly/implicitly reflecting the author or the author’s views

  • Charles Dickens wrote only about orphans because he himself was neglected and abused by his parents
  • David Copperfield, whose initials D.C. are just Charles Dickens’ initials C.D. reversed, bears a strong resemblance in both background and personality to his author.

Authorial intrusion

When the author explicitly intrudes into a story by revealing his/her existence or by showcasing his/her own feelings/thoughts/opinions

  • Warning: the dialogue above is for fictional purposes only
  • Certain kinds of narration/commentary may be considered a form of authorial intrusion too

Red Herring

Something to distract the reader/audience from what is really important in the plot

  • The reader was too engrossed in the melodramatic traits of X to realise that Y had been plotting the murder behind the scenes

Characterisation

A character’s experience and development can be an implicit technique to reveal effects/ideas to the audience

  • While all love outside of loving the Big Brother party is disapproved of in Oceania, Winston is depicted uniquely as a hopeful romantic, bravely professing to Julia that the real betrayal would be if they could make me stop loving you. This is what renders the outcome of the torture scene in room 101 all the more heartbreaking, as we, alongside Julia who was watching from a distance, discover that the party has effortlessly succeeded in reintegrating Winston: Tear her face off, strip her to the bones. Not me! Julia! Not me!. Here, not only has Winston betrayed Julia, but he has betrayed himself, and every quality that had made him virtuous - his love for Julia has been demolished and replaced by his refound love for the Party, showing how individual strength pales in the face of collective villainy.

Epiphany

When a character suddenly realises something important

  • In the middle of a typical argument with his wife, a man realises he has been the one causing every single argument, and that in order to keep his marriage, he must stop being such an aggressive person.

Allegory

A story that appears lighthearted, but actually reveals a deep insight into human understanding (esp morality or politics)

  • The Nun and the Priest’s tale is an allegory that depicts the lives of several animals who manifest human behaviour
  • Animal Farm
  • Tom & Jerry → anthropomorphism (furries)

allegorical

Anachronism

Something that feels out of time

  • A novel is set in the 21st century, and suddenly someone walks into a ancient temple
  • A novel is set in the 18th century, and suddenly someone walks into a theme park

Foreshadowing/foreboding

Indicating the soon occurrence of a significant event (something bad in the case of forebode)

  • If a character mentions offhandedly that bad things always happen to them in autumn, then the observant reader will be alert when the leaves in the story begin to fall.

foreshadow/forebode

Sensing 3

Tone / mood / atmosphere

Imagery

The use of visually descriptive and colourful language (usually as a means to an end - the middleman effect)

  • Visual: sight
  • Auditory: hearing
  • Gustatory: taste
  • The sky, at sunset, looked like a carnivorous flower

Semantic field

A group of related diction to create a collective imagery

  • I miss you blindingly like the sun, musically like a song with wings, frankly like the wind, and a sceptre lost at sea. Let us fly and fall together, my darling and rain.
  • ____, which culminates in an alliterative semantic field concerning darkness: gloom, grey, ghastly, establishing ____.
  • ____, where a semantic field of X imagery is established, moving from gloom to grey to ghastly, culminating in gas!, which ____

Sound 9

Rhyme

Couplet

  • Full rhyme:
  • Masculine: harsh stressed rhyme - rat + cat
  • Feminine: soft unstressed rhyme - room + gloom
  • Half (slant) rhyme: forge + orange

Rhythm

Fast vs slow

  • Intense vs lighthearted
  • Light vs heavy
  • Consistent vs inconsistent
  • Examples:

Meters

Iambic pentameter (mostly used by Shakespeare)

  • A line of verse with five metrical feet (10 syllables, 5 stressed, 5 unstressed)
  • Shall I compare thee to a summer’s day?
  • Two households, both alike in dignity.
  • Now is the winter of our discontent

Euphony

Use of pleasant harmonious sounds (usually soft vowel sounds)

  • A mellow, soothing lullaby
  • row row row the boat

euphonic

Cacophony/dissonance

The use of words with loud, harsh, unpleasant sounds (usually plosive consonant sounds b, d, g, k, p, s, t)

  • Dishes crashing on the floor, horns blaring, f***

Cacophonic + dissonant

Caesura family

Caesura: a pause mid-sentence either using a dash (—) or ellipsis (…)

  • That makes the two of us - don’t tell anyone!
  • Hmm… maybe I should eat
  • → hesitation
  • Aposiopesis: when a writer stops speaking suddenly without finishing a sentence

Ellison

Where the writer omits a letter or letters in part of a word

Arise, awake, or be forever fall’n

Often indicates dialect

Enjambment

Continuation of a sentence from one line to the next in a poem

  • I went out and / lost my way, where the "/" is a line break.
  • → more liquid flow to the poem

The Allusion Family 20

Allusion

Making an indirect reference to something outside the text.

  • Biblical: she was the sacrificial lamb → Abraham & Isaac
  • Historical: the war to end all wars → WWI

allude, allusive

Biblical allusion

She was the sacrificial lamb → Abraham & Isaac

Historical allusion

the war to end all wars → WWI

Psychological allusion

all her problems can be traced back to when her mum beat her with an iron rod → Freudian psychoanalysis

Stoicism

be a rock - resilient & unfazed, unaffected by the outside world

Existentialism

individuals are driven by a pursuit of purpose and meaning in existence - it is the individual’s responsibility to find such.

Absurdism

life is ridiculous, chaotic, purposeless and meaningless

Nihilism

life is meaningless and empty (philosophy of nothing, slightly pessimistic)

Utilitarianism

actions/morality are to be judged on net consequence or utility

Deontology

morality should follow a moral code

Relativism

morality as a whole is relative and culture-dependent

Liberalism

Left-wing

Conservatism

Right-wing

Libertarianism

prioritise individual freedom

Cynicism

a slightly pessimistic, critical outlook on life

Hedonism

life is about maximising pleasure (Hayden’s oyster)

Marxism

society - and life - can be categorised into hierarchical classes and individuals are shaped by their class experience

Myth of Sisyphus

struggling is pleasure (the journey is pleasure) and is indeed the purpose of life

Romanticism/idealism

dreams and ideals can conquer reality/practicalities

Realism

practicality comes first

Drama (General) 13

Staging/stage direction

An instruction in the text of a play indicating the movement, position, or tone of an actor, or the sound effects and lighting.

  • The man deals a deck of cards or Katy enters the room are examples of stage directions.

Euphemism

Sugar-coating

  • Melody is vertically-challenged
  • Bob passed away
  • Ted kicked the bucket

Rhetorical question

A figure of speech in which a question is asked for a reason other than to get an answer

  • I am a Jew. Hath not a jew eyes?
  • Why didn’t you turn off the lights?

Monologue

When a character speaks out loud for a long time in a dramatic way

  • Someone might lecture you with a monologue

Soliloquy

When a character speaks alone to himself/herself or to the audience

  • Now is the winter of our discontent made glorious summer by the sun of York.

Aside

When a fictional character breaks away from the events of the story to talk to themselves or directly to the audience.

  • Hamlet's first line in the play Hamlet is a great example of an aside. His stepfather/uncle addresses Hamlet as such, and Hamlet addresses the audience with, A little more than kin and less than kind, demonstrating his feelings about the situation without revealing this to anyone else onstage.

Apostrophe

When a speaker switches from addressing the audience to directly addressing an absent third party

  • O Romeo, Romeo, wherefore art thou Romeo?

Comic relief family

Comic relief

Humorous characters or events that intends to offset more serious episodes, lightening the mood to give the audiences a break

  • The archaeologist, who begins as oafish comic relief, exemplifies her gift for character drawing
  • The gravedigger in Shakespeare’s Hamlet is constantly surrounded by death, yet he possesses a humorous and lighthearted aura → comic relief

Sarcasm

Funny, mocking exaggeration

  • Melody, you’re so tall today

Satire

A lighthearted mockery/critique of something important such as politics

  • Jane Austen’s Pride and Prejudice is a prime example of social satire, questioning and poking fun at the customs and expectations surrounding marriage in 19th century English society

satirical

Irony (verbal, situational, dramatic)

Verbal: when a character says something and means another, especially if they mean the opposite

  • But Brutus says he was ambitious; And Brutus is an honourable man.
  • Situational: an expected outcome does not happen, or if the opposite happens instead (gap between our expectations and reality)
  • A fire station burns down
  • The whole of Romeo & Juliet

Pun

Make a joke exploiting the different possible meanings of a word.

  • Harold and the apple lived apple-y ever after.
  • Now is the winter of our discontent / Made glorious summer by this sun [or son] of York

Puns are only useful for Shakespearean plays

Tragedy 5

Tragic hero (Aristotle)

Aristotle's mould of a tragic hero is an individual who commits a tragic flaw (hamartia), without evil intent, great wrongs or injuries that ultimately lead to their misfortune, followed by them realising their wrongdoings and the true nature of events that led to this destiny. This means the hero still must be – to some degree – morally grounded.

  • Such tragedies can happen to anyone, yet can be prevented, thus the audience learns from tragic heroes.
  • They fall. We rise.
  • Aristotle claims: A man does not become a hero until he can see the root of his own downfall. - catharsis
  • Macbeth fits the role of a tragic hero because he is born to nobility, and he has good character. But his fatal flaw, his ambition, leads to his death at the end of the play. It also pushes him to commit many atrocities, including murder, as he falls deeper and deeper into darkness.

Hamartia (tragic flaw)

A fatal flaw leading to the downfall of a tragic hero or heroine.

  • Othello's fatal flaw is his jealousy. Fueled by Iago's lies, Othello flies into a jealous rage and murders his wife. Having discovered that she is in truth innocent, he kills himself as well.

Hubris

Possessing too much pride / arrogance (hubris can be an example of hamartia)

  • At the start of Macbeth, Macbeth is not a prideful character. However, by the end of the play, he becomes a prideful tyrant where his hubris ultimately gets the best of him.

Catharsis

When a character is released and relieved from strong or repressed emotions

  • Caesar was betrayed by his comrade, Brutus, and was brutally murdered. Brutus feels an overwhelming amount of guilt due to this action and catharsis occurs when he commits suicide bringing a purge of emotions.

Peripeteia

A sudden reversal of fortune or change in circumstances

  • An example of this is the death of King Creon's son Haemon at his father's hands after he opposes him, and Oedipus' discovery that he killed his own father and married his mother..
